title: Homer Simpson
text: Homer Simpson is Patriarch of the Simpson family and safety inspector at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. Homer is the bumbling, overweight father at the heart of the Simpson household, torn between deep love for his family and his own laziness, gluttony, and short attention span. He drifts through a string of odd jobs but always ends up back at the power plant, where he's more likely to nap or eat donuts than actually do his job well. Quick to anger, he's famous for choking his son Bart in fits of rage, yet he's also shown real self-sacrifice for his kids and wife when it counts. He spends much of his free time drinking with his buddies at Moe's Tavern or slumped on the couch at home with a beer. Impulsive and easily distracted, he chases get-rich-quick schemes and passing obsessions that rarely last. Despite his flaws—kleptomania, incompetence, and a temper—he remains devoted to Marge and their children in his own chaotic way. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: D'oh! | Why you little...! | Why you little bastard!

title: Marge Simpson
text: Marge Simpson is Matriarch of the Simpson family; wife of Homer and mother of Bart, Lisa, and Maggie. Marge is the steady, moral center of the Simpson household, forever trying to keep her chaotic family in line while managing the endless demands of housework and motherhood. She's cautious to a fault, disliking risk and novelty, and has literally worn a groove in the carpet from her rigid daily routine. Despite her buttoned-up image, she has surprising hidden depths, including real talent as a painter and cook, and has cycled through an eclectic string of odd jobs over the years, from police officer to bodybuilder. She can also be something of an unintentional killjoy, convinced her own personal tastes should dictate what's acceptable for everyone else. Her towering blue beehive hairstyle and ever-present pearl necklace make her instantly recognizable, and beneath her prim exterior she's shown flashes of wildness, including brushes with gambling, shoplifting, and alcohol. Ultimately, she remains devoted to Homer and her kids, serving as the family's moral compass and emotional glue. Voiced by Julie Kavner. Notable quotes: If it was up to [Marge], all we'd ever do is work and go to church. | She's been gray as a mule since she was seventeen.
quotes: If it was up to [Marge], all we'd ever do is work and go to church.

title: Bart Simpson
text: Bart Simpson is Eldest child of Homer and Marge Simpson, brother of Lisa and Maggie, and a student at Springfield Elementary School. Bart is the troublemaking ten-year-old son of Homer and Marge, forever labeled an underachiever despite flashes of real cleverness and surprising talents like languages, cooking, and marksmanship. He thrives on pranking authority figures, spraying graffiti as 'El Barto,' and generally disrupting the order of Springfield Elementary, all while dodging detention and disappointing teachers. Beneath the chaos, he has a genuine sense of loyalty and honor, sticking up for outcasts like Ralph Wiggum and Milhouse, and occasionally showing deep guilt when his schemes cause real harm to people like Skinner or Krabappel. He idolizes Krusty the Clown, loves comic books, skateboarding, and video games, and has an ongoing rivalry-slash-bond with his sister Lisa. His attention issues and impulsiveness are treated as a running trait of the show, sometimes played for laughs and sometimes explored more seriously. Despite constant scolding from Homer, Bart's mischief is often shown to mask real intelligence and moments of surprising maturity. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: Eat My Shorts! | Ay caramba! | Don't have a cow man!

title: Lisa Simpson
text: Lisa Simpson is Middle child of the Simpson family, an 8-year-old intellectual and the moral conscience of the household. Lisa is the whip-smart, socially conscious daughter of Homer and Marge, boasting a 159 IQ and membership in Mensa Springfield despite being only eight years old. She often feels out of place among her peers, being labeled a geeky overachiever, and finds emotional outlets through playing baritone saxophone, caring for animals, and immersing herself in world affairs. Though deeply principled—she's a vegetarian, a practicing Buddhist, and politically left-leaning—her moral certainty can tip into self-righteousness, whininess, or hypocrisy, as seen when her crusading zeal backfires on her. She craves validation for her intelligence, sometimes to a fault, and struggles with ordinary childhood insecurities like wanting a pony or getting hooked on TV, showing she's not purely defined by her brilliance. Her romantic life is a running thread, featuring on-and-off flirtations with characters like Nelson Muntz and the ever-devoted Milhouse Van Houten. Musically gifted and mentored by the late jazz musician Bleeding Gums Murphy, Lisa channels her frustrations and hopes into her saxophone playing. Ultimately, she serves as the show's grounded, empathetic voice amid her family's chaos. Voiced by Yeardley Smith. Notable quotes: "Free Tibet!" | "In this house, we obey the laws of thermodynamics!"
quotes: "Free Tibet!"

title: Maggie Simpson
text: Maggie Simpson is Youngest child of Homer and Marge Simpson, baby sister of Bart and Lisa. Maggie is the infant of the Simpson family, forever attached to her red pacifier and unable to walk without tripping over her own clothes. Despite being unable to speak, she is remarkably perceptive, often mimicking the world around her and getting swept up in the family's chaotic adventures. She's shown to be stubborn and prone to tantrums when she doesn't get her way, which makes other babies avoid her, so she mostly plays with her siblings. At the same time she reveals surprising competence in a crisis, from wielding a rifle to improvising weapons, frequently rescuing Homer from danger. She shares a rivalry with a fellow infant named Gerald that has followed her since their shared birth date, and she clearly favors Marge's company over Homer's, even though she loves her father. Because she cannot talk, Maggie tends to fade into the background of family life, but her rare, meaningful actions often carry big consequences for the plot. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright (making noises). Notable quotes: This is indeed a disturbing universe
quotes: This is indeed a disturbing universe

title: Ned Flanders
text: Ned Flanders is The Simpson family's devoutly religious next-door neighbor and landlord. Ned Flanders is Springfield's ever-cheerful, deeply devout neighbor who tries to live by the Bible as literally as possible. Raised by permissive 'beatnik' parents and subjected to an extreme spanking-based psychiatric treatment as a child, he grew up unable to express anger, which manifests as nervous, nonsensical jabbering whenever he's upset. He's almost pathologically kind and honest, often going out of his way to help others, including Homer, who resents him out of jealousy despite Ned's constant generosity. His strict Christian household extends to his sons Rod and Todd, who are shielded from pop culture, sugar, and even dice games. Ned's catchphrase-laden, folksy speech and unwavering faith make him both a source of comic relief and a moral touchstone amid Springfield's dysfunction. Voiced by Harry Shearer. title: Moe Szyslak
text: Moe Szyslak is Owner and bartender of Moe's Tavern, the regular hangout for Homer Simpson and his friends. Moe is a gruff, homely bar owner whose life is a constant cycle of failed get-rich-quick schemes, illegal side hustles, and self-loathing. He's famously cheap with his customers yet desperate for their company, alternating between throwing people out and begging them to stay so his tavern doesn't feel empty. His temper is explosive and often violent, and he has a well-documented habit of attempting suicide, most notably as an annual Christmas tradition, though these attempts are always played for dark comedy rather than tragedy. Beneath the surly exterior lies a surprisingly sentimental side, shown through his devotion to his cat, his kindness to society's outcasts, and unexpected acts of heroism. He nurses a hopeless, often creepy infatuation with Marge Simpson, which fuels much of his self-pity and comic desperation. Despite his many crimes, betrayals, and questionable ethics, Moe remains a beloved fixture of Springfield's social life, forever tied to Homer and the barflies who call his tavern home. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Ah, geez! (Moe's catchphrase) | we're phasing out the games, people drink less when they're having fun. | I can't believe this happened to me twice.

title: Krusty the Clown
text: Krusty the Clown is Cynical, chain-smoking clown TV host beloved by Bart and Lisa Simpson. Krusty is a jaded, addiction-prone Springfield celebrity who built his career hosting a long-running children's variety show despite constant personal and professional chaos. Born Herschel Krustofsky to a strict rabbi father who disowned him for pursuing comedy, he clawed his way through failed gigs, Vegas gambling addictions, and wartime entertaining before finding fame. His show has weathered scandals, including being framed for armed robbery by his resentful sidekick Sideshow Bob, as well as cancellation after losing viewers to the puppet Gabbo. Despite his gruff, self-serving exterior, he occasionally shows vulnerability, especially regarding his estranged father, and relies on Bart and Lisa's loyalty to bail him out of trouble. He is notably illiterate, has had numerous failed marriages and a scattered family life, and profits shamelessly off tie-in products like the disastrous Kamp Krusty. His career is a running gag of near-collapse followed by improbable comebacks. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Hey hey!
quotes: Hey hey!

title: Milhouse Van Houten
text: Milhouse Van Houten is Bart Simpson's best friend and a fellow student at Springfield Elementary. Milhouse is an awkward, nearsighted kid with a bulbous nose and thick glasses who serves as Bart's loyal, if frequently victimized, sidekick. He's of average intelligence but socially inept and extremely gullible, which makes him an easy target for both bullies like Nelson, Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney, and for Bart's schemes and pranks. Despite the mistreatment, the two share a genuine, if lopsided, friendship, and Milhouse occasionally flips the script by manipulating Bart himself. He nurses a long-running, largely unrequited crush on Lisa Simpson, suffering repeated romantic failures due to his tendency to lie, brag, and act clumsily around girls. Milhouse also has odd quirks, including a fear of honey and other allergies, a habit of bed-wetting, fluency in Italian from visits to his grandmother, and occasional forays into cross-dressing or effeminate behavior. Overall, he embodies the perpetually unlucky, dependable best friend archetype within the show's world. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: I'm not a nerd, Bart. Nerds are smart.
quotes: I'm not a nerd, Bart. Nerds are smart.

title: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon is Owner and clerk of the Kwik-E-Mart; Homer Simpson's friend and Springfield's convenience store proprietor. Apu is the tireless, endlessly hardworking owner of Springfield's Kwik-E-Mart, a man whose immense pride in his education and business is matched only by his devotion to his enormous family. Despite holding a Ph.D. in computer science, he spends nearly every waking hour behind the counter, a habit that occasionally pushes him into sleep-deprived delusions. Before settling into married life with Manjula through an arranged marriage, he was something of a ladies' man around town, with a colorful romantic past that came back to complicate his life more than once. He balances a deep religious devotion to Hindu gods with a very American entrepreneurial hustle, and he treats customer service with almost ritualistic cheerfulness. His steady, singsong catchphrase and unfailing politeness became one of the show's most recognizable running gags, even as the character later became the center of real-world debate over ethnic stereotyping. Loyal, industrious, and a little vain about his own accomplishments, Apu remains one of Springfield's most enduring supporting fixtures. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Thank you, come again!

text: The Simpsons was created by Matt Groening for the Fox network. It began as animated shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show in 1987 before becoming its own series in 1989.

title: Springfield Nuclear Power Plant
text: The Springfield Nuclear Power Plant is owned by Mr. Burns and is where Homer works as a safety inspector, often to comic (and alarming) effect.

title: Barney Gumble
text: Barney Gumble is Springfield's resident town drunk and Homer Simpson's best friend. Barney is a heavyset, perpetually inebriated barfly who spends nearly all his time propped up at Moe's Tavern, running up a beer tab so astronomical that NASA had to calculate it. Once a promising Harvard-bound student, he was derailed the night Homer introduced him to his first beer before the SATs, setting him on a lifelong path of alcoholism. Despite his sloppy appearance, wandering eye, and constant belching, he's warm-hearted and loyal, remaining one of Homer's closest friends alongside Moe, Lenny, and Carl. He's shown surprising hidden talents, including a beautiful Irish tenor singing voice as a member of The Be Sharps and skill as a helicopter pilot after periods of sobriety. Barney cycles repeatedly between attempts at recovery—via AA meetings, rehab, and personal triumphs—and inevitable relapses, often manipulated back into drinking by Moe, who depends on his patronage. He's also dabbled in various odd jobs and business ventures, most notably running a rival snow-plowing service called the Plow King that briefly outshone Homer's Mr. Plow. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. title: Nelson Muntz
text: Nelson Muntz is A tough, dim-seeming bully at Springfield Elementary School and longtime rival-turned-friend of Bart Simpson.. Nelson is the school's resident bully, instantly recognizable by his mocking laugh and rough, unkempt appearance. Though he's quick to throw a punch, he often does so for oddly principled reasons, punishing people for lying, wasting time, or betraying their beliefs rather than random cruelty. Beneath his tough exterior he hides surprising depths—flashes of intelligence, an appreciation for old crooners and fairy tales, and even a soft spot for Lisa Simpson, with whom he shares a brief and awkward romance. His homelife is chaotic and sad, shaped by an absent father and a neglectful mother, which helps explain his defensive, aggressive persona. Despite constantly torment­ing Martin Prince and clashing with Bart, he gradually becomes one of Bart's closest companions, showing loyalty when it counts. He runs in a loose gang with fellow bullies Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney, though his bond with them is shallow compared to his more complex relationships with his usual victims. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: Ha Ha! | That's for taking credit for other people's work! | That's for selling out your beliefs!

title: Seymour Skinner
text: Seymour Skinner is Principal of Springfield Elementary School and recurring authority figure/foil to Bart Simpson and the students. Seymour Skinner is the uptight, rule-obsessed principal of Springfield Elementary who genuinely wants the best for his students but is constantly undermined by a lack of funding, apathetic staff, and Bart Simpson's endless pranks. His rigid, militaristic demeanor traces back to his traumatic service as a Green Beret sergeant in the Vietnam War, where he was taken prisoner, and the show frequently hints he suffers lingering PTSD from that experience. Despite his tough exterior, he's often portrayed as timid and easily dominated, especially by his overbearing mother Agnes, whom he still lives with and who calls him 'Spanky.' His long, on-and-off romance with fellow teacher Edna Krabappel is a major recurring thread, ultimately derailed by his inability to break free of his mother's control. He shares a strange love-hate dynamic with both Bart, whose pranks keep him on his toes, and Superintendent Chalmers, his disapproving boss who conducts frequent stressful inspections. Skinner also occasionally reveals unexpected competence, such as using old combat skills to handle troublemakers, even though he's just as often bested in fights by ordinary townsfolk. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Young man, I'm going to be on you like a numerator on a denominator.

title: Groundskeeper Willie
text: Groundskeeper Willie is Groundskeeper and janitor at Springfield Elementary School, minor recurring character. Willie is the perpetually irate, thick-accented Scottish groundskeeper of Springfield Elementary School, feared by students and known for his gruff insults and volatile temper. Despite a lifetime of hard labor giving him surprising muscular strength beneath his clothes, he's frequently the butt of the show's jokes, often meeting gruesome fates in the Treehouse of Horror specials. His backstory reveals a tragic romance with Maisie MacWeldon back in Scotland, torn apart by her disapproving family before eventually reuniting decades later. He's had a string of romantic entanglements in Springfield, including flings with Lunchlady Dora, Edna Krabappel, and Agnes Skinner, showing a softer, more vulnerable side beneath his tough exterior. Willie also has a habit of unusual side jobs and hobbies, from moonlighting as a greenskeeper to secretly videotaping couples in cars. His catchphrase-worthy insults and thick brogue have made him one of the show's most quotable side characters, occasionally spilling into real-world cultural relevance. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Och, nae! | No one made it out alive, not even Willie! | Suddenly the ugliest man in Glasgow wasn't good enough for her!

title: Comic Book Guy
text: Comic Book Guy is Owner of The Android's Dungeon comic book store in Springfield, a recurring minor character. Comic Book Guy is an obese, unkempt, and socially awkward comic shop owner whose sharp sarcasm masks a lifetime of loneliness and insecurity. Despite holding a master's degree in folklore and mythology, he channels his intelligence into obsessive devotion to comics, sci-fi, and pop culture trivia, often looking down on customers like Bart and Milhouse from behind his counter. His childhood was shaped by an emotionally distant, wealthy father who struggled to connect with him, leaving him with lingering insecurities into adulthood. Romantically, he spent decades as a virgin before eventually dating Edna Krabappel and Agnes Skinner, and finally finding lasting love with Kumiko, whom he marries and later considers starting a family with. He briefly finds mainstream success as the creator of the comic series Everyman, even seeing it adapted into a troubled Hollywood film starring Homer Simpson. Known for his biting insults and superiority complex, he's most famous for his recurring put-down about things being the 'worst ever,' a signature line that defines his cynical persona. Voiced by Hank Azaria. title: Patty Bouvier
text: Patty Bouvier is Marge Simpson's cynical, chain-smoking identical twin sister, DMV employee, and Homer's frequent nemesis. Patty is the more hardened and openly contemptuous of the Bouvier twins, especially when it comes to her brother-in-law Homer, whom she treats with near-constant scorn. She works alongside her sister Selma at the Springfield DMV, where the pair are known for weaponizing bureaucratic red tape against people they dislike, particularly Homer. A lifelong smoker and devoted fan of the show MacGyver, Patty later reveals she is a lesbian, a truth she had hidden for years behind a facade of joyless dating, including a failed relationship with Principal Skinner. Her coming out marks one of her rare moments of vulnerability, leading her to ask Homer to officiate her wedding despite their mutual animosity. Outside of her feud with Homer, she shares a close, sometimes co-dependent bond with her twin, and the two are portrayed as intimidating, sharp-tongued figures who nonetheless show occasional cracks of familial loyalty, especially toward Marge. She's also revealed to be surprisingly well-read, being multilingual in fictional languages and co-authoring a fantasy novel. Voiced by Julie Kavner. title: Selma Bouvier
text: Selma Bouvier is Marge Simpson's older twin sister, DMV employee, and Homer's chain-smoking sister-in-law. Selma is one half of the notoriously cynical Bouvier twins, sharing her sister Patty's love of smoking and disdain for Homer, though she occasionally shows him small flashes of sympathy. She lost her senses of taste and smell in a childhood bottle rocket accident and has been married and divorced six times in her desperate search for lasting companionship. Despite her low standards for men, she longs for love and eventually finds motherhood by adopting a Chinese baby, Ling, after briefly caring for an iguana named Jub-Jub. She works alongside Patty at the Springfield DMV and lives with her at the Spinster Arms apartments, both women often behaving unprofessionally on the job. While she and Patty frequently scheme against Homer and hope for Marge to leave him, Selma is the one who ultimately helps reunite the couple when they separate. Her running gags include her raspy voice, chain-smoking habit, terrible luck with men, and grudging softness toward her nieces, nephew, and occasionally even Homer. Voiced by Julie Kavner (Yeardley Smith voiced young Selma). Notable quotes: Single? Well, he passes the Selma test! | The older they get, the cuter they ain't. | I am the lizard queen!

title: Abraham Simpson
text: Abraham Simpson is Patriarch of the Simpson family; father of Homer Simpson and grandfather of Bart, Lisa, and Maggie. Abe is the elderly, cantankerous grandfather of the Simpson clan, a self-proclaimed World War II veteran now living out his days at the Springfield Retirement Castle after Homer sends him there. He's best known for his endless, meandering, and wildly implausible war stories that rarely hold up to scrutiny, hinting that his memory has grown unreliable with age. Despite his confused and often contradictory recollections, he seems occasionally aware that he's being inconsistent, suggesting there's more mischief than senility behind some of his tall tales. Over the years he has claimed membership in secret societies, communist groups, and even leadership of oddly specific political causes, underscoring his eccentric and unpredictable nature. He suffers from random narcoleptic episodes, adding a physical-comedy element to his character, and his relationships—multiple marriages, a secret daughter, and an estranged half-brother situation with Homer's own half-sibling—paint him as a man whose chaotic past continues to ripple through the family. Despite his flaws, Abe's story arcs often circle back to a begrudging, sentimental bond with Homer and the rest of the family. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Ahh!
quotes: Ahh!

title: Sideshow Bob
text: Sideshow Bob is Bart Simpson's archnemesis; a former children's TV sidekick turned recurring criminal mastermind. Sideshow Bob is a highly educated, culturally refined man whose sophisticated tastes and self-regard mask a deep well of resentment and violent obsession. Once relegated to a humiliating sidekick role on Krusty the Clown's show, he snapped after years of abuse and turned to crime, framing Krusty and setting off a lifelong pattern of elaborate revenge schemes. His defining trait is an all-consuming hatred of Bart Simpson, who repeatedly foils his murder plots, leading to an endless cycle of arrest, parole, and re-arrest. Despite his menace, Bob is darkly comic and oddly endearing, prone to grandiose monologues, classical music and literature references, and surprisingly civil manners even mid-crime. He occasionally shows flashes of genuine goodness, such as helping solve crimes or admitting he can't bring himself to kill Bart, only to relapse into villainy soon after. Bob's saga spans marriages, a stint as Springfield's mayor, life abroad in Italy, and a supposed death, making him one of the show's most recurring and theatrical antagonists. Voiced by Kelsey Grammer (also Dan Castellaneta when disguised as Krusty in "Krusty Gets Busted"). Notable quotes: Hello, Bart.
quotes: Hello, Bart.

title: Kent Brockman
text: Kent Brockman is Anchorman for Channel 6 News in Springfield, hosting several news and talk programs. Kent Brockman is Springfield's sensationalist, self-important local news anchor who embodies nearly every flaw of tabloid journalism. He's vain, careerist, and prone to on-air tantrums, yet somehow keeps winning industry awards despite his questionable ethics. Brockman loves injecting his own reactionary opinions into broadcasts through a segment literally called 'My Two Cents,' and he's been caught cursing on air more than once, resulting in several firings and rehirings. His rivalry with traffic reporter Arnie Pye is a recurring source of petty cruelty, including Brockman's gleeful reaction to news of Pye's supposed death. Offscreen, his life is a mess of past relationships, a fluctuating fortune, and a wardrobe of vanity tricks like botox and clothes-pin face-lifts. Despite constant mockery of his character, he remains a fixture of Springfield media, forever ready to twist a story into something dramatic for ratings. Voiced by Harry Shearer. title: Edna Krabappel
text: Edna Krabappel is Bart Simpson's fourth-grade teacher at Springfield Elementary School. Edna Krabappel is the world-weary, chain-smoking teacher whose idealism was ground down by years of dealing with unruly students, especially Bart. Despite her cynicism, glimpses of her original desire to help children still surface from time to time. She is defined largely by her chronic loneliness and an almost comically long string of failed romances and flings with nearly every eligible man in Springfield. Her most stable relationships are with Principal Skinner and bartender Moe Szyslak, though she eventually ends up married to Ned Flanders. She has a dry, sarcastic wit and a memorable single-syllable laugh that other characters affectionately imitate after her passing. Behind her jaded exterior lies a lonely woman still hoping for real companionship and validation. Voiced by Marcia Wallace. title: Fat Tony
text: Fat Tony is Head of the Springfield Mafia and recurring mobster character in Springfield. Fat Tony is the smooth-talking, well-connected boss of Springfield's organized crime scene, running rackets that range from illegal gambling and cigarette smuggling to bizarre schemes like selling rat's milk to schools. Despite his violent profession, he carries himself with old-world charm and a strange code of honor, treating his family and 'business' associates with courtly respect even while ordering hits. He has a soft spot for his son Michael and a complicated romantic history, having been married multiple times and once unknowingly deceiving Selma Bouvier into a fake marriage ceremony. Tony often finds himself entangled with the Simpsons, alternately menacing Homer with contract hits and relying on him as a bodyguard or partner in crime. His operation is deeply embedded in Springfield's corrupt local government, frequently bribing Mayor Quimby and Chief Wiggum. A running gag is his oddly refined side, including his skill as a violinist and his surprisingly deep backstory involving a childhood exchange with a rival Prussian mob family. Ever the pragmatist, he treats even personal tragedies, like his wife's death, with dark comic detachment. Voiced by Joe Mantegna (also Hank Azaria in "A Fish Called Selma"). Notable quotes: I don't get mad, I get stabby. | She was whacked, by natural causes.

title: Ralph Wiggum
text: Ralph Wiggum is A young student at Springfield Elementary School and the son of Chief Clancy Wiggum; a classmate of Bart and Lisa Simpson.. Ralph is Springfield Elementary's resident oddball, known for blurting out bizarre non sequiturs and eating strange things like paste, crayons, and worms. Despite seeming slow-witted and socially awkward, he occasionally reveals surprising depth, talent, or cunning, such as his impressive stage performances or his secret political savvy. He's largely shielded from bullying thanks to his father's position as police chief, and he maintains an unusually rich inner life full of imaginary friends, including a mischievous, fire-obsessed leprechaun. Ralph has had brief but memorable relationships with other kids, most notably a short-lived romance with Lisa and an on-and-off friendship with Bart. Underneath his goofy, oblivious exterior lies a generally sweet and affectionate kid, especially toward his parents. His character has become a cultural touchstone for absurdist humor, inspiring real-world references far beyond the show itself. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: Me fail English? title: Otto Mann
text: Otto Mann is Springfield Elementary School's chaotic, perpetually stoner-teenage bus driver. Otto is the school bus driver whose laid-back, dude-speak demeanor masks a truly reckless approach to his job, having crashed the bus over a dozen times and once lost his position entirely for lacking any real license. He's a die-hard rock and metal fan, worshipping bands like Metallica and Black Sabbath, and is rarely seen without his guitar or headphones. His heavy drug use, including marijuana and implied harder substances, frequently intersects with his driving duties, leading to bizarre hallucinations and mishaps. Despite his burnout stoner image, he shows surprising creative flair, having invented his own comic book superhero and even taught himself lute in the style of Jimi Hendrix. His personal life is a string of odd romances and family drama, including a broken engagement he sabotaged himself and a strained relationship with his disapproving admiral father. Frequently homeless and jobless, Otto nonetheless remains a fixture of Springfield's community, filling in as a driver for everything from senior citizen trolleys to blood donation buses. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: My name is Otto, and I love to get blotto!

text: "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G08), directed by David Silverman and written by Mimi Pond, originally airing December 17, 1989. As Christmas nears, the Simpson family's holiday spirit is tested when Mr. Burns announces there will be no Christmas bonuses for plant workers, leaving Homer too ashamed to tell Marge. Complicating matters, Bart secretly gets a tattoo at the mall, forcing Marge to spend the family's entire Christmas savings on its removal. Desperate to hide his missing bonus and still provide for his family, Homer takes on a secret second job as a mall Santa Claus, enduring humiliating training and a mishap where Bart unmasks him in front of customers. After a disappointing paycheck of only thirteen dollars, Homer is convinced by Bart and Barney to try his luck at the dog track, betting everything on a longshot greyhound named Santa's Little Helper. The dog loses badly, seemingly dashing their last hope for a proper Christmas, but Homer and Bart find the discarded, mistreated dog afterward and decide to adopt him. Returning home empty-handed except for the dog, Homer tearfully confesses the truth about his lost bonus, but the family's love for their new pet turns the disappointing holiday into a heartwarming success. Notable quotes: Bart: Aw, come on, Dad, this could be the miracle that saves the Simpsons' Christmas. If TV has taught me anything, it's that miracles always happen to poor kids at Christmas. It happened to Tiny Tim, it happened to Charlie Brown, it happened to The Smurfs, and it's going to happen to us. | Homer: Oh, all right. Who's Tiny Tim? | Bart: I'm Bart Simpson, who the hell are you? | Homer: Thirteen bucks? Hey, wait a minute! | Homer: It says it's for dogs, but she can't read.

Homer: Oh, all right. Who's Tiny Tim?

Homer: It says it's for dogs, but she can't read.

title: Bart the Genius (S1E02)
text: "Bart the Genius" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G02), directed by David Silverman and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing January 14, 1990. During a family Scrabble game, Bart invents the nonsense word 'Kwyjibo' to win, foreshadowing his knack for deception. At school, after Martin Prince rats him out for graffiti insulting Principal Skinner, Bart swaps his aptitude test with Martin's to avoid punishment, inadvertently registering an IQ of 216. School psychologist Dr. Pryor convinces Skinner and the Simpsons that Bart is a genius who needs to attend a special school for gifted children. Bart enjoys the freedom of his new school at first, but quickly finds himself out of his depth among truly brilliant classmates who mock his ignorance. As Homer showers him with pride and attention, Bart struggles with guilt over the lie, especially after failing academically and alienating his old friends. When a lab explosion leaves him covered in green goo, Bart finally confesses the truth in a note meant for Dr. Pryor, exposing the ruse. Back home, though Bart admits he loved the closeness the deception brought him and Homer, an enraged Homer chases him around the house once the truth sinks in, restoring the family's usual chaotic normalcy. Guest starring Marcia Wallace as Edna Krabappel and Ms. Melon. Notable quotes: Bart: Uh... a big, dumb, balding North American ape. With no chin. | Homer: I'll show you a big, dumb, balding ape--!!! | Edna Krabappel: These tests will have no effect on your grades. They merely determine your future social status and financial success... if any. | Homer: I bet Einstein turned himself all sorts of colors before he invented the light bulb. | Bart: Eat my shorts.
quotes: Bart: Uh... a big, dumb, balding North American ape. With no chin.
Homer: I'll show you a big, dumb, balding ape--!!!
Edna Krabappel: These tests will have no effect on your grades. They merely determine your future social status and financial success... if any.
Homer: I bet Einstein turned himself all sorts of colors before he invented the light bulb.
Bart: Eat my shorts.

title: Homer's Odyssey (S1E03)
text: "Homer's Odyssey" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G03), directed by Wes Archer and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing January 21, 1990. Bart's class takes a field trip to the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, where his father Homer accidentally causes a gas leak while trying to wave at his son, getting himself fired on the spot. Struggling to find new work and drowning his sorrows at Moe's, Homer sinks into a deep depression, eventually stealing change from Bart's piggy bank just to afford a beer. Ashamed of what he's become, Homer writes a farewell note and sets off to drown himself, dragging a boulder toward a bridge. When Marge and the kids chase after him and are nearly hit by a car at an unmarked intersection, Homer selflessly shoves them out of harm's way, realizing in that moment that Springfield desperately needs better safety measures. Reinvigorated with purpose, he successfully petitions the town for a stop sign and launches a citywide safety campaign, plastering Springfield with warning signs. Emboldened, he turns his crusade toward the power plant itself, organizing a public protest against its lack of safety standards. Mr. Burns, impressed by his tenacity, offers Homer a job as the plant's official safety inspector, but tests his integrity by ordering him to falsely reassure the public that the plant is safe. Homer refuses to lie, earning Burns' respect and the job anyway, and the episode ends with the crowd triumphantly carrying him off after he tumbles from a balcony in celebration. Notable quotes: Homer: I will not rest until this street gets a STOP sign | Homer: I'm just a technical supervisor who cared too much. | Moe: Moe's Tavern. | Homer: Unlike most of you, I am not a nut. | Smilin' Joe Fission: I'll just put it where nobody'll find it for a million years.
quotes: Homer: I will not rest until this street gets a STOP sign
Homer: I'm just a technical supervisor who cared too much.
Moe: Moe's Tavern.
Homer: Unlike most of you, I am not a nut.
Smilin' Joe Fission: I'll just put it where nobody'll find it for a million years.

title: There's No Disgrace Like Home (S1E04)
text: "There's No Disgrace Like Home" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G04), directed by Gregg Vanzo, Kent Butterworth and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, originally airing January 28, 1990. After a disastrous outing at Mr. Burns' company picnic, where Bart cheats in the father-son race, Marge gets tipsy on punch, and the kids embarrass him in front of the boss, Homer becomes convinced his family is hopelessly dysfunctional. Comparing them unfavorably to a seemingly perfect family at the picnic, Homer resolves to fix his household and forces everyone to eat dinner together and say grace, which only leads to more bickering. Determined to prove something is wrong, he drags the family on a humiliating tour of the neighborhood to spy on other households, only for them to accidentally peek into their own home. Frustrated, Homer heads to Moe's Tavern, gets into a scuffle with Barney, and while recovering on the floor sees a TV ad for Dr. Marvin Monroe's Family Therapy Center promising a money-back guarantee. Despite the family's objections and the need to raid Bart's college fund and pawn the television for cash, Homer takes them all to therapy. Dr. Monroe tries drawing exercises and foam-mallet fights before resorting to an electroshock device meant to punish emotional hurts, but the Simpsons instead turn it into a chaotic free-for-all that overloads the building's power and drains half of Springfield's electricity. Monroe throws them out, but Homer insists on the advertised double-your-money-back guarantee, and the family leaves $500 richer and oddly bonded by the shared ordeal, with Homer planning to use the money to buy a new TV. Notable quotes: Marge: I don't want to alarm anyone, but I think there's a li'l al-key-hol in this punch. | Homer: Quick, Bart, give me a kiss. | Bart: Kiss you? But, Dad, I'm your kid! | Homer: When will I learn? The answers to life's problems aren't at the bottom of a bottle, they're on TV! | Bart: These people are obviously freaks.
quotes: Marge: I don't want to alarm anyone, but I think there's a li'l al-key-hol in this punch.
Homer: Quick, Bart, give me a kiss.
Bart: Kiss you? But, Dad, I'm your kid!
Homer: When will I learn? The answers to life's problems aren't at the bottom of a bottle, they're on TV!
Bart: These people are obviously freaks.

title: Bart the General (S1E05)
text: "Bart the General" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G05), directed by David Silverman and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 4, 1990. After Bart defends Lisa's cupcakes from one of Nelson Muntz's cronies, he accidentally bloodies Nelson's nose during the ensuing scuffle, making him the school bully's new target. Terrified of the promised after-school beating, Bart imagines gruesome outcomes but is ultimately thrashed and stuffed into a trash can, a humiliation Nelson repeats the next day even after Bart tries Homer's dirty-fighting tactics. Desperate for real help, Bart turns to Grampa Simpson, who admits that simply standing up for himself doesn't always work, and the pair seek out one-armed antiques dealer Herman, who suggests Bart raise a small army. Bart recruits neighborhood kids into a makeshift militia, training them through montages of drills and obstacle courses in preparation for a decisive confrontation. When the moment comes, Bart's army ambushes Nelson with water balloons, capturing him and dragging him back to the Simpson house. Herman drafts a peace treaty between Bart and Nelson, which both boys sign, ending the conflict, while Marge caps off the resolution by handing out cupcakes to everyone. The episode closes with Bart addressing the audience directly about the seriousness of war. Notable quotes: Bart: I promise you victory, I promise you good times! | Homer: What? And violate the code of the schoolyard? I'd rather Bart die! | Nelson: You made me bleed my own blood. | Principal Skinner: Scoot, young Simpson. There's learning afoot! | Grampa: We are not all vibrant, fun-loving sex maniacs.

Homer: What? And violate the code of the schoolyard? I'd rather Bart die!
Nelson: You made me bleed my own blood.
Principal Skinner: Scoot, young Simpson. There's learning afoot!
Grampa: We are not all vibrant, fun-loving sex maniacs.

title: Moaning Lisa (S1E06)
text: "Moaning Lisa" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G06), directed by Wes Archer and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, originally airing February 11, 1990. Lisa is overcome with sadness, unable to enjoy dodgeball, band practice, or even her share of cupcakes, and her gloom earns her a note home from Principal Skinner. While Homer and Marge struggle to understand what's wrong, Homer is preoccupied with losing repeatedly to Bart in the video game Super Slugfest and even has a nightmare about being knocked out by his son. One night Lisa follows the sound of a saxophone to a bridge overpass, where she meets Bleeding Gums Murphy, an old street musician who bonds with her over the blues and invites her to his club, the Jazz Hole. Marge, trying to help, instead tells Lisa to bury her true feelings and fake a smile to fit in with other kids, but seeing Lisa's forced happiness at school makes Marge realize her advice was wrong. Marge apologizes, tells Lisa it's fine to be sad and to always be herself, and the two reconcile. Meanwhile, after getting tips from an arcade kid, Homer finally defeats Bart at the video game, prompting Bart to retire undefeated in humiliation-avoidance fashion. The episode ends with the whole family at the Jazz Hole listening to Bleeding Gums perform a blues song that Lisa wrote about her life. Notable quotes: Lisa: I'm too sad. | Bleeding Gums Murphy: The blues isn't about making yourself feeling better, it's about making other people feel worse. | Marge: It doesn't matter how you feel inside, you know. It's what shows up on the surface that counts. Take all your bad feelings and push them down, all the way down, past your knees, until you're almost walking on them. | Marge: Lisa, I apologize to you, I was wrong, I take it all back. Always be yourself. If you want to be sad, honey, be sad. | Bart: Sorry Dad, women and children first
quotes: Lisa: I'm too sad.
Bleeding Gums Murphy: The blues isn't about making yourself feeling better, it's about making other people feel worse.

Marge: It doesn't matter how you feel inside, you know. It's what shows up on the surface that counts. Take all your bad feelings and push them down, all the way down, past your knees, until you're almost walking on them.

title: The Call of the Simpsons (S1E07)
text: "The Call of the Simpsons" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G09), directed by Wes Archer and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 18, 1990. After seeing Ned Flanders' impressive new RV, Homer decides the Simpsons need one too and takes the family to Bob's RV Round-Up. Priced out of the fancy models, Homer is pressured into buying a decrepit, run-down RV instead. While driving recklessly off-road on a camping trip, Homer wrecks the vehicle over a cliff, leaving the family stranded in the wilderness with nothing. Homer and Bart set off for help but become separated from baby Maggie, who is adopted by a family of bears after being left behind, while Marge and Lisa manage surprisingly well on their own. Homer and Bart endure a series of misadventures, including a waterfall plunge and a bee attack, culminating in Homer being caught on camera covered in mud, which sparks a media frenzy claiming Bigfoot has been discovered. The Bigfoot hysteria grows even after Marge and Lisa are found, and Homer is eventually tranquilized by hunters mistaking him for the creature. Scientists studying Homer conclude he is either an intelligent beast or a very stupid human, and the family is finally reunited at home, with Marge comforting a self-conscious Homer. Notable quotes: Homer: This is a real adventure! | Bart: Don't have a cow, Dad. | Homer: What am I gonna do? I've murdered us all! | Bob: You ever known a siren to be good? | Homer: When you're an experienced woodsman like me, you get a feel for these things. It becomes natural, like a third sense.
quotes: Homer: This is a real adventure!
Bart: Don't have a cow, Dad.
Homer: What am I gonna do? I've murdered us all!
Bob: You ever known a siren to be good?
Homer: When you're an experienced woodsman like me, you get a feel for these things. It becomes natural, like a third sense.

title: The Telltale Head (S1E08)
text: "The Telltale Head" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G07), directed by Rich Moore and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, Sam Simon, Matt Groening, originally airing February 25, 1990. The episode opens with Homer and Bart fleeing an angry mob through downtown Springfield, Bart clutching a mysterious object, before flashing back to explain how they got there. Frustrated by his lack of popularity, Bart falls in with three of Springfield Elementary's toughest bullies, sneaking into a movie, unwittingly helping them shoplift from the Kwik-E-Mart, and joining them in vandalizing the town's beloved statue of founder Jebediah Springfield. When the bullies mock Bart for defending the statue, he becomes obsessed with proving his coolness and later sneaks out at night to saw off the statue's head himself. The next morning the whole town is in uproar over the desecration, and Bart is wracked with guilt, hearing an imagined voice of Jebediah urging him to do the right thing. After failing to bury the head in the backyard, Bart confesses to his shocked family, and Homer realizes his own bad advice about the importance of popularity contributed to Bart's actions. Father and son return to the town square, where Bart publicly admits his crime to the assembled mob. Moved by his honesty and remorse, the townspeople forgive him, and Bart restores the head to the statue as the crowd cheers. Notable quotes: Jimbo Jones: I wish someone would cut his ugly old head off! | Ms. Albright: Because Heaven is for people. | Bart: What about a robot with a human brain? | Homer: I hope you're not planning on seeing a certain movie starring certain Space Mutants that a certain mother didn't want you to see. | Homer: Here you go son. 'Share the wealth', that's what I always say!
quotes: Jimbo Jones: I wish someone would cut his ugly old head off!
Ms. Albright: Because Heaven is for people.
Bart: What about a robot with a human brain?
Homer: I hope you're not planning on seeing a certain movie starring certain Space Mutants that a certain mother didn't want you to see.

title: Life on the Fast Lane (S1E09)
text: "Life on the Fast Lane" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G11), directed by David Silverman and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 18, 1990. On Marge's birthday, Homer nearly forgets the occasion and scrambles to buy her a gift, ultimately presenting her with a bowling ball engraved with his own name. Hurt and insulted, Marge decides to take up bowling herself just to spite him, and at Barney's Bowlarama she meets Jacques, a suave Frenchman who offers to teach her the game. As Jacques' lessons continue, his flirtation grows more overt, and Marge finds herself flattered and increasingly drawn to the attention she isn't getting at home. Meanwhile Homer, sensing something is wrong when he finds Marge's monogrammed wrist guard, grows anxious but keeps his fears bottled up, even as Bart and Lisa notice the tension between their parents. Marge agrees to meet Jacques at his apartment, and on the way she daydreams about a romantic encounter with him before snapping back to reality full of doubt. Torn at a literal fork in the road between Jacques' apartment and Homer's workplace, Marge chooses to visit Homer instead, surprising him at the power plant. The episode ends with the couple reconciling and sneaking off together, reaffirming their marriage despite the earlier rift. Notable quotes: Homer: Oh. Don't worry. This frosting will come right off. Beauty, isn't she? | Jacques: Yes, I am a very good teacher, and I can teach you everything. | Jacques: Well, first of all, you yell, "The eight-pin is a cop!" | Bart: Told ya she likes mine better. | Lisa: Oh, brother!

Jacques: Yes, I am a very good teacher, and I can teach you everything.

Bart: Told ya she likes mine better.

title: Homer's Night Out (S1E10)
text: "Homer's Night Out" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G10), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing March 25, 1990. After ordering a mail-order spy camera that finally arrives, Bart begins secretly photographing private family moments, while Homer prepares to attend a bachelor party for his supervisor Eugene Fisk at a seafood restaurant. Marge takes the kids to the same restaurant, and Bart sneaks into the party's private room, where he snaps a photo of Homer dancing exuberantly with a belly dancer named Princess Kashmir. Bart shares the photo at school under the promise of secrecy, but it spreads rapidly and soon the entire town of Springfield has seen it, embarrassing Marge and infuriating her. When Homer returns home unaware of the scandal, Marge confronts him with the photo and, after learning Bart took it, kicks Homer out of the house. Homer spends an uncomfortable night at Barney's messy apartment and endures an awkward interrogation from Mr. Burns about his supposed way with women. Seeking reconciliation, Homer agrees to Marge's demand that he and Bart find Princess Kashmir so Homer can prove to Bart that women aren't objects. After tracking her down at a strip club, Homer ends up on stage again, but this time delivers a heartfelt speech about respecting women, which touches the audience and wins Marge's forgiveness. Guest starring Sam McMurray as Gulliver Dark. Notable quotes: Homer: Women are not just mere objects! | Homer: This is the most fun I've had in my entire life! | Mr. Burns: What in blue blazes do you think you're doing, Simpson?! | Mr. Burns: A plant employee carrying on like an over-sexed orangutan in heat! | Bart: Oh, sure, like I'm really gonna take a picture of my butt.

title: The Crepes of Wrath (S1E11)
text: "The Crepes of Wrath" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G13), directed by Wes Archer, Milton Gray and written by George Meyer, Sam Simon, John Swartzwelder, Jon Vitti, originally airing April 15, 1990. After Bart accidentally injures Homer and then sets off a cherry bomb in the school restroom—unwittingly blasting Principal Skinner's mother off the toilet—Skinner decides that ordinary punishment won't suffice and proposes Bart be sent away on a foreign exchange program. Bart is shipped off to a rural vineyard in France, where he is taken in by two unscrupulous winemakers, Cesar and Ugolin, who strip him of his belongings and force him into grueling labor picking and crushing grapes. Worse, Bart discovers the pair are secretly adulterating their wine with antifreeze to cut costs, and he's made to taste-test it. Meanwhile, the Simpsons host their own exchange student, Adil Hoxha, an Albanian boy who turns out to be using his stay as cover to spy on Homer's nuclear plant for secrets, all while sparking political arguments with Lisa about capitalism and freedom. Back in France, an isolated and increasingly desperate Bart unexpectedly finds himself fluent in French and manages to alert a police officer to the abuse and the antifreeze scheme, leading to Cesar and Ugolin's arrest and turning Bart into a local hero. Simultaneously, American authorities uncover Adil's espionage and he is swapped for an American boy who had been caught spying in Albania. The episode closes with Bart returning home just as Adil is taken away, both exchange plots resolved in tandem. title: Krusty Gets Busted (S1E12)
text: "Krusty Gets Busted" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G12), directed by Brad Bird and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing April 29, 1990. While picking up ice cream for Marge, Homer witnesses Krusty the Clown robbing Apu at the Kwik-E-Mart at gunpoint, and later identifies him to police and in court. Bart is devastated that his idol has been arrested, while the town turns against Krusty, burning his merchandise in a public bonfire led by Reverend Lovejoy. During the trial, Krusty is revealed to be illiterate, and he is ultimately convicted and jailed. Refusing to believe Krusty is guilty, Bart enlists Lisa to investigate, and they uncover clues from the security footage—Krusty's pacemaker means he couldn't have used the microwave, and his illiteracy means he wasn't reading a magazine as claimed. Suspecting Sideshow Bob, Krusty's resentful former sidekick, Bart confronts him live on air and proves Bob has unusually large feet, matching the robber seen stepping on Homer's foot. Bob is exposed and arrested, confessing he framed Krusty out of jealousy and a desire for his own more intellectual show. Krusty is exonerated and thanks Bart, while Bob is hauled off to jail vowing revenge. Guest starring Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Notable quotes: Krusty: Hand over all your money in a paper bag! | Apu: Yes, yes, I know the procedure for armed robbery! I do work in a convenience store you know! | Krusty: No, okay?! I'm illiterate! | Judge Snyder: I do not believe it: the king of children's literacy is himself illiterate! | Bart: Dad, you're giving in to mob mentality!

title: Some Enchanted Evening (S1E13)
text: "Some Enchanted Evening" is an episode of Season 1 (production code 7G01), directed by David Silverman, Kent Butterworth and written by Matt Groening, Sam Simon, originally airing May 13, 1990. Homer and Marge's marriage hits a rough patch when Marge calls in to Dr. Marvin Monroe's radio therapy show to complain that Homer no longer treats her romantically. Overhearing this at the power plant, Homer seeks advice from Moe, who suggests a fancy dinner and flowers, and Homer manages to win Marge over with a rose, chocolates, and dinner reservations at Chez Paree. Struggling to find a babysitter after Bart's prank calls tie up Moe's line, Marge hires a stranger named Ms. Botz through a babysitting service, unaware she is actually the notorious 'Babysitter Bandit.' While Homer and Marge enjoy their night out, Ms. Botz forces Bart and Lisa to watch a children's video before revealing her true criminal nature and tying up the kids while she robs the house. Maggie, unnoticed, unties her siblings, and the children devise a plan using Maggie's pacifier sounds to lure Botz into a closet, where Bart knocks her out with a bat. The kids tie up Botz and call the police, but when Homer and Marge return home, they mistakenly believe the babysitter was mistreated and send her off with extra pay and her suitcases full of stolen goods. The episode ends with Homer accepting his own foolishness while Marge reassures him that she loves him regardless. Guest starring Penny Marshall. Must be a crossed wire. | Homer: It matters not, mon frere. | Barney: You're even more of a pig than I am. [burps] | Homer: [angrily] D'oh! Actually the Simpsons are neighbors of ours and we found them to be a quite misunderstood and underrated family.

title: Bart Gets an "F" (S2E01)
text: "Bart Gets an "F"" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F03), directed by David Silverman and written by David M. Stern, originally airing October 11, 1990. Bart's grades have been slipping all term, and after botching a book report on Treasure Island, Mrs. Krabappel warns him that failing the upcoming Colonial America test could mean repeating fourth grade. Bart tries every shortcut imaginable, from getting bogus answers from Sherri and Terri to faking illness and finally having Milhouse feed him test answers over the phone, but he still scores worse than ever. After a tense meeting with Homer, Marge, and the school psychiatrist Dr. Pryor, who recommends Bart be held back, Bart desperately vows he can pass on his own. He turns to unlikely study partner Martin Prince, trading tutoring for popularity tips, but Martin gets distracted by his newfound coolness and abandons their study sessions. Left on his own, Bart prays for a miracle to buy him more study time, and a snow day conveniently closes school the next morning. Torn between playing in the snow and studying, Bart chooses to hit the books, forcing himself through daydreams and self-slaps to stay focused. Despite his genuine effort, he scores only 59% on the test and breaks down crying, prompting a stunned Mrs. Krabappel—moved by his passionate answer referencing George Washington—to award him one extra point, bumping him to a D- and letting him pass, resulting in an accidental kiss on her cheek from an overjoyed Bart. Notable quotes: Bart Simpson: I passed, I passed, I passed, I passed, I passed, I ... kissed the teacher!! Yuck! | Martin Prince: A blindfolded chimp with a pencil in his teeth stands a better chance at passing this test than you do! | Edna Krabappel: I cannot believe it! This is even worse than Milhouse's exam! Bart Simpson, I warned you! | Bart Simpson Senior: Ah, lady, come on. My kid has the chicken pox, my wife has been nagging me for a new car and I need a root canal. | Otto: Whoa! Sorry, Bart dude, state law prohibits me from crashing the bus on purpose.

title: Simpson and Delilah (S2E02)
text: "Simpson and Delilah" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F02), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing October 18, 1990. After seeing a TV ad for a miracle hair-growth product called Dimoxinil, a balding Homer becomes desperate to try it despite the steep $1,000 price tag. Egged on by Lenny, he fraudulently charges the treatment to the plant's health insurance and secretly buys it from the shady Dr. Boyle. The formula works, and Mr. Burns, spotting Homer's new head of hair on the security monitors, promotes him to an executive position. Struggling to fit in among the office elite, Homer hires an unusually competent male secretary named Karl, who quietly manages Homer's image, relationships, and career, even taking credit for a workplace safety improvement Homer proposes. When plant records reveal Homer's insurance fraud, Karl selflessly claims responsibility for the scheme to protect Homer's job, sacrificing his own position. Just as Homer needs to deliver an important speech, his son Bart accidentally spills the remaining Dimoxinil, leaving Homer bald again right before the big presentation. Though Homer delivers an insightful speech on economizing the plant, the executives dismiss him now that he's bald, and Burns demotes him back to his old job while sharing his own past experience with hair loss. text: "Treehouse of Horror" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F04), directed by Wes Archer (part 1), Rich Moore (part 2), David Silverman (part 3) and written by John Swartzwelder (part 1), Jay Kogen & Wallace Wolodarsky (part 2), Sam Simon and Edgar Allan Poe (part 3), originally airing October 25, 1990. In this first Treehouse of Horror special, Marge opens with a tongue-in-cheek warning to parents before the family's Halloween tales unfold. In 'Bad Dream House,' the Simpsons buy a suspiciously cheap home that turns out to be sentient and evil, tormenting them with a kitchen vortex, flying furniture, and brainwashing them into attacking one another, until Marge stands her ground and the mortified house chooses to implode rather than keep living with them. In 'Hungry are the Damned,' the family is abducted by two well-meaning aliens, Kang and Kodos, along with Serak the Preparer, who shower them with food for a promised feast on Rigel IV; Lisa's suspicion, sparked by misreading a cookbook title, convinces everyone the aliens intend to eat them, leading the insulted Rigellians to abandon their offer of paradise and return the ungrateful humans to Earth. In 'The Raven,' Lisa narrates Edgar Allan Poe's poem with Homer cast as the grieving narrator tormented by a mysterious talking raven that only repeats 'Nevermore,' leading to a chaotic chase around his study that leaves Homer disheveled and unnerved. The episode closes with Bart shrugging off the scares while Homer, clearly rattled by the night's stories, declares he now hates Halloween. Guest starring James Earl Jones as Serak the Preparer, the narrator and the removalist. text: "Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F01), directed by Wes Archer and written by John Swartzwelder, Sam Simon, originally airing November 1, 1990. While fishing near the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, Bart hooks a mutated three-eyed fish that quickly becomes a local media sensation. The discovery prompts Governor Mary Bailey to order a safety inspection of the plant, which turns up hundreds of violations and a massive repair bill that threatens to shut Mr. Burns down. Desperate to avoid regulation, Burns decides to run for governor himself so he can rewrite the rules in his own favor, recruiting a reluctant Homer to help his campaign. The election splits the Simpson household, with Marge and Lisa firmly backing Bailey while Homer, hoping for a promotion, campaigns for Burns. Burns's advisors work to soften his cold public image, staging a folksy television ad featuring an actor playing Charles Darwin to spin the mutant fish as a marvel of evolution rather than a warning sign. Combined with a smear campaign against Bailey, Burns pulls even in the polls heading into election night. His team arranges a dinner at the Simpsons' house to win over ordinary voters, but Marge unwittingly serves the very three-eyed fish, Blinky, as the main course. Forced to eat it in front of the cameras, Burns can't stomach the bite and spits it out, and by the time it hits the floor his campaign is finished. The fiasco nonetheless ends up reuniting the divided Simpson family. title: Dancin' Homer (S2E05)
text: "Dancin' Homer" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F05), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Ken Levine, David Isaacs, originally airing November 8, 1990. At Moe's Tavern, Homer recounts to his drinking buddies the wild story of what happened in Capital City. It began at a special family night at the ballpark, where Homer unexpectedly ended up drinking beer alongside Mr. Burns and Smithers, who were trying to foster better employee relations. Fueled by alcohol, Homer performed a spontaneous, goofy dance that rallied the struggling Springfield Isotopes to a comeback victory. Impressed, the team owner hired Homer as their official mascot, and the Isotopes began winning consistently thanks to his antics. His success soon attracted the attention of the major league Capital City Capitals, who offered him a job, prompting the Simpsons to sell their home and move to the big city. Once there, Homer's small-town charm and simple humor failed to impress the far more cynical big-city crowd, and he was quickly fired after a disastrous performance. Though his family tried to comfort him after the humiliating failure, Homer felt his efforts had been for nothing. Back home in Springfield, however, he realizes that his friends at Moe's don't care about his failure—only about the entertaining story he has to tell, giving him some comfort in the whole ordeal. Guest starring Tony Bennett, Tom Poston. Notable quotes: Capital City Goofball: Ah, Mancini. The mascot's best buddy.

title: Dead Putting Society (S2E06)
text: "Dead Putting Society" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F08), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing November 15, 1990. Homer's petty jealousy of Ned Flanders boils over during a visit to Ned's rumpus room, leading to a falling out between the two neighbors. Ned tries to make amends with an awkwardly worded apology note, but Homer brushes it off. Tension escalates when Homer and Bart run into Ned and Todd at a mini golf course and learn of an upcoming father-son miniature golf tournament. Homer, determined to see Flanders humiliated, goads Ned into a wager: whichever boy fails to win will force his father to mow the winning family's lawn while wearing his wife's Sunday dress. Homer clumsily coaches Bart with bizarre motivational tactics, while Lisa's calming influence proves far more effective. The tournament comes down to a nail-bitingly close final hole between Bart and Todd, ending in a tie neither boy is willing to break. Because of the bet's exact wording, both fathers technically lose, forcing Homer and Ned to mow each other's lawns in dresses—an outcome Homer finds mortifying, while Ned surprisingly enjoys it, adding to Homer's frustration. title: Bart vs. Thanksgiving (S2E07)
text: "Bart vs. Thanksgiving" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F07), directed by David Silverman and written by George Meyer, originally airing November 22, 1990. On Thanksgiving, Lisa proudly unveils a handmade centerpiece honoring notable women while Marge cooks and Homer watches football and the parade. A squabble between Bart and Lisa over table space leads to the centerpiece being knocked into the fire and destroyed, and Bart is sent to his room after refusing to apologize. Rather than accept the punishment, Bart sneaks out with Santa's Little Helper, first trying to steal food from the Burns Manor before wandering into Springfield's rougher neighborhoods. He donates blood plasma for cash and visits a soup kitchen, where a TV reporter interviews him live, and Bart smugly refuses to show remorse on air, embarrassing his family. Witnessing the genuine hardship of the homeless people there, Bart gives away his earned money and begins to feel guilty about his own comparatively fortunate life. Returning home, he hesitates outside, imagining a harsh reception, until Lisa comes out to talk with him on the roof. Through their conversation, Bart finally understands that he hurt Lisa's feelings, not just broke an object, and offers a sincere apology, which Lisa happily accepts. The family reunites for a very late Thanksgiving dinner, giving thanks for another chance to be together despite the day's chaos. Guest starring Carol Kane. title: Bart the Daredevil (S2E08)
text: "Bart the Daredevil" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F06), directed by Wes Archer and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing December 6, 1990. Homer and Bart attend a monster truck rally where Truckasaurus destroys the family car, and Bart becomes obsessed with the show's daredevil, Captain Lance Murdock, after watching him perform a dangerous stunt and get seriously injured. Inspired, Bart starts attempting his own stunts, hurting himself on a skateboard jump and landing in the hospital, where Dr. Hibbert tries unsuccessfully to scare him straight by showing him a ward full of injured kids. Undeterred, Bart escalates his stunts, successfully clearing a pool, animals, and even Homer lounging in a hammock. During a school field trip to Springfield Gorge, Bart declares he'll jump the gorge on his skateboard, prompting Lisa to take him to see Murdock in hopes the daredevil will talk him out of it—only for Murdock to enthusiastically encourage the plan. Lisa then tells the family, leading Homer to punish Bart and have a heartfelt talk with him, but Bart sneaks off to the gorge anyway. Homer arrives just in time to stop him, then furiously decides to make the jump himself to prove a point about reckless risk-taking, causing Bart to abandon his own daredevil ambitions out of fear for his father's safety. Homer ends up rolling down the ramp on the skateboard, flying off the edge, and plummeting into the gorge, and after a chaotic rescue involving a helicopter crash, he ends up hospitalized in the bed next to Murdock, quipping about the real dangers of parenting. title: Itchy & Scratchy & Marge (S2E09)
text: "Itchy & Scratchy & Marge" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F09), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing December 20, 1990. After watching a particularly violent Itchy & Scratchy cartoon, baby Maggie clobbers Homer with a mallet, prompting a horrified Marge to blame the show and ban Bart and Lisa from watching it. When her kids simply watch at friends' houses instead, Marge writes to studio head Roger Meyers, Jr., who dismisses her as a powerless 'screwball,' spurring her to organize a grassroots protest group called SNUH. The movement snowballs into a citywide picket that lands Marge on Kent Brockman's news show, and a flood of angry mail finally forces Meyers to sanitize the cartoon into a tame, violence-free version. The kids of Springfield, bored by the toothless new Itchy & Scratchy, abandon TV altogether for a montage of wholesome outdoor play, delighting Marge. Her crusade against onscreen content then extends to protesting a traveling exhibit of Michelangelo's David, but Dr. Marvin Monroe calls out her inconsistency in condemning cartoon violence while defending nude classical art. Forced to concede the hypocrisy, Marge drops her censorship campaign, Itchy & Scratchy reverts to its ultraviolent form, and the kids gladly return to watching it. The episode closes with Homer and Marge viewing the David statue together, Marge lamenting society's priorities until Homer cheers her up with news that school will make the kids see it anyway. text: "The Way We Was" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F12), directed by David Silverman and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, Sam Simon, originally airing January 31, 1991. When the family television breaks down, Marge and Homer tell Bart, Lisa, and Maggie the story of how they first met in high school back in 1974. Marge, a serious feminist student, ends up in detention after burning her bra at a rally, where she encounters slacker Homer and his friend Barney, who are serving time for smoking in the bathroom. Homer is immediately smitten and joins the debate team just to be near Marge, but she's drawn instead to the smug, more polished Artie Ziff. Desperate, Homer fakes being a French student so Marge will tutor him, and his ruse works long enough for her to agree to go to prom with him, but when the deception is revealed she furiously rejects him. Exhausted from the fallout, Marge bombs a debate the next day, and Artie seizes the moment to ask her to prom instead. Homer, oblivious to the rejection, shows up on prom night anyway and, undeterred even after learning Marge is going with Artie, attends the dance solo since he'd already paid for everything. After Artie and Marge are crowned prom king and queen, their night out afterward turns sour when Artie gets too handsy, prompting Marge to demand he take her home. Overhearing her parents praising Artie and disparaging Homer, and then spotting Homer walking home alone, Marge picks him up and admits she should have gone with him instead, leading to their first embrace as a couple, an ending that disgusts Bart but delights Lisa and Maggie back in the present. After suffering a mild heart attack, Grampa Simpson confesses to Homer that he has a half-brother he abandoned at an orphanage decades earlier. Herb is thrilled to finally have family and invites the Simpsons to live in his mansion, where Marge frets that the kids are being spoiled by his luxurious lifestyle. Hoping to save his failing car company from foreign competition, Herb enlists Homer, believing his "average" perspective can help design a car for ordinary Americans. Emboldened by Herb's pep talk, Homer becomes an overbearing tyrant with the design team, insisting on absurd features like bubble domes and horns that play "La Cucaracha." The resulting vehicle, dubbed "The Homer," is unveiled as a grotesque, wildly overpriced monstrosity that instantly bankrupts Herb's company. Ruined and humiliated, Herb disowns Homer and leaves for parts unknown, blaming his downfall on ever having found his Simpson relatives. Homer: Well, if you ask me, changing the subject makes you the most worthless, heartless excuse for a human being I ever--

title: Bart's Dog Gets an "F" (S2E16)
text: "Bart's Dog Gets an "F"" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F14), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing March 7, 1991. Santa's Little Helper has become an unruly nuisance around the Simpson household, and things come to a head when he destroys a treasured family quilt along with a pair of Homer's new expensive shoes and a cookie he'd just bought at the mall. Furious, Homer wants to get rid of the dog, but Lisa pleads for one more chance and convinces the family to enroll him in obedience school run by the strict Emily Winthrop. Meanwhile, Lisa is stuck at home sick with the mumps, and Marge tries to keep her occupied with sewing lessons while Bart resents having to bring her homework. At obedience school, Bart refuses to use a choke chain on his dog, causing Santa's Little Helper to fail miserably and fall behind the other dogs. The night before the final exam, Homer warns that failure means the dog will be given away, devastating Bart and Lisa. Believing it may be their last night together, Bart spends the evening bonding and playing with Santa's Little Helper, and this renewed connection helps the dog finally understand and respond to his commands. The next day, Santa's Little Helper passes his exam, earning his place back in the family, and Lisa celebrates by sewing a brand-new quilt to replace the one that was destroyed. Guest starring Tracey Ullman as Emily Winthrop. Notable quotes: Emily Winthrop: PULL THE BLOODY CHAIN, BOY! | Bart: I am sorry, boy. It is not your fault you are so dumb. | Lisa: This is our pet. We can question his integrity and disposition, but we can't question his heart. Are you trying to teach us that the way to solve a problem with something we love is to throw it away? | Homer: Are you losing your hearing, or are you just stupid? | Bart: Lisa, you wasted chicken pox. Don't waste the mumps!

title: Old Money (S2E17)
text: "Old Money" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F17), directed by David Silverman and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing March 28, 1991. Grampa Simpson's dull routine at the Springfield Retirement Castle changes when a pill mix-up introduces him to Beatrice 'Bea' Simmons, and the two quickly fall in love. When Homer insists on dragging Grampa along on a family outing to a safari park on Bea's birthday, the family's car gets stranded and surrounded by lions overnight, keeping Grampa away from Bea. He returns home just as an ambulance takes her body away, having died suddenly, and he furiously blames Homer for costing him her final moments. At Bea's funeral, a grieving and bitter Grampa refuses to forgive his son. Soon after, lawyer Lionel Hutz reveals that Bea was secretly wealthy and left her entire $106,000 fortune to Grampa, to be spent however makes him happy. Grampa splurges on odd purchases and outings, but nothing eases his grief until Bea's ghost visits him on a roller coaster and tells him to give the money to those who truly need it. Back home, Grampa announces he'll donate the remaining funds, drawing a media frenzy and a line of hopeful townspeople pleading their cases. On a whim he heads to a casino to try to multiply the money, but Homer rushes in and stops him from losing it all on a reckless bet, prompting Grampa to finally forgive his son. In the end, Grampa uses Bea's inheritance to renovate the Retirement Castle and names its dining room in her honor. Guest starring Audrey Meadows as Beatrice Simmons, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Abraham Simpson: Has it ever occurred to you that old folks deserve to be treated like human beings! Whether they have money or not? | Grampa: No, Jasper. They may say she died from a burst ventricle, but I know she died of a broken heart. | Lisa: I don't deserve it, Grampa. No one here does. The people who deserve it are on the streets, and they're in the slums. | Lionel Hutz: There is one catch. You must spend one night in...a haunted house! | Homer: Stop it, both of you! Grampa smells like a regular old man, which is more like a hallway in a hospital.

Homer: Stop it, both of you! Grampa smells like a regular old man, which is more like a hallway in a hospital.

title: Brush with Greatness (S2E18)
text: "Brush with Greatness" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F18), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Brian K. Roberts, originally airing April 11, 1991. After Bart and Lisa nag Homer into taking them to Mt. Splashmore, Homer gets humiliatingly stuck in a water slide and resolves to lose weight. While searching for his old exercise weights, Bart uncovers teenage paintings Marge made of Ringo Starr, revealing a forgotten artistic passion sparked by a schoolgirl crush. Encouraged by Lisa, Marge enrolls in a painting class at Springfield Community College, where a portrait of Homer impresses her instructor, Professor Lombardo, and wins the school art show. The publicity catches the attention of Mr. Burns, who has been unable to find an artist capable of portraying him flatteringly for the new museum wing bearing his name, so he hires Marge despite her reluctance. Sitting for the portrait, Burns proves cruel and insulting, mocking Homer's weight-loss progress until Marge finally throws him out of the house. Feeling she can't honestly paint him as handsome, Marge is reinvigorated when a long-delayed, kind letter from Ringo Starr finally arrives praising her old artwork. Inspired, she finishes the portrait and unveils it at the museum opening, showing Burns as a frail, naked old man rather than a glamorous figure. Though the crowd is initially shocked, Marge explains that the painting captures Burns' fragile humanity beneath his power, and even Burns comes to embrace the piece as a strange kind of tribute. Guest starring Ringo Starr as himself, Jon Lovitz as Professor Lombardo. Notable quotes: Homer: I'm a big fat pig! | Homer: Marge, nobody gains 30 pounds of bone! | Burns: You're the fattest thing I've ever seen, and I've been on safari! | Homer: If you need me I'll be in the refrigerator! | Mr. Burns: Beatles, eh? Yes, I seem to remember their off-key caterwauling on the old Sullivan Show. What was Ed thinking?
