title: Lisa's Substitute (S2E19)
text: "Lisa's Substitute" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F19), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing April 25, 1991. When Lisa's regular teacher Miss Hoover is sidelined by a supposed case of Lyme disease, the class gets a charismatic substitute, Mr. Bergstrom, whose unconventional style reignites Lisa's passion for learning and sparks an innocent crush. Meanwhile, Bart runs for class president against the studious Martin Prince, winning over his classmates with jokes during a debate. Lisa's admiration for Mr. Bergstrom deepens, but she's mortified when Homer embarrasses her in front of him at a museum, prompting the teacher to gently encourage Homer to be more attentive to his daughter. Just as Lisa gets permission to invite Mr. Bergstrom to dinner, she discovers Miss Hoover has returned and Bergstrom has already left for another teaching job. Lisa chases him down at the train station, and he leaves her with a comforting note reminding her of her own inner worth before departing. On election day, Bart's overconfident classmates fail to actually vote for him, handing the presidency to Martin by a mere two votes. Devastated and lashing out at Homer, Lisa calls him a baboon, but he later comforts her with a clumsy yet heartfelt attempt at connection, mending their relationship. Homer also cheers up a dejected Bart by pointing out the burdens of the presidency, ending the episode with Homer feeling proud of parenting all three of his children well. Guest starring Dustin Hoffman as Mr. Bergstrom. Notable quotes: Mr. Bergstrom: I'm Mr. Bergstrom. Feel free to make fun of my name if you want. Two suggestions are Mr. Nerdstrom and Mr. Boogerstrom. | Lisa: I'm glad I'm not crying, because I would hate for you to think that what I'm about to say is based on emotion, but you, sir, are a baboon! | Lisa: Where is Mr. Bergstrom?! | Miss Hoover: I do not know, but I would sure like to have words with him! | Lisa: When I fall asleep, Mr. Bergstrom is the last thing I think of and he's my first thought when I wake up.

Lisa: Where is Mr. Bergstrom?!
Miss Hoover: I do not know, but I would sure like to have words with him!
Lisa: When I fall asleep, Mr. Bergstrom is the last thing I think of and he's my first thought when I wake up.

title: The War of the Simpsons (S2E20)
text: "The War of the Simpsons" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F20), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing May 2, 1991. Homer embarrasses himself with drunken antics at a dinner party he and Marge host, prompting a furious Marge to sign them up for a weekend marriage retreat at Catfish Lake. With no babysitter willing to handle Bart, Marge reluctantly leaves Grampa in charge for the weekend. At the retreat, Homer becomes distracted by tales of a legendary giant catfish named General Sherman and sneaks his fishing gear along despite Marge's warnings. Back home, Bart and Lisa manipulate Grampa with a fake list of rules, indulging in junk food, video games, and eventually throwing a wild party that trashes the house. At the retreat, Marge's litany of complaints about Homer takes hours, and later Homer secretly slips away to fish, getting pulled into a boat by the fabled catfish. Realizing his priorities are hurting his marriage, Homer ultimately releases the fish to prove his devotion to Marge, and the couple reconciles. Meanwhile, guilt-ridden Bart and Lisa scramble to clean the house, unaware that Grampa was secretly playing them the whole time by faking tears to gain their obedience. Notable quotes: Reverend Lovejoy: Marge, as a trained marriage counselor, this is the first instance where I've ever told one partner that they were 100% right. It's all his fault. I'm willing to put that on a certificate you can frame. | Grampa: I can turn it on like a faucet! | Barney: Oh, ow, hey, [burp] [cough] Is that a new kind of Mace? It's really painful! | McBain: Bye, book. | Bait Shop Clerk: Yep, 'General Sherman'. They say he's five hundred pounds of bottom-dwelling fury, don't you know.

Grampa: I can turn it on like a faucet!
Barney: Oh, ow, hey, [burp] [cough] Is that a new kind of Mace? It's really painful!
McBain: Bye, book.

title: Three Men and a Comic Book (S2E21)
keys: three men and a comic book
text: "Three Men and a Comic Book" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F21), directed by Wes M. Archer and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing May 9, 1991. At a comic book convention, Bart becomes fixated on buying a rare first issue of Radioactive Man after Comic Book Guy tells him it costs $100. Desperate for cash, Bart empties his piggy bank, cashes in bottles and foreign coins, and even tries selling lemonade and beer, but Homer shuts down his beer stand before he can make real money. Marge arranges for Bart to earn cash doing chores for the cranky elderly Mrs. Glick, who makes him do painful yard work and then pays him a measly fifty cents. Frustrated but determined, Bart returns to the comic shop and discovers Martin and Milhouse are also after the same issue, so the three pool their money to buy it together. Unable to agree on who gets to keep the comic, they retreat to Bart's treehouse for an uneasy joint sleepover, with tensions rising as Martin tries to broker a fair-sharing plan. A storm hits during the night, and as Bart and Milhouse scuffle, Milhouse ends up dangling from the treehouse while the precious comic blows away. Bart chooses to save his friend instead of the comic, and the group wakes up to find the issue destroyed, its last surviving page landing in a bird's nest. Guest starring Cloris Leachman as Mrs. Glick, Daniel Stern as the narrator. Notable quotes: Bart Simpson: Wow, Radioactive Man #1! I bet it's worth a million bucks! | Marge: Homer, it is seriously starting to pour. Will you please check on the boys? | Homer: They are fine. | Comic Book Guy: Looks like you got more than you bargained for.
quotes: Bart Simpson: Wow, Radioactive Man #1! I bet it's worth a million bucks!
Marge: Homer, it is seriously starting to pour. Will you please check on the boys?
Homer: They are fine.
Comic Book Guy: Looks like you got more than you bargained for.

title: Blood Feud (S2E22)
text: "Blood Feud" is an episode of Season 2 (production code 7F22), directed by David Silverman and written by George Meyer, originally airing July 11, 1991. Mr. Burns falls gravely ill with a rare blood disorder that leaves him near death, and Smithers scrambles to find a matching double-O-negative donor among the plant's employees. Homer eagerly volunteers hoping for a huge reward, but it's Bart who turns out to have the right blood type, and Homer pressures him into donating despite his reluctance. The transfusion saves Burns, who becomes so revitalized he decides to write his memoirs, but he thanks the Simpsons with nothing more than a simple card. Furious at the stinginess, Homer drafts a scathing insulting letter to Burns, which Marge convinces him not to send. When Homer later tries to destroy the letter, he discovers Bart has already mailed it, sending Homer into a panic to intercept it before Burns reads it. Burns gets the letter anyway and, enraged, orders Homer fired and even instructs Smithers to have him beaten up. Smithers refuses, reminding Burns that Homer's son saved his life, prompting Burns to reconsider and instead gift the family an outlandishly expensive Olmec head statue. Homer remains unsatisfied with the bizarre gift, and the family ends up debating whether the whole ordeal had any real lesson to it. Notable quotes: Homer: Joke's on them. If the core exploded, there would not even be the power to light that sign! | Homer: Hello, my name is Mr. Burns. I believe you have a letter for me. | Homer: Great plan, Bart. | Marge: Whatever it does, it's doing it now. | Moe: Listen, you little puke! One of these days I'm going to catch you, and I'm going to carve my name on your back with an ice pick!

Homer: Hello, my name is Mr. Burns. I believe you have a letter for me.
Homer: Great plan, Bart.
Marge: Whatever it does, it's doing it now.
Moe: Listen, you little puke! One of these days I'm going to catch you, and I'm going to carve my name on your back with an ice pick!

title: Stark Raving Dad (S3E01)
text: "Stark Raving Dad" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 7F24), directed by Rich Moore and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, originally airing September 19, 1991. Homer's white shirt turns pink in the wash, and his outlandish appearance at the power plant convinces Mr. Burns he's some kind of unstable free-thinker, leading Homer to be sent for psychological evaluation. After Bart carelessly fills out Homer's take-home personality test, Homer is judged insane and committed to the New Bedlam Rest Home. There he befriends a large, bald white patient named Leon Kompowsky, who insists he is actually Michael Jackson. While Marge works to free Homer by proving Bart really exists, Bart spreads word around Springfield that Michael Jackson is coming to town, causing a huge crowd to gather at their house. Amid the excitement over Homer's release and Leon's arrival, everyone forgets about Lisa's birthday, and Bart's failure to get her a gift leaves her devastated. Leon, still believing he's Michael Jackson, convinces Bart to make amends by co-writing a heartfelt birthday song for Lisa. After performing the song for her and mending their sibling rift, Leon reveals his true identity as a bricklayer from New Jersey who found happiness by pretending to be Michael Jackson, then wanders off singing contentedly in his own voice. Guest starring Michael Jackson as Leon Kompowsky. Notable quotes: Burns: Why is that man in pink? | Lenny: Hey Homer, we saved this doughnut for you with pink frosting on it! | Security guard: Drop that doughnut now, Pinkie! | Homer: This isn't fair! How can you tell who's sane and who's insane? | Bart: Joe's Crematorium. You kill 'em, we grill 'em.

Lenny: Hey Homer, we saved this doughnut for you with pink frosting on it!
Security guard: Drop that doughnut now, Pinkie!
Homer: This isn't fair! How can you tell who's sane and who's insane?
Bart: Joe's Crematorium. You kill 'em, we grill 'em.

title: Mr. Lisa Goes to Washington (S3E02)
text: "Mr. Lisa Goes to Washington" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F01), directed by Wes Archer and written by George Meyer, originally airing September 26, 1991. After Homer becomes obsessed with a free copy of Reading Digest magazine, Lisa discovers an essay contest inside it that offers a trip to Washington, D.C. for the best patriotic essay written by a child. Inspired by a bald eagle she spots in Springfield National Forest, Lisa writes a moving essay and wins the regional competition, earning the family an all-expenses-paid trip to the capital. While touring Washington, the Simpsons meet Congressman Bob Arnold, Springfield's representative, and Lisa is initially charmed by him. However, she later secretly witnesses Arnold accepting a bribe from a timber lobbyist to allow the destruction of Springfield's forest, shattering her faith in the political system. Devastated, Lisa scraps her original essay and instead writes a scathing new one exposing government corruption, which she reads at the national finals. Her words reach a senator, prompting an FBI sting that leads to Arnold's arrest and expulsion from Congress. Though Lisa doesn't win the contest, seeing justice served restores her faith in democracy, and she inadvertently teaches Bart to stand up for his beliefs when he disrupts an annoying pianist's performance. Notable quotes: Congressman Arnold: Look Jerry, you are a hell of a lobbyist and you make a spectacular case for clear-cutting forests, but this is not like burying toxic waste. People are going to notice those trees are gone. | Mr. Burns: Simpson, eh? How very strange. His job description clearly specifies an illiterate! | FBI Agent: FBI! Bob Arnold, you are under arrest for graft! | President Bush the Elder: Oh yes sir! All 250 million of them! | Bart: Lis, you taught me to stand up for what I believe in.
quotes: Congressman Arnold: Look Jerry, you are a hell of a lobbyist and you make a spectacular case for clear-cutting forests, but this is not like burying toxic waste. People are going to notice those trees are gone.
Mr. Burns: Simpson, eh? How very strange. His job description clearly specifies an illiterate!
FBI Agent: FBI! Bob Arnold, you are under arrest for graft!
President Bush the Elder: Oh yes sir! All 250 million of them!
Bart: Lis, you taught me to stand up for what I believe in.

title: When Flanders Failed (S3E03)
text: "When Flanders Failed" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 7F23), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing October 3, 1991. At a backyard barbecue, Ned Flanders announces he's quitting his job to open the Leftorium, a store catering to left-handed customers, and Homer immediately begins hoping his neighbor's new venture will fail. Meanwhile, after Marge urges Bart to get more exercise, he signs up for karate lessons but quickly loses interest when he discovers it involves studying philosophy books rather than flashy fighting moves, so he starts skipping class to play arcade games instead. As Ned's business struggles, Homer does nothing to help, even ignoring left-handed customers who could use the store, and eventually buys up Ned's possessions cheaply at a garage sale after the Leftorium collapses. Bart's deception is exposed on the playground when bullies steal Lisa's saxophone and he proves unable to defend her, resulting in his humiliating suspension from a basketball hoop. Homer's guilt deepens when he discovers the Flanders family has been reduced to living in their car after losing their home. Moved by Ned's forgiveness and friendship despite everything, Homer resolves to make amends by personally calling in favors to drum up business for the Leftorium, helping Ned get back on his feet. Notable quotes: Ned: Homer, I'm ruined. | Homer: No, I was a swine! | Ned: You tried to warn me about gambling my family's future on some pig in a poke! I didn't listen! Homer, you were a true friend! | Bart: Excuse me. I already know how not to hit a man. Can I practice with nunchucks? | Marge: Bart, don't use the Touch of Death on your sister!

Homer: No, I was a swine!

title: Bart the Murderer (S3E04)
text: "Bart the Murderer" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F03), directed by Rich Moore and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing October 10, 1991. After a disastrous day at school that leaves him missing a coveted field trip, Bart stumbles into a mob hangout called the Legitimate Businessman's Social Club while riding his skateboard home. Impressing mafia don Fat Tony by picking a winning racehorse and mixing drinks better than the wiseguys can, Bart is hired as the club's personal bartender. He begins accepting expensive gifts and even unknowingly stashes a truckload of stolen cigarettes in his bedroom, all while keeping his new job secret from his family. When Marge grows suspicious, Homer confronts Fat Tony but is quickly won over by a rigged poker game and approves of Bart's employment. Bart's newfound confidence backfires at school when he tries to bribe Principal Skinner, leading to detention that causes him to miss an important gathering where Fat Tony wanted to showcase his skills. After Bart explains his absence was Skinner's fault, Fat Tony ominously decides to pay Skinner a visit, and soon after, Skinner vanishes without a trace. Racked with guilt and nightmares, Bart is horrified when the police raid Fat Tony's club and arrest everyone for Skinner's apparent murder, putting Bart on trial as the alleged head of the crime syndicate. Just as the case looks hopeless, Skinner bursts into the courtroom, revealing he had merely been trapped under a pile of newspapers in his garage, clearing Bart and ending his brief criminal career. Guest starring Joe Mantegna, Phil Hartman, Neil Patrick Harris. Notable quotes: Homer Simpson: A job's a job. I mean, take me. If my plant pollutes the water and poisons the town, by your logic, that would make me a criminal. | Chief Wiggum: Fat Tony is a cancer upon Springfield! And I am the, uh, whatever cures cancer. | (Fat) Tony: Bart, um, is it wrong to steal a loaf of bread to feed your starving family? | Bart: Uh, say, are you guys crooks? | Reverend Lovejoy: There, there. There, there.

Chief Wiggum: Fat Tony is a cancer upon Springfield! And I am the, uh, whatever cures cancer.

Reverend Lovejoy: There, there. There, there.

title: Homer Defined (S3E05)
text: "Homer Defined" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F04), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Howard Gewirtz, originally airing October 17, 1991. After a jelly donut splatters onto a warning gauge, the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant nears meltdown, and Homer, who never listened during his training and instead played with a Rubik's Cube, is the only one who can stop it. Relying on a childish eeny-meeny-miny-moe method, he blindly presses a button and miraculously averts disaster, instantly becoming Springfield's hero. Burns showers him with awards, a ham, and a call from Magic Johnson, and even Lisa starts admiring him, but Homer privately knows his success was pure luck. Meanwhile, Bart is devastated to learn Milhouse's mother has forbidden their friendship because she considers Bart a bad influence, leaving Bart to reluctantly bond with baby Maggie. Marge intervenes, visiting Luann Van Houten and convincing her to let the boys reunite once she sees how miserable they both are apart. Burns then pressures Homer into giving a motivational speech to workers at a rival plant in Shelbyville, where another meltdown crisis conveniently arises. Homer repeats his lucky button-pressing trick and saves that plant too, but this time the town mocks him as a foolish simpleton rather than praising him as a hero, and the phrase 'to pull a Homer' enters common usage—and even the dictionary—to describe succeeding through sheer idiocy. The episode closes with Lisa offering Homer a strange comfort, telling him he now 'belongs to the ages.' Guest starring Chick Hearn as himself, Magic Johnson as himself, Jon Lovitz as Aristotle Amadopolis. Notable quotes: Homer: D'oh! This is all your fault! | Mr. Burns: [sarcastically] Thank you, President Ford... | Bart: Bad influence my butt! How many times have I told you: never listen to your mother! | Milhouse: Bart, my mom won't let me be your friend anymore. That's why you couldn't come to the party. | Marge: If you spare this town from becoming a smoking hole in the ground, I'll try to be a better Christian.

title: Like Father, Like Clown (S3E06)
text: "Like Father, Like Clown" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F05), directed by Jeffrey Lynch, Brad Bird and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing October 24, 1991. Krusty the Clown finally accepts an overdue dinner invitation from the Simpsons after Bart nearly quits his fan club in frustration over repeated cancellations. During the meal, Krusty reveals he was born Herschel Krustofsky, the son of a strict rabbi who disowned him after catching him performing as a clown instead of following in the family's religious footsteps. Sharing the story leaves Krusty visibly shaken, and he lingers at the Simpsons' house late into the night poring over old photographs. Afterward, he tries to call his estranged father but loses his nerve each time, and his depression begins bleeding into his television show, alarming his young fans. Bart and Lisa take it upon themselves to track down Rabbi Krustofsky, eventually finding him hosting a religious radio program. The rabbi remains bitter and unwilling to forgive his son, so the kids call into his show and cleverly invoke a quote from Sammy Davis, Jr. to challenge his stance on forgiveness. Moved by their argument, Hyman relents, and the episode ends with father and son emotionally reconciling on the set of Krusty's show, with Bart and Lisa looking on proudly. Guest starring Jackie Mason as Rabbi Krustofsky. Notable quotes: Lisa Simpson: Poor Krusty. He's like a black velvet painting come to life. | Rabbi Krustofsky: A rabbi would never exaggerate. A rabbi composes. He creates thoughts. He tells stories that may never have happened. But he does not exaggerate. | Homer: He's talking funny-talk! | Lisa: No Dad, that's Hebrew! Krusty must be Jewish. | Moe: I've got something in my eye.

Rabbi Krustofsky: A rabbi would never exaggerate. A rabbi composes. He creates thoughts. He tells stories that may never have happened. But he does not exaggerate.

title: Treehouse of Horror II (S3E07)
text: "Treehouse of Horror II" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F02), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, Jeff Martin, George Meyer, Sam Simon, John Swartzwelder, originally airing October 31, 1991. After overindulging in Halloween candy, Homer, Bart, and Lisa each fall into unsettling dreams. In Lisa's nightmare, Homer brings home a cursed monkey's paw from Morocco that grants wishes at a steep price, leading to fame that turns into public scorn, a wish for world peace that leaves Earth defenseless against alien conquerors Kang and Kodos, and a seemingly safe wish for a turkey sandwich that infuriates Homer over a trivial flaw. In Bart's nightmare, he gains god-like mental powers that let him control and punish anyone in town who displeases him, including transforming Homer into a jack-in-the-box, until a family therapist's advice leads Homer and Bart to bond during a series of father-son outings that soften Bart's cruelty. In Homer's nightmare, he loses his job and becomes a cemetery worker, only to be mistaken for dead by Mr. Burns and Smithers, who remove his brain for a robotic worker experiment; when the experiment fails, Burns is crushed and his head is grafted onto Homer's body. The episode closes with Homer waking to find himself literally stuck with Burns' head, dreading a schedule conflict between a school spaghetti dinner and a royal reception for Queen Beatrix. Notable quotes: Kodos: They constructed a board with a nail in it, but they won't stop there. They'll construct bigger boards with bigger nails, and then they'll construct a board with a nail in it so large, it will destroy them all... | Mr. Burns: Have trouble breathing... organs leaking vital fluids... Smithers... I'm going to die. | Homer: Well, time to shake the dew off the lily. | Mr. Burns: Oh, that's right. It's all a dream... Or is it? | Homer: Oh, I hate having two heads. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 2): "Lisa's nightmare", "Bart's nightmare", and "Homer's nightmare".

Homer: Oh, I hate having two heads.

title: Lisa's Pony (S3E08)
text: "Lisa's Pony" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F06), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, originally airing November 7, 1991. Lisa desperately needs a new saxophone reed for that evening's school talent show, and after striking out with everyone else, she calls Homer at work to get one. Homer stops at Moe's for a quick beer beforehand and, after some delay convincing the shop owner to reopen, finally buys the reed—only to arrive too late, forcing Lisa to embarrass herself performing without it. Wracked with guilt, Homer tries various small gestures to win back Lisa's affection, but nothing works until he impulsively buys her a pony named Princess, instantly restoring her love for him while infuriating Marge over the expense. To cover the pony's costs, Homer takes a grueling second job at the Kwik-E-Mart working for Apu, leaving him perpetually exhausted and barely functional at either job. As the family's finances and Homer's health deteriorate, Marge finally tells the kids the truth about why their father is working himself to exhaustion. Touched by this sacrifice, Lisa makes the painful choice to give up Princess so Homer can quit the convenience store job, telling him that he is the "big dumb animal" she loves even more than her pony. Notable quotes: Homer: First you didn't want me to get the pony. Now you want me to take it back. Make up your mind! | Apu: He slept, he stole, he was rude to the customers. Still, there goes the best damned employee a convenience store ever had. | Homer: I work from midnight to eight, come home, sleep for five minutes, eat breakfast, sleep six more minutes, shower, then I have ten minutes to bask in Lisa's love, then I'm off to the power plant, fresh as a daisy. | Homer: Marge, with today's gasoline prices, we can't afford not to buy a pony. | Groundskeeper Willie: Sounds like the gopher I caught in me lawnmower.
quotes: Homer: First you didn't want me to get the pony. Now you want me to take it back. Make up your mind!
Apu: He slept, he stole, he was rude to the customers. Still, there goes the best damned employee a convenience store ever had.

Homer: I work from midnight to eight, come home, sleep for five minutes, eat breakfast, sleep six more minutes, shower, then I have ten minutes to bask in Lisa's love, then I'm off to the power plant, fresh as a daisy.
Homer: Marge, with today's gasoline prices, we can't afford not to buy a pony.
Groundskeeper Willie: Sounds like the gopher I caught in me lawnmower.

title: Saturdays of Thunder (S3E09)
text: "Saturdays of Thunder" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F07), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Ken Levine, David Isaacs, originally airing November 14, 1991. When Springfield's Soap Box Derby is announced, Bart is determined to win first prize, but the rules require him to build his own racer. Homer, having just discovered from a fatherhood quiz that he barely knows his own son, decides to bond with Bart by helping him construct the car. The resulting vehicle, Li'l Lightnin', is a rickety mess, especially compared to the sleek, scientifically engineered Honor Roller built by Martin Prince, who allies with Bart against the sinister bully Nelson Muntz and his fearsome Roadkill 2000. During the race, Bart struggles to get any speed out of Homer's creation while Martin loses control of his overpowered racer and crashes, leaving him unable to compete. Martin offers his newly repaired racer to Bart for the final heat, and Bart reluctantly accepts, devastating Homer, who initially responds by selfishly withdrawing his support. Left alone, Homer reflects on his failures as a father, finally passes the fatherhood test, and rushes to the track to encourage Bart before the big race. Despite Nelson's dirty tactics, Bart wins the race using Martin's car, and father and son reconcile, with Bart even meeting his diminutive childhood hero, three-time champion Ronnie Beck. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Bart: Dad, I don't know how to say this. I don't want to drive your car. It's slow, it's ugly, it handles like a shopping cart. | Nelson: Whoa, talk about your pieces of crap! | Homer: Thank you, Bill Cosby. You've saved The Simpsons! | Homer: Goodbye son! | Homer: Well, he's always chewing on the phone cord.

Nelson: Whoa, talk about your pieces of crap!

title: Flaming Moe's (S3E10)
text: "Flaming Moe's" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F08), directed by Rich Moore, Alan Smart and written by Robert Cohen, originally airing November 21, 1991. While Lisa hosts a sleepover that leaves Bart feeling like the butt of every joke, Homer heads to Moe's Tavern only to find the bar nearly empty and Moe desperate for customers. Homer recounts how he stumbled onto a strange new drink at home after mixing dregs of liquor with cough syrup and accidentally setting it ablaze with a dropped cigarette ash. Moe seizes on the recipe, renames it the Flaming Moe, and passes it off as his own creation, quickly transforming his failing bar into Springfield's trendiest hangout frequented by celebrities like Aerosmith. Betrayed and furious, Homer swears off the tavern and grows increasingly bitter watching Moe profit from his invention. Meanwhile, a representative from a rival chain, Tipsy McStaggers, tries repeatedly to buy the secret recipe from Moe, eventually offering a million dollars despite not being able to identify the final ingredient. Moe's new waitress learns the truth about the stolen recipe and urges him to cut Homer in on the profits, and Moe is on the verge of agreeing when a desperate Homer bursts in and publicly reveals that the secret ingredient is just cough syrup. The exposed secret ruins the drink's mystique, the corporate deal collapses, and copycat versions pop up all over town, tanking Moe's business. In the end, Moe and Homer reconcile, with Moe serving Homer a free 'Flaming Homer' as a peace offering. Guest starring Aerosmith (Tom Hamilton, Joey Kramer, Joe Perry, Steven Tyler, and Brad Whitford) as themselves, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Moe: I like your moxie kid! You're hired. | Mayor Quimby: Henceforth, this date shall forever be known as Flaming Moe's Day! | Homer: Oh, look at me! I'm making people happy! I'm the magical man from Happyland in a gumdrop house on Lollipop Lane! | Moe: The Flaming Moe is not for sale. Do you know how much of my blood and sweat are in this drink? | Hugh: All right, better luck next time.

Mayor Quimby: Henceforth, this date shall forever be known as Flaming Moe's Day!
Homer: Oh, look at me! I'm making people happy! I'm the magical man from Happyland in a gumdrop house on Lollipop Lane!
Moe: The Flaming Moe is not for sale. Do you know how much of my blood and sweat are in this drink?
Hugh: All right, better luck next time.

title: Burns Verkaufen der Kraftwerk (S3E11)
text: "Burns Verkaufen der Kraftwerk" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F09), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing December 5, 1991. Homer discovers he owns stock in the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant and hastily sells his shares to a shady broker for a paltry $25, only to learn the stock's value skyrocketed later that day, costing him thousands in potential profit. The reason for the surge is that a despondent Mr. Burns, bored with running the plant, decides to sell it to two eager German businessmen, Hans and Fritz, for $100 million. The new owners conduct an intense evaluation of the staff, and when Homer proves unable to answer basic questions about his job—drifting instead into a daydream about a fantastical 'Land of Chocolate'—he is promptly fired. Depressed and idle, Homer wallows at home while Burns, now retired, finds that without his plant he has lost the respect and fear he once commanded. When Burns visits Moe's Tavern, Homer and the other patrons mock him openly, wounding his pride. Meanwhile, the German owners discover the plant requires another $100 million in safety upgrades, making them desperate to unload it. Sensing an opportunity, Burns buys the plant back for only $50 million, restoring his power and status. He vows quiet revenge against Homer for the humiliation at the bar, promising it will come when Homer least expects it. In the end, Homer is rehired and joyfully tells his family the news, oblivious to Burns's lingering grudge. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure, Horst, and the stock broker. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: These two gentlemen are American as apple pie! Hans and Fritz, why that's just... John and Frank! | Horst: First, we need to deal with substance abuse. Are there any alcoholics here? | Homer: Doh! Lucky drunks! | Homer: Sock it to him, Horst! | Burns: Simpson, eh? As for him, many years will pass, where he will remain unaware the Sword of Damocles is dangling over him. And when he least expects it...
quotes: Mr. Burns: These two gentlemen are American as apple pie! Hans and Fritz, why that's just... John and Frank!
Horst: First, we need to deal with substance abuse. Are there any alcoholics here?
Homer: Doh! Lucky drunks!
Homer: Sock it to him, Horst!

title: I Married Marge (S3E12)
text: "I Married Marge" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F10), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing December 26, 1991. When Marge fears she might be pregnant again, Homer distracts the kids by recounting the story of how he and Marge got married and had Bart. He recalls working at a mini-golf course in 1980, where a romantic date after seeing The Empire Strikes Back leads to Marge getting pregnant. Homer proposes, they marry quickly at a roadside chapel, and move in temporarily with Marge's disapproving mother and sisters. Struggling to support his new family, Homer loses his job prospects and their belongings get repossessed, prompting him to abandon Marge in shame and take a low-paying job at a taco stand. Selma tells Marge the truth despite Patty's wishes, and Marge tracks Homer down, forgiving him and urging him to come home. Determined to prove himself, Homer boldly demands a job from Mr. Burns at the power plant and is hired on the spot, allowing him to reclaim the pawned wedding ring and baby supplies. Rushing to the hospital as Marge goes into labor, Homer stands up to Patty's insults and is present for Bart's birth, immediately experiencing his son's mischievous nature firsthand. Back in the present, Marge returns with the good news that she isn't pregnant, and the couple celebrates with a joyful high-five. Notable quotes: Lisa Simpson: It's not our fault our generation has short attention spans, Dad. We watch an appalling amount of TV. | Homer: Someday I will buy you a real castle. | Homer: It is the Champale talking! | Homer: This castle is impregnable. | Smithers: We have two openings, which means one of you will be rejected from this job...but it ain't gonna be my old frat buddy Lou Johnston!
quotes: Lisa Simpson: It's not our fault our generation has short attention spans, Dad. We watch an appalling amount of TV.
Homer: Someday I will buy you a real castle.
Homer: It is the Champale talking!
Homer: This castle is impregnable.
Smithers: We have two openings, which means one of you will be rejected from this job...but it ain't gonna be my old frat buddy Lou Johnston!

title: Radio Bart (S3E13)
text: "Radio Bart" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F11), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing January 9, 1992. For Bart's tenth birthday, Homer buys him a radio microphone that can transmit voice broadcasts, though Bart initially finds it unimpressive compared to his new label-maker. After testing the device on unsuspecting family members, Bart uses it to terrify Rod and Todd Flanders by posing as God, then escalates his pranking by lowering the microphone into an abandoned well and pretending to be a trapped orphan named Timmy O'Toole. Groundskeeper Willie falls for the hoax and alerts the town, sparking a massive rescue effort complete with news coverage, a charity carnival, and a benefit song performed by Krusty and Sting. The ruse unravels when Santa's Little Helper's growls over the radio convince everyone Timmy has gone feral, and Lisa realizes what Bart has done. When Bart sneaks back to retrieve the incriminating, labeled radio, police officers accidentally send him tumbling into the well himself, trapping his foot exactly as he'd fabricated. Once the town learns of his deception, public sympathy evaporates and Mayor Quimby refuses to authorize a rescue, leaving Bart stranded. Ultimately, Homer organizes a grassroots digging effort with fellow townspeople, including Sting, and after days of tunneling they finally free Bart, with Homer vowing the well will never endanger anyone else. In the final scene, Willie merely posts a warning sign by the well rather than sealing it properly. Guest starring Sting as himself. Notable quotes: Bart: People of Earth, this is Bartron, commander of the Martian invasion force. Your planet is in our hands. Resistance is useless. We have captured your President. He was delicious! | Bart: Whaddya mean, 'How did I get on the radio?' I created the universe! Stupid kid. | Willie: Outta my way! Look out, ya horse's ass! | Homer: It's not our fault! We didn't want the boy, he was an accident! | Eddie: Hey, I've got an idea for a prank. Let's go home and go to sleep.

Bart: Whaddya mean, 'How did I get on the radio?' I created the universe! Stupid kid.
Willie: Outta my way! Look out, ya horse's ass!

Eddie: Hey, I've got an idea for a prank. Let's go home and go to sleep.

title: Lisa the Greek (S3E14)
text: "Lisa the Greek" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F12), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing January 23, 1992. Homer settles in for a Sunday of football, dismissing Lisa's attempts to share her Malibu Stacy diorama with him, and loses money betting on a lopsided game. After Marge urges Lisa to bond with her father over his interests, Lisa joins Homer for the next game and casually picks the winning team, prompting Homer to start using her uncanny predictions to place bets with Moe. As Lisa's picks keep paying off, Homer declares Sundays 'Daddy-Daughter Day,' showers the family with gifts from his winnings, and lets Marge believe the bonding is genuine, even as he secretly plans to ditch Lisa for a bowling outing with Barney right after the Super Bowl. When Lisa learns the truth—that Homer only wanted her for her predictions—she is devastated, calls Marge's attention to his selfishness, and gives away the toys he bought her. Guilt-ridden, Homer tries to reconcile, but Lisa only leaves him a cryptic, emotionally loaded prediction for the Super Bowl: Washington winning means she still loves him, Buffalo winning means she doesn't. Homer watches the game anxiously at Moe's, and after Washington rallies late to win, he's overjoyed to learn Lisa still cares for him. In the end, Homer cancels his bowling plans and takes Lisa on the promised hike up Mount Springfield, repairing their relationship. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Smooth Jimmy Apollo and Larry. Notable quotes: Homer: D'OH! Why did you not say that before? | Lisa: What could be better than the savage ballet that is professional football? | Lisa: So gambling makes a good thing even better. | Homer: Yes, it is like there is some kind of bond between us. | Chief Wiggum: Oh, sure thing, Moe. I was just using it as a coaster.
quotes: Homer: D'OH! Why did you not say that before?
Lisa: What could be better than the savage ballet that is professional football?
Lisa: So gambling makes a good thing even better.
Homer: Yes, it is like there is some kind of bond between us.
Chief Wiggum: Oh, sure thing, Moe. I was just using it as a coaster.

title: Homer Alone (S3E15)
text: "Homer Alone" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F14), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by David M. Stern, originally airing February 6, 1992. Marge has been quietly worn down by her family's constant demands, and her frustration boils over when she halts traffic on the Springfield Memorial Bridge in a stress-induced daze. After being briefly arrested and then pardoned by Mayor Quimby, she sees an ad for the resort Rancho Relaxo and decides she desperately needs a getaway. She drops Bart and Lisa off with Patty and Selma, who subject them to bland food, cramped sleeping arrangements, and unwanted foot-rubbing duties, while Maggie refuses to be left behind and stays home with Homer. Homer struggles comically with basic baby care, from stapling Maggie's diaper to accidentally terrifying her with a puppet show that Santa's Little Helper turns into chaos. When Maggie mysteriously vanishes from the house overnight, Homer and Barney search frantically for her, eventually looping in the police as panic sets in. Meanwhile, Marge, refreshed from her vacation, decides to return home, and Homer nearly confesses the disaster before Chief Wiggum arrives with Maggie, found safely asleep near a giant ice-cream cone statue resembling Marge. Relieved, Homer secures Maggie for the ride and retrieves an eager Bart and Lisa from their aunts' house. The family reunites, with Marge and Homer agreeing to appreciate each other more, ending the episode on a note of restored (if imperfect) domestic harmony. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Marge: I need to unwind. | Lisa: You think you know fear? I've seen them naked! | Chief Wiggum: Well, I'm fresh out of ideas. | Patty: Probably will trade her for a beer and a Playboy. | Homer: D'oh!
quotes: Marge: I need to unwind.
Lisa: You think you know fear? I've seen them naked!
Chief Wiggum: Well, I'm fresh out of ideas.
Patty: Probably will trade her for a beer and a Playboy.
Homer: D'oh!

title: Bart the Lover (S3E16)
text: "Bart the Lover" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F16), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing February 13, 1992. Bored and lonely, Edna Krabappel places a personal ad in the newspaper begging to be saved from her solitude. Bart, serving detention for a yo-yo-related fish killing, spots the ad and decides to prank her by inventing a suave pen pal named 'Woodrow.' Using stolen lines from Homer's old love letters to Marge and dialogue lifted from romance movies, Bart carries on an increasingly passionate correspondence with his unsuspecting teacher, even sending her a photo of hockey player Gordie Howe as 'Woodrow.' When Edna asks to meet in person, Bart sets up a date at The Gilded Truffle but never intends to show up, instead going to see a movie. Watching Edna wait alone and then cry when Woodrow never appears fills Bart with genuine guilt, and he confesses everything to his family. With Lisa's help, he crafts a kind farewell letter that lets Edna down gently, leaving her sad but at peace with the imaginary romance's end. Meanwhile, Homer tries to curb his constant swearing after Ned Flanders complains that Todd is picking up bad language from him, agreeing to a deal where Ned will shave his mustache if Homer cleans up his mouth. Marge introduces a swear jar to help Homer's efforts, and though he struggles—especially while building a doghouse he ultimately destroys in frustration—the money collected ends up funding a surprise replacement doghouse from Marge and Lisa. Guest starring Marcia Wallace. Notable quotes: Bart: Gross, he's picking his nose! | Edna Krabappel: At least until tomorrow. | Todd: Hell, no. | Woodrow: Truly, yours is a butt that won't quit. | Homer: "Damn crappy nails! Superglue my butt!"

Edna Krabappel: At least until tomorrow.
Todd: Hell, no.
Woodrow: Truly, yours is a butt that won't quit.
Homer: "Damn crappy nails! Superglue my butt!"

title: Homer at the Bat (S3E17)
text: "Homer at the Bat" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F13), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 20, 1992. The Springfield Nuclear Power Plant softball team, led by Homer's clutch hitting with his homemade Wonder Bat, has gone undefeated all season and is set to face Shelbyville in the championship. Mr. Burns wagers a million dollars with Shelbyville's owner Aristotle Amadopoulos that his team will win, and decides to stack the roster with ringers. After Smithers informs him his first choice of legendary players are all long dead, Burns instead hires nine current MLB stars, giving them plant jobs so they qualify to play, which infuriates the regular employees who had actually earned their spot in the finals. On the eve of the big game, a series of bizarre mishaps—including radiation poisoning, a boxing injury, a hypnotism mix-up, and other calamities—take out all the ringers except Darryl Strawberry. Because Strawberry plays Homer's position, Burns benches Homer for most of the game despite his protests. In the ninth inning, with the score tied and the bases loaded, Burns sends Homer up to bat specifically to face a left-handed pitcher, only for the first pitch to strike Homer in the head, knocking him out cold and forcing in the winning run. Homer is carried off the field as an unlikely hero, still unconscious, securing the championship and Burns's bet. The episode closes with Terry Cashman's musical tribute, 'Talkin' Softball,' playing over the credits. Guest starring Wade Boggs, Terry Cashman, José Canseco, Roger Clemens, Ken Griffey, Jr., Don Mattingly, Steve Sax, Mike Scioscia, Ozzie Smith, Darryl Strawberry. Notable quotes: Dr. Hibbert: Oh my lord, gigantism! | Jose Canseco: Never fear ma'am, I'll save your cat! | Boggs: Pitt the Elder! | Barney: Lord Palmerston! | Mike Scioscia: Will... I... be... able... to... play... softball... tomorrow?

Jose Canseco: Never fear ma'am, I'll save your cat!
Boggs: Pitt the Elder!

title: Separate Vocations (S3E18)
text: "Separate Vocations" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F15), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by George Meyer, originally airing February 27, 1992. After taking a career aptitude test at school, Bart is stunned to learn he's suited to be a police officer, while Lisa is devastated to discover her ideal career is homemaker. Refusing to accept the results, Lisa seeks validation from a jazz musician, only to be told she's inherited her father's stubby fingers and can never be a professional saxophonist. Meanwhile, Bart embraces his new identity, riding along with police officers and later being appointed hall monitor by Principal Skinner, quickly becoming an efficient enforcer of school rules. As Bart thrives on authority, Lisa spirals into rebellion, quitting band, ignoring her studies, and falling in with a rough crowd. After repeated punishments from Miss Hoover, Lisa retaliates by stealing every teacher's edition textbook in the school, throwing the faculty into chaos. Bart, tasked with finding the culprit, discovers it was Lisa but chooses to take the blame himself, sacrificing his hall monitor status and earning 600 days of detention. Grateful and humbled, Lisa returns to her old self, serenading her brother with saxophone music outside his detention classroom as a gesture of thanks. Guest starring Steve Allen as Bart's warped courtroom voice. Notable quotes: Mrs. Krabappel: Some of you may discover a wonderful vocation you'd never even imagined. Others may find out life isn't fair, in spite of your Masters from Bryn Mawr, you might end up a glorified babysitter to a bunch of dead-eyed fourth graders while your husband runs naked on a beach with your marriage counselor! | Bart: Because I didn't want you to wreck your life. You got the brains and the talent to go as far as you want. And when you do, I'll be right there to borrow money. | Homer: No, the Army said I was too heavy. The police said I was too dumb. | Homer: We always have one good kid and one lousy kid. Why can't both our kids be good? | Bart: That's right, man. I got my first taste of authority. [rubs his hands] And I liked it!

Others may find out life isn't fair, in spite of your Masters from Bryn Mawr, you might end up a glorified babysitter to a bunch of dead-eyed fourth graders while your husband runs naked on a beach with your marriage counselor!

Homer: No, the Army said I was too heavy. The police said I was too dumb.
Homer: We always have one good kid and one lousy kid. Why can't both our kids be good?
Bart: That's right, man. I got my first taste of authority. [rubs his hands] And I liked it!

title: Dog of Death (S3E19)
text: "Dog of Death" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F17), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 12, 1992. As Springfield buzzes with excitement over a massive lottery jackpot, the Simpsons fail to notice that Santa's Little Helper has become seriously ill. A trip to the vet reveals he needs an emergency operation costing $750, money the family doesn't have. Determined not to let their dog die, Homer rallies the family to sacrifice their small pleasures—beer, lottery tickets, haircuts, books, and new clothes—to scrape together the funds. The operation succeeds, but the strain of their sacrifices breeds resentment toward the dog, especially after Marge discovers her usual lottery numbers would have won big money. Sensing the family's hostility, Santa's Little Helper runs away and is taken in by Mr. Burns, who trains him into a vicious attack dog through cruel conditioning. Wracked with guilt, the family searches for him, and Bart eventually finds him among Burns' guard dogs at the mansion. Just as the brainwashed dog is about to attack, memories of their bond break through, and he turns on the other dogs instead to protect Bart. The episode ends with the dog reunited with a loving, remorseful family. Notable quotes: Homer: I want to tell you about the most wonderful place in the world: Doggie Heaven. | Bart: I'm not gonna let our dog die and that's it! | Marge: You wouldn't want what he's eating – it's mostly just snouts and entrails. | Homer: The cat? What's the point? | Veterinarian: I love animals. I spend my life saving them and they can't thank me. Well, the parrots can.

Bart: I'm not gonna let our dog die and that's it!

Homer: The cat? What's the point?

title: Colonel Homer (S3E20)
text: "Colonel Homer" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F19), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Matt Groening, originally airing March 26, 1992. After a frustrating night at the movies with Marge, Homer storms off alone and drives into rural Spittle County, where he stumbles into a rowdy bar and hears a talented but unknown singer named Lurleen Lumpkin performing a heartfelt country song. Charmed by her voice, Homer befriends her and soon becomes her manager, helping her record a demo and get airplay on a local radio station, where her music unexpectedly soothes tempers and settles conflicts all across Springfield. As Lurleen's career takes off, Homer spends more and more time away from home arranging recording sessions and promotional appearances, leaving Marge feeling neglected and increasingly suspicious of his relationship with the singer. Marge's fears are confirmed when Lurleen begins writing songs with clear romantic undertones aimed at Homer, culminating in a seductive performance and an attempted kiss backstage at a television appearance. Caught in the moment, Homer suddenly realizes what he would lose if he gave in, and he flees the situation, quickly selling off his managerial rights to another agent for a paltry sum. He rushes home to reconcile with Marge, arriving just as Lurleen tearfully sings a new, heartfelt song on television expressing her unrequited feelings and acknowledging that Marge is lucky to have Homer. The episode closes with Marge and Homer reaffirming their bond as they watch the broadcast together. Guest starring Beverly D'Angelo as Lurleen Lumpkin. Notable quotes: Homer: They don't call me Colonel Homer because I'm some dumb-ass army guy. | Homer: Your song touched me in a way I've never felt before. And which way to the can? | Homer: Marge, it takes two to lie. One to lie, and one to listen. | Bart: As much as I hate that man right now, you gotta love that suit. | Homer: Well, right now she's an out-of-work cocktail waitress, but she's going to be a country music superstar, like, uh... that... jerk in the cowboy hat... and that dead lady.

title: Black Widower (S3E21)
text: "Black Widower" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F20), directed by David Silverman and written by Teleplay: Jon Vitti; Story: Sam Simon and Thomas Chastain, originally airing April 9, 1992. Selma announces she's marrying Sideshow Bob, a prison pen-pal she met through a correspondence program, and the family is shocked to learn he's Bart's old nemesis. Bob charms everyone at dinner with tales of his prison reform, and despite Bart's deep suspicion, the family and Selma quickly warm to him. A pre-wedding crisis over Bob's hatred of Selma's favorite show, MacGyver, is smoothed over thanks to Homer's marital advice, and the wedding proceeds with only Bart remaining wary. On their honeymoon, Bob sends home a video that tips Bart off to a suspicious obsession with having a fireplace in their hotel room. Piecing together clues about Selma's lost sense of smell and her habit of smoking after MacGyver airs, Bart realizes Bob has rigged the room to explode via a gas leak ignited by her cigarette. Bart and Marge race to the hotel and rescue Selma just before the room detonates, thanks to an unrelated mishap involving Chief Wiggum's cigar. Bob is arrested again, stunned that his elaborate murder plot was foiled, and the family finally acknowledges that Bart's stubborn distrust of Bob was justified all along. Guest starring Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Notable quotes: Sideshow Bob: Bart, I must know. How did you untangle my web? | Homer: Gee, if some snot-nosed little kid sent me to prison, the first thing out, I'd find out where he lives, and tear him a new belly button! | Selma: And here's another breathtaking sight... my brand new hubby! | Sideshow Bob: This is one more Emmy than you'll ever win, you bantering jack-in-the-box! | Bart: Don't be a fool, Aunt Selma. That man is scum.

Homer: Gee, if some snot-nosed little kid sent me to prison, the first thing out, I'd find out where he lives, and tear him a new belly button!
Selma: And here's another breathtaking sight... my brand new hubby!
Sideshow Bob: This is one more Emmy than you'll ever win, you bantering jack-in-the-box!
Bart: Don't be a fool, Aunt Selma. That man is scum.

title: The Otto Show (S3E22)
text: "The Otto Show" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F21), directed by Wes Archer and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing April 23, 1992. Homer takes Bart and Milhouse to a Spinal Tap concert, but the show ends in chaos and a riot after technical mishaps plague the aging rock band. Inspired by the concert, Bart decides he wants to be a rock star, prompting Homer and Marge to buy him an expensive guitar he turns out to be terrible at playing. When Bart lets bus driver Otto try the guitar, Otto reveals he's a surprisingly skilled rocker, but his antics behind the wheel cause an accident, and it's revealed he never had a driver's license. Skinner fires Otto and takes over driving duties himself, much to the students' dismay, while Otto is soon evicted from his apartment for not paying rent. Bart secretly lets the newly homeless Otto move into the Simpsons' garage, but Otto's slacker habits and freeloading quickly wear out his welcome with Homer and Marge. After being kicked out again, an furious Otto returns to the DMV, where Patty Bouvier—sharing his disdain for Homer—helps him cheat his way to passing the driving test. Otto triumphantly returns as the school bus driver, delighting the kids and leaving Skinner to watch begrudgingly as his tenure as driver ends. Guest starring Christopher Guest as Nigel Tufnel, Michael McKean as David St. Hubbins. Notable quotes: Principal Skinner: Well, that tears it. Until you get a license and wear your own underwear, mister, you are suspended without pay. | Otto Mann: No can do. Never got one. But if you need proof of my identity, I wrote my name on my underwear. | Skinner: Otto. That's one palindrome you won't be hearing for awhile. | Otto: A garage?! Oh, somebody up there likes me. | Homer: Forget it. That line didn't work for my dad and it's not gonna work for you.
quotes: Principal Skinner: Well, that tears it. Until you get a license and wear your own underwear, mister, you are suspended without pay.
Otto Mann: No can do. Never got one. But if you need proof of my identity, I wrote my name on my underwear.
Skinner: Otto. That's one palindrome you won't be hearing for awhile.
Otto: A garage?! Oh, somebody up there likes me.
Homer: Forget it. That line didn't work for my dad and it's not gonna work for you.

title: Bart's Friend Falls in Love (S3E23)
text: "Bart's Friend Falls in Love" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F22), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing May 7, 1992. After a chaotic Indiana Jones-style escape from Homer, Bart heads to school with Milhouse, whose Magic 8 Ball ominously predicts their friendship won't survive the day. That prophecy seems to come true when new student Samantha Stanky arrives from Phoenix and quickly becomes Milhouse's girlfriend, leaving Bart feeling abandoned as the couple monopolize his treehouse with constant kissing. Frustrated and jealous, Bart decides to sabotage the romance by tipping off Samantha's overprotective father, who yanks her out of school and ships her off to a strict all-girls convent. Milhouse is devastated and furious when he learns Bart was responsible, leading to a physical fight that only ends when Bart smashes the Magic 8 Ball over Milhouse's head. Seeking to make amends, Bart and Milhouse visit Samantha at her new school, where she reveals she's actually happy there and forgives Bart, though she still shares a rule-breaking farewell kiss with Milhouse. Meanwhile, after Lisa becomes alarmed by a documentary on obesity's dangers, Marge orders Homer a subliminal weight-loss tape, but a shipping mix-up sends a vocabulary-building tape instead, causing Homer to eat even more while inexplicably becoming eloquent, a side effect that vanishes once he discards the tape. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure, Kimmy Robertson as Samantha Stanky. Notable quotes: Milhouse: Bart, I don't want you to see me cry. | Bart: God shmod! I want my monkey-man! | Otto: Everybody on! No shoving! Hee, just kidding. You can shove all you want! | Edna: Oh, don't you worry. Most of you will never fall in love and marry out of fear of dying alone. | Bart: Yeah, but never a girl. What if I want to strut around nude?

Bart: God shmod! I want my monkey-man!
Otto: Everybody on! No shoving! Hee, just kidding. You can shove all you want!
Edna: Oh, don't you worry. Most of you will never fall in love and marry out of fear of dying alone.
Bart: Yeah, but never a girl. What if I want to strut around nude?

title: Brother, Can You Spare Two Dimes? (S3E24)
keys: brother, can you spare two dimes?
text: "Brother, Can You Spare Two Dimes?" is an episode of Season 3 (production code 8F23), directed by Rich Moore and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing August 27, 1992. Homer's routine physical at the power plant reveals that radiation exposure has left him sterile, prompting a worried Mr. Burns to invent a bogus honor—the First Annual Montgomery Burns Award for Outstanding Achievement in the Field of Excellence—to get Homer to sign a liability waiver disguised as an award certificate, complete with a $2000 cash prize. Meanwhile, Homer's estranged half-brother Herb, now homeless after losing his car company because of Homer's earlier meddling, spots a mother struggling to communicate with her baby and hits on the idea of inventing a baby translator, realizing he needs both a good idea and money to make it work. Herb tracks down news of Homer's award money and shows up at the Simpson house, first mistakenly visiting the Flanders, who clean him up, before finally confronting Homer with a punch and a plea for a second chance. Torn between his desire to buy an irresistible vibrating recliner called the Spinemelter 2000 and his family's urging, Homer reluctantly lends Herb the prize money to fund his invention. Herb spends hours studying Maggie's babbling and successfully builds a working baby translator, which becomes a sensation at a baby products convention, restoring his fortune. Grateful, Herb repays Homer and showers the family with gifts—including the very vibrating chair Homer coveted—symbolizing his forgiveness and renewed brotherly bond with Homer. Guest starring Danny DeVito, Joe Frazier. Notable quotes: Homer: Go to Hell. | Lisa: This show is the biggest farce I ever saw! | Herb: All right, a man needs two things. An idea, and money to get it off the ground. | Homer: Marge, there's an empty spot I've always had inside me. I tried to fill it with family, religion, community service ... but those were dead ends! I think this chair is the answer. | Herb: Discarded pizza boxes are an inexpensive source of cheese.
quotes: Homer: Go to Hell.
Lisa: This show is the biggest farce I ever saw!
Herb: All right, a man needs two things. An idea, and money to get it off the ground.
Homer: Marge, there's an empty spot I've always had inside me. I tried to fill it with family, religion, community service ... but those were dead ends! I think this chair is the answer.
Herb: Discarded pizza boxes are an inexpensive source of cheese.

title: Kamp Krusty (S4E01)
text: "Kamp Krusty" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 8F24), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by David M. Stern, originally airing September 24, 1992. As the school year ends, Bart panics when he receives failing grades, since Homer has promised he can only attend Kamp Krusty with a C average; Mrs. Krabappel and later a bus-ride forgery help him fake passing marks. Homer discovers the trick but decides not to punish Bart further and lets him go anyway. Bart and Lisa join other Springfield kids at the camp, only to discover Krusty is absent, replaced by the shady Mr. Black and cruel counselors Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney, who subject the campers to filthy cabins, pine-cone campfires, and fake gruel. Meanwhile, Homer and Marge relish their child-free summer, and Krusty is off in Wimbledon being knighted while ignoring the camp's problems. Letters home about the terrible conditions are dismissed by the parents as exaggeration, until a fake Krusty appearance (actually Barney in costume) triggers Bart to lead a full-scale rebellion, freeing the campers and the kids from the neighboring fat camp. News of the uprising reaches Krusty during his knighting ceremony, prompting him to rush back and personally apologize, admitting he only licensed his name for money. To make amends, Krusty whisks the children off to Tijuana for a wild, joyful finale as compensation for the disastrous camp experience. Notable quotes: Homer: Well, it is! | Homer: Sure do. When you're 18, you're out the door! | Mrs. Krabappel: Have a 'D'-lightful summer. | Dolph: Not quite. This is Krusty Brand Imitation Gruel. Nine out of ten orphans can't tell the difference! | Kearney: Well, it ain't gettin' any safer!
quotes: Homer: Well, it is!
Homer: Sure do. When you're 18, you're out the door!
Mrs. Krabappel: Have a 'D'-lightful summer.
Dolph: Not quite. This is Krusty Brand Imitation Gruel. Nine out of ten orphans can't tell the difference!
Kearney: Well, it ain't gettin' any safer!

title: A Streetcar Named Marge (S4E02)
text: "A Streetcar Named Marge" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 8F18), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing October 1, 1992. Marge auditions for a community theater production of Oh, Streetcar!, a musical adaptation of A Streetcar Named Desire, and is cast as Blanche DuBois under the direction of the eccentric, dramatic Llewellyn Sinclair. Feeling unsupported and dismissed by Homer, who shows little interest in her new hobby, Marge channels her resentment toward him into her performance, giving her portrayal real emotional depth. Her intensity boils over during rehearsals when she nearly attacks her co-star Ned Flanders, who plays Stanley Kowalski, with a broken bottle during a key scene. Meanwhile, Maggie is enrolled at the strict Ayn Rand School for Tots, where the humorless caretaker confiscates the babies' pacifiers, prompting Maggie to organize a covert rebellion among the infants to reclaim them. On opening night, Marge delivers a powerful performance that earns thunderous applause from the audience, but Homer sits stone-faced, seemingly unmoved. Furious and hurt, Marge confronts him afterward, only to discover that he was actually deeply affected by the story's themes of loneliness and disappointment. Realizing that Homer had truly connected with her performance in his own way, Marge forgives him, and the two reconcile. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure and Lionel Hutz, Jon Lovitz as Llewellyn Sinclair and Ms. Sinclair. Notable quotes: Llewellyn Sinclair: Hello! I am Llewellyn Sinclair. I've directed three plays in my career and I've had three heart attacks. That's how much I care, I'm planning for a fourth. | Lionel Hutz: Lionel Hutz, Attorney at Law. I'm filing a class-action suit against the director on behalf of everyone who was cut from the play. I also play Mitch! | Ms. Sinclair: She's saying "I am a leech". | Marge: For God's sakes, you can pull the lid off your own can of pudding! | Homer: I'm livin' in a cuckoo clock!

Lionel Hutz: Lionel Hutz, Attorney at Law. I'm filing a class-action suit against the director on behalf of everyone who was cut from the play. I also play Mitch!
Ms. Sinclair: She's saying "I am a leech".
Marge: For God's sakes, you can pull the lid off your own can of pudding!
Homer: I'm livin' in a cuckoo clock!

title: Homer the Heretic (S4E03)
text: "Homer the Heretic" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F01), directed by Jim Reardon and written by George Meyer, originally airing October 8, 1992. On a freezing Sunday morning, Homer refuses to go to church with Marge and the kids, choosing instead to enjoy a day of lazy indulgence at home. While his family suffers through a rambling sermon and a car that won't start in the cold, Homer revels in his freedom, cooking elaborate waffles and winning a radio contest. Furious at his newfound apathy toward religion, Marge prays for divine intervention, and that night Homer dreams of a conversation with God, who ultimately concedes that Homer's personal way of worshipping isn't so bad. Despite pressure from Marge, Reverend Lovejoy, and the Flanders family to return to church, Homer stays firm in skipping services again the next week, this time smoking a cigar while reading magazines. He falls asleep and accidentally sets the house on fire, nearly perishing before being saved by his neighbors—Hindu Apu, Jewish Krusty, and Christian Ned—who all rush to help regardless of their differing faiths. Lovejoy uses the incident to show Homer that God's influence works through people of all religions, convincing him to give church one more try. In the end, Homer attends church again but simply falls asleep during the sermon, showing that some things about him will never truly change. Notable quotes: Apu: Please do not offer my god a peanut. | Krusty: Hello. I'm collecting for the Brotherhood of Jewish Clowns. | Apu: Hindu! There are 700 million of us. | Homer: Oh, spiteful one, show me who to smite and they shall be smoten! | God: Well... okay. The meaning of life is...
quotes: Apu: Please do not offer my god a peanut.
Krusty: Hello. I'm collecting for the Brotherhood of Jewish Clowns.
Apu: Hindu! There are 700 million of us.
Homer: Oh, spiteful one, show me who to smite and they shall be smoten!
God: Well... okay. The meaning of life is...

title: Lisa the Beauty Queen (S4E04)
text: "Lisa the Beauty Queen" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F02), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing October 15, 1992. At the Springfield Elementary carnival, Lisa is devastated when a caricature artist's drawing convinces her she is unattractive. Wanting to lift her spirits, Homer sells his hard-won grand prize—a ride on the Duff blimp—to Barney so he can afford the entry fee for the 'Little Miss Springfield' beauty pageant sponsored by Laramie Cigarettes. Touched by her father's sacrifice, Lisa agrees to compete, even though she faces a formidable rival in Amber Dempsey, a manipulative girl with eyelash implants who easily charms the judges. Lisa finishes as runner-up, but when Amber is struck by lightning during a public appearance, Lisa is thrust into the role of Little Miss Springfield. Uncomfortable being used as a cigarette mascot, Lisa uses her new platform to speak out against smoking and to criticize Mayor Quimby's corruption, angering the pageant's sponsors. Quimby and the tobacco executives search for a way to remove her and discover that Homer accidentally invalidated her entry form by writing in a restricted area, allowing them to reinstate Amber. Though Lisa loses her crown, she and Homer share a warm moment reflecting on his efforts to boost her confidence, ending the episode on a heartfelt note. Guest starring Bob Hope as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: Oh it's no fair, we'll never have a buffer! | Homer: Moe, have you ever felt unattractive? | Homer: Well if I could gouge out somebody else's eyes and shove them into my sockets I would; but to me, she's beautiful! | Bart: She'll see through me like Grandma's underpants! | Homer: When it comes to compliments, women are ravenous blood-sucking monsters always wanting more...more... MORE!

title: Treehouse of Horror III (S4E05)
text: "Treehouse of Horror III" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F04), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Al Jean, Mike Reiss, Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, Sam Simon, Jon Vitti, originally airing October 29, 1992. Homer, imitating Alfred Hitchcock, warns viewers that this Halloween special may be too scary before the family settles in for their annual Treehouse of Horror stories. In the first tale, Homer buys Bart a talking Krusty doll from a sinister shop, unaware that a factory defect has switched it from 'Good' to 'Evil,' causing it to repeatedly attempt to murder Homer until a KrustyCo repairman fixes the malfunction. Next, in a black-and-white King Kong parody, Marge accompanies Mr. Burns and Smithers on an expedition to Ape Island, where they capture the giant King Homer and put him on display in New York, only for him to break free, kidnap Marge, and rampage through the city before their unlikely wedding. Finally, Bart discovers an occult book in the school library and tries to resurrect Lisa's dead cat to cheer her up, but instead accidentally raises an army of zombies that overrun Springfield, including a zombified Ned Flanders whom Homer shoots dead. Bart and Lisa race against time to find the correct reversal spell in the ravaged library, and Bart's spell backfires by briefly turning Lisa into a snail before he finally gets it right, banishing the zombies and restoring order. The episode closes with the family safely back on the couch, having survived all three of their own scary stories. This installment is made up of 4 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 3): "Opening segment", "Clown Without Pity", "King Homer", and "Dial "Z" for Zombies".

title: Itchy & Scratchy: The Movie (S4E06)
text: "Itchy & Scratchy: The Movie" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F03), directed by Rich Moore and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing November 3, 1992. After Bart's misbehavior earns a scathing report from Mrs. Krabappel and he breaks Grampa's dentures, Marge insists that Homer finally start disciplining their son properly. Bart and Lisa are thrilled about the upcoming Itchy & Scratchy Movie and buy tickets in advance, but Bart continues to act up, tricking Homer into overlooking his misdeeds until he neglects to watch Maggie, resulting in her joyriding the family car into a prison and freeing convicts. Furious, Homer tears up Bart's movie ticket and bans him from ever seeing the film, refusing to relent even as Bart grows miserable watching everyone else rave about it. Marge and Lisa plead with Homer to end the punishment after two months, but he stands firm, even preemptively blocking Bart from buying a ticket at the theater himself. Eight months and several Academy Awards later, the film finally leaves theaters, and Homer insists that his harsh discipline will ultimately make Bart a better person. In a non-canon epilogue set forty years later, an adult Bart—now Chief Justice of the Supreme Court—finally gets to watch the film's re-release with his father, suggesting Homer's tough love paid off after all. Guest starring Neil Armstrong. Notable quotes: Homer: Young man, since you broke Grampa's teeth, he gets to break yours. | Homer: If you don't start making more sense, we're going to have to put you in a home. | Marge: Do you want your son to grow up to be Chief Justice of the Supreme Court or a sleazy male stripper? | Homer: Can't he be both like the late Earl Warren? | Homer: Someday you'll thank me for this, son.

Homer: Can't he be both like the late Earl Warren?

title: Marge Gets a Job (S4E07)
text: "Marge Gets a Job" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F05), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing November 5, 1992. When the Simpsons' house begins sinking and needs $8,500 in foundation repairs, Marge reluctantly takes a job at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, filling the position vacated by the retiring Jack Marley. Mr. Burns quickly becomes infatuated with Marge and tries various schemes, including novelty theme days and hiring her favorite singer Tom Jones, to win her over. When Marge rebuffs his advances by revealing she is married, Burns fires her, prompting her to seek help from the inept lawyer Lionel Hutz, who is quickly overwhelmed by Burns' legal team. Meanwhile, Bart repeatedly fakes illness to avoid a test on Ivanhoe at school, drawing skepticism from Mrs. Krabappel who compares him to the boy who cried wolf. His deception backfires spectacularly when an escaped timberwolf from Krusty's studio actually attacks him outside his classroom, and no one believes his cries for help until Groundskeeper Willie intervenes. Bart, feeling guilty over his lies, tries to admit he made up the wolf story, only to collapse from his injuries and prove he was telling the truth. Burns has a change of heart after witnessing Homer's genuine devotion to Marge, and the episode ends with Homer and Marge enjoying a private, if awkwardly coerced, performance from the captive Tom Jones. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure and Lionel Hutz, Tom Jones as himself. Notable quotes: Grampa: Good news, boy! I found a pharmacy that carries leeches! Well, it wasn't actually a pharmacy – more of a bait shop. | Mr. Burns: I want you to show this woman the time of her life. | Homer: Gotcha! Marge, we're getting some drive-thru, then we're doing it twice! | Smithers: Heh, heh, heh. Marge, please! According to your resume, you invented this machine! | Tom Jones: Sorry, mate, I do not do private parties.

title: New Kid on the Block (S4E08)
text: "New Kid on the Block" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F06), directed by Wes Archer and written by Conan O'Brien, originally airing November 12, 1992. When elderly neighbors the Winfields decide to sell their house and move to Florida, Homer's refusal to tidy up the property nearly scuttles the sale. The house is soon bought by newly divorced Ruth Powers and her teenage daughter Laura, and Bart is instantly smitten with the older girl. Bart tries various schemes to impress Laura, including babysitting antics and a Hugh Hefner-style outfit, but she treats him more like a little brother than a potential boyfriend. Meanwhile, Homer gorges himself at the all-you-can-eat buffet at The Frying Dutchman and, after being kicked out before he's truly full, hires bumbling lawyer Lionel Hutz to sue the restaurant for false advertising. Bart's heart breaks when Laura reveals she's dating the school bully Jimbo Jones because she finds his rebellious attitude attractive. Seeking revenge, Bart tricks Moe into confronting Jimbo with a knife, which terrifies Jimbo and exposes him as a coward, leading Laura to dump him. In the courtroom, the Sea Captain proposes a solution that lets Homer's appetite become a promotional attraction for the restaurant, resolving the lawsuit. In the end, Laura tells Bart that if he were a few years older, she'd gladly date him, and gives him a kiss on the cheek before they team up to prank-call Moe again. Guest starring Sara Gilbert as Laura Powers, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz, Pamela Reed as Ruth Powers. Notable quotes: Laura Powers: If you had a bad teenage mustache, I'd go out with you in a second. | Homer: Marge, we're going to that restaurant. | Sea Captain: 'Tis no man. 'Tis a remorseless eating machine. Arrrr... | Lionel Hutz: Homer, I don't use the word "hero" very often. But you are the greatest hero in American history. | Homer: Son, a woman is a lot like, uh... ... a refrigerator. They're about six feet tall, 300 pounds... they make ice and ... Oh, wait a minute, actually, a woman is more like a beer!

title: Mr. Plow (S4E09)
text: "Mr. Plow" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F07), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing November 19, 1992. During a heavy Springfield snowstorm, Homer wrecks both family cars while rushing home from Moe's Tavern, then lies to an insurance adjuster to cover up where he'd really been. With the insurance payout, he's talked into buying a snowplow truck instead of a regular car, and launches his own business, Mr. Plow, complete with a catchy late-night TV jingle. The venture is a huge success, earning Homer the town's admiration and a key to the city from Mayor Quimby. When Barney, tired of dead-end jobs, asks for advice, Homer unwittingly inspires him to start a rival business called The Plow King, which soon steals all of Homer's customers with Linda Ronstadt's help on a slick ad campaign. Furious at losing his customers and his key to the city, Homer sends Barney on a fake plowing job up the treacherous Widow's Peak, only to hear reports of an avalanche there. Guilt-ridden, Homer rescues Barney from the mountain, and the two reconcile and decide to become business partners. Their boastful declaration that not even God could stop their partnership is answered when the snow miraculously melts, ending both of their businesses. Homer's truck gets repossessed, but he's satisfied that he and Barney are friends again, content to still wear his Mr. Plow jacket to bed. Guest starring Linda Ronstadt, Adam West. Notable quotes: Homer: It's a pornography store. I was buying pornography. | Grampa: I'm cold and frightened. | Bart: Who the hell is Robin? | Homer: Oh, you want the Mr. Plow who plows driveways. This is Tony Plow. You know, from Leave It To Beaver? Yeah, they were gay. | Barney: So long, Superman! You're secret identity is safe with me!
