title: Lisa's First Word (S4E10)
text: "Lisa's First Word" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F08), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing December 3, 1992. In the present, the Simpsons try unsuccessfully to coax Maggie into speaking, prompting Bart to ask about his own first word, which leads Marge to instead recount the story of how Lisa learned to talk. She flashes back to 1983, when the family lived in a cramped apartment on the Lower East Side with a mischievous toddler Bart, and Marge announces she's pregnant again, prompting the search for a bigger home. After Homer secures money from Grampa to buy 742 Evergreen Terrace, the family settles in, but Bart struggles with jealousy once baby Lisa arrives, acting out by cutting her hair and trying to give her away to the Flanders family. Homer, meanwhile, gets sidetracked by a Krusty Burger Olympics promotion and builds Bart an ill-conceived clown bed that terrifies him. As Bart prepares to run away from home in frustration over Lisa stealing the spotlight, he furiously blames her for his misery, and Lisa's very first word turns out to be "Bart," astonishing the whole family and easing the siblings' rivalry somewhat. Back in the present, Homer tucks Maggie into her crib, wishing aloud that she never learns to talk since talking leads to talking back, unaware that Maggie finally whispers her first word, "Daddy," just as he leaves the room. Guest starring Elizabeth Taylor. Notable quotes: Homer: The sooner kids talk, the sooner they talk back. I hope you never say a word. | Maggie: Daddy. | Homer: Did you hear that? She said "burlap." | Grampa: I ratted on everybody and got off scot free! | Bart: Can't sleep... Clown'll eat me... Can't sleep... Clown'll eat me...

Maggie: Daddy.

title: Homer's Triple Bypass (S4E11)
text: "Homer's Triple Bypass" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F09), directed by David Silverman and written by Gary Apple, Michael Carrington, originally airing December 17, 1992. Homer starts experiencing chest pains after years of poor diet and stress, dismissing the warning signs as everything from indigestion to car trouble. His condition worsens dramatically when Mr. Burns torments him with false hope of keeping his job before firing him, triggering a heart attack that briefly kills him until the mention of a ham revives him. Dr. Hibbert determines Homer needs an expensive triple bypass surgery, but the family's lack of health insurance and meager savings make the $40,000 procedure impossible to afford. After suffering additional heart attacks, including one while being rejected for insurance, Homer and Marge turn to the notoriously incompetent but cheap Dr. Nick Riviera, who offers the surgery for a fraction of the price. While recovering in the hospital, Homer bonds awkwardly with roommate Ned Flanders over prayer, drawing the ire of a strict nurse. On the day of surgery, Dr. Nick's ignorance nearly proves disastrous when he forgets the procedure, but Lisa, who has studied cardiology, guides him from the observation gallery. Against all odds, the surgery succeeds, and Homer makes a full recovery, his heart even beating out the show's theme song by the episode's end. Notable quotes: Homer: Oh, Doctor, I was in a wonderful place filled with fire and brimstone, and there were all these guys in red pajamas sticking pitchforks in my butt! | Mr. Burns: Look at that pig, stuffing his face with donuts on *my time*! That's right, keep eating... Little do you know you're drawing ever closer to the poison donut! | Homer's astral body: Mmm... ham. | Mr. Burns: Oh, good. Cancel the ham! | Attendant: It's your heart. And I think it's on its last thump.

Mr. Burns: Look at that pig, stuffing his face with donuts on *my time*! That's right, keep eating... Little do you know you're drawing ever closer to the poison donut!
Homer's astral body: Mmm... ham.

title: Marge vs. the Monorail (S4E12)
text: "Marge vs. the Monorail" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F10), directed by Rich Moore and written by Conan O'Brien, originally airing January 14, 1993. After Mr. Burns is fined $3 million by the EPA for illegally dumping toxic waste in the park, Springfield holds a town meeting to decide how to spend the windfall. Marge proposes repairing the town's crumbling Main Street, but a charismatic con man named Lyle Lanley sweeps in and, through an infectious song, convinces the townspeople to instead build a monorail. Homer, seeing his 'lifelong dream' fulfilled, trains at Lanley's institute and is selected as the monorail's conductor, while Marge grows suspicious after discovering a sketch in Lanley's notebook showing the train derailing in flames. She travels to North Haverbrook, where she meets engineer Sebastian Cobb, who reveals that Lanley previously sold the town a shoddy monorail that was destroyed after cutting corners on construction. Racing back to Springfield, Marge arrives just as the monorail's inaugural run begins with celebrity guest Leonard Nimoy aboard, and the brakes fail, sending the train speeding out of control. As Lanley flees with the money, only to be confronted by an angry mob in North Haverbrook, Homer must improvise a solution, using a stolen rope tied to the train's giant 'M' as a makeshift anchor. The plan works, dragging the runaway monorail to a stop in a donut shop, saving the town, while Nimoy comically takes credit for the rescue. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lyle Lanley, Leonard Nimoy as himself. Notable quotes: Lyle Lanley: Well, sir, there's nothing on earth like a genuine, bona-fide, electrified, six-car monorail. | Homer: Marge, I want to be a monorail conductor. | Marge: Your life-long dream was to run out on the field during a baseball game, and you did it last year, remember? | Mr. Burns: Hello. My name is Mr. Snrub, and I come from... eh, someplace far away. | Sebastian Cobb: He cut corners everywhere... bad wiring... faulty brakes... and the celebrity on the maiden voyage was Gallagher.

Marge: Your life-long dream was to run out on the field during a baseball game, and you did it last year, remember?
Mr. Burns: Hello. My name is Mr. Snrub, and I come from... eh, someplace far away.
Sebastian Cobb: He cut corners everywhere... bad wiring... faulty brakes... and the celebrity on the maiden voyage was Gallagher.

title: Selma's Choice (S4E13)
text: "Selma's Choice" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F11), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by David M. Stern, originally airing January 21, 1993. After Great Aunt Gladys passes away, the Simpson family attends her funeral and the reading of her video will, in which she warns Patty and Selma about dying alone without a husband or children. Rattled by this message, Selma becomes anxious about her biological clock and begins exploring ways to have a baby, from video dating to considering an anonymous sperm donor. Meanwhile, Homer had promised Bart and Lisa a trip to Duff Gardens, but he falls ill after eating a spoiled sandwich, forcing Marge to find a replacement chaperone. Seeing an opportunity for Selma to test her maternal instincts, Marge sends her to take the kids to the amusement park instead. The outing quickly becomes chaotic as Bart and Lisa run Selma ragged, with Lisa hallucinating after drinking suspicious water on a ride and Bart getting picked up by park security. Exhausted and disillusioned by the experience, Selma concludes that she isn't cut out for motherhood after all. In the end, she decides to fulfill her need for companionship by adopting Gladys's iguana, Jub-Jub, instead of pursuing having a child. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Homer: I'm not pouting. I'm mourning. Stupid dead woman. | Lionel Hutz: You'd be surprised how often that works, you really would! | Mrs. Bouvier: Why didn't she just leave me the bowel obstruction that killed her? | Selma: Get out of my car. | Homer: And I'm a college student!
quotes: Homer: I'm not pouting. I'm mourning. Stupid dead woman.
Lionel Hutz: You'd be surprised how often that works, you really would!
Mrs. Bouvier: Why didn't she just leave me the bowel obstruction that killed her?
Selma: Get out of my car.
Homer: And I'm a college student!

title: Brother from the Same Planet (S4E14)
text: "Brother from the Same Planet" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F12), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing February 4, 1993. After Homer forgets to pick him up from soccer practice, leaving him stranded in a storm, Bart decides he's had enough of his father's neglect. He fabricates a sob story to the Bigger Brothers Agency claiming he's been abandoned, and is paired with Tom, a cool, athletic mentor voiced by Phil Hartman. As Bart enjoys motorcycle rides, paragliding, and workouts with Tom, Homer eventually spots them together and feels betrayed and humiliated. Seeking revenge, Homer signs up with the same agency and is paired with a real orphan named Pepi, showering him with attention and gifts meant for Bart. Meanwhile, a subplot follows Lisa's growing addiction to a pricey celebrity phone hotline, which Marge helps her overcome just as Homer and Bart's rivalry comes to a head. At a Bigger Brothers event at Marine World, Homer and Tom collide, leading to a wild citywide brawl that ends with Homer injured on a fire hydrant. In the hospital, Homer and Bart finally reconcile, and Bart cleverly pairs Tom and Pepi together so both can have a companion, while Homer teaches Bart the fighting moves he used against Tom. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Eddie Muntz and Tom. Notable quotes: Homer: I know you're mad at me right now, and I'm kinda mad too... I mean, we could sit here and try to figure out "who forgot to pick up who" till the cows come home. But let's just say we're both wrong and that'll be that. | Bart: Yeah... he left me out on the curb for the ashman. What a revoltin' development. | Homer: Marge, when kids these days say bad, they mean good. And to shake your booty means to wiggle one's butt. Permit me to demonstrate. | Tom: Bart, I could kiss you, if the Bigger Brothers hadn't made me sign a form promising I wouldn't. | Homer's brain: Don't say revenge. Don't say revenge.

Bart: Yeah... he left me out on the curb for the ashman. What a revoltin' development.

title: I Love Lisa (S4E15)
text: "I Love Lisa" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F13), directed by Wesley Archer and written by Frank Mula, originally airing February 11, 1993. On Valentine's Day, Lisa feels sorry for Ralph Wiggum when he doesn't receive any cards, so she gives him one out of pity. Ralph misreads the gesture as romantic interest and begins pursuing Lisa relentlessly, using his father Chief Wiggum's influence to get them tickets to Krusty's 29th Anniversary Special and a starring role opposite her in the school's President's Day Pageant. Miss Hoover rigs the casting so Ralph plays George Washington to Lisa's Martha Washington, having been coerced by Chief Wiggum. At Krusty's taping, Ralph publicly declares his love for Lisa on live television, prompting her to snap and cruelly reject him in front of everyone, revealing she never liked him and only gave him the valentine out of pity. Ralph is devastated, and Lisa feels guilty, especially after Bart replays the humiliating moment on video. Meanwhile, Chief Wiggum takes his frustration out on Homer with a bogus traffic stop, only to be unsettled by Homer's warning about citizens rising against corrupt cops. At the pageant, despite Bart's irreverent antics as John Wilkes Booth, Ralph delivers a surprisingly moving performance as George Washington that earns him respect from his classmates. Afterward, Lisa gives Ralph a new, friendlier valentine, and the two reconcile as friends, with Chief Wiggum watching contentedly as they sit together on the swings. Notable quotes: Ralph: I Choo-Choo-Choose you. | Groundskeeper Willie: I didn't cry when me own father was hung for stealing a pig, but I'll cry now. | Homer: Ah, sweet pity. Where would my love life have been without it? | Chief Wiggum: They are!? Oh no! Ha-have they set a date? | Homer: Six simple words: I'm not gay, but I'll learn.
quotes: Ralph: I Choo-Choo-Choose you.
Groundskeeper Willie: I didn't cry when me own father was hung for stealing a pig, but I'll cry now.
Homer: Ah, sweet pity. Where would my love life have been without it?
Chief Wiggum: They are!? Oh no! Ha-have they set a date?
Homer: Six simple words: I'm not gay, but I'll learn.

title: Duffless (S4E16)
text: "Duffless" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F14), directed by Jim Reardon and written by David M. Stern, originally airing February 18, 1993. After Bart's science fair prank leads Lisa to a new plan, the episode kicks off with Homer sneaking away from work to join Barney on a free tour of the Duff Brewery. While Barney drinks heavily and Homer barely partakes, a waiting police trio pulls Homer over and arrests him for DUI despite passing a sobriety test, forcing him into traffic school and AA meetings. Meanwhile, Lisa's genetically engineered tomato project is ruined when Bart uses it as a prank on Principal Skinner, prompting her to devise a new experiment comparing Bart's intelligence to a hamster's. Marge, worried about Homer's drinking, convinces him to abstain from beer for a month, leading Homer through humorous withdrawal, newfound clarity about life without alcohol, and a shrinking belly. At the science fair, Bart's flashy "Can hamsters fly planes?" project steals the show and the prize, crushing Lisa's more scientifically valid experiment. Homer struggles through his AA meetings, confessing embarrassing behavior, but grows healthier and even saves money during his sober month. When the month ends, he initially heads back to Moe's for a drink, but after witnessing the sorry state of the regular barflies, he decides to walk away and return home to Marge instead. The episode ends with Homer and Marge riding off together on a bike, symbolizing his renewed outlook on life. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz and Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Marge: Homie, I'd like you to do something for me. | Homer: You got it. No deer for a month. | Chief Wiggum: Mrs. Simpson, I have some bad news; your husband was found DOA. | Homer: I would kill everyone in this room for a drop of sweet beer. | Principal Skinner: Well, Edna, for a school with no Asian kids, I think we put on a pretty darn good science fair.

Homer: You got it. No deer for a month.

title: Last Exit to Springfield (S4E17)
text: "Last Exit to Springfield" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F15), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jay Kogen, Wallace Wolodarsky, originally airing March 11, 1993. When the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant's union leader mysteriously vanishes, Mr. Burns seizes the opportunity to draft a new contract that strips away the workers' dental plan. Homer initially shrugs off the news until he realizes that losing the plan means he'll have to pay for Lisa's newly needed braces out of pocket. Fired up, Homer rallies his coworkers with an impassioned speech and is unexpectedly elected union president, putting him directly at odds with Burns. Burns tries every trick to win Homer over, from confusing gestures for exercise to awkward innuendo-laced negotiations that Homer misinterprets as a pass, and later resorts to strikebreakers and even robotic replacements when Homer calls a strike. As the plant goes dark and the town loses power, Burns steps outside expecting to find a broken, demoralized workforce, but instead hears the strikers singing in defiant unity. Humbled, Burns agrees to restore the dental plan on the condition that Homer step down as union president, a deal Homer happily accepts without realizing he's been outmaneuvered. With insurance restored, Lisa gets her braces fixed properly, and the family shares a laugh with the dentist as the episode closes on a note of triumph and absurdity. Guest starring Joyce Brothers as herself. Notable quotes: Lenny: So long, dental plan! | Homer: If we give up our dental plan...I'll have to pay for Lisa's braces! | Homer: Sorry, Mr. Burns, but I don't go in for these backdoor shenanigans. Sure, I'm flattered, maybe even a little curious, but the answer is no! | Mr. Burns: This is a thousand monkeys working at a thousand typewriters. Soon they'll have written the greatest novel known to man. | Mr. Burns: Look at them all, through the darkness I am bringing. They're not sad at all. They're actually singing.

title: So It's Come to This: A Simpsons Clip Show (S4E18)
keys: so it's come to this: a simpsons clip show
text: "So It's Come to This: A Simpsons Clip Show" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F17), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing April 1, 1993. On April Fools' Day, Homer spends the morning tormenting Bart with pranks like taping his eyes shut and swapping his milk for a sour version. Seeking revenge, Bart shakes up a can of beer in a paint shaker and leaves it for Homer, but the resulting explosion sends Homer to the hospital with severe injuries. As Homer recovers, Dr. Hibbert cruelly pranks Marge by claiming Homer has died before revealing he may never walk again, and Barney's attempt to comfort Homer only leads Moe to worry about his friend's loneliness. Determined to prove he can walk, Homer struggles toward a candy machine, but chokes on a mouthful of candy and slips into a coma. While keeping vigil at his bedside, the family recalls a series of memorable past experiences together, shown through flashback clips. Mr. Burns, irritated by the cost of Homer's care, tries to have him taken off life support, and Dr. Nick nearly agrees before signs of life appear. Bart eventually confesses that he caused the explosion, prompting a furious Homer to wake from his coma and strangle him, much to the relief of the rest of the family. Marge reveals that Homer has been in a coma for weeks and lost five percent of his brain in the process. Notable quotes: Dr. Hibbert: Mrs. Simpson, I'm afraid your husband is dead. [laughs] April Fools. He's very much alive, although I'm afraid he may never walk again. | Grampa: Coma? Pfffft. Why, I go in and out of comas all the – [falls asleep] [wakes up] French toast, please. | Mr. Burns: This man is costing my health plan $5000 a day! I demand that he die with dignity. | Homer: You couldn't fool your mother on the foolingest day of your life if you had an electrified fooling machine. | Marge: You lost 5% of your brain.

title: The Front (S4E19)
text: "The Front" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F16), directed by Rich Moore and written by Adam I. Lapidus, originally airing April 15, 1993. After watching an especially poor episode of The Itchy & Scratchy Show, Bart and Lisa decide they could write better material and pen a script inspired by Homer's mishap with hedge shears in Marge's hair. When producer Roger Meyers Jr. dismisses the script because it's from children, they resubmit it under Grampa's name, and it's accepted, landing Grampa a job as a staff writer. Bart and Lisa keep churning out scripts under Grampa's name while splitting the paychecks three ways, even as Grampa grows uneasy about the deception. Meanwhile, Homer and Marge attend their high school reunion, where Homer is celebrated with a string of joke awards until the principal reveals Homer never actually graduated, stripping him of his honors in front of everyone. Stung by the embarrassment, Homer enrolls in a remedial science class to reclaim his silly awards rather than out of any real desire for self-improvement, and ultimately passes the class and finally earns his diploma. At the Annual Cartoon Awards, Grampa is honored for his writing, but after being shown a compilation of the show's graphic violence for the first time, he's disgusted and delivers a scathing anti-violence speech to the booing crowd before storming off. He hands the award over to Bart and Lisa, revealing the truth of who really wrote the scripts. The episode closes with a satirical Ned Flanders cartoon short mocking his overly pious family life. Guest starring Brooke Shields. Notable quotes: Grampa: Dear Mr. President, there are too many states nowadays. Please eliminate three. I am not a crackpot! | Grampa: Well, whenever I'm confused, I just check my underwear. It holds the answer to all the important questions. | Homer: Marge! Ix-nay on the uclear-nay echnician-tay. | Grampa: That's right. I did the Iggy. | Bart: I'll never watch an awards show again.

title: Whacking Day (S4E20)
text: "Whacking Day" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F18), directed by Jeff Lynch and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing April 29, 1993. As Springfield gears up for its annual Whacking Day celebration, Bart is expelled after Principal Skinner tricks him and several bullies into hiding in a utility basement during an inspection, leading to a tractor accident involving Superintendent Chalmers. With Bart out of school, Marge tries homeschooling him and gets him hooked on reading through the book Johnny Tremain. Meanwhile, Lisa becomes increasingly outraged over Whacking Day, a tradition where townsfolk herd snakes into the town square and beat them to death, supposedly started by Jebediah Springfield. While researching for school, Bart discovers that Whacking Day was actually invented decades later as an excuse to persecute Irish immigrants, not by Jebediah at all. Bart and Lisa team up to save the snakes by luring them into their house using bass-heavy music, aided unexpectedly by Barry White, the disgusted celebrity Grand Marshal of the event. When the mob arrives to reclaim the snakes, Bart reveals the holiday's true racist origins, turning the crowd against the tradition and humiliating Mayor Quimby, who arrives with pre-killed snakes. In the end, Skinner reinstates Bart at school, but realizes in a panic that he's forgotten about the bullies still trapped in the basement. Guest starring Barry White. Notable quotes: Barry White: You people make me sick! | Bart: According to this, snakes hear by sensing vibrations in the ground. So, if we put our stereo speakers on the ground and play something with a lot of bass, those snakes will be in here like Oprah on a baked ham. | Grampa: I'm an old man, I hate everything but Matlock. Ooh, it's on now. | Homer: That's my boy! Mmm... beer... What!? | Principal Skinner: We give them their bikes, no one sues.

title: Marge in Chains (S4E21)
text: "Marge in Chains" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F20), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing May 6, 1993. When a batch of Japanese 'Juice Loosener' machines brings the Osaka Flu to Springfield, Marge is left exhausted from nursing her sick family and absentmindedly walks out of the Kwik-E-Mart without paying for a bottle of bourbon for Grampa. An overzealous police response leads to her arrest, and with only the bumbling Lionel Hutz to defend her, Marge is convicted and sentenced to thirty days in the Springfield Women's Prison. While she's locked up, Homer and the kids fall into domestic chaos, letting the house and their hygiene fall apart, and Marge struggles to adjust to prison life alongside her eccentric cellmate. Meanwhile, without Marge's famous marshmallow squares, the town's annual bake sale flops, leaving the Springfield Park Commission unable to afford a planned Abraham Lincoln statue and forced to settle for an unwanted Jimmy Carter statue instead, sparking a furious riot. Sensing a political disaster and hoping to win back the town's female voters, Mayor Quimby engineers Marge's early release from prison. Springfield welcomes her home with celebration, even repurposing the reviled Carter statue by topping it with a likeness of Marge's hair as a makeshift tribute. Guest starring David Crosby, Phil Hartman. Notable quotes: Homer: My name is Mr. Burns! | Chief Wiggum: All right, come out with your hands up, two cups of coffee, an auto freshener that says 'Capricorn', and something with coconut on it! | Flanders: Oh, the network slogan is true. Watch Fox and be damned for all eternity. | Lionel Hutz: I move for a bad court thingy. | Judge Snyder: This verdict is written on a cocktail napkin. And it still says "guilty." And "guilty" is spelled wrong!

title: Krusty Gets Kancelled (S4E22)
text: "Krusty Gets Kancelled" is an episode of Season 4 (production code 9F19), directed by David Silverman and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing May 13, 1993. A mysterious new TV character named Gabbo, a ventriloquist's dummy with a grating catchphrase, is heavily marketed across Springfield and soon debuts a show airing directly opposite Krusty the Clown's long-running program. Gabbo's slick production and stolen content, including snatching away Itchy & Scratchy, quickly siphon off Krusty's audience, and Krusty's own desperate attempt with a creepy dummy backfires horribly. Reduced to airing a cheap foreign cartoon called Worker and Parasite, Krusty's ratings collapse and his show is cancelled, sending him into a deep depression and financial ruin. Bart and Lisa, who never bought into the Gabbo hype, hatch a plan to revive Krusty's career by exposing Gabbo's off-camera rudeness and organizing a star-studded comeback special. The kids secretly capture Gabbo insulting his audience on a hot mic, discrediting him publicly, while lining up celebrities like Bette Midler, Johnny Carson, the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and Krusty's half-brother Luke Perry to appear on the special. A setback occurs when Krusty, misled into drinking fattening milkshakes he thought were diet shakes, balloons in weight right before the show, forcing the Simpson family to help whip him back into shape. The comeback special is a triumphant success, restoring Krusty's fame, and the episode ends with a celebratory party at Moe's Tavern where Bart toasts Krusty as the greatest entertainer in the world. Guest starring Johnny Carson, Hugh Hefner, Bette Midler, Luke Perry, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Elizabeth Taylor, Barry White. Notable quotes: Krusty: Ugh, 35 years in show business and already no one remembers me, just like what's-his-name and whose-it, and you know that guy, always wore a shirt? | Krusty: Pffp, know him?! He's my worthless half-brother. | Reverend Lovejoy: Everyone is saying "Gabbo this" and "Gabbo that" – but no one is saying "Worship this" and "Jericho that". | Moe: He is so stupid. And now back to the wall. | Krusty: I lost to Channel Ocho? What the hell is that?

title: Homer's Barbershop Quartet (S5E01)
text: "Homer's Barbershop Quartet" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 9F21), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jeff Martin, originally airing September 30, 1993. While browsing the Springfield Swap Meet, Bart and Lisa are stunned to find an old album cover featuring their father, prompting Homer to recount his brief stardom as a member of a barbershop quartet in 1985. He explains how his casual singing sessions at Moe's with Wiggum, Skinner, and Apu grew popular enough to attract a slick agent, who insisted Wiggum be replaced after a string of comically bad auditions from Grampa, Willie, and Jasper. Barney is discovered singing beautifully in the bar's restroom and joins the newly renamed group, the Be Sharps, while Apu reluctantly changes his surname for marquee purposes. Inspired by Marge's 'Baby on Board' sign, Homer writes a hit single that launches the group to national fame, culminating in a Grammy win and a star-studded performance at the Statue of Liberty's centennial, where Homer briefly meets George Harrison. As their celebrity grows, merchandising deals and creative tension mount, and Barney's new girlfriend—an Ono-esque artist—drives a wedge between the bandmates, echoing The Beatles' breakup. The group implodes after a bizarre experimental recording session, and each member quietly returns to his old life in Springfield. Back in the present, after dodging his kids' lingering questions, Homer joins his old bandmates for a spontaneous reunion performance atop Moe's Tavern, which is wryly interrupted by George Harrison's passing limousine. Guest starring David Crosby, George Harrison. Notable quotes: George Harrison: It's been done. | Homer: Oh, my god. OH, MY GOD! Where did you get that brownie? | Apu: That is a great dishonor to my ancestors and God...but okay. | Bart: Dad, I can't even remember what happened eight minutes ago. | Man: Yeah, they took her off the market after some kid put both his eyes out.

title: Cape Feare (S5E02)
text: "Cape Feare" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 9F22), directed by Rich Moore and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing October 7, 1993. Bart begins receiving anonymous, blood-written death threats, and while the family investigates, they discover most of them come from Sideshow Bob, currently up for parole. Despite his prison tattoos of Bart with a broken neck and 'Die Bart Die' on his chest, Bob convinces the parole board he's reformed and is released. He soon confronts the Simpsons at a movie theater, confirming he wrote the threats, prompting Marge to seek police help. Chief Wiggum enrolls the family in the Witness Relocation Program, renaming them the Thompsons and moving them to a houseboat at Terror Lake, unaware that Bob has secretly hitched a ride on the underside of their car. After a series of mishaps repeatedly injure Bob, he tracks the family down at their new home and eventually sneaks aboard their houseboat, cutting it loose and tying up the family before cornering Bart. Bart cleverly delays his own murder by asking Bob to perform the entire score of H.M.S. Pinafore, buying time as the boat drifts back into Springfield's jurisdiction. Just as Bob prepares to strike, the boat crashes into a rock, separating them long enough for the police to arrive and arrest Bob again. The family returns home to normal life, save for Grampa's bizarre transformation from missing his medication. Guest starring Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Notable quotes: Sideshow Bob: Very well, Bart. I shall send you to Heaven before I send you to Hell. | Homer: Oh my god, someone's trying to kill me! Oh wait, it's for Bart. | Bart: Who'd want to hurt me? I'm this century's Dennis the Menace. | Chief Wiggum: Sideshow Bob has no decency. He called me "Chief Piggum". | Sideshow Bob: Heavens No! That's German for 'the Bart, the'.

Homer: Oh my god, someone's trying to kill me! Oh wait, it's for Bart.

title: Homer Goes to College (S5E03)
text: "Homer Goes to College" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F02), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Conan O'Brien, originally airing October 14, 1993. When surprise inspectors from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission catch Homer causing a fake meltdown in their testing van, Mr. Burns is forced to get him enrolled at Springfield University for remedial physics training after every other college rejects him. Expecting a stereotypical campus full of jock-versus-nerd rivalries, Homer instead finds a laid-back, approachable dean, Bobby Peterson, who frustrates his preconceived notions of college life. After causing chaos in his nuclear physics class, Homer is assigned tutoring with three genuine nerds, whom he tries to loosen up with a beer-soaked road trip and later a prank involving kidnapping a rival school's pig mascot. The prank backfires when the nerds, not Homer, are caught and expelled thanks to the pig's politically connected owners, including former President Nixon. Guilt-ridden, Homer lets the homeless nerds stay with his family, but their annoying habits push Marge and Bart to the breaking point. Homer's plan to stage a heroic rescue of Dean Peterson to win back the nerds' enrollment goes wrong and Peterson ends up hospitalized, but Homer's honest confession moves him to reinstate the nerds. Homer initially cheats his way to passing grade via the nerds hacking the system, but Marge insists he retake the course honestly, and after a montage of classic college antics, he finally earns his diploma the right way—flashing the audience at graduation. Notable quotes: Homer: [singing] I am so smart. I am so smart. I am so smart. S-M-R-T... Uh, I mean S-M-A-R-T. | Mr. Burns: Hello, Simpson. My lawyers and I were in the neighborhood and thought we'd stop by. | Dean Peterson: I'm sorry, boys. I've never expelled anyone before, but that pig had some powerful friends. | Bart: So it's a prank you're looking for, is it? I'll give you your prank. | Homer: Ahh, the college road trip. What better way to spread beer-fueled mayhem.

Mr. Burns: Hello, Simpson. My lawyers and I were in the neighborhood and thought we'd stop by.
Dean Peterson: I'm sorry, boys. I've never expelled anyone before, but that pig had some powerful friends.
Bart: So it's a prank you're looking for, is it? I'll give you your prank.
Homer: Ahh, the college road trip. What better way to spread beer-fueled mayhem.

title: Rosebud (S5E04)
text: "Rosebud" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F01), directed by Wes Archer and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing October 21, 1993. Mr. Burns is haunted by dreams of Bobo, the teddy bear he abandoned as a child, and Smithers realizes his boss is desperate to reclaim it. Tracing the bear's bizarre journey through history—passing through the hands of Charles Lindbergh and Adolf Hitler before ending up frozen in a block of ice—Burns learns it has resurfaced in Springfield. Bart discovers the bear inside a bag of ice from the Kwik-E-Mart and brings it home, where Maggie instantly adopts it as her own. Homer sees a chance to cash in, planning to trade the bear to Burns for a fortune and a couple of Hawaiian islands, but Burns balks at actually paying up. Torn between greed and his daughter's attachment to the toy, Homer decides to keep Bobo, prompting a furious Burns to cut off Springfield's beer and television service until the bear is returned. The enraged townspeople force Homer to hand it over, but when they see how heartbroken Maggie is, they give it right back to her. Ultimately, Burns personally pleads with baby Maggie, and she willingly surrenders Bobo without the family receiving any reward. In a coda set a million years in the future, a robotic Burns fights off apes to reclaim the buried Bobo, with a now-robotic dog Smithers in pursuit. Guest starring Joey Ramone, Johnny Ramone, C. J. Ramone, Marky Ramone. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: Have the Rolling Stones killed. | Homer: Well, I also do a delightful impression of him. I paint a frowny face on my butt and pull down my pants! | Homer: Marge, the comedy roast is an American tradition. It's what gives us the freedom to criticize our social betters. | Nelson: My old man can't get a beer because his old man won't give a bear to another old man! Let's get him! | Mr. Burns: Bobo? Duh..uh, I meant Lobo...Sherrif Lobo, they should have never canceled that show.

Homer: Well, I also do a delightful impression of him. I paint a frowny face on my butt and pull down my pants!
Homer: Marge, the comedy roast is an American tradition. It's what gives us the freedom to criticize our social betters.

Mr. Burns: Bobo? Duh..uh, I meant Lobo...Sherrif Lobo, they should have never canceled that show.

title: Treehouse of Horror IV (S5E05)
text: "Treehouse of Horror IV" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F04), directed by David Silverman and written by Conan O'Brien, Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, Greg Daniels, Dan McGrath, Bill Canterbury, originally airing October 28, 1993. This Halloween special features three horror-themed vignettes framed by Bart's mock-scary introductions. In 'The Devil and Homer Simpson,' Homer sells his soul to Flanders-as-the-Devil for a donut, leading to a courtroom battle over the contract's validity that Marge ultimately wins by revealing Homer already pledged his soul to her, though the Devil gets a final petty revenge by turning Homer's head into a donut. In 'Terror at 5 1/2 Feet,' Bart becomes convinced a gremlin is destroying the school bus, but no one believes him until his warning proves true, resulting in Bart being sent to a mental institution despite being vindicated. In 'Bart Simpson's Dracula,' the family visits Mr. Burns, who turns out to be a vampire, and he bites Bart, turning him into one of the undead. Lisa discovers the truth and convinces the family to stake Burns to save Bart, but the twist ending reveals that Marge has secretly been the family's true vampire matriarch all along. Each segment blends comedic horror tropes with the show's usual family dynamics, and the episode closes with a lighthearted Peanuts-style musical sign-off. Notable quotes: Homer: Mmmm ... forbidden donut. | Flanders the Devil: It's always the one you least suspect! | Mr. Burns: Hmm... Who's that goat-legged fellow? I like the cut of his jib. | Skinner: The only monster on this bus is a lack of proper respect for the rules. | Homer: They're dogs! And they're playing poker! [crazed laughter] This installment is made up of 6 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 4): "Wraparound part 1", "The Devil and Homer Simpson", "Terror at 5 1/2 Feet", "Wraparound part 2", "Bart Simpson's Dracula", and "Title Cards".
quotes: Homer: Mmmm ... forbidden donut.
Flanders the Devil: It's always the one you least suspect!
Mr. Burns: Hmm... Who's that goat-legged fellow? I like the cut of his jib.
Skinner: The only monster on this bus is a lack of proper respect for the rules.
Homer: They're dogs! And they're playing poker! [crazed laughter]

title: Marge on the Lam (S5E06)
text: "Marge on the Lam" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F03), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Bill Canterbury, originally airing November 4, 1993. Marge wins ballet tickets and Homer reluctantly agrees to go, but he gets both arms stuck in vending machines at the plant and misses the show. Marge instead spends the evening with her neighbor Ruth Powers, and the two hit it off so well that Marge decides to go out with her again the following night. Feeling excluded and mocked by his kids, Homer tries to arrange his own night out but fails to find anyone available, so he hires the inept lawyer Lionel Hutz to babysit while he wanders Springfield alone. Meanwhile Marge and Ruth go line dancing, shoot up a farmer's antique can collection, and drive around in Ruth's car, which turns out to be stolen from her ex-husband. When Chief Wiggum tries to pull them over, Ruth flees, sparking a wild, long-distance car chase involving Homer riding along with Wiggum. The chase ends when Homer pleads with Marge over a megaphone to stop before a canyon, and though Wiggum's car plunges in, everyone survives thanks to a landfill cushioning the fall. In the aftermath, Ruth's charges are dropped and her ex is ordered to pay child support, Marge is fined for the shot-up cans, and Homer happily gets shipped off to a military testing camp. Guest starring George Fenneman, Phil Hartman, Pamela Reed. Notable quotes: Ruth Powers: Tonight has nothing to do with 'nice'. | Homer: Come on, Marge, it's fun to smash things! | Lisa: I always knew someday Mom would violently rise up and cast off the shackles of our male oppressors. | Chief Wiggum: Quiet! I can't hear the eggs. | Lionel Hutz: Mr. Simpson, I was just going through your garbage, and I couldn't help overhearing that you need a babysitter. Of course, being a highly-skilled attorney, my fee is $175 an hour.

Homer: Come on, Marge, it's fun to smash things!
Lisa: I always knew someday Mom would violently rise up and cast off the shackles of our male oppressors.

title: Bart's Inner Child (S5E07)
text: "Bart's Inner Child" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F05), directed by Bob Anderson and written by George Meyer, originally airing November 11, 1993. After Homer's ill-fated attempt to profit from a backyard trampoline ends in injuries and marital strife, Marge turns to a self-help infomercial featuring guru Brad Goodman for guidance. Homer and Marge apply his feel-good philosophy at home, and encouraged by the results, they bring Bart to one of Goodman's live seminars hoping to fix his behavior. Instead, Bart's outspoken heckling during the event inspires Goodman to declare Bart a model of living freely and following one's inner child, and soon the whole town adopts Bart as their icon of impulsive self-expression. Springfield descends into chaos as citizens abandon responsibility and duty in favor of doing whatever they feel, capped by a disastrous unsupervised carnival where a neglected Ferris wheel breaks loose and crashes into the zoo, releasing wild animals into the streets. As pandemonium spreads, the townspeople turn their anger on Bart, blaming him for the mess, and a mob forms to confront him until Homer swoops in to rescue his son. Having lost interest in getting revenge, the mob simply wanders off toward the old mill for cider instead. Back home, the family reflects on the ordeal, with Lisa clarifying that true self-improvement takes real effort rather than shortcuts, before they settle back into their normal routine watching TV together. Guest starring Albert Brooks as Brad Goodman, James Brown as himself, Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Homer: Checkmate, Mr. Trampoline. | Homer: All right. All right, you win for now ... But someday you'll rust! Rust, I tell ya! | Snake: All right! I got me a bed. | Homer: Tramampoline! Trambomboline! | Skinner: I'M A GROWN MAN NOW! AND I CAN RUN MY OWN LIFE!!!
quotes: Homer: Checkmate, Mr. Trampoline.
Homer: All right. All right, you win for now ... But someday you'll rust! Rust, I tell ya!
Snake: All right! I got me a bed.
Homer: Tramampoline! Trambomboline!

title: Boy-Scoutz 'n the Hood (S5E08)
text: "Boy-Scoutz 'n the Hood" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F06), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Dan McGrath, originally airing November 18, 1993. After finding a stray twenty-dollar bill, Bart and Milhouse buy an all-syrup Squishee and go on a sugar-fueled rampage through Springfield, blacking out by the end of the night. Bart wakes up with no memory of the previous evening and discovers he accidentally joined the Junior Campers, while Milhouse ends up with a shaved head after a prank gone wrong. Reluctant at first, Bart warms up to the group once he realizes its skills are useful for pranking Homer and earning badges. When the father-son rafting trip arrives, Bart dreads bringing his embarrassing dad along, and his fears are confirmed when Homer's incompetence—losing the map, wasting supplies, and shooting down a rescue plane—sends their raft drifting out to the open ocean with Ned Flanders and Rod in tow. Just as their situation turns dire, Homer's keen sense of smell leads them to an unlikely oasis: a Krusty Burger built on an offshore oil rig. Meanwhile, the rest of the Junior Camper troop, led by celebrity dad Ernest Borgnine, takes the correct river fork but ends up terrorized by hillbillies and stalked by a mysterious attacker in the woods, vanishing without explanation by episode's end. Guest starring Ernest Borgnine. Notable quotes: Homer: Awww ... 20 dollars!? I wanted a peanut. | Homer's Brain: 20 dollars can buy many peanuts! | Homer: Mmm... free goo. | Homer: Ooh, floor pie! | Homer: Bring me 700 Krusty burgers!

title: The Last Temptation of Homer (S5E09)
text: "The Last Temptation of Homer" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F07), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Frank Mula, originally airing December 9, 1993. After a parking-lot prank backfires on him, Bart is punished by Mrs. Krabappel, leading Marge to have him checked by Dr. Hibbert, who diagnoses a slew of ailments and turns Bart into a bespectacled, orthopedic-shoed nerd who becomes a target for bullies. At the power plant, a horseplay accident causes a meltdown and reveals the emergency exit is only painted on, prompting Mr. Burns to fire Charlie for complaining rather than fix the problem. Government pressure forces Burns to hire a female employee, and he brings on Mindy Simmons, a beautiful redhead who shares eerily identical tastes with Homer, from doughnuts to beer to television. Homer becomes consumed with guilt and desire, seeking advice from Barney and even calling a marital hotline, all while battling his conscience and vivid hallucinations about Mindy. Meanwhile, Bart finds temporary refuge among fellow nerds led by Martin until his two weeks of forced nerd-dom end and the bullying resumes. When Homer and Mindy are chosen to represent the plant at an energy convention in Capital City, they end up sharing a hotel room and are crowned King and Queen of Energy, intensifying Homer's fear that he might leave Marge. After an unsettling fortune cookie and a heartfelt talk with Mindy, Homer resists temptation, and Marge arrives at the hotel just as Mindy leaves, allowing Homer to reaffirm his love for her through song, comically undercut by him knocking out a hotel worker. Guest starring Werner Klemperer as Colonel Klink, Michelle Pfeiffer as Mindy Simmons. Notable quotes: Bart: The beauty of it is each parking space is a mere one foot narrower. Indistinguishable to the naked eye. But therin lies the game. | Edna: I'm in the lines! You got a problem, go tell your mama. | Mr. Burns: Why, that's a fabulous idea. Anything else you'd like? How about real lead in the radiation shields? Urinal cakes, maybe? Smithers, throw this at him. | Homer: Foul temptress. I'll bet she thinks Ziggy's gotten too preachy, too! | Homer: Hello, hotline? I'm very tempted by another woman!

title: Homer the Vigilante (S5E11)
text: "Homer the Vigilante" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F09), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing January 6, 1994. A cat burglar begins terrorizing Springfield, stealing valuables and leaving a calling card, including Lisa's saxophone, while the overwhelmed police remain unable to catch him. Frustrated, Homer forms a neighborhood vigilante group that quickly becomes reckless and causes more chaos than the crimes it's meant to prevent. During a planned stakeout at the museum to protect a giant zirconium, Homer gets distracted by underage drinking kids and gets drunk, allowing the burglar to steal the gem uninterrupted. Disgraced and abandoned by his group, Homer is redeemed when Grampa reveals that the thief is Molloy, a fellow resident at the retirement home, and helps expose him by showing off the stolen zirconium in his room. Molloy calmly confesses and returns the stolen goods, and though the townspeople are moved by his apology, Chief Wiggum insists on justice and jails him. Molloy then teases the town with cryptic clues about hidden treasure buried under a “Big T,” sparking a chaotic town-wide treasure hunt. The search leads to a palm tree shaped like a T, where they discover only a note revealing that the treasure never existed and that Molloy has already escaped from jail. Despite this, Mayor Quimby stubbornly orders everyone to keep digging. Guest starring Sam Neill as Molloy. Notable quotes: Homer: Oh my God! Underage kids drinking without a permit! | Chief Wiggum: NO, no, Dig UP Stupid! | Ned Flanders: Welcome, neighbors. Since the police can't seem to get off their dufferoonies to do something about this burglarino, I think it's time we started our own neighborhood watch... eroony! | Homer: Oh people can come up with statistics to prove anything Kent, forfty per cent of all people know that. | Marge: I don't think the guns are a good idea.

Chief Wiggum: NO, no, Dig UP Stupid!
Ned Flanders: Welcome, neighbors. Since the police can't seem to get off their dufferoonies to do something about this burglarino, I think it's time we started our own neighborhood watch... eroony!
Homer: Oh people can come up with statistics to prove anything Kent, forfty per cent of all people know that.
Marge: I don't think the guns are a good idea.

title: Bart Gets Famous (S5E12)
text: "Bart Gets Famous" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F11), directed by Susie Dietter and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 3, 1994. During a school field trip to the local box factory, Bart sneaks away out of boredom and wanders into the nearby Channel 6 studio. There he runs into Krusty the Clown, who is furious that his Danish pastry hasn't arrived, so Bart steals one from Kent Brockman to appease him and is rewarded with a job as Krusty's personal assistant. Back at school, Bart's disappearance sends Skinner and eventually Homer into a panic, fearing he was killed in the factory machinery, but he turns up safe. As Krusty's overworked and unappreciated gofer, Bart grows tired of the gig until Krusty lets him deliver one line on air; Bart fumbles it, wrecks the set, and blurts out "I didn't do it," which becomes an instant sensation with the studio audience. Krusty quickly exploits the catchphrase, turning Bart into a media sensation with merchandise and talk-show appearances, including an interview with Conan O'Brien where Bart tries to seem more substantial than just a fad. Worried his fame is fleeting, Bart's fears prove true as the phrase's novelty wears off and the public loses interest. Marge presents Bart with a keepsake box of mementos from his brief stardom, and later, when Homer breaks a lamp, the family reflexively responds with their own signature catchphrases, highlighting that Lisa is the only one without one, leaving her characteristically unimpressed by the whole spectacle. Guest starring Conan O'Brien as himself. Notable quotes: Lisa: If I ever become famous, I want it to be for something worthwhile, not because of some obnoxious fad. | Bart: Have any of your workers ever had their hands cut off by the machinery? | Bart: And then the hand started crawling around and try to strangle everybody? | Homer: What kind of a catchphrase is that? | Lisa: ...if anyone wants me, I'll be in my room.
quotes: Lisa: If I ever become famous, I want it to be for something worthwhile, not because of some obnoxious fad.
Bart: Have any of your workers ever had their hands cut off by the machinery?
Bart: And then the hand started crawling around and try to strangle everybody?
Homer: What kind of a catchphrase is that?
Lisa: ...if anyone wants me, I'll be in my room.

title: Homer and Apu (S5E13)
text: "Homer and Apu" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F10), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Greg Daniels, originally airing February 10, 1994. After eating expired hot dogs from the Kwik-E-Mart and getting food poisoning, Homer decides to expose Apu on a consumer-complaint TV show by wearing a hidden camera hat. The footage catches Apu putting a dropped hot dog back on the rack, and the manager fires him on the spot. A guilt-ridden Homer lets the newly unemployed Apu stay at the Simpson house, where the family slowly warms to his help around the home. Meanwhile, the Kwik-E-Mart hires actor James Woods to work the counter as research for an upcoming film role. Still unable to shake his longing for the store, Apu convinces Homer to accompany him to India to petition the Kwik-E-Mart's corporate headquarters for his old job back, but Homer wastes their limited questions with the CEO and the trip ends in a fistfight between the two friends. Back in Springfield, Apu returns to the Kwik-E-Mart to confront his past and meets an admiring James Woods, only for a robber to burst in and shoot at Woods. Apu heroically takes the bullet, which ricochets harmlessly off another bullet already lodged in his chest from a prior robbery, and a grateful Woods arranges for Apu to get his job back before departing for his next acting gig. Guest starring James Woods as himself. Notable quotes: Apu: Surprisingly expensive. | Homer: No, don't kill me! I didn't know there was film in that camera in that hat! I was unaware! I WAS UNAWAAARE! | Apu: I am selling only the concept of karmic realignment. | Homer: Apu, if it'll make you feel any better, I've learned that life is one crushing defeat after another until you just wish Flanders was dead. | Apu: Ah! The searing kiss of hot lead—how I missed you! I mean, I think I'm dying.

Apu: I am selling only the concept of karmic realignment.

Apu: Ah! The searing kiss of hot lead—how I missed you! I mean, I think I'm dying.

title: Lisa vs. Malibu Stacy (S5E14)
text: "Lisa vs. Malibu Stacy" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F12), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing February 17, 1994. After witnessing his idol Ben Matlock get mobbed at the opening of a geriatric center, Grampa Simpson becomes fixated on his own mortality and hands out early inheritances, giving Lisa his old letters and the rest of the family a box of silver dollars. At the mall, Lisa is swept up in the frenzy over the new Talking Malibu Stacy doll, only to be horrified by its shallow, sexist catchphrases, prompting her to publicly denounce the toy and hurl it out a window. Frustrated that no one shares her outrage, Lisa complains to the toy company and tours its factory, uncovering the doll's sexist design history, while Grampa takes a humiliating job at Krusty Burger before quitting in a fit of senior solidarity. Determined to create something better, Lisa tracks down Stacy Lovell, the doll's reclusive original creator, and convinces her to help make an alternative toy. Together they produce Lisa Lionheart, a doll voiced by Lisa herself with empowering messages for girls, which quietly hits shelves amid a wave of local media attention. On release day, the rival toy company sabotages Lisa's efforts by rolling out a 'new' Malibu Stacy with just a different hat, and most girls abandon Lisa Lionheart for the familiar doll. Only one little girl chooses Lisa's doll, but Lisa decides that reaching even one child makes the effort worthwhile, while Stacy Lovell cynically hopes the girl's family will keep spending money on it. Guest starring Kathleen Turner as Stacy Lovell. Notable quotes: Malibu Stacy: I wish they taught shopping in school! | Malibu Stacy: Let's bake some cookies for the boys! | Malibu Stacy: Don't ask me, I'm just a girl. | Bart: Right on! Say it, sister. | Homer: Dad, I love you, but you're a weird, sore-headed old crank and nobody likes you!
quotes: Malibu Stacy: I wish they taught shopping in school!
Malibu Stacy: Let's bake some cookies for the boys!

title: Deep Space Homer (S5E15)
text: "Deep Space Homer" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F13), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by David Mirkin, originally airing February 24, 1994. Homer is furious when the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant's coveted 'Worker of the Week' award goes to an inanimate carbon rod instead of him, leaving him feeling unappreciated. Around the same time, NASA is worried about declining public interest in its space program and decides to boost ratings by sending an ordinary, relatable citizen into orbit. When Homer calls NASA to complain about boring shuttle broadcasts, officials mistake his gripe for the perfect everyman attitude and recruit him, though he initially tries to pin the call on Barney. Homer and Barney are pitted against each other in astronaut training, and Barney's natural talent while sober nearly wins him the seat until a bout of drinking ruins his chances, leaving Homer to go to space by default despite his fear. Once aboard the shuttle with Buzz Aldrin and another astronaut, Homer's smuggled potato chips lead to a genuine crisis when ants stowed away in an ant farm overrun the ship's systems. With help from a radio pep-talk by James Taylor, the crew vents the ants into space, but Homer's mishandling of the airlock nearly kills him before he seals the hatch shut using the same carbon rod that once snubbed him. Though Homer saves the mission, the media instead hails the carbon rod as the true hero of the flight, giving it parades and magazine covers while Homer returns home to a quieter, more personal appreciation from his family. Guest starring Buzz Aldrin as himself, James Taylor as himself. Notable quotes: Kent Brockman: And I, for one, welcome our new insect overlords. | Jack Stillwater: Gentlemen, you've both worked very hard, and in a way, you're both winners. But in another more accurate way, Barney is the winner. | Marge: When I found out about this, I went through a range of emotions. First I was nervous, then anxious, then wary, then apprehensive, then... kind of sleepy, then worried, and then concerned. | Dr. Babcock: Maybe we should finally tell them the big secret, that all the chimps we sent into space came back super intelligent. | Homer: Marge, I don't really wanna go through with this. But being an astronaut is how I got you to respect me!
quotes: Kent Brockman: And I, for one, welcome our new insect overlords.
Jack Stillwater: Gentlemen, you've both worked very hard, and in a way, you're both winners. But in another more accurate way, Barney is the winner.
Marge: When I found out about this, I went through a range of emotions. First I was nervous, then anxious, then wary, then apprehensive, then... kind of sleepy, then worried, and then concerned.
Dr. Babcock: Maybe we should finally tell them the big secret, that all the chimps we sent into space came back super intelligent.
Homer: Marge, I don't really wanna go through with this. But being an astronaut is how I got you to respect me!

title: Homer Loves Flanders (S5E16)
text: "Homer Loves Flanders" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F14), directed by Wes Archer and written by David Richardson, originally airing March 17, 1994. Homer is desperate to attend the big Pigskin Classic football game but loses out on tickets when a scalper buys the entire allotment. When Ned Flanders unexpectedly wins tickets on the radio, he generously invites Homer along, and the two end up having a wonderful time together, capped off by Ned securing Homer an autographed football. Overwhelmed with gratitude, Homer becomes obsessively devoted to Ned, showering him and his family with attention to the point of exhaustion, while Bart and Lisa worry that their father's newfound niceness will ruin the family's usual chaotic dynamic. Tensions boil over during a family outing to Lake Springfield, where Homer's clumsy enthusiasm wrecks Ned's boat and car and sparks a food fight, pushing Ned to the breaking point. Ned tries to flee Homer's suffocating friendship, leading to a frantic car chase that ends with Chief Wiggum pulling him over and humiliating him with a roadside sobriety test just as the church bus passes by. Ashamed, the Flanders family is shunned at church the next Sunday, but Homer's heartfelt public apology repairs the rift and restores goodwill between the two families. By the next week, however, everything reverts to normal, with Homer back to disliking Ned and the Simpsons once again caught up in a bizarre adventure, this time spending the night in a haunted house. If this were a more perfect world, we'd all be known as the Flimpsons. | Homer: Can't talk, seeing Flanders. title: Bart Gets an Elephant (S5E17)
text: "Bart Gets an Elephant" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F15), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 31, 1994. While the Simpson family is forced by Marge to clean the house, Bart becomes obsessed with winning a radio contest on KBBL by repeatedly answering the phone with the station's catchphrase. He finally wins and is given a choice between $10,000 in cash or an elephant, and to his family's horror he picks the elephant, naming him Stampy. The novelty quickly wears off as Stampy terrifies the pets, costs a fortune to feed, and generally wreaks havoc around the house, souring Homer and Marge on the idea while Bart and Lisa remain attached to him. Facing mounting expenses, Homer rejects donating Stampy to a nature preserve for free and instead strikes a deal with a shady ivory dealer, Mr. Blackheart, to sell the elephant. Before the sale can happen, Stampy escapes and rampages through Springfield, and the family searches for him after Police Chief Wiggum dismisses their reports. They find Stampy mourning at the Springfield Tar Pits, and when Homer blurts out his plan to have Stampy's tusks turned into piano keys, the family is disgusted. Homer then accidentally sinks into the tar pit himself, and after a chaotic rescue involving a self-immolating Barney, Stampy saves Homer's life. Moved by this, and pushed by his family, Homer finally agrees to donate Stampy to the elephant preserve instead of selling him, though he remains bitter about not profiting from the ordeal. Can't we just buy a new house? | Marge: Aw, cleaning doesn't have to be a chore. Just work to the music!

title: Burns' Heir (S5E18)
text: "Burns' Heir" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F16), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jace Richdale, originally airing April 14, 1994. After nearly drowning in his bathtub, an anxious Mr. Burns decides he needs to name an heir to safeguard the future of his power plant. He holds auditions for Springfield's children, cruelly rejecting most of them, including Bart, whom he insults with a mechanical kicking device. When Bart retaliates by vandalizing Burns' mansion, the old man is so impressed by his malice that he names Bart his heir. Homer is thrilled, and Bart soon moves in with Burns, enjoying luxuries like private pizza deliveries from Krusty. When Bart briefly returns home, he finds his family's modest life unsatisfying and goes back to Burns, prompting a desperate but failed rescue attempt involving the police, incompetent lawyer Lionel Hutz, and a bumbling private investigator scheme that leaves Hans Moleman brainwashed into thinking he's a Simpson. Burns manipulates Bart further by staging a fake video of his family expressing indifference toward him, but Bart begins to feel isolated despite the plant's amusing power games, such as firing employees for sport. When ordered to fire Homer, Bart refuses and instead tries to fire Burns himself, causing Burns to disown him as his heir. Bart returns home to his real family, who reveal Burns' deception, and the episode ends with the Simpsons reconciling — plus Homer jokingly welcoming Hans Moleman as a new 'brother.' Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: Look, Smithers -- a creature of pure malevolence. He's the perfect one to suckle at my proverbial teat. | Nelson: Give me your fortune or I'll pound your withered old face in! | Mr. Burns: Ooh, I like his energy. Put him on the callback list. | Homer: Can I keep him anyway, huh, huh? | Homer: There sure is. Kids, you tried your best, and you failed miserably. The lesson is, "Never Try."

title: Sweet Seymour Skinner's Baadasssss Song (S5E19)
text: "Sweet Seymour Skinner's Baadasssss Song" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F18), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing April 28, 1994. On show-and-tell day, Bart brings Santa's Little Helper to Springfield Elementary, and the dog escapes into the school's air vents, causing chaos. When Superintendent Chalmers witnesses the ensuing pandemonium, he immediately fires Principal Skinner, leaving Bart wracked with guilt. Skinner re-enlists in the Army but forms an unlikely, easygoing friendship with Bart, even sharing meals at Luigi's. Meanwhile, Ned Flanders takes over as principal and proves disastrously permissive, letting the students run wild, vandalize school property, and even cage Martin Prince. Determined to fix what he broke, Bart tries repeatedly to convince Chalmers that Flanders is unfit for the job, but Chalmers dismisses his complaints during an inspection. It's only when Chalmers overhears Flanders proselytizing over the intercom that he fires him for violating the separation of church and state. Skinner is reinstated as principal, and though he and Bart have grown close, they both recognize their friendship can't continue now that the old order is restored, so they part on good terms. Um, I'm real sorry about my dog getting you fired, and biting you, and then getting it on with your leg. | Willie: There's nary an animal alive that out-run a greased Scotsman. | Skinner: That's not true. I can buy a new pair! [checks his wallet] No I can't. I needed those, I really did. | Ralph: [sees Santa's Little Helper in the airduct] Um, Miss Hoover? There's a dog in the vent. | Luigi: Get some red crap for the ugly kid-a!

title: The Boy Who Knew Too Much (S5E20)
keys: the boy who knew too much
text: "The Boy Who Knew Too Much" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F19), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing May 5, 1994. Bart skips school by faking a dentist appointment, evading Principal Skinner and hitching a ride with the arrogant, New England-accented Freddy Quimby, nephew of Mayor Quimby. At Freddy's birthday lunch, Freddy bullies a French waiter over the pronunciation of 'chowder,' and Bart, hiding nearby, overhears violent noises and sees the injured waiter afterward. Freddy is arrested for the assault and put on trial, while Homer is chosen for jury duty on the same case. Mayor Quimby bribes witnesses like Moe to give false testimony, and courtroom tempers flare when Freddy explodes in a rage about the word 'chowder,' making him look guilty. Homer manipulates the jury into a deadlock so they can be sequestered at a hotel, rooming with Skinner, while Bart wrestles with guilt over staying silent since testifying would expose his truancy. With encouragement from Lisa, Bart finally takes the stand and reveals that the waiter's injuries were actually the result of his own clumsiness after Freddy stormed off. Freddy is cleared of the charges, but Bart is punished with months of detention for skipping school. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: Oh my God! Someone's taken a bite out of the big Rice Krispie square! Oh yeah, and the waiter's been brutally beaten. | Homer: Marge, it was horrible. Everyone was against me in that jury room. But I stood by the courage of my convictions and I prevailed. I believe Freddy Quimby should walk out of here a free hotel. | Bart: I can't let Dad see me playing hooky!

title: Lady Bouvier's Lover (S5E21)
text: "Lady Bouvier's Lover" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F21), directed by Wes Archer and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing May 12, 1994. During Maggie's first birthday party, Marge notices that both her mother Jacqueline and Homer's father Abe seem lonely, so she arranges for them to spend time together. Grampa and Mrs. Bouvier hit it off and begin dating, but their budding romance is disrupted when Mr. Burns meets Jacqueline and is instantly smitten by her, sweeping her off her feet with wealth and charm despite Smithers' jealousy and Marge's disapproval. Meanwhile, Bart becomes obsessed with buying an expensive Itchy & Scratchy animation cel off a TV shopping channel using Homer's credit card, only to receive a disappointing severed cartoon arm instead of a full image; he later gets reimbursed by Mr. Burns for the mix-up. As Burns and Jacqueline's wedding approaches, Grampa grows increasingly heartbroken watching the woman he loves prepare to marry his old rival. On the wedding day, Grampa dramatically bursts into the ceremony, echoing a famous scene from 'The Graduate,' pleading with Jacqueline not to go through with the marriage. In the end, Jacqueline realizes she doesn't want to marry either man and leaves with Grampa on a bus, both uncertain but free, ending the episode on an ambiguous, comedic note about lonely hearts in old age. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Comic Book Guy: This – this is a Snagglepuss drawn by Hig Heisler; it is worth something. title: Secrets of a Successful Marriage (S5E22)
text: "Secrets of a Successful Marriage" is an episode of Season 5 (production code 1F20), directed by Carlos Baeza and written by Greg Daniels, originally airing May 19, 1994. After being called slow during a poker game at Lenny's house, Homer worries about his intelligence and heads to the Adult Education Annex to take a class. Finding all his friends teaching courses instead of learning, he decides he wants to teach one too, and the center's manager convinces him to lead a class called Secrets of a Successful Marriage since he's actually married. Lacking real advice, Homer resorts to sharing embarrassing private stories about his relationship with Marge, which infuriates her when she finds out and forces him to promise to stop. He can't resist continuing, even inviting his students over for dinner to observe a real marriage in action, which pushes Marge over the edge and gets him thrown out of the house. Living alone in the treehouse, Homer spirals into squalor and delusion, eventually building a makeshift replacement wife out of a plant and old clothes. On the verge of giving up on the marriage entirely, he has a moment of clarity and tells Marge that what he offers her is total, helpless dependence on her. Though she doesn't see this as a compliment at first, his honesty about being unable to survive without her trust wins her over, and after only a day apart, she forgives him and lets him return home. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Homer: Good news, Lisa. I don't need your mother anymore. I've created a replacement that's superior to her in almost every way! | Homer: Lisa! You will respect your new mother. Now, give her a kiss! BURNS OUT OF THIS!!!! *GAHN!! | Bart: Wow, I've never seen Mom so mad at Homer before.

title: Bart of Darkness (S6E01)
text: "Bart of Darkness" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 1F22), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Dan McGrath, originally airing September 4, 1994. During a scorching summer, the Simpsons' fridge dies and Otto's Pool-Mobile visit only makes the kids crave a pool of their own. After a botched first attempt yields a barn instead of a pool, the family successfully builds one, instantly making Bart and Lisa the most popular kids in the neighborhood. Bart breaks his leg attempting a treehouse dive into the pool after being distracted by Nelson, leaving him housebound while Lisa enjoys the social spotlight. Bored and increasingly isolated, Bart uses Lisa's telescope to spy on the neighbors and becomes convinced he's witnessed Ned Flanders murdering his wife and burying her body. As his paranoia grows, Bart fears Ned intends to kill Rod and Todd next, and later believes Lisa is in danger when she sneaks into the Flanders house to investigate and Ned returns home carrying an axe. Bart drags himself across town on his broken leg to rescue her, only to discover Ned was merely mounting the axe as decoration. The 'murder' turns out to be Ned's panicked burial of Maude's overwatered ficus plant, and Maude herself was simply away at Bible camp the whole time. Meanwhile, Martin Prince's rival pool becomes the neighborhood hotspot until it bursts from overcrowding, restoring Bart and Lisa's status once things return to normal. I've got friends now. I don't need you anymore.

title: Lisa's Rival (S6E02)
text: "Lisa's Rival" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 1F17), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Mike Scully, originally airing September 11, 1994. Lisa's confidence is shattered when Allison Taylor, a brilliant new student who matches or surpasses her in academics and saxophone skill, joins her class at Springfield Elementary. As jealousy consumes her, Lisa struggles to maintain a friendly facade while secretly resenting Allison's talents, especially after losing First Chair to her in band. Tensions peak during the school's Diorama-rama competition, where Lisa, egged on by Bart, sabotages Allison's Edgar Allan Poe-themed diorama by swapping it with one containing a rotting cow's heart. When Principal Skinner publicly humiliates Allison over the ruined project, Lisa's guilt forces her to confess, and both girls end up losing the contest to Ralph Wiggum's sentimental Star Wars diorama. In the end, Lisa and Allison bond over their shared experience and become genuine friends. Meanwhile, Homer discovers an overturned truck spilling sugar and greedily hauls off hundreds of pounds of it, hoping to profit from the windfall. His attempts to sell or exploit the sugar go nowhere, and the situation worsens when it attracts a swarm of bees from a local apiary. Just as beekeepers offer to pay Homer for the bees' return, a rainstorm dissolves the sugar, causing the bees to leave on their own and leaving Homer's scheme for naught. A minor subplot has Bart tormenting Milhouse by falsely reporting him as a fugitive on a look-alike TV crime show. Guest starring Winona Ryder as Allison Taylor. I mean stop blowing your sax, your sax, stop it. | Lisa: I never made Miss Hoover "yowie." | Homer: Ooh, a blasting cap.

title: Another Simpsons Clip Show (S6E03)
text: "Another Simpsons Clip Show" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F33), directed by David Silverman and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing September 25, 1994. One night Marge reads The Bridges of Madison County and, unsettled by its passion, wakes Homer to ask whether romance has faded from their marriage. He responds by grumbling and tossing the book into their oddly placed bedroom fireplace, and the two bicker before falling back asleep. The next morning Marge insists the family sit down together to talk about love and romance, hoping to reconnect emotionally with everyone. Instead of new stories, each family member dredges up old memories of failed romantic entanglements, shown through clips from previous episodes. Homer and Marge recall his flirtation with Mindy Simmons and Marge's near-affair with Jacques the bowling instructor, while other past crushes and heartbreaks are revisited as well. The children, especially Bart and Lisa, grow cynical about love, comparing the exercise to a rehashed Itchy & Scratchy episode made of old footage. Just when the conversation seems to fall apart, Homer redeems the moment by recounting the story of how he and Marge first fell in love. In the end, Bart and Lisa lose interest and wander off to watch cartoons, while Homer and Marge share a quiet, affectionate moment together. Guest starring Albert Brooks as Jacques, Sara Gilbert as Laura Powers, Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob, Jon Lovitz as Artie Ziff, Michelle Pfeiffer as Mindy Simmons, Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. title: Itchy & Scratchy Land (S6E04)
text: "Itchy & Scratchy Land" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F01), directed by Wesley Archer and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing October 2, 1994. Bart and Lisa see a commercial for the new Itchy & Scratchy Land theme park and beg their parents to take them, overriding Marge's plan for a quiet bird sanctuary vacation once they learn there's an adult-oriented area called Parents' Island. The family flies in by helicopter and Marge is uneasy about the park's extreme violence-themed attractions, though she initially enjoys herself while Homer relaxes at Parents' Island. Bart and Lisa explore rides and a documentary theater showcasing classic Itchy & Scratchy cartoons, but the trip sours when Bart sets off a stink bomb on a costumed employee and Homer kicks an Itchy mascot, leading to both being arrested and Marge mortified in front of other parkgoers. Meanwhile, Professor Frink, who oversees the park's animatronic robots, warns that chaos theory predicts the robots will inevitably turn against people—moments before they do exactly that. As Marge scolds Bart and Homer after their release, the power goes out and a horde of malfunctioning Itchy and Scratchy robots begins attacking guests. Homer discovers that camera flashes short-circuit the robots, so the family raids a gift shop for cameras and uses the flashes to destroy the entire robotic army. Hailed as heroes for saving the park, the Simpsons agree it was the best vacation ever, but decide never to mention it again. Notable quotes: Homer: Oh, everything's too damned expensive these days. Look at this Bible I just got. Fifteen bucks! And talk about a preachy book! Everybody's a sinner except for this guy. | Homer: Okay, let's make a pact. title: Sideshow Bob Roberts (S6E05)
text: "Sideshow Bob Roberts" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F02), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing October 9, 1994. After calling into right-wing radio host Birch Barlow's show to complain about prison conditions, Sideshow Bob becomes a media sensation and is released by a pressured Mayor Quimby. Bob then decides to run for mayor himself, prompting Bart and Lisa to campaign hard for Quimby, who is defending his job despite his own checkered record. Bob wins the election by an overwhelming, suspicious margin, and soon after takes office, he orders a new expressway built directly through the Simpsons' neighborhood, threatening their home. Convinced something is amiss, Bart and Lisa investigate the vote and are secretly tipped off by Waylon Smithers, leading them to discover that nearly all of Bob's votes came from dead people and deceased pets. At a hearing, the kids goad Bob's ego until he proudly and foolishly confesses to rigging the election, providing all the evidence needed to convict him. Bob is sent back to prison, Quimby is reinstated as mayor, the Simpsons' house is saved, and Bart is forced to return to his regular fourth-grade class after enjoying a stint in kindergarten. Guest starring Henry Corden as Fred Flintstone, Dr. Demento as himself, Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz, Larry King as himself. Your guilty conscience may force you to vote Democratic, but deep down inside, you secretly long for a cold-hearted Republican to lower taxes, brutalise criminals and rule you like a king! | Kent Brockman: The results are in: for Sideshow Bob, one hundred percent; and for Joe Quimby, one percent. And, we remind you, there is a one percent margin of error. | Bart: "Oh, my God ... the dead have risen ... and they're voting Republican!"
