title: Treehouse of Horror V (S6E06)
text: "Treehouse of Horror V" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F03), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Greg Daniels, Dan McGrath, David S. Cohen, Bob Kushell, originally airing October 30, 1994. In this fifth Halloween anthology episode, three separate nightmarish tales unfold after a mock warning from Marge and a chaotic introduction from Bart and Homer. In 'The Shinning,' the Simpsons become caretakers of Mr. Burns' isolated hotel, where the lack of beer and television drives Homer into a murderous, axe-wielding frenzy egged on by the ghost of Moe, until Groundskeeper Willie is killed trying to help and the family narrowly escapes, only to freeze to death outside while watching TV. In 'Time and Punishment,' Homer accidentally invents a time machine out of a broken toaster and repeatedly alters history with small changes, creating a series of increasingly bizarre alternate realities including a world ruled by Ned Flanders and one where donuts don't exist, ultimately settling for a version of the present close enough to his own despite everyone having long tongues. In 'Nightmare Cafeteria,' Springfield Elementary's staff discover that misbehaving students taste delicious and begin secretly cooking and eating them as cafeteria specials, prompting Bart, Lisa, and Milhouse to try to escape once they realize what's happening, but they ultimately fall into a giant blender after Willie is killed trying to save them. The episode closes with Bart waking from the nightmare, only for a real inside-out-turning fog to invade the house, leading the entire family and Willie into a macabre musical number about their gruesome transformation. Guest starring James Earl Jones as Alternate universe Maggie. Notable quotes: Bart: There's nothing wrong with your television set. Do not attempt to adjust your picture. We are controlling the transmission. | Marge: Homer, did you remember to lock the front door of the house? | Moe: Uh, they'd be much happier as ghosts. | Marge: Hello, police? This is Marge Simpson. My husband is on a murderous rampage. Over. | Maggie: This is indeed a disturbing universe. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 5): "The Shinning", "Time and Punishment", and "Nightmare Cafeteria".

title: Bart's Girlfriend (S6E07)
text: "Bart's Girlfriend" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F04), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Jonathan Collier, originally airing November 6, 1994. Bart becomes infatuated with Jessica Lovejoy, the reverend's daughter, after seeing her recite scripture in church. Determined to win her over, he tries acting like a model student, returning to Sunday school and resisting the urge to misbehave, but Jessica remains unimpressed. When Bart pulls a prank on Groundskeeper Willie during Scotchtoberfest and gets caught, Jessica is intrigued by his rebellious side and invites him to dinner. The date goes disastrously with her parents, but Jessica reveals she actually likes bad boys, and the two begin sneaking around pulling pranks together. Bart soon realizes Jessica is reckless and even cruel, especially after she forces him into dangerous stunts and a school fire alarm prank. Things escalate when Jessica steals the church collection plate and frames Bart, turning the whole town against him. With Lisa's help, Bart exposes Jessica during a church service, and the stolen money is found hidden in her room. Jessica admits she only wanted attention and shows no remorse, leaving Bart humiliated and manipulated as she moves on to another boy. Guest starring Meryl Streep as Jessica Lovejoy. Notable quotes: Groundskeeper Willie: There's not? You used me Skinner! You used me! | Bart: I'm bad to the bone, honey. | Ms. Albright: Ralph, Jesus did not have wheels. | Reverend Lovejoy: Never have I heard such gratuitous use of the word "butt". | Bart: There's only one thing to do at a moment like this... strut.

Bart: I'm bad to the bone, honey.
Ms. Albright: Ralph, Jesus did not have wheels.
Reverend Lovejoy: Never have I heard such gratuitous use of the word "butt".
Bart: There's only one thing to do at a moment like this... strut.

title: Lisa on Ice (S6E08)
text: "Lisa on Ice" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F05), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Mike Scully, originally airing November 13, 1994. After a wave of low test scores, Principal Skinner introduces academic alerts to warn parents about their children's failing grades, and Lisa is mortified to receive one for gym class. Desperate to avoid embarrassment, she tries out various sports before settling on a pee-wee hockey team sponsored by Apu, only to discover it's set up as a rival to Bart's own team. As Lisa proves to be a natural athlete and even keeps excelling academically, Bart grows jealous and decides to try becoming a better student, but years of slacking off leave him hopelessly behind in class. The sibling rivalry escalates and divides the whole family, culminating in a tense championship game where Bart's and Lisa's teams face off, splitting the stadium crowd into competing factions. When the game comes down to a dramatic penalty shot with Bart shooting against goalie Lisa, both flash back to small acts of kindness they once showed each other as young children. Overwhelmed by nostalgia and affection, they abandon the game entirely, throwing down their equipment and embracing on the ice. Homer, missing the emotional moment entirely, calls them both losers, which promptly sparks a riot among the enraged fans in the stands. Notable quotes: Ralph Wiggum: Me fail English? That's unpossible! | Chief Wiggum: We won! We won! Unfortunately, since I bet on the other team, we won't be going out for pizza. | Üter: Don't make me run, I'm full of chocolate! | Homer: Sucker! Competitive violence! That's why you're here! | Lisa: Milhouse, knock him down if he's in your way! Jimbo, Jimbo, go for the face! Ralph Wiggum lost his shin guard! Hack the bone! Hack the bone.

title: Homer Badman (S6E09)
text: "Homer Badman" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F06), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Greg Daniels, originally airing November 27, 1994. Homer and Marge head to a candy convention, leaving feminist college student Ashley Grant to babysit the kids. At the convention Homer becomes obsessed with stealing the rare Gummi Venus de Milo, using Marge as a distraction and a soda-and-Pop Rocks 'grenade' to make his escape. That night, while dropping Ashley off at home, Homer spots the missing candy stuck to the back of her pants and grabs it, but his lustful expression makes Ashley believe he sexually assaulted her. The accusation snowballs into a media frenzy, with tabloid show Rock Bottom airing a deceptively edited interview and Fox broadcasting a lurid TV movie starring Dennis Franz as Homer. Protesters camp outside the Simpson home and the family's every move becomes tabloid fodder, ruining Homer's reputation. Desperate, Homer records a public-access rebuttal that mostly just confuses onlookers, until Groundskeeper Willie comes forward with a videotape proving Homer was only grabbing the candy. Ashley and the media retract their accusations, but Rock Bottom immediately shifts its scorn to Willie, branding him a pervert instead, and Homer smugly admits he's learned nothing from the ordeal. Guest starring Dennis Franz as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: Marge, they can't carry enough candy! They have puny little muscles, not big ropy ones like you. | Ashley Grant: You grabbed me in the car! | Homer: Oh that, no. I was just grabbing a gummy Venus De Milo that got stuck to your pants. | Kent Brockman: Simpson scandal update - Homer sleeps nude in an oxygen tank which he believes gives him sexual powers. | Homer: Hey, that's a half-truth!
quotes: Homer: Marge, they can't carry enough candy! They have puny little muscles, not big ropy ones like you.
Ashley Grant: You grabbed me in the car!
Homer: Oh that, no. I was just grabbing a gummy Venus De Milo that got stuck to your pants.
Kent Brockman: Simpson scandal update - Homer sleeps nude in an oxygen tank which he believes gives him sexual powers.
Homer: Hey, that's a half-truth!

title: Grampa vs. Sexual Inadequacy (S6E10)
text: "Grampa vs. Sexual Inadequacy" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F07), directed by Wes Archer and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing December 4, 1994. Homer and Marge's marriage is strained by a lack of intimacy, prompting Grampa to concoct a homemade tonic that reignites their passion. Seeing an opportunity, Homer and Grampa hit the road selling the tonic across nearby towns, becoming surprisingly successful entrepreneurs. As parents across Springfield become distracted and affectionate again, the neglected children—including Bart, Milhouse, and Nelson—hatch theories that their parents have been possessed by aliens or turned into reverse vampires. On one sales trip, Homer and Grampa visit their old family farmhouse, where a nostalgic conversation turns into a bitter argument about Grampa's lack of encouragement during Homer's childhood. Grampa cruelly reveals that Homer was an unplanned pregnancy and says he wishes Homer had never been born, causing Homer to storm off and abandon him. Back home, Homer tries but fails to reconnect with his kids, while Grampa attempts to keep the tonic business alive with Barney as his new partner, without success. Both men, unaware of each other, return separately to the abandoned farmhouse and each accidentally starts a fire. As the house burns around them, father and son reconcile, admitting they are both flawed 'screw-ups' who forgive one another. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Grampa: Step right up, folks, and witness the magnificent medicinal miracle of Simpson & Son's patented revitalizing toniiic. | Grampa: What, seeex? What's so unappealing about hearing your elderly father talk about sex? I had seeeeex. | Homer: Ooh, mama! This is finally, really happening. After years of disappointment with get-rich-quick schemes, I know I'm gonna get rich with this scheme... and quick! | Nelson: Who cares? With no adults, I run this city. | Milhouse: Jeez... if it's in a book, it's gotta be true!

Homer: Ooh, mama! This is finally, really happening. After years of disappointment with get-rich-quick schemes, I know I'm gonna get rich with this scheme... and quick!
Nelson: Who cares? With no adults, I run this city.

title: Fear of Flying (S6E11)
text: "Fear of Flying" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F08), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by David Sacks, originally airing December 18, 1994. After Homer's harmless prank backfires and gets him banned from Moe's Tavern, he wanders Springfield searching for a new bar, eventually bluffing his way into a private pilots' lounge. Mistaken for an actual pilot, he's forced to fly a plane and crashes it, and the embarrassed airline bribes the family with free tickets to keep quiet. The trip turns disastrous when Marge has a panic attack mid-flight, revealing a long-hidden fear of flying that she can't explain. As Marge's anxiety manifests in increasingly strange behavior, Lisa urges her to see a psychiatrist, much to Homer's discomfort, since he worries the therapist will turn Marge against him. Through therapy sessions, Marge unearths a series of childhood traumas, including being teased as a child, a chaotic dream casting her family as characters from Lost in Space, and painful memories tied to her father, whom she once believed was a pilot but discovered was actually a male flight attendant. Additional buried memories surface, including a baby-feeding mishap, a toy plane catching fire, and being attacked by a crop duster as a child. Homer pulls Marge out of the session just before the psychiatrist can address his role in her anxiety. Newly confident, Marge boards a plane without fear, only for the flight to end anticlimactically when the plane overshoots the runway and lands in the ocean. Guest starring Anne Bancroft, Ted Danson, Woody Harrelson, Rhea Perlman, John Ratzenberger, George Wendt. Notable quotes: Homer: Wait a minute ... there's something bothering me about this place. I know! This lesbian bar doesn't have a fire exit. Enjoy your death trap, ladies. | Marge: Letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff... | Bart: Oh, great. I specifically asked not to be seated next to a baby. | Marge: You might even say he was an American hero. | Dr. Zweig: Let us not go overboard.

Marge: Letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff, letmeoff...
Bart: Oh, great. I specifically asked not to be seated next to a baby.
Marge: You might even say he was an American hero.
Dr. Zweig: Let us not go overboard.

title: Homer the Great (S6E12)
text: "Homer the Great" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F09), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing January 8, 1995. Homer grows suspicious when Lenny and Carl start receiving mysterious perks at the power plant, and discovers they belong to a secretive fraternal organization called the Stonecutters. Desperate to join, he learns membership requires either saving a member's life or being the son of one, and is thrilled to find his own father is already a Stonecutter, granting him entry after a series of bizarre and painful initiation rites. Homer revels in the group's absurd privileges, from secret handshakes to a hidden shortcut through Springfield's traffic, but his carelessness leads him to accidentally destroy the society's sacred founding parchment, resulting in his humiliating expulsion. A twist reveals that a birthmark on Homer's body matches an ancient prophecy naming him 'The Chosen One' destined to lead the Stonecutters to glory, and he is quickly reinstated as their leader in a ceremony mocking epic historical dramas. However, Homer's erratic and self-serving rule alienates the other members, who abandon him to form a rival club, the Ancient Mystic Society of No Homers, deliberately excluding him despite his name literally being Homer. Feeling rejected and directionless, Homer is comforted by Marge, who reminds him that his true and only club is his family, and the episode ends with the family playfully subjecting him to a mock hazing ritual at home. Guest starring Patrick Stewart as Number One. Notable quotes: Homer: Why won't those stupid idiots let me in their crappy club for jerks? | Homer: I always wondered if there was a god. And now I know there is. And it's me. | Lisa: Beware the Ides of March. | Number One: Now, let's all get drunk & play ping-pong! | Homer: You better run, egg!
quotes: Homer: Why won't those stupid idiots let me in their crappy club for jerks?
Homer: I always wondered if there was a god. And now I know there is. And it's me.
Lisa: Beware the Ides of March.
Number One: Now, let's all get drunk & play ping-pong!
Homer: You better run, egg!

title: And Maggie Makes Three (S6E13)
text: "And Maggie Makes Three" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F10), directed by Swinton O. Scott III and written by Jennifer Crittenden, originally airing January 22, 1995. When Lisa notices there are no baby photos of Maggie in the family album, Homer explains why while recounting the story to the family. Fed up with the stress of the power plant, Homer had finally paid off his debts and pursued his dream of working at a bowling alley, accepting lower pay for a happier life. That same night, he and Marge conceived their third child, and Marge, knowing another baby would force Homer back into a job he hated, tried desperately to keep the pregnancy secret. Patty and Selma discover the truth and, despite promising discretion, spread the news through Springfield's gossips, culminating in a surprise baby shower that reveals the secret to Homer. Furious and dreading the financial strain, Homer reluctantly quits the bowling alley and begs Mr. Burns for his old job back, who agrees but mounts a demeaning plaque reading 'Don't forget: you're here forever' at his workstation as a permanent reminder. Despite his resentment toward the pregnancy, Homer's heart melts the moment Maggie is born and grips his thumb. Back in the present, Homer reveals that he keeps Maggie's baby pictures at work, arranged around Burns' plaque so that it now reads 'Do it for her,' transforming his bitter reminder into a symbol of love for his daughter. Notable quotes: Homer: This is getting very abstract, but thank you, I do enjoy working at the bowling alley. | Homer: New job? Marge is pregnant!? Nooooooooo! Aahhhhhhh! | Homer: Come on, Marge, show a little enthusiasm. | Mr. Burns: I ought to be defending myself, but I am paralyzed with rage...and soothing island rhythms. | Carl: Homer, you should see a doctor. I don't think a healthy man can make that kind of smell.
quotes: Homer: This is getting very abstract, but thank you, I do enjoy working at the bowling alley.
Homer: New job? Marge is pregnant!? Nooooooooo! Aahhhhhhh!
Homer: Come on, Marge, show a little enthusiasm.
Mr. Burns: I ought to be defending myself, but I am paralyzed with rage...and soothing island rhythms.
Carl: Homer, you should see a doctor. I don't think a healthy man can make that kind of smell.

title: Bart's Comet (S6E14)
text: "Bart's Comet" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F11), directed by Bob Anderson and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 5, 1995. During Science Week at Springfield Elementary, Bart sabotages Principal Skinner's weather balloon launch, earning himself early-morning detention assisting Skinner with astronomical observations. While Skinner chases his runaway balloon, Bart plays with the telescope and discovers a comet, which gets named after him despite Skinner's jealousy. Bart's nerdy admirers, the Superfriends, later notice the comet has grown alarmingly close and realize it's on a collision course with Springfield. The town panics as Mayor Quimby and Professor Frink's rocket plan to destroy the comet instead destroys the only bridge out of town, trapping everyone. A congressional bill to evacuate Springfield fails due to an unrelated funding rider, leaving the townspeople to fend for themselves. The Simpsons take refuge in Ned Flanders' bomb shelter, but it becomes overcrowded, and the group votes to kick out Ned himself. Ned climbs a nearby hill to await the end alone, and one by one the Simpsons and other townspeople join him rather than stay in the shelter. In the end, the comet burns up in the atmosphere just as Homer predicted, destroying only the abandoned bomb shelter, sparing the town and leaving everyone stunned that Homer was right. Notable quotes: Homer Simpson: What's everyone so worked up about? So there's a comet. Big deal. It'll burn up in our atmosphere, and what's ever left will be no bigger than a chihuahua's head. | Principal Skinner: Curse the man who invented helium. Curse Pierre Jules César Janssen. | Bart: I knew you'd try to find something wrong with my comet, Lisa. You've always been petty and small, right from the beginning. | Kent Brockman: I've said it before, and I'll say it again: Democracy simply doesn't work. | Homer: Ah, Lisa. The whole reason we have elected officials is so we don't have to think all the time.
quotes: Homer Simpson: What's everyone so worked up about? So there's a comet. Big deal. It'll burn up in our atmosphere, and what's ever left will be no bigger than a chihuahua's head.
Principal Skinner: Curse the man who invented helium. Curse Pierre Jules César Janssen.
Bart: I knew you'd try to find something wrong with my comet, Lisa. You've always been petty and small, right from the beginning.
Kent Brockman: I've said it before, and I'll say it again: Democracy simply doesn't work.
Homer: Ah, Lisa. The whole reason we have elected officials is so we don't have to think all the time.

title: Homie the Clown (S6E15)
text: "Homie the Clown" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F12), directed by David Silverman and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 12, 1995. After overspending and losing yet another bet with the mob, Krusty the Clown's accountant Bill convinces him to open a clown college to train regional Krusty impersonators. Homer, obsessed by a billboard advertisement, decides on a whim to enroll, shocking his family. He graduates and begins performing official Krusty duties around Springfield, including unveiling a new burger and appearing at Milhouse's birthday party, all while wearing his official clown makeup and costume. Homer soon discovers that Springfield residents, including Chief Wiggum, mistake him for the real Krusty, and he starts exploiting this to dodge trouble. Meanwhile, Krusty skips town to avoid Fat Tony's mob after losing another bet, and the mobsters mistakenly target Homer for retribution, repeatedly failing to gun him down. Krusty, having gotten cosmetic surgery in Switzerland that only made him younger-looking with unwanted new features, returns to face the mob himself. The two clowns are captured together and forced to perform Krusty's signature bicycle stunt to save their lives, ultimately succeeding and impressing the mob boss Don Vittorio, who lets them go after Krusty pays off his debt. Guest starring Dick Cavett, Joe Mantegna, Johnny Unitas. Notable quotes: Krusty the Clown: How about letting me go double or nothing on the big opera tonight? | Fat Tony: OK. But we're only letting the bet ride because you crack us so consistently up. | Homer: That's it! You people have stood in my way long enough. I'm going to clown college! | Lisa: If there has to be a bastardized version of Krusty, I'm glad it's you. | Homer: Being a clown sucks. You get kicked by kids, bit by dogs, and admired by the elderly.
quotes: Krusty the Clown: How about letting me go double or nothing on the big opera tonight?
Fat Tony: OK. But we're only letting the bet ride because you crack us so consistently up.
Homer: That's it! You people have stood in my way long enough. I'm going to clown college!
Lisa: If there has to be a bastardized version of Krusty, I'm glad it's you.
Homer: Being a clown sucks. You get kicked by kids, bit by dogs, and admired by the elderly.

title: Bart vs. Australia (S6E16)
text: "Bart vs. Australia" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F13), directed by Wes Archer and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing February 19, 1995. Bart and Lisa argue over the Coriolis effect after a bathroom race, prompting Bart to place a collect call to a boy in rural Australia to settle the debate. When the call drags on for hours as the boy fetches neighbors, his family is left with a staggering $900 phone bill that Bart refuses to pay, mocking the man's pleas. His defiance escalates into an international incident when Australia formally indicts him for fraud, and the U.S. State Department decides the best resolution is to send the whole Simpson family to Australia so Bart can apologize in person. Once there, the family sightsees and clashes with local customs, including the country's fondness for corporal punishment, before Bart's apology is deemed insufficient and officials demand he receive a ceremonial boot to the backside. Bart and Homer make a break for the American embassy, gathering the rest of the family along the way in a chaotic escape. Ultimately Bart agrees to accept the punishment but defiantly moons the crowd with a patriotic message written on his buttocks, turning the humiliation into a statement. The family flees the furious nation by helicopter in a scene styled after the Fall of Saigon. Throughout the trip, Bart's smuggled pet frog escapes and breeds uncontrollably, devastating the Australian ecosystem as a nod to real-world invasive species, a fact the family remains blissfully unaware of as they fly home. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Evan Conover. Notable quotes: Lisa Simpson: I'm impressed you were able to write so legibly on your own butt! | Bart: Hey, I think I hear a dingo eating your baby. | Homer: When will you Australians learn? In America, we stopped using corporal punishment, and things have never been better. | Evan Conover: Mr. Simpson, shush! Disparaging the boot is a bootable offense! It's one of their proudest traditions! | Homer: There it is! Aus-tra-li-a. I'll be damned. Look at this country: U-R-Gay!
quotes: Lisa Simpson: I'm impressed you were able to write so legibly on your own butt!
Bart: Hey, I think I hear a dingo eating your baby.
Homer: When will you Australians learn? In America, we stopped using corporal punishment, and things have never been better.
Evan Conover: Mr. Simpson, shush! Disparaging the boot is a bootable offense! It's one of their proudest traditions!
Homer: There it is! Aus-tra-li-a. I'll be damned. Look at this country: U-R-Gay!

title: Homer vs. Patty and Selma (S6E17)
text: "Homer vs. Patty and Selma" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F14), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Brent Forrester, originally airing February 26, 1995. Homer sinks the family's savings into pumpkin futures, mistakenly believing they'll peak in January, and loses everything just before a mortgage payment is due. Desperate for cash, he's forced to ask Patty and Selma for a loan, and they agree only if he becomes their personal servant, subjecting him to endless humiliating chores. When Marge finds out about the arrangement, she's furious and puts a stop to it, so Homer instead tries moonlighting as a chauffeur, only to get pulled over for lacking a proper license. At the DMV, his sisters-in-law preside over his driving and written exams and fail him out of spite, but Homer gets a lucky break when their supervisor catches them smoking on duty, threatening their recent promotions. Wanting to protect Marge from disappointment in her sisters, Homer nobly takes the blame for the cigarettes, and in exchange pressures Patty and Selma into forgiving his debt entirely. Meanwhile, Bart arrives late to sign up for gym class and ends up stuck in ballet, which he initially finds embarrassing but soon discovers he has real talent for. He's invited to perform in a recital and does so while wearing a mask to hide his identity, revealing himself only after winning over the crowd. Bullies who recognize him chase him afterward, and though he gets away from the beating itself, he's injured jumping a ditch, with Lisa briefly comforting him before leaving him without real help. Guest starring Mel Brooks as himself, Susan Sarandon as the ballet teacher. Notable quotes: Moe Szyslak: Sure, Homer, I can loan you all the money you need. However, since you have no collateral, I'm going to have to break your legs in advance. | Selma: You came to us in order to be bailed out of your money problems. Now we own you like Siegfried owns Roy. | Marge: Not too good, Lisa. Frankly, he's under the table. | Carl: Quit drowning in self-pity and come get drunk with us. | Selma: When are you going to wake up and smell your husband, Marge?

Selma: You came to us in order to be bailed out of your money problems. Now we own you like Siegfried owns Roy.
Marge: Not too good, Lisa. Frankly, he's under the table.
Carl: Quit drowning in self-pity and come get drunk with us.
Selma: When are you going to wake up and smell your husband, Marge?

title: A Star Is Burns (S6E18)
text: "A Star Is Burns" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F31), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Ken Keeler, originally airing March 5, 1995. After Kent Brockman reports that Springfield is the least popular city in America, Marge proposes a town film festival to boost civic pride, and invites TV critic Jay Sherman to serve as judge. Jay arrives and stays with the Simpsons, quickly clashing with Homer over everything from pork chops to burping contests, leaving Homer feeling inadequate and insecure about his marriage. Meanwhile, Mr. Burns, upset over falling plant profits, hires a bargain director named Señor Spielbergo to produce a self-glorifying film for the festival in hopes of winning public affection. As the festival unfolds, entries range from Apu's and Moe's amateur films to Hans Moleman's crude slapstick short and Barney's surprisingly poignant art film 'Pukahontas.' When the jury—including a begrudgingly recruited Homer—convenes, corruption and personal bias threaten to sway the vote toward Burns' egotistical film, but Marge and Jay convince Homer to give Barney's film a fair viewing. Moved by its sincerity, Homer changes his vote, and Barney wins the festival, receiving a lifetime supply of Duff Beer instead of sobriety. Months later, Burns' bribery-fueled Oscar campaign fails when his film loses to a Hollywood remake of 'Man Getting Hit by Football.' Guest starring Phil Hartman as Charlton Heston, Jon Lovitz as Jay Sherman, Maurice LaMarche as George C. Scott. Notable quotes: Burns: Listen, Spielbergo, Schindler and I are like peas in a pod: We're both factory owners, we both made shells for the Nazis, but mine worked, dammit! Now go out there and win me that festival! | Homer: This contest is over! Give that man the ten thousand dollars! | Jay Sherman: This isn't America's Funniest Home Videos. | Smithers: Oh, no, sir. They're saying "Boo-urns, Boo-urns". | Hans Moleman: I was saying "Boo-urns".

Homer: This contest is over! Give that man the ten thousand dollars!
Jay Sherman: This isn't America's Funniest Home Videos.
Smithers: Oh, no, sir. They're saying "Boo-urns, Boo-urns".
Hans Moleman: I was saying "Boo-urns".

title: Lisa's Wedding (S6E19)
text: "Lisa's Wedding" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F15), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Greg Daniels, originally airing March 19, 1995. At the Springfield Renaissance Fair, Lisa wanders away from her gluttonous family and stumbles upon a mysterious fortune teller who reveals a vision of her future. In the year 2010, a 23-year-old Lisa meets Hugh Parkfield, a witty British classmate, and after a rocky start the two fall deeply in love and become engaged. When Hugh travels to Springfield to meet Lisa's family, he is dismayed by their crude behavior, especially Homer's antics and Bart's crass jokes, though he tries to hide his discomfort from Lisa. Homer gives Hugh a pair of tacky heirloom cufflinks as a token of family tradition, which Hugh reluctantly agrees to wear but privately resents. On the wedding day, Lisa discovers Hugh never intended to wear the cufflinks and that he plans to cut ties with her family after the marriage, prompting her to call off the wedding rather than abandon the people she loves despite their flaws. Back in the present, the fortune teller confirms that this future is fixed and that Lisa is destined for more romantic disappointment before finding lasting happiness. The episode closes with Lisa affectionately listening to Homer recount his ridiculous day at the fair, reaffirming her bond with her family. Guest starring Mandy Patinkin as Hugh Parkfield, Phil Hartman as Troy McClure. Notable quotes: Homer: Sweet maiden of the spit, grant now my boon, that I mightst sup on suckling pig this noon. | Marge: Homer, don't take this personally, but I've obtained a court order to prevent you from planning this wedding. | Homer: So, Hugh. Have you heard all the latest American jokes? Uh, here's a good one. Pull my finger. | Marge: You know, Fox turned into a hard-core sex channel so gradually, I didn't even notice. | Homer: I ate seven pounds of fudge!
quotes: Homer: Sweet maiden of the spit, grant now my boon, that I mightst sup on suckling pig this noon.
Marge: Homer, don't take this personally, but I've obtained a court order to prevent you from planning this wedding.
Homer: So, Hugh. Have you heard all the latest American jokes? Uh, here's a good one. Pull my finger.
Marge: You know, Fox turned into a hard-core sex channel so gradually, I didn't even notice.

title: Two Dozen and One Greyhounds (S6E20)
text: "Two Dozen and One Greyhounds" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F18), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Mike Scully, originally airing April 9, 1995. Santa's Little Helper's excess energy leads the Simpsons to a dog track, where he falls for a greyhound named She's the Fastest, whose owner gives her away once she loses her racing drive. The two dogs soon produce a litter of 25 puppies, whose adorable chaos—destroying socks, stealing snacks, and ruining a dinner party—pushes Homer and Marge to decide the family can't keep them all. Before they can find new homes, Mr. Burns swoops in and secretly whisks the puppies away to his mansion, claiming he wants to care for them. Suspicious, Bart and Lisa sneak onto the estate and discover Burns has selected a favorite pup, Little Monty, intending to turn all the dogs into a fur tuxedo. The kids attempt a daring rescue through a laundry chute, but Burns catches them and nearly shoots the dogs and the children themselves. Moved by the sight of the puppies and kids standing on their hind legs, Burns has a change of heart, vows never to wear fur again, and instead adopts all 25 dogs, raising them into champion racers. The episode closes with a comedic misdirection involving Homer, a light bulb, and Marge's momentary panic. Guest starring Frank Welker. Do not attempt sexual relations, as years of TV radiation have left your genitals withered and useless. | Homer: Awwww, so that's what's been wrong with the little fellow: He misses casual sex! | The Rich Texan: She's yours now! Once they fall in love, they lose their racing spirit. | The Rich Texan: Lady, you're all right!

title: The PTA Disbands (S6E21)
text: "The PTA Disbands" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F19), directed by Swinton O. Scott III and written by Jennifer Crittenden, originally airing April 16, 1995. After a disastrous school field trip that seems to have cost Üter his life, Edna Krabappel calls an emergency teachers' strike to protest Principal Skinner's stingy budgeting on school supplies and activities. With classes suspended, the kids scatter in different directions: Lisa becomes desperate for grades, Milhouse is forced into private tutoring by his parents, Jimbo gets hooked on soap operas, and Bart happily embraces his freedom while secretly working to keep Skinner and the union from reconciling. As the standoff drags on, Skinner insists that state budget cuts have left him with no more money to give, while the union demands restored funding. Frustrated parents, urged on by Marge, step in to run makeshift classes themselves, but the amateur instruction proves even more chaotic than the strike itself, especially once Marge starts smothering Bart with her overbearing teaching style. Desperate to escape his mother's classroom, Bart teams up with the newly tutoring-savvy Milhouse to trick Krabappel and Skinner into Skinner's office, locking them inside together. Forced to spend hours confined like prisoners, the two adversaries bond and devise a plan to generate extra revenue for the school. The strike ends and normal classes resume, but the school's cloakrooms are now rented out as annexes to Springfield Prison, placing jail cells at the back of every classroom—including one right behind Bart's desk holding Snake Jailbird, whom Bart hints he intends to help escape. Notable quotes: Bart: Well, at least it's safer than the old bus. | Skinner: Otto, we need you to fill up the bus. Here's the "credit card". | Skinner: Five dollars a child?! Last year it was free! | Ticket lady: Hmph. New ownership. | Otto: Damn! I shouldn't have eaten the mint first.

title: 'Round Springfield (S6E22)
text: "'Round Springfield" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F32), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Teleplay: Joshua Sternin and Jennifer Ventimilia; Story: Al Jean and Mike Reiss, originally airing April 30, 1995. Bart develops a stomach ache after accidentally eating a jagged metal Krusty-O, but Homer and Marge dismiss his complaints and send him to school. After Mrs. Krabappel finally lets him see the nurse, he collapses and is rushed to Springfield General Hospital for emergency appendix surgery. During a hospital visit, Lisa is thrilled to discover her idol, jazz musician Bleeding Gums Murphy, recovering in a nearby bed, and the two bond over their shared love of music. When Bleeding Gums lends her his saxophone for a school recital, Lisa turns a disastrous performance into a triumphant solo, but she returns to the hospital only to learn he has died. Grief-stricken, Lisa resolves to make sure Springfield remembers his legacy, while Bart separately wins a $100,000 lawsuit against Krusty over the faulty cereal, only to have lawyer Lionel Hutz's fees whittle it down to $500. Lisa finds Bleeding Gums' rare album at the Android's Dungeon, but the price doubles once the owner learns of his death, leaving her unable to afford it. Remembering that Lisa was the only one who believed him about his illness, Bart uses his settlement money to buy the album for her. Lisa gets the record played on a local jazz station, and a lightning strike unexpectedly boosts the signal so all of Springfield can hear it. In a heartfelt farewell vision featuring Bleeding Gums alongside Darth Vader and Mufasa, he tells Lisa she made him happy, and the two share one last musical jam together. Guest starring Ron Taylor as Bleeding Gums Murphy, Steve Allen as himself, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Homer: Lisa, when you get to be our age, you learn a few things. | Bart: Mrs Krabappel, I can't take the test, I have a stomach ache. | Mrs. Krabappel: Well, that's a lame excuse for an excuse - Ha! | Bart: No teacher shall be held accountable if Bart Simpson dies. | Homer: What I'm saying is, all we have to do is go down to the pound and get a new jazzman.

Bart: Mrs Krabappel, I can't take the test, I have a stomach ache.
Mrs. Krabappel: Well, that's a lame excuse for an excuse - Ha!
Bart: No teacher shall be held accountable if Bart Simpson dies.
Homer: What I'm saying is, all we have to do is go down to the pound and get a new jazzman.

title: The Springfield Connection (S6E23)
text: "The Springfield Connection" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F21), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jonathan Collier, originally airing May 7, 1995. After helping catch a con man running a three-card monte scam, Marge realizes she craves excitement in her humdrum life. She decides to join the Springfield Police Department, enduring Chief Wiggum's chaotic training before becoming a full-fledged officer. On the job, Marge takes her duties extremely seriously, strictly enforcing the law even against friends and family, which alienates her from the community and even leads her to arrest Homer for illegal parking. Meanwhile, Homer's poker buddy Herman uses Homer's garage as a front for a counterfeit jeans operation. When Marge stumbles upon the scheme, she and Herman have a wild confrontation in Bart's treehouse, ending comically when his makeshift zip-line escape fails due to the shoddy denim. Though the police arrive, Chief Wiggum and his corrupt officers make the evidence disappear for their own gain, letting Herman off the hook. Disillusioned by the corruption within the force, Marge decides to resign from the police, and Wiggum reluctantly lets her go. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Skinner: Well, I could send it back to Taiwan for repair. But why should I have to?! I've done nothing wrong! And I don't give permission for my face to be on TV. I want it blurred! | Moleman: Are you really allowed to execute people in a local jail? | Homer: Boy... when Marge first told me she was going to the police academy, I thought it'd be fun and exciting! You know, like that movie, Spaceballs! But instead it's been painful and disturbing, like that movie Police Academy. | Moe: The garage? Hey, fellas, the garage! Well, ooh-la-di-da, Mr. Frenchman. | Moe: A car hole.

title: Lemon of Troy (S6E24)
text: "Lemon of Troy" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F22), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Brent Forrester, originally airing May 14, 1995. After Marge scolds Bart for vandalizing wet cement, her lecture on town pride sticks with him, and he starts taking interest in Springfield's history. Bart and Milhouse learn the legend of the town's cherished lemon tree, planted by founder Jebediah Springfield after he split from his rival Shelbyville Manhattan over a dispute about cousin marriage. When the boys discover the lemon tree has been stolen, with tracks leading to Shelbyville, Bart leads Milhouse, Nelson, Martin, Todd, and Database on a raid into the rival town to reclaim it. Marge discovers the boys are missing and enlists Homer and the other fathers, who set off in Ned Flanders' RV to find them. The kids track the tree to a Shelbyville impound lot, but their attempt to retrieve it is thwarted, and the arriving parents are similarly rebuffed by a mocking lot owner. Bart devises a clever scheme, deliberately getting Flanders' RV illegally parked so it gets impounded, allowing them to sneak in and reclaim the tree during the resulting chaos. The lemon tree is triumphantly returned to Springfield, and the episode ends with both towns' old-timers spinning their own exaggerated, self-flattering versions of the legend for a new generation of children. Notable quotes: Bart: And now I'm going to teach some kids a lesson. | Marge: I choose to take that literally. | Milhouse: That kid said radical. I say radical! That's the thing that I say! | Martin: A car impound lot. The impenetrable fortress of suburbia. | Homer: This is the darkest day in Springfield history, If anyone wants me I'll be in the shower.

Marge: I choose to take that literally.
Milhouse: That kid said radical. I say radical! That's the thing that I say!

title: Who Shot Mr. Burns? (Part One) (S6E25)
text: "Who Shot Mr. Burns? (Part One)" is an episode of Season 6 (production code 2F16), directed by Jeffrey Lynch and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing May 21, 1995. The school week begins with the discovery that Superdude the gerbil has died, and while burying it, Willie accidentally strikes oil beneath Springfield Elementary. The windfall thrills the faculty and students, who begin requesting lavish new equipment, but Mr. Burns covets the oil for himself and secretly taps the well using an illegal slant-drilling rig. The resulting oil geyser wreaks havoc across town, destroying Bart's treehouse, injuring Santa's Little Helper, collapsing Grampa's retirement home, and shutting down Moe's Tavern, while the school's newfound wealth evaporates, costing several staff their jobs. Fury mounts against Burns, especially from Homer, who resents Burns's constant failure to remember his name, and from Smithers, who finally refuses to support Burns's cruelty. Undeterred, Burns unveils his most audacious scheme yet: a massive device to block out the sun and force Springfield to depend on his electricity forever, prompting Smithers to quit and be fired in the same breath. At a chaotic town meeting, nearly every resident voices a grievance against Burns, and many are seen carrying guns as tensions boil over. After Burns activates his sun-blocking machine, he is confronted in a dark alley and shot, collapsing dramatically onto the town sundial. As the shocked townsfolk realize almost everyone had a motive, Chief Wiggum is tasked with unraveling the mystery, leaving the identity of the shooter unresolved as the episode ends on a cliffhanger. Guest starring Tito Puente. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: Since the dawn of time, man has yearned to destroy the Sun. I will do the next best thing; block it out! | Smithers: Sir, this is insane! Darkness is a boon for muggers; owls will bother us with incessant hooting; the town's sundial will be rendered useless. I want no part of this! | Mr. Burns: My name is the return address, you senseless dunderpate. Smithers, who is this nincompoop? | Ned Flanders: Dear Lord, that's the loudest profanity I ever heard! | Barney: Me too! Ahh... now there's the inflated sense of self-esteem!

title: Who Shot Mr. Burns? (Part Two) (S7E01)
text: "Who Shot Mr. Burns? (Part Two)" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 2F20), directed by Wes Archer and written by Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, originally airing September 17, 1995. In the aftermath of Mr. Burns' shooting, Waylon Smithers becomes convinced his own drunken rage led him to pull the trigger, and he confesses to what he thinks is a priest, only to be arrested by Chief Wiggum in disguise. As Springfield buzzes with theories, Lisa methodically works through a list of suspects, including Tito Puente and Principal Skinner, all of whom are cleared through absurd but airtight alibis. Smithers is eventually exonerated when it's revealed he only shot Jasper's wooden leg after leaving the town meeting early to catch a TV show. The investigation turns toward Homer after his fingerprints are found on a gun in his car, and he becomes the prime suspect, prompting a wild police chase after he escapes custody. Convinced Burns will name him as the shooter once he wakes from his coma, Homer sneaks into the hospital to confront him, leading to a chaotic scene where Burns finally regains full speech. To everyone's shock, Burns reveals that his true attacker was baby Maggie Simpson, who shot him accidentally while he tried to wrestle a lollipop away from her in the family car. The episode resolves with Burns demanding Maggie's arrest, Wiggum joking that no jury would convict a baby, and a final ambiguous shot of Maggie's eyes hinting she may not be as innocent as she seems. Guest starring Tito Puente as himself. Notable quotes: Willie: It's impossible for me to fire a pistol. If you'll check me medical records, you'll see I have a cripplin' arthritis in me index fingerrrs. | Kent Brockman: Dozens of people are gunned down each day in Springfield, but until now none of them was important. | Lisa: Everyone in Springfield had a reason to shoot Mr. Burns, even us. | Grampa: Yeah, Smingers did it. Case closed. Now where's my hat? I'm going to the outhouse. | Homer: Sure. I've had it up to here with these damn rickets!

title: Radioactive Man (S7E02)
text: "Radioactive Man" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 2F17), directed by Susie Dietter and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing September 24, 1995. Bart and Milhouse are ecstatic when their favorite comic book hero, Radioactive Man, is being made into a live-action film starring Rainier Wolfcastle, and production comes to Springfield after the studio spots a cheap classified ad. Both boys audition for the coveted role of sidekick Fallout Boy, but Bart is rejected for being an inch too short, and the part instead goes to a reluctant Milhouse. Bart tries desperately to alter his height with props and clothing, but ultimately accepts a lesser role as the star's confidant, encouraged by Lisa. As filming progresses, Milhouse grows miserable with the pressures of stardom, culminating in him vanishing during the shoot of the movie's most costly and dangerous scene involving real acid. The town searches frantically for him, and Bart eventually discovers Milhouse hiding in his treehouse, having decided to quit acting despite a pep talk from aging former child star Mickey Rooney. With its sidekick gone and Springfield townsfolk gouging the production with outrageous costs, the film collapses into bankruptcy, and the disillusioned filmmakers pack up and return to Hollywood, remarking that people there treat each other better than in Springfield. Guest starring Mickey Rooney, Phil Hartman. I'm wearing a jacuzzi suit. | Rainier Wolfcastle: My eyes! The goggles do nothing!

title: Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily (S7E03)
text: "Home Sweet Homediddly-Dum-Doodily" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F01), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing October 1, 1995. Homer surprises Marge with a trip to a relaxation center, leaving the kids in Grampa's ineffective care. While they're away, Bart catches lice from Milhouse's monkey and Lisa's shoes are stolen by bullies, leaving both looking disheveled at home. When Homer and Marge return, they find that Principal Skinner has tipped off the child welfare agency, which misreads the household's temporary messiness as neglect and takes Bart, Lisa, and Maggie into custody. The kids are placed in foster care right next door with the ultra-religious Flanders family, where they endure strange food, early bedtimes, and constant scripture. Ned is horrified to learn the children were never baptized and resolves to remedy that himself, while Maggie surprisingly warms up to the attentive Flanders household. Meanwhile, Homer and Marge are required to attend remedial parenting classes to prove their fitness as guardians, with Homer oddly excelling and Marge feeling humiliated by the basic lessons. After being cleared, the couple rushes to stop Ned from baptizing Bart in the river, and Homer accidentally takes the holy water meant for his son, briefly becoming unnervingly polite before reverting to normal. In the end, Marge's call convinces a wavering Maggie to come home, and the family reunites, joking about Ned's overly organized garage as they leave. Guest starring Joan Kenley. Notable quotes: Marge: Enjoy it while you can kids! Because when you are grown up and I am dead, you will have no one to look after you! | Homer: Marge! A spider got near the car keys! | Maude Flanders: I don't judge Homer and Marge. That's for a vengeful God to do. | Ned Flanders: Until this I never thought Homer and Marge were bad parents, but now I know you kids need a less-hellbound family. | Marge: The only thing I am high on is love! Love for my son and daughters. Yes, a little L.S.D. is all I need!

title: Bart Sells His Soul (S7E04)
text: "Bart Sells His Soul" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F02), directed by Wes Archer and written by Greg Daniels, originally airing October 8, 1995. During a Sunday church service, Bart secretly swaps the hymn for Iron Butterfly's psychedelic rock song 'In the Garden of Eden,' scandalizing the congregation before Rev. Lovejoy catches on. When Milhouse is spooked by a crow into ratting Bart out, both boys are forced to clean the church organ pipes as punishment. Bart mocks Milhouse's fear of losing his soul, insisting souls don't exist, so Milhouse dares him to sell his for five dollars—which Bart does without hesitation. Strange things soon start happening: animals avoid him, doors won't open automatically for him, and he loses his sense of humor, convincing him he really has lost something vital. Bart tries repeatedly to buy back the scrap of paper from Milhouse, but Milhouse has already traded it away for Alf pogs to the Comic Book Guy, sending Bart on a frantic overnight search across Springfield. Unable to recover it, a desperate and rain-soaked Bart prays for his soul's return, and Lisa—having tracked it down and bought it back—drops it into his room from above. Meanwhile, Moe attempts to reinvent his tavern as a wholesome family restaurant called Uncle Moe's Family Feedbag, but his volatile temper and the strain of running it alone cause the venture to collapse, and he reverts back to his seedy bar. Bart's arc ends with him gratefully devouring the paper soul and sleeping peacefully, having learned to take the idea of a soul seriously. Notable quotes: Bart: You traded my soul for pogs?!? | Bart: Soul? Come on, Milhouse, there is no such thing as a soul. It's just something they make up to scare kids, like the Boogeyman or Michael Jackson. | Milhouse: Well, I didn't want hungry birds pecking my soul forever. | Bart: Any time, chum...p. | Bart: I can't take this anymore! I want my soul, and I want it now!

title: Lisa the Vegetarian (S7E05)
text: "Lisa the Vegetarian" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F03), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by David S. Cohen, originally airing October 15, 1995. After petting an adorable lamb at Storytown Village's petting zoo, Lisa finds she can no longer stomach eating meat, and she pushes away the lamb chops Marge serves for dinner. Her new vegetarianism isolates her at school, where she refuses to dissect a worm and struggles to find anything meatless in the cafeteria, triggering Principal Skinner's suspicion of an 'independent thinker' among his students. At home, Homer and Bart mock her choice and stage a mocking song-and-dance number, and tensions boil over when Homer throws a big backyard barbecue featuring a whole roast pig. Humiliated and furious after being laughed at for bringing gazpacho and struck by a stray flying burger, Lisa steals the roast pig using a riding lawnmower, sending it careening downhill into a river and eventually launching it comically into the sky past Mr. Burns' office window. After a bitter fight with Homer, Lisa runs away and is worn down by relentless pro-meat propaganda and peer teasing, finally biting into what she believes is a real hot dog at the Kwik-E-Mart. Apu reveals it was actually a tofu dog and introduces her to his rooftop garden, where Paul and Linda McCartney help restore her conviction and teach her to influence others without forcing her views on them. Lisa returns home, reconciles with a relieved and apologetic Homer, and the episode ends with him offering her a 'veggieback' ride instead of a piggyback one. Guest starring Phil Hartman, Linda McCartney, Paul McCartney. Notable quotes: Lisa: I can't eat this. I can't eat a poor little lamb. | Homer: Lisa, get ahold of yourself. This is lamb, not a lamb. | Bart: This one spent two hours in the broiler! | Dora: Yum. It's rich in bunly goodness. | Homer: It's just a little airborne. It's still good, it's still good!

title: Treehouse of Horror VI (S7E06)
text: "Treehouse of Horror VI" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F04), directed by Bob Anderson and written by John Swartzwelder (part 1), Steve Tompkins (part 2), David X. Cohen (part 3), originally airing October 29, 1995. This Halloween special is split into three separate horror tales. In 'Attack of the 50-Foot Eyesores,' Homer's outrage over false advertising at Lard Lad Donuts leads him to steal the statue's giant donut, which somehow causes a freak storm that animates Springfield's advertising mascots into rampaging monsters. The town is saved only when an ad executive and a musical cameo from Paul Anka convince citizens to simply stop paying attention to the creatures, draining their power, though Homer's stubborn fixation on reclaiming his donut nearly ruins everything. In 'Nightmare on Evergreen Terrace,' the ghost of Groundskeeper Willie, killed years earlier in a furnace accident caused by Homer's tampering with the thermostat, begins murdering Springfield Elementary students in their dreams in a parody of A Nightmare on Elm Street. After Willie kills Martin and injures several other kids, Bart enters the dream world to fight back, and with help from Lisa and baby Maggie, who jams Willie's bagpipe-spider form with a pacifier, the ghost is destroyed for good. Finally, in 'Homer³,' Homer hides from his visiting sisters-in-law behind a bookcase and stumbles into a bizarre three-dimensional realm rendered in computer animation. When his careless actions tear open the fabric of this dimension, a black hole threatens to consume everything, and despite Bart's attempt at a rescue, Homer is ultimately ejected from the collapsing universe into the real, live-action world, landing dazed but strangely delighted on a real street in Los Angeles. Guest starring Paul Anka. Notable quotes: Homer: D'oh, nuts! That's false advertising! | Homer: I got your donut, Lard Lad! And what are you going to do about it? | Chief Wiggum: Eh, they're not so tough. | Homer: Don't you ever get tired of being wrong all the time? | Marge: These monsters are destroying everything and everyone we hold dear! And you kids should have jackets on. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 6): "Attack of the 50-Foot Eyesores", "Nightmare on Evergreen Terrace", and "Homer³".

title: King-Size Homer (S7E07)
text: "King-Size Homer" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F05), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing November 5, 1995. When Mr. Burns institutes a mandatory exercise program at the power plant, Homer desperately tries to avoid it, first by attempting to injure himself and then by learning that employees on disability get to work from home. Discovering that morbid obesity qualifies as a disability, he sets a goal of reaching 300 pounds, enlisting Bart's enthusiastic help despite Marge's worries about his health and their marriage. With guidance from the dubious Dr. Nick, Homer gorges on outrageous food combinations and eventually tips the scale past his goal, even resorting to eating one of Maggie's Play-Doh creations. Once hooked up to a home computer terminal, Homer discovers he can coast through his job by repeatedly hitting the 'yes' key, and he even rigs a mechanical drinking bird to do it for him while he sneaks out to the movies. Humiliated when a theater refuses to seat him because of his size, Homer returns home determined to prove that overweight people can matter, only to find the bird has failed and the plant is on the verge of a nuclear meltdown. Racing to the reactor, Homer heroically uses his massive girth to physically plug a leaking gas valve, averting disaster and saving the plant. As a reward, Mr. Burns promises to pay for Homer to become thin again, and after Homer's own exercise attempts fail, Burns funds his liposuction instead. Guest starring Joan Kenley as the telephone operator. Notable quotes: Homer: [reads] "To start, press any key." Well where's the "any" key? I see Esc, Catarl, and PigUp. There doesn't seem to be any "any" key! | Smithers: Boy, I never saw a man so desperate to get out of five minutes of calisthenics. | Lenny: Yeah, he got injured on the job and they sent him home with pay. It's like a lottery that awards stupidity. | Homer: I'm purposely gaining 61 pounds to get on disability! | Homer: All my life I've been an obese man trapped inside a fat man's body.

title: Mother Simpson (S7E08)
text: "Mother Simpson" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F06), directed by David Silverman and written by Richard Appel, originally airing November 19, 1995. Mr. Burns forces his employees to spend a Saturday cleaning up a highway for a publicity photo, and a disgruntled Homer decides to skip out by rigging a dummy to fall off a cliff, making everyone believe he died at work. When the ruse causes the family's utilities to be shut off because the house is in Homer's name, Marge insists he go straighten things out at the Hall of Records. While there, Homer discovers his mother Mona, long believed dead, is actually still alive, and he tracks her down at what he thinks is her grave. Mona reunites tearfully with Homer and meets the family, quickly bonding with Lisa, but her nervous reaction to a passing police car raises suspicions about her past. Bart and Lisa uncover evidence that Mona has been living under multiple aliases, prompting the family to press her for the truth about why she abandoned Homer as a child. In flashback, Mona reveals she became a radical 1960s activist who bombed one of Mr. Burns' germ-warfare labs, forcing her into decades of hiding from the law. Burns recognizes her and alerts the FBI, leading to a tense standoff that Mona escapes with help from a grateful Chief Wiggum. In the end, Mona must go underground once again, leaving Homer to bid her a bittersweet goodbye as she drives off into the night. Guest starring Glenn Close as Mona Simpson, Harry Morgan as Bill Gannon. title: Sideshow Bob's Last Gleaming (S7E09)
text: "Sideshow Bob's Last Gleaming" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F08), directed by Dominic Polcino and written by Spike Feresten, originally airing November 26, 1995. Krusty the Clown hosts a charity food drive that's really an excuse for a messy obstacle-course stunt show, which enrages Sideshow Bob, watching from his minimum-security prison, as it reminds him how debased television has become. During work duty at an airfield preparing for an air show, Bob impersonates an Air Force colonel to sneak into a restricted hangar and steal a nuclear bomb. He hijacks the airshow's broadcast to announce that Springfield must abandon television entirely or he will detonate the weapon, and a panicked Mayor Quimby agrees to shut down all TV transmissions. Krusty, unwilling to lose his audience, secretly keeps broadcasting from a civil defense shelter, provoking Bob's fury when he discovers the bomb was a dud and television survives anyway. Bob then kidnaps Bart, crashes a stolen Harrier jet, steals the historic Wright Brothers plane, and attempts a kamikaze crash into Krusty's hideout while Lisa works to reveal his location to the authorities. The suicide attack fizzles harmlessly, Bob is captured, Bart is safely reunited with his family, and the stolen antique plane is accidentally destroyed by a tank in the chaos. Guest starring R. Lee Ermey as Colonel Hapablap, Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Notable quotes: Sideshow Bob: Sweet Enola Gay, son! Get moving or I'll tear you up like a Kleenex at a... snot party. | Sergeant: Sir! Right away Sir!

title: The Simpsons 138th Episode Spectacular (S7E10)
text: "The Simpsons 138th Episode Spectacular" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F31), directed by David Silverman and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing December 3, 1995. Troy McClure hosts a retrospective special celebrating The Simpsons' history, mixing clips, deleted scenes, and answers to viewer questions. He recounts the show's origins with Matt Groening, James L. Brooks, and Sam Simon, and airs the original animated short 'Good Night' along with several other vintage shorts. Viewer questions probe Homer's escalating stupidity, an angry and armed Matt Groening's writing process, and the true nature of Smithers' devotion to Mr. Burns, each answered with a barrage of clips. The special then showcases previously unseen deleted scenes from episodes like 'Krusty Gets Kancelled,' '$pringfield,' 'Mother Simpson,' 'Treehouse of Horror IV,' 'Homer and Apu,' and 'Burns' Heir.' A major segment revisits the 'Who Shot Mr. Burns?' mystery, replaying various suspects' hypothetical confessions before revealing the alternate ending where Smithers is unmasked as the shooter and receives a pay cut as punishment. Throughout, the special pokes fun at the show's production quirks, low-budget early animation, and mock accusations of hidden right-wing messaging. It ends with Troy McClure teasing a final, risqué montage before the show wraps up its clip-show tribute to the series. Guest starring Buzz Aldrin as himself, Glenn Close as Mona Simpson, Phil Hartman as Troy McClure and Lionel Hutz. They were never popular. | Bart: I'd sell my soul for a Formula One racing car! | Mr. Burns: Smithers, for attempting to kill me, I'm giving you a five percent pay cut.

title: Marge Be Not Proud (S7E11)
text: "Marge Be Not Proud" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F07), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Mike Scully, originally airing December 17, 1995. Bart becomes obsessed with getting the violent fighting game Bonestorm after seeing it advertised during a Krusty Christmas special, but Marge refuses to buy it for him. After failing to rent, borrow, or play the game through legitimate means, Bart succumbs to temptation at the Try-N-Save discount store and shoplifts a copy, only to be caught by the store's intimidating security officer, Don Brodka. Bart manages to erase Brodka's warning message from the family's answering machine and hides his crime, but the secret unravels when Marge schedules the family Christmas photo at that very store and Brodka exposes Bart's shoplifting on the store's surveillance monitors. While Homer's reaction devolves into a rambling non-lecture about Police Academy movies, Marge grows quietly distant and heartbroken, excluding Bart from family Christmas traditions. Wracked with guilt, Bart secretly returns to the store to make amends with Brodka and buys Marge a nicely dressed studio photo of himself as an early Christmas gift. Touched, Marge forgives him and gives Bart his own present early—a video game she was told everyone wants—which turns out to be the notoriously boring golf simulator Lee Carvallo's Putting Challenge instead of Bonestorm. Despite his disappointment, Bart embraces his mother warmly, resolving the emotional rift between them. Guest starring Lawrence Tierney as Don Brodka. Notable quotes: Comic Book Guy: Ah, ah, ah! It seems we are unfamiliar with sarcasm. | Nelson: Shoplifting is a victimless crime, like punching someone in the dark. | Troy McClure: I'm here today to give you the skinny on shoplifting, thereby completing my plea bargain with the good people at Foot Locker of Beverly Hills. | Gavin: No, Mom, you idiot! I have Bloodstorm, and Bone Squad, and Bloodstorm II, stupid. | Bart: Those are all good points, but the problem is, they don't result in me getting the game.

title: Team Homer (S7E12)
text: "Team Homer" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F10), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Mike Scully, originally airing January 7, 1996. Homer, bored with his routine at Moe's Tavern, decides to start a bowling team with Moe, Apu, and Otto, but they lack the funds to enter the league. He visits Mr. Burns just as the executive is under the influence of medication, and a hallucinating Burns mistakes Homer for a beloved doughboy mascot and hands over $500. The newly formed Pin Pals dominate the league until Burns realizes he's been duped and forces his way onto the team, souring their winning streak with his incompetence. Meanwhile, Bart sparks a school-wide riot after wearing a provocative anti-homework shirt, prompting Principal Skinner to institute strict uniforms that drain the students of their individuality. During a surprise visit from Superintendent Chalmers, a rainstorm turns the uniforms into vibrant tie-dye patterns, restoring the students' spirits. Back with the bowling team, Homer's teammates nearly kick Burns off after his blunders keep costing them games, but relent when he buys them new uniforms. In the championship against the Holy Rollers, Burns unexpectedly wins the game, then selfishly keeps the trophy for himself, prompting Homer to break into his mansion to steal it back, only to be foiled by Burns' guard dogs while his teammates flee. Notable quotes: Chalmers: Skinner! Why, are there, children, walking on, my head?! | Superintendent Chalmers: Well, Seymour, I must say for once, I am impressed. In fact, I am going to give this school a perfect ten.

title: Two Bad Neighbors (S7E13)
text: "Two Bad Neighbors" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F09), directed by Wesley Archer and written by Ken Keeler, originally airing January 14, 1996. When Evergreen Terrace hosts a neighborhood garage sale, the Simpsons discover that former President George H. W. Bush and his wife Barbara have moved into the house across the street. Homer immediately resents the attention his new famous neighbors receive, while Bart takes an interest in visiting them, charming Barbara but grating on George with his casual manners. Tensions boil over when Bart accidentally destroys George's manuscript for his memoirs, prompting the exasperated ex-president to spank him. Furious, Homer declares war on George, leading to an escalating series of pranks including fireworks, a humiliating wig switch before a big speech, and George retaliating by tearing up the Simpsons' lawn with his car. Barbara repeatedly urges her husband to make peace, but the feud continues until George, worn down by the chaos Springfield has brought into his life, finally apologizes and decides to sell the house and leave. The home is quickly purchased by another former president, Gerald Ford, who immediately bonds with Homer over beer, nachos, and football, offering a much friendlier ending to the saga of presidential neighbors. title: Scenes from the Class Struggle in Springfield (S7E14)
keys: scenes from the class struggle in springfield
text: "Scenes from the Class Struggle in Springfield" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F11), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Jennifer Crittenden, originally airing February 4, 1996. After Grampa breaks the family TV, the Simpsons head to the Ogdenville outlet mall, where Marge finds a marked-down Chanel suit and becomes obsessed with wearing it. A chance encounter with old classmate Evelyn Peters gets Marge and the family invited into the exclusive Springfield Country Club, and Marge grows increasingly desperate to fit in with its snobbish members, even as she starts neglecting her family. Meanwhile, Homer discovers a natural talent for golf and is challenged to a match by Mr. Burns, only to catch Smithers secretly swapping Burns' ball to make him look better; Burns blackmails Homer into silence by threatening the family's club membership. As Marge tries to alter her suit for an upcoming club party, Lisa's pestering causes her to ruin it, forcing Marge to buy an even pricier real Chanel dress. At the party, Marge's snobbery toward her own family reaches a breaking point, and Homer's gentle offer to stay silent all night makes her realize how much she's changed. Rejecting the country club world, Marge takes her family to Krusty Burger instead, only for them to learn the party was actually meant to celebrate the Simpsons' full club membership, sponsored by Evelyn. title: Bart the Fink (S7E15)
text: "Bart the Fink" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F12), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Teleplay: John Swartzwelder, Story: Bob Kushell, originally airing February 11, 1996. After the Simpsons inherit money from Great Aunt Hortense, Marge insists the kids deposit it in the bank rather than blow it on tacos or public broadcasting donations. Bart, hoping to collect Krusty the Clown's autograph, slips a check into the clown's pocket for him to sign, but instead it comes back stamped by a mysterious holding company. When Bart questions the bank about the odd stamp, his innocent inquiry triggers an IRS investigation that exposes Krusty's illegal offshore account in the Cayman Islands. Krusty is arrested for tax evasion, and his empire collapses as the government seizes his assets, guts his TV show's budget, and takes over Krusty Burger. Wracked with guilt over destroying his idol, Bart is devastated further when Krusty's plane crashes and he is presumed dead. However, Bart and Lisa discover Krusty is alive, hiding under the alias Rory B. Bellows as a dockside salvager to escape his debts. The siblings track him down and convince him to give up his new identity, and Krusty decides to use his fraudulent life-insurance payout to settle his debts with the government, casually blowing up his boat as a parting gesture. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure, Bob Newhart as himself. title: Lisa the Iconoclast (S7E16)
text: "Lisa the Iconoclast" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F13), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Jonathan Collier, originally airing February 18, 1996. With Springfield's bicentennial parade approaching, Lisa researches town founder Jebediah Springfield for a school essay contest and befriends museum curator Hollis Hurlbut. While digging through an old flute, she uncovers a hidden scroll revealing that Jebediah was actually a murderous pirate named Hans Sprungfeld who faked his heroic legacy. Meanwhile, Homer eagerly takes over as the parade's town crier after Flanders steps aside, reveling in the attention. Convinced Lisa is right, Homer helps her try to prove the truth by exhuming Jebediah's body to find his telltale silver prosthetic tongue, but the grave yields nothing, leaving them mocked and ostracized. Lisa is later visited by the ghost of George Washington, who directs her to a torn portrait that leads her back to the museum, where she discovers Hurlbut himself hid the tongue to protect the town's cherished myth. Faced with the truth, Lisa ultimately decides not to shatter the town's belief in Jebediah, realizing the legend inspires unity and civic pride. The episode ends with the bicentennial parade proceeding joyfully, Homer proudly serving as town crier with Lisa perched on his shoulders. Guest starring Donald Sutherland as Hollis Hurlbut. It's a perfectly cromulent word. | Bart: Well, yeah, Dad, you're a big fat loudmouth and you can walk when you have to. | Chief Wiggum: Good God, he is fabulous. | Lisa: Oh my God, our town hero is a fraud!

title: Homer the Smithers (S7E17)
text: "Homer the Smithers" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F14), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 25, 1996. After a disastrous employee appreciation night at a drag racing track, Waylon Smithers snaps under the strain of catering to Mr. Burns' every whim and tries to drown himself in an office water cooler. Burns orders him to take a vacation, but Smithers insists on finding the most incompetent worker possible as a temporary replacement so Burns will be eager to have him back. He settles on Homer, who throws himself into the job despite constant mockery from Burns and being exploited by his own kids for homework help and rides. Homer's patience finally snaps and he punches Burns, then flees home convinced he has killed his boss. Terrified of further violence, Burns begins doing his own work and unexpectedly starts to enjoy his newfound independence, deciding he no longer needs Smithers and firing him outright. Desperate and unable to hold down other jobs, Smithers schemes with Homer to get rehired by faking a call from Burns' mother, but the plan collapses and Burns catches them in the act. A fight between Homer and Smithers knocks over Burns' bear statue, sending Burns crashing out of his office window and back into dependence on Smithers during his recovery. In the end, Smithers regains his old position and, rather than punishing Homer, quietly thanks him with a gift basket for engineering his return. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: You call this a super computer! | Homer: Smithers probably selected me because of my ability to motivate people. Everyone says they have to work a lot harder when I am around. | Mr. Burns: Good Lord, Smithers! You look atrocious! I thought I ordered you to take a vacation. | Homer: Uh, Smithers already left, sir. I am his replacement, Homer Simpson. | Mr. Burns: Homer, you have done more for me than any man ever could. Your brutal attack forced me to do things for myself.

title: The Day the Violence Died (S7E18)
text: "The Day the Violence Died" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F16), directed by Wesley Archer and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 17, 1996. During the 75th anniversary celebration of Itchy & Scratchy, Bart wanders off the parade route into a rundown part of town and meets Chester J. Lampwick, a destitute old man who claims he invented Itchy decades ago. Chester shows Bart and Milhouse an old nitrate film reel proving his claim, but it disintegrates in flames moments later, destroying their only evidence. Determined to help, Bart takes Chester in, causing friction when the old man brawls with Grampa, and later they attempt to confront studio head Roger Meyers Jr. directly, only to be tossed out by security. The dispute goes to court, where Chester's lack of proof nearly loses him the case despite a comic courtroom scuffle with Krusty. At the last minute, Bart finds an old autographed drawing in a comic shop proving Meyers' father stole the Itchy character from Chester years earlier. Chester wins a massive $800 million judgment, bankrupting the Itchy & Scratchy studio and putting the show on indefinite hiatus. Guilt-ridden, Bart and Lisa try to fix the mess they caused, only to discover that two suspiciously perfect kid detectives, Lester and Eliza, have already resolved the studio's financial crisis and rescued other beloved characters from scandal. The episode closes with Bart and Lisa grumbling about being upstaged by someone else's tidy resolution. Guest starring Kirk Douglas as Chester J. Lampwick, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz, Alex Rocco as Roger Meyers, Jr., Jack Sheldon as the Amendment To Be, Suzanne Somers as herself. If it wasn't for The Honeymooners, we would of never had The Flinstones! | Roger Meyers, Jr.: Thanks a lot kid, you just kill Itchy & Scratchy.

title: A Fish Called Selma (S7E19)
text: "A Fish Called Selma" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F15), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jack Barth, originally airing March 24, 1996. Troy McClure, a washed-up actor with a mysterious aquarium scandal in his past, gets pulled over by Chief Wiggum and sent to the DMV for an eye exam, where he meets Selma Bouvier. He charms her into passing his test in exchange for a date, and their subsequent public outings reignite tabloid interest in his career. His agent, MacArthur Parker, pushes him to keep dating Selma for the publicity, leading to a whirlwind romance, a proposal during a drive-in movie, and a quick marriage. Behind the scenes, Troy confides to Homer that the relationship is a sham designed purely to revive his fading fame, a secret that eventually reaches Selma through Marge and Patty. Confronted, Troy admits the truth but convinces Selma to stay married for the financial security and comfort it offers her and her pet iguana Jub-Jub. When Parker pressures Troy to have a baby to complete his wholesome image, Selma and Troy attempt it but both realize they can't go through with bringing a child into a loveless marriage. Selma leaves with Jub-Jub, ending the marriage, while Troy's career rebounds enough that he turns down a big sequel role to pursue a passion project instead.
