title: Bart on the Road (S7E20)
text: "Bart on the Road" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F17), directed by Swinton O. Scott III and written by Richard Appel, originally airing March 31, 1996. When Principal Skinner needs a day off to catch a flight, he schedules a 'Take Your Kids to Work Day,' sending Bart, Lisa, and their classmates off with their parents. Bart, bored at the DMV with his aunts, forges himself a fake driver's license, and teams up with Nelson, Milhouse, and a newly rich-then-broke Martin to rent a car for a secret road trip, lying to their parents about a grammar competition in Canada. With no real destination in mind, the boys end up chasing an old brochure to a long-faded World's Fair site in Knoxville, Tennessee, only to wreck their rental car and find themselves stranded and penniless. Meanwhile, Lisa spends her day happily shadowing Homer at the power plant, growing suspicious of Bart's story and eventually learning the truth over a phone call. Desperate to get his friends home without alerting his parents, Bart takes a job as an international courier, flying as far as Hong Kong to earn money. Lisa, unable to keep the secret from Homer, reveals everything, prompting a furious but secretly resourceful Homer to arrange for a giant crate to be shipped to Springfield—one large enough to smuggle Nelson, Milhouse, and Martin home. In the end, the boys make it back safely, but Marge remains blissfully unaware of the whole ordeal, fielding a string of confusing phone calls about her son's misadventures. title: 22 Short Films About Springfield (S7E21)
text: "22 Short Films About Springfield" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F18), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Richard Appel, David Cohen, Jonathan Collier, Jennifer Crittenden, Greg Daniels, Brent Forrester, Rachel Pulido, Steve Tompkins, Bill Oakley, Josh Weinstein, Matt Groening, originally airing April 14, 1996. Bart and Milhouse muse on a bridge about whether anything interesting ever happens to the ordinary people of Springfield, prompting a series of interwoven vignettes about the town's residents. Apu sneaks away from the Kwik-E-Mart for five minutes to attend a party, only to return and find Hans Moleman had been waiting inside the whole time. Mr. Burns and Smithers' tandem bike ride turns disastrous when Smithers is stung by a bee and suffers an allergic reaction, leading to a crash where only the unconscious Burns gets medical attention. Dr. Nick faces a malpractice review board but saves his license with an absurd improvised treatment on Grandpa Simpson. Principal Skinner desperately disguises Krusty Burger food as home cooking for Superintendent Chalmers' visit, then must explain away his burning kitchen as an indoor aurora borealis. Meanwhile, Homer accidentally traps Maggie in a newspaper vending machine and resorts to stealing the whole machine, while Snake and Chief Wiggum end up taken hostage by Herman at his military antiques shop. Lisa spends the episode trying to get gum out of her hair, eventually getting a haircut that boosts her confidence, only for Nelson to mock her—leading to Nelson's own humiliation at the hands of a very tall man and a ketchup-and-mustard ambush from Bart and Milhouse. The episode closes with Bart and Milhouse concluding that everyone has a story worth telling, just as Professor Frink tries to share his before being cut off by the credits. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz and the hospital board chairman. Notable quotes: Skinner: Superintendent, I hope you're ready for mouthwatering hamburgers! | Skinner: Oh no, I said 'steamed hams'. That's what I call hamburgers. | Chalmers: Aurora Borealis? At this time of year! At this time of day! In this part of the country! Localized entirely within your kitchen?!? | Milhouse: I try not to. It makes it harder to spit on 'em. | Dr. Nick: Holy smokes! title: Much Apu About Nothing (S7E23)
text: "Much Apu About Nothing" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F20), directed by Susie Dietter and written by David S. Cohen, originally airing May 5, 1996. After a bear wanders into Springfield and causes minor panic, Homer whips up a mob demanding protection, prompting Mayor Quimby to create an expensive, high-tech Bear Patrol funded by a tiny tax hike. When the townspeople balk at even this small increase, Quimby cleverly redirects their anger toward illegal immigrants, proposing a referendum to deport them. Apu is horrified to learn he could be deported since his student visa expired years ago and he never became a citizen. Panicked, he buys forged citizenship papers from Fat Tony, but guilt and memories of his parents' advice to always be himself push him to take the legitimate citizenship test instead. Homer 'helps' him study by feeding him absurdly wrong facts about American history, leaving Apu to cram alone all night, only to fall asleep and forget everything. Despite this, Apu passes the test alongside a colorful group of fellow test-takers, including a disguised Moe, and is welcomed home with a citizenship party by the Simpsons. The episode closes ironically with Groundskeeper Willie being deported anyway, shouting his displeasure as his ship departs. Guest starring Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony. title: Homerpalooza (S7E24)
text: "Homerpalooza" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F21), directed by Wes Archer and written by Brent Forrester, originally airing May 19, 1996. After Otto crashes the school bus, Homer starts driving Bart, Lisa, and their classmates to school, only to discover the kids find his classic rock tastes hopelessly outdated. Stung by feeling uncool, Homer resolves to reconnect with his youth and takes Bart and Lisa to the Hullabalooza music festival in Capitol City. There, after being humiliated for wearing a Rastafarian hat, Homer accidentally intercepts a cannonball meant for Peter Frampton's stage finale and discovers he can withstand the blow unharmed. The festival's manager hires him as a sideshow act, and Homer becomes a minor celebrity touring with bands like the Smashing Pumpkins, signing autographs on spent cannonballs. When Hullabalooza reaches Springfield, a veterinarian warns Homer that another hit could kill him, but he stubbornly insists on performing anyway. At the climactic show, Homer loses his nerve and dodges the cannonball at the last second, drawing boos from the crowd and getting fired from the tour. Marge comforts him with a sandwich, and the family drives home debating what it truly means to be 'cool.' Guest starring Cypress Hill, Peter Frampton, Sonic Youth, The Smashing Pumpkins. Notable quotes: Homer: I used to rock and roll all night and party ev-a-ry day. Then it was every other day. Now I'm lucky if I can find half an hour a week in which to get funky. I've got to get out of this rut and back into the groove! | Bart: Dad! No one cares about any of your stupid dinosaur bands! You have the worst, lamest taste in music ever! | Homer: Why do you need new bands? Everyone knows rock attained perfection in 1974. It's a scientific fact. | Grampa: I used to be "with it." But then they changed what "it" was. Now what I'm with isn't "it," and what's "it" seems weird and scary to me. It'll happen to you. | Lisa: Wow, it's like Woodstock. Only with advertisements everywhere and tons of security guards.

title: Summer of 4 Ft. 2 (S7E25)
text: "Summer of 4 Ft. 2" is an episode of Season 7 (production code 3F22), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing May 19, 1996. As the school year ends, Lisa is crushed when none of her classmates bother to sign her yearbook despite her academic achievements. When the Simpsons head to Flanders' beach house in Little Pwagmattasquarmsettport for the summer, Lisa sees a chance to reinvent herself, adopting a cooler look and attitude and quickly befriending a group of laid-back teens, including Erin, Dean, Rick, and Ben. To fit in, she distances herself from Bart, calling him her nerdy brother, which fuels his jealousy since he only has Milhouse for company. Bart retaliates by exposing Lisa's yearbook to her new friends during a beach party, revealing her true nerdy reputation and humiliating her in front of everyone. The siblings clash bitterly at a carnival the next day, with Lisa devastated by the betrayal. However, when she returns to the beach house, she finds her new friends have decorated the family car with seashells spelling out 'Lisa Rules,' showing that her yearbook status doesn't matter to them. Before the family leaves, Bart secretly has Lisa's friends sign her yearbook, and he returns it to her as a heartfelt peace offering. The episode ends with the family driving home, seagulls chasing the shell-covered car because the kids never washed off the leftover food. Guest starring Christina Ricci as Erin. Notable quotes: Lisa: Like, you know, whatever. Like, you know, whatever. | Lisa: I don't get it. Straight A's, perfect attendance, Bathroom Timer... I should be the most popular girl in school. | Homer: Um... let me have one of those porno magazines... a large box of condoms... a bottle of Old Harper... a couple of those panty shields... and some illegal fireworks... and one of those disposable enemas. No, make it two. | Bart: I guess my little yearbook stunt was pretty rough, but it did teach you a lesson: It's important to be yourself. | Dean: You taught us about cool things like nature and why we shouldn't drink sea water.

title: Treehouse of Horror VII (S8E01)
text: "Treehouse of Horror VII" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F02), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Ken Keeler, Dan Greaney, David S. Cohen, originally airing October 27, 1996. In this Halloween special, three unrelated horror tales unfold. In 'The Thing and I,' Bart and Lisa investigate strange noises in the attic and discover Homer and Marge have been secretly keeping Bart's deformed conjoined twin, Hugo, locked away; when Hugo tries to reunite with Bart surgically, Dr. Hibbert's examination reveals a shocking twist—Bart, not Hugo, was actually the evil twin, and Bart ends up confined to the attic in his place. In 'The Genesis Tub,' Lisa accidentally creates a microscopic civilization inside a science fair cola experiment, and the tiny society rapidly advances technologically; after Bart interferes and nearly destroys their world, the miniature people shrink Lisa down and worship her as a deity, while Bart steals her project for himself and wins the science fair. In 'Citizen Kang,' aliens Kang and Kodos abduct Homer during a fishing trip, then kidnap presidential candidates Bill Clinton and Bob Dole, impersonating them to manipulate the 1996 election; Homer's attempt to expose the ruse backfires when he accidentally kills the real candidates in space, and despite unmasking the aliens, the American public votes for Kang anyway due to the two-party system, resulting in humanity's enslavement. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Bill Clinton. Notable quotes: Homer: We chained Hugo up in the attic like an animal and fed him a bucket of fish heads once a week. | Dr. Hibbert: Wait a minute, Hugo's scar is on the wrong side! He couldn't have been the evil left twin! That means the evil twin is, and always has been... Bart. | Lisa: Principal Skinner, wait! I created the universe! Give me the gift certificate! | Homer: Oh my God... space aliens! Don't eat me! I have a wife and kids! Eat them! | Kang: Stop. We have reached the limits of what rectal probing can teach us. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 7): "The Thing and I", "The Genesis Tub", and "Citizen Kang".

title: You Only Move Twice (S8E02)
text: "You Only Move Twice" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 3F23), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing November 3, 1996. When the family's aging house begins literally falling apart, Homer jumps at an opportunity to work for the mysterious Globex Corporation, uprooting the family to the shiny new town of Cypress Creek. While Homer thrives under his charismatic new boss, Hank Scorpio, the rest of the family struggles: Marge grows bored and starts drinking since household chores are all automated, Bart is humiliated by being placed in a remedial class, and Lisa suffers constant allergy attacks from the local vegetation. Meanwhile, Homer remains completely unaware that Scorpio is secretly a global supervillain building a doomsday device and battling a spy and government strike teams from his volcano fortress. Homer even unwittingly helps thwart an assassin sent to stop Scorpio, mistaking the attack for an ordinary workplace scuffle. Torn between his family's misery and his newfound professional success, Homer confronts Scorpio about quitting just as a full-scale military assault hits the compound. Scorpio graciously accepts Homer's resignation despite the chaos, and the Simpsons return home to Springfield. As a parting gift, Scorpio sends Homer ownership of an NFL team, and while it isn't Homer's beloved Dallas Cowboys, he happily accepts the Denver Broncos instead. Guest starring Albert Brooks as Hank Scorpio. Notable quotes: Scorpio: Don't call me that word. I don't like things that elevate me above the other people. I'm just like you. | Homer: Sir, I need to know where I can get some business hammocks. | Apu: Thank you, come again! | Scorpio: We don't have bums in our town, Marge, and if we did they wouldn't rush. They'd be allowed to go at their own pace. | James Bont: So, do you expect me to talk?

title: The Homer They Fall (S8E03)
text: "The Homer They Fall" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F03), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Jonathan Collier, originally airing November 10, 1996. After buying a novelty belt off Comic Book Guy, Bart shows it off at school and is beaten up and robbed by the local bullies. When Homer confronts the bullies' parents at Moe's Tavern, he too is thoroughly beaten, but astonishingly refuses to fall down, no matter how many punches he takes. Moe notices Homer's odd resilience and, revealing his own past as a boxer, convinces Homer to train as a fighter, devising a strategy where Homer simply waits out his opponents' exhaustion before shoving them over. Homer racks up a string of wins against weak, malnourished opponents, drawing the attention of Moe's old promoter, Lucius Sweet, who arranges a high-profile bout against the terrifyingly powerful champion Drederick Tatum. Marge reluctantly allows Homer to fight only after Moe promises to stop the match if Homer's safety is truly at risk. In the ring, Tatum proves far too strong and relentless for Homer's passive strategy to work, and Homer is quickly overwhelmed. Just as Tatum prepares to deliver a potentially fatal blow, Moe swoops in and rescues Homer using a parachute-powered paramotor, ending the fight before disaster strikes. The episode closes with Moe using his flying rig for good, shown rescuing disaster victims in India. Guest starring Michael Buffer as himself, Paul Winfield as Lucius Sweet. Notable quotes: Moe: Fun's over, fellas! If you're gonna beat up my friend in my bar, there's a two-drink minimum. | Moe: Yup. They called me Kid Gorgeous. Later on, it was Kid Presentable. Then Kid Gruesome. And finally, Kid Moe. | Homer: Big deal. I didn't even get my kid's belt back. The only thing a loser like me is good for is taking beatings. | Comic Book Guy: Hey, I... uh, de—oh... | Marge: Homer, you don't know how to box, you're 38 years old, and you haven't gotten any exercise since grade school.

title: Burns, Baby Burns (S8E04)
text: "Burns, Baby Burns" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F05), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing November 17, 1996. During a family outing to a cider mill, the Simpsons run into Ned Flanders while, elsewhere, Mr. Burns's train is delayed by a couch on the tracks. A down-on-his-luck souvenir vendor named Larry hitches a ride with the Simpsons and turns out to be Mr. Burns's long-lost illegitimate son. Burns is initially delighted, but Larry's crude jokes and lack of refinement quickly embarrass him, especially after a disastrous gala and a failed attempt to get Larry into Yale. To keep him occupied, Burns gives Larry a job at the power plant, where he strikes up a friendship with Homer. When Burns' patience with Larry runs out, Homer hatches a scheme for Larry to fake his own kidnapping so Burns will realize how much he values him. The plan backfires when Burns reacts with outrage over being "robbed" rather than concern for his son, and the pair are forced to hide out, first in the Simpsons' basement and then in a nearly empty movie theater, before being discovered by the police. In the end, Burns admits he cannot give Larry the family bond he craves, but Larry shrugs it off since he already has a family of his own, and the episode ends with an impromptu party at the Burns mansion. Guest starring Rodney Dangerfield as Larry Burns. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: Who are you? How dare you interrupt my lime rickey! | Larry: Mr. Burns, I am your son! | Female Admissions Officer: Let me put it this way. Larry spelled Yale with a 6. | Mr. Burns: Blast you! I am not made of airports! Get out! | Kent: Appearing in broad daylight with police everywhere. Ladies and gentlemen, there's only one word for that: idiocy.

title: Bart After Dark (S8E05)
text: "Bart After Dark" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F06), directed by Dominic Polcino and written by Richard Appel, originally airing November 24, 1996. When Lisa learns of an oil spill devastating Baby Seal Beach, she convinces Marge to take her there to help clean up the wildlife, leaving Homer and Bart alone at home. While playing with friends at the park, Bart accidentally damages the roof of a strange old house while retrieving Milhouse's remote-control plane. The house's owner, the mysterious Belle, demands compensation, and Homer volunteers Bart to work off the debt through chores. Bart soon discovers the building is actually a burlesque house, and he becomes oddly enthusiastic about his new job, even as the rest of Springfield's parents grow suspicious. When Marge returns early from a disappointing seal-cleaning trip, she's horrified to learn where Bart has been working and confronts Belle, demanding the club be shut down. Marge rallies the town into an angry mob determined to demolish the burlesque house, but Homer and Bart intervene with a heartfelt musical plea that temporarily wins the crowd over. Marge, arriving late with a bulldozer, accidentally crashes into the building anyway, and in an ironic twist, ends up performing there herself to pay for the damage she caused. You can stay right here and give the dog a bath. Or trim the cat's nails. | Homer: Gotcha. Cat in the furnace. | Mr. Burns: I don't like being outdoors, Smithers. For one thing, there are too many fat children. | Milhouse: It's a secret lab where they take the brains out of zombies and put them in the heads of other zombies to create a race of super-zombies.

title: A Milhouse Divided (S8E06)
text: "A Milhouse Divided" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F04), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Steve Tompkins, originally airing December 1, 1996. Marge throws a dinner party to break the monotony of family life, inviting the Flanders, Lovejoys, Hibberts, and Van Houtens. The evening is ruined when Kirk and Luann Van Houten's constant bickering erupts into a full-blown fight, ending with Luann demanding a divorce. Kirk moves into a dreary apartment and loses his job at the cracker factory, while Luann quickly moves on with a buff American Gladiator named Chase. Watching Kirk's failed attempts to rebuild his life rattles Homer, who suddenly fears that his own marriage to Marge could collapse just as unexpectedly. Homer turns to Lisa for advice on how to prove his devotion, recalling their unglamorous wedding at a truck stop and Marge's lingering disappointment over it. His clumsy romantic gestures, like recreating ocean sounds to help her sleep, only leave Marge unimpressed. Convinced the marriage is doomed, Homer secretly files for divorce, but he actually plans an elaborate surprise: gathering their friends and proposing a full, proper wedding ceremony to remarry Marge. Inspired by their happy reconciliation, Kirk tries to win Luann back with a heartfelt song, but she laughs at his attempt, and he is humiliated and thrown out by Chase. Notable quotes: Homer: Marge, can't we get some clear plates? I can't see the TV! | Bart: Hey, this ain't the Ritz. | Homer: You know what you two need? A little comic strip called "Love Is...". It's about two naked eight-year-olds who are married. | Homer: Oh, we can't afford that. Who do you think I am, Liz Taylor? | Otto: Man, that is flagrant false advertising!

title: Lisa's Date with Density (S8E07)
text: "Lisa's Date with Density" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F01), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Mike Scully, originally airing December 15, 1996. After Superintendent Chalmers' new car is vandalized, Nelson Muntz is caught and punished with janitorial duty under Groundskeeper Willie. Watching him from her classroom window, Lisa develops an unexpected crush on the school bully. A misdirected love note leads Nelson to mistakenly pummel Milhouse, but Lisa still pursues a relationship with Nelson, hoping she can reform him into a better person. She takes him shopping for new clothes and a haircut, and the two share a romantic evening and first kiss at the observatory. Just as Lisa believes she is succeeding, Nelson's old friends Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney pressure him into vandalizing Skinner's house, and his subsequent lie to Lisa reveals he hasn't truly changed, prompting her to end things while Milhouse rejoices. Meanwhile, Homer finds a discarded autodialer machine used for telemarketing scams and uses it to run his own "Happy Dude" panhandling scheme, driving the entire town to distraction with his recorded messages. Chief Wiggum eventually catches Homer and forces him to apologize to his victims via the same device, though Homer can't resist tacking on another request for money at the end.

title: Hurricane Neddy (S8E08)
text: "Hurricane Neddy" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F07), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Steve Young, originally airing December 29, 1996. As a hurricane bears down on Springfield, most residents panic and stock up on supplies while Ned Flanders calmly braces his home. When the storm passes, everyone else is unscathed but the Flanders house is completely destroyed, leaving Ned's family homeless and forcing them into the church basement. Ned, who lacks insurance, sinks into despair and questions his faith after seeing his store looted on the news. Marge organizes the neighbors to rebuild the Flanders home, but the shoddy, hastily done reconstruction—dirt floors, a toilet in the kitchen, a door too small to fit through—pushes Ned over the edge when it collapses. He erupts in a furious tirade against nearly everyone in town, shocking his neighbors, then checks himself into Calmwood Mental Hospital. There, Dr. Foster reveals that Ned's ultra-permissive parents made him a wild child, and a harsh spanking-based therapy overcorrected him into suppressing all anger. With Homer's help, Ned finally confronts and vents his repressed rage, admitting he hates his parents, and is declared cured. He returns home determined to express his feelings more honestly, unsettling his neighbors with his newfound bluntness. Guest starring Jon Lovitz as Jay Sherman. Notable quotes: Ned: It's all gone. Everything gone-diddilly-on. Maude? Rod? Todd? | Marge: Remarkable. There doesn't seem to be any damage at all. It just goes to show you that everything will work out if you have faith. | Apu: No, no, no, do not listen to that man. Remain calm. You will all have a chance to be gouged. | Grampa: I ain't leaving! I was born in this nursing home, and I'll die in this nursing home. | Homer: Hey, I got off pretty easy.

title: El Viaje Misterioso de Nuestro Jomer (S8E09)
keys: el viaje misterioso de nuestro jomer
text: "El Viaje Misterioso de Nuestro Jomer" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 3F24), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Ken Keeler, originally airing January 5, 1997. Marge tries desperately to keep Homer from learning that the annual Springfield Chili Cook-Off is happening, fearing a repeat of his drunken antics from the previous year. When Homer discovers it anyway, she reluctantly agrees to let him attend on the condition that he avoid beer. At the event, Homer's legendary tolerance for spicy food is destroyed by Chief Wiggum's chili, secretly laced with the incredibly potent Guatemalan Insanity Peppers. After nearly breaking his promise to Marge, Homer discovers that candle wax numbs his mouth, allowing him to eat the peppers in triumphant fashion, but the peppers send him into a surreal hallucination. In this vision, a mystical desert landscape and a wisecracking Space Coyote spirit guide urge him to seek out his true soulmate, casting doubt on his marriage to Marge. Waking up in a sand trap on a golf course, Homer rationalizes the whole experience, but the coyote's message nags at him, especially after Marge is furious that he seems to have gotten drunk again. Convinced he must find his true soulmate, Homer explores lonely corners of town, eventually fixating on the town's lighthouse keeper, only to find the lighthouse is run by a robot named E.A.R.L. After clumsily damaging the light, Homer is joined by Marge, and together they repair it just in time to try to warn an oncoming ship. Despite their effort, the ship still runs aground, spilling a cargo of hot pants that the townspeople gleefully scavenge, while Homer and Marge reaffirm that they truly are soulmates after all. title: The Springfield Files (S8E10)
text: "The Springfield Files" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 3G01), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Reid Harrison, originally airing January 12, 1997. After ditching work with a rigged security tape, Homer spends a drunken Friday night at Moe's and, walking home through the woods, encounters a glowing, gently-voiced figure that tells him not to be afraid. Nobody believes his story, not even Marge, Lisa, or the police, and his coworkers and Chief Wiggum mock him for it. News of the sighting reaches FBI agents Mulder and Scully, who travel to Springfield to investigate but find no solid evidence after testing Homer and revisiting the scene. Frustrated by the ridicule, Homer teams up with Bart, who believes him, and the two stake out the woods the next Friday, managing to film the mysterious creature before it flees. Once the footage airs on Kent Brockman's news report, the whole town turns out the following Friday to confront the alien, arming themselves with weapons. Lisa exposes the truth by shining a light on the figure, revealing it to be Mr. Burns, whose weekly rejuvenation treatments with Dr. Nick leave him disoriented and glowing from decades of nuclear plant exposure. After a booster shot restores his usual nastiness, the disturbance ends with the town joining Burns in song, and Marge tells Homer she's proud of him for bringing the town together. Guest starring Gillian Anderson as Dana Scully, David Duchovny as Fox Mulder, Leonard Nimoy as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: No! Well...ten beers. | Mr. Burns: Good morning starshine, the earth says hello... | Lisa: You want an alien? This is your alien! | Mulder: I hardly think the FBI is concerned with matters like that. | Squeaky-Voiced Teen: I'm Leonard Nimoy, goodnight, and keep watching the skis! ... I mean, skies.

title: The Twisted World of Marge Simpson (S8E11)
keys: the twisted world of marge simpson
text: "The Twisted World of Marge Simpson" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F08), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by Jennifer Crittenden, originally airing January 19, 1997. Marge is expelled from the Springfield Investorettes after admitting she's too cautious to invest in risky ventures, so she sets out to prove herself by buying into a modest pretzel-cart franchise called Pretzel Wagon. Early sales attempts flop spectacularly, first when the flashier Fleet-A-Pita van steals her customers at the power plant, and then when a free pretzel giveaway at an Isotopes game ends in a riot after fans, angry over a car raffle, pelt the field with pretzels and injure Whitey Ford. Crushed by repeated failure, Marge sinks into despair, telling her kids to aim low so they'll never be disappointed. Worried about his wife, Homer secretly seeks help and ends up striking a deal with mob boss Fat Tony after learning that Frank Ormand and his estate's executor are both dead. Business suddenly booms as Fat Tony's goons intimidate rival vendors, including blowing up the Investorettes' van and squeezing out the Girl Scouts and Luigi's restaurant, but the mob then demands repayment for their 'favor.' When Homer refuses to pay, Fat Tony corners Marge and claims he's owed all her profits, forcing Homer to admit what he's done. Marge and Homer resolve to stand their ground rather than pay the mob, and when Fat Tony's crew arrives to collect, the rival Investorette-backed Yakuza show up and a gang war erupts, allowing the Simpsons to escape safely home. Homer apologizes for dragging Marge into the mess, and the two reconcile. Guest starring Jack Lemmon as Frank Ormand, Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony. Notable quotes: Fat Tony: You have 24 hours to give us our money. And to show you we're serious... you have 12 hours. | Homer: Marge needs help... and God knows I'm not the man to provide it. But I know who can! | Bart: Oh, cheer up, Mom. You can't buy publicity like that. Thousands and thousands of people saw your pretzels injuring Whitey Ford. | Marge: I'm not wild about these high-risk ventures. They sound a little risky. | Homer: You mean the mob only did me a favor to get something in return? Oh, Fat Tony! I will say good day to you, sir!

title: Mountain of Madness (S8E12)
text: "Mountain of Madness" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F10), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 2, 1997. After a disastrous fire drill at the power plant, Mr. Burns decides the employees need a lesson in teamwork and organizes a mountain race to a remote cabin, with the last team to arrive facing termination. Homer is paired with Burns himself, while Smithers, upset at not being chosen as Burns's partner, is forced to go it alone and ends up reluctantly accompanied by Bart and Lisa, who slow him down more than help. Burns convinces Homer to cheat by using a snowmobile, and the two arrive at the cabin hours ahead of everyone else, bonding over champagne. Their celebratory toast triggers an avalanche that buries the cabin, trapping them, and every subsequent escape attempt only causes more snow to seal them in further. Isolated and suffering from cabin fever, Homer and Burns dress snowmen for company before descending into paranoid madness and violently turning on each other. Their fight ignites a propane tank, blasting the cabin out of the snow and sending it hurtling toward the rest of the astonished workers just as they reach the ranger station. Once the smoke clears, Burns reinstates the contest rules, declares Lenny the loser for arriving last, then abruptly changes his mind and cancels everyone's firing. The episode ends with Burns and Homer eyeing each other warily while a furious Lenny stalks off to confront Burns, only to comically fall into an icy crevasse. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: I've seen more orderly behavior in a Ritz Brothers film! You all need a serious lesson in teamwork! | Mr. Burns: Cheating is the gift man gives himself. | Homer: Mr. Burns, I insist that we cheat! | Bart: Mom, can Lisa and I play outside... away from the bear? | Mr. Burns: Yes. You won, all right. You won more than you bargained for.

title: The Itchy & Scratchy & Poochie Show (S8E14)
text: "The Itchy & Scratchy & Poochie Show" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F12), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by David S. Cohen, originally airing February 9, 1997. Facing sliding ratings for 'Itchy & Scratchy,' producer Roger Meyers Jr. takes Lisa's offhand suggestion to heart and decides the cartoon needs a fresh character, settling on a dog named Poochie to complete the mouse-cat-dog chain. Homer, egged on by his family, auditions for the voice role and unexpectedly lands the part, becoming fast friends with veteran voice actress June Bellamy along the way. Poochie's debut episode airs to universally scathing reviews, since network-mandated changes strip away the violent slapstick fans love and instead make him a toothless, catchphrase-spouting mascot. Humiliated executives quietly plot to kill the character off, and when Homer overhears them he tries to save his job by writing a heartfelt speech for Poochie's next appearance. The studio secretly replaces his dialogue with a hasty explanation that Poochie has died returning to his home planet, delighting the staff and fans but devastating Homer. Meanwhile, the show's mysterious extra houseguest Roy, who has apparently been living with the Simpsons for a while without explanation, decides it's finally time to move out. In the end, Bart and Lisa are relieved to see 'Itchy & Scratchy' return to its simple, violent roots, and they casually flip the channel to see what else is on. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Troy McClure, Alex Rocco as Roger Meyers, Jr.. Notable quotes: Roger Meyers, Jr.: Hey, Krusty, you look great. You get your teeth bleached? | Krusty: I oughta replace it right now with a Chinese cartoon where the robots that turn into... blingwads! | Ralph: My knob tastes funny. | Man: Please refrain from tasting the knob. | Roger Myers Jr.: You kids don't know what you want! That's why you're still kids; 'cause you're stupid!

title: Homer's Phobia (S8E15)
text: "Homer's Phobia" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F11), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Ron Hauge, originally airing February 16, 1997. After Bart's prank destroys the family's gas line, the Simpsons need money and attempt to pawn what Marge believes is a priceless antique doll, only to learn from shop clerk John that it's actually a cheap old whiskey bottle. Despite this, the family befriends the charming, witty John and invites him home, where he bonds with Homer over dancing and shared interests. When Marge reveals that John is gay, Homer spirals into panic and irrational homophobia, convinced that Bart's newly picked-up mannerisms and phrases mean his son is 'turning gay' too. Homer attempts a series of misguided manly bonding exercises—sending Bart to loiter by a cigarette billboard, touring a steel mill that turns out to be run by gay employees, and finally taking him deer hunting with Barney and Moe. The hunting trip goes awry when the group breaks into Santa's Village and provokes a herd of aggressive reindeer, leaving Homer and Bart in danger. John arrives just in time, using a robotic Santa Claus to scare off the reindeer and save their lives. Humbled by John's heroism, Homer realizes his prejudice was baseless, while Bart finally understands why his father had been acting so strangely. The episode ends with the family relationship restored and Homer's fears thoroughly dispelled. Guest starring John Waters. Notable quotes: Homer: Oh my God! Oh my God! Oh my God! Oh my God! I danced with a gay! Marge, Lisa, promise me you won't tell anyone. Promise me! | Homer: You know me, Marge. I like my beer cold, my TV loud, and my homosexuals FA-LAMING! | Bart: Anything slim. | Bart: Oh, Dad. You are the living end. | Homer: Look, John, you seem like a perfectly nice guy and all. Just stay the hell away from my family!

title: Brother from Another Series (S8E16)
text: "Brother from Another Series" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F14), directed by Pete Michels and written by Ken Keeler, originally airing February 23, 1997. After a decade of increasingly deranged crimes, Sideshow Bob is released from prison into the custody of his estranged brother Cecil, Springfield's chief hydrological engineer, who is overseeing construction of a new dam. Bart is convinced Bob's reformation is a lie and becomes obsessed with proving his old nemesis is still evil, even sabotaging Bob's date with Edna Krabappel and spying on him at the construction site. When Bart and Lisa sneak into Bob's trailer, they discover a briefcase of stolen money, but before they can make sense of it, Bob catches them and chases them into the dam's turbine room. There Cecil reveals himself as the true villain: he has been embezzling construction funds and framing Bob for it, and he traps all three of them in the turbine room, intending to detonate the dam. Bob, proving his change of heart, helps Bart and Lisa escape and battles Cecil to stop the explosion, ultimately saving Bart's life in a dramatic rescue on the dam's face. Cecil is arrested, but manipulates Bob into vowing revenge on Bart again, undoing the fragile trust Bart had begun to place in him. Despite their efforts, the dam bursts anyway and floods the town, though little real damage results, and the episode ends with Bob and Cecil bickering as cellmates in jail. Guest starring Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob, David Hyde Pierce as Cecil Terwilliger. Notable quotes: Cecil: Off the record, yes. But officially, I did it for the money! | Bart: Guess who? | Cecil: Maris? | Bob: You only get one chance with Edna Krabappel. I hope you're happy. | Bart: Inside every hardened criminal beats the heart of a ten-year-old boy.

title: My Sister, My Sitter (S8E17)
text: "My Sister, My Sitter" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F13), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing March 2, 1997. After reading a book about babysitting twins, Lisa decides to launch her own babysitting career and quickly builds a reputation for reliability. Her resolve is tested when Homer and Marge leave her in charge of Bart and Maggie for an evening, since Bart is furious at being watched by his younger sister. Bart wages a campaign of sabotage, refusing dinner, watching forbidden TV, spiking Maggie's ice cream with caffeine, and ordering absurd deliveries just to humiliate Lisa. When Lisa finally loses her temper and chases him, he tumbles down the stairs, dislocating his arm and bumping his head, but keeps aggravating the injury to use as evidence against her. Desperate to protect her babysitting business, Lisa secretly sneaks Bart out of the house in a wheelbarrow, with Maggie stashed in a pet carrier, intending to get him medical help without her parents finding out. Her covert mission goes awry as she dodges Chief Wiggum, loses Bart down a muddy hill, and ends up exposed by a spotlight at the grand opening of the Springfield Squidport, right in front of Marge, Homer, and a crowd of horrified onlookers who assume the worst. Dr. Hibbert steps in to clear up the misunderstanding and treat Bart's injuries, and a chastened Bart apologizes for nearly wrecking Lisa's reputation. In the end, Lisa's ordeal actually enhances her standing, as she receives babysitting requests from both Dr. Hibbert and Ned Flanders. Notable quotes: Homer: You could be Abe Lincoln's father's boss! | Lisa: I sell peace of mind for a dollar an hour. Two dollars after 9 o'clock. | Homer: Take it like a man, boy, and do everything your sister says. | Lisa: But I'm very mature for my age. People often mistake me for 9! | Homer: I love these pedestrian malls. There's practically no traffic.

title: Homer vs. the Eighteenth Amendment (S8E18)
text: "Homer vs. the Eighteenth Amendment" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F15), directed by Bob Anderson and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 16, 1997. Springfield's St. Patrick's Day beer bash leads to Bart getting drunk in public, prompting an outraged group of women to demand a ban on alcohol. An old law is discovered that technically outlaws drinking, and Mayor Quimby is forced to enforce prohibition. Duff Beer collapses after a failed non-alcoholic relaunch, while the mafia begins bootlegging beer to Moe's, now disguised as a pet shop. When corrupt, tipsy Chief Wiggum fails to stop the drinking, humorless federal agent Rex Banner is brought in and cracks down hard. Homer secretly becomes Springfield's underground beer supplier, using an elaborate bowling-ball delivery system to funnel booze into Moe's, earning fame as the mysterious 'Beer Baron.' As demand grows, Homer moves into risky homemade liquor production, drawing Banner's suspicion. After Homer helps a broken Wiggum regain his dignity, he is caught and sentenced to a humiliating catapult exile, but is saved when it's revealed the prohibition law was repealed 199 years earlier. Springfield quickly returns to its beer-loving ways, with the mafia flooding the town with alcohol once again. Guest starring Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony, Dave Thomas as Rex Banner. Somebody to kiss you goodbye? | Homer: Oh honey you're not the world's worst mother. What about that freezer lady in Georgia?

title: Grade School Confidential (S8E19)
text: "Grade School Confidential" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F09), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Rachel Pulido, originally airing April 6, 1997. Martin Prince throws himself a lavish but dull birthday party, which ends in disaster when the kids get food poisoning from bad oysters. Bart skips the illness and stumbles upon Principal Skinner and Edna Krabappel sharing a secret kiss in Martin's playhouse. Fearful of losing their jobs, the two educators swear Bart to secrecy and make him their go-between, rewarding him by letting Milhouse take the blame for his poor school record. As the arrangement drags on, Bart becomes increasingly humiliated by having to relay their romantic messages in front of his peers. Pushed too far, he snaps and exposes the couple's relationship to the entire school by throwing open a closet door on them. The scandal spreads through Springfield with wild exaggeration, prompting Superintendent Chalmers to fire both Skinner and Krabappel after Chief Wiggum gets involved. Feeling guilty, Bart urges Skinner to fight back, leading the couple to barricade themselves in the school and make televised demands for reinstatement and privacy. After Skinner publicly and awkwardly clears up rumors about their intimacy by revealing he's a virgin, the town relents and Chalmers restores their jobs, with the couple pretending to Bart that they've broken up so they can continue dating in secret. Notable quotes: Principal Skinner: The fact is, I haven't ever had relations. I am a virgin. | Maude Flanders: Just a minute, Edna. I don't think we're talking about love here. We are talking about S-E-X, in front of the C-H-I-L-D-R-E-N! | Krusty: Sex Cauldron? I thought they closed that place down! | Principal Skinner: We have barricaded ourselves in the school, and we're not coming out 'til our demands our met! | Groundskeeper Willie: Willie hears ya. Willie don't care.

title: The Canine Mutiny (S8E20)
text: "The Canine Mutiny" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F16), directed by Dominic Polcino and written by Ron Hauge, originally airing April 13, 1997. Bored with never receiving mail, Bart fills out a credit card application using his dog Santa's Little Helper's name, misspelled as 'Santos L. Halper,' and lists his occupation as 'butt doctor.' The card is approved, and Bart goes on a lavish shopping spree, buying gifts for the family and, most extravagantly, a $1,200 purebred collie named Laddie. The family quickly falls for the well-trained Laddie, largely ignoring Santa's Little Helper, and Bart soon finds himself unable to pay off the mounting credit card debt. When debt collectors arrive to repossess everything, Bart panics and claims Santa's Little Helper is the expensive collie, resulting in his own loyal dog being taken away instead of Laddie. Guilt-ridden, Bart searches the town for his missing pet while Laddie becomes a local hero and is given to the police force after saving a baby. Bart eventually tracks Santa's Little Helper to a lonely blind man, Mr. Mitchell, who has grown attached to the dog, complicating Bart's attempt to reclaim him. After a tense late-night confrontation involving the police, Bart and Mitchell let the dog choose, and Santa's Little Helper picks Bart, allowing the family to reunite while Mitchell is left to deal with the police over an unrelated matter. Guest starring Frank Welker as Laddie. Notable quotes: Homer: Well, crying isn't gonna bring him back... unless your tears smell like dog food. | Comic Book Guy: Oh, pardon me, Santos, if that is your real name, Bart Simpson, but your phony credit card is no good here. Now make like my pants, and split. | Marge: Homer, are you wearing a tie to impress Laddie? | Homer: You gave both dogs away?? You know how I feel about giving! | Chief Wiggum: Hello! Police! Aw, man, if this one's not the right house, I quit!

title: The Old Man and the Lisa (S8E21)
keys: the old man and the lisa
text: "The Old Man and the Lisa" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F17), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing April 20, 1997. Lisa and Principal Skinner run a recycling drive for the Junior Achievers Club, and Mr. Burns is invited to give the kids a speech on business success. During his talk, Lisa points out from his own biography that Burns' fortune isn't as large as he believes, prompting him to check his finances. His fearful, yes-man lawyers never warned him about risky investments, and he ends up completely bankrupt, forcing the bank to seize the power plant and sell his mansion to pro wrestler Bret Hart. After a humiliating stint living with Smithers and a disastrous grocery store trip, Burns is committed to the Springfield Retirement Castle. Desperate, he begs Lisa for help, and she agrees to assist him only if he abandons his ruthless ways, teaching him to earn money through recycling. Their venture grows into the successful Little Lisa Recycling Plant, and Lisa is thrilled that Burns seems reformed—until he reveals the plant's true purpose: turning recycled plastic into giant nets to strip the ocean of sea life for profit as animal slurry. Horrified, Lisa tries to warn the town, but everyone is too enamored with recycling to listen. Burns later visits Lisa after selling the plant for $120 million and offers her a 10% cut as thanks, which she refuses once she realizes its tainted origin, leading to a series of heart attacks for Homer when he misunderstands (and then correctly understands) how much money was turned down. Guest starring Bret Hart. Notable quotes: Homer: Please be Flanders, Please be Flanders. | Bret "The Hitman" Hart: Eww. title: In Marge We Trust (S8E22)
text: "In Marge We Trust" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F18), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Donick Cary, originally airing April 27, 1997. After a dull sermon from Reverend Lovejoy leaves the congregation restless, Marge confronts him about the church's lack of outreach and impulsively volunteers to counsel parishioners over the phone. Meanwhile, Homer and the kids visit the dump, where Bart finds a box of Japanese detergent, Mr. Sparkle, whose mascot bears an uncanny resemblance to Homer. As Marge's phone counseling proves surprisingly effective, Lovejoy grows jealous and resentful of losing his flock's attention. Homer becomes fixated on solving the mystery of Mr. Sparkle, eventually learning via a videotaped commercial that the logo is simply a coincidental merger of two unrelated Japanese company logos. Back at church, Marge's advice to Ned Flanders to confront some bullying teens backfires, leading to Ned being chased across town and trapped in the zoo's baboon enclosure. Marge and the Simpsons track him down with help from a gas station attendant, and Lovejoy dramatically rescues Ned by driving a zoo train through the baboon pit and fighting off the animals. Reinvigorated by his heroics, Lovejoy retells the rescue story as his new sermon, winning back the congregation's admiration and resolving his rivalry with Marge. Guest starring Sab Shimono, Gedde Watanabe, Frank Welker. Notable quotes: Homer: In that case, he should've made the week an hour longer. Do you know that so-called "volunteers" don't even get paid? | Akira Kurosawa: Ah yes, this is a product called "Mr. Sparkle." Very popular dish detergent. Hey, he looks like you!

title: Homer's Enemy (S8E23)
text: "Homer's Enemy" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F19), directed by Jim Reardon and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing May 4, 1997. After a sympathetic news report about his hard-luck life, Frank Grimes is hired at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, only to be passed over for the executive vice president job in favor of a dog when Mr. Burns forgets his earlier promise. Working alongside Homer, Grimes is horrified by his new coworker's laziness and incompetence, especially since Homer still enjoys a comfortable home, family, and reputation despite doing almost nothing to earn it. Meanwhile, in a lighter subplot, Bart impulsively buys a condemned warehouse at a tax auction for a dollar and 'employs' Milhouse as its night watchman, though the building eventually collapses and releases a swarm of rats into Moe's Tavern. Homer tries to win Grimes over with a fancy dinner, but the visit backfires spectacularly when Grimes sees firsthand just how much Homer has despite his mediocrity, and the two are declared enemies. Desperate to discredit Homer, Grimes tricks him into entering a children's power-plant design contest, hoping to publicly humiliate him, but Homer wins anyway thanks to Mr. Burns' amusement. Pushed past his breaking point, Grimes has a full mental breakdown, mimicking Homer's slovenly behavior around the plant before fatally electrocuting himself while imitating Homer's careless demeanor. At Grimes' funeral, the episode ends on a dark comedic note as Homer sleep-talks through the service, oblivious and unbothered, drawing laughter from the mourners instead of the reflection Grimes' death might have warranted. It's supposed to be a power plant, not Aunt Beulah's Bordello! | Homer: Change the channel, Marge! | Milhouse: I was watching. I saw the whole thing. First it started falling over, then it fell over.

title: The Simpsons Spin-Off Showcase (S8E24)
text: "The Simpsons Spin-Off Showcase" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F20), directed by Neil Affleck and written by Story by: Ken Keeler, Written by: David S. Cohen, Dan Greaney, Steve Tompkins, originally airing May 11, 1997. Troy McClure hosts a special from the Museum of TV and Television, explaining that Fox needed new shows to fill its fall schedule, so the Simpsons producers created three spin-off pilots. In 'Chief Wiggum, P.I.,' Wiggum and Skinner relocate to New Orleans as crime-fighting partners and must rescue Ralph after he's kidnapped by a Cajun gangster called Big Daddy, leading to a wild boat chase through the bayou. Next, 'The Love-Matic Grampa' finds Grampa's spirit trapped inside Moe's Love Tester machine after Grampa dies in a freak accident, and the ghostly grandfather tries to coach the lonely bartender through a date, with disastrous but ultimately heartwarming results after bullies destroy the machine. The final segment, 'The Simpson Family Smile-Time Variety Hour,' reimagines the family as hosts of a cheesy 1970s-style musical variety show at Radio City Music Hall, complete with novelty skits, a candy-themed karaoke number, and a guest appearance by Tim Conway, ending in a chaotic pillow fight. Throughout, Troy McClure provides ironic narration, treating the absurd pilots as legitimate hits. In the epilogue, he previews outlandish and mostly fictional storylines for the upcoming season, most of which never materialize. The special closes on a self-mockingly optimistic note about the future of these 'spin-offs,' none of which are ever seen again except for a brief cameo by the alien Ozmodiar. Guest starring Tim Conway, Phil Hartman, Gailard Sartain. Swampy. | Ralph: Daddy, these rubber pants are hot. | Chief Wiggum: You wear 'em until you learn, son. | Bart: Mardi Gras, man! When the Big Easy calls, you gotta accept the charges!

title: The Secret War of Lisa Simpson (S8E25)
keys: the secret war of lisa simpson
text: "The Secret War of Lisa Simpson" is an episode of Season 8 (production code 4F21), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Richard Appel, originally airing May 18, 1997. During a field trip to the Springfield Police Station, Bart mischievously blasts a wall of megaphones set to full volume, shattering every window in town. As punishment, Homer and Marge decide to enroll him at Rommelwood Military School, and to everyone's surprise, Lisa asks to attend too, becoming the academy's first female cadet. The other cadets resent having to give up their dorm space for Lisa and retaliate by hazing both her and Bart with brutal chores and pranks. Bart quickly wins acceptance among the boys, but Lisa remains isolated and struggles with the school's grueling physical demands, growing homesick and discouraged. After feeling guilty for abandoning her, Bart secretly begins training Lisa at night for the dreaded final test, a rope-crossing obstacle called the Eliminator. On the day of the test, Lisa falters and nearly falls, but Bart breaks ranks to publicly cheer her on, giving her the strength to finish. Their bond restored, both siblings graduate, with Lisa even earning a medal from the Commandant. The episode ends on a comedic note as Homer and Marge, instead of taking the kids to Disneyland as promised, drive them to the dentist. Guest starring Willem Dafoe. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: Aw, can't anybody in this town take the law into their own hands? | Lisa: It's not my nature to complain, but so far today we've had three movies, two film strips, and an hour and a half of "magazine time." title: The City of New York vs. Homer Simpson (S9E01)
keys: the city of new york vs. homer simpson
text: "The City of New York vs. Homer Simpson" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 4F22), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing September 21, 1997. After a bar drawing forces Barney into designated-driver duty, he ends up borrowing Homer's car and abandons it in New York City for two months while on a drunken bender he barely remembers. Homer, sick of waiting, cobbles together a makeshift car from spare parts, only for Lisa to bring news that his real car has been impounded in Manhattan and will be dumped in the river if not claimed within 72 hours. Despite deep-seated trauma from a previous disastrous trip to the city, Homer reluctantly agrees to go because the fare is cheap, even burning his wallet so New York can't 'steal' it. Once there, the rest of the family heads off to enjoy Broadway shows and ethnic neighborhoods while Homer discovers his car covered in tickets and locked under a wheel boot at the World Trade Center. Forced to wait all day for a parking officer who never shows, Homer suffers through hunger, questionable street food, and a desperate search for a bathroom that leads him to the top of the North Tower. When he finally relieves himself, the officer appears out of nowhere and slaps him with a new ticket for leaving his vehicle. Enraged, Homer rips the boot off using a stolen jackhammer and a lot of kicking, wrecking the car in the process. He races through the city to reunite with his family, and they speed away from New York covered in garbage truck debris, with Homer ambiguously promising they might return someday. Guest starring Joan Kenley as the telephone operator. Notable quotes: Homer: Hehe, Homer one. New York nothin'. | Duffman: Ah, that's swell. Duff Beer wholeheartedly supports the designated driver system. Now, who wants to party?! | Bart: Hey, immigrants! Beat it! Country's full! | Marge: No, no, Lisa they're just sleeping, upside down... and inside out. | Homer: New York is a hellhole. And you know how I feel about hellholes.
quotes: Homer: Hehe, Homer one. New York nothin'.
Duffman: Ah, that's swell. Duff Beer wholeheartedly supports the designated driver system. Now, who wants to party?!
Bart: Hey, immigrants! Beat it! Country's full!
Marge: No, no, Lisa they're just sleeping, upside down... and inside out.
Homer: New York is a hellhole. And you know how I feel about hellholes.

title: The Principal and the Pauper (S9E02)
text: "The Principal and the Pauper" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 4F23), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Ken Keeler, originally airing September 28, 1997. Springfield gathers to celebrate Principal Skinner's twentieth anniversary, but the festivities are derailed when a stranger arrives claiming to be the real Seymour Skinner. Under questioning, Skinner confesses that he is actually Armin Tamzarian, a soldier who assumed his fallen commanding officer's identity after returning from Vietnam. The real Skinner, played by Martin Sheen, takes over as principal, but his rigid military demeanor clashes badly with the town's affection for the familiar impostor. Even Agnes, who initially disowned Tamzarian, comes to miss him, and the Simpsons hatch a scheme to track him down in Capital City where he has resettled into an ordinary life. After convincing him to return, the townspeople forcibly remove the real Sergeant Skinner by tying him to a chair aboard a departing freight train. Judge Snyder then issues an absurd ruling restoring Armin Tamzarian to his role as Principal Skinner and forbidding anyone from ever mentioning the name Tamzarian again, resetting the status quo as if nothing happened. Guest starring Martin Sheen. Notable quotes: Skinner/Armin: My real name is... Armin Tamzarian! | Homer: Keep looking shocked... and move slowly towards the cake. | Agnes Skinner: I have no son! | Chalmers: Armin Tamzarian's reign of terror is over! Now let us welcome our new principal Skinner... principal Seymour Skinner! | Edna: Is this the line for people who want to badmouth Sergeant Skinner?
quotes: Skinner/Armin: My real name is... Armin Tamzarian!
Homer: Keep looking shocked... and move slowly towards the cake.
Agnes Skinner: I have no son!
Chalmers: Armin Tamzarian's reign of terror is over! Now let us welcome our new principal Skinner... principal Seymour Skinner!
Edna: Is this the line for people who want to badmouth Sergeant Skinner?

title: Lisa's Sax (S9E03)
text: "Lisa's Sax" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 3G02), directed by Dominic Polcino and written by Al Jean, originally airing October 19, 1997. After Bart accidentally hurls Lisa's saxophone out the window during a squabble, it is destroyed in the street by passing vehicles and pedestrians. Grieving over the loss, Lisa realizes she has no memory of how she got the instrument, prompting Homer to tell an exaggerated, self-serving story about Bart's traumatic first day of school. Lisa dismisses his tale as irrelevant, so Marge steps in with the real account. She recalls how Bart's enthusiasm for school was crushed by a dismissive teacher, turning him into a troublemaker, while a psychologist discovered that young Lisa was remarkably gifted after she solved a complex puzzle. Homer and Marge struggled with how to nurture Lisa's talents, briefly considering an expensive private school they couldn't afford. During a brutal heat wave, Homer had saved money for an air conditioner, but Marge convinced him to instead use the funds to buy Lisa her first saxophone. The purchase came with an inscription mishap that ended in Homer's signature 'D'oh!' being engraved on the instrument. The story resolves in the present as Homer, moved by the memory, buys Lisa a new saxophone with a similar engraving, just as another heat wave strikes Springfield. Guest starring Fyvush Finkel as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: Lisa, knock off that racket! | Bart: Oh yeah? My dear Lisa, you are eight, and I am ten. And in my two extra years on this planet, I've learned a few tricks. | Homer: Lisa, honey, if it'll make you feel better I'll destroy something Bart loves. | Grampa: Homer, you're dumb as a mule and twice as ugly, if a strange man offers you a ride, I say take it! | Principal Skinner: Welcome kindergarteners, I'm Principal Sinner... Skinner!
quotes: Homer: Lisa, knock off that racket!
Bart: Oh yeah? My dear Lisa, you are eight, and I am ten. And in my two extra years on this planet, I've learned a few tricks.
Homer: Lisa, honey, if it'll make you feel better I'll destroy something Bart loves.
Grampa: Homer, you're dumb as a mule and twice as ugly, if a strange man offers you a ride, I say take it!
Principal Skinner: Welcome kindergarteners, I'm Principal Sinner... Skinner!

title: Treehouse of Horror VIII (S9E04)
text: "Treehouse of Horror VIII" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F02), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Mike Scully, David S. Cohen, Ned Goldreyer, originally airing October 26, 1997. This Halloween anthology opens with a Fox censor being gruesomely stabbed to death by a sword emerging from the ratings icon, pushing the show's rating to absurd extremes. In 'The HΩmega Man,' Mayor Quimby's insulting joke about France provokes a neutron bomb attack that seemingly wipes out all of Springfield except Homer, who survives by hiding in a bomb shelter he was shopping for. Believing himself the last man alive, Homer briefly revels in his freedom until he's confronted by mutated townsfolk who want to eliminate 'normal' humans, but he escapes home to find his family alive thanks to their lead-paint-covered house, and together they gun down the mutants before driving off to loot Ferraris. In 'Fly vs. Fly,' Homer's newly purchased teleporter causes chaos when Bart swaps bodies with a housefly after his pets are accidentally merged in the device; the family unknowingly welcomes fly-Bart into the house until Lisa helps reverse the swap, leaving Homer to furiously chase Bart with an axe for misusing his invention. Finally, in 'Easy-Bake Coven,' Puritan-era Springfield is gripped by witch hysteria, and Marge is accused and thrown off a cliff to prove her innocence—only to reveal she truly is a witch. She and her equally witchy sisters, Patty and Selma, terrorize the town until Maude Flanders's gift of gingerbread men saves the local children and inadvertently creates the tradition of Halloween trick-or-treating. The episode closes with modern-day Homer accusing Lisa of witchcraft after his own Halloween prank backfires, sparking a mob chase through the neighborhood. Notable quotes: Homer: Now, that's the Marge I married. Now, who wants to go steal some Ferraris?! | Chief Wiggum: The Bible says a lot of things. NOW SHOVE HER!! | Homer: Something I should have done a long time ago. | Moe: Uh, we don't like the word `mutant,' Homer. We prefer "freaks." Or "monsters." | Comic Book Guy: But, Aquaman, you cannot marry a woman without gills! You're from two different worlds! This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 8): "The HΩmega Man", "Fly vs. Fly", and "Easy-Bake Coven".
quotes: Homer: Now, that's the Marge I married. Now, who wants to go steal some Ferraris?!
Chief Wiggum: The Bible says a lot of things. NOW SHOVE HER!!
Homer: Something I should have done a long time ago.
Moe: Uh, we don't like the word `mutant,' Homer. We prefer "freaks." Or "monsters."
Comic Book Guy: But, Aquaman, you cannot marry a woman without gills! You're from two different worlds!

title: The Cartridge Family (S9E05)
text: "The Cartridge Family" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F01), directed by Pete Michels and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing November 2, 1997. After a soccer match between Mexico and Portugal erupts into a citywide riot, Homer decides the family needs protection and buys a handgun rather than pay for a security system. Marge is horrified by the weapon and insists he get rid of it, but Homer instead treats the gun recklessly, using it to grab cereal off the roof of the Kwik-E-Mart and to shoot clay-pigeon-style at dinner plates. After the gun nearly injures Marge during dinner, Homer promises to dispose of it but secretly stashes it in the vegetable crisper. Bart and Milhouse find it and start a dangerous game of William Tell, which Marge interrupts just in time, finally giving Homer an ultimatum to choose between his gun and his family. Marge leaves with the kids for a motel, and Homer, hosting an NRA meeting at home, is thrown out of the organization for his careless gun handling. Realizing his mistake, Homer rushes to the motel, reconciles with Marge, and claims he's finally gotten rid of the weapon. Just then, Snake attempts to rob the motel clerk at knifepoint, and Homer's hidden gun foils the robbery, though Snake steals the gun and escapes. In the end, as Marge prepares to throw the recovered gun away, she catches her own reflection looking dangerous and, intrigued, decides to keep it instead. Notable quotes: Homer: A gun is not a weapon, Marge, it's a tool. Like a butcher's knife or a harpoon, or... or an alligator. | Homer: I'd like to buy your deadliest gun, please. | Gun Shop Owner: Aisle six, next to the sympathy cards. | Moe: And that's how, with a few minor adjustments, you can turn a regular gun into five guns. | Homer: I'm sorry I lied to you Marge, but this gun had a hold on me. I felt this incredible surge of power, like God must feel when he's holding a gun.
quotes: Homer: A gun is not a weapon, Marge, it's a tool. Like a butcher's knife or a harpoon, or... or an alligator.
Homer: I'd like to buy your deadliest gun, please.
Gun Shop Owner: Aisle six, next to the sympathy cards.
Moe: And that's how, with a few minor adjustments, you can turn a regular gun into five guns.
Homer: I'm sorry I lied to you Marge, but this gun had a hold on me. I felt this incredible surge of power, like God must feel when he's holding a gun.

title: Bart Star (S9E06)
text: "Bart Star" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F03), directed by Dominic Polcino and written by Donick Cary, originally airing November 9, 1997. After a town health fair exposes Bart and other kids as out of shape, Homer pushes Bart into joining the newly formed Springfield Wildcats pee-wee football team, coached by Ned Flanders. Nelson turns out to be a natural quarterback and leads the team to victory, but Homer becomes obsessed with tearing down Ned's coaching and needling him until Ned angrily quits and hands the coaching job to Homer. Determined to prove himself, Homer benches star player Nelson and installs an unqualified Bart as quarterback, ignoring the team's protests. Bart is humiliated in a lopsided loss, and after enduring bullying from his teammates and pressure from his father, he fakes an injury and then quits outright, getting himself and Milhouse cut from the team. Homer's guilt over pushing Bart too hard mirrors his own childhood resentment toward Abe, and the two eventually reconcile over sodas at the Kwik-E-Mart. With Bart back in his old tackle role and Nelson restored at quarterback, the Wildcats win the championship, with Bart nobly taking the blame for a foul to let Nelson score the winning touchdown, leading to Bart's arrest by Chief Wiggum for humorously exaggerated charges. Guest starring Roy Firestone, Mike Judge as Hank Hill, Joe Namath. Notable quotes: Dr. Hibbert: Your cholestral level is lethally high, Homer, but I'm more concerned about your gravy level. | Lisa: Hey, tubby! Want another Pop-Tart, tubby? | Bart: I'm comfortable with who I am. | Nelson: I won't give you a B, but I'll tear you a new A. | Homer: I believe in you! Hug meeee!
quotes: Dr. Hibbert: Your cholestral level is lethally high, Homer, but I'm more concerned about your gravy level.
Lisa: Hey, tubby! Want another Pop-Tart, tubby?
Bart: I'm comfortable with who I am.
Nelson: I won't give you a B, but I'll tear you a new A.
Homer: I believe in you! Hug meeee!

title: The Two Mrs. Nahasapeemapetilons (S9E07)
text: "The Two Mrs. Nahasapeemapetilons" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F04), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Richard Appel, originally airing November 16, 1997. When a bachelor auction to benefit the Springfield fire brigade flops, Marge nominates Apu, whose surprising popularity earns him a string of dates and a taste of the single life. His fun is cut short by a letter from his mother in India reminding him of an arranged marriage to a woman named Manjula. Panicked, Apu takes Homer's advice and claims he's already married, and when his mother unexpectedly shows up in Springfield, Marge reluctantly agrees to pose as his wife. The ruse grows more complicated when Homer, hiding out at the retirement home under a fake identity, returns and climbs into bed with Marge just as Apu's mother arrives to say goodbye, blowing the whole scheme. Furious at being dragged into the lie, Marge insists Apu come clean, and his mother declares the arranged marriage will happen regardless. At the backyard wedding, Apu is still uneasy until he reconnects with Manjula and discovers they share the same favorite food, book, and movie, all being Fried Green Tomatoes. Homer makes a last-ditch, poorly costumed attempt to disrupt the ceremony as a Ganesha figure but is driven off, and Apu and Manjula are happily married. Guest starring Jan Hooks, Andrea Martin. Notable quotes: Apu: All Kwik-E-Mart employees must be skilled with firearms. | Luann Van Houten: Who is up for some clog dancing? | Apu: Why do you not try and stop me!
quotes: Apu: All Kwik-E-Mart employees must be skilled with firearms.
Luann Van Houten: Who is up for some clog dancing?
Apu: Why do you not try and stop me!

title: Lisa the Skeptic (S9E08)
text: "Lisa the Skeptic" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F05), directed by Neil Affleck and written by David S. Cohen, originally airing November 23, 1997. After Homer's supposed boat prize turns out to be a scam to collect unpaid parking tickets, Lisa notices bulldozers preparing to destroy Sabertooth Meadow, a site rich in fossils, to build a new mall. With help from Lionel Hutz, she convinces the mall's developer Sid to let students dig for fossils there as a publicity move. During the dig, Lisa unearths a skeleton with wing-like bone structures, which the town immediately declares to be an angel. Homer takes the bones home and starts charging townspeople admission to view them, while Lisa's attempts to apply scientific skepticism are drowned out by mass hysteria, even causing a rift with Marge, who believes in the angel. Lisa secretly sends a sample to paleontologist Stephen Jay Gould, but his tests are inconclusive, and religious fervor escalates into vandalism against Springfield's scientific institutions. When the skeleton vanishes and reappears with an ominous doomsday message, the town prepares for the end of the world, only for sundown to pass uneventfully. The skeleton then rises and reveals itself as an animatronic promotional gimmick for the grand opening of the Heavenly Hills Mall, exposing the entire affair as a hoax. Lisa and Marge reconcile as the townspeople rush off to shop at the new mall. Guest starring Stephen Jay Gould as himself, Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Homer: I didn't like it. The mast had termites. | Mr. Burns: Oh, fiddle-faddle. Everyone knows our mutants have flippers. Oops. I've said too much. Smithers, use the amnesia ray. | Homer: No one's calling it an angel, Lisa. If you'll look carefully, you'll notice I never once used the word "angel". | Kent Brockman: Oh, that's a bunch of baloney, Lisa. Everyone knows leprechauns are extinct. | Chief Wiggum: Oh, oh yeah, yeah, we're outraged. Very, uh... Very much so... But look at all the stores! A Pottery Barn!
quotes: Homer: I didn't like it. The mast had termites.
Mr. Burns: Oh, fiddle-faddle. Everyone knows our mutants have flippers. Oops. I've said too much. Smithers, use the amnesia ray.
Homer: No one's calling it an angel, Lisa. If you'll look carefully, you'll notice I never once used the word "angel".
Kent Brockman: Oh, that's a bunch of baloney, Lisa. Everyone knows leprechauns are extinct.
Chief Wiggum: Oh, oh yeah, yeah, we're outraged. Very, uh... Very much so... But look at all the stores! A Pottery Barn!

title: Realty Bites (S9E09)
text: "Realty Bites" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F06), directed by Swinton O. Scott III and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing December 7, 1997. Bored with domestic life, Marge convinces Homer to take her out, and they end up at a police auction where Homer impulsively buys Snake's prized car, the Lil' Bandit, infuriating the incarcerated criminal. While walking home in protest, Marge meets Lionel Hutz, who works at Red Blazer Realty, and decides to become a real estate agent herself. She passes her licensing exam but struggles in the job because her relentless honesty about houses' flaws scares away every potential buyer. Meanwhile, Snake breaks out of jail specifically to reclaim his car and get revenge on Homer, leading to a chaotic car chase. Facing termination for not making a single sale, Marge finally convinces the Flanders family to buy a house with a gruesome hidden history as a murder site. Guilt-ridden, she rushes back to warn them, only to discover a scene that looks like a bloody massacre but turns out to be leftover red paint from redecorating. Just as she tries to return their money, Snake and Homer's brawling car crashes into the house, and Chief Wiggum's pursuit finishes the job, destroying the home entirely. Ned tears up the check anyway, Marge loses her real estate job, and Homer helps her look into filing for unemployment. Guest starring Phil Hartman as Lionel Hutz. Notable quotes: Lionel Hutz: You see, the law business is a little slow, and since most of my clients wind up losing their houses, this was a natural move for me. | Marge: 200 dollars for doing nothing?! I feel like such a crook... | George Bush: Don't worry, it gets easier every week. | Lionel Hutz: The right house is the house that's for sale. The right person is anyone. | Lenny: Please don't tell anyone how I live.

Marge: 200 dollars for doing nothing?! I feel like such a crook...
George Bush: Don't worry, it gets easier every week.
Lionel Hutz: The right house is the house that's for sale. The right person is anyone.
Lenny: Please don't tell anyone how I live.

title: Miracle on Evergreen Terrace (S9E10)
text: "Miracle on Evergreen Terrace" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F07), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Ron Hauge, originally airing December 21, 1997. In the days before Christmas, Homer and Marge brave chaotic crowds at the Try-N-Save to secure the season's hottest toys, with Homer resorting to a sneaky cashier scam to grab extra gifts. On Christmas Eve, Marge confiscates all the alarm clocks to prevent early present-opening, but Bart outsmarts her by chugging water so he'll wake up early needing the bathroom. Sneaking downstairs before dawn, Bart plays with his new remote-controlled fire truck, which crashes into the tree and sets the presents ablaze. Panicking, Bart hides the charred remains outside and later fabricates a story about a burglar stealing everything. Kent Brockman's sympathetic news report triggers an outpouring of community generosity, netting the family a new tree and $15,000, which Homer promptly squanders on a car he crashes into a lake. Guilt eventually forces Bart to confess the truth to his furious family, and the lie unravels publicly when the burned tree remnants are discovered during a follow-up news segment. Branded as frauds, the Simpsons are pressured by the town to repay the $15,000, leading Marge to attempt winning it back on Jeopardy!, where she fails miserably. Fed up with waiting, the townspeople raid the Simpson home and take nearly everything they own as repayment, though they ultimately forgive the family. The episode ends with the Simpsons left with only a ragged washcloth, squabbling over it as their last possession. Guest starring Alex Trebek. Notable quotes: Bart: ...aren't we forgetting the true meaning of this day? The birth of Santa. | Marge: I know you're used to getting hate mail, but I'm not! | Kent: In my long career, I've seen some pretty shabby things. But this putrid fraud out stinks them all. | Homer: Eh, yes... Kent. Uh, hello... jerk. We may never find you, and we should probably all stop looking. But one thing's for sure... you do exist. | Krusty: Fifteen thousand mazoolians? Holy shlamola! Whaddya gonna do with all that kablingy?

Marge: I know you're used to getting hate mail, but I'm not!
Kent: In my long career, I've seen some pretty shabby things. But this putrid fraud out stinks them all.
Homer: Eh, yes... Kent. Uh, hello... jerk. We may never find you, and we should probably all stop looking. But one thing's for sure... you do exist.
Krusty: Fifteen thousand mazoolians? Holy shlamola! Whaddya gonna do with all that kablingy?

title: All Singing, All Dancing (S9E11)
text: "All Singing, All Dancing" is an episode of Season 9 (production code 5F24), directed by Mark Ervin and written by Steve O'Donnell, originally airing January 4, 1998. Homer brings home a rental he's sure will be a violent Clint Eastwood-Lee Marvin Western, only for the family to discover it's actually the musical Paint Your Wagon. Disgusted, Homer declares singing to be the lowest form of communication and swears he never sings, prompting Marge to counter that he and the rest of Springfield burst into song all the time. To prove her point, she recounts a string of memorable musical moments from the family's past, including Homer's barbershop quartet days, Springfield's tourism jingle, Bart's rebellious anthems, Apu's love song, Krusty's showbiz lament, Ned Flanders' vest tribute, the ill-fated monorail pitch, Bart's soul-searching hymn, and Homer's induction into the Stonecutters. As the family keeps breaking into song at home, small-time crook Snake Jailbird becomes increasingly irritated by their singing and repeatedly breaks in to kill them, but each time is foiled by lacking a loaded gun or losing his motivation when the singing stops. In a darkly comic running joke, Snake's own attempts to intimidate the family come out as song as well, showing he's not immune to the phenomenon he despises. The tension escalates until Marge, humming while cleaning up, gives Snake an excuse to finally fire his gun, though no one is hurt as the shot merely shatters some glass. The episode closes with Snake, now thoroughly sick of music, trying in vain to stop the closing theme song from playing. Guest starring George Harrison, Phil Hartman. Notable quotes: Homer: Singing is the lowest form of communication. | Homer: No I don't. I hate to rhyme. | Snake: A singing family! it's worse than I feared. For hostage purposes, you're just too weird! | Snake: Because of you all, I got a tune in my head. And the only way to stop it is to make you all dead! | Homer: Ugh, I knew I should have shut that window.
