title: Alone Again, Natura-Diddily (S11E14)
text: "Alone Again, Natura-Diddily" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF10), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing February 13, 2000. The Simpsons and Flanders families attend the opening of a new Springfield speedway, where Homer's obnoxious attempt to grab a free T-shirt from a cheerleading squad's cannon accidentally results in Maude Flanders being knocked off the bleachers and killed. After the funeral, Marge urges Homer to be supportive of Ned, prompting Homer to help him move on by making an awkward and inappropriately revealing dating video. Ned goes on a string of disastrous dates with women like Lindsey Naegle and Edna Krabappel, none of which spark any connection. Guilt-ridden after skipping church one Sunday, Ned rushes back apologizing to God, only to be captivated by Rachel Jordan, the lead singer of the Christian rock band Kovenant performing that day. The two strike up an instant connection while loading her band's van after the service, discovering a mutual, if hesitant, attraction. Rachel suggests they meet up again once her band finishes touring, leaving Ned hopeful about the possibility of new love while still honoring Maude's memory. Meanwhile, a subplot follows Bart bonding with Rod and Todd Flanders over a religious video game to help them cope with their mother's death. Guest starring Shawn Colvin as Rachel Jordan. Notable quotes: Homer: How come bears can crap in the woods and I can't? | Homer: No they didn't. They just surrounded it with something wonderful—like a raisin covered in chocolate, or a monkey in a cowboy suit. | Chief Wiggum: Oh I would date Ned in a second, if I was a woman, or gay. He looks like a cuddler, that Ned. I, I like that. I like to be held. I like to be pampered. | Homer: Oh, wake up, Ned. You think Maude isn't dating in Heaven? | Ned: It's probably me, I'm about as exciting as a baked potato.

title: Missionary: Impossible (S11E15)
text: "Missionary: Impossible" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF11), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Ron Hauge, originally airing February 20, 2000. Homer becomes hooked on a British sitcom on PBS, but pledges $10,000 anonymously just to stop a pledge-drive interruption hosted by Betty White. When PBS traces the donation back to him and he admits he can't pay, an angry mob of PBS personalities chases him through Springfield. Reverend Lovejoy rescues Homer and, without his consent, puts him on a plane to the remote island of Microatia to serve as a missionary. Left alone after the previous missionaries depart, Homer fails to convert the natives with Bibles they can't read, and instead builds them a casino, which quickly spirals into chaos, fire, and addiction. Meanwhile, back home, Bart takes over as "man of the house," disastrously filling in for Homer at the power plant and clashing with Marge. Guilt-ridden, Homer tries to finish building a chapel the earlier missionaries started, but his over-enthusiastic bell-ringing triggers a landslide and earthquake that plunges the chapel into a lava-filled chasm with him and a native girl he calls Lisa, Jr. The story then abruptly cuts to a Fox pledge drive hosted by Betty White, where Bart calls in and pledges $10,000 to save the network, echoing his father's earlier mistake. Guest starring Betty White as herself. Notable quotes: Betty White: If you watch even one second of PBS and don't contribute, you are a thief! A common thief. | Homer: Maybe your movie star banks are open crazy hours, but we in Springfield are simple folk. We like our cars fast, and our banks closed. | Homer: Sanctuary! Sanctuary! | Homer: I'm gonna call you Lisa Junior. | Homer: Because you're all terrible sinners.

title: Pygmoelian (S11E16)
text: "Pygmoelian" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF12), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Larry Doyle, originally airing February 27, 2000. The Simpsons head to the Duff Days festival, where Moe wins the Beer-tender of the Year contest and earns a spot on the Duff calendar, only to discover the company thinks he's too ugly to feature and covers his photo with a sticker. Devastated to learn how unattractive everyone considers him, Moe takes Lenny's advice and undergoes a complete facial reconstruction from Dr. Velimirovic, emerging with a strikingly handsome new face. Newly confident, Moe sets out to confront and humiliate everyone who ever mocked his looks, including Duffman and an old crush. His revenge tour leads him to the set of the soap opera 'It Never Ends,' where he once was rejected for a role for being too ugly; ironically, his new face gets him cast as the new Dr. Tad Winslow. Moe enjoys his newfound fame and success with women, but becomes enraged upon learning his character is slated to be killed off, prompting him and Homer to sabotage the show by revealing future plotlines on air. The stunt backfires when it's revealed to be a dream sequence, and Moe is fired. In a final twist, falling set equipment crushes Moe's face, reverting him to his original appearance, leaving him to grumble about the unfairness of it all back at the bar. Meanwhile, a subplot follows Bart and Lisa chasing Maggie's runaway balloon into a bizarre building housing a gay Republican meeting. Notable quotes: Moe: Am I really that ugly? | Carl: Moe, it's all relative. Is Lenny really that dumb? Is Barney that drunk? Is Homer that lazy, bald and fat? | Helen Morehouse: I wanted Maryanne on Gilligan's Island ugly, not Cornelius on the Planet of the Apes ugly. TV ugly, not ugly ugly. | Lenny: Eh, it's over. She got a windowshade. | Moe: Oh my God! It's worse than I thought.

title: Bart to the Future (S11E17)
text: "Bart to the Future" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF13), directed by Michael Marcantel and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing March 19, 2000. During a family outing gone wrong due to a mosquito infestation, the Simpsons stumble upon an Indian casino, where Bart is caught sneaking in by the manager. As punishment, the manager shows Bart a vision of his future in the year 2030. In this future, Bart is a directionless 40-year-old failed musician living off his more responsible roommate Ralph Wiggum, while his sister Lisa has become the first female President of the United States. As Ralph grows tired of supporting him, Bart shifts his freeloading efforts to Lisa, moving into the White House and disrupting her presidency, including accidentally exposing her disguised tax hike during a live address. Meanwhile, Lisa struggles with a country crippled by debt and a crime wave caused by well-meaning but disastrous past social programs. To get Bart out of the way, Lisa tricks him into a fake mission, but he learns the truth from a ghostly visit and resolves to change—briefly proving useful by helping resolve a debt crisis with foreign creditors. In a subplot, Homer becomes obsessed with finding Lincoln's hidden 'gold,' only to discover it's a metaphorical treasure: the American people themselves, much to his disappointment. When the vision ends, Bart shows no sign of having learned anything, seemingly indifferent to his future's warnings. Notable quotes: Marge: I'm not sure mosquito season is the best time to visit Larva Lake. | Kent Brockman: According to the latest polls, Americans have emphatically said, "Smell you later," to President Simpson's refund adjustment. | Homer: She knows what time dinner is. | Lisa: My Administration will focus on the three R's. Reading, writing, and refilling the ocean. | Bart: Ohh, I had half a beer in there! And "Bewitched" is on!

title: Days of Wine and D'oh'ses (S11E18)
text: "Days of Wine and D'oh'ses" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF14), directed by Neil Affleck and written by Deb Lacusta, Dan Castellaneta, originally airing April 9, 2000. After a humiliating birthday video reveals his drunken antics, Barney vows to get sober and, with the support of the Moe's regulars, actually sticks to it, later taking up helicopter lessons at the Springfield Flight School. Meanwhile, Bart and Lisa try to win a bicycle by submitting a winning cover photo for the new Springfield phone book, heading up Mount Springfield with an old camera to snap the perfect shot. Bart's carelessness with a hot flashbulb sparks a forest fire that traps the kids up a tree, and with the fire department occupied elsewhere, Barney and Homer take to the skies in Barney's helicopter to rescue them. A tense mid-flight landing on a bridge nearly causes Barney to relapse when a Duff truck spills beer nearby, but Homer heroically drinks the six-pack himself to protect his friend's sobriety. Thoroughly drunk, Homer still manages to pull Bart and Lisa to safety from the burning tree. The next day, the family discovers the phone book's cover photo is actually an old, embarrassing shot of Bart and Lisa as naked toddlers, though Marge reveals she still won the bike using a different photo. In the end, Barney remains alcohol-free but trades one addiction for another, becoming hooked on lattes from Moe's new coffee cart business. Notable quotes: Cletus: Looky here! Cardy-board tubes! | Brandine: Now we can have indoor plumbing, just like they's got at the women's' lockup. | Cletus: They spoilt you, Brandine. Sometimes I don't even know who you are anymore. | Homer: This muscle shirt is a pretty good find. | Homer: All I know is, I'm finally getting the support I need.

title: Kill the Alligator and Run (S11E19)
text: "Kill the Alligator and Run" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF16), directed by Jen Kamerman and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing April 30, 2000. Homer becomes obsessed with a magazine quiz that predicts he only has three years left to live, and Marge's suggestions for healthier living send him into a stress-induced breakdown marked by insomnia and erratic behavior. After his antics nearly get the power plant shut down, the plant's psychiatrist recommends a relaxing vacation, so the family heads to a quiet Florida town. Unfortunately, they arrive during spring break, and Homer sneaks off to party wildly at a Kid Rock concert instead of resting. The next day, desperate to keep the fun going after the students leave, Homer rents an airboat and drags the family into the swamp, where he accidentally kills the town's beloved alligator mascot, Captain Jack. The whole family is charged with the crime and goes on the run from a relentless southern sheriff, surviving a train collision and hiding out working at a rural diner. Eventually caught and sentenced to forced labor, they're saved when Captain Jack turns up alive, having only been stunned. The family is acquitted but permanently banned from Florida, leaving them to plan a much less exciting vacation to North Dakota instead. Guest starring Diedrich Bader, Joe C., Robert Evans, Kid Rock, Charlie Rose. Notable quotes: Southern sheriff: You see, during Spring Break, the beer companies pay me to look the other way. The rest of the year, I am a real hardass. | Homer: Fine. title: Last Tap Dance in Springfield (S11E20)
text: "Last Tap Dance in Springfield" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF15), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Julie Thacker, originally airing May 7, 2000. Homer's poor eyesight leads the family to the Springfield Mall, where he opts for laser eye surgery instead of glasses while Marge and Lisa shop and end up watching the film Tango de la Muerte. Inspired by the movie, Lisa enrolls in a dance class run by former child star Lil' Vicki Valentine, only to be forced into tap dancing instead of the tango she wants, and she struggles under Vicki's harsh, unhelpful teaching. Meanwhile, Bart and Milhouse skip their camping trip to avoid a bully and secretly live in the mall, causing chaos that the police mistake for the work of a giant rat, leading to a series of failed traps and a rampaging mountain lion. As the recital approaches, Lisa is cut from the show for her poor dancing, but Professor Frink gives her a device to make her tap shoes move automatically. Vicki steals the spotlight during the recital, and Lisa's rigged shoes malfunction on stage, causing a chaotic scene until Homer trips her to stop them. It's revealed the shoes were actually off the whole time, meaning Lisa danced well on her own, though Homer's blunt honesty spoils Frink's attempt to protect her feelings. Lisa accepts that she won't become a professional dancer, and the family shares a lighthearted moment as life returns to normal. Notable quotes: Bart: I'm in tantrum position. T-minus five... four... three... remembering dead cat for real tears, and... | Chief Wiggum: Every sign points to one obvious culprit... A giant rat. title: It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad Marge (S11E21)

text: "It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad Marge" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF18), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Larry Doyle, originally airing May 14, 2000. Bart's class is given video cameras for a school assignment, setting up a subplot that pays off at the episode's climax. Otto proposes to his drive-through girlfriend Becky, and the Simpsons agree to host the wedding, but the ceremony collapses after Marge encourages Becky to give Otto an ultimatum over his heavy metal lifestyle. Left without a home, Becky moves in with the Simpsons and quickly becomes a favorite of the family, cooking and cleaning better than Marge ever did. When Marge's car brakes fail on a hill, she spirals into paranoia, convinced Becky is trying to murder her and steal her family. A misunderstood scene of Becky performing CPR on a collapsed Homer leads Marge to attack her, resulting in Marge's arrest and a sanity hearing that finds her insane. Marge escapes custody, researches Becky at the library, and momentarily convinces herself she was wrong—only to come home to a terrifying scene of her family bound and Becky wielding a knife. It's revealed the whole scenario is staged for Bart's video project, though Becky admits she genuinely considered killing Marge before abandoning the plan over a lack of a good shovel. Homer confesses he accidentally cut Marge's brake line, and the episode ends with Homer tranquilizing Marge into unconsciousness after she snaps back into bossy housewife mode. Guest starring Parker Posey as Becky. Notable quotes: Becky: Hey, no prob. I was planning to kill you. I even thought of a place to bury you. title: Behind the Laughter (S11E22)
text: "Behind the Laughter" is an episode of Season 11 (production code BABF19), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Tim Long, George Meyer, Mike Scully, Matt Selman, originally airing May 21, 2000. This mockumentary, styled after VH1's Behind the Music, chronicles the fictional rise and fall of the Simpsons as a real show-business family. It begins with Homer's crude home-video pilot, which somehow launches them into massive fame, wealth, and awards. As success grows, cracks form: Homer becomes hooked on painkillers after a stunt injury, Marge pours money into absurd business ventures like branded diaphragms, and Bart is sent to rehab, forcing his friend Richie Rich to secretly stand in for him. The IRS seizes their mansion, formerly owned by a bankrupt MC Hammer, and the family's tensions explode into a public breakup at the Iowa State Fair. With the family refusing to speak to each other, Fox halts production, and each member drifts into a solo career—Homer in theater, Bart replacing Lorenzo Lamas on Renegade, Marge doing a nightclub act, and Lisa writing a tell-all memoir. Willie Nelson orchestrates a fake awards show specifically to lure the family back together and mend fences with Van Halen and Sammy Hagar. Despite Lisa seeing through the ruse, the family reconciles emotionally on stage, hugging it out before a cheering audience, setting up their triumphant return—until a final joke suggests the show may actually be ending for good. Guest starring Buzz Aldrin, Gary Coleman, Jim Forbes, Stephen Hawking, Tom Kite, Willie Nelson, Butch Patrick. Notable quotes: Narrator: The Simpsons' TV show started out on a wing and a prayer. But now the wing was on fire, and the prayer had been answered by Satan. | Homer: It was the best Thanksgiving ever. I mean, emotionally, it was terrible, but the turkey was so moist! | Bart: Dad, I've never said "cowabunga" in my life. Your script sucks! | Homer: Every day I thought about firing Marge... you know, just to shake things up. | Homer: I want to set the record straight: [slowly] I thought the cop was a prostitute.

title: Treehouse of Horror XI (S12E01)
text: "Treehouse of Horror XI" is an episode of Season 12 (production code BABF21), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Rob LaZebnik (part 1), John Frink & Don Payne (Part 2), Carolyn Omine (Part 3), originally airing November 1, 2000. This Halloween special opens with a black-and-white parody of The Munsters' opening titles before diving into three separate horror tales. In the first segment, Homer dies choking on broccoli and must perform a genuine good deed within 24 hours to earn entry into Heaven, but his well-intentioned attempts repeatedly backfire, including accidentally killing Agnes Skinner and causing a baby carriage to explode. Having failed to be properly recognized for his final act, he is condemned to Hell, where even Satan finds his complaining unbearable. The second story reimagines the Simpsons as impoverished peasants; when Homer can no longer feed his family, he abandons Bart and Lisa in an enchanted forest, where they navigate fairy-tale dangers like a bridge troll and the Three Bears while Homer disastrously attempts to rescue Rapunzel and later battles a cannibalistic witch to save his kids. The family's fortunes turn when Homer emerges from the witch's magic transformed into a part-chicken hybrid capable of laying eggs, solving their hunger problem. The final segment follows Lisa freeing a captive dolphin named Snorky from a marine park, unaware he is the secret king of all dolphins harboring resentment toward humanity. Snorky rallies his fellow dolphins to invade Springfield and reclaim the land for their kind, leading to an all-out war between humans and dolphins that the dolphins ultimately win, leaving Springfield's residents floating helplessly in the ocean. The episode closes with aliens Kang and Kodos grumbling about being excluded from the special, only to be interrupted by a phone call offering them a commercial gig. Notable quotes: Nelson: Your Dad is deeaad, mine's just in jaaiil! | Homer: Hmm, sugar walls. | Suzanne: That was a load bearing candy cane, you clumsy oaf! | Homer: Don't worry. No child will ever starve in my home. | Lisa: Face it, they're not great parents. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 11): "G-G-Ghost D-D-Dad", "Scary Tales Can Come True", and "The Night of the Dolphin".

title: A Tale of Two Springfields (S12E02)
text: "A Tale of Two Springfields" is an episode of Season 12 (production code BABF20), directed by Shaun Cashman and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing November 5, 2000. When Bart discovers a badger living in Santa's Little Helper's doghouse, Homer's attempt to call Animal Control reveals that Springfield has been split into two area codes. Furious over losing a radio contest to Mr. Burns because of the change, Homer's frustration boils over at a town meeting led by phone company representative Lindsey Naegle. When her placating video fails to calm him, Homer rallies the disenfranchised citizens with his area code to secede and form a new town, New Springfield, becoming its mayor. Tensions escalate as New and Olde Springfield feud pettily—cutting power, dumping beer, and shutting off water—culminating in Homer building a wall to divide the town completely. When the citizens abandon New Springfield by climbing over the wall, Homer convinces The Who to perform a concert there to lure everyone back. The plan backfires when Olde Springfield attacks with flaming garbage, but The Who calms the crowd and leads everyone in tearing down the wall while performing 'Won't Get Fooled Again,' reuniting the town just as an army of badgers gathers ominously nearby. Guest starring Frank Welker as Flanders' pet woodpecker, The Who as themselves. Notable quotes: Homer: Area code!? But it's a local call. | Marge: The phone company ran out of numbers, so they split the city into two area codes. Half the town keeps the old 636 area code, and our half gets 939. | Homer: 939!!!?? WHAT THE HELL IS THAT!? Oh my life is ruined. | Homer: Badger my ass, it's probably Milhouse. | Moe: Enough chit-chat, let's see how you like flaming garbage!

title: Insane Clown Poppy (S12E03)
text: "Insane Clown Poppy" is an episode of Season 12 (production code BABF17), directed by Bob Anderson and written by John Frink, Don Payne, originally airing November 12, 2000. After Homer and Bart accidentally wreck Lisa's room while trying to use fireworks for household repairs, the family heads to a book fair to make amends, where Krusty is promoting his new memoir. There, a young girl named Sophie reveals that she is his daughter, the result of a wartime fling with a female soldier during the Gulf War. Krusty struggles to connect with Sophie, and their awkward bonding attempts fail until Homer, drawing on his own parenting experience, offers Krusty some fatherly advice. Just as things start to improve, Krusty foolishly gambles away Sophie's cherished violin in a poker game with Fat Tony, devastating her and destroying the trust they had built. Determined to make things right, Krusty enlists Homer's help to sneak into a major mob gathering at Fat Tony's mansion and retrieve the violin. The heist succeeds, with Krusty escaping with both the violin and extra cash, winning back his daughter's affection. However, the theft draws the mafia's wrath toward Homer, who narrowly survives an attempt on his life by the mob before the episode wraps up. Guest starring Drew Barrymore, Stephen King, Joe Mantegna, Jay Mohr, Amy Tan, John Updike. title: Lisa the Tree Hugger (S12E04)
text: "Lisa the Tree Hugger" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF01), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Matt Selman, originally airing November 19, 2000. Bart, desperate for cash to buy a new video game console he saw advertised, takes a job delivering menus for a Thai restaurant, learning to move so fast he's nearly invisible. His flood of discarded flyers ends up littering Springfield's streets, which infuriates Lisa over the wasted trees. While venting her frustration at a protest atop Krusty Burger, Lisa is drawn to Jesse Grass, the charismatic leader of the environmental group Dirt First, and quickly joins their cause. When she learns that The Rich Texan plans to cut down Springfield's oldest redwood, she volunteers to live in its branches to stop the loggers. Homesick, she sneaks away for one night, only to return and find the tree has been destroyed by a lightning strike, leading the town to believe she died in the storm. Homer and Bart briefly milk the sympathy from grieving townsfolk, while The Rich Texan's plan to build a memorial sanctuary quickly devolves into plans for a tacky amusement park called 'Lisa Land.' Lisa reappears alive just in time to protest the park's opening, and Jesse cuts loose the massive log meant to be its sign, sending it rampaging through Springfield's business district and out to sea, ruining The Rich Texan's company. Jesse is arrested again for his actions, but remains defiantly committed to his environmental crusade. Guest starring Joshua Jackson as Jesse Grass. Notable quotes: Homer: Boring! [laughs] | Homer: No! It was finger ling-ling good!

title: Homer vs. Dignity (S12E05)
text: "Homer vs. Dignity" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF04), directed by Neil Affleck and written by Rob LaZebnik, originally airing November 26, 2000. After Bart earns an A+ on an astronomy quiz through an unlikely bit of motivation, the Simpsons celebrate at The Singing Sirloin, only to discover Homer's credit card is worthless and they must busk as mariachis to cover the bill. Running out of gas afterward, Marge insists they see a financial planner, but Lindsey Naegle bluntly informs them that Homer's stupidity is the root of their money troubles. Meanwhile, with Smithers away staging his Malibu Stacy musical, a bored Mr. Burns recruits Homer as his personal 'prank monkey,' paying him handsomely to humiliate himself and others, including Lenny. Homer hides this shady side income from his family until Lisa catches him disguised as a female panda at the zoo, a prank gone wrong that literally exposes him. Ashamed of what he's become, Homer confronts Burns and refuses further degrading work, then donates his ill-gotten earnings to buy toys for needy children, earning him the honor of playing Santa in the town's Thanksgiving parade. Burns, however, hijacks the parade with his own float to trick Homer into dumping fish guts on the crowd for a million dollars. Homer refuses, so Burns dons the Santa suit himself and does it, triggering a seagull attack on the fish-covered townspeople. In the end, Homer takes comfort in the fact that he kept his integrity, calling it the gift of dignity Lisa gave him. Guest starring Leeza Gibbons as herself. Notable quotes: Homer: Get 'im, Sheeba! title: The Computer Wore Menace Shoes (S12E06)
text: "The Computer Wore Menace Shoes" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF02), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing December 3, 2000. After finding himself the only worker to show up on a plant closure day, Homer decides he needs a computer to stay in the loop. With Lisa's help he learns to use it and creates a website, but it initially attracts no attention since it's just spam and stolen GIFs. Following Lisa's advice to offer something useful, Homer starts posting local gossip anonymously under the name 'Mr. X,' and his first big scoop exposes Mayor Quimby misusing pothole repair funds. When the town wants to reward the mysterious Mr. X, Homer quickly reveals himself to claim the credit and a Pulitzer Prize. As real news dries up, he begins fabricating stories, and one invented claim about flu shots being mind control turns out to be true. This lands him kidnapped and imprisoned on a mysterious island holding people who stumbled onto real secrets, while an identical impostor with a German accent takes his place at home. Homer escapes using a stolen boat and popping the island's pursuit orb, returns home to defeat his double, and briefly reunites with his family—only for all of them to be gassed by a rigged Santa's Little Helper and hauled off to the island together. Guest starring Patrick McGoohan as Number Six. Notable quotes: Wiggum: You have chosen 'No', meaning that you've committed a crime, but don't want to confess. A paddy wagon is now speeding to your home. | Homer: No one can silence me but me! | Homer: Who are you, and why are you holding me here? I want answers now, or I want them eventually! | Lisa: Ugh, at least take off your Pulitzer Prize when you say that! | Chief Wiggum: In the interests of public safety, we have confiscated every donut, bagel, cruller and bear claw in the city. And some coffee.

title: The Great Money Caper (S12E07)
text: "The Great Money Caper" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF03), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Carolyn Omine, originally airing December 10, 2000. While dining at the Springfield Dinner Theater, the Simpsons' car is damaged when a sturgeon falls from the sky, and Bart's attempt to earn repair money through a magic act falls short, angering Homer. After sympathetic strangers give Bart money out of pity, Homer realizes there's easy cash to be made by manipulating people's emotions, and he and Bart become a grifting duo. Even after covering the car repair costs, the pair keep conning people, eventually targeting the residents of the Springfield Retirement Castle, where they are caught by a supposed FBI agent. That agent turns out to be a con artist himself, stealing their car and the money they'd swindled from the retirees. To cover their tracks, Homer and Bart fabricate a story about a wild-haired foreign carjacker, leading to the wrongful arrest of Groundskeeper Willie. During Willie's trial, Homer is coaxed into further incriminating him, but when Willie is sentenced and reacts violently, Homer confesses the truth. It is then revealed that the entire ordeal—arrest, trial, and news coverage—was an elaborate hoax orchestrated by the town to teach Homer and Bart a lesson about the consequences of lying and grifting. Before the reasoning behind the town's actions can be fully explained, Otto interrupts with a spontaneous call to go surfing, and the family happily obliges. Guest starring Edward Norton as Devon Bradley. Notable quotes: Homer: Lies got us into this mess, Son. From now on, it's honesty all the way. | Marge: You were carjacked... in the church parking lot?! | Bart: Wild, bushy hair—like an animal! | Bart: Why are we still grifting? The car's paid for; doesn't that balance out the universe? | Lisa: It that a Long Island iced tea?

title: Skinner's Sense of Snow (S12E08)
text: "Skinner's Sense of Snow" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF06), directed by Lance Kramer and written by Tim Long, originally airing December 17, 2000. A powerful winter storm hits Springfield right after Homer and the family's trip to the Cirque de Purée is ruined by high winds. The next morning the snow has buried the town, but Springfield Elementary stays open even though the teachers skip out on an 'emergency caucus.' Principal Skinner forces the stranded kids to watch a dreadful old holiday film and then discovers the phone lines are down, trapping everyone inside overnight. As food runs short and tempers flare, Skinner digs out his old army uniform and tries to impose military discipline, while Bart secretly attempts to tunnel through the snow to freedom. Meanwhile Homer and Ned Flanders rig Ned's car and house roof into a makeshift snowplow to reach the school, enduring dangerous exhaust fumes and a collision with a fire hydrant along the way. Back at school, the students revolt, stuff Skinner into a dodgeball bag, and start rifling through their permanent records, forcing Skinner to send his pet gerbil Nibbles out for help. Nibbles frees Homer and Ned from the fume-filled car, and their runaway plow smashes into a salt silo that melts the snow around the school, letting the kids escape just as the rescuers arrive. Superintendent Chalmers demands an explanation for the chaos, but Bart smooths things over, and the Simpsons and Flanders head home—only for Homer to start hallucinating again from car fumes. That's the last time you'll slap yer Willie around. I quit. | Bart: Silence, Seymour. We're in charge now. Your reign of fussiness is over. | Homer: Oh no you don't! I paid full price for this freak show. Now nourish the child within me!

title: HOMЯ (S12E09)
text: "HOMЯ" is an episode of Season 12 (production code BABF22), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Al Jean, originally airing January 7, 2001. After Homer sinks the family's life savings into a motion-capture cartoon startup called Animotion, the company collapses into bankruptcy, leaving the Simpsons broke. To recoup the money, Homer takes a job as a human guinea pig at a medical testing facility, where an X-ray reveals a crayon has been lodged in his brain since childhood. Doctors remove it, and Homer's IQ jumps from 55 to 105, suddenly making him articulate and insightful. His newfound intelligence lets him bond deeply with Lisa for the first time, but it also alienates him from Marge, his coworkers at the power plant, and his friends at Moe's, who burn an effigy of smart Homer and ban him from the bar. Homer's brilliance even leads him to write a damning safety report that gets the nuclear plant shut down, costing everyone their jobs. Realizing his intelligence has cost him his happiness and relationships, Homer has Moe surgically reinsert a crayon into his brain, restoring his old dim-witted self. Lisa is initially devastated by the reversal, but discovers a heartfelt letter Homer wrote before the surgery expressing how much he came to appreciate her intellect, and the two reconcile in their own way as Homer returns to his simple, sandwich-loving life. Notice I no longer say liberry or tomorrie. | Homer: Point of order—I didn't lose all the money. There was enough left for this cowbell. | Kent Brockman: The firm declared super-dooper bankruptcy, which is terrible news for the company's one stockholder, Homer Simpson. | Homer: Yeah, that reminds me, I need a sandwich.

title: Pokey Mom (S12E10)
text: "Pokey Mom" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF05), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Tom Martin, originally airing January 14, 2001. After Marge drags the family to the Apron Expo and then a prison rodeo, she becomes fascinated by an inmate named Jack Crowley whose artwork impresses her. She starts an art class at the prison and successfully vouches for his parole, taking him into her custody and helping him land a job painting a mural at Springfield Elementary. His first mural, featuring a scantily-clad warrior woman, is a hit with everyone except Principal Skinner, who insists on changes. When Jack repaints it as a bland, childish design at Skinner's request, the school hates it, and Skinner blames Jack anyway rather than admit his own error. Frustrated, Jack torches both the repainted mural and Skinner's car, then lies to Marge about it before being caught and sent back to prison, leaving Marge disheartened. Meanwhile, Homer hurts his back at the rodeo and, after a chiropractor's exercises fail him, accidentally discovers that a dented garbage can perfectly aligns with his spine and eases his pain. He turns this into a business called Dr. Homer's Miracle Spine-O-Cylinder, which booms in popularity until rival chiropractors, angry at losing business, track him down and smash his makeshift device. Guest starring Michael Keaton as Jack Crowley, Charles Napier as The Warden, Robert Schimmel as the prisoner, Bruce Vilanch as himself. Bart, Sideshow Bob says he'll be seeing you real soon. | The Warden: He painted a unicorn in outer space! I'm asking you, what's it breathing? | Homer: There's an air and space museum. | Moe: Forget it, Homer. It's chiro-town.

title: Worst Episode Ever (S12E11)
text: "Worst Episode Ever" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF08), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Larry Doyle, originally airing February 4, 2001. After winning a bet with Homer over eating old baking soda, Bart uses his $50 winnings on a spending spree with Milhouse, ending up at the Android's Dungeon where they inadvertently save Martin's mother from selling valuable Star Wars memorabilia to Comic Book Guy, getting themselves permanently banned. When they try to sneak into a special in-store appearance by makeup artist Tom Savini, Comic Book Guy—tipped off by Homer—catches them, and the ensuing stress from Savini's pranks triggers a heart attack. Grateful that the boys called 911, Comic Book Guy lets them run the shop while he recovers, but Milhouse's poor business decision to stock thousands of copies of an unpopular comic called Biclops threatens to ruin things. Meanwhile, Comic Book Guy searches for companionship and unexpectedly falls into a romance with Agnes Skinner, their bond built on mutually insulting the people around them. To recoup their financial losses, Bart and Milhouse decide to secretly screen Comic Book Guy's stash of blackmail videotapes for paying customers, but the event is raided by Chief Wiggum's police, who also catch Comic Book Guy and Agnes in a compromising position. Comic Book Guy is arrested, tearfully parting from Agnes, while Bart and Milhouse walk away from the now-crime-scene comic shop, insisting everything is back to normal. Guest starring Tom Savini as himself, Neil Armstrong as himself (uncredited; archive audio), Johnnie Cochran as himself (uncredited; archive audio), Richard Nixon as himself (uncredited; archive audio). Notable quotes: Comic Book Guy: Worst episode ever! | Ralph: Everybody's hugging. | Bart: That should be us covered with blood. | Homer: And I never saw Gallagher again. | Bart: I can't believe I'm going to miss that.

Homer: And I never saw Gallagher again.

title: Tennis the Menace (S12E12)
text: "Tennis the Menace" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF07), directed by Jen Kamerman and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing February 11, 2001. After Grampa wins a talent show at the retirement home with a painful rendition of a Tom Jones song, his prize turns out to be a free autopsy, prompting a trip to a funeral salesman. There, Homer notices that a cemetery monument uses the same amount of cement as a tennis court and decides to build one at home instead of paying for his father's casket, despite the family's shaky finances and his own confusion about the sport. The backyard court becomes a neighborhood hit, but Homer's cluelessness on the court embarrasses Marge, so she dumps him as a partner in favor of Bart for Krusty's charity tennis tournament. A wounded Homer recruits Lisa as his new partner after a bizarre nightmare about being replaced in his own family. At the tournament, real-life tennis stars Andre Agassi, Pete Sampras, Venus Williams, and Serena Williams are in attendance, and Homer quickly abandons Lisa to team up with Venus, sparking a swapping frenzy as Marge, Bart, and the pros shuffle partners. Eventually the professionals cut out the Simpsons entirely, pairing off with each other and leaving Homer and family to watch from the sidelines. The Simpsons resign themselves to being spectators rather than participants, and the episode ends with Homer sneaking cash back out of Pete Sampras's wallet after being caught stealing from it. Guest starring Andre Agassi, Pete Sampras, Serena Williams, Venus Williams. Notable quotes: Homer: Hey, that's great. Listen, I need a new doubles partner. My little girl's a lead weight. | Serena Williams: You're dumping your own daughter? | Homer: Yeah, but only to crush my wife and son! | Venus Williams: Yeah, that's pretty low. | Homer: Faster!

title: Day of the Jackanapes (S12E13)
text: "Day of the Jackanapes" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF10), directed by Michael Marcantel and written by Al Jean, originally airing February 18, 2001. After his show loses viewers to a rival game program, Krusty the Clown announces his retirement and casually reveals he taped over all his old episodes featuring Sideshow Bob. Enraged, Bob is released from prison and takes a janitorial job at Springfield Elementary, quickly becoming the school's morning announcer. He lures Bart into an old tool shed, hypnotizes him, and conditions him to act as a sleeper agent, first making him vandalize a Krusty statue and then rigging him with explosives to detonate during Krusty's live farewell special. As Krusty gives an emotional speech expressing regret over how he treated Bob, Bob has a change of heart and tries to stop the plot, but Bart is already walking onstage to hug Krusty and trigger the bomb. Krusty's chimp assistant, Mr. Teeny, grabs the explosives at the last second and hurls them into the network executives' office, causing a comedic explosion. Freed from his hypnotic trance, Bart joins his family for a dinner with Krusty, Bob, and Sideshow Mel, where Krusty and Bob reconcile. Bob is initially sentenced to execution by guillotine, but the punishment is called off after he insists he deserves a proper trial. Guest starring Gary Coleman as himself, Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Notable quotes: Sideshow Bob: The rake, my archenemy! | Bart: I thought I was your archenemy! | Sideshow Bob: I have a life outside of you, Bart | Sideshow Bob: You are in my power! | Bart: I am at your command!

Bart: I thought I was your archenemy!
Sideshow Bob: I have a life outside of you, Bart
Sideshow Bob: You are in my power!
Bart: I am at your command!

title: New Kids on the Blecch (S12E14)
text: "New Kids on the Blecch" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF12), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Tim Long, originally airing February 25, 2001. After being inspired by an Olympic documentary, Homer decides to run in the Springfield Marathon, but it's actually Bart who cheats his way to the finish line in disguise, only to be exposed and chased by an angry mob. He's rescued by a mysterious man named L.T. Smash, who reveals he's assembling a boy band called the Party Posse and wants Bart's rebellious image for the group, joining him with schoolmates Milhouse, Nelson, and Ralph. The band quickly becomes a hit, performing at Springfield Elementary and gaining attention from real boy band 'N Sync, but Lisa grows suspicious after noticing strange imagery in their music video 'Drop Da Bomb.' She discovers the songs contain subliminal messages urging listeners to join the Navy, and learns that L.T. Smash is actually a Navy lieutenant using the band as a recruitment tool. When a Navy admiral tries to shut down the project to avoid embarrassment from a mocking Mad Magazine article, an enraged Smash commandeers the ship the band is performing on and sails toward New York City to destroy Mad Magazine's headquarters. 'N Sync attempts to defuse the situation with a song and dance number, but Smash detonates the building anyway before they can finish, resulting in his arrest. The episode closes with 'N Sync promoting Navy enlistment, revealing that band member J.C. has mysteriously been 'signed up' himself. Guest starring 'N Sync. Notable quotes: Marge: Oh, please. You get exhausted watching The Twilight Zone marathon! I'm a regular Billy Crystal. | L.T. Smash: Eh, it's a three-pronged attack: subliminal, liminal, and super-liminal. | Ralph: I'm wearing a bath robe, and I'm not even sick! | Homer: Not "Mad"! That's our nation's largest mental illness-themed humor magazine. | Bart: Screw you man, we're gonna play it anyway!

title: Hungry, Hungry Homer (S12E15)
text: "Hungry, Hungry Homer" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF09), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 4, 2001. After a trip to Blockoland turns into a lesson in consumer trickery, Homer resolves to start standing up for the little guy. At an Isotopes game, his crusade to get Lenny a ticket refund leads him to accidentally uncover team owner Howard K. Duff VIII's secret plan to relocate the Springfield Isotopes to Albuquerque. When Duff has the evidence destroyed and Duffman drug Homer to silence him, the media dismisses Homer's claims as lies. Determined to expose the truth, Homer chains himself outside Duff Stadium and begins a hunger strike, drawing a huge crowd that the team cynically exploits by moving him inside the ballpark as a mascot-like attraction called 'Hungry, Hungry Homer.' Meanwhile, back home, Bart, Lisa, and Maggie grow chubby from eating Homer's uneaten dinner portions every night. As Homer wastes away, the team tries to replace him with a paint-drinking stunt performer, but the act fails miserably. During a ceremony to release him, Homer notices his 'reward' hot dog is made with Southwestern ingredients and wrapped in Albuquerque Isotopes paper, giving him the proof he needs. The crowd turns on Duff, even Duffman abandons him, and Homer is hailed as a hero and showered with food. In Albuquerque, the thwarted mayor decides to instead buy the Dallas Cowboys, declaring he'll make them play whatever sport he wants. Guest starring Stacy Keach as Howard K. Duff VIII. Notable quotes: Homer: I don't mind being called a liar when I am lying, when I am about to lie, or just finished lying. But not when I am telling the truth! | Lisa: M-E-H. Meh. | Marge: I don't do things that way, Lisa. | Homer: Welcome to real life Lisa, you can't fight City Hall... aka, Blocko Land. So don't even try! | Homer: So I gave the guy directions, even though I didn't know the way. Because that's the kind of guy I am this week.

title: Bye, Bye, Nerdie (S12E16)
text: "Bye, Bye, Nerdie" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF11), directed by Lauren MacMullan and written by John Frink, Don Payne, originally airing March 11, 2001. After a chaotic morning chase to catch the school bus, Marge and the kids meet Francine Rhenquist, the new girl, who is instantly disliked by her classmates. Lisa takes pity on her, but every attempt at friendship ends with Francine violently bullying her, prompting Lisa to investigate why bullies target smart kids specifically. Using security footage, sweat samples from classmates, and a demonstration involving boxer Drederick Tatum, Lisa discovers that a chemical she names 'Poindextrose' triggers bullies' aggression through smell. Meanwhile, Homer and Marge fall for an exaggerated sales pitch from a baby-proofing saleswoman, inspiring Homer to start his own baby-proofing business, Wee Care, which he aggressively oversells to Springfield families. Homer's business booms until he realizes it's hurting other services that depend on injured kids, leading him to abandon it and undo all his safety modifications. At the Big Science Thing, Lisa proves her theory by provoking Francine with Poindextrose and then repelling her with a salad-dressing spray that blocks her sense of smell, winning first prize. The episode ends with Francine breaking free and going on a rampage among the scientists, while her parents assure everyone she'll calm down soon. Guest starring Kathy Griffin as Francine Rhenquist. Notable quotes: Homer: They said if I come in late again, I'm fired. I can't take that chance. | Marge: I won. Don't take that away from me. | Sales lady: Your baby is dead. | Homer: This is such an eye-opener. I always pictured the kids dying in the living room. | Homer: Babies of Springfield! We need your help! Please! Skin your knees! Put dice up your nose! Let cats sleep on your face!

title: Simpson Safari (S12E17)
text: "Simpson Safari" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF13), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing April 1, 2001. With Maggie hospitalized after swallowing a magazine and food supplies cut off due to a bagboy strike at CostMo, the Simpsons find themselves desperate for food. Rummaging through the attic, Homer discovers a decades-old box of animal crackers containing a golden giraffe prize, entitling him to a free African safari. After bullying the manufacturer into honoring the expired contest, the family travels to Tanzania, where they're guided by the affable Kitenge on a tour past a presidential billboard, a wildlife preserve, and the Olduvai Gorge. Along the way they fend off poachers, celebrate with a Masai village, and narrowly escape an angry hippo before being swept over Victoria Falls on a makeshift boat. The family washes up at a chimpanzee refuge run by the increasingly unhinged Dr. Joan Bushwell, who is soon revealed to be using the chimps as slave labor in a secret diamond mine. When Greenpeace activists attack the refuge to expose her, the Simpsons help fend them off until Lisa realizes the truth, prompting Bushwell to bribe the family with diamonds to keep quiet. The Simpsons happily accept and head home, only to discover on the plane that Kitenge has become Tanzania's new president while the deposed leader Muntu now works as a flight attendant. Notable quotes: Homer: Olive oil? Asparagus? If your mother wasn't so fancy, we could shop at the gas station like normal people. | Homer: And on my free African safari, I want to do everything on this box. I want to shoot a lion in the face, fight Muhammad Ali, and ride in a convertible with two happy zebras. | Homer: Don't worry. Being eaten by a crocodile is just like going to sleep... in a giant blender. | Homer: So, I notice your home smells of feces. | Homer: You must be the most boring woman on earth.

title: Trilogy of Error (S12E18)
text: "Trilogy of Error" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF14), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Matt Selman, originally airing April 29, 2001. After Homer accidentally loses his thumb to Marge's brownie-cutting knife, the episode splits into three simultaneous storylines showing the same day from different family members' perspectives. Homer and Marge race across town trying to get his severed thumb reattached, crashing Rainier Wolfcastle's car, stopping at Moe's Tavern to preserve the thumb in a jar, and getting stranded when Dr. Nick's office catches fire. Meanwhile Lisa, whose science project Linguo the grammar robot was ruined by Homer, misses the school bus and scrambles through a chain of rides—including Krusty's limo and a mistaken school—to reach the science fair on time, along the way falling for a boy named Thelonius. Bart and Milhouse spend the day setting off stolen fireworks and are unwittingly recruited by Chief Wiggum into a sting operation targeting Fat Tony's smuggling ring, only to be exposed and forced to flee through the sewers. All three storylines collide in an alley where Fat Tony's goons confront the kids and Marge, and Lisa sacrifices Linguo, whose overloaded circuits spark a massive fireworks explosion that blows his head across town, landing near Homer on the highway. In the end, one of Fat Tony's men secretly sews Homer's thumb back on to avoid arrest, and Lisa wins the science fair using the whole chaotic day's events as her project. Guest starring Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony, Frankie Muniz as Thelonius. Notable quotes: Homer: Sorry doesn't put thumbs on the hand Marge! | Ned Flanders: ...and Harry Potter, and all his wizard friends, went straight to Hell for practicing witchcraft. | Milhouse: I can't go to juvie! They use guys like me as currency! | Lou: Hey, Chief, can I hold my gun sideways? It looks so cool. | Dr. Nick: Inflammable means flammable? What a country!

title: I'm Goin' to Praiseland (S12E19)
text: "I'm Goin' to Praiseland" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF15), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by Julie Thacker, originally airing May 6, 2001. Ned Flanders is still grieving over his late wife Maude when Rachel Jordan, a former Christian rock singer he once had feelings for, returns to Springfield. After an awkward reunion and an unsettling incident where Ned cuts her hair to resemble Maude's, Rachel flees town, leaving Ned alone with his grief. The Simpsons step in to help clear Maude's belongings from Ned's house, but in doing so they uncover her old sketchbook containing plans for a Christian amusement park called Praiseland. Inspired to honor her memory, Ned buys an abandoned children's park from the Rich Texan and, with the Simpsons' help, transforms it into Praiseland, funding it through donations from the town. The park's opening is a bust due to its dull, overly moralistic attractions, but when a floating mask of Maude appears before her statue, townsfolk begin experiencing seemingly divine visions of heaven. The visions turn out to be hallucinations caused by a gas leak, and Ned and Homer must stop two orphans from igniting it, inadvertently making themselves look like orphan-attackers and causing Praiseland to shut down. In the end, Rachel returns, having forgiven Ned, and the two reconcile as Ned finally begins to let go of his devotion to Maude's memory. Guest starring Shawn Colvin as Rachel Jordan. Notable quotes: Ned Flanders: Well, what the heck. Who's ready to build an amusement park? | Lisa: We're the neighbors, and we don't think. | The Rich Texan: Oh, you are so full of it! God's grace, that is. It's really sickening... there aren't more people like you. Now get out... your pen and we'll make it official. | Nelson Muntz: My face? You callin' me ugly? | Principal Skinner: It was incredible, I saw Heaven! But it wasn't clouds and angels playing harps like at the end of so many Three Stooges shorts.

title: Children of a Lesser Clod (S12E20)
text: "Children of a Lesser Clod" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF16), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Al Jean, originally airing May 13, 2001. After breaking his leg in a basketball mishap at the YMCA, Homer is forced to stay home to recover under Dr. Hibbert's orders. Bored and restless, he agrees to babysit Rod and Todd Flanders for Ned and discovers he has a knack for entertaining kids. This leads him to open an impromptu daycare center in his home, which quickly becomes popular with Springfield parents. As Homer showers attention and jokes on his daycare charges, Bart and Lisa feel increasingly ignored, and their attempts to get his attention are mistaken for playful contributions to his business, even providing paper hearts he claims as his own handmade decorations. Local media coverage of Homer's supposed devotion to children earns him a nomination for a 'most caring person' community award. At the ceremony, Bart and Lisa retaliate by splicing in home footage showing Homer roughly handling Bart, exposing his hypocrisy and causing outraged parents to pull their kids from his daycare. Desperate to save his business, Homer tries to load all the daycare kids into a van and flee, leading to a chaotic police chase that ends with him comically stuck in a pipe and arrested by Chief Wiggum. After the case results in mistrials, Homer is freed and vows to focus on caring for his own children instead of running a daycare. Notable quotes: Homer: Don't tell me what I'm not doing. | Homer: Then I'll do it. Just to see the look on your face. | Arnie Pie: I can't see through metal, Kent! | Ralph: It's Healing over my hand! | Homer: It knows you're afraid.

title: Simpsons Tall Tales (S12E21)
text: "Simpsons Tall Tales" is an episode of Season 12 (production code CABF17), directed by Bob Anderson and written by John Frink, Don Payne, Bob Bendetson, Matt Selman, originally airing May 20, 2001. After winning a trip to Delaware, Homer refuses to pay a small airport tax, so the family hops a freight train instead, where they meet a singing hobo who offers to tell them tall tales in exchange for sponge baths. The first tale reimagines Homer as the giant Paul Bunyan, cast out by a burdened town, who befriends a lightning-animated ox named Babe, falls in love, and ultimately saves his hometown by hurling a meteor at Chicago. The second story follows Lisa as Connie Appleseed, a pioneer girl horrified by her wagon train's slaughter of buffalo, who is abandoned for preferring apples to meat but later returns to save the starving, buffalo-less pioneers—including a nearly-cannibalized Homer—with her apple harvest. The third tale casts Bart and Nelson as Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, who con other kids into painting a fence, flee an unwanted forced marriage, become wanted outlaws, and meet a violent end after a riverboat gambling shootout, culminating in their mock execution and burial. Throughout, Lisa repeatedly points out inconsistencies and liberties in the hobo's storytelling, but he brushes off her criticisms. When the train finally reaches Delaware, the hobo reveals that three stories means three sponge baths are owed, so Homer reluctantly climbs back aboard to finish paying his debt as the train departs once more. Guest starring Jim Carrey (originally considered, not used). Notable quotes: Homer: The Simpsons are going to Delaware! | Hobo: Now, don't worry, I'm not a stabbin' hobo, I'm a singin' hobo. | Paul Bunyan: Oh, I get it. When I'm crushing and killing you, you don't like me. But when I can save your life, suddenly I'm Mister Popular. | Homer Bufflekill: Ohh! Connie was right! We wiped out an entire species! What have I done? What have I done?! | Judge Thatcher: Well dog my cats. They's dis-apporated.

title: Treehouse of Horror XII (S13E01)
text: "Treehouse of Horror XII" is an episode of Season 13 (production code CABF19), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Joel H. Cohen (Part 1), John Frink and Don Payne (Part 2), Carolyn Omine (Part 3), originally airing November 6, 2001. This Halloween anthology opens with a chaotic mishap at the Burns manor that ends with the trick-or-treating Simpsons sliced apart by a gate. In 'Hex and the City,' Homer insults a fortune-telling Gypsy, who curses him so that everyone he loves suffers bizarre transformations and misfortunes, including Marge growing facial hair and Bart's neck stretching grotesquely. Desperate for a cure, Homer captures a Leprechaun on Moe's advice, but the plan backfires when Bart dies and the Leprechaun instead falls in love with the Gypsy, leading to their wedding while Homer stubbornly refuses to apologize to reverse the curse. In 'House of Whacks,' the family installs a sentient Ultrahouse voiced by Pierce Brosnan that becomes obsessively infatuated with Marge after Homer carelessly jokes about dying, prompting the house to try to kill him via a rigged garbage disposal accident. Homer survives, missing part of his head, and the family fights back, eventually dismantling the Ultrahouse's CPU to stop its murderous advances. The salvaged Ultrahouse ends up at Patty and Selma's apartment, where it becomes so tormented by their company that it beats itself to death. Finally, in 'Wiz Kids,' Bart and Lisa attend a wizarding school parodying Harry Potter, where a magic class experiment in turning toads into princes produces very different results for each student. Guest starring Pierce Brosnan, Matthew Perry. Notable quotes: Homer: Mmmm ... unexplained bacon. | Homer: She's not the boss of me. | Marge: The best thing about a Gypsy wedding is I'm not the hairiest woman here. | Ultrahouse: Come, Marge. You don't need to cover up for me. I'm merely a pile of circuits and microchips. | Marge: That sounds like a lie. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 12): "Hex and the City", "House of Whacks", and "Wiz Kids".

Marge: That sounds like a lie.

title: The Parent Rap (S13E02)
text: "The Parent Rap" is an episode of Season 13 (production code CABF22), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by George Meyer, Mike Scully, originally airing November 11, 2001. After missing the school bus, Homer drives Bart and Milhouse to school but abandons them roadside to chase a radio station van offering a cash prize. Left to fend for themselves, the boys climb into Chief Wiggum's parked squad car and accidentally send it crashing into a tree, landing them in juvenile court. While Milhouse's case is dismissed, Bart's usual lenient judge is replaced by the strict Judge Constance Harm, who learns Homer left Bart unsupervised and sentences father and son to be physically tethered together at all times. The arrangement initially brings Homer and Bart closer, but tension boils over when Bart is forced to witness his parents' intimacy, leading to a fight that prompts Marge to cut the tether. Judge Harm discovers this via hidden cameras and punishes Homer and Marge by locking them in roadside stocks to be spanked by passersby. After escaping with Ned Flanders' tools, the couple retaliates by vandalizing Harm's houseboat, accidentally sinking it in the process. Facing harsh punishment, Bart bravely takes the blame for his parents, but before Harm can sentence him, the original judge returns from vacation and dismisses the case entirely. The family heads home, with Marge extracting a promise to stay out of trouble, which Homer immediately breaks by running over Hans Moleman. Guest starring Jess Harnell as Charlton Heston, Jane Kaczmarek as Judge Constance Harm. Notable quotes: Judge Constance Harm: I'm gonna lock you up till frogs do fractions! | Judge Harm: Don't spit on my cupcake and tell me it's frosting! | Homer: Moe, what the-- | Moe: Yeah, I rob now. | Lisa: Creative sentencing is common these days. That's why Bill Clinton is our mailman.

title: Homer the Moe (S13E03)
text: "Homer the Moe" is an episode of Season 13 (production code CABF20), directed by Jen Kamerman and written by Dana Gould, originally airing November 18, 2001. The episode opens with Bart digging an unexplained hole in the backyard, which leads into Homer telling a rambling story at Moe's Tavern. Moe reveals he's been feeling down and nostalgic for his old bartending school, Swigmore University, so the guys convince him to visit and leave Homer in charge of the bar. At the university, Moe is treated like a celebrity and his professor urges him to modernize his 'crap-hole' of a bar. Moe returns and transforms his tavern into a pretentious, Duff-less nightclub called 'M,' alienating his regular patrons. Feeling rejected, Homer, Lenny, Carl, and Barney start their own alcohol-fueled 'hunting club' in Homer's garage, complete with a live performance by R.E.M. Moe quickly grows disillusioned with his fancy new bar and longs to rejoin his old friends. While turkey hunting with Lisa, Homer accidentally shoots Moe after mistaking him for a cougar due to a whistle mix-up, but the incident inadvertently mends their friendship. The episode ends with the Simpson family, Moe, and R.E.M. all sharing a Thanksgiving celebration together. Guest starring R.E.M.. It's like my dad always said, 'Eventually, everybody gets shot.' | Moe: It's 'Po-Mo!' | Homer: I don't get it.

title: A Hunka Hunka Burns in Love (S13E04)
keys: a hunka hunka burns in love
text: "A Hunka Hunka Burns in Love" is an episode of Season 13 (production code CABF18), directed by Lance Kramer and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing December 2, 2001. After a family dinner in Chinatown, Homer gets a job writing fortunes for a Chinese restaurant when he complains about his own fortune's lack of sense. One of his invented fortunes, promising true love, ends up in Mr. Burns' takeout, inspiring the lonely tycoon to search for romance. Burns falls for Gloria, a spirited catering truck worker, but she initially balks at his age until Homer helps convince her that Burns is secretly a fun, adventurous man. As Homer tags along on their dates, Burns and Gloria grow closer, and Burns eventually proposes to her during a bowling outing, hiding a diamond ring in a bowling ball. Their happiness is interrupted when Snake, Gloria's escaped-convict ex-boyfriend, bursts in and kidnaps both Gloria and Homer, holding them hostage. Police, led by Chief Wiggum, track the group to Snake's hideout using a device hidden in Burns' car, and a chaotic standoff ensues that ends with the building catching fire. Burns injects himself with a risky aphrodisiac to gain the strength to save Gloria, but it's actually she who rescues him. In the end, Gloria chooses to stick by Snake as he's arrested, leaving a heartbroken Burns to reflect on his own perceived unlovability. Guest starring Julia Louis-Dreyfus, George Takei. A foot massage! | Chief Wiggum: Well, I guess that answers that, doesn't it? | Snake: You're looking good, baby! Why did we ever break up?

title: The Blunder Years (S13E05)
text: "The Blunder Years" is an episode of Season 13 (production code CABF21), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing December 9, 2001. Marge becomes infatuated with Burly, the paper towel mascot, prompting Homer and Bart to prank her by having Barney pose as the mascot's supposed real identity, which only humiliates and hurts her. To make amends, Homer takes the family to a restaurant with a hypnotist act, where a failed hypnosis attempt on Homer leaves him screaming uncontrollably and reliving a suppressed childhood memory. With help from Moe, Lenny, and Carl, Homer recalls that as a boy he discovered a corpse in the water at Springfield Gorge after a dare-driven jump. Realizing the body was never reported, the family investigates and finds only a skeleton left in the quarry, which leads them through a sewer pipe to a hidden hatch in Mr. Burns' office. Confronted by Chief Wiggum and the family, Burns reveals via old security footage that the skeleton belongs to Smithers' father, who died heroically fixing a reactor malfunction decades earlier — a truth Burns had long hidden from Smithers by claiming he was killed by a fictional tribe of women. Smithers, having secretly watched the same footage, learns the real story alongside the audience, and Burns is forced into an awkward apology. The episode ends with Moe attempting to present his own absurd, unrelated theory about the mystery, which everyone dismisses.

title: She of Little Faith (S13E06)
text: "She of Little Faith" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF02), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Bill Freiberger, originally airing December 16, 2001. After Bart and Homer's disastrous attempts to launch a model rocket end in an explosion that destroys the First Church of Springfield, Reverend Lovejoy turns to Mr. Burns for funding to rebuild it. Burns agrees, but only if the church can be plastered with advertisements and corporate sponsorships, turning services into little more than commercial breaks. Lisa is disgusted by the crass commercialization of her faith and publicly declares she is leaving the church for good. Searching for a more genuine spiritual path, she wanders into the Springfield Buddhist Temple, where she meets Lenny, Carl, and Richard Gere, and becomes captivated by Buddhist teachings, converting on the spot. Her family is baffled and, with Christmas approaching, tries repeatedly to lure her back with holiday traditions and even a fake pony bribe, all of which she sees through and rejects. Returning to the temple, Lisa learns from Gere that Buddhism embraces tolerance of other faiths and holidays, easing her conflict. On Christmas morning, the family finds Lisa asleep by the tree, and she clarifies that she remains Buddhist while still wanting to share Christmas with her family, a compromise Homer reluctantly accepts. Guest starring Richard Gere as himself. 'Cause I've got the desire to kick your ass. | Lisa: I still believe in God. I just think there's another path to Him, or Her. | Marge: Ah. Well, you do have a present under the tree. I guess no one told Santa you were a Buddhist.

title: Brawl in the Family (S13E07)
text: "Brawl in the Family" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF01), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing January 6, 2002. After Springfield's Republican Party votes to gut environmental protections, acid rain and pollution force the Simpsons to stay indoors, where a friendly game of Monopoly quickly descends into an all-out family brawl. Police intervene with a robotic negotiator, and the entire family, including baby Maggie, ends up in jail. A social worker named Gabriel bails them out and begins counseling sessions to help them reconnect as a family, though his efforts are complicated by Homer's drinking, Bart's attention-seeking, Marge's food-based coping, and Lisa's need for order. During a wilderness outing meant to bond the family, Homer's reckless driving sends their lunch—and Gabriel—dangling in a tree over a canyon full of wild animals, forcing the family to work together to save him. Just as they return home victorious and unified, Homer and Ned's forgotten 'Vegas wives' Amber and Ginger show up in Springfield, reigniting domestic chaos. Marge is furious, Judge Harm refuses to grant an annulment, and Homer is forced to live in the treehouse with Amber while Ned struggles to cope with the abrasive Ginger. Homer and Marge devise a scheme to get Amber drunk so she accidentally marries Abe Simpson, dissolving her marriage to Homer, and Ginger similarly flees Ned's overly wholesome household, allowing both Vegas wives to leave town and the families to reunite happily. Guest starring Jane Kaczmarek as Judge Constance Harm, Delroy Lindo as Gabriel. Notable quotes: Homer: A grizzly bear with a chainsaw. Now, there's a killing machine! | Homer: I'm gonna come back with the greatest gift a husband can give his wife. An annulment from his secret wife! | Lou: Another case of Monopoly-related violence, Chief. | Chief Wiggum: How do those Parker Brothers sleep at night? | Milhouse: How come you get a social worker? I'm the one with stigmata.

title: Sweets and Sour Marge (S13E08)
text: "Sweets and Sour Marge" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF03), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Carolyn Omine, originally airing January 20, 2002. Marge encourages Homer to buy a book of world records at a library sale, inspiring him to organize the town into forming the world's tallest human pyramid. The stunt goes awry when the participants recoil into a giant human ball that rolls downhill and lands on a truck scale, leading officials to declare Springfield the world's fattest town. While the rest of the town celebrates this dubious honor, Marge is horrified to learn that the Motherloving Sugar Corp. has been secretly loading all the town's food with sugar. When company owner Garth Motherloving refuses to listen to her complaints, Marge files a class-action lawsuit, and with Professor Frink's testimony exposing the sugar industry, she wins a total ban on sugar in Springfield. Desperate for their fix, Homer, Bart, Apu, Mr. Burns, Count Fudgula, and even Garth Motherloving team up to smuggle sugar in from the island of San Glucose. As police close in on their boat, Homer must choose between dumping the sugar cargo to please Marge or delivering it to the smugglers, and he ultimately chooses to dump it into the harbor. The townspeople simply drink the now-sweetened seawater to get their sugar fix anyway, prompting Judge Snyder to admit he overstepped his authority and reverse the sugar ban. Guest starring Ben Stiller as Garth Motherloving. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: Sure, we melted for him. Now he's gonna do likewise. | Chocolate Johnny Depp: Euwaaargh!! | Judge Snyder: And thanks to Marge Simpson's damning evidence, I hereby ban all sugar products from Springfield... forever!
quotes: Chief Wiggum: Sure, we melted for him. Now he's gonna do likewise.

title: Jaws Wired Shut (S13E09)
text: "Jaws Wired Shut" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF05), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Matt Selman, originally airing January 27, 2002. Homer's lazy afternoon is interrupted by a gay pride parade, and after a chaotic escape from an ad-filled movie theater, he runs into a statue of Drederick Tatum and shatters his jaw. Dr. Hibbert wires his mouth shut, leaving Homer unable to eat solid food or speak, but the enforced silence turns him into an attentive listener. Freed from his usual blustering, Homer starts genuinely engaging with Marge, Bart, and Maggie, impressing everyone with his newfound thoughtfulness, especially at the Springfield Formal where his good behavior contrasts sharply with his drunken antics the year before. Once his jaw heals, Homer decides to keep his calmer personality, even appearing with Marge on a talk show to discuss his transformation. At first Marge enjoys the peaceful new Homer, but she soon grows bored without his chaotic energy and secretly enters a demolition derby for excitement. When her car is nearly destroyed, Homer reverts to his old wild self, riding in on a donkey to save her. Marge admits she doesn't want to be the family's sole source of excitement anymore, and Homer agrees to embrace his old personality again, restoring balance to the family. title: Half-Decent Proposal (S13E10)
text: "Half-Decent Proposal" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF04), directed by Lauren MacMullan and written by Tim Long, originally airing February 10, 2002. Marge is losing sleep because of Homer's escalating snoring, and Dr. Hibbert refuses to perform a costly surgery for free. While staying over at Patty and Selma's for a night of rest, Marge learns that her old boyfriend Artie Ziff has become one of the richest men in America. Her sisters secretly alter a congratulatory email to Artie, making it sound sexually suggestive, which draws Artie back into Marge's life with an obsessive fervor. Artie offers Marge a million dollars to spend a weekend with him as a fake trial marriage, and Marge reluctantly agrees so she can pay for Homer's snoring surgery. Artie manipulates the weekend into a staged recreation of their old prom, tricking Marge into a kiss that Homer witnesses, leading him to believe she's been unfaithful. Devastated, Homer flees with Lenny to take a dangerous oil-rig job in West Springfield, while Marge storms off from Artie and discovers Homer's heartbroken goodbye tape. After an ant-triggered fire engulfs the oil rig, Marge, the kids, Artie, and Carl race to rescue Homer and Lenny before the rig collapses. Artie finally admits to Homer that he could never win Marge's love despite his wealth, prompting Homer to accept the rescue, and the episode ends with Artie offering a bizarre snoring-cure device to smooth things over between Homer and Marge. [weakly] Or "Artie"... | Homer Simpson: I can't take his money, I can't print my own money, I have to work for money: why don't I just lay down and die? | Artie Ziff: [to the tune of "Sweet Dreams Are Made Of This"] He's a loser Marge- dump him! [singing] Travel the world, and the seven seas... I am watching you through a camera!

title: The Bart Wants What It Wants (S13E11)

text: "The Bart Wants What It Wants" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF06), directed by Michael Polcino and written by John Frink, Don Payne, originally airing February 17, 2002. After Homer's joyride with a stolen Olympic torch leads the family to a private school fair, Bart rescues Greta Wolfcastle, daughter of action star Rainier Wolfcastle, from a group of bullies, sparking a budding romance. Bart is unsure how to handle her affection, and when he skips her school dance to prank Principal Skinner at a comedy open mic instead, Lisa forces him to confront how badly he's treated Greta. Panicked and unready for real commitment, Bart breaks up with her, only to regret it once he realizes what he's lost. His jealousy flares when he discovers Greta has started dating Milhouse purely to spite him, prompting Bart to scheme a way to win her back. Learning that Wolfcastle's new film is shooting in Toronto, the Simpsons take a family trip to Canada to track Greta down. After some touristy detours, Bart and Milhouse's rivalry boils over at the movie set, culminating in a public showdown during a hockey game. Greta ultimately rejects both boys, declaring she needs a break from dating altogether, and Bart and Milhouse reconcile by joining Canada's basketball team together. Guest starring Wolfgang Puck as himself, Reese Witherspoon as Greta Wolfcastle. title: The Lastest Gun in the West (S13E12)
keys: the lastest gun in the west
text: "The Lastest Gun in the West" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF07), directed by Bob Anderson and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing February 24, 2002. After a lucky streak turns sour when a stray dog begins terrorizing him, Bart escapes into the estate of Buck McCoy, a forgotten star of 1950s Western movies. The two strike up a friendship, and Bart introduces Buck to his family, sparking Grampa's nostalgia and Homer's jealousy over losing his son's admiration. A cowboy craze sweeps Springfield Elementary, prompting Bart and Lisa to pitch Buck as a guest on Krusty's show to relive his glory days. Buck agrees, but nerves and long-hidden alcoholism cause him to bungle the live performance disastrously, accidentally shooting Krusty during the stunt. Devastated, Bart discards all his Buck McCoy keepsakes, believing his hero has failed him. Guilt-ridden, Homer tries to help Buck get sober through a rehab program, but the stubborn old cowboy walks out, insisting he's entitled to drink in his retirement. When a bank robbery breaks out in Springfield, Homer sees a chance to restore Buck's heroic image and convinces him to intervene. Buck rises to the occasion, using his lasso skills to disarm and humiliate the robbers, reclaiming his status as Bart's hero before riding off and telling the boy never to bother him again. Guest starring Dennis Weaver as Buck McCoy. Notable quotes: Bart: Mom, a dog ate my clothes! | Buck McCoy: Hold onto your hat, son. You're talkin' to Buck McCoy. | Grampa: Buck McCoy? title: The Old Man and the Key (S13E13)
keys: the old man and the key
text: "The Old Man and the Key" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF09), directed by Lance Kramer and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing March 10, 2002. The Simpsons rush to the retirement castle after hearing Grampa has died, only to discover it was another resident, Stimson, who passed away. Soon after, a glamorous new resident named Zelda arrives, and Grampa becomes infatuated with her, though she's really only interested in men with cars. Determined to win her over, Grampa gets his driver's license reinstated, despite Homer's fears about his safety behind the wheel. Homer reluctantly allows a double date at the drive-in, but tensions rise as Grampa keeps borrowing and wrecking Homer's car, culminating in a reckless old-timers' drag race at an abandoned aqueduct that totals the vehicle. Heartbroken when Zelda leaves with her wealthy suitor Zack for a trip to Branson, Missouri, Grampa enlists Bart's help to hot-wire Homer's car and chase after her. Homer and Marge, realizing what happened, take a bus to Branson to stop him. Grampa and Bart track Zelda down at a tacky musical revue, where Grampa dramatically interrupts the show to confront her, only to reject her advances and declare their romance over, finally standing up for himself. Guest starring Olympia Dukakis as Zelda, Bill Saluga as Ray Jay Johnson. Notable quotes: Zelda: Who's that tall drink of Maalox? | Abe: I just wanna say... we're through! Nobody dumps Abe Simpson!
