title: Tales from the Public Domain (S13E14)
text: "Tales from the Public Domain" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF08), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Andrew Kreisberg, Josh Lieb, Matt Warburton, originally airing March 17, 2002. Homer receives an overdue notice from the library for a children's classics book he checked out when Bart was born but never got around to reading. When Lisa finds the book, Homer finally reads three stories aloud to the kids. In the first, Homer plays Odysseus, who tricks and destroys Troy, angers the gods, and endures a perilous voyage home past sirens and the sorceress Circe before slaughtering the suitors pursuing his wife Penelope, only to abandon her for Moe's Tavern once he's home. In the second tale, Lisa plays Joan of Arc, chosen by God to lead the French army, but she is captured and sentenced to burn at the stake; Marge intervenes to give the story a happier, if absurd, ending. The final story casts Bart as Hamlet, who learns from his father's ghost that Uncle Claudius murdered him to marry Gertrude, leading to a bloody chain of revenge, accidental deaths, and poisonings that leaves nearly the entire cast dead by the end. Afterward, Bart complains that Hamlet was boring, but Homer insists it's a classic that later became a great movie, Ghostbusters, prompting the family to dance to its theme song. Notable quotes: Krusty: If your idea of a date is to burn down her village then you just might be a Viking! | Bart: Are you crazy? I can't believe a play where every character becomes murdered can be so boring. | Homer: Son, it's not only a great play, but also became a great movie called... Ghostbusters! | Lisa: And that's the greatest story ever written.

title: Blame It on Lisa (S13E15)
text: "Blame It on Lisa" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF10), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Bob Bendetson, originally airing March 31, 2002. After the Simpsons receive an unusually large phone bill, they discover the charges are from calls to Brazil, initially blaming Bart for another prank call. When Marge and Homer confront the phone company about the bill, Lisa finally admits she has secretly been sponsoring and calling a Brazilian orphan named Ronaldo, who has since gone missing. Determined to find him, the family travels to Brazil, splitting up to search the city, but their efforts quickly go awry. Homer and Bart are kidnapped by an unlicensed taxi driver, and the kidnappers demand a hefty ransom for Homer's return while Bart manages to escape. Meanwhile, Lisa tracks down Ronaldo and discovers he has become a wealthy child star, secretly performing in a children's show while wearing the shoes she once gave him. Ronaldo generously pays the ransom to free Homer, who has grown oddly attached to his captors during his ordeal. The family is joyfully reunited, though the happy ending is undercut when Bart is unexpectedly eaten by an anaconda. Notable quotes: Homer: So it's opposite land! Crooks chase cops, cats have puppies! | Homer: I have a bladder the size of a brazilnut! | Woman: No. I was just distracting you while my children rob you. | Homer: The Simpsons are goin' to Brazil. | Kidnapper: Around here we just call them nuts.

title: Weekend at Burnsie's (S13E16)
text: "Weekend at Burnsie's" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF11), directed by Michael Marcantel and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing April 7, 2002. After Marge grows genetically modified vegetables and then switches to her own backyard garden, a flock of crows begins attacking the plot, prompting her to build a scarecrow. Homer mistakes the scarecrow for an intruder and destroys it, earning the crows' respect as an 'alpha,' but when he later drives them off after they endanger Maggie, the birds retaliate by injuring his eyes. Dr. Hibbert prescribes medical marijuana for the pain, and despite Homer's traumatic teenage memory involving a police dog, he agrees to try it, becoming mellow and more affectionate with his family and neighbor Ned Flanders. Unbeknownst to him, Ned tricks Homer into signing a petition to recriminalize medical marijuana. Meanwhile, Homer's stoned laughter impresses Mr. Burns during a mix-up at the plant, earning him a surprise promotion to executive vice president over Smithers. When Homer and Otto learn of the marijuana recriminalization vote, they organize a Phish concert rally to fight it, but arrive a day too late as the law has already passed, forcing Homer to quit smoking and repair his strained friendships. At an important investors meeting, Homer and Smithers get high to endure Burns' bad jokes, only to discover Burns has apparently died in his bathtub; they disguise his 'death' by puppeteering his body until he suddenly revives during a dance number and has Smithers slap them both repeatedly for their scheme. Guest starring Phish as themselves. Mr. Burns is gonna be so mad. | Marge: I've tried heckling them, I've tried jeckling them, it's time I made myself a scarecrow. | Homer: Marge, I just realized: I am the "ow" in the word "now". And if you tell anyone...

title: Gump Roast (S13E17)
text: "Gump Roast" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF12), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Deb Lacusta, Dan Castellaneta, originally airing April 21, 2002. Homer is discovered sitting on a park bench dressed as Forrest Gump, prompting Chief Wiggum to question him about impersonating movie characters, which leads Homer into a rambling recollection of his life story. Unbeknownst to him, Marge and the kids are secretly organizing a special event, and they eventually blindfold him and drive him to the Springfield Friars Club, where he learns he is the guest of honor at a roast. A parade of Springfield residents, including Bart, Lisa, Mr. Burns, Grampa, and Mrs. Skinner, take turns mocking Homer's incompetence and misadventures, each anecdote triggering a flashback clip from earlier episodes. A drunken Homer briefly humiliates himself before Reverend Lovejoy and Ned Flanders perform a musical duet that ends in an argument over altered lyrics. The proceedings are interrupted when aliens Kang and Kodos crash the party, announcing they will judge humanity's worth through Homer's memories and destroy Earth if it is found lacking. When the aliens deem humanity too brutish, Lisa pleads for them to examine baby Maggie's innocent mind instead, hoping her purity might save the planet. The aliens are so overwhelmed by Maggie's saccharine memories that they vomit, but ultimately relent and spare Earth, later mingling with celebrities at an awards show. Guest starring Ed Asner, Alec Baldwin, Kim Basinger, Stephen Hawking, Ron Howard, Elton John, Lucy Lawless, Joe Namath, 'N Sync, Elizabeth Taylor, U2. Notable quotes: Wiggum: Hold it right there, Forrest Plump! This town has laws against impersonating movie characters. | Homer: Are the proceeds going to charity? | Burns: Just look at all of his catastrophic nincompoopery. | Agnes: You fruits wouldn't know what to do with me! | Krusty: This can't be good for my pacemaker.
quotes: Wiggum: Hold it right there, Forrest Plump! This town has laws against impersonating movie characters.

text: "I Am Furious (Yellow)" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF13), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing April 28, 2002. During a lackluster Career Day at Springfield Elementary, Lisa and Principal Skinner recruit cartoonist Geoff Jenkins to inspire the students, but his blasé attitude toward his craft backfires. Inspired anyway, Bart tries drawing his own comic strip and gets harsh but constructive criticism from Comic Book Guy and a visiting Stan Lee. After watching Homer struggle comically through his day, Bart creates "Angry Dad," a comic based on his father's short temper, which becomes a school sensation and eventually an online cartoon produced by BetterThanTV.com. Homer is initially amused until he realizes the cartoon mocks him, leading to public humiliation and a violent confrontation with Bart. Urged by Lisa to address his anger issues, Homer suppresses his rage, causing strange boils to form on his neck each time he holds back an outburst. When BetterThanTV.com abruptly goes out of business, Bart rushes to stop a prank trap he had set to provoke new material from Homer, but arrives too late. Homer falls into the trap and lands in a vat of green paint, causing a panicked town to mistake him for the Hulk, resulting in a chaotic rampage before police subdue him. At the hospital, Dr. Hibbert reveals that Bart's prank actually saved Homer's life by releasing his dangerously bottled-up anger, and the episode ends with father and son bonding over fishing, with Bart still trying to provoke him for fun. Apu's chaotic home life with Manjula and their eight children pushes him toward an affair with Annette, the flirtatious Squishee delivery woman, at the Kwik-E-Mart. Homer accidentally discovers the tryst while returning a beer keg from the town's inaccurate Civil War reenactment, and he and Marge struggle to keep the secret from Manjula while trying to convince Apu to end the affair. Manjula eventually uncovers the truth herself using the store's security footage, kicks Apu out, and files for divorce despite Homer and Marge's clumsy attempts to reconcile the couple over a surprise dinner. Living alone and despondent, Apu is nearly driven to suicide before Manjula, having had a change of heart after seeing her children's first words spell out a plea for their father's return, arrives just in time to stop him. Marge suggests Manjula make a list of atonement tasks for Apu to complete, ranging from losing weight to performing an octuplet-cast Broadway show, and Apu dutifully completes them all. The episode ends with Manjula finally forgiving Apu and welcoming him back into their bed, much to the traumatized horror of Homer, who witnesses it all again from a ladder outside their window. title: The Frying Game (S13E21)
text: "The Frying Game" is an episode of Season 13 (production code DABF16), directed by Michael Polcino and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing May 19, 2002. Homer gives Marge a koi pond for their anniversary, but it attracts a rare, constantly shrieking bug called the Screamapillar, and federal law makes the family responsible for its welfare. After a mishap makes it look like Homer killed the creature, the EPA arrests him and he's sentenced to community service delivering Meals on Wheels. While on his rounds he meets a seemingly frail elderly woman, Mrs. Bellamy, and out of pity begins helping her around her house, eventually dragging a reluctant Marge into the same trap as the old woman manipulates them into becoming unpaid servants. When Mrs. Bellamy turns up stabbed to death and her diamond necklace goes missing, Homer and Marge become the prime suspects, especially once it's revealed they stand to inherit her estate. Despite spotting the real culprit, a mysterious man with braces, at the scene, the couple is convicted with Gil as their inept defense attorney and sentenced to death, while their kids are sent to live with the Spuckler family. Just as Homer sacrifices himself to save Marge from the electric chair, the whole ordeal is exposed as an elaborate hidden-camera reality show called Frame Up, with the man with braces as host and Mrs. Bellamy revealed to be co-host Carmen Electra in disguise. Homer is freed and reunites with his family, and after angrily lecturing Carmen Electra about exploiting people for ratings, he immediately undercuts his own indignation by staring at her chest. Trouble escalates when Springshield busts Fat Tony for fraud, prompting the mobster to publicly threaten to kill Homer unless he leaves town. Homer is later crowned King of the Springfield Mardi Gras through a rigged election, and during the parade Bob deduces that the same wrench used to jam the spa door was used to sabotage Homer's car brakes. While cooped up, Marge begins lifting the weights Homer bought from Wolfcastle's sale, and the workouts unexpectedly restore her confidence enough to leave the house and confront and beat up her mugger. Emboldened, Marge dives into bodybuilding, reconnecting with old friend Ruth Powers, who introduces her to steroids to prepare for a competition called The Iron Maidens. The drugs make Marge freakishly strong but only earn her second place, sending her into a rage-fueled spiral where she starts brawling at Moe's Tavern and losing her femininity. Homer finally convinces her that the steroids are changing her for the worse, prompting Marge to give up bodybuilding and destroy her weights in the furnace, restoring peace to the family. title: Pray Anything (S14E10)
text: "Pray Anything" is an episode of Season 14 (production code EABF06), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Sam O'Neal, Neal Boushell, originally airing February 9, 2003. After watching Ned Flanders win big at a WNBA game by playing fair and praying, Homer decides prayer might be a shortcut to getting whatever he wants. When his small requests seem to be answered instantly, he becomes convinced of prayer's power. His luck turns when a prayer outside the First Church of Springfield leads him to fall into a hole and break his leg, prompting a lawyer to help him sue Reverend Lovejoy's church for damages. Lovejoy loses the case and, unable to pay the judgment, is forced to hand over the church deed to the Simpsons. Homer immediately turns the church into the site of an endless, debauched housewarming party, while a humiliated Lovejoy retreats to preaching out of Barney's Bowlarama before deciding to leave Springfield for good. As Homer's party spirals into a display of nearly every biblical sin, a massive storm floods the town, driving everyone onto the church roof where an angry mob nearly turns on Homer. Reverend Lovejoy returns dramatically by helicopter to pray for mercy, and the rain miraculously stops, saving the town. Homer is left uncertain whether it was truly divine intervention, but claims to have learned a lesson about respecting God's power. Guest starring Ken Burns as himself, Lisa Leslie as herself. It's hypnotic. | Homer: Eh. God's cool. | God: Keep that popcorn chicken coming, colonel.

title: Barting Over (S14E11)
text: "Barting Over" is an episode of Season 14 (production code EABF05), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Andrew Kreisberg, originally airing February 16, 2003. After Bart and Lisa dig up an old baby commercial Bart starred in, Bart learns Homer spent all the money buying back embarrassing photos of himself dropping baby Bart off a balcony. Furious at years of mistreatment, and provoked further when Homer declares he can do whatever he wants to Bart until he's 18, Bart seeks out the family's shady lawyer to file for emancipation. In court, Judge Constance Harm sides with Bart after Homer's temper gets the better of him, ordering Homer to hand over half his paycheck until Bart's stolen money is repaid. Bart moves into a downtown loft, where he unexpectedly befriends his new neighbor Tony Hawk and parties with the band Blink-182, finally enjoying life away from his father. Marge pushes Homer to make amends, but Bart, though willing to forgive, chooses to stay independent and join Hawk's skateboard tour instead. Desperate to win back his son's respect, Homer schemes with Tony Hawk to rig a skateboarding contest in his favor, but the plan spirals into a real aerial duel that leaves Tony injured. Bart finally gets Homer to understand that his hurt wasn't about money or coolness but about feeling uncared for, and Homer sincerely vows to change. To pay off his debt, Homer takes a humiliating job as the face of an impotence drug commercial, a decision that follows him even in death decades later. Guest starring Blink-182, Tony Hawk, Jane Kaczmarek. Notable quotes: Marge: Bart, you're suing us? | Bart: Yes, I want to be emancipated. | Homer: Emancipated? Don't you like being a dude?! | Homer: ...You're mine until you're 18.

As a new school year begins, Lisa wins Springfield Elementary's spelling bee and advances through the state finals toward the national Spellympics. When the Ribwich is finally discontinued because its source animal has gone extinct, Homer gives up his last sandwich to trade for a car so he can rush to support Lisa at the finals. Inspired by his arrival, Lisa refuses to throw the competition and publicly exposes Plimpton's scheme, but she then accidentally misspells her word and is eliminated anyway, leaving her without the promised scholarship reward. Despite her loss, the Simpsons return home to find the whole town celebrating her integrity, and Mayor Quimby unveils a giant mountain carving made in her honor, turning her defeat into a moral victory. title: A Star Is Born Again (S14E13)
text: "A Star Is Born Again" is an episode of Season 14 (production code EABF08), directed by Michael Marcantel and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing March 2, 2003. During Springfield's annual Jellyfish Festival, Ned Flanders feels lonely at a beachside dance since losing Maude, so he retreats to the Leftorium to do paperwork. There he meets a mysterious customer who turns out to be famous actress Sara Sloane, and after a surprise date at the Squidport, the two begin an unlikely romance. Their relationship quickly attracts tabloid chaos, wrecking the Flanders home and forcing Ned to navigate the strange world of Hollywood, including visiting Sara's film set and helping rewrite a nude scene so she won't have to appear naked. Ned struggles to adapt to Sara's celebrity lifestyle, clashing with her over a revealing dress and being unsettled when ex-boyfriend Rainier Wolfcastle shows up begging her to reconcile. Marge tries to bond with Sara through her book club, inviting author Helen Fielding, but the meeting falls apart when no one has actually read the assigned book. After a romantic night together, Ned proposes marriage, but Sara turns him down, unwilling to be tied to one place, and the couple splits. Ned later watches news of Sara's whirlwind marriage and divorce from Bob Balaban, wistfully noting that his own relationship with her lasted longer, before moving on with his ordinary Springfield life. Guest starring James L. Brooks as himself, Helen Fielding as herself, Marisa Tomei as Sara Sloane. title: Mr. Spritz Goes to Washington (S14E14)
text: "Mr. Spritz Goes to Washington" is an episode of Season 14 (production code EABF09), directed by Lance Kramer and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing March 9, 2003. After Mayor Quimby secretly reroutes airport traffic directly over Evergreen Terrace so he can enjoy peace with his girlfriends, the Simpsons endure months of deafening noise until Lisa develops an uncanny ability to identify planes by sound alone. When their sympathetic congressman dies of a heart attack before he can help them, Bart convinces a reluctant Krusty the Clown to run for the vacant seat, hoping Krusty's own grievances with government red tape will motivate him. Krusty's campaign nearly implodes after he unknowingly insults Latino voters with a mistranslated Spanish phrase and his opponent airs old clips of Krusty's show mocking various ethnic and social groups. Lisa steps in to reshape his image by having him connect personally with everyday Springfield families, and his popularity rebounds enough for him to win the election. Once in Congress, however, Krusty discovers that freshman representatives are powerless and ignored, leaving him disillusioned and drinking in a bar until the Simpsons rally him to keep fighting for his constituents. With help from a mysterious janitor (implied to be Walter Mondale) and Homer getting a key congressman drunk, they blackmail one representative with incriminating tape and sneak the air traffic bill into an unrelated piece of legislation. The scheme works, the bill passes, and the Simpsons finally get relief from the noisy skies above their home. Notable quotes: Krusty: I vow to reach out to the Latino community! title: C.E. D'oh (S14E15)
text: "C.E. D'oh" is an episode of Season 14 (production code EABF10), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Dana Gould, originally airing March 16, 2003. On a disappointing Valentine's Day, Homer's rejected advances from Marge send him spiraling until he stumbles into a business seminar, having first been booted from a stripping class taught by Dr. Hibbert. Inspired by the corporate self-help lessons, Homer begins pitching efficiency ideas at the power plant, only to be humiliated and dropped into a tank of electric eels by Mr. Burns. Discovering that the plant's true owner is actually Burns' pet canary, Homer and Bart hatch a scheme, freeing the bird and shipping it off to the Canary Islands to strip Burns of his ownership claim. When Homer fakes an inspection crisis, a panicked Burns names him the new owner, and Homer immediately fires his old boss. As the new head of the plant, Homer finds himself consumed by work and increasingly absent from his family, causing tension at home. A ghostly nighttime visit from Burns forces Homer to confront how much he's neglected his loved ones, prompting him to quit. Enraged, Burns drugs Homer and tries to bury him alive in a cemetery crypt, but he's too feeble to finish the job before sunrise. Homer casually walks free, reclaims the plant one last time to hand it back symbolically, and ends the episode playing baseball with Bart, having repaired their relationship. Meanwhile, Homer and Bart team up with local Native Americans to destroy a beaver dam that had flooded their land, hoping to help them reclaim it for a casino. Lisa, jealous upon overhearing Luke mention a woman named Clara, misdirects her into the dangerous flooded woods, only to learn Clara is Luke's sister, prompting a rescue mission with Bart's help using the very beavers they'd angered. text: "Treehouse of Horror XIV" is an episode of Season 15 (production code EABF21), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing November 2, 2003. This Halloween special opens with Bart and Lisa in a Peanuts-themed parody that devolves into family violence before Kang and Kodos mock the Simpsons for airing the special in November. In 'Reaper Madness,' Homer accidentally kills the Grim Reaper trying to save Bart, causing everyone in Springfield to become unable to die, so Homer takes over as the new Reaper until he's ordered to kill Marge, leading to a tense standoff with God himself. In 'Frinkenstein,' Professor Frink revives his deceased father for a Nobel Prize ceremony, only for the reanimated corpse to go on a rampage stealing body parts and brains to make himself superior, forcing Frink Jr. to subdue him with a swift kick. Finally, in 'Stop the World, I Want to Goof Off,' Bart and Milhouse acquire a stopwatch that freezes time, which they use for pranks until it breaks, trapping them as the only moving people in a frozen world for fifteen years of crime and excess. When they finally repair the watch and frame Martin Prince to escape blame, Bart returns as a wealthy grown man, prompting Lisa to demand a turn with the device, which she uses to warp reality with bizarre transformations before everything resets to normal. Guest starring Oscar De La Hoya as himself, Jennifer Garner as herself, Dudley Herschbach as himself, Jerry Lewis as Jonathan Frink Sr.. Notable quotes: Moe: If I knew this would take so long I'd put out a TV. | Homer: Death! Death! We miss you so much! You were a busboy in the restaurant of life. | Homer: No way, forget it. I might occasionally kill out of anger, or to illustrate a point. But I am not a Grim Reaper! | Agnes Skinner: Lost your spine, huh? You just keep finding new ways to disappoint me. | Homer: Let the baby have her bottle. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 14): "Reaper Madness", "Frinkenstein", and "Stop the World, I Want to Goof Off".

title: My Mother the Carjacker (S15E02)
text: "My Mother the Carjacker" is an episode of Season 15 (production code EABF18), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Michael Price, originally airing November 9, 2003. After Marge wins a shirt from Kent Brockman's 'Oops Patrol' for spotting a funny headline, Homer becomes obsessed with earning one too and starts poring over old newspapers late at night. He believes a strange article about the 'World's Biggest Pizza' is a coded message meant for him, and it turns out to be from his long-lost fugitive mother, Mona Simpson, who has used newspaper stories to secretly contact him before. Mona reveals she's still wanted for sabotaging one of Mr. Burns' germ labs decades earlier, and she's returned because a childhood memento made her miss Homer. Their reunion is repeatedly interrupted by the law: Chief Wiggum's officers, a courtroom battle instigated by Mr. Burns, and finally the FBI, who arrest her for using fake names in theme park guestbooks. Determined not to lose her again, Homer and Bart hijack the prison bus transporting her to a federal facility, freeing the other inmates but sending the vehicle on a runaway chase that ends with it plunging off a cliff into a lake, seemingly killing Mona. After a chaotic funeral where the coffin goes missing, a grieving Homer searches the papers again and finds a hidden message reading 'IMOK,' revealing that Mona survived the crash and is alive and hiding once more. Guest starring Glenn Close as Mona Simpson. Notable quotes: Grampa: Mona, I'll always remember raspberry trolley cars, because my mind is shot. | Homer: I barely know my mother. And every time I see her, she's taken away again. And when a man doesn't have his mother, he winds up like me. | Mona: Pizza was the first food he choked on. | Homer: Candlepin bowling? That's a great idea. We'll play right after I break your grandmother out of prison. | Convict: I never want this trip to end. Because I'm getting executed when we stop.

title: The President Wore Pearls (S15E03)
text: "The President Wore Pearls" is an episode of Season 15 (production code EABF20), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Dana Gould, originally airing November 16, 2003. After a chaotic casino night fundraiser exposes Martin Prince's incompetence as class president, Springfield Elementary holds a new election. Lisa decides to run against the far more popular Nelson Muntz, and despite an awkward debate performance, she wins the crowd over with a heartfelt campaign song and ultimately wins the vote. As the new student body president, Lisa gets a dramatic makeover and enjoys the perks of the office, but Principal Skinner secretly manipulates her into unknowingly authorizing the elimination of gym, art, and music programs to save money. When the cuts are revealed, Lisa is devastated and blamed by her peers, prompting Homer to encourage her to fight back against the administration. Lisa confronts Skinner and organizes a student strike that grows into a citywide spectacle, drawing police, news crews, and even documentarian Michael Moore. To defuse the situation, the school transfers Lisa to a magnet school, where she briefly considers staying before Homer insists on bringing her home. In the end, the school restores the cut programs through creative and ethically dubious budget cuts, closing the episode on a satirical note about school funding priorities. Guest starring Michael Moore. Notable quotes: Marge: Bet... system... betting system! God is telling me to gamble! | Drederick Tatum: Welcome to Springfield Elementary Casino Night. My fee for this evening goes to victims of my criminal recidivism. So relax, have fun and, please God, don't piss me off. | Skinner: Yeah. The students will do anything she says. She's captured their imagination like a bright piece of construction paper. | Skinner: Any student caught striking will be severely disciplined. Unless all of you do it. Then I'm stymied. | Bart: Lisa is a nut. She has a rubber butt. Every time she turns around it goes "putt putt."

title: The Regina Monologues (S15E04)
text: "The Regina Monologues" is an episode of Season 15 (production code EABF22), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Swartzwelder, originally airing November 23, 2003. After Mr. Burns loses a $1000 bill that ends up in Bart's possession, Bart briefly turns his treehouse into a profitable museum before Burns reclaims the cash using a bruise on his chest as proof. Realizing the museum earnings could give Marge the vacation she's never truly enjoyed, the kids convince the family to use the money for a trip, and Grampa pushes for London so he can reunite with Edwina, a wartime sweetheart. In London, Bart and Lisa binge on rich British chocolate while Homer embarrasses the family by mistaking Tony Blair for Mr. Bean and cursing actor Ian McKellen with repeated 'Macbeth' jinxes. Disaster strikes when Homer, trapped on a roundabout, smashes through the gates of Buckingham Palace and crashes into the Queen's carriage, leading to a brutal beating from the guards. Put on trial, Homer's inept self-defense and insults toward the judge and Queen result in a death sentence, and he's imprisoned in the Tower of London awaiting execution. Using directions from Lisa, Homer escapes through a secret tunnel that unfortunately leads into the Queen's bedroom, triggering another guard chase. He is ultimately pardoned on the condition that the family smuggle Madonna out of England in a suitcase. As they prepare to leave, Grampa is reunited with Edwina, who introduces her daughter Abbey—a woman who bizarrely resembles Homer—prompting Grampa to flee while Homer finds her oddly attractive. Guest starring Tony Blair, Jane Leeves, Ian McKellen, Evan Marriott, J. K. Rowling. You have my word as a gentlemen and a lady. Now let's see, which rifle should I bring? | Homer: Wow, I can't believe we just met Mr. Bean!

title: The Fat and the Furriest (S15E05)
text: "The Fat and the Furriest" is an episode of Season 15 (production code EABF19), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing November 30, 2003. After buying Marge a duplicate Mother's Day gift, Homer purchases a 'Kitchen Carnival' machine and uses it to create an enormous, disgusting ball of deep-fried, caramel-coated cotton candy. When Marge demands he dispose of it, Homer heads to the dump and is confronted by a menacing grizzly bear, from which he cowers in terror until the bear wanders off. A video of his humiliation spreads around town, turning Homer into a laughingstock among his coworkers and even Bart's friends. Spurred by Grampa's taunts, Homer resolves to confront the bear again, building makeshift armor and enlisting hunter Grant Connor's help, then sneaking off into the woods with Bart, Lenny, and Carl. During the trip, the bear attacks Homer again and drags him to its den, where Homer discovers the animal's aggression stems from a painful prod stuck in its ear. After freeing the bear, the two form an unlikely friendship, bonding over shared habits like dumpster diving. Meanwhile, Marge and Lisa track Homer down with Grant's help, but when Homer tries to escort the now-friendly bear to a wildlife refuge, Grant, Cletus, and other hunters ambush them. Homer saves the bear by dressing it in his bulletproof armor, allowing it to safely reach the refuge, where it immediately gets into a scuffle with an elephant. Guest starring Charles Napier as Grant Connor. Notable quotes: Candy Ball: I think you should get rid of ''her''. ''[cocks shotgun]'' | Grant: Well, we all feel that way sometimes. ''[cocks shotgun]''

title: Today I Am a Clown (S15E06)
text: "Today I Am a Clown" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF01), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing December 7, 2003. After Maggie gets accidentally locked in the bathroom, the Simpsons end up adopting a litter of puppies when Santa's Little Helper impregnates Dr. Hibbert's poodle. While giving away the puppies, Krusty the Clown discovers he has no star on the Jewish Walk of Fame because he never had a bar mitzvah, since his father Rabbi Krustofsky withheld it fearing Krusty would mock the ceremony. Determined to earn his place, Krusty begins studying Judaism with his father, but this means he can't work on the Sabbath, so he hires Homer to host his show as a fill-in. Homer's low-key talk show, featuring Moe, Barney, Disco Stu, and Carl, becomes an unexpected hit, leading to Krusty's show being cancelled by Channel 6. When Lisa convinces Homer to use his newfound influence for good, his moralizing tanks his ratings and his show is cancelled too. Krusty pitches a lavish televised bar mitzvah to Fox, which becomes a massive ratings success but disappoints his father with its crass spectacle. Feeling guilty, Krusty insists on having a genuine, traditional bar mitzvah at the temple, achieving a heartfelt reconciliation with his father. Meanwhile, the Simpson family's own storyline ends on a comically bleak note when Homer strangles Bart and their car gets thrown away to be shredded. Guest starring Jackie Mason as Rabbi Hyman Krustofsky, Mr. T as himself. Notable quotes: Lisa: I tried the coat hanger again. I don't understand why we only try ideas once. | Krusty: I just found out I'm not Jewish! I got turned down by all those country clubs for nothing! | Homer: Who has more power? Miss America or Miss USA? | Lisa: I have a Jewish imaginary friend. Her name is Rachel Cohen and she just got into Brandeis. | Chief Wiggum: Simpson, I hate to bother you when you're eating. But you're always eating.

title: 'Tis the Fifteenth Season (S15E07)
text: "'Tis the Fifteenth Season" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF02), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Michael Price, originally airing December 14, 2003. As Christmas approaches at the power plant, a gift exchange goes awry when Homer gives Lenny only a pack of Certs while receiving a valuable Joe DiMaggio baseball card, which he unwittingly sells for cash to Comic Book Guy. Rather than using the windfall to buy a nice tree, Homer secretly spends it on an extravagant talking astrolabe for himself, leaving his family with cheap keychains and a tree that catches fire. When Marge discovers his selfishness, she freezes him out, forcing him to sleep on the couch. A televised Christmas special about a miserly character inspires Homer to reform, and he sets out to become the kindest man in Springfield, performing generous deeds that outshine even Ned Flanders. Ned, humiliated, retaliates by renting out his house to fund gifts for the whole town, reigniting a rivalry over who is more charitable. Taking Lisa's Buddhist-inspired advice about Christmas not being about material things too literally, Homer sneaks out at night and steals back all the presents he and Ned gave away. The townspeople wake up furious and nearly turn on Homer, but a mistaken 'star' in the sky—actually a flare from a stranded Hans Moleman—unites everyone in song, restoring holiday peace, while Snake makes off with Homer's prized astrolabe. title: Marge vs. Singles, Seniors, Childless Couples and Teens and Gays (S15E08)

text: "Marge vs. Singles, Seniors, Childless Couples and Teens and Gays" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF03), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing January 4, 2004. After a channel-surfing mishap, Maggie becomes obsessed with a children's entertainer named Roofi, and Marge insists his CD be played constantly, irritating the rest of the family. Marge takes Maggie to a packed Roofi concert at Cletus Spuckler's farm, but rain and overcrowding spark a chaotic baby riot dubbed the "Tot Offensive." Furious over the resulting damages and taxes, Springfield's childless and single residents, led by Lindsay Naegle, form a lobbying group called SSCCATAGAPP to strip the town of child-friendly services and policies. Outraged, Marge organizes a counter-movement, "Families Come First," to push Proposition 242 and protect children's interests, though her efforts falter until Mr. Burns unexpectedly lends his support. Homer's clumsy attempts to help the campaign, including a botched ad and undistributed bumper stickers, nearly derail things further. As election day approaches, Bart and Lisa devise a scheme using children's charm to sway voters at the polls. Their plan works, as swarms of adorable, hugging kids melt the resolve of Proposition 242's opponents. SSCCATAGAPP collapses, and Marge's pro-family initiative triumphs. Children are the future... today belongs to me! | Bart: Mom, that's Roofi. title: I, (Annoyed Grunt)-bot (S15E09)
text: "I, (Annoyed Grunt)-bot" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF04), directed by Lauren MacMullan and written by Dan Greaney, Allen Glazier, originally airing January 11, 2004. After bullies humiliate Bart's newly customized bike, Bart sabotages it to get a replacement, accidentally killing Snowball II in the process while Homer proves useless at fixing anything mechanical. Homer's attempt to build a robot for the Robot Rumble competition falls apart, so he decides to build a robot suit he can secretly operate from the inside, creating Chief Knocka-Homer to compete for Bart's sake. Meanwhile, Lisa struggles to move past Snowball II's death, adopting first Snowball III, who quickly drowns, then Coltrane, who leaps to his death after being startled by her saxophone playing. As Knocka-Homer wins fight after fight, Homer takes a beating inside the suit but keeps going to make Bart proud, all while hiding the truth from him. Lisa's search for a new pet ends when the Crazy Cat Lady gives her a cat identical to Snowball II, whom she renames Snowball II to simplify things. In the championship match against Killhammad Aieee, Homer is finally exposed when he pops out of the damaged robot, but the opposing robot's programming prevents it from harming a human, handing Knocka-Homer the win. Bart learns the truth about his father's sacrifice and is thrilled rather than upset, leading to a heartfelt bonding moment between father and son. I am the luckiest kid in the world. | Homer: There's nothing worse than the look on a boy's face when he says "Dad I don't think you can build a fully-functional robot."

title: Diatribe of a Mad Housewife (S15E10)
text: "Diatribe of a Mad Housewife" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF05), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Robin J. Stein, originally airing January 25, 2004. After a food-related car accident gets Homer fired from the Power Plant, he hides his unemployment from Marge and stumbles into a job as a car salesman at Boris' Car Loft, eventually quitting to buy an old ambulance and become a freelance ambulance driver. Meanwhile, Marge is inspired by romance novelist Esme Delacroix to try writing her own book, drawing on a whaling painting to create the story of Temperance Barrows and her rough husband Captain Mordecai. As Homer's boorish behavior at home annoys her, Marge unconsciously models Mordecai after him, and creates a dashing love interest, Cyrus Manley, inspired by Ned Flanders. Homer lies about reading the finished manuscript, telling Marge he loved it, which allows her to get it endorsed by celebrities and published to citywide acclaim. When the whole town recognizes Homer as the buffoonish Mordecai and mocks him, he finally has the book read aloud to him and confronts Marge, furious over the implied romance with Ned. Homer storms off to confront Flanders, chasing him to a cliff in a scene mirroring the novel's dramatic climax, only to realize he only wants advice on being a better husband. The episode ends with Homer and Marge reconciling and deciding to collaborate on a new book together about the JFK assassination.

title: Margical History Tour (S15E11)
text: "Margical History Tour" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF06), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing February 8, 2004. When the Springfield kids find the public library nearly empty of useful books, Marge steps in to help them with their history reports by acting out stories herself. In the first tale, Homer plays a lustful King Henry VIII who divorces and executes a string of wives, including Marge's own alter ego Margarine of Aragon, in his obsessive quest for a son, only to be smothered by her decades later on his deathbed. Next, Marge tells Lisa about Sacagawea, who guides the bickering explorers Lewis and Clark through the wilderness despite their ingratitude, ultimately saving the expedition and earning their respect after a near-fatal encounter with a mountain lion. Finally, Marge spins a tale for Bart about a young, rebellious Mozart who overshadows and torments his jealous sister Sally Salieri, leading her to sabotage his opera and hasten his tragic, impoverished death. Salieri's triumph is short-lived, as she is quickly replaced in the Emperor's favor by Beethoven, driving her to madness. The episode closes with Homer musing about the actor who played Mozart also appearing in Animal House, prompting a parody send-up of that film's ending captions applied to the historical figures just depicted. title: Milhouse Doesn't Live Here Anymore (S15E12)
text: "Milhouse Doesn't Live Here Anymore" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF07), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Julie Chambers, David Chambers, originally airing February 15, 2004. Bart is devastated when his best friend Milhouse moves to Capital City with his mother after she separates from Kirk. Struggling to find a replacement friend, Bart visits Milhouse only to discover he's dyed his hair, changed his style, and adopted a rebellious new attitude, even using Bart as a prop to look cool in front of his new friends. Back home, a lonely Bart starts spending time with Lisa, and the two unexpectedly bond over car washing, bike rides, and exploring an old Indian burial mound, becoming close siblings. When a court order forces Milhouse back to Springfield, Lisa is hurt to learn Bart revealed their secret burial mound to Milhouse, feeling used as a temporary substitute. Bart reassures her with a heartfelt gift of coupons promising to be a better brother, restoring their bond. Meanwhile, Homer forgets his wedding anniversary and, desperate for gift money, begins panhandling on the street, eventually earning enough to buy Marge diamond earrings. His continued begging embarrasses Marge when other homeless people bring her to witness it, though she can't bring herself to reject the earrings despite her anger. title: Smart and Smarter (S15E13)
text: "Smart and Smarter" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF09), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Carolyn Omine, originally airing February 22, 2004. The Simpsons tour an exclusive pre-nursery school run by the imperious Henry, hoping to enroll Maggie after seeing the Flanders and Apu's octuplets attend. Maggie initially seems unable to qualify since she can't talk, but Lisa unwittingly feeds her the right answers during testing, revealing an off-the-charts IQ of 167 that surpasses Lisa's own 159. Devastated at losing her identity as the family's genius, Lisa cycles through a series of new personas—goth, cheerleader, rapper, athlete, cowgirl, and comedian—none of which stick. Bitter and jealous, she starts secretly teaching baby Maggie incorrect facts, prompting Homer and Marge to confront her about undermining her sister. Ashamed, Lisa runs away and hides out in the Natural History Museum until police find her inside a walk-through model of the human body, where the rest of the family is touring. Maggie panics and hits buttons that swallow Homer, Marge, and Bart into the exhibit's digestive system, but with a visual cue from Lisa, she manages to hit the evacuate button and save them. Afterward, Henry exposes video proof that Lisa had been silently signaling Maggie's answers during the test, deflating the 'baby genius' narrative and enraging Homer enough to attack Henry. In the end, Maggie contentedly plays with Lisa's saxophone, and the sisters reach a quiet understanding as Lisa reclaims her rightful place as the sax player of the family. Guest starring Simon Cowell. Notable quotes: Lisa: I can't believe I'm jealous of a baby! | Nelson: Well... you're gay! | Lisa: People who call other people gay are often covering up their own latent homosexuality. | Henry: Do you nurse with that mouth? | Homer: We've all learned something today. Never be something you're not, namely food.

title: The Ziff Who Came to Dinner (S15E14)

text: "The Ziff Who Came to Dinner" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF08), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Deb Lacusta, Dan Castellaneta, originally airing March 14, 2004. Homer takes Bart, Lisa, and the Flanders boys to a scary movie after finding all the kid-friendly films sold out, leaving the children thoroughly spooked once they get home. When strange noises come from the attic that night, Homer and Marge investigate and discover Marge's old prom date Artie Ziff secretly living there after his internet company, ZiffCorp, collapsed. Artie convinces the reluctant Simpsons to let him stay while he gets back on his feet, but he conceals the fact that he is being pursued by the SEC for defrauding his stockholders. During a poker game, Homer unwittingly wins a controlling stake in ZiffCorp's stock, which makes him the target of the SEC investigation once agents arrive to arrest Artie. Artie manipulates the situation so that Homer takes the fall, and Homer is put on trial, humiliates himself in court, and is sentenced to ten years in prison. Furious, Marge throws Artie out of the house, and he ends up at Moe's Tavern, where he reconnects with Selma, who once had a crush on him. After a night together, Artie has a change of heart and decides to turn himself in and hand over evidence to clear Homer's name. Homer is released from prison, and Artie is incarcerated in his place, ending up as an oddly cheerful nuisance to his fellow inmates. Guest starring Jon Lovitz as Artie Ziff, Jay Sherman, Professor Lombardo, Aristotle Amadopolis and Llewellyn Sinclair. Notable quotes: Homer: Relax, stupid. Everything you see is make-believe. Although it is based on a true story. | Homer: Well, what do you know? It's unkillable! | Lenny: Classic Hollywood story. The director saw my photo in a medical book. | Artie: Doesn't your father ever read to you? | Lisa: He tried once, but he got confused and thought the book was real. He's still searching for that chocolate factory. It consumes him.

Homer: Well, what do you know? It's unkillable!
Lenny: Classic Hollywood story. The director saw my photo in a medical book.
Artie: Doesn't your father ever read to you?
Lisa: He tried once, but he got confused and thought the book was real. He's still searching for that chocolate factory. It consumes him.

title: Co-Dependent's Day (S15E15)
text: "Co-Dependent's Day" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF10), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Matt Warburton, originally airing March 21, 2004. The Simpsons attend the premiere of a new Cosmic Wars film, but the movie turns out to be a disappointing bore, prompting Bart and Lisa to write an angry complaint letter to creator Randall Curtis. When Curtis brushes them off, the family travels to Northern California so the kids can confront him at his ranch, while Homer and Marge visit a nearby winery. There, Homer and Marge discover a shared love of drinking together, which sparks a fun new phase in their marriage but soon spirals into frequent boozy outings, including a trip to Oktoberfest. After getting extremely drunk and crashing the car on the way home, Homer switches seats with Marge to make it look like she was driving, letting her take the blame and legal consequences. Marge becomes a pariah in town and checks into a rehab facility called Quitters, but Lisa figures out that Homer was actually responsible and confronts him. Homer confesses to Marge, who reacts with fury and briefly relapses with fellow rehab patients before realizing she'd rather spend her time with Homer than drinking. She checks herself out despite counselor Kyle's warnings that Homer is the real alcoholic, and Homer promises to cut back on drinking to save their relationship. Meanwhile, the Bart and Lisa subplot wraps up with them convincing Curtis to return his films to their original creative roots. Guest starring Brave Combo as themselves. Notable quotes: Comic Book Guy: Worst. Cosmic Wars. Ever. | Otto: Aw, man! I waited three weeks at the wrong ticket window! | Homer: Ah, Summer in Tuscany. | Marge: Stop it, Seinfeld. | Homer: Heh-heh. Come on. We'll have a blast. Kids, while we're out, the TV's in charge. Go to bed when it says.

Otto: Aw, man! I waited three weeks at the wrong ticket window!
Homer: Ah, Summer in Tuscany.
Marge: Stop it, Seinfeld.

title: The Wandering Juvie (S15E16)
text: "The Wandering Juvie" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF11), directed by Lauren MacMullan and written by John Frink, Don Payne, originally airing March 28, 2004. Bart pulls an elaborate prank by registering himself and a fake bride, 'Lotta Cooties,' at Costington's department store, inviting the town to a nonexistent wedding so he can pocket unused gifts for store credit. Chief Wiggum arrests him before he can cash in, and Judge Constance Harm sentences Bart to six months at the Springfield Juvenile Correctional Facility. Inside, Bart struggles to fit in and is targeted by tough inmate Gina Vendetti, who threatens him before eventually bonding with him. Homer takes a job as a prison guard to protect his son, but his protection is short-lived once his shift ends. When a dance is held at the facility, Gina partners with Bart and later engineers a daring escape, dragging him along as they flee together. On the run, Gina opens up about her troubled past and lack of a real family, leading to an emotional clash and a fierce fight with Bart after he thoughtlessly reminds her of her loneliness. The police catch up and arrest them both, but Gina takes full responsibility for the escape, freeing Bart from extra punishment while she returns to juvie alone. In a heartwarming coda, Gina finds the Simpson family visiting Bart in her old cell for taco night and happily joins them, while the lonely Warden is left to his own sad evening plans. Guest starring Sarah Michelle Gellar as Gina Vendetti, Jane Kaczmarek as Constance Harm, Charles Napier as the Warden. Notable quotes: Bart: Yeah, I'm gonna scam this town out of so many presents. And, what I don't use, I'm gonna return... for store credit. | Chief Wiggum: Um. What does it say on my badge? Cash bribes only. Let's go. | Homer: I believe that children are the future... unless we stop them now. | Ralph Wiggum: Your eyes need diapers. | Homer: It's not all your fault. All these years, I watched you turn our son into a time bomb, and yet I did nothing. So, in a way, I too, am victim... of you.
quotes: Bart: Yeah, I'm gonna scam this town out of so many presents. And, what I don't use, I'm gonna return... for store credit.
Chief Wiggum: Um. What does it say on my badge? Cash bribes only. Let's go.
Homer: I believe that children are the future... unless we stop them now.
Ralph Wiggum: Your eyes need diapers.
Homer: It's not all your fault. All these years, I watched you turn our son into a time bomb, and yet I did nothing. So, in a way, I too, am victim... of you.

title: My Big Fat Geek Wedding (S15E17)
text: "My Big Fat Geek Wedding" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF12), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Kevin Curran, originally airing April 18, 2004. Principal Skinner and Edna Krabappel are set to marry, but after separate bachelor parties, Skinner confesses to Homer that he has cold feet. Edna discovers his hesitation at the ceremony and flees, calling off the wedding entirely. Homer and Marge try to reconcile the couple, even as their own marriage hits a rocky patch. Meanwhile, Edna returns a wedding gift to Comic Book Guy and unexpectedly finds him charming, sparking a new romance. Homer arranges for Skinner to win Edna back with a serenade performed by Bart, Milhouse, and Martin, but the plan collapses once he learns of her new relationship. The family confronts Comic Book Guy at the Bi-Mon-Sci-Fi-Con, where he proposes to Edna after being inspired by a chance encounter with Matt Groening. Skinner, comically costumed as Catwoman, battles Comic Book Guy for Edna's affection, but she stops the fight and rejects both suitors, choosing independence instead. The episode closes with Homer and Marge renewing their vows in a whimsical Klingon-style ceremony. Guest starring Matt Groening as himself. Notable quotes: Milhouse: Mr. Groening, can you please autograph my Bender doll? | Homer: And now Padre, if you would do the honers. | Marge: I do. | Homer: Marge, you just agreed to raise the kids Klingon. | Marge: D'oh!
quotes: Milhouse: Mr. Groening, can you please autograph my Bender doll?
Homer: And now Padre, if you would do the honers.
Marge: I do.
Homer: Marge, you just agreed to raise the kids Klingon.
Marge: D'oh!

title: Catch 'Em If You Can (S15E18)
text: "Catch 'Em If You Can" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF14), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing April 25, 2004. After a chaotic day of sibling fighting and a disastrous family movie night, Marge announces the family will travel to Dayton, Ohio for Uncle Tyrone's birthday, but Bart and Lisa opt to stay home with Grampa instead. At the airport, Homer and Marge impulsively ditch the family trip and fly to Miami for a secret second honeymoon. Back home, the kids grow suspicious after hearing about a tornado near their supposed hotel and then getting a call from Marge, and Bart traces the call to discover their parents are actually in Miami. Bart and Lisa convince Grampa to take them there, and the couple is forced to flee their own children across the country, hopping from Atlantic City to other cities in a cross-country chase, using disguises and tricks to escape, all while Ned Flanders' credit card is secretly footing the bill for their travel. The chase culminates in Niagara Falls, where the kids finally corner their parents, leading to an uneasy truce. Later, Bart and Lisa, feeling guilty for ruining their parents' romantic getaway, try to give them privacy at an amusement park, but a mix-up sends Homer and Marge fleeing into a bouncy castle that breaks free and plunges over the falls. Rescued by feuding Canadian and American rescue teams, Homer and Marge are found alive and unabashedly continue their romantic moment beneath the falls, resolving the story on a happy, if ridiculous, note. Notable quotes: Marge: That boy failed show and tell, but he's on our ass like Sherlock Holmes! | Homer: Your mother and I are trying to lose each other in this movie, so shut the hell up! | U.S. Customs Officer: Beat it, you puck-slapping maple suckers. | Homer: As the Bible says, to hell with that. | Grampa: I'm only rotting on the right side!
quotes: Marge: That boy failed show and tell, but he's on our ass like Sherlock Holmes!
Homer: Your mother and I are trying to lose each other in this movie, so shut the hell up!
U.S. Customs Officer: Beat it, you puck-slapping maple suckers.
Homer: As the Bible says, to hell with that.
Grampa: I'm only rotting on the right side!

title: Simple Simpson (S15E19)
text: "Simple Simpson" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF15), directed by Jim Reardon and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing May 2, 2004. Homer becomes obsessed with a bacon-themed contest and ends up winning only a minor prize as a fair judge. When the Rich Texan ruins Lisa's entry in the place-setting competition and makes her cry, Homer disguises himself in a pie-tin mask to avoid being arrested for assault and pies the bully in the face, accidentally becoming a masked vigilante known as Pie Man. Pie Man becomes a local celebrity after humiliating the Comic Book Guy in front of visiting Star Trek actress Nichelle Nichols, but his crusade against a hospital closing leads to a police shootout where he is wounded and barely escapes. Lisa quickly deduces her father's secret identity, and Homer promises her he'll retire the costume, but he can't resist another appearance when Mr. Burns mistreats the plant workers. This time Burns catches and unmasks Pie Man, blackmailing Homer into becoming his personal enforcer, forcing him to pie innocent targets on command. When Burns orders Homer to humiliate the visiting Dalai Lama, Homer's conscience and Lisa's Buddhist beliefs stop him from going through with it, and he publicly reveals his identity—only for no one to believe the bumbling Homer could really be Pie Man. Freed from Burns' control, Homer embraces his alter ego permanently, recruiting Bart as his sidekick 'Cupcake Kid,' though their heroics are quickly reduced to mundane chores when Marge puts them to work cleaning the gutters. Guest starring Nichelle Nichols. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: Simpson! You'll rue the day you took a pie tin, made two holes for eyes and tied a rubber band around the back! | Homer: It's not a rubber band, it's a scrunchy. | Apu: Mr. Simpson, if you really want to kill yourself, I also sell handguns! | Homer: Wherever injustice shows its ugly face, I will be there, for I am the Pie Man. | Homer: Please forgive me, talking llama
quotes: Mr. Burns: Simpson! You'll rue the day you took a pie tin, made two holes for eyes and tied a rubber band around the back!
Homer: It's not a rubber band, it's a scrunchy.
Apu: Mr. Simpson, if you really want to kill yourself, I also sell handguns!
Homer: Wherever injustice shows its ugly face, I will be there, for I am the Pie Man.
Homer: Please forgive me, talking llama

title: The Way We Weren't (S15E20)
text: "The Way We Weren't" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF13), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing May 9, 2004. Bart tricks Milhouse and Ralph into yard work, then a game of spin the bottle in the treehouse ends with Milhouse accidentally kissing Homer, leading to a family court session presided over by Lisa. During testimony, Homer reveals that Marge wasn't actually his first kiss, and recounts being sent to a camp for underprivileged boys where he worked at a rich girls' camp across the lake. He returns a lost retainer to an unseen girl and arranges a nighttime meeting, but fails to show up the next night after a series of misadventures involving a fat camp run by Quimby, Wiggum, and Comic Book Guy. Marge then shares her side, revealing she was the girl at the camp who waited for him, believing she'd been stood up, which left her wary of boys for years. The two eventually realize they were each other's mystery first kiss all those years ago, and Marge is initially skeptical that their love can last. Homer proves his devotion by producing his half of a heart-shaped stone he kept for decades, and Marge reveals she kept her half too, leading to a heartfelt reconciliation and kiss. Notable quotes: Homer: I'm Elvis! Elvis Jagger. Elvis Jagger Abdul-Jabbar. | Lisa: Dad, how could you? | Bart: Men are dogs, the worse we treat you, the more you want us. | Bart: I've kissed 3 girls. | Marge: You won't be kissing anyone for a while.

Lisa: Dad, how could you?
Bart: Men are dogs, the worse we treat you, the more you want us.
Bart: I've kissed 3 girls.
Marge: You won't be kissing anyone for a while.

title: Bart-Mangled Banner (S15E21)
text: "Bart-Mangled Banner" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF17), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by John Frink, originally airing May 16, 2004. After a chaotic vaccination visit involving Barney and Moe impersonating Dr. Hibbert, Bart ends up temporarily deafened by his shot. At a school donkey basketball game, Bart's prank with a carrot backfires when the donkey rips off his shorts during the National Anthem, exposing him just as a photo is snapped with the flag behind him, making it look like he deliberately mooned it. The Springfield Shopper twists the story, turning the whole town against the Simpsons. When the family appears on the talk show Head Butt to defend themselves, a loaded question from host Nash Castor provokes Marge into saying she hates America too, which causes the entire country to turn on Springfield. Mayor Quimby rebrands the town 'Libertyville' and forces exaggerated patriotic displays, but after Lisa criticizes this forced patriotism in church, the family is arrested under the 'Government Knows Best Act.' They're sent to the Ronald Reagan Reeducation Center, actually Alcatraz, where they encounter other blacklisted celebrities, and stage an escape by swimming away, only to be rescued by a French ship and taken to France. Though they adapt well to French life, they miss their belongings back home and ultimately return to the U.S. disguised as old-fashioned immigrants. Notable quotes: Drederick Tatum: Black on black violence must end! That was for Dr. King. | Bart: Don't feel bad doc. I won't even let my mom cut my toenails. | Dr. Hibbert: I guess you just too smart for me Bart. | Moe: Okay well I really enjoyed being you Dr. Hibbert. Oh by the way you're not welcome at the library no more. Sorry.
quotes: Drederick Tatum: Black on black violence must end! That was for Dr. King.
Bart: Don't feel bad doc. I won't even let my mom cut my toenails.
Dr. Hibbert: I guess you just too smart for me Bart.
Moe: Okay well I really enjoyed being you Dr. Hibbert. Oh by the way you're not welcome at the library no more. Sorry.

title: Fraudcast News (S15E22)
text: "Fraudcast News" is an episode of Season 15 (production code FABF18), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Don Payne, originally airing May 23, 2004. Springfield unveils its newest national landmark, Geezer Rock, but the dedication ceremony is ruined when Homer accidentally destroys it while trying to remove a small tree from its 'eye.' Mr. Burns is caught in the resulting landslide and, though he survives, is enraged to discover that no one in town even noticed he was missing. Determined to fix his public image, Burns buys up every media outlet in Springfield, using them to spread flattering propaganda about himself, including taking over Itchy & Scratchy. Lisa, disturbed by this media monopoly, starts her own independent newspaper, The Red Dress Press, recruiting Bart, Milhouse, and Nelson to help her report the truth. Burns tries bribing Lisa with ponies and then retaliates by cutting off the Simpsons' electricity, but Lisa presses on using an old mimeograph machine. Burns finally breaks Lisa's spirit by manipulating a drugged Homer into revealing embarrassing personal details, which are published to humiliate her, causing Lisa to shut down her paper in defeat. However, Homer starts his own newspaper in her honor, and other townspeople follow suit, proving that ordinary citizens can still resist corporate media control. Frustrated that he still can't silence all criticism despite owning everything, Burns concedes that total media domination is impossible for anyone but Rupert Murdoch, and copes by going on a shopping spree with Smithers. Notable quotes: Homer: All my daughter ever did was tell people to think for themselves. I may be her father, but when I grow up, I wanna be just like her, except still a dude. | Burns: My god, are you always on!? | Burns: Well, I guess it's impossible for one man to control all the media. Unless, of course, you're Rupert Murdoch. | Nelson: I dunno, making nerds cry? | Bart: What's the big deal about a rock that looks like a dude? I've got a dad that looks like a monkey!
quotes: Homer: All my daughter ever did was tell people to think for themselves. I may be her father, but when I grow up, I wanna be just like her, except still a dude.
Burns: My god, are you always on!?
Burns: Well, I guess it's impossible for one man to control all the media. Unless, of course, you're Rupert Murdoch.
Nelson: I dunno, making nerds cry?
Bart: What's the big deal about a rock that looks like a dude? I've got a dad that looks like a monkey!

title: Crook and Ladder (S18E19)
text: "Crook and Ladder" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF13), directed by Lance Kramer and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing May 6, 2007. After following bad advice from a parenting magazine secretly published by Larry Flynt, Marge takes away Maggie's pacifier, sparking a destructive tantrum that is only calmed when Santa's Little Helper offers her a squeaky toy. Meanwhile, Homer starts taking a sleep aid called Nappien to cope with stress, and Bart and Milhouse exploit his zombie-like state by having him drive them around at night. Homer wakes mid-drive and crashes into the Springfield Fire Department, badly injuring the firefighters and sending them to the hospital. With no professionals available, Homer, Apu, Moe, and Principal Skinner form a volunteer fire department and are showered with gifts and gratitude for their rescues. When they save Mr. Burns' mansion and he refuses to reward them, the volunteers grow bitter and begin stealing valuables from the people they rescue, blaming the losses on fire damage. Marge and the kids discover Homer's thefts and shame him with sorrowful looks wherever he goes until he can't bear it anymore. Homer convinces the other volunteers to stop stealing after helping save Moe and Apu from a dangerous situation, and the group ultimately donates all their stolen loot to the homeless. Notable quotes: Homer: I have three kids and no money. Why can't I have no kids and three money? | Bart: Why am I sleeping when right next door is every boy's dream; a fat, suggestible zombie dad. | Man in burning building: Not as bad as knowing that somewhere, gays are marrying each other. That's the real emergency, Kent. | Moe Szyslak: Lousy civilians... I wish I could burn them all! | Homer: Hey, it's the least they can do after we saved them from being melty-faced weirdos.
quotes: Homer: I have three kids and no money. Why can't I have no kids and three money?
Bart: Why am I sleeping when right next door is every boy's dream; a fat, suggestible zombie dad.
Man in burning building: Not as bad as knowing that somewhere, gays are marrying each other. That's the real emergency, Kent.
Moe Szyslak: Lousy civilians... I wish I could burn them all!
Homer: Hey, it's the least they can do after we saved them from being melty-faced weirdos.

title: Future-Drama (S16E15)
text: "Future-Drama" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF12), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Matt Selman, originally airing April 17, 2005. Bart and Lisa, bickering over childish insults, tumble into Professor Frink's basement, where he uses his 'astrology' machine to show them a vision of their lives eight years in the future, on the eve of their high school graduation. In this future, Lisa is graduating early and headed to Yale, reluctantly dating a buff, emotional Milhouse, while Bart is smitten with a girl named Jenda who rejects his marriage proposal because he lacks prospects. Meanwhile, Homer and Marge have separated after Homer sank the family's savings into an underwater house, and Homer takes Bart out on the town in a failed attempt to find companionship. Bart takes a job at the Kwik-E-Mart and heroically saves Mr. Burns from Snake, earning a Yale scholarship originally meant for Lisa, which he accepts hoping to win back Jenda. This betrayal enrages Lisa, and while Homer publicly scuffles with Krusty (Marge's new boyfriend), Bart's plan seems to work as Jenda takes him back. Guilt-stricken after seeing a bleak vision of Lisa's future married to Milhouse, Bart gives up the scholarship to save his sister, causing Jenda to dump him for good. Back in the present, Frink assures a heartbroken Bart he'll eventually find true love just moments before his own death, while Homer's beating from Krusty ironically helps him win Marge's heart back. Guest starring John DiMaggio as Bender, Amy Poehler as Jenda. Notable quotes: Moleman: Nobody's gay for Moleman. | Skinner: It's what turned Superintendent Chalmers into a vegetable. | Moe: You moron! Oh, why did I think I ever needed a clone? | Homer: Come on, boy! We're hitting the town! | Bender: Alright! You guys are my new best friends!
quotes: Moleman: Nobody's gay for Moleman.
Skinner: It's what turned Superintendent Chalmers into a vegetable.
Moe: You moron! Oh, why did I think I ever needed a clone?
Homer: Come on, boy! We're hitting the town!
Bender: Alright! You guys are my new best friends!

title: Springfield Up (S18E13)
text: "Springfield Up" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF07), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by Matt Warburton, originally airing February 18, 2007. Documentary filmmaker Declan Desmond returns to Springfield to continue his decades-long project chronicling local children every eight years as they grow up. His subjects include Chief Wiggum, whose lifelong obsession with police work leads him to a corrupt but comfortable position as chief, and Professor Frink, whose attempt to fix his own past with a time machine ends in comic disaster. Eleanor Abernathy's rise from brilliant dual-degree professional to the deranged Crazy Cat Lady provides another darkly comic thread, while Marge's abandoned dreams of photography reveal quiet disappointment beneath her cheerful exterior. The main focus falls on Homer, embarrassed by his lack of accomplishments, who fools Declan into believing he's become a wealthy inventor living in a mansion, when in reality the mansion belongs to a vacationing Mr. Burns. When Burns unexpectedly returns and exposes the ruse, Declan feels betrayed and Marge angrily defends Homer's dignity, banning Declan from their home. Realizing he's grown fond of Homer despite the deception, Declan makes amends by interviewing Springfield residents about their genuine affection for Homer, editing together a heartfelt tribute that restores Homer's faith in his life. The episode ends on a lighthearted note as Homer and Declan bond over a spontaneous musical performance. Guest starring Eric Idle as Declan Desmond. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: And here we are in now-times. As you can see, I have gotten everything I've ever wanted. | Homer: Why do you sound so shocked? This is our fifth take. | Homer: I don't know. You can put horseradish on your dead mother for all I care. | Marge: Oh yes. I'm so proud, I feel my chest might burst. Can you edit that? I don't wanna say "chest" in a movie. | 8-Year-Old Homer: I will! I will be rich! I'll own a football team and a basketball team and I'll make them play baseball!
quotes: Chief Wiggum: And here we are in now-times. As you can see, I have gotten everything I've ever wanted.
Homer: Why do you sound so shocked? This is our fifth take.
Homer: I don't know. You can put horseradish on your dead mother for all I care.
Marge: Oh yes. I'm so proud, I feel my chest might burst. Can you edit that? I don't wanna say "chest" in a movie.
8-Year-Old Homer: I will! I will be rich! I'll own a football team and a basketball team and I'll make them play baseball!

title: Marge Gamer (S18E17)
text: "Marge Gamer" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF10), directed by Bob Anderson and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing April 22, 2007. After being embarrassed at a PTA meeting for not having an email address, Marge buys a computer and quickly becomes engrossed in an online fantasy game called Earthland Realms, where she discovers most of Springfield's residents playing as various fantasy characters. Her fascination turns to alarm when she realizes that the game's most feared and violent character, the Shadow Knight, is actually her son Bart, and she begins trying to mother him within the game itself, embarrassing him in front of his in-game allies. Meanwhile, Homer takes up refereeing at Lisa's soccer games, and after initially struggling, he studies the rules to improve, only to end up penalizing Lisa harshly after a player named Ronaldo accuses her of "flopping," causing a rift between father and daughter. Bart, furious at his mother's meddling and redecorating of his in-game lair, lashes out and accidentally kills her character, but later revives her out of guilt. Believing Elf Marge to be an easy target, the other players ambush and gruesomely kill the Shadow Knight, celebrating with a grotesque victory dance. Touched by her son's earlier act of contrition, Marge takes up the mantle of the new Shadow Knight and sets out to avenge Bart by hunting down and defeating everyone involved in his character's death. Meanwhile, Homer and Lisa reconcile after he shows her a documentary proving that soccer flopping is real, helping her see that Homer's call was justified. Guest starring Ronaldo. Notable quotes: Marge: And all this time I thought Googling yourself meant the other thing. | Homer: Oh, Marge, you gotta get on the Net. It's got all the best conspiracy theories. Did you know that Hezbollah owns Little Dolly Snack Cakes? This stuff will rock your world. | Shadow Knight: Mom, what are you doing in my game? How would you like it if I suddenly started going shopping with you? | Troll Moe: What? No, my character's supposed to look like me. Why does everyone keep thinking I'm a troll? | Cobra King: The prison guards think I'm getting my online law degree. Ha, ha!

Homer: Oh, Marge, you gotta get on the Net. It's got all the best conspiracy theories. Did you know that Hezbollah owns Little Dolly Snack Cakes? This stuff will rock your world.
Shadow Knight: Mom, what are you doing in my game? How would you like it if I suddenly started going shopping with you?
Troll Moe: What? No, my character's supposed to look like me. Why does everyone keep thinking I'm a troll?

title: Jazzy and the Pussycats (S18E02)
text: "Jazzy and the Pussycats" is an episode of Season 18 (production code HABF18), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Daniel Chun, originally airing September 17, 2006. After a chaotic paddle-ball incident at the funeral of Homer's late Vegas wife Amber, Bart is sent to a psychiatrist who recommends drumming as an outlet, and Bart quickly proves to be a natural talent. His nonstop practicing annoys Homer and Marge, so Lisa offers to channel his energy by bringing him to a jazz brunch, only to watch him effortlessly outshine her and her quintet, earning an invitation to join a famous jazz group. As Bart becomes a local celebrity, Lisa grows resentful and, to cope, is encouraged by Marge to adopt a puppy from the shelter. She initially picks the cutest dog over a sicker one, but after being haunted by the guilt-tripping spirit of the rejected dog, she returns and ends up adopting every sick animal there, plus stray circus animals she meets along the way, stashing them all in the attic. Bart discovers her menagerie while jamming with his jazz friends in the same attic, and in the chaos a tiger bites his arm, severely damaging his nerves and ending his drumming career. To pay for the surgery he needs, Bart organizes a benefit concert with his musician friends, while Lisa desperately searches for homes for her animals before they're taken to the pound. After the concert proves a huge success, Bart has a change of heart and uses the proceeds to build a permanent shelter for all of Lisa's rescued animals, resolving both siblings' conflicts. Guest starring Jack White as himself, Meg White as herself. Notable quotes: Meg White: Let's kick his ass! | Homer: I love you so much. Damn you! | Lisa: It's jazz! Jazz! You don't even know the name of the thing you're stealing from me! | Dog Spirit: You suuuck, You suuuck! | Bart: My arm! It hurts where the tiger's biting it!
quotes: Meg White: Let's kick his ass!
Homer: I love you so much. Damn you!
Lisa: It's jazz! Jazz! You don't even know the name of the thing you're stealing from me!
Dog Spirit: You suuuck, You suuuck!
Bart: My arm! It hurts where the tiger's biting it!

title: Treehouse of Horror XV (S16E01)

text: "Treehouse of Horror XV" is an episode of Season 16 (production code FABF23), directed by David Silverman and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing November 7, 2004. This Halloween special opens with a twisted 'Keepin' It Kodos' segment where the Simpsons are served as an alien family dinner. In 'The Ned Zone', a bowling ball accident gives Ned Flanders the psychic ability to foresee people's deaths, and he is horrified to learn he is destined to shoot Homer. Despite Ned's attempts to avoid this fate by fleeing town and destroying a gun, a bizarre chain of accidents leads to Homer being shot and then accidentally blowing up the power plant with his tongue, sending both men to heaven. In 'Four Beheadings and a Funeral', a Victorian-era Eliza Simpson and her sidekick Dr. Bartley investigate the Mutton Chop Murderer terrorizing London, following a trail of clues through the Emporium of Exotica and an opium den before unmasking Inspector Wiggum himself as the killer. Finally, in 'In the Belly of the Boss', Maggie is accidentally shrunk and swallowed by Mr. Burns, prompting the rest of the Simpson family to shrink down and journey through his body to rescue her. After a chaotic trip through Burns' bloodstream and heart, they save Maggie but must leave Homer behind as he grows too large, resulting in a comedic finale where the whole cast gathers for a musical dinner at the Gilded Truffle. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 15): "The Ned Zone", "Four Beheadings and a Funeral", and "In the Belly of the Boss".

title: The Seemingly Never-Ending Story (S17E13)
text: "The Seemingly Never-Ending Story" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF06), directed by Raymond S. Persi and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, originally airing March 12, 2006. Trapped with his family in a hidden cavern after wrecking a fragile stalactite, Homer waits out the delay while Lisa spins a rambling tale to pass the time. Her story leads into Mr. Burns recounting how he lost everything to The Rich Texan in a bizarre scavenger hunt and was forced to take a job at Moe's Tavern. That story unfolds into Moe's own tragic romance with Edna Krabappel, which he sabotaged by stealing Snake's Mayan coins to fund an escape from Springfield, only for Edna to change her mind after meeting a troubled Bart. Nested within is Edna's account of resolving to stay and help Bart succeed, plus a brief detour into a vengeful goat's simple tale about returning Lisa's lost necklace. Back in the present, Homer reveals his own hidden motive for the cave trip: he'd seen The Rich Texan stash gold there and hoped to dig it up. When the Texan, Burns, Snake, and Moe all converge on the treasure, a tense standoff erupts until Marge threatens to hurl the gold into a bottomless pit, shaming everyone into abandoning their greed. Finally, the entire saga is revealed to be Bart's own invented excuse to Principal Skinner for skipping his test prep, though its final twist—Moe and Edna reuniting with a kiss—suggests some of it may be true. Guest starring Maurice LaMarche as Commander McBragg. title: The Girl Who Slept Too Little (S17E02)
