text: "The Girl Who Slept Too Little" is an episode of Season 17 (production code GABF16), directed by Raymond S. Persi and written by John Frink, originally airing September 18, 2005. After noisy construction on Evergreen Terrace sparks a neighborhood protest, Mayor Quimby relocates the project by swapping it with the Springfield Cemetery, which ends up right behind the Simpsons' house and in clear view of Lisa's bedroom. Terrified by the graveyard and haunted by nightmares, Lisa starts crawling into Homer and Marge's bed every night, straining the household routine. She strikes a deal to return to her own room once the family visits the new Springfield Stamp Museum, but her fear proves too strong and she breaks the promise, leading Marge and Homer to spend a night in her room themselves to test how scary it really is. Realizing the problem may stem from Lisa never being properly nurtured as a baby, they seek help at a shady psychiatric row, but Lisa decides instead to confront her fears head-on by venturing into the cemetery at night with Bart and Santa's Little Helper. Left alone after both abandon her, she encounters a gravedigger, a grave-robbing Dr. Nick, and a menacing owl before falling and knocking herself out on a tombstone. In her ensuing dream she faces a series of surreal monsters, including a spider with Bart's head and a slime-covered Milhouse-slug, before meeting whimsical creatures from Dr. Burkhart's book who teach her that being scared doesn't mean she isn't smart. Homer and Marge find and comfort her, resolving her fear of the cemetery, while a subplot follows Chief Wiggum, who strips down and hides terrified in a tree, only to be hilariously extracted with the help of a pizza bagel. When the Simpsons discover Springfield Park is run-down, they attend a charity carnival where Homer wins a giant stuffed octopus with an over-the-top victory dance, which Ned unwittingly records and Comic Book Guy posts online, turning Homer into an internet joke. Football player Deion Overstreet pays Homer to invent flashy touchdown celebrations for him, and word spreads until stars like LeBron James, Michelle Kwan, Tom Brady, Yao Ming, and Warren Sapp all enroll in Homer's new 'Showboating Academy.' Meanwhile, Ned channels his frustration over racy TV ads into making increasingly violent, low-budget Bible films starring his sons, which Mr. Burns agrees to fund after seeing their popularity, much to Marge's horror. Marge's campaign against the graphic religious films eventually costs Ned Burns' backing when Burns gets distracted by a threat to his nuclear power monopoly. Homer, having built a reputation for spectacle, is hired to produce the Super Bowl halftime show but struggles for ideas until he teams up with Ned, who suggests a dramatic retelling of Noah's Ark. Their over-the-top, faith-heavy halftime extravaganza destroys the field and offends the sports-loving audience, making Homer despised again. The episode ends with the Simpsons and Homer's celebrity students gathered peacefully at home for a dinner of omelettes. text: "Girls Just Want to Have Sums" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF12), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Matt Selman, originally airing April 30, 2006. After Principal Skinner publicly suggests that girls are naturally worse at math than boys, outraged mothers and teachers stage a protest at Springfield Elementary. Skinner's clumsy attempts to smooth things over backfire spectacularly, leading Superintendent Chalmers to replace him with a new principal, Melanie Upfoot, who immediately splits the school into separate boys' and girls' campuses. Lisa is thrilled at first by the girls' school's beauty, but is dismayed to discover its math class focuses on abstract 'magic' rather than real problem-solving. Determined to get a proper math education, Lisa disguises herself as a boy named Jake Boyman and sneaks into the boys' school, where she excels academically but struggles with the crude, aggressive social dynamics, even getting beaten up by Nelson. Bart discovers her secret and, feeling protective, teaches her how to act tougher like a boy. Lisa's newfound toughness pays off when she wins a math award as 'Jake,' prompting her to reveal her true identity to the stunned school. When Bart tries to diminish her achievement by saying she only succeeded because she acted like a boy, an enraged Lisa hurls her trophy at him but accidentally hits Ralph instead, forcing her to confront how far she's strayed from herself. The episode ends with the implication that Skinner is reinstated as principal, restoring order to Springfield Elementary. Guest starring Frances McDormand as Melanie Upfoot. title: Mommie Beerest (S16E07)
text: "Mommie Beerest" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF01), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Michael Price, originally airing January 30, 2005. After finally paying off their mortgage, the Simpsons' brunch is ruined by a fight between Bart and Lisa, sending Homer to Moe's Tavern to vent. Marge convinces Moe to transform the dive into a trendy British-style pub called The Nag and Weasel, which quickly becomes a hit with Springfield's elite. As Marge and Moe spend more and more late nights together working on the bar, Homer grows increasingly jealous and insecure about their close bond. Lenny and Carl warn Homer that Marge is having an 'emotional affair' with Moe, urging him to become a better friend to his wife before it's too late. When Marge flies off with Moe to a bar owners' convention in Aruba, Homer races to the airport and boards the plane to win her back, only to concede defeat until Marge herself rejects Moe and reaffirms her love for Homer. The episode ends with the couple reconciled in Aruba, while a hotel mix-up forces Homer to share a bed with Moe instead of Marge, and the family belatedly realizes no one is watching the kids, who are off in a balloon race over Paris. text: "Treehouse of Horror XVI" is an episode of Season 17 (production code GABF17), directed by David Silverman and written by Marc Wilmore, originally airing November 6, 2005. After a cosmic mishap involving Kang and Kodos' Accele-Ray destroys the entire universe, the Halloween special proceeds anyway in three separate tales. In the first, Bart falls into a coma after a reckless stunt, prompting his grieving family to adopt a robotic replacement son named David, whose perfection sparks a jealous rivalry once Bart wakes up and Homer callously abandons him in the woods. Bart returns as a scrap-metal cyborg seeking revenge, leading to a gruesome showdown that turns out to be nothing more than a nightmare brought on by Homer being possessed by a demon, resolved in an 'Exorcist' parody. The second story finds Mr. Burns luring Homer and half of Springfield to his estate under the guise of a hunting trip, only for the guests to discover they are the actual prey being stalked by Burns' rifle and attack helicopter. Homer barely survives the massacre by disguising himself with Barney's corpse, and is ultimately saved when Marge knocks out both Burns and Smithers before scolding her husband for being out all night. In the final segment, a witch loses a Halloween costume contest after being disqualified for not actually wearing a costume, and retaliates by magically transforming every Springfield resident into the literal character they were dressed as. The Simpsons are hit especially hard, with Homer's head falling off and Bart becoming a real werewolf, until Lisa realizes that baby Maggie, dressed as a witch, has the power to reverse the curse. Maggie's uncertain magic instead turns everyone into giant pacifiers, and she flies off on a broomstick before returning to seemingly restore order as the credits roll. Guest starring Terry Bradshaw, Dennis Rodman. Notable quotes: Lisa Simpson: Dad, you're not a robot. You're just posessed by the Devil. | Kang: It will be fine. I'll just leave a note. | Homer: Yeah, a robot son will be great. We can confuse him and make his head explode! | Dr. Hibbert: They're pretty much the same thing except this way I get to keep billing you! | David: I will comply. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 16): "B.I.: Bartificial Intelligence", "Survival of the Fattest", and "I've Grown a Costume on Your Face".

Kang: It will be fine. I'll just leave a note.
Homer: Yeah, a robot son will be great. We can confuse him and make his head explode!
Dr. Hibbert: They're pretty much the same thing except this way I get to keep billing you!
David: I will comply.

title: G.I. (Annoyed Grunt) (S18E05)
text: "G.I. (Annoyed Grunt)" is an episode of Season 18 (production code HABF21), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Daniel Chun, originally airing November 12, 2006. When Army recruiters trick Springfield Elementary students into signing delayed-enlistment contracts, Bart proudly brings his home to Marge, who panics and sends Homer to get it voided. Homer bullies the recruiters into tearing up Bart's contract, but they cleverly maneuver him into signing up himself instead. Shipped off to Fort Clinton, Homer coasts through basic training while being pampered as a joke, infuriating the base's colonel, and is eventually placed with a group of hopeless recruits assigned to OPFOR duty during a live-ammunition war game. Homer's mistaken flare launch exposes his unit's position, sparking a chaotic escape into Springfield with real soldiers in pursuit. Using a loophole in a broccoli-day proclamation, the colonel declares martial law over the town, rounding up any man deemed fat, bald, or amused by Homer. While Homer hides among the elderly at the Retirement Castle, Marge organizes the townsfolk into a resistance using an old-fashioned phone tree. The citizens spike the reservoir with alcohol, incapacitating the occupying soldiers, and the hungover colonel is forced to surrender, only demanding that Homer finish out his service. Homer ends up working as an unsuccessful mall recruiter, closing the story on a comedic anti-climax. Guest starring Maurice LaMarche, Kiefer Sutherland. Notable quotes: Homer: Hey baby. Ya like obstacle courses? | Homer: Bring it on chumps! [The tank runs over the manhole he's peeping out of] Oooh! Fingers, fingers, fingers! | Army colonel: Yes, I can. Congress slipped it into the National Broccoli Day proclamation | Marge: Don't worry. I have a secret weapon. One more deadly then any gun. | Superintendent Chalmers: Ugh, I'm not bald, I'm balding. Why doesn't anyone honor the ding?

title: All's Fair in Oven War (S16E02)
text: "All's Fair in Oven War" is an episode of Season 16 (production code FABF20), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Matt Selman, originally airing November 14, 2004. After touring a neighbor's house with an impressive kitchen, Marge convinces Homer to renovate their own, and his clumsy demolition unearths a stash of his old Playdude magazines. Marge cuts the nude photos out before tossing them, but Bart and Milhouse rescue the discarded issues and become obsessed with the sophisticated lifestyle articles inside, leading Bart to remodel the treehouse into a swinging bachelor pad and host a party that scandalizes the neighborhood parents. Meanwhile, Marge hires a real contractor to finish the kitchen, and her newfound culinary skill inspires her to enter the Ovenfresh Bakeoff with her novelty Dessert Dogs. At the competition she faces vicious, cutthroat rivals who mock and sabotage her, prompting Marge to retaliate by secretly spiking the other contestants' dishes with Maggie's ear medicine. Lisa is horrified by her mother's cheating and pressures her to come clean. In the final round against Cletus's wife Brandine, Marge confesses her sabotage rather than win dishonestly, restoring Lisa's respect for her, and Brandine takes the trophy from celebrity judge James Caan. The episode closes with Cletus vowing revenge after Brandine leaves him for Caan, ending in a comically violent ambush on the actor's car. Guest starring James Caan, Thomas Pynchon. Notable quotes: Marge: I think you used too much plaster. | Ralph Wiggum: Can you taste the thumbtacks? | Bart: Listen up, ring-a-ding-dingers. I'm throwin' a little sip'n'quip at the Playdude Treehouse. | Luigi Risotto: Yo, Marge. Your recipe, she's-a pathetic! | Marge: It's going to be weird cooking without your tipsy father grabbing me from behind. But I think I'm up to it.

title: Homer Simpson, This Is Your Wife (S17E15)

text: "Homer Simpson, This Is Your Wife" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF08), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Ricky Gervais, originally airing March 26, 2006. Homer becomes obsessed with Lenny's new plasma-screen TV after a party, spending days at Lenny's apartment until he's finally kicked out. Desperate to own one himself, he leaps at a contest Marge entered, but the family only wins a consolation trip to the Fox Studios in Los Angeles instead of a television. While touring the studio, Homer discovers a reality show called Mother Flippers that swaps wives between families for a cash prize, and he convinces a reluctant Marge to sign up so they can finally afford their own plasma TV. Back in Springfield, Marge is paired with mild-mannered Charles Heathbar, while Homer, Bart, and Lisa must endure the harsh discipline of Charles's domineering wife Verity. Charles finds Marge's kindness intoxicating and eventually confesses his love for her through a song, but she gently rebuffs him and urges him to be honest with his own wife instead. Meanwhile, Verity decides she's had enough of both her husband and Homer, and ends up pairing off with Patty, united by their mutual disdain for Homer. Charles brings Marge home to a joyous reunion with Homer and the kids, and the episode closes with Homer happily serenading his beloved new plasma TV—with Marge as an afterthought. Guest starring Ricky Gervais as Charles Heathbar. title: Pranksta Rap (S16E09)
text: "Pranksta Rap" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF03), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Matt Selman, originally airing February 13, 2005. After Santa's Little Helper swallows the TV remote and accidentally lands on a hip-hop show, Bart becomes obsessed with rapper Alcatraaaz and buys a ticket to his concert despite Homer and Marge forbidding him to go. Bart sneaks out anyway, ends up performing onstage with Alcatraaaz, and is driven home in style, only to panic when he realizes his parents know he snuck out. To avoid punishment, he fakes his own kidnapping. Chief Wiggum traces a background noise from the fake ransom call to a rare brand of popcorn, leading him to mistakenly arrest Kirk Van Houten, Milhouse's father, as the culprit. As Wiggum is hailed a hero and Kirk becomes an unlikely celebrity, Bart's guilt grows, but Wiggum convinces him that everyone is happier believing the lie. Lisa uncovers evidence proving Bart faked the kidnapping, and along with Principal Skinner, seeks proof from Alcatraaaz's mansion, prompting a tense confrontation involving Homer, Bart, and Wiggum. The situation is defused when Alcatraaaz decides to throw a party instead of retaliating, and the episode ends with Skinner jokingly asking about a place for himself in the hip-hop world. title: There's Something About Marrying (S16E10)
text: "There's Something About Marrying" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF04), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing February 20, 2005. When a professional tourism critic exposes Springfield's many flaws, the town's economy collapses, prompting Lisa to suggest legalizing same-sex marriage to attract new visitors. Reverend Lovejoy refuses to perform any such ceremonies, so Homer, lured by the $200-per-couple fee, gets ordained online and begins marrying every gay couple in town. Once he runs out of same-sex couples, a greedy Homer starts officiating absurd unions between people and inanimate objects. Meanwhile, Patty confides in Marge that she is a lesbian and plans to marry a professional female golfer named Veronica, forcing Marge to confront her own uneasy feelings about her sister's sexuality despite publicly supporting gay marriage. At the wedding, Marge discovers that Veronica is secretly a man, Leslie Robin Swisher, posing as a woman to compete on the women's golf tour. Torn by guilt over Patty's genuine happiness, Marge exposes the truth mid-ceremony, and Leslie admits his deception. Patty firmly rejects him, reaffirming her identity as a lesbian, and the episode ends with her and Selma continuing to look for love in their own unconventional way. title: The Seven-Beer Snitch (S16E14)
text: "The Seven-Beer Snitch" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF08), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing April 3, 2005. After a trip to Shelbyville leaves Marge insulted by how Springfield is mocked, she writes a letter urging the town to build a cultural center, inadvertently inspiring architect Frank Gehry to design an elaborate concert hall. The expensive building flops when locals lose interest in classical music almost immediately, giving Mr. Burns the opportunity to convert it into a new state prison. To fill the cells, Chief Wiggum revives obscure old laws, and Homer is arrested for repeatedly kicking a beer can. Inside prison, Homer accidentally becomes a snitch after reporting Snake's escape attempt, and the guards reward him with perks like a plasma TV, angering the other inmates when Marge blabs about his snitching during a visit. Fat Tony and the mob use a fake breakout plan to expose and punish Homer, leading to a tense chase that ends in a gas chamber standoff where Homer exposes the prison's brutal conditions to the governor. As a result, Homer is freed and the prisoners are shipped off to a barge to fight for dominance. Meanwhile, Bart and Lisa discover that Snowball II has been secretly living a double life with another family who spoils her, and Bart's attempt to reclaim her is thwarted when he gets distracted by their generous home cooking. The episode ends with Homer and Snowball crossing paths at Moe's Tavern, silently agreeing to keep each other's secrets. Guest starring Frank Gehry as Frank Gehry, Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony, Charles Napier as Officer Krackney. title: Midnight Rx (S16E06)
text: "Midnight Rx" is an episode of Season 16 (production code FABF16), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Marc Wilmore, originally airing January 16, 2005. After Mr. Burns cancels the power plant's employee prescription drug program, similar cutbacks spread across Springfield, leaving many residents unable to afford their medications. Homer struggles to find new work while Marge and Lisa's attempt to secure cheap drugs through a shady company goes nowhere. Meanwhile, Grampa and other seniors at the retirement home are left to go through withdrawal with makeshift substitutes. Desperate, Homer and Grampa travel to Canada using fake health cards obtained from a veteran named Johnny Canuck, successfully smuggling back cheap medication for the town, including insulin for Rod Flanders and relief for an exhausted Apu. Their scheme eventually gets them caught by Canadian border patrol and banned from the country, devastating the town's drug supply once again. When Smithers' untreated illness turns into a goiter, a guilt-ridden Mr. Burns personally flies to Canada in his old prop plane to retrieve more medicine, bringing Homer and Grampa along. The plane crashes back in Springfield during a storm, but the grateful townspeople—thankful for the returned medication—convince Chief Wiggum to let the men go free. Burns reinstates the prescription drug program to save Smithers, but the episode ends with Homer discovering a mysterious lump on his own neck. Notable quotes: Homer: Hola señor! title: Kiss Kiss Bang Bangalore (S17E17)
text: "Kiss Kiss Bang Bangalore" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF10), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Dan Castellaneta, Deb Lacusta, originally airing April 9, 2006. When the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant is outsourced to India, Homer is the only employee offered a job at the new facility and reluctantly relocates overseas. Confused about geography and initially disoriented, Homer settles in and, using a self-help book Marge gave him, unintentionally convinces the Indian workers to cheer enthusiastically, which Mr. Burns and Smithers mistake for genuine productivity. Impressed, Burns puts Homer in complete charge of the plant while he takes a leisurely trip down the Ganges, and Homer's ego swells to the point that he starts believing he might be a god. Meanwhile, back in Springfield, Patty and Selma kidnap their idol Richard Dean Anderson from a Stargate SG-1 convention, only to discover he despises being reminded of MacGyver; however, he soon becomes obsessed with orchestrating elaborate escapes from their captivity. Burns and the Simpson family eventually travel upriver to check on Homer, finding him ruling the plant like a deity, though the workers reveal they actually just appreciate the American workplace perks he introduced, like coffee breaks. Furious at the deception, Burns fires everyone and decides to move the plant back to Springfield, delighting the workers thanks to lucrative severance clauses Homer had unknowingly written into their contracts. The episode closes with a joyous musical celebration featuring the Simpsons, Lenny, Carl, Patty, Selma, Smithers, and Richard Dean Anderson dancing with the plant's native workers. title: Little Big Girl (S18E12)
text: "Little Big Girl" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF04), directed by Raymond S. Persi and written by Don Payne, originally airing February 11, 2007. When Cletus's farm mishaps spark a chain-reaction wildfire that spreads across Springfield, Bart accidentally saves the day using stolen fire extinguishers during a wild wagon ride, earning him a town-granted wish. He chooses a driver's license, but quickly grows tired of being Homer's personal chauffeur for absurd errands. Fleeing to North Haverbrook, Bart lies about his age to impress Darcy, a teenage girl who falls for him, and their whirlwind romance leads to a hasty engagement and a trip to Utah to marry. A pregnancy scare complicates things until Darcy's mother reveals she herself is expecting, allowing the family to cover up the truth by passing the babies off as twins, and Bart and Darcy part amicably. Meanwhile, Lisa fabricates a fictional Native American tribe called the Hitachi for a school heritage project, and her lie spirals out of control as she's asked to represent her invented people at increasingly important events. Wracked with guilt, she publicly confesses the deception, inspiring others to admit their own false claims of heritage. The episode ends with Homer casually revealing that his great-great-grandmother actually was Native American, undercutting Lisa's entire ordeal. Guest starring Natalie Portman as Darcy. title: Regarding Margie (S17E20)
text: "Regarding Margie" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF13), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Marc Wilmore, originally airing May 7, 2006. Bart, Milhouse, and Nelson start a curbside scam, painting house numbers for cash, but leave the Simpsons' address incomplete after Homer refuses to pay, causing mail mix-ups. Meanwhile, Marge receives a bogus prize letter promising a maid, and out of pride scrubs the house spotless herself, mixing cleaning chemicals that leave her dizzy. She slips, hits her head on a stool, and wakes up in the hospital with amnesia, unable to recognize her own family. As the days pass, small sensory triggers—Maggie's pacifier, Lisa's vocabulary, Milhouse's news about lactose tolerance—slowly restore her memories of everyone except Homer, whom she finds repulsive once she learns how much of a slob he is. Devastated, Homer tries increasingly desperate schemes to win her back, only to be rejected and thrown out of the house. Patty and Selma push Marge into speed dating, where she connects with a seemingly perfect match until her amnesia and family become dealbreakers for him. Homer intercepts the man to passionately defend Marge's virtues, but the man still leaves, unmoved by Homer's speech. Driving home together afterward, Homer casually mentions his newfound love of beer, which somehow triggers Marge's full memory return, and the two reconcile as an oddly perfect, imperfect couple, ending with Homer driving drunkenly into the sunset. Guest starring Sal Bando, Gene Tenace. Notable quotes: Homer: You monster! What have you done to my face?! | Marge: Don't answer the door! I don't want that judgmental bitch in my house! | Bart: What? Honest work for honest pay? | Homer: The wisest, wettest man you'll ever meet. | Marge: I remember everything now. You get drunk all the time!

title: Simpsons Christmas Stories (S17E09)
text: "Simpsons Christmas Stories" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF01), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Don Payne, originally airing December 18, 2005. When Reverend Lovejoy fails to show up for the church Christmas service due to a mishap with his model trains, Homer ends up leading the congregation through a series of holiday tales. The first, a retelling of the Nativity, casts Homer and Marge as Joseph and Mary, with Lisa as the angel Gabriel and various townsfolk as the wise men, shepherds, and King Herod, culminating in baby Jesus's first miracle and a chaotic escape from Herod's soldiers. Back home, Bart and Lisa catch Grampa trying to trap Santa Claus in the chimney, prompting him to recount a wild WWII story about being shot down with Mr. Burns, surviving on a deserted island, and having Burns steal Santa's sleigh and presents after accidentally shooting him down. Grampa manages to retrieve the sleigh and return it to Santa, but is left stranded on the island for years, and the present-day visit reveals his long-lost brother Cyrus is alive and living happily in Tahiti with many wives. A third segment follows the Springfield Elementary Nutcracker performance, Krusty's disastrous old Christmas special, and Moe's recurring failed attempts at suicide during the holidays. The episode closes with Homer's panicked last-minute gift search for Marge, only for her to reveal she anticipated his forgetfulness by giving him a gift to re-gift to her, showing the family's imperfect but genuine love for one another. text: "Stop, or My Dog Will Shoot!" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF12), directed by Matthew Faughnan and written by John Frink, originally airing May 13, 2007. Homer's hopes for a beer-soaked Oktoberfest are dashed when Marge redirects the family to a dry Harvest Festival instead. While trying to sneak away, Homer wanders into a cornfield maze and gets hopelessly lost, forcing Lisa to devise a scientific escape route while Bart calls on Santa's Little Helper to track down his missing father. The dog's heroic rescue makes him a local celebrity, and Chief Wiggum convinces the family to enroll him in the police canine academy, where he's partnered with Lou. After a successful bust of Snake Jailbird ends in a courtroom loophole that lets the criminal walk free, the disillusioned dog lashes out and bites Bart, prompting the family to give him up to live with Lou. Marge tries to fill the pet-shaped hole in Bart's life with a giant pet python named Strangles, but the snake causes chaos at school by knocking over chemicals and creating a toxic gas cloud that leaves Bart unconscious. In the climax, both Santa's Little Helper and Strangles rush to save Bart, but he chooses his loyal dog, who is welcomed back into the Simpson household. Strangles finds a new home with Groundskeeper Willie, coiled up in a fire hose. Guest starring Stephen Hawking, Maurice LaMarche, Rudy Giuliani. title: The Haw-Hawed Couple (S18E08)
text: "The Haw-Hawed Couple" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF02), directed by Chris Clements and written by Matt Selman, originally airing December 10, 2006. After Bart and Lisa walk in on Homer and Marge, a traumatized Bart is targeted by Nelson for lunch money but also invited to his birthday party. Bart convinces his classmates to skip the party out of spite, but Marge forces him to attend anyway. Following the party, Nelson takes Bart under his wing as a bodyguard and best friend, though his intense jealousy forbids Bart from spending time with Milhouse. When Nelson discovers Bart's secret friendship with Milhouse, he angrily ends their bond, only to later confront Bart during a class field trip to the tidepools. Despite his anger, Nelson saves Bart from a rising tide simply because of their field-trip buddy obligation, and Bart is left reflecting fondly on their strange friendship. Meanwhile, Homer becomes engrossed in Lisa's beloved 'Angelica Button' book series, and upon discovering that a beloved character dies in the final chapter, he can't bear to break the news to Lisa. Instead, Homer improvises a happier ending for her, only to later mourn the real, sadder conclusion himself at Moe's Tavern. Notable quotes: Nelson Muntz: Ha-ha! title: Milhouse of Sand and Fog (S17E03)
text: "Milhouse of Sand and Fog" is an episode of Season 17 (production code GABF19), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Patric M. Verrone, originally airing September 25, 2005. After Ned Flanders suggests deliberately exposing children to chicken pox for immunity, Homer hosts a paid 'pox party' at the Simpson house, only to catch the illness himself since he never had it as a child. During the outbreak, Kirk and Luann Van Houten reconcile, but their son Milhouse feels ignored now that his parents are no longer competing for his attention. Determined to split them up again, Milhouse convinces Bart to help by planting one of Marge's bras in the Van Houten's bed, hoping to frame Homer and Marge for an affair. The scheme backfires spectacularly when Luann accuses Marge of infidelity, causing Homer to doubt Marge's loyalty and triggering a real rift between Bart's own parents. Realizing his mistake, Bart tries to fix things by faking a fall off a cliff into a river using a dummy, but Milhouse's bad eyesight causes Bart to actually plunge into the water for real. Homer dives in heroically to save his son, and Marge's trust in Homer allows the family to pull each other from the dangerous rapids just before a waterfall. The near-tragedy repairs the Simpsons' relationship, and in a final twist, Milhouse leaps into the water too, unwilling to be without his best friend. title: Marge and Homer Turn a Couple Play (S17E22)

text: "Marge and Homer Turn a Couple Play" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF16), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing May 21, 2006. When a kiss between Marge and Homer is broadcast on the Isotope Stadium Jumbotron, struggling slugger Buck Mitchell notices it and asks the couple for marital advice, hoping it will help fix his rocky marriage to provocative pop star Tabitha Vixx. Marge reluctantly agrees to counsel them, while Homer sees the sessions as an opportunity to score free baseballs and flirt shamelessly with Tabitha. As Marge's advice about spending quality time together helps Buck and Tabitha reconnect, Buck's batting improves, but everything falls apart after Homer gives Tabitha an inappropriate backstage massage, prompting Buck to punch Homer and end the counseling. Buck's performance collapses again, and local radio blames Homer for the team's slump, leading to Homer and Bart getting attacked by angry fans. Determined to fix what he broke, Homer hijacks the Duff Blimp to fake a loving message from Tabitha, convincing Buck to play well again, though the stunt ends with the blimp crashing after Buck hits a home run through it. Believing he's been tricked, Buck nearly attacks Homer again until Tabitha appears on the Jumbotron and offers to reconcile if he can guess the game's attendance. The couple reunites, restoring harmony just as the season ends. Guest starring Stacy Keach as Howard K. Duff VIII, Mandy Moore as Tabitha Vixx. Notable quotes: Homer: What a game! title: The Wettest Stories Ever Told (S17E18)
text: "The Wettest Stories Ever Told" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF11), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Jeff Westbrook, originally airing April 23, 2006. While the Simpsons wait at The Frying Dutchman for a delayed meal, Captain McCallister suggests passing the time with a sea story, and the family takes turns telling three tall tales. Lisa recounts a comic version of the Mayflower voyage in which a stowaway Homer disguises himself as a Puritan, clashes with a jealous suitor named Moezekiel, and ends up drunkenly steering the ship safely to the New World after the captain is injured. Bart then tells an exaggerated take on the mutiny on the Bounty, where Captain Bligh's cruelty and obsession with rationing water push his crew, led by Fletcher Christian, into rebellion, leaving the ship rudderless and adrift toward Antarctica. Finally, Homer narrates a disaster story about the cruise ship Neptune, which capsizes after being struck by a massive wave while the Simpsons perform onstage as the ship's band. The survivors band together to climb through the overturned vessel and are eventually rescued, and as they escape by lifeboat they pass the ghostly, skeleton-crewed Bounty still searching for Tahiti. The framing device closes as the family's storytelling wraps up around their long-awaited dinner at the restaurant. Notable quotes: Captain McCallister: Until then, perhaps an old sea yarn may pass the time. Too bad I don't know any. | Homer: What kind of booze cruise is this? Where's the hooch? | Ned Flandish: Heh, heh, heh, we Puritans have no place for drunkenness... or colorful clothes, or dreaming, or poetry. | Moezekiel: We're engaged! I didn't kill her husband just so.... I-I mean, I-I didn't kill her husband. | Reverend Lovejoy: Lord, we thank you for the many ways you show your love: the sun which bakes our lips to the point of bleeding.

title: The Italian Bob (S17E08)
text: "The Italian Bob" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF02), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Frink, originally airing December 11, 2005. Mr. Burns sends Homer and the family to Italy to pick up his new luxury sports car, and after a mishap with a giant wheel of cheese damages the vehicle, they find themselves stranded in the small village of Salsiccia. There they discover that the town's beloved mayor is none other than Sideshow Bob, who fled to Italy after his last attempt on Bart's life, reformed himself, married a local woman named Francesca, and had a son named Gino. Bob pleads with the Simpsons to keep his criminal past secret so he can keep his new life, and they agree in exchange for getting their car repaired. Things go smoothly until Lisa gets drunk at a village celebration and accidentally exposes Bob's prison uniform and true identity to the shocked townspeople, who promptly strip him of his mayoral title. Enraged, Bob swears a vendetta against the Simpsons and pursues them with his wife and son, chasing them across the Italian countryside and eventually cornering them at the Colosseum during a performance of Pagliacci starring Krusty the Clown. Bob seizes the opportunity to perform the opera's dramatic climax to a standing ovation before the family narrowly escapes in Krusty's limo. The episode ends with the vengeful Terwilliger family walking off scheming further revenge, while little Gino comically declares a vendetta of his own against a butterfly. title: 24 Minutes (S18E21)
text: "24 Minutes" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF14), directed by Raymond S. Persi and written by Ian Maxtone-Graham, Billy Kimball, originally airing May 20, 2007. Principal Skinner launches the Counter Truancy Unit, a covert student squad led by Lisa, to keep tabs on troublemakers like Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney. When Homer is forced to get rid of a horrifically expired container of yogurt from the power plant, it ends up in the bullies' hands and becomes the key ingredient in a homemade stink bomb meant to ruin the school bake sale. Milhouse's surveillance attempt fails, so Bart is recruited and negotiates immunity for his pranks in exchange for infiltrating Jimbo's house to find the bomb. While investigating, Bart's phone gets crossed with a call meant for Jack Bauer, sparking a bizarre subplot where Bauer's real CTU mistakes Bart for a terrorist. Meanwhile, Marge scrambles to bake a raisin cake for the sale after forgetting about it, resulting in a rock-hard, ruined dessert. Bart discovers Martin has secretly betrayed the group to the bullies and is captured and trapped in a flooding ventilation room just as the bomb's timer starts at the bake sale. With Bart's guidance, Lisa manages to shut off the fan and defuse the bomb using a simple switch, while Marge's indestructible cake is used to smash the window and free Bart. Just as the crisis is resolved, the real Jack Bauer and his agents storm the bake sale to arrest Bart for the prank call, and the episode ends with a nuclear explosion in the distance—revealed to have happened harmlessly in Shelbyville. Guest starring Mary Lynn Rajskub as Chloe O'Brian, Kiefer Sutherland as Jack Bauer. We're dumpster folk. | Chalmers: I'm very happy to hear that. You don't know me at all. | Nelson: Can't a guy enjoy a catchy tune?

title: The Boys of Bummer (S18E18)
text: "The Boys of Bummer" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF11), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Michael Price, originally airing April 29, 2007. After catching a game-winning fly ball for the Springfield Isotots, Bart becomes a local hero, but his fortune reverses at the championship game against Shelbyville when he drops an easy pop-up, allowing the other team to score a walk-off grand slam. The town turns viciously on Bart, mocking and humiliating him at every turn, while Lisa's attempt to console him by introducing him to a washed-up ballplayer who made the same mistake backfires spectacularly. Overwhelmed with guilt and shame, Bart spirals into a breakdown, vandalizing the town and staging a public suicide attempt that shocks the community into remorse. Marge finally confronts the mob, shaming them for their cruelty and declaring Springfield the 'Meanest City in America.' The town atones by restaging the championship game dozens of times until Bart finally makes the catch cleanly. Meanwhile, Homer takes a job as a mattress salesman and foolishly trades away his and Marge's mattress to the Lovejoys to fix their marital problems, tanking his and Marge's own sex life in the process. After a botched attempt to steal the mattress back, Homer and Marge instead rekindle their intimacy the old-fashioned way, parking behind a billboard just like on their honeymoon. The episode closes decades later with an elderly Bart still lying about the game to preserve his pride, watched over by the ghosts of Homer and Marge. title: The Monkey Suit (S17E21)
text: "The Monkey Suit" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF14), directed by Raymond S. Persi and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing May 14, 2006. As summer ends, a museum visit to the evolution exhibit sparks a town-wide controversy when Ned Flanders convinces Mayor Quimby to appoint Reverend Lovejoy as a 'Morality Czar' to promote creationism in schools. Rather than allowing both theories to be taught, Springfield bans evolution outright, leaving Lisa and a handful of classmates as lone defenders of Darwin's ideas while scientific buildings across town are destroyed. When Lisa defies the ban by secretly teaching evolution, she is arrested and put on trial, represented by an unlikable New York lawyer against a charming Southern prosecutor. Marge unexpectedly becomes the swing vote after reading Lisa's copy of 'On the Origin of Species' and having a change of heart, prompting her to help call Ned to the stand. Meanwhile, Homer's comedic struggle to open a beer bottle turns him into an ape-like spectacle in the courtroom, which so rattles Ned that he blurts out an insult comparing Homer to a 'monkey-faced gorilla.' Lisa's lawyer seizes on this outburst to argue that Homer resembles the missing link the prosecution had been citing, collapsing their case. In the end, Lisa reconciles with a dejected Ned, telling him she respects his faith but believes science and religion should remain separate, a sentiment he ultimately accepts. The episode closes with the reveal that 'Todd' was actually Nelson in disguise all along. Guest starring Melanie Griffith as herself, Larry Hagman as Wallace Brady. title: Fat Man and Little Boy (S16E05)
text: "Fat Man and Little Boy" is an episode of Season 16 (production code FABF21), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing December 12, 2004. Bart, unsettled by the realization that he's losing his last baby tooth, worries he's growing up too fast and stages a Viking funeral for his childhood toys. Following Lisa's advice to channel his feelings into writing, he starts scrawling cynical slogans on T-shirts, which unexpectedly become a local sensation. After Chief Wiggum shuts down his unlicensed sidewalk stand and Krusty's flashy booth crushes his expo table, a fast-talking entrepreneur named Goose Gladwell literally runs Bart over and offers to mass-produce his shirts. As Bart's merchandise empire takes off, Homer feels obsolete as the family's provider and instead throws himself into bonding with Lisa, inspired by a wildlife documentary about lions and fatherhood. Their bonding time turns disastrous when Homer sabotages Lisa's school science project by swapping in real plutonium to beat Martin's robot CHUM, reigniting her resentment toward him. Meanwhile, Gladwell secretly sells the rights to Bart's shirts to Disney without paying him a cent. When Homer discovers the scam, he confronts Gladwell, forces him to make things right for Bart, and reclaims his place as the family's protector and father. Guest starring Eric Idle as Declan Desmond. title: The Bonfire of the Manatees (S17E01)
text: "The Bonfire of the Manatees" is an episode of Season 17 (production code GABF18), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing September 11, 2005. Homer's gambling debts to the Springfield Mafia force him to let Fat Tony use the Simpson house as a filming location for an adult movie starring Carl and Lenny. To keep Marge and the kids away, Homer sends them to Santa's Village, but they return early and Marge is horrified to discover what has happened to her home. Disgusted, she walks out on Homer and soon meets the charming manatee researcher Dr. Caleb Thorn, who helps her see that Homer's flaws are part of the man she originally fell for, even as she still longs for him to improve. Meanwhile, Homer and the kids move in with their surprisingly refined country cousins while searching for Marge. Determined to win her back, Homer attempts to rescue a group of manatees from aggressive jet skiers, but his plan backfires when the jet skiers attack him after he insults them. His country cousin arrives with a legal court order that finally drives the thugs away. Witnessing Homer's clumsy but genuine heroism, Marge decides to take him home, calling him the real endangered species worth saving. Guest starring Alec Baldwin as Caleb Thorn, Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony. Notable quotes: Homer: Hello, Marge? Does the pizza guy take a check? If so, where do we keep the checks? Bart and Lisa's bus ride ends in chaos when Bart steals Otto's bus, leading to Otto's suspension and Marge being stuck carpooling the neighborhood kids. Among the carpool is Michael D'Amico, who the kids soon realize is the son of mob boss Fat Tony, and Lisa befriends him over his passion for cooking. When Fat Tony's rival, the Calabresi family, tries to have him killed, the two families hold a sit-down that seems to end peacefully, but the Calabresis return to shoot up Fat Tony's mansion after mocking Michael's cooking, leaving Fat Tony hospitalized. With Fat Tony recovering, Michael is forced to take over the family business, and Homer and Bart eagerly help him collect debts around town, getting a little too into the mob lifestyle for Michael's taste. Wanting to keep the Simpsons separate from his world, Michael invites the Calabresi family to a dinner he cooks himself, and all three of them mysteriously drop dead afterward. Michael insists it was just an unfortunate recipe mishap, but lets Fat Tony believe he intentionally took out their rivals, warning Lisa to stay out of his business before returning to playing with his toy cars. title: Home Away from Homer (S16E20)
text: "Home Away from Homer" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF15), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing May 15, 2005. Strapped for cash, Ned Flanders rents his rumpus room to two college women, unaware they are secretly running a soft-core webcam show from the room. Bart and Milhouse stumble onto the stream online, and Homer eagerly spreads the word around Springfield, reveling in his oblivious neighbor's misfortune. Marge pressures Homer into confessing to Ned, and the resulting scandal turns Ned into the town's laughingstock. Wracked with guilt, Homer visits with a gift basket only to discover the Flanders family has already relocated to Humbleton, Pennsylvania, an idyllic town built around Ned's beloved figurine collection. Ned initially thrives there, but the town's obsessive, judgmental perfectionism—over things like facial hair and mailbox etiquette—soon wears him down, especially once a difficult new neighbor moves in. Meanwhile, back in Springfield, an obnoxious sports coach named Clay has taken over the vacated Flanders house and refuses to budge. Homer convinces Ned to return home, and together they manage to talk Clay into giving up the house. The episode ends with Homer and Ned reconciling, celebrating Ned's homecoming with a backyard party featuring a pipe organ Homer procured, which Ned mistakenly believes was a gift from the church. title: Thank God It's Doomsday (S16E19)
text: "Thank God It's Doomsday" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF14), directed by Michael Marcantel and written by Don Payne, originally airing May 8, 2005. After a chaotic haircut mishap forces Bart, Lisa, and Homer to hide in a movie theater, Homer watches a Christian apocalypse film and becomes convinced the Rapture is imminent. Fueled by a series of misinterpreted events—mistaking an advertising mascot for the Devil and an injured whale's blood for a sign from heaven—Homer calculates a specific doomsday date using nonsensical methods. When a bizarre coincidence involving a blimp accident at a Krusty event seems to validate his prediction, the town rallies behind him, only to be left disappointed and angry when nothing happens at the predicted time. Humiliated, Homer discovers a miscalculation involving the number of apostles at the Last Supper, leading him to believe the real Rapture is actually a day later, but no one will listen to him this time. He heads out alone to face the apocalypse, and to his shock, the Rapture actually happens, sweeping him up to heaven while his skeptical family and friends are left behind to suffer under the Devil's torment. In heaven, Homer negotiates with a reluctant God, eventually forcing Him through a chaotic tantrum to reverse the Rapture and restore everything to normal. Homer wakes back on Earth reunited with his family, uncertain if it was all a dream, until subtle changes—like a restored Moe's Tavern—suggest it really happened. My Son went down to Earth once. I don't know what you people did to him, but he hasn't been the same since. | Krusty: Well, that's our show for tonight. I'd like to thank all the really talented people who broke my fall. | Homer: Marge, in a world gone mad, only a lunatic is truly insane. | God: Deus ex machina.

title: She Used to Be My Girl (S16E04)

text: "She Used to Be My Girl" is an episode of Season 16 (production code FABF22), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Tim Long, originally airing December 5, 2004. When a sex scandal engulfs Mayor Quimby, Springfield is overrun by reporters, among them Chloe Talbot, Marge's glamorous former high school friend and journalism partner. Marge invites Chloe to dinner, but watching her family fawn over Chloe's cooking, stories, and career success stirs up old insecurities about the path she chose, staying in Springfield to raise a family instead of pursuing journalism like Chloe did. Lisa becomes fascinated by Chloe's exciting, worldly lifestyle and is invited to accompany her to a women's conference in Capital City, which infuriates Marge and leads to a jealous confrontation that leaves Marge with a black eye. Lisa ends up operating the camera during the dangerous report, prompting Homer and Marge to race to the volcano to rescue her. title: Yokel Chords (S18E14)
text: "Yokel Chords" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF09), directed by Susie Dietter and written by Michael Price, originally airing March 4, 2007. After Homer botches making school lunches, Bart invents a gruesome cafeteria legend called Dark Stanley to scare classmates into abandoning their food, causing chaos at school. As punishment, Skinner sends Bart to see psychologist Dr. Stacey Swanson, and though he's initially resistant, he grows attached to their sessions and eventually opens up about why he acts out. Meanwhile, Groundskeeper Willie rounds up Cletus Spuckler's many uneducated children, and Lisa is assigned to tutor them after objecting to the school's plan to deny them enrollment. Lisa takes the Spuckler kids on an educational tour of Springfield, where they burst into song, catching Krusty the Clown's attention. Krusty exploits the children for his show, even bringing in Stephen Sondheim to write for them, much to Lisa's dismay as their exploitation grows. Meanwhile, Bart's final therapy session lets him realize he misbehaves to keep his parents' anger focused on him rather than each other, giving him closure. Lisa and Brandine intervene to stop Krusty from using the children further, with Brandine revealing only two of the kids are actually Cletus's, forcing Krusty to let the rest go. The episode ends with the Spuckler children thanking Lisa, and Brandine and Cletus reconciling. Guest starring Peter Bogdanovich, Andy Dick, James Patterson, Meg Ryan, Stephen Sondheim. title: Sleeping with the Enemy (S16E03)
text: "Sleeping with the Enemy" is an episode of Season 16 (production code FABF19), directed by Lauren MacMullan and written by Jon Vitti, originally airing November 21, 2004. After being teased by classmates about her weight, Lisa becomes obsessively self-conscious about her body, a problem Homer's talk of the 'Simpson butt' only worsens. Meanwhile, Bart finally earns the perfect test score he was promised a party for, only to learn the whole class got 100 because Mrs. Krabappel forgot to fold up a map, and his celebration turns into a dull, awkward gathering. Feeling unappreciated by her own children, Marge finds neighborhood bully Nelson eating tadpoles in the park and impulsively takes him under her wing, paying him for chores and mothering him at the Simpson house. When Nelson's mother confronts Marge for meddling, a heated exchange leaves Lisa so startled that she finally eats a vegetable. After his mother leaves town to pursue an acting career, Nelson moves into Bart's room, displacing Bart to the floor, while Lisa bonds with Nelson over her own insecurities and enlists his help in getting revenge on her tormentors with a skunk prank. Bart, meanwhile, tracks down Nelson's estranged father, discovering he was mistaken for a sideshow freak after a bizarre allergic reaction at the Kwik-E-Mart. With his father found and his mother back from a successful stint playing Lady Macbeth, Nelson's family is reunited, though he makes clear to Bart that this won't stop him from bullying him. Lisa, still anxious about her weight, is left with only Homer's reassurance that everything is fine. My God. | Marge: Go home to your son, Mrs Muntz, and try not to have intercourse on the way. | Terri: She might crush us all with her giant butt | Willie: Shut up you, stop teasing the big bottomed lass.

title: Rome-Old and Juli-Eh (S18E15)
text: "Rome-Old and Juli-Eh" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF08), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Daniel Chun, originally airing March 11, 2007. After Homer splurges on a lavish new rec room and is forced into court-ordered financial austerity, he decides the cheapest fix is to move Grampa out of the retirement home and into the family's basement. When Homer and Marge leave Grampa to babysit, Marge insists Selma supervise him, and to Homer's horror, Grampa and Selma end up falling for each other. Determined to sabotage the romance, Homer teams up with Patty, who despises the match as much as he does, and the two stage an elaborate scheme involving disguises to catch Grampa 'cheating.' The plan backfires spectacularly when the real Selma catches Homer and Patty in their ruse, and an indignant Grampa proposes marriage to Selma on the spot. The newlyweds move in together, but domestic bliss quickly sours as Grampa's cluelessness wrecks their kitchen appliances while Selma struggles as the family's sole earner, eventually leading her to accept that their whirlwind romance has run its course. Meanwhile, Bart and Lisa trick a delivery driver out of a mountain of cardboard boxes and construct an elaborate fort, which they successfully defend—with unexpected help from Nelson—against an invading army of shipping employees. After their hard-won victory, however, the kids immediately grow bored and hose the fort into oblivion. Guest starring Jane Kaczmarek as Judge Constance Harm. Notable quotes: Homer: Aah! A bear is eating my father! | Grampa: Yeah, I know who I was kissing, and I also know why. I'm a little shaky on when and where, but I got my theories! | Homer: It's not right. It's like an old sea turtle dating a suitcase that fell out of a plane. | Moe Szyslak: Uh, gee, Homer, you, uh, ain't exactly open-casket material yourself. | Bart: Hmm... Build a fart! title: Million-Dollar Abie (S17E16)
text: "Million-Dollar Abie" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF09), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Tim Long, originally airing April 2, 2006. When the NFL announces plans to expand, Homer spearheads a bid to bring a franchise to Springfield, pitching an elaborate stadium funded by corporate sponsorships. After a smear campaign from Los Angeles backfires, the league awards Springfield the new team. As the town celebrates and rebrands itself in the team's honor, Grampa mistakes the visiting commissioner for a burglar and ties him up, causing the league to yank the franchise and the town to turn against him. Devastated by the town's hatred, Grampa seeks out an assisted-suicide clinic, but a last-minute rescue by police saves him just as he's about to go through with it. Believing himself dead, Grampa wanders through town in a daze before realizing he survived, and resolves to start living boldly. He becomes a local celebrity by taking up bullfighting in the abandoned stadium, delighting the town but troubling Lisa, who sees the sport as cruel. After winning one fight, Grampa has a change of heart mid-bout and frees all the bulls instead of killing them, causing chaos throughout Springfield. Lisa is proud of his moral choice, and the two reconcile while floating above the town, though their peace is disrupted by escaped bulls rigged with balloons. Guest starring Rob Reiner. I'd look pretty stupid in this outfit walkin' around fightin' oysters! | Grampa: You're all dead too? So, who went berserk? Fatso or the little guy?

title: The Wife Aquatic (S18E10)
text: "The Wife Aquatic" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF03), directed by Lance Kramer and written by Kevin Curran, originally airing January 7, 2007. During a family outing to a park movie screening, Marge is moved to nostalgia by an old home movie of a childhood vacation to Barnacle Bay. Wanting to please her, Homer decides to take the whole family back to the island, only to discover it has decayed into a rundown, foul-smelling shell of its former self due to the collapse of the local Yum-Yum Fish population from overfishing. Determined to cheer Marge up, Homer secretly repairs the old carousel and arranges a fireworks show, but a stray spark burns down the town's boardwalk, leaving him in debt to the furious townsfolk. As punishment, Homer is forced to work off his debt as a fisherman aboard the ramshackle boat The Rotting Pelican, run by the gruff Captain Jack. When Homer accidentally reverses the bait and batter for the crew's dinner, he inadvertently discovers a new way to lure back the elusive Yum-Yum Fish. A massive storm then sinks the ship, and Bart—who had secretly stowed away—is caught in the danger along with the crew, all of whom are presumed dead. To Marge's relief, they turn out to have been rescued by a passing Japanese fishing vessel. In the end, Lisa convinces Jack not to repeat the mistake of overfishing, so the townspeople decide to become lumberjacks instead. Guest starring Maurice LaMarche, Sab Shimono. [Lisa gasps] Yeah, that's right, I know about Milhouse. | Homer: Finally. Something even I wouldn't eat.

title: Bart Has Two Mommies (S17E14)
text: "Bart Has Two Mommies" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF07), directed by Michael Marcantel and written by Dana Gould, originally airing March 19, 2006. After Homer's cheating fails to win a church rubber-duck race, Ned Flanders takes home a female-oriented computer called FeMac but has no use for it, so he gives it to Marge in exchange for her babysitting Rod and Todd. As Marge spends more time with the Flanders boys, Homer is left in charge of Bart and Lisa, largely neglecting them while they wreck the house playing knights on their bikes. When Lisa pushes for an outing, Homer takes them to a retirement shelter for movie animals, where Bart is seized and held hostage by a monkey named Toot-Toot after offering her ice cream. Meanwhile, Marge lets Rod and Todd enjoy real childhood fun, including a foam-covered activity center, which horrifies the overprotective Ned when Rod gets a minor injury. Ned bans Marge from watching his sons just as news breaks that Bart is trapped with Toot-Toot atop the church's unfinished steeple, in a King Kong-style standoff. Marge convinces Ned to trust Rod, who uses his newfound climbing courage to scale the scaffolding and trade Toot-Toot's baby monkey, Mr. Teeny, to free Bart. Rod successfully rescues Bart, misunderstanding Bart's use of the word 'gay' to mean brave, and proudly (and confusingly) announces to Ned that Mrs. Simpson made him 'gay.' The episode closes with Ned displeased but Maude watching approvingly from heaven as her son grows more confident. Guest starring Antonio Fargas, Randy Johnson, Susan Sarandon, Dave Thomas. Notable quotes: Homer: He has to finish paying off the planets. Did you see that ring He gave Saturn? | Rod: I'm gay, Daddy! I'm gay! Mrs. Simpson made me gay! | Homer: What are you talking about? Monkeys don't have feelings. If they did, my experiments on them could be called cruel. | Ned: A sliver from a band-aid wrapper! Call me Ned Zeppelin, but is one of my boys abraised and contused?! | Rod: The secular humanist in the school house with misinformation!

title: My Fair Laddy (S17E12)
text: "My Fair Laddy" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF05), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Michael Price, originally airing February 26, 2006. When regular gym teacher Brunella Pommelhorst goes on leave, the sadistic substitute Coach Krupt torments students with his relentless dodgeball drills called 'Bombardment.' Fed up, Bart freezes a dodgeball overnight and hurls it at Krupt during class, but the icy projectile misses and smashes into Groundskeeper Willie's shack, destroying it. Marge takes pity on the newly homeless Willie and invites him to live with the Simpsons, giving Lisa the idea to civilize him as a school science project, betting Bart she can transform him into a proper gentleman before the fair. While Lisa coaches Willie through etiquette lessons, Homer rips his beloved blue pants in a go-kart accident and discovers the brand has been discontinued due to low sales, so he launches an unconventional marketing scheme—literally advertising on the back of his own head—that revives the pants' popularity across town. Willie initially resists refinement, but on the eve of the fair he surprises everyone by speaking eloquently, and he wows the crowd at the science fair with his newfound sophistication, winning Lisa's bet. Despite his success and newfound respect, Willie realizes he misses his old rough-and-tumble life as groundskeeper, especially after learning his job and shack were taken over by the music teacher. Understanding his true nature, Lisa lets him return to his old ways, and Willie happily resumes his life of grime and solitude in his rebuilt shack. title: A Star Is Torn (S16E18)
text: "A Star Is Torn" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF13), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Carolyn Omine, originally airing May 8, 2005. After the Simpsons get food poisoning from unfamiliar organic vegetables, Lisa nurses them back to health by singing a lullaby, revealing a hidden talent. Inspired, she decides to enter Krusty's Li'l Starmaker, a televised singing contest offering the winner a spot in an Itchy & Scratchy cartoon, with Homer serving as her enthusiastic songwriter. Lisa advances through several rounds against rivals Clarissa Wellington and the young heartthrob Cameron, but Homer's increasingly ruthless, stage-parent behavior backstage embarrasses and unsettles her. Fed up with his aggressive tactics, Lisa fires him, prompting Homer to switch sides and become Cameron's manager instead, rebranding him as "Johnny Rainbow." Hurt but still supportive, Homer secretly helps Lisa with a small performance tip before the finale, showing he still cares. For the final round, Lisa performs a heartfelt original song about her bond with her father, moving the crowd to tears, while Homer, working against her, has coached Cameron into performing an alienating song that turns the audience against him. Cameron's meltdown leaves Lisa the clear winner, and father and daughter reconcile, ending the episode with a sweet, silly celebration of jazz hands. Guest starring Fantasia Barrino as Clarissa Wellington. Notable quotes: Homer: Lisa sings so sweetly and Bart is my pillow... everyone's good for something. | Bart: Why? Just because she sings like Whitney Houston brought to life? | Homer: Much of the tune is plagiarized. Now go, go, go! | Lisa: Dad, I'm sorry you're hurt, but you left me no choice. You were obnoxious at a level not even permitted in show business. | Homer: I'm not Mr. Simpson. That ship has sailed. I'm Colonel Cool! And I'm the Captain on this rocket to the stars.

title: Mobile Homer (S16E13)
text: "Mobile Homer" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF07), directed by Raymond S. Persi and written by Tim Long, originally airing March 20, 2005. After a series of freak accidents, including nearly being decapitated by the garage door, Homer is declared uninsurable when he applies for life insurance. Terrified of being left destitute like the widow in a cheesy TV movie, Marge starts hoarding money by buying cheap knockoff groceries, sending the kids to school in charity clothes, and forcing Homer to smuggle his own drinks into Moe's Tavern. Fed up with the miserly lifestyle, Homer secretly spends the family's savings on an extravagant RV, which he then lets a rowdy convoy of traveling friends, including a couple resembling George and Martha from Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, park and party around at the Simpson house. Marge's fury boils over when she cuts the power to drive the freeloaders away, sparking a huge fight between her and Homer. Bart and Lisa decide to solve the problem themselves by driving the RV back to the dealership, but using a bizarre Flintstones-themed map, they get lost and end up stowed aboard a Turkish cargo ship bound for Kahramanmaraş. Marge and Homer chase after them in Homer's pink car, and Marge manages to negotiate the kids' release by trading canned goods with the ship's captain. The family shares an unexpectedly pleasant dinner aboard the ship, and Homer's attempt to return the RV via crane ends in disaster when it crashes into the water. Despite this chaotic ending, Marge remains strangely calm, later revealed to be because the Turkish crew had secretly slipped hashish into her food. [whispering] I want her to think I'm cool. | Lisa: Well, I think, in these days of petro-terrorists and ozone depletion, a Sunday drive reeks of bio-hubris. | Homer: You can't enjoy money when you're dead so why not have fun now!! | Bart: You know what started this trouble? This motorhome! How could a vehicle this cool destroy a marriage that crappy?

title: See Homer Run (S17E06)
text: "See Homer Run" is an episode of Season 17 (production code GABF21), directed by Nancy Kruse and written by Stephanie Gillis, originally airing November 20, 2005. On the eve of Father's Day, Homer's excitement clashes with Lisa's disappointment when he dismisses the heartfelt handmade book she gives him in favor of a fancy multi-tool from Bart. When Homer carelessly ruins Lisa's gift and blames her for it, she spirals into resentment toward men in general, acting out at school and alarming Principal Skinner and Dr. Pryor. Desperate to repair his image in his daughter's eyes, Homer takes on the role of the school's safety mascot, the Safety Salamander, but his early attempts are disastrous, including nearly injuring students on the school bus and setting the auditorium on fire. Fate intervenes when a massive highway pileup—caused indirectly by Bart's theft of a street sign—gives Homer a chance to become a genuine hero while in costume, rescuing drivers from the wreckage. His newfound fame coincides with a political crisis after Mayor Quimby faces a recall election, and Lisa encourages Homer to run for mayor, believing the town's love for the Salamander could restore his self-worth. Homer's campaign soars until his costume, freshly washed by Marge, disintegrates during the final debate, exposing that the public only loved the costume, not the man. Though his political ambitions collapse and Quimby retains his position by default, Homer's genuine effort to do right by the town restores Lisa's faith in him as her hero, and father and daughter reconcile through an emotional embrace and dance. It's my day. | Dolph Shapiro: Yeah, if a sign's got your name on it you can take it, and the cops can't do nothin' about it. | Homer: What happened to the last Safety Salamander? | Homer: Look, Lisa. I made safety happen! | Lenny Leonard: Uh, what special powers would a salamander bring to the office of mayor?

title: The Last of the Red Hat Mamas (S17E07)

text: "The Last of the Red Hat Mamas" is an episode of Season 17 (production code GABF22), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing November 27, 2005. After an Easter egg hunt at Mayor Quimby's mansion turns into a brawl between Homer and Hugs Bunny, Marge is humiliated and abandoned by her usual friends. Determined to help, Homer's clumsy attempt to find her a new friend backfires, but Marge herself soon connects with Tammy and her social club, the Cheery Red Tomatoes. Marge is thrilled to be invited to join, only to discover that initiation requires helping the group break into Mr. Burns' mansion to steal a $1 million donation he reneged on giving to a children's hospital. Torn between her morals and her desire for friendship, Marge reluctantly agrees to take part in the heist. Homer discovers her plans and rushes to stop her, arriving just as Chief Wiggum and Burns catch the women in the act. After the chaos settles, Marge realizes she doesn't need a club to have a true friend, since she already has Homer, though she keeps a stolen Fabergé egg for the group. In a parallel story, Lisa hires Milhouse to teach her Italian for a school trip, and the two grow closer during their lessons, but Lisa is furious to catch him with another girl, ending their budding romance with a beating.

title: Revenge Is a Dish Best Served Three Times (S18E11)

text: "Revenge Is a Dish Best Served Three Times" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF05), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing January 28, 2007. After The Rich Texan cuts him off in traffic, Homer becomes obsessed with getting revenge, prompting his family to each tell a cautionary tale. Marge recounts a version of The Count of Monte Cristo in which Homer, wrongly imprisoned by a rival named Meaux, spends years plotting an elaborate and gruesome revenge that ultimately costs him his family's love. Lisa then tells of Milhouse building a device called the Get-back-inator to stop school bullies, only for him to become drunk on power and turn on his friends and even Lisa herself before Nelson seizes the device and turns it against him. Bart's story reimagines him as the superhero Bartman, who is created after criminals kill Homer and Marge, and who spends his crime-fighting career hunting down villains until he finally confronts and kills the Serpent, his parents' true murderer. Each story illustrates a different consequence of seeking vengeance, from personal loss to addiction to violence to bittersweet closure. Despite hearing all three tales, Homer's desire for revenge isn't fully quashed by logic, but he and The Rich Texan end up reconciling anyway by the episode's end. title: Homer's Paternity Coot (S17E10)
text: "Homer's Paternity Coot" is an episode of Season 17 (production code HABF03), directed by Mike B. Anderson and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing January 8, 2006. When a mailman frozen since the 1960s is found thawed out on Mount Springfield, decades-old undelivered mail finally reaches its recipients, including a letter to Mona Simpson from an old lifeguard boyfriend hinting he might be Homer's real father instead of Abe. Meanwhile, Marge's attempt to dodge a new toll booth on the way to a fire-sale bargain store sparks chaos with Mayor Quimby and Chief Wiggum, ultimately leading to the tire fire that melts the mountain snow and reveals the frozen mailman. Homer tracks down the letter writer, wealthy adventurer Mason Fairbanks, by posing as a reporter, and the two hit it off over tales of sunken treasure. A DNA test appears to confirm Mason is Homer's biological father, delighting Homer but devastating Abe, who is left out of the family's admiration for the charming Mason. While the rest of the family awkwardly visits Grampa, Homer and Mason go treasure hunting in polluted waters, and Homer nearly dies after his submarine gets stuck and his oxygen runs out. Homer wakes from a three-day coma to learn from Grampa that Abe secretly swapped the DNA samples so Homer would believe Mason was his father and be happy, but the truth is that Abe really is his dad after all. The episode ends with father and son reconciling emotionally, while Mason gives Homer one last piece of paternal advice about not touching a hot stove. Guest starring Joe Frazier, William H. title: Moe'N'a Lisa (S18E06)
text: "Moe'N'a Lisa" is an episode of Season 18 (production code HABF19), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Matt Warburton, originally airing November 19, 2006. Homer wakes up covered in reminders but still can't figure out what he's forgotten, and the family heads off to watch Grampa compete in the Senior Olympics, where he recalls a bizarre brush with Adolf Hitler decades earlier. It turns out Homer forgot his promise to take Moe fishing for his birthday, and a furious Moe delivers a scathing note to the Simpsons that Lisa finds unexpectedly poignant. Struggling to find an interesting subject for a school report, Lisa visits Moe's cluttered hotel room and discovers his scattered thoughts on post-it notes, which she compiles into a poem she titles herself. The piece becomes a sensation, earning Moe recognition as a gritty poet and an invitation to a prestigious writers' retreat called Wordloaf in Vermont. At the convention, Moe rubs shoulders with real literary figures like Tom Wolfe, Gore Vidal, Michael Chabon, and Jonathan Franzen, but his ego swells and he publicly claims sole credit for the poem, devastating Lisa. She cuts ties with him, and when he tries to write alone, geese destroy his new work, sending him into a rage. Homer and Bart plot revenge with maple syrup after learning how Moe hurt Lisa, but their plan comically fails due to the syrup's thickness. In the end, Moe redeems himself by publicly crediting Lisa for her contribution during his big reading at Wordloaf. Guest starring Michael Chabon, Jonathan Franzen, J. K. Simmons, Gore Vidal, Tom Wolfe. Notable quotes: Lisa: You're a heartless jerk! | Moe: Where did that come from? title: The Father, the Son and the Holy Guest Star (S16E21)

text: "The Father, the Son and the Holy Guest Star" is an episode of Season 16 (production code GABF09), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Matt Warburton, originally airing May 15, 2005. Bart is expelled from Springfield Elementary after Groundskeeper Willie, seeking revenge for being cast as the village idiot in a medieval festival, unleashes a pie full of rats that gets blamed on Bart. Marge enrolls him at St. Jerome's Catholic School, where the kind Father Sean welcomes him and sparks his curiosity about Catholicism with a saints comic book. Homer, initially intending to confront Father Sean, instead gets drawn in by pancake dinners, Bingo nights, and an elaborate confession, and considers converting himself. Alarmed that her husband and son might end up in a separate Catholic Heaven, Marge enlists Reverend Lovejoy and Ned Flanders to intervene and reclaim Bart's faith. A chaotic chase ensues, culminating in a standoff at a Protestant Youth Festival where Homer and Father Sean arrive on a motorcycle to clash with Marge, Lovejoy, and Ned. Bart points out the absurdity of the various Christian factions fighting each other, prompting an uneasy truce between the groups. The episode closes with a wild flash-forward one thousand years into the future, showing humanity locked in holy war over the true meaning of Bart's teachings. Guest starring Liam Neeson as Father Sean. Notable quotes: Father Sean: I was laying in the gutter, pickin' up me teeth when St. Peter himself appears before me. | Saint Peter: Sean, you wanker. | Saint Peter: Repent of your wicked ways or sod off. | Father Sean: Then he gobbed in my face and turned back into a streetlight.

Saint Peter: Sean, you wanker.
Saint Peter: Repent of your wicked ways or sod off.
Father Sean: Then he gobbed in my face and turned back into a streetlight.

title: Homerazzi (S18E16)
text: "Homerazzi" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF06), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing March 25, 2007. On Homer's birthday, a mishap with trick candles sets his party hat and eventually the whole house on fire. Following Flint Drywall's advice, the family buys a fireproof safe to protect their most treasured possessions, each family member choosing a sentimental item. A chain reaction involving a wind-up Krusty doll, Lisa's toy car, and Homer's old cologne bottle causes the safe's contents to catch fire and be destroyed, including the family photo album that Marge cherished. Devastated, Marge decides to recreate the lost family photos rather than mourn them, but while staging one of these photos, she accidentally captures proof of a secret affair between Duffman and Booberella. This discovery pushes Homer into a new career as a tabloid paparazzo, chasing down embarrassing photos of Springfield's celebrities for cash. His photography spree angers the local celebrity community, who hire their own ruthless paparazzo, Enrico Irritazio, to turn the tables on Homer. As Homer becomes the hunted instead of the hunter, he must find a way to escape the world of gossip journalism he helped create. The situation is eventually resolved, restoring peace between Homer and Springfield's offended celebrities. Guest starring Jon Lovitz, J. K. Simmons, Betty White. Notable quotes: Bart: Lisa, you fool! You've doomed us all! | Homer: Whee! I'm sort of rich! I can rent anything I want! | Marge: Well, at least it got made.
quotes: Bart: Lisa, you fool! You've doomed us all!
Homer: Whee! I'm sort of rich! I can rent anything I want!
Marge: Well, at least it got made.

title: Kill Gil, Volumes I & II (S18E09)
text: "Kill Gil, Volumes I & II" is an episode of Season 18 (production code JABF01), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Jeff Westbrook, originally airing December 17, 2006. During a chaotic Christmas ice show, Homer's holiday cheer is threatened by a strange creature called The Grumple, setting an odd tone for the season. At Costington's department store, Gil, working as Santa, generously finds Lisa a sold-out toy that was actually reserved for his boss's daughter, and he gets fired for it. Marge, feeling sorry for him, invites Gil to spend the holiday with the Simpsons, but her inability to say no lets his stay stretch from Christmas into New Year's and beyond. As months pass, Gil disrupts the household—eating Homer's Valentine's chocolates, keeping the family up with drunken St. Patrick's Day singing, and even hijacking the family Christmas card the following year. Homer's frustration grows, and he also keeps running into The Grumple, culminating in a bar brawl. Marge finally resolves to kick Gil out, only to discover he's already left for a sales job in Scottsdale, so the family travels there to confront him properly. They find Gil thriving as a successful realtor, but when Marge finally unleashes her pent-up refusals on him, his coworkers realize he's a fraud and he loses the job again. Feeling guilty, the Simpsons buy a house in Scottsdale and spend Christmas there with Gil, and the episode ends with The Grumple and his family joining them for a heartfelt, if bizarre, holiday singalong. Guest starring Elvis Stojko as himself. Notable quotes: Moe Szyslak: Don't you hags know that all male figure skaters are "twinkly in the lutz"? | The Grumple: Grumply, grumply groo, I'll throw my net over you! | Homer: Give back that Holiday Cheer, you bastard! | Homer: Your present is leaving. | Marge: And that's why I have trouble saying "no" to people—even Gil!
