title: Bart's in Jail! (S33E02)
text: "Bart's in Jail!" is an episode of Season 33 (production code QABF18), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Nick Dahan, originally airing October 3, 2021. Grampa and his elderly friends fondly recall their first paychecks from the Springfield Meatball Factory before returning to the present to demand their withheld pension taxes back. After a shopping spree and a game of cribbage, Grampa is jolted awake by a phone call claiming Bart has been arrested and needs bail money fast. Panicked, he wires ten thousand dollars—money meant to be Homer's inheritance—only to discover the next day that Bart was never in trouble at all. When the family learns Grampa was scammed, Homer is furious about the lost money but soon falls for a pyramid scheme himself at a support meeting for scam victims, forcing him to eat his own words. Using Lisa's tech skills, the family traces the scam operation to a call center where they find Moe working as one of the scammers, though police can't arrest the low-level employees. After a mishap with stolen gift cards leads them to a lavish dinner, the mysterious mastermind behind the scams is revealed to be the trickster god Loki in disguise. In the aftermath, Marge tests her restored faith in humanity by lending money to a stranger, and though she credits the stranger for repaying her, it was secretly Grampa who returned the funds to reassure her—while Moe, unrepentant, goes right back to scamming. Guest starring Alan Cumming as Loki, Scott Hanson as Punt Zone anchor, Alex Hirsch as Bill Cipher. Notable quotes: Grampa: I don't care what you've done. All that matters is that no grandson of mine's gonna go to jail. | Homer: I had an inheritance and you gave it away? I'm so mad I could kill you, but now I'd get nothing. title: The Longest Marge (S33E11)
text: "The Longest Marge" is an episode of Season 33 (production code UABF05), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing January 2, 2022. When rookie football star Grayson Mathers is drafted by the Springfield Atoms, Mr. Burns seizes the opportunity to make him the new face of his struggling liquor brand, Mr. Gentleman Sipping Brandy. Grayson's reckless partying quickly spirals out of control, leading to a disastrous drunken appearance at a game and a humiliating meltdown while giving a motivational speech at Springfield Elementary. After collapsing from overindulgence, he ends up in the school infirmary under Marge's care, prompting her to strike an unusual deal with Burns: she'll manage Grayson's home life while Burns handles his public image. Marge welcomes Grayson into the Simpson household, teaching him domestic responsibility, healthy habits, and family values, while he opens up about a childhood devoid of parental warmth due to his football career. As Grayson thrives under Marge's nurturing and Burns' management, tension grows between the two adults, each wanting credit and control over him, culminating in a fight that forces Grayson to choose sides and triggers an emotional breakdown. He storms off, only to later invite Marge to a prestigious sports awards ceremony as his date—though Burns also receives an invitation, leading to an unexpected moment of bonding between the two rivals. Just as it seems the family conflict might resolve into a strange harmony, Grayson's acceptance speech reveals a shocking twist: he's already engaged to a woman he met days earlier, whom he's named his manager, abruptly severing his connections with both Marge and Burns. Guest starring Beck Bennett as Grayson Mathers, John Mulaney as Warburton Parker, Adam Schefter as himself. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: How dare they jeer that boy? He's like the arrogant, out-of-control son I never sent to boarding school and forgot about. | Grayson: I actually have six identical Ferraris. I want to own all the blue ones. | Marge: You listen here, young man. Just because you're embarrassed by your own behavior is no reason to lash out at me. | Grayson: In a family, you don't do you. title: The Man Who Flew Too Much (S36E10)

text: "The Man Who Flew Too Much" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF02), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Al Jean, originally airing December 22, 2024. After the Pin Pals qualify for the state bowling championship, Springfield throws them a hero's send-off before Barney flies the team to Capital City in a helicopter he pilots himself. Overloaded with extra-heavy bowling balls, the chopper develops engine trouble and crashes on a remote, snowy mountainside, leaving the team stranded and out of contact. Moe destroys the only working phone in a fit of rage after mistaking a call from Bart for a prank, cutting off their last hope of rescue. As the group struggles down the mountain, Fausto succumbs to his injuries, Moe suggests cannibalism out of desperation, and exhaustion nearly claims them all. Back home, the Simpsons and the town assume the worst, holding a funeral for the presumed-dead bowlers while Marge cooks Homer's favorite meal in mourning. The smell of the food somehow reaches Homer's hallucinating mind, jolting him awake and giving him the strength to dig free and rescue his unconscious teammates using a rope. Homer triumphantly carries the survivors into the middle of their own funeral, turning grief into celebration, and in a final twist, Fausto reappears alive and well after the service ends. title: Mad About the Toy (S30E11)
text: "Mad About the Toy" is an episode of Season 30 (production code YABF03), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Michael Price, originally airing January 6, 2019. Homer and Marge, unable to find a babysitter, leave the kids with Grampa so they can rush through an anniversary date before returning him to the Retirement Castle. While playing, Bart and Lisa dig up a set of vintage toy army men that send Grampa into a screaming panic. Assuming it's wartime PTSD, the family takes him to the V.A. Hospital, but doctors find no connection to his actual combat history. Lisa notices the toy soldiers' faces resemble Grampa, leading him to recall being scouted after WWII by the Whiz-Bang Toy Company to model for the figures, only for the memory to go blank after that. After a chaotic TV appearance demanding unpaid royalties, the family is flown to New York to confront the toy company's CEO, who reveals Grampa fled the original photoshoot and was blacklisted from claiming credit. Grampa remembers that he ran off in a panic after photographer Philip Hefflin, mistaking his friendliness for flirtation, kissed him, resulting in Philip being fired for being gay. Feeling guilty, the family travels to Marfa, Texas, where Grampa reconciles with Philip, finishes the interrupted photoshoot, and apologizes with a kiss on the cheek, reaffirming his own heterosexuality. The episode ends with Grampa proudly displaying a photo of himself and Philip, while Bart, Milhouse, and Nelson decide to microwave the infamous army men.

title: I, Carumbus (S32E02)
text: "I, Carumbus" is an episode of Season 32 (production code ZABF18), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Cesar Mazariegos, originally airing October 4, 2020. At the Springfield History Museum's Ancient Rome exhibit, Marge and Homer clash over his lack of ambition, prompting the curator to spin a Roman parable starring an alternate version of Homer named Obeseus the Wide. Sold into slavery by his own father, Obeseus becomes a gladiator, survives a brutal Colosseum duel, and wins the heart of Marjora, his owner's daughter, after she spares his life. Forced into marriage when he gets her pregnant, Obeseus repeatedly promises to free his fellow gladiator friends but keeps breaking his word as he rises from urine-collecting launderer to wealthy landowner. Pushed by an ambitious Marjora, he schemes his way toward political power, eventually helping assassinate the emperor, though he refuses to take the throne himself. Marjora then poisons the emperor and installs their son Bartigula, who becomes a cruel, self-declared god-emperor and turns on his own father, sentencing him to death by lions. Reunited with his betrayed friends and confronted by his neglected daughter, Obeseus refuses to flee and instead battles Bartigula, and both die in the confrontation. A guilt-ridden Marjora poisons herself, and Rome eventually falls centuries later. Back in the present, the Simpsons squabble over what lesson the story taught, while bickering gods watching from above debate whether the whole show—implied to be The Simpsons itself—has gone on far too long. Guest starring Joe Mantegna as Gordus Antonius, Michael Palin as the Springfield History Museum curator. title: Coming to Homerica (S20E21)
text: "Coming to Homerica" is an episode of Season 20 (production code LABF12), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Brendan Hay, originally airing May 17, 2009. After Krusty Burger's health rating hits an all-time low, Krusty launches an all-vegetarian 'Mother Nature Burger,' which turns out to be made from tainted barley grown in nearby Ogdenville. The food poisoning outbreak devastates Ogdenville's economy, forcing its Norwegian-descended residents to flee to Springfield in search of work. At first the Simpsons and their neighbors welcome the newcomers, hiring them for odd jobs and even finding romance, but resentment builds as hospitals, bars, and public services become overwhelmed. A skateboarding accident lands Bart in an overcrowded ER, pushing Homer and Marge to their breaking point, and Homer's night of drinking Ogdenvillian aquavit costs him his job at the power plant. Mayor Quimby responds by sealing the town borders, and Homer joins a ragtag citizen patrol called the Star-Spangled Goofballs to keep Ogdenvillians out, eventually building a giant wall between the two towns. While constructing the wall, Springfield and Ogdenville residents bond over their shared humanity, realizing their differences are trivial. In the end, both communities miss each other so much that the Ogdenvillians use a secret door in the wall to rejoin Springfield for a joyous reunion party. Notable quotes: Marge: Oh! I can't read this sloopy-blooby writing! | Homer: I do have a history of going up on roofs and ending up in hospitals. | Marge: Maggie's first words are Ogdenvillese! | Homer: Those burly burgers were tainted! Why did I eat twelve of them? WHY??? | Lisa: Herling!

title: Eternal Moonshine of the Simpson Mind (S19E09)
keys: eternal moonshine of the simpson mind
text: "Eternal Moonshine of the Simpson Mind" is an episode of Season 19 (production code KABF02), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing December 16, 2007. Homer wakes up in the snow with no memory of the previous night and returns home to find his family gone and Santa's Little Helper attacking him. At Moe's Tavern, he learns he asked for a 'Forget-Me-Shot' to erase the last 24 hours, and Chief Wiggum reveals there was a domestic disturbance at his house reported by Ned Flanders. Piecing together fragmented flashbacks, Homer becomes convinced Marge gave herself a black eye and later fears she's cheating on him with Duffman. Seeking clarity, he uses Professor Frink's painful memory-sorting machine and enlists Bart and Lisa, leading to a chaotic detour where past and present versions of Homer get beaten up. Distraught and believing his life is meaningless, Homer heads to Suicide Bridge, where Patty and Selma push him off before he can change his mind. As he falls, his memories return in full: Marge had been secretly planning a surprise party for his completed community service, and the black eye came from a champagne cork accident, not abuse. Homer lands safely on a moon bounce at the party, reunites with his family, and even predicts details of the night using his restored memories, resolving all his misunderstandings. title: Wad Goals (S32E13)
text: "Wad Goals" is an episode of Season 32 (production code QABF06), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing February 28, 2021. After stumbling into a hidden playground behind a hedge, Ralph Wiggum leads Bart, Milhouse, and the other kids to discover a golf club has been operating secretly in the middle of Springfield. Bart and Milhouse land jobs as caddies, with Bart quickly excelling by flattering his client Kent Brockman, while Milhouse bungles his assignment caddying for Mr. Burns. As Bart's earnings grow, he becomes increasingly obsessed with money and flattery, even sucking up to Marge for cash, which deeply unsettles her. Marge tries to warn Homer that their son is changing for the worse, but Homer dismisses her concerns as just how America works. When Bart's newfound wealth causes friction with his friends over a shared ATV, Marge and Lisa start an online petition to shut down the exclusive golf club, inadvertently giving it a controversial acronym that boosts its popularity. To save the club from Marge's petition, Bart convinces club president Bildorf and Mayor Quimby to declare golf an official religion, making it tax-exempt and legally untouchable. Furious at being dropped as Bildorf's caddy despite saving the club, Bart lets his friends destroy the golf course with the ATV. The police then raid the club, revealing it has secretly devolved into a sex cult, and arrest Bildorf, ending the golf club's reign over the town.

title: Funeral for a Fiend (S19E08)
text: "Funeral for a Fiend" is an episode of Season 19 (production code KABF01), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Michael Price, originally airing November 25, 2007. After Homer buys a free battery bundled with a TiVo subscription at Circuit Circus, Marge becomes obsessed with skipping commercials, until a guilty dream about Keith Olbermann convinces her to start watching ads again. One of those ads leads the family to a suspicious new restaurant, which turns out to be a trap set by Sideshow Bob, who has disguised himself as its owner to lure the Simpsons to their deaths. Bob's overly elaborate bomb plot fails when he gets distracted correcting a Shakespeare quote, and he is captured and put on trial. During the trial, Bob paints himself as a sympathetic victim of Bart's childhood torment, and when Bart lunges to stop him from using a vial of nitroglycerin, Bob collapses and is declared dead by Dr. Hibbert. The town turns against Bart and reveres Bob as a martyr, culminating in a lavish funeral, but Bart is convinced by Bob's brother Cecil to make peace at the funeral home. There, Bob reveals he faked his death as part of a scheme to fake-cremate Bart in his place and escape with his equally deranged family. Lisa deduces the ruse just in time, and Homer and Marge rescue Bart from the furnace, leading to Bob and his family's arrest, while an unrepentant Bob vows revenge from his prison cell. Guest starring Kelsey Grammer, John Mahoney, Keith Olbermann, David Hyde Pierce. title: Lisa's Belly (S33E05)
text: "Lisa's Belly" is an episode of Season 33 (production code QABF20), directed by Timothy Bailey and written by Juliet Kaufman, originally airing October 24, 2021. The Simpsons head to what Homer remembers as the wild and dangerous Riot Rivers water park, only to discover it has been rebranded as the safety-obsessed Quiet Rivers. Determined to relive the old thrills, Homer drags Bart and Lisa to the forbidden Devil's Deluge ride, which dumps them into contaminated water. The exposure forces Dr. Hibbert to prescribe a steroid that causes Bart and Lisa to gain noticeable belly weight just as school starts. Bart happily uses his new bulk to bond with the school bullies at their makeshift gym, the Meat Castle, while Lisa spirals into body-image anxiety, worsened when Marge carelessly calls her "chunky." Marge's attempts to fix the problem with new clothes and apologies only deepen Lisa's insecurity, especially when Marge implies Lisa will return to being her "perfect" self once the medication wears off. Patty and Selma try to help Lisa stop caring what others think, but it's a hypnotherapy session with Dr. Wendy Sage that finally gets to the root of the issue, revealing matching childhood wounds in both Lisa's and Marge's minds. Recognizing and sharing this generational pain allows both of them to feel lighter, and the episode closes on the suggestion that everyone, especially Homer, is carrying similar hidden burdens. title: You Don't Have to Live Like a Referee (S25E16)

Homer is recruited to serve as a referee for the FIFA World Cup after impressing officials with his supposed integrity, prompting Lisa to deliver a proud speech about his honesty. Meanwhile, Bart and other family members experience their own culture clashes and comedic mishaps amid the World Cup festivities. Marge's language struggles create friction with locals, including a short-tempered samba school teacher who mocks her reliance on a translation app. As Homer tries to extract himself from the gangster's scheme without getting killed, the family's Brazilian adventure builds to a chaotic climax at the match itself. title: Warrin' Priests: Part One (S31E19)
text: "Warrin' Priests: Part One" is an episode of Season 31 (production code ZABF12), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Pete Holmes, originally airing April 26, 2020. Reverend Lovejoy's dwindling congregation at the First Church of Springfield gets a jolt when charismatic young preacher Bode Wright arrives in town looking for work. Helen Lovejoy, who posted the job listing, hires him as junior minister and even invites him to stay in their home, infuriating her husband. As Homer and Marge attend marriage counseling after Homer secretly sells their house, tension builds between Lovejoy and Bode, culminating in Lovejoy losing his voice right before a big service. Bode steps in, wows the congregation with music and warmth, and quickly becomes the town's favorite spiritual leader, sparking a genuine religious revival that even wins over Homer. Lisa forms a bond with Bode over shared interests like vegetarianism and meditation, while Lovejoy's old-fashioned, tone-deaf humor alienates the crowd further. After the church council fires Lovejoy in favor of Bode, he and Helen travel to Michigan to dig up damaging information about their rival's past. The episode ends on a cliffhanger as Lovejoy uncovers a newspaper article in Traverse City that may reveal a scandal capable of ending Bode's rising influence. title: Homer's Adventures Through the Windshield Glass (S34E22)

text: "Homer's Adventures Through the Windshield Glass" is an episode of Season 34 (production code OABF13), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Tim Long, originally airing May 21, 2023. After storming out of the bank in a rage, Homer drives recklessly while texting Marge and crashes into a fire hydrant, flying through the windshield in slow motion. Guided by Goobie-Woo, Maggie's talking doll, Homer relives the moment he learned that Marge's late father Clarence left her a secret $1,000-a-month inheritance that she never told him about. He grows angrier upon discovering that Bart and Lisa already knew about the money, and imagines wild reasons for Marge's secrecy before learning the truth: she's been using the funds to quietly bail him out of his own disasters. Just as Homer starts to appreciate Marge, Goobie-Woo reveals that Clarence never liked or respected him, prompting a vision of Clarence privately dismissing Homer to Marge. Realizing he must be dead, Homer ends up in Hell, where he's forced to wait in an eternal queue for punishment alongside history's worst tyrants, including a poker game with Clarence, Stalin, and Genghis Khan. Clarence shows Homer a future vision of Lisa dating the insufferable Mercer, helping Homer understand Clarence's disdain for him by seeing his own judgmental reaction mirrored. This epiphany allows Homer to escape Hell and wake up from the crash, though when he tries to tell Marge he's changed, his injuries leave him unable to speak clearly, so Marge simply pays the paramedic for pain relief as Goobie-Woo sings them off. title: Double, Double, Boy in Trouble (S20E03)
text: "Double, Double, Boy in Trouble" is an episode of Season 20 (production code KABF14), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing October 19, 2008. At a lavish party thrown to celebrate Lenny's lottery win, Bart's mischief with runaway Vac-U-Bots ruins the event, leaving Marge furious and Bart's belongings confiscated. Sulking in the bathroom, Bart meets his exact double, Simon Woosterfield, heir to Springfield's richest family, and the two impulsively agree to swap lives. While Simon settles into the modest but loving Simpson household and slowly warms to Marge and Homer's affection, Bart revels in the Woosterfield mansion's luxury and rubs elbows with celebrities like Joe Montana. However, Bart soon notices that his new step-siblings, Devan and Quenly, are unusually cruel, and a conversation with Mr. Burns about his own family's suspicious inheritance history tips Bart off that the siblings may be plotting to kill him for the family fortune. Meanwhile, Lisa grows suspicious of 'Bart's' odd behavior and confronts Simon, forcing him to admit the truth about the switch and the danger Bart is in. The Simpsons rush to save Bart during a ski trip staged by Devan and Quenly, with Homer comically saving the day by turning into a giant snowball. Bart and Simon return to their rightful families, with Simon cryptically reassuring Bart that Devan and Quenly won't be a problem anymore, hinting the two siblings will turn on each other instead. The episode ends with Bart, comforted by Marge's tender bedtime routine, happily deciding that his own life is pretty great after all. Guest starring Joe Montana as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: Why you little... You ruin everything! | Homer: This looks like a job for Captain Crazy! Up! Up! And away! | Homer: Ahhhh! Come on gravity, you used to be cool! | Lisa: Okay, listen, you. I don't know who you are or what you've done with the real Bart, but God help me, I want him back. | Bart: This is the life.

Homer: This looks like a job for Captain Crazy! Up! Up! And away!
Homer: Ahhhh! Come on gravity, you used to be cool!
Lisa: Okay, listen, you. I don't know who you are or what you've done with the real Bart, but God help me, I want him back.
Bart: This is the life.

title: Convenience Airways (S36E08)
text: "Convenience Airways" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF01), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Loni Steele Sosthand, originally airing December 8, 2024. In a congressional hearing, Marge testifies about a chaotic Convenience Airways flight the family took to Louisiana for a Bouvier family boucherie. On the flight, Marge is unexpectedly upgraded to first class, leaving Homer, Bart, Lisa, and Maggie to endure a coach cabin filled with rude, unstable, and downright bizarre passengers, including a mischievous flight attendant named Joel who trades barbs with Bart. As the flight descends into chaos—with fistfights, bathroom cooking, and viral video moments—Homer struggles to keep Maggie calm while trying not to disturb Marge, who is blissfully unaware in first class alongside a drunken Krusty and Drederick Tatum. When the unruly passengers vanish one by one, Homer and Lisa discover they've been dropped into a secret in-flight jail run by the airline as punishment for disruptive behavior. Homer eventually calms a prison riot after misreading a text from baby Maggie as wisdom from Marge, urging the passengers to act with basic decency. Back in court, it's revealed that BurnsCo designed the punitive system, which airline executives want to expand industry-wide, but when Marge objects, she too gets trap-doored away, closing the loop on the story's darkly comic bureaucracy. Guest starring Kate Berlant, John Early, Jay Pharoah, John Pirruccello. Notable quotes: Marge: Oh, my God. I'm turning left. I didn't know planes had a left. | Homer: Aw, come on. You choke out one guy with a seat belt extender and you're labeled for life. | Homer: Somebody shut that brat up! Oh, that's my brat. Stop judging her! | Female passenger: That's not a baby, that's a hate crime. | Homer: They can't do this to us! Buying a ticket gives us the right to do what we want. There's no law in the sky.

Homer: Aw, come on. You choke out one guy with a seat belt extender and you're labeled for life.

title: Abe League of Their Moe (S36E15)
text: "Abe League of Their Moe" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF08), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing April 27, 2025. In a flashback to 1944, a young Abe Simpson watches baseball with his own grandfather, who predicts Abe will one day share the game with his grandson. Decades later, Grampa tries to make that happen by calling Bart, who brushes him off, but he instead bonds with Moe over heckling the Yankees at a game, and the two become fast friends. When Macedonian star Aeropos Walkov announces he's coming to America, Moe and Grampa team up to make him a heartfelt recruitment video, and their sincerity (helped by a shared love of tire fires) convinces him to sign with the Springfield Isotopes. As Walkov's fame grows, Moe becomes his translator and manager, prioritizing money and sponsorships over Grampa's friendship and Bart's wish to meet his hero. Grampa grows disillusioned watching the sport get overrun by gambling ads, and things worsen when Walkov himself becomes hooked on betting, while Bart secretly starts gambling too. At a tense press conference, Moe initially covers up Walkov's guilt-ridden breakdown with fake translations, but Grampa and Bart's arrival forces the truth into the open. Moe publicly confesses his role in exploiting Walkov, blaming the gambling-saturated broadcasts, though he ultimately takes the fall in the ensuing investigation. In the end, Walkov moves on to sign with the newly rebranded San Francisco Draft-Pigs, while Bart continues gambling in secret, only slightly relieved that he isn't losing money. Guest starring Kevin Burkhardt, Jamie Demetriou, Steve Gelbs, Kevin Millar, Jimmy "Jomboy" O'Brien, Chris Rock, Danny Trejo. Notable quotes: Bart: Eh, baseball's just a bunch of guys in tight pants barely moving. I can watch that here. | Moe: Yeah, us, you lovable bag of Alzheimer's. | Chris Rock: What a city! Where else can you get a sandwich at 3:00 a.m. and a gun at the same bodega? | Aeropos Walkov: In Macedonia, our widows chant mournful dirges for your garbage Marlins. | Moe: Sorry, kids, the big lug's teaching himself English by watching Family Guy.

Moe: Sorry, kids, the big lug's teaching himself English by watching Family Guy.

title: Take My Life, Please (S20E10)
text: "Take My Life, Please" is an episode of Season 20 (production code LABF01), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Don Payne, originally airing February 15, 2009. When Mayor Quimby unveils a plaque honoring Vance Connor's success, Homer is reminded of his bitter defeat to Vance in a high school class president election decades earlier. At Moe's Tavern, Lenny and Carl reveal that Principal Dondelinger secretly buried the actual ballot box instead of announcing the results. Determined to learn the truth, Homer digs up the box and has Lisa tally the votes, discovering that he was the real winner all along. Furious, Homer and Bart track down the retired Dondelinger, who explains he hid the results to protect Homer from being mocked, since students had only planned to vote for him as a cruel joke. Still consumed by regret over his lost alternate life, Homer visits Luigi's, where a mysterious old Italian man who stirs the restaurant's sauce offers to show the family a vision of what might have been. In this fantasy, Homer becomes a popular, wealthy class president who marries Marge but never has children, leading Homer to realize that this version of his life is empty and unfulfilling. Yanked back to reality, a depressed Homer sulks until his family cheers him up by revealing a new plaque honoring him has been placed on the Springfield Wall of Fame. Content with his real life, Homer notices another plaque nearby belongs to Principal Skinner, and the family heads off to decide where to eat. Notable quotes: Homer: I'm going to find out what Dondelinger did last summer! Twenty-two years ago! In the winter! | Homer: Detention!? Thanks a lot, you dumb-delinger! | Homer: Guys that popular and confident are never truly happy. | Homer: I would've been a winner, instead of some idiot spending his Saturday night staring into a bowl of sauce. Why did fate do this to me? | Old Italian man: Hey everyone! The stupid fat man's talking to garlic bread!

Homer: Detention!? Thanks a lot, you dumb-delinger!
Homer: Guys that popular and confident are never truly happy.

title: The Town (S28E03)
text: "The Town" is an episode of Season 28 (production code VABF17), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Dave King, originally airing October 9, 2016. After Homer humiliates himself cheering against Boston at Moe's Tavern, he's shocked to discover Bart has become a fan of the rival Boston Americans. Determined to cure his son of this betrayal, Homer plans a 'hate-cation' to Boston, hoping the trip will show Bart how awful the city truly is. Once there, the family is repeatedly surprised: Homer is rescued by an impressively efficient team of doctors after a bobblehead cart accident, while Marge, Lisa, and Maggie discover the city's charm and intellectual culture. Homer himself begins to warm to Boston after trying candlepin bowling with Bart, and soon the whole family decides to relocate there permanently. Life in Boston initially seems perfect—Homer gets a cozy job at a candy factory and Lisa thrives at her new school—but Bart discovers that even detention there is filled with well-behaved, singing students, making him realize the city just isn't built for troublemakers like him. Desperate to get the family to move back, Bart lures Homer into attending a parade celebrating Boston's controversionally-won championship, banking on his father's temper. Sure enough, Homer snaps a Boston hat in half and reignites his hatred of the team's cheating ways, prompting the family's return to Springfield. Back home, Bart has fully flipped to rooting for Boston, Marge is upset about the abrupt move, and Lisa is left daydreaming about the school she left behind.

title: Shoddy Heat (S36E04)
text: "Shoddy Heat" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 35ABF16), directed by Gabriel DeFrancesco and written by Jeff Westbrook, originally airing October 27, 2024. On a scorching day in Springfield, the Simpsons take refuge at the Retirement Castle, where Grampa's feud with Homer over air conditioning is interrupted by police investigating a grave at Shady Oaks that contains two bodies instead of one. A business card for the old Simpson and O'Donnell Detective Agency ties Grampa to the mystery, forcing him to recount his 1982 partnership with Billy O'Donnell and a case involving Agnes Skinner, who suspected her boyfriend Mr. Burns of cheating. As Lisa digs into forensic clues despite Grampa's warnings, she uncovers that Billy vanished the night he and Agnes tailed Burns and Smithers, eventually piecing together a romance between young Grampa and Agnes. Grampa's flashbacks reveal that Burns actually killed Billy, and that Grampa struck a secret deal with Burns guaranteeing Homer's job security no matter how many mistakes he made. When the truth comes out, Homer is touched by the sacrifice Grampa made for him, while Burns cheekily reveals he faked his own death and is living on a tropical island. Agnes admits she manipulated events all along, hoping Grampa would kill Burns so she could inherit his fortune, but she ultimately spares him a confrontation with a kiss instead. The subplot resolves when Lisa learns the second body belongs to Harold Baumgartner, a business card printer buried per his own wishes, closing out the investigation as Ralph comically threatens the precinct with a gun. Guest starring Topher Grace as Billy O'Donnell. Notable quotes: Grampa: You monster! Elder abuse! | Bart: Grampa, you were a private detective? It takes you an hour to find your socks. | Young Grampa: The part where there's someone younger and sexier than you. | Grampa: Got new business cards. "Abe Simpson and nobody. Private investigators." | Grampa: I'd call that an upgrade.
quotes: Grampa: You monster! Elder abuse!
Bart: Grampa, you were a private detective? It takes you an hour to find your socks.
Young Grampa: The part where there's someone younger and sexier than you.
Grampa: Got new business cards. "Abe Simpson and nobody. Private investigators."
Grampa: I'd call that an upgrade.

title: Little Orphan Millie (S19E06)
text: "Little Orphan Millie" is an episode of Season 19 (production code JABF22), directed by Lance Kramer and written by Mick Kelly, originally airing November 11, 2007. At a family picnic, Kirk and Luann Van Houten announce they are remarrying, delighting Milhouse but setting off a chain of odd events. While getting ready for the wedding, Homer casually reveals he has no idea what color Marge's eyes are, prompting an offended Marge to hide her eyes from him until he figures it out. On their honeymoon cruise, Kirk and Luann are tossed overboard during a storm and presumed dead, leaving Milhouse to stay with the Simpsons and spiral into a brooding, poetic persona that unexpectedly makes him the coolest kid at school. As Milhouse's popularity soars at Bart's expense, a jealous and desperate Bart tries everything from krumping to enlisting Milhouse's eccentric Danish relative, 'Uncle Zack,' to win back attention, only to accidentally help Milhouse plan an escape by hot air balloon. Meanwhile, Homer frantically searches the house for clues to Marge's eye color, finally recalling an old love song with Abe's help, which reveals the answer as hazel and reconciles the couple. Bart, realizing he actually misses Milhouse, joins him and Zack on the balloon flight, during which they discover Kirk and Luann alive and stranded on a deserted island. The estranged couple use a makeshift hang-glider to reach the balloon, reuniting with Milhouse, while Zack and Kirk fall into a squabble over their Danish versus Dutch heritage. Notable quotes: Milhouse: Oh, my God! I've become the world's oldest baby. Men don't get their moo-moo from a baa-baa. They get their moo-moo from a big-boy cup! | Homer: Marge, give me a break! I don't know the colors of peoples' eyes! I just judge them on the color of their skin. | Bart: Is it that you're brother and sister? Because you really look a lot alike. | Marge: Stop naming things! | Second Officer: And we have to search all of them -- 'cause they all, you know, connect.
quotes: Milhouse: Oh, my God! I've become the world's oldest baby. Men don't get their moo-moo from a baa-baa. They get their moo-moo from a big-boy cup!
Homer: Marge, give me a break! I don't know the colors of peoples' eyes! I just judge them on the color of their skin.
Bart: Is it that you're brother and sister? Because you really look a lot alike.
Marge: Stop naming things!
Second Officer: And we have to search all of them -- 'cause they all, you know, connect.

title: Do PizzaBots Dream of Electric Guitars? (S32E15)

text: "Do PizzaBots Dream of Electric Guitars?" is an episode of Season 32 (production code QABF08), directed by Jennifer Moeller and written by Michael Price, originally airing March 14, 2021. In a flashback, teenage Homer works at Razzle Dazzle's Pizza-Tainment Palace under Gil Gunderson, DJing alongside a malfunctioning animatronic band until an FBI raid reveals the restaurant was a front for drug trafficking. Back in the present, Homer becomes despondent after passing the old building during Ralph's birthday party, worrying Marge and Moe that he's lost his youthful spark. Bart and Lisa track down the auctioned-off animatronics, discovering that Wakkety Yak has just been sold to filmmaker J. J. Abrams for a Mission: Impossible movie. The kids sneak into Abrams' studio and steal Yak back using BB-8 robots, but Abrams follows them home and pitches an exploitative nine-movie franchise, upsetting Homer further. Homer bonds with Comic Book Guy over shared fandom trauma, and the two begin trolling Abrams online in hopes of tanking his new animatronic-themed film, Agents of P.I.Z.Z.A. At the film's premiere, Homer tries to disrupt the screening, but Grampa intervenes and reminds Abrams that he's the one who truly ruined Homer's childhood, not the movie. Abrams and Homer reconcile, and Abrams reveals he's repurposed the animatronics into frozen yogurt dispensers for the after-party. The episode ends with Comic Book Guy leading the trolls as the newly formed 'Troll Force Five.' Guest starring J. J. Abrams, Greg Grunberg. Notable quotes: Grampa: Son, I don't know quite how to put this, but you're a fool and your dreams are garbage. Now, get out of here before I say something I'll regret. | Gil Gunderson: I'm gonna get those robots back, and start a new kiddie pizza place, then use that as a front to sell even better drugs! | Herman Hermann: I liked the way he would sing about pizza every time I shot him in the chest. | Homer: Six feelings with extra cheese. An order of French feelings, and a super chocolate frosty depression. | Grampa: Son, a movie can't ruin your childhood. I ruined it by being a terrible father.

title: There Will Be Buds (S28E06)
text: "There Will Be Buds" is an episode of Season 28 (production code VABF22), directed by Matthew Faughnan and written by Matt Selman, originally airing November 6, 2016. After a smoke-filled pee-wee football game sends several kids to the hospital, Springfield residents gather to find a safer sport. Kirk, struggling to be heard, suggests lacrosse, and the town agrees to let him coach on the condition that Homer serves as his assistant. The team starts winning, but as Kirk grows increasingly attached to Homer, treating him as his best friend, Homer becomes uncomfortable with the closeness. Kirk overhears Homer venting about how much he secretly dislikes him, and hurt, Kirk quits just before the championship game. With the kids about to forfeit, Homer tracks Kirk down to a strip club where he's hiding out, and after some comic mishaps involving chicken wings and rice burgers, convinces him to return. The team wins the championship, and in a final gag, Homer and Kirk celebrate so hard they both break their wrists and end up sharing a hospital room together. Notable quotes: Homer: Kirk is like a sports genius who everyone hates. | Marge: Worse than Jim Harbaugh? | Lenny: They over-fogged the run-in! | Carl: They put those kids in danger just to psych up the crowd! [yelling] Yeah, are you psyched up now? Huh? Are you?! | Homer: Concessions!!

title: Murder, She Boat (S35E09)
text: "Murder, She Boat" is an episode of Season 35 (production code 35ABF04), directed by Chris Clements and written by Broti Gupta, originally airing December 17, 2023. After Marge finds two stimulus checks stuck to the mailbox, the family uses the money to go on a nerd-culture themed cruise aboard the Pacific Princess Leia, much to Homer's disgust. Comic Book Guy brings a rare Radioactive Man action figure with erroneous Wolverine claws, only for its head to be stolen during a blackout at dinner, and Bart—who holds a grudge after Comic Book Guy destroyed his comic—becomes the prime suspect due to scratches on his face. Lisa refuses to believe her brother is guilty and teams up with fellow passenger and film director Taika Waititi to investigate, interviewing suspects like Milhouse, Sideshow Mel, and Kumiko. Just as Lisa starts to doubt Bart after finding the figure's head under his bed, Rainier Wolfcastle is knocked out before he can reveal the true culprit, and Comic Book Guy himself disappears. Taika accuses a fleeing Comic Book Guy of insurance fraud, but Lisa deduces from a spelling clue on the box that Taika himself swapped in a broken duplicate figure, leading to his arrest. The group eventually finds Comic Book Guy hiding in the ship's gym, devastated that everyone secretly resents him and fearing he's losing his wife's affection. With the mystery solved, Bart is freed and thanks Lisa for standing by him, and Comic Book Guy ultimately throws the prized figure overboard to save his marriage with Kumiko. Guest starring Maurice LaMarche, Taika Waititi. Notable quotes: Comic Book Guy: Behold, I have brought the jewel of my collectible collection. The rarest treasure in all of geekdom: A Radioactive Man action figure accidentally manufactured with Wolverine claws. Gaze upon it and lose your mind. | Kumiko Albertson: When I first met Comic Book Guy, I was his priceless collectible. But now, when we make love, my husband calls out the doll's serial number. | Sideshow Mel: It would! But it didn't. But it could! And if I did, I would lie about it to you now! But I'm not. But I would! | Taika Waititi: We're in the middle of Lake Springfield. I can see the Lard Lad statue from here. | Homer: No, I hate the theme and the people and the boat. But I love the food.

title: Estranger Things (S36E18)
text: "Estranger Things" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF11), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Tim Long, originally airing May 18, 2025. Years earlier, Homer ignores Marge's instructions and lets young Bart and Lisa discover Itchy & Scratchy, sparking a shared obsession that Marge hopes will keep them close forever. In the present, the siblings decide the show is too babyish and move on to separate interests, worrying Marge that they are drifting apart despite their promises to stay close. The story then jumps decades into the future, where Marge has died and Lisa has become a powerful basketball commissioner while Bart secretly runs a scam retirement home out of the family house. When Lisa returns to Springfield for a school speech, she uncovers Bart's fraud, clashes with him over their unequal burdens caring for Homer, and accidentally gets Homer taken away by Senior Protective Services after reporting Bart. Searching the attic for answers, Lisa finds a video will from Marge urging the siblings to stay close, which reignites their bond. Together they stage a ridiculous Itchy & Scratchy-inspired rescue to save Homer from being shipped off to a Florida retirement facility, succeeding just in time to watch a new Itchy & Scratchy reboot as a family. In heaven, Marge is relieved to see her children reconciled before moving on to enjoy the afterlife with Ringo Starr. Guest starring Zooey Deschanel, Max Greenfield, Sarah McLachlan. Notable quotes: Marge: I knew my kids were growing up, but I never thought they'd grow apart. And I think I'm the only one who cares. | Homer: Yeah, but if I may pose a counterargument: Eh, whaddya gonna do? | Bart: Okay, I've told a few fibs, but since when is fraud a crime? | Lenny Leonard: Car drive Lenny crash good? | Lisa: How dare you interrupt my onstage breakdown!

title: Pulpit Friction (S24E18)
text: "Pulpit Friction" is an episode of Season 24 (production code RABF11), directed by Chris Clements and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing April 28, 2013. A bedbug infestation sweeps through Springfield, sending the town into a panic and leaving Reverend Lovejoy struggling to keep his congregation's attention amid the chaos. Into this vacuum steps Elijah Hooper, a charismatic new minister whose calm confidence and modern approach quickly win over nearly everyone in town, overshadowing Lovejoy almost entirely. Only Ned Flanders and Bart remain skeptical of Hooper, suspecting something is off about his sudden rise in popularity, and they team up to track down the disheartened Lovejoy to convince him to reclaim his pulpit. Meanwhile, Marge discovers that her cherished wedding dress was accidentally swapped at the dry cleaners with one of Krusty's clown costumes, sending her on a mission to recover it. Lisa steps in to help her mother, using surprisingly effective detective work to trace the dress through a garbage man, a failed theater production of Mamma Mia, and finally a bankruptcy sale to a young couple. As Bart and Ned dig into Hooper's past, they uncover the truth behind his charm and expose him, paving the way for Lovejoy's redemption and return to his rightful place in the church. In the end, both plots resolve with the town's faith restored in its true reverend and Marge inching closer to reclaiming her prized dress. Guest starring Edward Norton as Elijah Hooper. Notable quotes: Marge: Are there any two wordsmore exciting than "couch shopping"? | Bart: Don't know. Why are your friends such drunks? | Lisa: I'm only eight. I might get married someday, even if it's only a green card marriage to keep a Chinese dissident from being deported. | Ned: He's in a place full of brimstone and exposed flesh. | Bart: You mean he's selling hot tubs?

title: Better Off Ned (S31E16)
text: "Better Off Ned" is an episode of Season 31 (production code ZABF11), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Al Jean (Story); Joel H. Cohen, Jeff Westbrook (Teleplay), originally airing March 15, 2020. After Grampa scares Bart with a dud grenade prank, Bart repeats the trick at a school assembly, causing panic until Ned Flanders heroically throws himself on the grenade to save everyone. When Bart is nearly suspended, Ned steps in as a mentor figure, teaching him fishing, cooking, and choir singing, which leaves Homer feeling jealous and useless. Determined to get his own protégé, Homer stumbles upon a heartbroken Nelson Muntz at the dump and decides to mentor him, partly to spite Bart. Lisa, worried about the family tension, pays for Homer to see a therapist, but his sessions go poorly. When Homer learns the truth about Nelson's troubled home life, Nelson feels betrayed and plots revenge on Bart during the Christian Pride Parade using a mechanism built by Ned and Bart. Homer discovers Nelson's plan just in time and sacrifices himself to save Bart, getting crushed by giant praying hands instead. The incident brings Homer and Bart closer again, while Ned welcomes Nelson and his mother into his own family circle, restoring balance between the two mentor relationships. Notable quotes: Grampa: Yeah, the nursing home finally stopped using me as the placebo and gave me real meds. | Superintendent Chalmers: Well, Simpson, thanks to you, now no one can bring grenades to school. | Ned Flanders: I can make that real blood, you little punk. | Dr. Hibbert: Mm. Remarkable. I thought the only way to turn Bart into a little angel was a downed power line at a water park. | Nelson Muntz: I get my hair cut by hiding in the bushes when the gardener comes by.

title: The Winter of His Content (S25E14)
text: "The Winter of His Content" is an episode of Season 25 (production code SABF09), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by Kevin Curran, originally airing March 16, 2014. When the Retirement Castle is shut down for health violations, Marge takes pity on Grampa and two of his elderly friends and lets them move into the Simpson household. At first Homer is welcoming, but he soon starts adopting the habits and mindset of the old-timers, wearing sock garters, complaining about his health, and generally acting decades older than he is. Marge grows increasingly annoyed as Homer's newfound 'old person lifestyle' turns him into a version of his own father, and she struggles to get her husband to act like himself again. Meanwhile, at school, Bart is unexpectedly pulled into Springfield Elementary's bully clique when Nelson, Jimbo, and Dolph name him an honorary bully and give him a strange necklace as a symbol of initiation. Reluctant but unable to refuse, Bart is dragged along to a citywide 'Bully Summit' where bullies from other schools gather. Bart must navigate his discomfort with this new social role while figuring out how to extract himself from the group. By the episode's end, Marge manages to snap Homer out of his premature old-age routine, restoring some balance at home, while Bart's brief stint among the bullies comes to its own resolution. Guest starring Kevin Michael Richardson as Chester, Julius Hibbert's father, and SAT Prepper. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: Aw, Lou, you got a suspicious mind, you know? title: Lisa the Drama Queen (S20E09)
text: "Lisa the Drama Queen" is an episode of Season 20 (production code KABF22), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing January 25, 2009. Homer takes Bart and Lisa to the Springfield Recreation Center, where Lisa meets a kindred creative spirit, Juliet Hobbes, in an art class. The two girls quickly bond over shared interests and begin inventing an elaborate fantasy world called Equalia, writing a book together and even crafting paper models of its characters. As their friendship deepens, Juliet increasingly uses Equalia as an escape from tension with her strict, intellectual parents, and Lisa starts to worry as her own schoolwork suffers from spending so much time immersed in the fantasy. When Marge insists Lisa cut back on seeing Juliet, the girls instead run away together, hiding out in an abandoned seafood-themed restaurant they imagine as an Equalia castle. There they're captured by bullies Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney, but Kearney becomes strangely enchanted by their Equalia stories and turns on his friends, allowing the girls to escape. Once safe, Lisa admits she no longer wants to pretend Equalia is real and would rather live in the real world, which devastates and angers Juliet, ending their friendship. Months later, a rejection letter for their book pushes Lisa to move on, while Homer channels the experience into his own goofy fantasy reimagining of the family. Guest starring Emily Blunt as Juliet Hobbes, Fall Out Boy as end credits performers. Notable quotes: Comic Book Guy: Welcome to Shaolin Kung Fu. title: Fan-ily Feud (S34E18)
text: "Fan-ily Feud" is an episode of Season 34 (production code OABF11), directed by Timothy Bailey and written by Broti Gupta, originally airing April 23, 2023. At an Isotopes game, Homer and Bart are drowned out by a crowd of girls celebrating pop star Ashlee Starling's new single, and when a reporter mistakes Homer for a fan, he repeats Bart's dismissive insult and it airs publicly. Ashlee Starling's devoted fan army, the Murmur Nation, turns on Homer, subjecting him to glitter-bomb car crashes, bird attacks at work, and social ostracism, while Bart refuses to take the blame. Desperate, Homer is rescued by rival pop star Echo and her fanbase, the Echolaliacs, who offer him protection, sparking an all-out street war between the two fandoms that trashes Springfield. Meanwhile, Bart infiltrates the Murmur Nation (which secretly includes Lisa) to use its members for pranks, but gets expelled for not being enthusiastic enough about a fan's dog. Ashlee Starling manipulates Marge with a fancy dinner and alcohol, then releases a spiteful song exposing the low points of Homer and Marge's marriage. Learning that Bart and Lisa orchestrated the attacks against him, a hurt Homer retreats to Echo Studios for several days. With Echo's help, he writes and performs a heartfelt song for his family that repairs the rift and reminds everyone of his love for them. The warring fandoms eventually call off their feud, and the Simpsons reflect on the dangers of fanatical devotion before rushing off, running late for church. Guest starring Billy Eichner as Krusty the Clown, Jade Novah as Ashlee Starling and Echo. Notable quotes: Bart: I disagree. title: My Life as a Vlog (S34E12)
text: "My Life as a Vlog" is an episode of Season 34 (production code OABF05), directed by Debbie Mahan and written by Jessica Conrad, originally airing January 1, 2023. The episode unfolds as an unseen YouTube viewer clicks through a series of recommended videos chronicling the meteoric rise and mysterious disappearance of "The Simpson Family Vlog." After a viral clip of baby Maggie causes a sensation, the family parlays their fame into individual YouTube series, moves into a lavish sponsored mansion, and becomes wildly wealthy. Milhouse, posing online as anonymous whistleblower "Truth Wizard," leaks behind-the-scenes footage exposing that the family's wholesome content is largely staged, including Homer's off-camera temper and Lisa's fake beach cleanups. Tension escalates when Homer, desperate for sponsorship money, forces a terrified Maggie into a promotional Nom-Noms stunt, straining the family's relationship. After an ominous announcement teaser, the Simpsons vanish from the internet entirely, spawning wild conspiracy theories from Frink, Skinner, and others about kidnapping or alien possession. A mob of fans and rival vloggers eventually tracks down the mansion and discovers the family trapped inside a panic room whose door was installed backwards by an inexperienced NFT-house company. Having survived on unused sponsor products, the Simpsons emerge having reconciled their differences and vow to quit vlogging for good. The framing viewer is revealed to be author George R. R. Martin, who abandons the videos in frustration to get back to writing, only to be distracted again by an unrelated clip of drag queens fighting. Guest starring Bob the Drag Queen, Michael Rapaport, Monét X Change. Notable quotes: Homer: Come on in. Take your shoes off first. All 50 million of you. [laughs] | Mike Wegman: Leave Homer Simpsons alone! Leave him alone! | Homer: I'm getting a hammer. | Marge: We were trapped, and it was all Homer's fault. | Professor Frink: Um... in summary, I have concluded that the Simpsons are being held hostage by a major tech company.

title: Homer and Her Sisters (S36E09)
text: "Homer and Her Sisters" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF03), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Nick Dahan, originally airing December 15, 2024. Homer ruins Patty and Selma's birthday celebration at an escape room by wasting hints and insulting the sisters, deepening their long-standing feud with him. Meanwhile, Krusty is coaxed by his Aunt Sadie into confronting the fact that he's isolated from his own crew, including Sideshow Mel and Wayne the Grip, who host a podcast he didn't know existed. As Homer refuses to reconcile with the twins, Marge fakes an injury to lure her sisters home so Sadie can mediate their family conflict, only for Sadie to point out that Marge herself thrives on being the family's perpetual victim and peacekeeper, which enrages Marge. Determined to prove he can get along with Patty and Selma without Marge as a buffer, Homer takes them out for a day of bowling, drinks, and a movie, and they genuinely bond, leaving Marge to realize she might be the actual source of the family's dysfunction. Simultaneously, Lindsey Naegle turns Sadie's psychological insights into a reality show called 'The Problem Is You,' featuring the Simpsons and other Springfield families airing their grievances. During the show's chaotic season finale, old arguments resurface, Marge insists real relationship problems can't be fixed in 30 minutes, and the families dissolve into fighting once more. Tragedy strikes when a stage prop mishap caused by Percival kills Sadie, and at her funeral Krusty remains oblivious to any personal growth until getting a literal flick to snap him back to his old self. Guest starring Ike Barinholtz as Wayne the Grip, Susie Essman as Sadie Krustofsky, Jay Pharoah as Drederick Tatum. title: Treehouse of Horror XXIX (S30E04)
text: "Treehouse of Horror XXIX" is an episode of Season 30 (production code XABF16), directed by Matthew Faughnan and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing October 21, 2018. This Halloween special opens with the Simpsons entering an oyster-eating contest that turns out to be a trap set by the cosmic entity Cthulhu, whom Homer improbably defeats and then eats. In 'Intrusion of the Pod-Y Switchers,' an alien impersonating a Mapple executive unleashes spores that replace Springfield's citizens with docile copies, and after Bart and Lisa's escape attempt fails, Lisa is taken to a seemingly utopian alien world that turns out to have its own consumerist problems. In 'Multiplisa-ty,' Lisa develops multiple violent personalities after being pushed too far by Bart's mockery and cheating, trapping and eventually killing Milhouse and Nelson while Bart scrambles to survive her escalating rage, only earning a reprieve when he owns up to his misdeeds. The final segment, 'Geriatric Park,' finds Mr. Burns opening a retirement community where elderly residents are injected with dinosaur DNA, granting them youthful vigor until rising temperatures trigger a monstrous transformation. The rejuvenated seniors, including Grampa and Jacqueline Bouvier, go on a rampage against visitors, but Lisa manages to calm Grampa by appealing to his need for respect, allowing the family to flee via helicopter—piloted, unsettlingly, by a pterodactyl version of Agnes Skinner. Notable quotes: Announcer: Here at Geriatric Park, we combine speculative theories with untested technologies to give our seniors a better life. This installment is made up of 3 segments (also called Treehouse of Horror 29): "Intrusion of the Pod-Y Switchers", "Multiplisa-ty", and "Geriatric Park".

title: Replaceable You (S23E04)
text: "Replaceable You" is an episode of Season 23 (production code NABF21), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Stephanie Gillis, originally airing November 6, 2011. Bart initially struggles to find a science fair project while Lisa boasts about her doom-and-gloom asteroid prediction model. After recruiting the reluctant Martin Prince, Bart builds the Robopet, a robotic baby seal, which becomes a surprise hit at the fair and later a beloved companion for the elderly residents of the Springfield Retirement Castle. Meanwhile, Homer gets a seemingly perfect new assistant, Roz Davis, who turns out to be secretly undermining him to Mr. Burns and stealing credit for his work. When funeral directors, worried that happy seniors mean fewer deaths, sabotage the Robopets to turn violent, one resident is killed and the toys are impounded, prompting Bart and Martin to enlist Professor Frink and a group of nerds to break the robots out and fix them. Simultaneously, Homer discovers Roz's aversion to physical touch and uses this knowledge, along with Ned Flanders' help, to expose her true nature during a company awards ceremony, causing her to attack Mr. Burns and get fired. With the Robopets repaired and returned, the retirement home residents celebrate, and even in the afterlife the deceased resident joins in the joyous dancing. Bart earns newfound respect from Lisa for his invention's positive impact, while Homer reclaims his rightful place at the plant. Guest starring Jane Lynch as Roz Davis. Notable quotes: Roz Davis: Who told you?! | Homer: I wont say, but his initials are S.F. | Roz: Stupid Flanders!

title: Forgive and Regret (S29E18)
text: "Forgive and Regret" is an episode of Season 29 (production code XABF09), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing April 29, 2018. After losing a pickle-egg eating bet at Moe's, Homer wrecks his car and unwittingly sells it into the Springfield Demolition Derby, leading the family to attend the event. Amid the chaos of the derby, Grampa suffers a heart attack and, believing he's dying, confesses to Homer that he once did something terrible involving Mona and threw away something important connected to her. Homer forgives him, but when Grampa unexpectedly recovers thanks to a new drug, Homer is left furious that his forgiveness was given under false pretenses. The two clash bitterly, trying and failing to reconcile through a bar visit and an escape-room outing, until Homer finally reveals to the family that Grampa destroyed a box of Mona's recipes out of anger years ago and lied about it. Determined to make amends, Grampa sets off to retrieve the box from a cliff where he'd discarded it, and Homer follows him into a dangerous climb that nearly costs them both their lives. Though the box turns out to be empty, they discover that a diner owner had found and used Mona's recipes for years, and she happily returns them to Homer. The episode ends with father and son reconciling over a shared meal, while Homer also recovers his car—only to be scratched by Snowball II, who had been trapped inside during the derby the whole time. Guest starring Glenn Close as Mona Simpson. Notable quotes: Homer: Mom left, but you were there. Frankly a little drunk, sometimes not there, but you were always there. | Lisa: Oh, I hate confrontation. | Bart: So just leave your body. | Lisa: I never thought I'd say this word, but here it comes — coot!

After Lisa overhears Marge admit she doesn't actually enjoy Lisa's jazz saxophone playing, Lisa feels hurt and starts distancing herself from her mother, even refusing to wear the pearl necklace Marge once gave her. Determined to repair their relationship, Marge takes Lisa on a mother-daughter trip to Capital City, but her efforts to bond only seem to push Lisa further away. As a last resort, Marge brings Lisa to see a cheesy musical called 'Bad News Bears: The Musical,' where Lisa realizes she has been just as dismissive of Marge's tastes as Marge was of hers. After the show, they meet the musical's star, Andrew Rannells, who gently calls Lisa out for ignoring her mother's attempts at connection. Lisa and Marge reconcile, culminating in Lisa singing atop a Capital City building. Meanwhile, back in Springfield, Bart grows frustrated that his pranks no longer fool anyone, so he enlists baby Maggie as an unwitting partner in a new round of tricks targeting Rod, Todd, and Gil. Their prank spree comes to an abrupt halt when Bart tries to fool Homer by disguising Maggie as a baby version of Bart, prompting Homer to nearly throttle her. The episode ends with the family settling back into their usual routines, with Lisa rejoining her friends and Marge finding peace with her daughter's individuality. Guest starring Andrew Rannells. While on a school research trip, Lisa is stunned to find that Sideshow Bob has reinvented himself as the chief scientist at a massive chemical engineering company. Despite Bart's warnings, Lisa is drawn to Bob's cultured intellect and convinces her family to let her get to know him better, even as her instincts warn her something is off. It turns out Bob has been secretly developing dangerous genetic engineering experiments, and his ambitions spiral out of control when he uses his own research on himself, transforming into a monstrous, out-of-control creature. Bart and Lisa must team up to stop Bob's rampage before he can cause widespread destruction with his mutated abilities. Meanwhile, Marge reluctantly takes charge of a teen church group's abstinence education program after all the more desirable volunteer positions are taken. Her attempts to discuss healthy sexuality with the teens go awkwardly, especially with Ned Flanders' overly restrictive views clashing with her more practical approach. The subplot builds to a chaotic climax involving the church youth, mirroring the escalating madness of Bob's plot. In the end, Bob is defeated and neutralized, and Marge's group survives its bumpy educational journey with some lessons learned about honesty and boundaries. Elon Musk crash-lands his rocket in the Simpsons' backyard, claiming he's in Springfield searching for inspiration. Homer quickly befriends him and brings him along to the power plant, where Musk realizes Homer's offhand "Homerisms" are a goldmine of inventive ideas. Musk uses this inspiration to pitch Mr. Burns a series of flashy new projects, including a magnetohydrodynamic generator, a Hyperloop, self-driving cars, and the mysterious "Glavinator," all while refusing Burns' attempts to hire him outright. While the town celebrates these innovations, Smithers grows suspicious of Musk's true motives, and Bart and Lisa sneak off in one of the new self-driving cars, disabling its autopilot and causing chaos. It's eventually revealed that the plant is hemorrhaging $50 million a quarter because of Musk's schemes, prompting Burns to order massive layoffs that cost Lenny, Carl, and other plant workers their jobs. Homer, upset that his friendship with Musk led to this disaster for his coworkers, decides—with Marge's encouragement—to end the friendship gently. After surviving an assassination attempt by Burns meant for Musk, Homer thanks him but still breaks off their friendship, and the two share a farewell hug before Musk departs for space, briefly returning to retrieve a stowaway Lisa and leave the family a futuristic birdhouse as a parting gift. title: Waverly Hills 9-0-2-1-D'oh (S20E19)
text: "Waverly Hills 9-0-2-1-D'oh" is an episode of Season 20 (production code LABF10), directed by Michael Polcino and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing May 3, 2009. After overindulging in free samples of a trendy bottled water, Marge is forced to use the restroom at Springfield Elementary and is horrified to see how run-down and neglected the school has become. Determined to give Bart and Lisa a better education, she and Homer rent a cheap, run-down apartment in the wealthy Waverly Hills district so the kids can enroll in the district's elite school, while Homer stays behind in their real house. At Waverly Hills Elementary, Bart stages a fake arrest by Chief Wiggum to build his tough-guy reputation, while Lisa struggles to fit in until Bart spreads a rumor that she's friends with pop star Alaska Nebraska, instantly making her popular. When the family learns a city inspector will visit to verify residency, Homer moves into the sham apartment, reveling in a carefree bachelor lifestyle with two college students while he and Marge rekindle their romance long-distance. Lisa's popularity collapses after she sneaks backstage to beg Alaska Nebraska for help and is rebuffed and thrown out, exposing her lie to the fickle friends who abandon her. The inspector nearly fails the family until toys and evidence convince him kids truly live there, but Bart and Lisa beg to return to their old school and lives, preferring genuine acceptance over a fake persona. The family reunites at their real home, with Homer and Marge nostalgically repurposing the backyard treehouse as their new 'love nest,' annoying Bart. text: "The Flandshees of Innersimpson" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF05), directed by Chris Clements and written by Dan Vebber, originally airing March 30, 2025. During a family road trip, the Simpsons notice billboards celebrating wealthy teenage DJs, inspiring Homer to push Bart into becoming one himself. After a destructive party and a humiliating public dispute, Ned finally reaches his breaking point, returns Homer's last borrowed item, and vows never to speak to him again—delighting Homer at first. Over the following months, Homer tries increasingly desperate schemes to force Ned to break his silence, from disguises to stealing a nativity Jesus, but nothing works, and he begins to spiral into loneliness. Marge urges Homer to write a genuine apology, but when he finally does, Ned reveals the letter only proves Homer knowingly wronged him for years, and Ned furiously reclaims and destroys everything he'd ever lent the Simpsons. A chaotic car chase lands both men in court, where Judge Harm sentences them to couples counseling instead of jail. Their therapist eventually turns to a hallucinogenic drug, sending Homer and Ned into a surreal shared vision where they see how much they secretly value each other. They reconcile with a hug, restoring their status quo, though Homer immediately reverts to his old borrowing habits by swiping Ned's newspaper the next morning. title: Homerland (S25E01)

When Homer fails to return home from a nuclear plant convention with Lenny and Carl, the family panics until he shows up acting strangely calm, sober, and health-conscious. Lisa becomes convinced her father has been brainwashed after overhearing Chief Wiggum discuss a terrorist threat and spotting Homer praying on a mat and marking an 'X' on a blueprint of the power plant. Ignored by her distracted mother, Lisa secretly contacts the FBI and is assigned jumpy, unstable Agent Annie Crawford to investigate. As Annie tries to extract information from Homer, Lisa sneaks into the plant disguised as a technician to stop him from causing a disaster. Homer reveals the truth: he was actually picked up by environmental activists who detoxed him from alcohol, and his 'device' is just a foul-smelling canister meant to shut down the plant to protect the environment, not blow it up. text: "In the Name of the Grandfather" is an episode of Season 20 (production code LABF11), directed by Ralph Sosa and written by Matt Marshall, originally airing March 17, 2009 (UK/Ireland), March 22, 2009 (USA). After buying a hot tub and neglecting a family gathering, Homer resolves to make it up to Grampa by fulfilling his wish to revisit O'Flanagan's Pub in Dunkilderry, Ireland, where he once had the best night of his life. The family arrives to find Ireland transformed into a modern, tech-driven society, and the old pub is nearly empty since its patrons have traded drinking for yuppie pursuits. While Marge, Bart, and Lisa tour famous Irish sights like the Giant's Causeway, Blarney Castle, and the Guinness Brewery, Homer and Grampa settle in for a long night of drinking at the pub. The next morning, they discover they've drunkenly bought the failing bar from its owner, Tom O'Flanagan. Struggling to attract customers, Homer calls on Moe Szyslak, who suggests exploiting Ireland's smoking ban by turning the pub into an illegal 'smokeasy.' The scheme brings in brisk business until Irish authorities raid and shut them down. Homer and Grampa are fined and deported back to America, with a judge quipping that America is where Ireland sends its idiots and half-wits, punctuated by a cameo of the bumbling Chief Wiggum. Guest starring Glen Hansard, Markéta Irglová, Colm Meaney. Notable quotes: Homer: Why don't you join us, Flanders? Are you afraid to get your moustache wet? | Bart: Come on, Ned. Baptize your buns. | Grampa: Moe?! You shipped yourself here? | Moe Szyslak: No, it's how you fly coach on Delta now. | Grampa: You good-for-nothing jellyfish!

title: The Winter of Our Monetized Content (S31E01)

text: "The Winter of Our Monetized Content" is an episode of Season 31 (production code YABF19), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Ryan Koh, originally airing September 29, 2019. After embarrassing himself on a sports call-in show, Homer decides to start his own internet show, 'Walkoff Homer,' but Bart's mocking interruptions turn into an armpit-farting brawl that raccoons stumble into, and the resulting video goes viral. Slick agent Warburton Parker swoops in to monetize Bart and Homer's newfound fame, coaching them to stage increasingly commercialized fights and cash in on sponsorships like Buzz Cola and a restaurant tie-in. As the money rolls in, the father-son duo become minor celebrities, but when a candid moment of them hugging leaks online, their fanbase turns on them for breaking the 'brand.' Meanwhile, at school, Lisa accidentally starts a food fight and is blamed after her joking explanation backfires, landing her in detention just as the school outsources its punishment system to Lindsey Naegle's privatized R.O.C.C. facility. Detention becomes a for-profit labor operation making license plates, prompting the students to organize a strike, which forces teachers to take over the manual labor instead. Parker tries to revive Bart and Homer's fading fame with a violent 'Mortal Kombat Live Online' stunt for Netflix, but the pair can't bring themselves to actually hurt each other, and the stream flops with only Maggie watching. In the end, Homer abandons the monetized spectacle and returns to his original passion project, inviting his sports rival Anger Watkins onto a marathon episode of 'Walkoff Homer.' title: Loan-a Lisa (S22E02)
text: "Loan-a Lisa" is an episode of Season 22 (production code MABF17), directed by Matthew Faughnan and written by Valentina L. Garza, originally airing October 3, 2010. Grampa decides to give each family member $50 from his savings before he dies, setting off two separate schemes. Marge accidentally buys an expensive designer handbag, discovers that carrying it earns her better treatment at restaurants, and this inspires Homer to start a scam where he and Marge buy pricey goods, use them, and return them for refunds. Meanwhile, Lisa invests her $50 in Nelson's bike-repair business, Snot Wheels, through a microloan website, and the business booms so quickly that Nelson considers dropping out of school to run it full time. Lisa tries to convince him education still matters by taking him to an entrepreneurs' expo, but meeting a successful college dropout like Mark Zuckerberg only strengthens Nelson's resolve to quit. Homer's return-scam subplot collapses when he's caught and publicly shamed on a hidden-camera consumer-fraud show hosted by Chris Hansen. Nelson's business also implodes when the cheap glue holding his bikes together fails, ruining his product and his fledgling company. Humbled, Nelson decides to stay in school after all, and he and Lisa end the episode bonding at a roller rink, accidentally knocking over Zuckerberg in the process. title: Simpsorama (S26E06)
text: "Simpsorama" is an episode of Season 26 (production code SABF16), directed by Bob Anderson and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing November 9, 2014. When Springfield Elementary buries a time capsule containing Milhouse's rabbit's foot and a sandwich tainted with Bart's germs, the mix combines with radioactive ooze to create disastrous mutant creatures a thousand years later. In the present, Bender arrives from the future with a secret mission to kill Homer, since Homer and Marge's future child is somehow responsible for the chaos plaguing New New York. Bender bonds with Homer over beer and mischief, making him unable to complete his assassination, prompting the Planet Express crew—Leela, Fry, Farnsworth, Hermes, Zoidberg, and Amy—to travel back in time themselves to finish the job. Working together with Professor Frink, the two crews determine that digging up the time capsule is the key to stopping the future catastrophe, but the mutant creatures destroy the time portal before they can act, stranding most of the Simpsons and the Futurama crew in the ruined future. There, Homer battles the Bart-mutants while Lisa devises a clever plan to lure the creatures into Madison Cube Garden using fake Butterfinger bars so the Planet Express ship can launch them into space. Meanwhile, back in the past, Bender and baby Maggie spend their time gambling and squandering money at the horse track. With the crisis resolved and the portal repaired, the Simpsons return home, and Bender powers down in their basement for another thousand years. The episode closes with a coda on Omicron Persei 8, where Lrrr and Ndnd bicker over the crashed, monster-filled Madison Cube Garden. Guest starring John DiMaggio, David Herman, Phil LaMarr, Maurice LaMarche, Katey Sagal, Peter Sagal, Lauren Tom, Frank Welker, Billy West. Notable quotes: Bender: My name is Bender and I come from... [ominous] ...the future! | Homer: Prove it. What happens to Homer Simpson in the future? | Bender: I don't know. You die? | Scruffy: No, they just got my mustache. But a life without a mustache ain't worth living. | Professor Farnsworth: Little girl, time machines are physical impossibilities. We teleported through a singularity that I quantum entangled to Bender under the guise of fixing his collar.

title: Let's Go Fly a Coot (S26E20)
text: "Let's Go Fly a Coot" is an episode of Season 26 (production code TABF13), directed by Chris Clements and written by Jeff Westbrook, originally airing May 3, 2015. At Milhouse's absurdly lavish birthday party, Homer learns the Van Houtens went into debt to throw it, prompting him to start sabotaging other kids' extravagant parties out of principle. When the birthday party committee catches him, the Simpson kids are banned from ever having parties again unless Homer redeems himself by throwing Rod Flanders a spectacular party. At that party, Grampa reconnects with his old Air Force buddies, but Homer dismisses him as useless and refuses to let him socialize, angering the veterans, who force Homer at gunpoint to apologize and admit he loves his father. Meanwhile, Bart falls for Milhouse's visiting Dutch cousin Annika and takes up vaping to impress her, buying her e-cigarettes and getting caught by Marge in the process. When Bart learns Annika is being sent home, Grampa inspires him with a story about a reckless plane stunt he once pulled to impress a girl named Sunny, who turns out to be Mona Simpson. Bart rushes to the airport for a grand gesture, but instead rejects Annika, revealing he'd grown tired of her complaining, and dumps a bag of e-cigarettes on the crowd as she storms off cursing in Dutch. Milhouse, unfazed by rejection dynamics within his family, suggests Bart date another cousin, showing he's fine with marrying relatives to strengthen family ties. In a closing gag, Homer turns Grampa's disliked steak into vapor for an e-cigarette, which Grampa declares the best steak he's ever 'breathed.' Guest starring Glenn Close as Mona Simpson, Carice van Houten as Annika Van Houten. Notable quotes: Homer: Dad I apologize. I only say this at gunpoint, but it's true. I love you. | Grampa: That's Mock Rickly, my old Air Force buddy. | Grampa: That's the kind of mix up that used to happen when I was in the Marines. | Marge: Geez kids, guess you've had your last birthday. You're going to stay your current ages for the rest of your lives.

title: The Miseducation of Lisa Simpson (S31E12)
text: "The Miseducation of Lisa Simpson" is an episode of Season 31 (production code ZABF06), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing February 16, 2020. Captain McCallister spends decades hunting sunken treasure near Springfield, only to lose it when his wife tips off Mayor Quimby to redraw the town's boundaries and claim it as municipal property. Marge persuades the town to use the windfall to build a flashy new STEM Academy, enlisting John Legend for a musical pitch. Bart and Lisa enroll at the new school, where Lisa is funneled into an advanced 'gifted' track while Bart, thrilled by gamified lessons, is unknowingly being trained for menial future jobs like elder care and warehouse work. As Lisa digs into the school's algorithm-driven curriculum, she uncovers that most students are being groomed for low-wage servant labor while automation eliminates traditional careers. Meanwhile, Homer tries to convince his fellow power plant workers that human labor still matters, staging a stunt to prove machines can't replace him, even as Mr. Burns quietly brings in robots anyway. Lisa and Bart, aided by reluctant CEO Zane Furlong, expose the school's true purpose to the student body, prompting a wave of scathing reviews that crash and destroy the academy's servers. The students return to their old, now-repurposed school building, left to wonder what jobs will remain for humans as technology advances unchecked. The episode closes with Zane delivering food via a gig app and a bleak vision of a future where humans serve an all-powerful machine, alongside a comedic aside of Superintendent Chalmers seeking widows on a riverboat cruise.
