title: The Fat Blue Line (S31E03)
text: "The Fat Blue Line" is an episode of Season 31 (production code YABF22), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Bill Odenkirk, originally airing October 13, 2019. During the San Castellaneta Festival, Jason Momoa regales the crowd with the gruesome legend of a martyred saint just before a wave of pickpocketing sweeps through the townsfolk. State investigator Lenora Carter takes over the case from Chief Wiggum, humiliating him and sidelining him from his own department. Using Homer's famously large backside as bait, the police plant a tracking device in his wallet, leading them to a storage unit stuffed with stolen goods where Fat Tony and his uncle are caught and framed for the crime. Wiggum, despondent over being pushed aside, nonetheless senses that Fat Tony is innocent and visits him in prison to get the real story. Fat Tony reveals his rock-solid alibi of singing alone in his room, then agrees to wear a wire to help expose the true culprit, his old associate Johnny Tightlips, who betrayed him to seize control of the Springfield Mafia. During the sting at Luigi's, Homer wanders in at the wrong moment and takes a bullet in the buttocks, which Wiggum bravely sucks out to save him. With Homer recovering safely at the hospital and Fat Tony's name cleared, Wiggum's confidence as a police officer is restored, and the trio toast to a job well done. Guest starring Joe Mantegna as Fat Tony, Jason Momoa as himself, Bob Odenkirk as the mob lawyer. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: I can tell he's innocent, with a certainty you can only develop putting hundreds of innocent people in jail. | Lenora Carter: You are the worst police officer I've ever had the pleasure of humiliating in front of his men. | Fat Tony: Whatever you think I want you to do, just do the opposite! | Chief Wiggum: Ah, you work with two guys all your life and you think you know 'em. Betrayed by Lou and, uh, the other guy. What is his name again? I-I want to say Greg. | Homer: Dear Lord, please bring back plastic straws. The paper ones get soggy so fast.

title: Parahormonal Activity (S37E11)
text: "Parahormonal Activity" is an episode of Season 37 (production code 37ABF03), directed by Chris Clements and written by Loni Steele Sosthand, originally airing December 14, 2025. In the near future, Marge finds herself struggling to manage her teenage children Bart and Lisa as they navigate the awkward changes of puberty, while also noticing troubling signs of her own aging and mood swings. As Homer helps Ned Flanders write wedding vows for his upcoming marriage to Pam, Marge suspects she is entering perimenopause after suffering hot flashes and emotional outbursts, and even considers Botox after a chance meeting with Artie Ziff, who no longer feels attracted to her. Tension boils over when Marge discovers Bart viewing inappropriate content and confiscates the family's devices, only for Homer to install an internet-connected smart fridge that undermines her efforts. Meanwhile, Lisa hides her first period from Marge after their earlier argument about the burdens of womanhood, leaving Marge devastated that she failed as a mother. Homer's own medical treatment for erectile dysfunction spirals out of control, causing him to behave erratically and eventually take Marge's menopause medication before Ned's wedding, resulting in an unexpectedly heartfelt speech instead of a roast. After a chaotic car ride to the wedding driven by Bart, Marge and Lisa reconcile, with Marge assuring her she doesn't have to perform on stage—only to find Lisa performing anyway, on her own terms, showing her growing independence. Guest starring Lindsay Lohan, Jon Lovitz, Megan Mullally. Notable quotes: Marge: Maybe 43 is the year I change my hairstyle. No, I don't have that kind of courage. | Maggie: Please. Don't let Bart drive. It's too scary. He drives so wiggly and everybody honks at us and yells bad words and shows us fingers! | Marge: Heroin. I've heard it's amazing, but I'm not sure it's for me. | Homer: Little boys will stare at a rock if it's got big boobs. Ooh. Look, a rock with big boobs. | Lisa: What tone did you take when you found out your mother was a raging hypocrite?

title: McMansion & Wife (S35E03)
text: "McMansion & Wife" is an episode of Season 35 (production code OABF20), directed by Debbie Bruce Mahan and written by Dan Vebber, originally airing October 22, 2023. The Simpsons meet their new neighbors, Anne and Thayer Blackburn, and Homer grows suspicious when Thayer—a Lambuggini dealer—starts showering him with friendship, fearing it's a sales tactic. As Homer bonds with Thayer over pickleball, ice cream, and double dates, he casually agrees to sign whatever documents Thayer wants, not realizing he's approved a massive home renovation next door. Meanwhile, at Springfield Elementary, an anti-bullying presentation backfires spectacularly, emboldening Nelson to bully even more students than before. Lisa fights back by posting embarrassing videos of Nelson online, forcing him to back off until he hires tech-savvy classmate Hubert Wong to help him regain control and retaliate. Homer discovers the Blackburns' house has become an enormous McMansion blocking his sunlight, revealing that Thayer's kindness was really a bribe to smooth over the construction. Lisa and Hubert eventually abandon their online feud, realizing it could hurt their college prospects, while Bart and Nelson simply forget why they were fighting and reconcile on the playground. Hubert then uncovers that Evergreen Terrace sits on a historically protected site, meaning the Blackburns' mansion violates preservation laws and can't be expanded further—though it also means the Simpsons can't get repairs done on their own home. Homer returns the borrowed Lambuggini to Thayer and drives off with Marge, settling back into their normal, humble life. Guest starring Dick Van Dyke as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: Hey, I have friends in this neighborhood. There's the guy whose lawn I used as a shortcut, the guy whose mailbox crashed into our car, and Mrs. Bad Halloween candy. | Homer: See, Marge? Strangling the boy has paid off. Just kidding. I don't do that anymore. Times have changed. | Homer: Nothing should be named food that isn't food. | Homer: I hate phonies. At least I pretend to because I think it's cool. | Jebediah Springfield: Eh, we better stop here 'cause the horses are dead. Spring, field? We'll call it Fieldspring.

title: Four Regrettings and a Funeral (S25E03)
text: "Four Regrettings and a Funeral" is an episode of Season 25 (production code RABF18), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Marc Wilmore, originally airing November 3, 2013. Following the funeral of beloved but obscure neighbor Chip Davis, Reverend Lovejoy's sermon on regrets sends several Springfielders into introspective flashbacks. Marge frets that her habit of listening to KISS albums while pregnant may have caused Bart's misbehavior, while Homer mourns having sold his Apple stock in 2001 to buy a prized bowling ball. Mr. Burns recalls a lost love, Lyla, a Parisian crêpe vendor (and his cousin) he abandoned out of selfishness, and resolves to track her down and rekindle the romance. Kent Brockman regrets never leaving local news to join his former partner Rachel Maddow at a bigger network, and briefly tries out for a job at Fox News before losing his nerve over ethical concerns. Meanwhile, Bart's balloon-basket prank sends him drifting dangerously high above town, drawing a crowd desperate to rescue him. Burns' reunion with Lyla ends tragically when she disintegrates into dust, prompting Smithers to convince him to honor her wish by spending time helping others. Professor Frink devises a plan using a cannon and Homer's cherished bowling ball to safely bring Bart back to earth, reuniting the Simpson family. In the end, Marge decides that being together as a family makes every past choice worthwhile, and Kent turns down Maddow's job offer, content with his life in Springfield. Guest starring Rachel Maddow, Joe Namath. Notable quotes: Mr. Burns: If it makes you feel worse, I'm the man who bought the stock you sold. | Homer: I'll bet a rich man like you has no regrets at all. | Agnes: Oh, I didn't see you there. | Bart: 50% attention-seeking, 50% to drop things on people. | Marge: You know what I think about regrets? As long as your family is together, every choice you've ever made is the right one.

title: Gal of Constant Sorrow (S27E14)
text: "Gal of Constant Sorrow" is an episode of Season 27 (production code VABF06), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Carolyn Omine, originally airing February 21, 2016. When Bart accidentally sends homeless woman Hettie Mae Boggs's shopping cart into a frozen river during a sled race, he guiltily invites her to secretly live in his closet, charging her rent to keep the arrangement quiet. Lisa uncovers the scheme but is soon won over by Hettie's extraordinary folk-singing talent, offering her own closet rent-free and setting out to launch Hettie's music career. She enlists a reluctant Mr. Largo, then arranges a radio interview and a public concert through Mayor Quimby and Krusty the Clown. The plan unravels when Hettie confesses on air to being a drug addict with a violent past, shattering Lisa's idealized image of her. Meanwhile, Homer's attempt to prove his handyman skills by fixing a loose tile spirals into disaster, trapping Snowball II and then Santa's Little Helper inside the walls, damage Marge reveals she's been quietly covering up all along. As the concert nears, Hettie disappears to drink at Cletus's farm, forcing Homer and Bart to track her down while Lisa stalls the crowd with a saxophone performance. They arrive too late and the audience has left, but Hettie sings one final, deeply personal song for Lisa that mends their broken trust, leading Lisa to invite her to stay on the family couch instead. Guest starring Bob Boilen as himself, Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob, Kate McKinnon as Hettie Mae Boggs, Natalie Maines as Hettie's singing voice. Notable quotes: Homer: It's handyman! | Bart: Face it, Homeboy, you ain't handy! Unless we need a big fat paperweight. | Homer: I'll paperweight you!! [sits on Bart] | Marge: There's no stopping what I've started here. Here's your tile! [puts the tile on Homer's plate] Have fun! Handy [pause] man! | Bart: I can't die now! I actually did my homework!

title: Woo-Hoo Dunnit? (S30E22)
text: "Woo-Hoo Dunnit?" is an episode of Season 30 (production code YABF15), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing May 5, 2019. After Marge and Lisa discover that Lisa's college fund, hidden in a cleanser can under the sink, has vanished, a true-crime documentary crew descends on the Simpson home to investigate. Chief Wiggum and Lou lead the probe, and suspicion rotates through the family one by one. Marge is first accused after a tip implicates her gambling, but security footage clears her while exposing the actual tipster's own vices. Homer becomes a suspect when his bar tab is mysteriously paid off, though his alibi involves a bizarre marathon phone call and compulsively licking sauce off the kitchen walls rather than touching the cash. Bart is revealed to have been running a slime-selling operation at school, having borrowed from the stash but always replacing what he took. Lisa is briefly implicated over a saxophone purchase at King Toot's, but it turns out to be Krusty buying the instrument to impress his disapproving father. With every family member cleared, the Simpsons throw the documentary crew out and demand a retraction, leaving the case officially unsolved. In a private coda, it's revealed that Marge herself took the money to secretly fund a snap-on coaster invention, and Homer agrees to cover for her by blaming rats, and the two share a quiet moment together on the beach. Guest starring Ken Burns as himself, Will Forte as King Toot, Jackie Mason as Hyman Krustofsky, Liev Schreiber as the Dateline: Springfield narrator. Notable quotes: Chief Wiggum: You try not to dwell on your innumerable failures, instead you stare out to sea and try to look like you're thinking deep thoughts. | Lisa: There's been a robbery! Send help! Evergreen Terrace. | 911 Operator: Sounds like what's been stolen are your manners. | Bart: Hey, nothing is my fault 'cause Dad raised me so rotten. | Grampa: Don't blame me. It was a race out the door and your mother won.
quotes: Chief Wiggum: You try not to dwell on your innumerable failures, instead you stare out to sea and try to look like you're thinking deep thoughts.
Lisa: There's been a robbery! Send help! Evergreen Terrace.
911 Operator: Sounds like what's been stolen are your manners.
Bart: Hey, nothing is my fault 'cause Dad raised me so rotten.
Grampa: Don't blame me. It was a race out the door and your mother won.

title: Haw-Haw Land (S29E10)
text: "Haw-Haw Land" is an episode of Season 29 (production code XABF03), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Tim Long, Miranda Thompson, originally airing January 7, 2018. While attending a STEM Conference with her family, Lisa becomes infatuated with Brendan Beiderbecke, a jazz-loving 11-year-old pianist who is about to transfer to Springfield Elementary. Meanwhile, Bart discovers an unexpected talent and passion for chemistry after meeting a chemical engineer at the conference. Back home, Lisa and Brendan's musical rehearsals annoy Homer, while Marge and Homer grow suspicious that Bart's newfound interest in chemistry might be a cover for making drugs. A rivalry develops between Brendan and Nelson Muntz for Lisa's affection, escalating into serenades, staged confrontations, and jealous outbursts. At the school talent show, Brendan is disqualified for not actually attending the school, ending his romance with Lisa, while Nelson gracefully bows out after revealing he prioritized his workouts over winning her over. Bart is nearly arrested by Chief Wiggum for allegedly spiking Superintendent Chalmers' vodka with acid, but Marge's trust in him allows his chemistry demonstration to dazzle the crowd, and Groundskeeper Willie confesses to the acid prank, which was meant for Principal Skinner. The episode closes with a meta joke as Marge apologizes to viewers for the episode's mistaken movie parody, and the family decides to watch a different movie instead. title: Fatzcarraldo (S28E14)
text: "Fatzcarraldo" is an episode of Season 28 (production code WABF07), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Michael Price, originally airing February 12, 2017. After a reckless domino stunt nearly triggers a meltdown at the Power Plant, Homer wins a work reprieve from Mr. Burns, only to have his celebration ruined when Patty and Selma drag the family to a tedious DMV awards ceremony. Craving greasy comfort food, Homer discovers that Krusty Burger has been overhauled with healthy Japanese cuisine, and in desperation prays for guidance, which leads him to Deuce's Caboose Chili Dogs, a run-down hot dog cart he used to visit as a child with Grampa and Grandma Mona. Homer becomes obsessed with reclaiming this nostalgic haunt, returning again and again, even as Deuce fails to remember him. Meanwhile, Lisa's school radio station faces closure due to budget cuts, leaving her and her fellow broadcasters, including Martin and Milhouse, dispirited after being overshadowed by a rival bully-run show. Homer's world crumbles further when he learns the caboose has been sold to none other than Krusty, prompting him to literally steal the cart with his car in a desperate, police-chased rescue mission. Fellow junk-food lovers rally to help him refuel along the way, and after a chaotic chase that ends with a crash over a bridge barrier set up by Lindsey Naegle and Krusty, Deuce saves Homer from disaster and finally acknowledges that he remembers him after all. Guest starring Glenn Close as Mona Simpson. title: How Munched Is That Birdie in the Window? (S22E07)

text: "How Munched Is That Birdie in the Window?" is an episode of Season 22 (production code NABF02), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Kevin Curran, originally airing November 28, 2010. During a thunderstorm, an injured carrier pigeon crashes into the Simpson house, and Bart nurses it back to health, naming it Ray. Once healed, Bart grows too attached to release Ray into the wild and instead keeps him as a pet, eventually training him to deliver messages after being inspired by a documentary on wartime carrier pigeons. Bart and Homer use Ray for mischievous pranks on Mrs. Krabappel and Mr. Burns, while Marge helps Lisa work through her fear of pigeons by comparing it to her own fear of opossums. Tragedy strikes when Santa's Little Helper eats Ray right in front of the family, sending Bart into a grief-stricken rage against the dog. A psychologist, Dr. Thurston, tries to help Bart forgive Santa's Little Helper, but he remains unmoved and the family decides to send the dog away to Ostrich World. Before they can leave him there, an escaped ostrich attacks the family, and Bart must call on Santa's Little Helper for help, ultimately forgiving him after the dog's confused but earnest defense. The family beats the ostrich and takes it home for dinner, but on the drive back the seemingly dead bird revives and begins attacking Homer, leaving the episode on a chaotic note. title: Days of Future Future (S25E18)
text: "Days of Future Future" is an episode of Season 25 (production code SABF13), directed by Bob Anderson and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing April 13, 2014. After years of poor health, Homer dies falling down the stairs, prompting Professor Frink to unveil a secret cloning project that repeatedly replaces him, though each clone dies in increasingly absurd ways. Thirty years later, the cloning finally fails for good, and Frink instead uploads Homer's memories onto a flash drive plugged into a TV screen, leaving Marge to care for a digital husband. Meanwhile, adult Bart struggles with joint custody and heartbreak after divorcing Jenda, so he undergoes a memory-erasing treatment called Moving On to forget her, only to discover the entire ordeal was a simulated dream meant to cure his obsession. In a parallel subplot, Lisa is married to a zombified Milhouse and must decide whether to have Dr. Hibbert cure his undead condition after he heroically fights off Springfield's bullies, ultimately deciding she prefers him as a zombie. Marge, drowning her sorrows at Moe's, reflects on why she's stayed with Homer through decades of chaos, inspiring Lisa to embrace her unconventional marriage. By the end, Milhouse is cured and mortified by his own zombie urges, Bart wakes up from his dream-therapy determined to move forward, and Marge chooses to electronically merge her consciousness with Homer's so they can be together in his digital form forever. title: Any Given Sundance (S19E18)
text: "Any Given Sundance" is an episode of Season 19 (production code KABF11), directed by Chuck Sheetz and written by Daniel Chun, originally airing May 4, 2008. During a tailgate party before a college football game, Lisa begins filming everyday moments around the parking lot for a school video project, discovering a passion for filmmaking. After her teacher gives the film a mediocre grade, Principal Skinner—revealing his own frustrated love of cinema—encourages her to find drama closer to home, prompting Lisa to make a candid documentary about the Simpson family. Superintendent Chalmers, eager to boost the school's reputation, pushes to get the finished film, "Capturing the Simpsons," accepted into the Sundance Film Festival, and it is. At the premiere in Utah, the family is mortified to see their private dysfunction—Homer's tantrums, Bart's messiness, Marge's exhaustion—exposed on screen for an audience that finds them ridiculous, and the film becomes an unexpected hit, with distributors and press mocking the family as villains. Guilt-ridden, Lisa is comforted by real-life director Jim Jarmusch, who shows her a rival documentary about Nelson's grim home life to prove that fame at Sundance is fleeting and that every family has its own troubles. Sure enough, buzz shifts to Nelson's film, the Simpsons fade back into anonymity, and the family reconciles, with Marge firmly declaring there will be no more "Simpsons movies." Guest starring Jim Jarmusch as himself, John C. Reilly as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: I never wanted to be famous for being mean. I wanted to be famous for catching Santa Claus. | Homer: Whaaat, I'm going for the Shia LaBeouf thing. Not quite a nerd, not quite a hunk. Shia LaBeouf! | Marge: No more Simpsons movies! One was plenty. | Marge: Call me old-fashioned, but I usually don't like movies that humiliate our family in front of the world. | Nelson: I like to cry at the ocean, because only there do my tears seem small.

title: Todd, Todd, Why Hast Thou Forsaken Me? (S31E09)

text: "Todd, Todd, Why Hast Thou Forsaken Me?" is an episode of Season 31 (production code ZABF04), directed by Chris Clements and written by Tim Long, Miranda Thompson, originally airing December 1, 2019. Still grieving his mother Maude, Todd has a nightmare in which she appears faceless, leaving him unable to remember what she looked like. When Reverend Lovejoy asks the Sunday school children what they would say to baby Jesus, Todd erupts in anger, declaring he no longer believes in God because his mother is gone forever. Horrified, Ned tries everything from scripture lessons to prayer to scare his son back into faith, even sending him to stay with the Simpsons hoping the chaotic household will make Todd appreciate religion again. Meanwhile, Lisa attempts to convert Todd to Buddhism without success, and Homer's own attempts to use pareidolia and forced breakfast rituals to restore Todd's belief similarly fail. When Todd finally confronts Homer about the permanence of loss, it triggers Homer's own grief over his mother Mona, sending him and Ned to Moe's to drown their sorrows together. After being struck by Hans Moleman's car, both men have near-death, out-of-body experiences in Heaven, encountering Maude, Edna Krabappel, John the Baptist, God, and Abraham Lincoln. Seeing his father's spirit in danger, Todd prays earnestly for the first time, successfully bringing Ned back to his body, while Homer gets a final emotional goodbye from Mona before he too revives. The families are reunited, Lisa gives up on converting Todd and instead brings the bizarre Ralph Wiggum to blow Buddha's mind, and Maude's spirit is shown still watching over her sons at bedtime. title: Donnie Fatso (S22E09)
text: "Donnie Fatso" is an episode of Season 22 (production code MABF19), directed by Ralph Sosa and written by Chris Cluess, originally airing December 12, 2010. After racking up a series of petty fines and then attempting to bribe a court official, Homer is arrested and thrown in Springfield Penitentiary. Homer stages a fake beating to earn the trust of Louie and the rest of the gang, prompting Fat Tony to break him out of prison. As Homer proves his loyalty—even unwittingly getting credit for Moe torching his own bar—Fat Tony grows to see him as a kindred spirit and welcomes him fully into the family. The two bond deeply, but the operation reaches a breaking point during a weapons deal at the docks with Belgian gun runners, where the FBI is still secretly listening in. Homer tries to warn Fat Tony away, but the mob boss realizes his friend is an informant, and the shock triggers a fatal heart attack. Grief-stricken, Homer is later abducted by Fat Tony's cousin Fit Tony, who spares his life upon sensing Fat Tony's spirit living on in him. Lisa competes in an alternative energy derby but loses when the Duff Blimp disrupts her solar-powered car, leading her to learn about Amelia Vanderbuckle, a forgotten female inventor once committed to Springfield Asylum. Determined to restore Amelia's legacy, Lisa recruits Bart to break into the asylum, where Bart instead becomes fascinated with the diary of a former sociopathic patient named Nathan. Bart brings the diary to school to scare Ralph, which spirals into Chief Wiggum warning Marge that Bart may be a sociopath. Homer and Marge secretly administer a disguised psychological test, and once Bart realizes what's happening, he intentionally answers as menacingly as possible, alarming his parents further. Convinced he needs help, they send him to a facility where he and other supposedly troubled kids are recruited by the Air Force to test drone simulators. Bart excels at destroying targets until he discovers the drones were real and caused real casualties, and his guilt-driven reaction proves he's mentally healthy, earning his release. Meanwhile, Lisa and Milhouse enlist Groundskeeper Willie to dig beneath a Knockers restaurant built over a former feminist club, uncovering Amelia's true invention: an early computing device rather than a simple loom. Lisa succeeds in getting the invention donated to a museum, even though her efforts to celebrate Amelia go largely unnoticed by everyone except her. title: The Blue and the Gray (S22E13)
text: "The Blue and the Gray" is an episode of Season 22 (production code NABF06), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Rob LaZebnik, originally airing February 13, 2011. Moe recruits Homer to act as his wingman at a bar, hoping that Homer's presence will help him attract women. The plan backfires spectacularly when every woman they meet becomes interested in Homer instead of Moe, leaving Moe increasingly humiliated and resentful. As Moe's frustration grows, he must confront the reality that his approach to dating is fundamentally flawed rather than simply unlucky. Meanwhile, at home, Marge notices her first gray hairs appearing and initially worries about aging. Instead of hiding or dyeing them, she decides to embrace her graying hair, surprising her family with her new look and confidence. Her decision sparks reactions from Homer and the kids, forcing the family to grapple with changing perceptions of beauty and aging. Both storylines explore themes of self-acceptance versus insecurity, as Moe struggles with jealousy and self-image issues while Marge finds empowerment in accepting a natural change. By the episode's end, Moe gains some perspective on his romantic failures, while Marge's embrace of her gray hair becomes a small but meaningful triumph for her sense of identity. title: Homer the Father (S22E12)
text: "Homer the Father" is an episode of Season 22 (production code NABF05), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing January 23, 2011. Homer becomes fixated on 'Thicker than Waters,' an old family sitcom written by David Mamet, and starts imitating its wise, no-nonsense television father in his own parenting. This new attitude leads him to refuse Bart the expensive dirt bike he desperately wants, insisting the boy earn it instead. Frustrated and desperate for cash, Bart is approached by a trio of Chinese spies who convince him to sell secrets about the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant in exchange for enough money to buy the bike. Bart's espionage scheme quickly spirals out of control, putting him in real danger once the spies expect more information than a ten-year-old can safely provide. Meanwhile, Homer's obsession with the sitcom continues as James Lipton interviews the show's cast for 'Inside the Actors Studio,' further feeding his fantasy of movie-perfect fatherhood. Homer eventually realizes his rigid, sitcom-inspired parenting pushed Bart toward the risky secret-selling scheme. He steps in to rescue Bart from the spies and the situation, learning that real fatherhood requires more flexibility and understanding than any TV dad could show. The episode closes with the family reconciling, as Homer abandons his imitation of a fictional father to be more genuinely present for his own son. When Homer drives to the seedy town of Guidopolis for milk, his car gets towed, and he becomes fascinated with the towing business. After sleeping through a meltdown at the power plant, Homer is diagnosed with narcolepsy but comes home drunk instead of with his medication, angering Marge. Picking up his prescription, Homer meets pharmacist Candace, and after mixing pills with alcohol, the two end up sleeping together, pushing Homer to start dating her despite the age gap. Their relationship deepens until Candace insists Homer meet her father, who turns out to be Mayor Quimby's rival Roger, who is dating Marge and proposes to her at dinner—prompting Candace to reveal she's pregnant. The shock wakes Homer, revealing it was a dream inside Dr. Zilowitz's office, and he and Marge reconcile, with Homer vowing to stop drinking. text: "The Serfsons" is an episode of Season 29 (production code WABF17), directed by Rob Oliver and written by Brian Kelley, originally airing October 1, 2017. In the medieval fantasy realm of Springfieldia, the Serfson family lives in squalid feudal poverty while nobles like Lord Montgomery and Rainier Wolfcastle lord over them. When Marge's mother Jackie is bitten by an Ice Walker she once dated, the family learns she'll freeze to death within a week unless they can buy a costly Amulet of Warmfyre. Homer, despite his devotion to the feudal system, is pushed by Marge to find the hundred gold pieces needed to save her. Lisa secretly reveals she possesses real magic and uses it to transform Homer's lucky lead nugget into gold, allowing them to purchase the amulet, though Jackie initially resists being saved. The kingdom's sorcerers detect Lisa's magic use and teleport into the Serfson home to seize her as royal property, prompting Homer to abandon his love of feudalism and lead a peasant uprising against Lord Montgomery's castle. During the chaotic siege, Wolfcastle attacks on the last dragon in the realm, and Jackie sacrifices herself by removing her amulet and freezing solid to destroy the beast from within. With the dragon dead, Lisa warns that all magic will fade since dragonfire fuels it, so a horrified Homer relights the dragon's flame, reviving it and inadvertently causing it to burn the town down as the episode ends. title: Screenless (S31E15)
text: "Screenless" is an episode of Season 31 (production code ZABF09), directed by Michael Polcino and written by J. Stewart Burns, originally airing March 8, 2020. The Simpson family becomes absorbed in television and devices, ignoring baby Maggie's attempts to communicate, even as she tries to warn them that Hans Moleman is trapped under a fallen tree. After noticing how screens are stunting Maggie's development, Marge imposes strict limits on everyone's screen time, but the kids find ways to cheat until Raphael confiscates all devices entirely. Forced offline, Homer discovers a talent for word puzzles, Patty and Selma's lives improve, Bart rediscovers imaginative play with Jimbo and Dolph, and Lisa falls back in love with reading physical books. Meanwhile, Marge struggles without her phone and laptop for recipes and everyday tasks, and when the family returns home unexpectedly, they catch her secretly using her devices in a closet. Realizing she is the one truly addicted, Marge checks the whole family into a screen-rehab facility called Messages, even though she's the only one who needs it. The retreat initially seems idyllic, but the family soon uncovers that the staff, led by Dr. Lund, secretly use technology to run identity theft and spam scams on the patients. The Simpsons escape and expose Dr. Lund, ending the ordeal and returning to a more balanced relationship with technology. title: Bart's Not Dead (S30E01)
text: "Bart's Not Dead" is an episode of Season 30 (production code XABF19), directed by Bob Anderson and written by Stephanie Gillis, originally airing September 30, 2018. After refusing to pull a fire alarm to sabotage Lisa's sad recital performance, Bart is pressured by Homer to prove his toughness and later accepts a dare from bullies to jump off a dam at Echo Canyon. He lands face-first and wakes up in the hospital, where, desperate not to disappoint Marge, he fabricates a story about visiting Heaven and meeting Jesus. The lie makes Bart a local celebrity, drawing attention from Ned Flanders and even the police, and soon Christian movie producers arrive to offer the Simpsons a deal to turn his story into a film. Homer eagerly takes the deal and is forced into an uneasy partnership with Ned to produce the movie, interviewing celebrities like Emily Deschanel and Gal Gadot for roles. As filming progresses, guilt and anxiety consume Bart, culminating in a nightmare where he actually visits Heaven and is confronted by Jesus and Bart's late grandfather figure, Clarence Bouvier. When the finished movie becomes a massive hit, Bart can no longer bear the deception and confesses the truth to Marge and Lisa, sparking outrage throughout Springfield. Homer and Ned resolve the backlash by donating the film's profits to charity, restoring most of the town's goodwill. In a final twist, Bart and Lisa fall from the roof of their house while discussing forgiveness but survive by landing on a pile of leaves, while a comedic epilogue shows Homer's afterlife fate involving Hindu Heaven and reincarnation as a turtle. Guest starring Dave Attell, Emily Deschanel, Gal Gadot, Jonathan Groff, Pete Holmes, Leonard Nimoy, Katy Perry, Kiefer Sutherland. title: Clown in the Dumps (S26E01)
text: "Clown in the Dumps" is an episode of Season 26 (production code SABF20), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Joel H. Cohen, originally airing September 28, 2014. During a televised comedy roast, Krusty the Clown is stung by the harsh jokes and seeks reassurance from his father, Rabbi Krustofsky, only to have the Rabbi criticize his humor before suddenly collapsing and dying. Convinced that he has lost his comedic touch and that nobody finds him funny anymore, Krusty announces his retirement from show business. Bart tries to cheer him up by having him binge-watch old episodes of his show, but this backfires when Krusty notices how repetitive and stale his jokes have become, sending him into a drunken stupor. While passed out, he dreams of a Jewish version of Heaven where he meets Rodney Dangerfield and is visited by his father's spirit, who explains that Jews don't believe in an afterlife and urges Krusty to focus on helping others instead of seeking laughs. A hollow act of charity fails to lift his spirits, but when Bart brings him to synagogue, Krusty overhears a beloved rabbi quoting his own religious jokes approvingly, proving that his father secretly appreciated his humor after all. Meanwhile, Lisa becomes fixated on preventing any harm from befalling Homer following the Rabbi's sudden death, going so far as to wrap her father in bubble wrap for his own safety. Her overprotectiveness pays off unexpectedly when Otto's out-of-control school bus crashes through the Simpsons' garden, and the bubble wrap cushions Homer from injury. The episode closes with Krusty reconciling with his late father's memory, envisioning him laughing alongside Dangerfield and Jesus in the afterlife. Guest starring Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob, Don Hertzfeldt as Futuristic "Sampsans" Creatures, David Hyde Pierce as himself, Jackie Mason as Rabbi Krustofsky, Jeff Ross as himself, Sarah Silverman as herself. Larry's mother gives the group his diary, which contains a drawing of all of them at Serenity Falls, prompting them to set off on a road trip to scatter his ashes there. Along the way, Homer accidentally knocks over the urn and discovers sapphires hidden in the ashes, which Moe recognizes and tries to keep secret from the others. The group's bickering over the jewels and reckless driving leads to the urn spilling and their arrest by a sheriff who turns out to be mob enforcer Mickey No-Loose-Ends, sent by Fat Tony to retrieve the smuggled gems. After a tense standoff and a botched flare-gun attempt by Homer, the men's car nearly plunges off a ravine, but Mickey ultimately spares them and helps save Homer from falling. Reaching Serenity Falls, the group realizes Larry's true wish was simply to belong with them back at Moe's, so they honor him there instead, and Moe reveals he swallowed the lost sapphires to keep them safe. As summer break begins, Bart retreats into his VR headset for a week while Lisa channels her energy into writing welcome notes for next year's teachers, worrying Marge and Homer, who ends up joining Bart in his slump instead of intervening. Marge pushes Homer to take Bart outside, and a search for a fishing spot instead leads them to lounge on the couch, mirroring a town-wide malaise among Springfield's men. Frustrated and unable to afford therapy, Marge turns to Amazon Alexa for help, accidentally summoning the police before the 'real' Alexa suggests sending the town's men and boys to Man Camp and Boys Camp to fix their emotional shortcomings. At Man Camp, the enigmatic Greg leads Homer and the other men through awkward exercises in empathy, hugging, and vulnerability, guided by a talking stick and painful personal confessions, while Coach Krupt teaches them how to handle rejection without violence. Meanwhile, at Boys Camp, Greg tries to teach the boys about the dangers of bullying and phone addiction, even as the kids form their own bonds, with Bart building a makeshift TV to reenact Itchy and Scratchy antics and the group banding together to rescue Ralph from a rushing stream. Back in town, the wives enjoy their newfound freedom while the men undergo a final test at the camp's closing campfire: killing a duck for dinner. Homer refuses to harm the duck, choosing kindness instead, prompting Greg to declare all the men have truly become 'men.' The camp's lessons carry over as the men return home to loving reunions with their families, though Moe's reunion with Maya is cut short by his mother, who reminds him their five-year separation isn't over yet.

title: Sashes to Sashes (S37E07)
text: "Sashes to Sashes" is an episode of Season 37 (production code 36ABF18), directed by Mike Frank Polcino and written by Ryan Koh, originally airing November 16, 2025. After Alice Glick dies and leaves her estate to fund a new school music program, Joe Quimby III hijacks the money for a music festival and uses the promise of headliner Chunk Mafia to win votes for student council president. Lisa, disgusted by the Quimbys' unchecked influence over Springfield, initially plans to run herself but instead convinces a reluctant Bart to challenge Joe. As the election heats up, Lisa digs into the Quimby family's dark history, discovering flashbacks spanning generations: Joe Quimby, Sr. fleeing Ireland after a theft and murder, ruthlessly building his fortune, and later forcing his son Joe Quimby to marry campaign aide Beatrice Bouvier (Marge's aunt) for political gain rather than love. When Joe publicly denies being unfaithful, the scandal backfires and costs him his father's approval, driving home a legacy of ambition over love. In the present, Lisa and Marge visit an estranged Beatrice, learning the full truth of her heartbreak, which inspires Lisa to write a moving concession speech for the newly-elected Joe. Touched by the story, Joe steps down from the presidency in favor of Bart, but a technicality hands the role to Martin Prince instead, who ultimately preserves the music program. The episode ends with Joe reconciling with his father's ghostly memory, finally earning his approval. Guest starring Carrie Coon, Cole Escola, Brendan Gleeson, Domhnall Gleeson. Notable quotes: Devin: Two votes. That's all you get. You and Milhouse... maybe. | Bart: It's weird, but it turns out I love popularity. | Beatrice Bouvier: So you'll respect me privately, but humiliate me publicly? | Agnes Skinner: If he can't even cheat on his wife, how can he repave our highways? I say we turn on him. | Joe Quimby, Sr.: I stole the family turnip. I left the land of my birth. I killed a man with a corned beef sandwich. All to make our name in this country.

title: Peeping Mom (S26E18)
text: "Peeping Mom" is an episode of Season 26 (production code TABF11), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by John Frink, originally airing April 19, 2015. After a bulldozer mysteriously plows through part of Springfield, suspicion immediately falls on Bart, who insists he had nothing to do with it. Unconvinced by his denials, Marge decides to shadow Bart's every move, determined to catch him in the act if he really is responsible. Her constant surveillance strains their relationship, echoing an old argument between her and Homer about trust and giving up on people, which resurfaces as she reflects on standing by Homer during his failed sumo league venture. Meanwhile, Ned Flanders adopts a new dog, and Homer quickly grows attached to the animal, even preemptively apologizing to it for future messes he plans to blame on her. As Marge's investigation continues, Chief Wiggum and Lou pursue their own clumsy attempt to pin the bulldozer incident on Bart despite lacking real evidence. Bart's insistence on his innocence eventually leads to the truth coming out, easing Marge's suspicions and mending the tension between mother and son. By the episode's end, the real culprit or explanation behind the bulldozer chaos is revealed, and family trust is restored, while Homer's bond with Ned's new dog continues to grow. Notable quotes: Homer: Moes before bros. | Homer: Oh, you must be Flanders' new dog. I just want to apologize in advance for the things I'm gonna blame on you. | Chief Wiggum: I've got everything I need to convict your boy, except for motive, means, and opportunity. | Lou: You also have no evidence. | Chief Wiggum: That's implied.

Chief Wiggum: I've got everything I need to convict your boy, except for motive, means, and opportunity.
Lou: You also have no evidence.
Chief Wiggum: That's implied.

title: The Great Phatsby: Part One (S28E12)
text: "The Great Phatsby: Part One" is an episode of Season 28 (production code WABF04), directed by Chris Clements and written by Dan Greaney, originally airing January 15, 2017. Mr. Burns, nostalgic for his youth, decides to throw a lavish party at his Summer Mansion, sending Smithers on a dangerous errand to Canada for hand-cut lake ice while cheaping out on everything else. The Simpsons and other Springfield residents attend, but the party proves so disappointing that most guests leave early. Spotting a livelier party across the lake, Burns and Homer row over and crash the mansion of Jay G, a wealthy music mogul who idolizes Burns as his inspiration. Jay G lavishes Burns with a special unlimited credit card and whisks him and Homer off on a spending spree, secretly draining Burns' fortune. Meanwhile, Lisa is wooed by Blake Black, a spoiled rich boy, and their outings—including a cruel whale-watching trip and a horse show—reveal his true, self-serving nature, leading her to abandon him for another admirer. Bart briefly encounters a mysterious candle vendor who Homer's narration hints will matter later, though he can't recall why. Smithers endures a string of disastrous mishaps in the Canadian wilderness, losing his phone and glove while trying to stay in contact with Burns. Back home, Burns discovers his credit card has been declined and repossessors arrive to strip his mansion bare, and Homer reveals that Jay G's rap video lyrics prove he deliberately engineered Burns' financial ruin, leaving Burns devastated. Guest starring Keegan-Michael Key, Charles Barkley. Notable quotes: Homer: [narrating] In my younger and more vulnerable years, my father gave me some advice. He said, "The laziest way to tell a story is through voice-over narration." | Mr. Burns: Now, you head up to Northern Canada and get me a quarter ton of lake ice. Hand-sawn and tong-carried. | Waylon Smithers: Risk my life in the arctic wilderness just to bring you some ice. It would be an honor. | Chief Wiggum: Hey, everyone, hey! I'm off-duty, so please don't feel weird doing drugs in front of me, or with me. | Mr. Burns: A charge plate? But I've never had one of those newfangled swipe-a-ma-jigs!

Chief Wiggum: Hey, everyone, hey! I'm off-duty, so please don't feel weird doing drugs in front of me, or with me.
Mr. Burns: A charge plate? But I've never had one of those newfangled swipe-a-ma-jigs!

title: Daddicus Finch (S30E09)
text: "Daddicus Finch" is an episode of Season 30 (production code YABF01), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Al Jean, originally airing December 2, 2018. During a chaotic second grade play at Springfield Elementary, Lisa storms the stage in protest of a violent skit, leading to the show's cancellation. Afterward, Marge encourages Homer to comfort a frustrated Lisa, and their outing to the mall sparks a new closeness between them. Lisa, immersed in reading 'To Kill a Mockingbird,' begins to see Homer as a noble, Atticus Finch-like figure, praising him constantly at home and school. This newfound admiration leaves Bart feeling pushed aside, and he seeks advice from Dr. Jessup while acting out through pranks, including sabotaging car keys at Shauna's bat mitzvah. Homer, channeling his inner Atticus, calmly defuses the resulting mob, further cementing Lisa's idealized view of him. As tension mounts between Lisa and Bart over their father's attention, Marge intervenes and consults Dr. Jessup to restore balance in the family. Eventually, Lisa's idolization fades naturally, while Maggie steps in to comfort Homer once the spotlight shifts away from him. In a non-canon epilogue, Marge promises Bart a moment just for himself, and he retaliates by kicking a robot-suited Homer in the backside. Guest starring Jon Lovitz, J. K. Simmons, Gregory Peck, Mary Badham, Phillip Alford, John Megna. Notable quotes: Homer: Give attention to Lisa, give attention to Bart. What am I, made of attention? | Lenny Leonard: I never got along with my old man. He was always disappointed I didn't follow him in the family business. | Moe Szyslak: Yeah, my dad left when I was most vulnerable: the day after mom left. That was a tough week there. | Grampa: I'm the greatest!!!! Oh... someone put down my dukes!

Lenny Leonard: I never got along with my old man. He was always disappointed I didn't follow him in the family business.
Moe Szyslak: Yeah, my dad left when I was most vulnerable: the day after mom left. That was a tough week there.
Grampa: I'm the greatest!!!! Oh... someone put down my dukes!

title: Friend with Benefit (S27E06)
text: "Friend with Benefit" is an episode of Season 27 (production code TABF21), directed by Matthew Faughnan and written by Rob LaZebnik, originally airing November 8, 2015. Homer becomes obsessed with a self-lifting chair he sees advertised on TV, and after failing to raise money through a heartfelt but embarrassing crowdfunding video, he unexpectedly gets enough donations to buy it. When Springfield realizes their money went to something so frivolous, an angry mob descends on the Simpson house and destroys the chair. Meanwhile, Lisa befriends Harper, a wealthy new classmate at school, and Homer bonds with Harper's internet-billionaire father over their shared love of luxury and excess. Homer is drawn into Harper's father's world of VIP concerts, magic shows, and a private island vacation, while Lisa grows increasingly frustrated that Harper is controlling and doesn't let her speak or participate. Tensions boil over when Harper gives Lisa an expensive bike as a gift, which Lisa refuses out of sentimental attachment to her old one, causing the girls to end their friendship. Despite the family's anger at Lisa for jeopardizing their island vacation, Homer ultimately chooses to leave the island and side with his daughter after witnessing how entitled and unkind Harper truly is. The episode ends on a comedic note as the family realizes, while flying home, that they accidentally left Bart behind on the island. Guest starring Kristen Bell as Harper Jambowski, David Copperfield as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: It's like being from North Korea and finding out there's a South Korea! | Homer: There comes a time in everyone's life when you need a little extra help getting up from your chair. | Lisa: My dad assembled it on Christmas Day. Which is why I have to pedal backward to go forward, but I love it. | Mike Jambowski: When I'm happy, I make holes! When I'm sad, I buy a hockey team! They cost, like, nothin', man!
quotes: Homer: It's like being from North Korea and finding out there's a South Korea!
Homer: There comes a time in everyone's life when you need a little extra help getting up from your chair.
Lisa: My dad assembled it on Christmas Day. Which is why I have to pedal backward to go forward, but I love it.
Mike Jambowski: When I'm happy, I make holes! When I'm sad, I buy a hockey team! They cost, like, nothin', man!

title: Whiskey Business (S24E19)
text: "Whiskey Business" is an episode of Season 24 (production code RABF13), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Valentina L. Garza, originally airing May 5, 2013. After attending a trade show in Capital City, Moe returns to Springfield with a batch of his homemade bourbon that suddenly attracts the attention of wealthy venture capitalists eager to invest in his tavern's secret recipe. As Moe is thrust into the unfamiliar world of corporate branding and investor meetings, he struggles to balance his newfound success with his usual barfly instincts, risking everything he's built. Meanwhile, Lisa discovers that the memory of her late jazz idol, Bleeding Gums Murphy, is being exploited when a shady promoter resurrects him as a cheesy holographic performer for profit. Determined to protect his legacy, Lisa sets out to confront the exploitation and restore dignity to his memory. In a third storyline, Grampa is injured while babysitting Bart, forcing the two to spend an unexpected two weeks together during his recovery. Despite their rocky start, Grampa comes to cherish being cared for by his grandson far more than the impersonal treatment he receives at the retirement home. By the episode's end, Moe's business venture unravels in typical Springfield fashion, Lisa manages to bring some closure to Bleeding Gums' exploited image, and Grampa and Bart's bond is strengthened by their time together. Guest starring Tony Bennett, Kevin Michael Richardson, Sonny Rollins, Ron Taylor. Notable quotes: Moe Szyslak: My name is Moe Szyslak of Makers Moe Bourbon, ticker symbol: M-O-E. | Homer: Now, wait a minute. Got to make sure you're okay. Who's the president now? | Homer: He's back! | Bart: Well, you are the first thing I took care of that didn't die. | Grampa: But what you did wasn't for nothing. It was the best two weeks of this final horrible part of my life.
quotes: Moe Szyslak: My name is Moe Szyslak of Makers Moe Bourbon, ticker symbol: M-O-E.
Homer: Now, wait a minute. Got to make sure you're okay. Who's the president now?

Grampa: But what you did wasn't for nothing. It was the best two weeks of this final horrible part of my life.

title: Diggs (S25E12)
text: "Diggs" is an episode of Season 25 (production code SABF08), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Dan Greaney, Allen Glazier, originally airing March 9, 2014. After hearing a missionary's tale about a troubled village boy, Bart guilt-trips himself into borrowing $20 from Homer for charity, then desperately tries to earn it back by eating disgusting things at school, including a formaldehyde-soaked dead frog offered by bullies. This stunt lands him in the hospital and makes him a school pariah, until Diggs, a falconry-obsessed transfer student with a trained falcon named Freedom, rescues him from further bullying. Bart joins Diggs in reviving the school's falconry club and grows close to him, worrying his family with his late nights. During a tree-climbing outing, Diggs suddenly jumps out of the tree in an apparent attempt to prove something, injuring himself and revealing a fixation on the idea that humans can still learn to fly. Bart discovers Diggs has been sent to a psychiatric hospital, and despite his family's concerns, insists on staying loyal to his troubled friend. When Diggs gets a day pass to attend a falconry competition, he enlists Bart's help in freeing all the caged falcons before his time runs out. As Diggs returns to the hospital, he hands leadership of the falconry club to Bart, and Milhouse reconciles with him. The episode ends with the Simpson family sharing a mundane dinner, gently deflating the emotional weight of Bart's adventure. Guest starring Daniel Radcliffe as Diggs. Notable quotes: Homer: Pressure's how you make your beloved diamonds, Marge. | Nelson Muntz: I named the frog Herb! | Diggs: I wanted to fly. I know it sounds a little crazy now, but I suddenly thought maybe we can all fly, but somehow we've forgotten that we can. | Lisa: Want a hug? | Jimbo: Making fun of the mentally ill. Real classy.

Diggs: I wanted to fly. I know it sounds a little crazy now, but I suddenly thought maybe we can all fly, but somehow we've forgotten that we can.

title: Mr. Lisa's Opus (S29E08)
text: "Mr. Lisa's Opus" is an episode of Season 29 (production code XABF01), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Al Jean, originally airing December 3, 2017. While writing her Harvard admission essay, an older Lisa reflects on formative moments from her childhood, beginning with a painful memory of her family forgetting her seventh birthday and only Ned Flanders remembering to give her a gift. The narrative then leaps forward to a non-canon future in which Homer's drinking has put serious strain on his marriage to Marge, even as the family gathers for Lisa's fourteenth birthday with an awkward cake and a special song from Leon Kompowsky. Lisa discovers evidence suggesting Marge is planning to leave Homer and take the kids to run a bed and breakfast, prompting her to intervene before the situation truly unravels. She confronts her father at Moe's Tavern, where Moe now sports bizarre spider-like prosthetic legs, and extracts a promise from Homer to quit drinking for good. Homer calls on Ned, who turns out to be his sponsor, and walks him through a comedic version of the twelve-step program, ultimately helping him get sober and save his marriage. Later, Lisa receives her acceptance to Harvard via a competitive drone delivery, and though she struggles with homesickness on her first day of college, Bart helps cheer her up before the family departs. She bonds with her new roommate, easing her transition into this new chapter of life. The episode closes with a nostalgic musical montage and a tongue-in-cheek meta appearance by Norman Lear, followed by a tour of Springfield teasing a fictional spin-off, 'Simpson and Son.' Guest starring Kat Dennings, Valerie Harper, Kipp Lennon, Norman Lear, Jon Lovitz. Notable quotes: Homer: Sweetie, marriages are like water heaters—they sit peacefully for years until they explode in a fireball ruining everything you own. | Homer: Stop drinking? That's like asking a golfer to stop drinking! | Ned: Al right, soberino, it's just 12 simple steps. | Homer: Dear Lord, the Satan of Heaven, I order you to fix me. | Lisa: Very much. But I won't.
quotes: Homer: Sweetie, marriages are like water heaters—they sit peacefully for years until they explode in a fireball ruining everything you own.
Homer: Stop drinking? That's like asking a golfer to stop drinking!

title: That '90s Show (S19E11)
text: "That '90s Show" is an episode of Season 19 (production code KABF04), directed by Mark Kirkland and written by Matt Selman, originally airing January 27, 2008. When the Simpsons' heat goes out because Homer forgot to pay the bill, Lisa stumbles upon Marge's old university diploma, prompting Marge and Homer to recount a rocky chapter of their relationship from the 1990s. Back then, the young couple lived happily but poor until Marge secretly enrolled at Springfield University, forcing Homer to take a humiliating job at his father's laser tag business to pay her tuition. Marge grows infatuated with her pretentious professor, Steffan August, while Homer feels increasingly shut out, eventually reinventing his mellow music group as an angry grunge band called Sadgasm. After Homer catches Marge with August, the couple breaks up, sending Homer into a spiral of fame, addiction-seeming behavior, and heartbreak, while Marge dates August and slowly realizes his progressive ideals mask arrogance and hypocrisy. A humiliating date with August, followed by hearing Homer's raw, heartfelt song about her, convinces Marge that she still loves Homer. She rushes to his side, discovers his "drug" stash is actually diabetes medication, and the two reconcile for good. Back in the present, Homer and Marge finish their story, having reaffirmed how much they've grown together since their turbulent college days. Guest starring Kurt Loder as himself, "Weird Al" Yankovic as himself. Notable quotes: Homer: I had finally achieved every rock star's dream: hating being famous. | Marge: We wouldn't be in this trouble if you'd just paid the heating bill! | Homer: I thought global warming would take care of it. Al Gore can't do anything right. | Young Homer: You know these IKEA foam futons do Velcro together. | Dean: If you did the former better we'd use the latter less.

title: You Won't Believe What This Episode Is About – Act Three Will Shock You! (S33E14)
keys: you won't believe what this episode is about – act three will shock you!
text: "You Won't Believe What This Episode Is About – Act Three Will Shock You!" is an episode of Season 33 (production code UABF07), directed by Jennifer Moeller and written by Christine Nangle, originally airing March 13, 2022. After Marge kicks the family out during a frantic house-cleaning test, Homer ends up watching Santa's Little Helper alone, and a series of mishaps leaves the dog locked in a hot car, giving onlookers the false impression that Homer abandoned him. The incident goes viral on NeighborHub and Instasnap, and Homer's botched public apology at church only makes things worse, causing Mr. Burns to sever ties with him and the town to shun him completely. Isolated and banned from his usual hangouts, Homer discovers his family celebrating without him at Dead Lobster and there meets Theo, founder of a reputation-repair group called The Institute. Joining fellow disgraced Springfieldians like Helen Lovejoy, Kirk Van Houten, and Larry Doogan, Homer performs charitable acts to rebuild his image, but public goodwill isn't enough, so Theo proposes a drastic plan: infiltrating ChumNet Island to erase all bad publicity using a universal eradication code. During the break-in, Homer realizes the code would wipe out countless innocent people's records along with his own, and he refuses to go through with it, instead broadcasting Lisa's heartfelt apology to win back the town's forgiveness. Theo faces consequences for his failed scheme, while the Simpsons finally reunite for a peaceful dinner at Dead Lobster. Guest starring Kumail Nanjiani as Theo, Jay Pharoah as Drederick Tatum. I'm sorry that you all have skin thinner than gas station toilet paper. | Mr. Burns: My fellow Springfielders, here at Burns Industries, we release the hounds on all forms of disrespect, and to tolerance we say, "excellent." | Homer: Oh, I've never been so viciously lampooned. title: Thursdays with Abie (S21E09)
text: "Thursdays with Abie" is an episode of Season 21 (production code MABF02), directed by Michael Polcino and written by Mitchell H. Glazer, Don Payne, originally airing January 3, 2010. During a family trip to the aquarium, Grampa strikes up a conversation with Marshall Goldman, a Springfield Shopper reporter who becomes fascinated by his old stories, including tales of taming a shark and meeting Clark Gable. When Marshall publishes these anecdotes and Grampa becomes a minor celebrity, Homer grows jealous that his father never shared such stories with him and tries to find his own interesting subject to interview, first attempting a disastrous chat with Mr. Burns. Sneaking into the newspaper office, Homer discovers Marshall's real plan: a Pulitzer-worthy story about Grampa's death, revealing that Marshall intends to murder him aboard a train for a dramatic finale. Homer races to intercept the train, eventually being lowered into the car by Lenny and Carl, where he finds Marshall attempting to smother Grampa. After a struggle, Grampa manages to pull the emergency brake, sending Marshall crashing into a pile of hat boxes, and Homer and his father reconcile over the ordeal. In a parallel subplot, Lisa loses Bart's beloved classroom stuffed lamb, Larry, down a sewer drain, prompting Bart to venture into the sewers himself, battling rats and cats, only to find the toy torn beyond repair. The episode ends with the family gathered together as Grampa begins telling Homer a rambling, exaggerated story, symbolizing their renewed bond. Guest starring Mitch Albom as himself. Notable quotes: Grampa: You're in the newspaper business? Something that's gonna die before I do! | Marshall Goldman: Now I know how a radio feels! | Homer: Marge, my brain is like a computer, and I file away Grampa's stories in a very special place. | Homer: Dad, I don't have the right words to say how I really feel about you, but at least I know how to beat up a guy who does. | Lisa: I'm a freaking Buddhist! A Buddhist!

title: King Leer (S29E16)
text: "King Leer" is an episode of Season 29 (production code XABF10), directed by Chris Clements and written by Daniel Furlong, Zach Posner, originally airing April 15, 2018. When Bart is forced to join the school band, Homer's fear of paying for a broken instrument leads him to smash Bart's violin himself. Meanwhile, Homer and Marge tail Moe after he abruptly closes the bar following a mysterious phone call, and discover him brawling with his estranged father, Morty Szyslak, at a warehouse. Moe reveals his family runs Mattress King, a business built on secretly infesting mattresses with bed bugs to drive repeat sales, and that he was cast out for refusing to sabotage a rival store, which led to his family's business collapsing anyway. Marge pushes for reconciliation, arranging a tense family dinner that Homer manages to salvage with a nostalgic old commercial. Morty then retires and splits the business among his three children, but Moe's siblings sabotage his store's reopening commercial out of lingering resentment, tanking his new venture. Moe retaliates by vandalizing his siblings' stores, and Marge again intervenes, bringing Morty back to mediate as Moe prepares to unleash bed bugs on his family's mattresses. Ultimately Moe can't go through with the betrayal, but the bugs escape anyway, sending the whole family fleeing and scratching from the warehouse. title: Bart the Cool Kid (S33E15)
text: "Bart the Cool Kid" is an episode of Season 33 (production code UABF08), directed by Steven Dean Moore and written by Ryan Koh, originally airing March 20, 2022. When Ralph shows up at school wearing the trendy Slipreme Caliphates sneakers, Bart becomes desperate to get a pair, and Homer waits in line to buy them. Unwilling to actually stand in line, Homer secretly buys counterfeit shoes from shady vendor Mike Wegman, and the fakes fall apart at school, humiliating Bart in a viral video. Guilt-ridden, brand owner Orion Hughes visits the Simpsons to apologize and gives them real merchandise, and he and Bart strike up a friendship, eventually deciding to co-design a new sneaker called the Bartman One. Meanwhile, Homer discovers a taste for the cool clothes Orion gave him, and photos of him spread online, turning the Slipreme brand into an unlikely middle-aged fad as Moe and the barflies adopt the trend. This uncool surge threatens to ruin the brand's image right before the Bartman One launch party, and Bart traces the problem back to his father. With Marge's help, Homer is coaxed away from the spotlight and redirects the aging crowd to a museum, saving the brand's cool reputation. Bart and Homer reconcile, but when they try once more to get real shoes from Wegman, the fakes fall apart yet again, while it's revealed that Orion's father Darius created his son as a literal clone of himself. Guest starring Michael Rapaport as Mike Wegman, The Weeknd as Orion and Darius Hughes. Notable quotes: Ralph: My daddy took my cat to the cat doctor, and when Daddy came home, my cat had turned into these shoes. | Bart: I love you, Dad. title: Pork and Burns (S28E11)
text: "Pork and Burns" is an episode of Season 28 (production code WABF06), directed by Matthew Nastuk and written by Rob LaZebnik, originally airing January 8, 2017. After discovering a bestselling book about a Japanese tidying philosophy, Marge insists the family purge anything that no longer brings them joy. title: P.S. I Hate You (S36E14)
text: "P.S. I Hate You" is an episode of Season 36 (production code 36ABF07), directed by Mike Frank Polcino and written by Cesar Mazariegos, originally airing April 13, 2025. After an embarrassing run-in with Helen Lovejoy over discount shopping, Marge retreats upstairs to vent her frustrations by writing one of her secret hate letters, a longtime coping habit the family knows nothing about. Her birthday party that night is a huge success, with the town praising her as the nicest woman in Springfield, but the next day she discovers her hidden box of letters has vanished from the closet. A mysterious caller demands $5,000 or threatens to expose the letters to the whole town, and after the police and Marge's dismissive sisters offer no real help, Homer takes matters into his own hands by threatening the blackmailer directly. When one letter is read aloud at church, Helen wrongly assumes Agnes Skinner wrote it, causing a minor uproar, while Marge eventually realizes from a clue in the ransom call that the culprit is actually her babysitter, Shauna, who found the letters and roped in Jimbo to extort her. Marge and Homer stage a break-in at the Chalmers house to retrieve the box, only to find it filled with decoy novels, then chase Shauna and Jimbo across town until cornering them on a rooftop. During the confrontation Shauna nearly falls, forcing Marge to choose between saving her or catching the scattering letters, and she chooses Shauna, letting her secret feelings blow away and land in the hands of the townspeople. Rather than hide from the fallout, Marge publicly embraces her flaws during a parade, admitting she's not just endlessly nice but a person with real emotions, and the episode ends with Tim Meadows adopting her hate-letter habit himself. title: Homer Is Where the Art Isn't (S29E12)
