He also has a habit of driving unconventional solar-powered vehicles, which nearly gets him killed during a freak solar eclipse in Springfield. Despite the mishaps, he remains a good-natured, dedicated advocate for clean energy. His fame within Springfield is subtly reinforced by having his picture displayed in local businesses like The Penny Loafer. Voiced by Ed Begley, Jr. (Himself).

title: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (character)
text: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (character) is Real-world basketball legend who makes a guest appearance in Springfield. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar appears as a real-world celebrity guest in The Simpsons, playing a fictionalized version of himself. His most notable involvement comes when Dr. Zander enlists him to help Homer Simpson understand the sensation of being strangled, tying him into one of the show's recurring physical comedy bits. Outside of canon storylines, he is also depicted attending a glitzy Hollywood premiere event, poking fun at celebrity culture surrounding the show itself. As a former professional athlete, his towering height and calm demeanor are used for comedic contrast against the show's more chaotic characters. He functions primarily as a cameo character rather than a recurring cast member with deep characterization. Voiced by Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (Himself).

title: Abbey
text: Abbey is Abe Simpson's illegitimate English daughter, making her Homer Simpson's half-sister. Abbey is a previously unknown relative who surfaces when the Simpsons visit England, revealing a secret from Abe's past. She was born after Abe had a brief wartime fling with a woman named Edwina while stationed there before D-Day, a tryst Abe never knew resulted in a child. When the family runs into Edwina and the now middle-aged Abbey at the airport, Abe is so horrified by the reminder of his indiscretion that he flees in a panic. In contrast, Homer immediately warms up to his newfound half-sister, largely because she looks and behaves so much like him. Abbey herself is mostly defined by this uncanny resemblance to Homer, played for comedic effect given their shared mannerisms and demeanor. She remains a minor, one-episode character who nonetheless expands the Simpson family tree in an unexpected way. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: See you in Heaven.
quotes: See you in Heaven.

title: Zapp Brannigan
text: Zapp Brannigan is Futurama character (Captain of the Nimbus and Commander of the D.O.O.P. army) who appears in a non-canon Simpsons/Futurama crossover comic. Zapp Brannigan is a crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe from Futurama, appearing when the citizens of Springfield are transported to New New York. He is portrayed as a blustery, self-important military commander who is easily distracted by romantic pursuits, seen flirting with Edna Krabappel in a bar. His second-in-command, Kif Kroker, is often at his side, tasked with helping manage the chaos he causes. Brannigan proves gullible and easily manipulated, as Waylon Smithers manages to win his trust and use it to stage a mutiny aboard his own ship, the Nimbus. This leads to a humiliating turn of events where Zapp and Kif are forced to go-go dance in cages, underscoring his tendency to be outsmarted despite his authoritative position.

title: Brain Spawn
text: Brain Spawn is A non-canon species of evil brains appearing in Simpsons/Futurama crossover comics. Brain Spawn are not individual characters but an entire species of malevolent, disembodied brains. They exist outside the show's main canon, appearing only in a Bongo comic book crossover story. Their most notable trait is being trapped in liquid diamond after the Planet Express ship lands on Nerdanus XII, sealing them away. As a species rather than a single personality, they lack the usual character development or running gags seen in mainline Simpsons characters. Their appearances are tied specifically to comic-book storylines that blend Simpsons and Futurama elements.

title: Charlie Brown
text: Charlie Brown is Crossover character from the Peanuts comic strip, referenced/appearing in various Simpsons episodes. Charlie Brown is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover figure borrowed from the classic Peanuts comic strip, appearing mostly as a reference, mention, or costume rather than a fully voiced character. He's frequently invoked as a cultural shorthand for hard luck and perseverance, such as when Bart compares his family's hoped-for Christmas miracle to the kind that happens to Charlie Brown. His image shows up in odd corners of Springfield, from a poster parody of The Matrix to a bootleg costume worker posing for photos in Capital City. He even factors into a surreal hallucination sequence where Homer and Ned imagine themselves as Lucy and Charlie Brown after taking a strange drug. In a non-canon Halloween segment, Bart dresses as Charlie Brown while Lisa becomes Lucy Van Pelt, playing on their real-life sibling dynamic. Overall, Charlie Brown functions as a recurring nostalgic pop-culture nod rather than a character with his own arc within the show. Notable quotes: We've been through more hardships than the Jews and Charlie Brown put together. | Good grief!
quotes: We've been through more hardships than the Jews and Charlie Brown put together.
Good grief!

title: Carnac the Magnificent
text: Carnac the Magnificent is A parody character based on Johnny Carson's recurring 'Tonight Show' persona, appearing within The Simpsons universe. Carnac the Magnificent is not an original Simpsons character but a recreation of Johnny Carson's famous comedic bit from The Tonight Show, brought into the show's universe as a crossover reference. He appears as a turban-wearing mystic who humorously 'predicts' answers to unseen questions, a gag lifted directly from Carson's real-life act. In one canonical flashback, his appearance angers Chief Wiggum after he randomly names Wiggum alongside fictional castaways Gilligan and the Skipper, prompting Wiggum to shoot his television in frustration. In a separate non-canon nightmare sequence, Bart and Lisa are shown watching him perform on television. His inclusion in the show serves as a nostalgic, comedic nod to classic American late-night television culture rather than developing him as a true series character. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Bestimus Mucho
text: Bestimus Mucho is A transforming robot toy character appearing in a Treehouse of Horror parody segment. Bestimus Mucho is a non-canon transforming robot who began life as a simple toy truck before becoming a Malibu Stacy car. He serves as the leader of the Pos-i-bots, a faction that stands opposed to the villainous Carnage Destructicus. The character exists as part of a parody of transforming robot franchises, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror Halloween special segment. Beyond his brief animated appearance, he later found a more expanded role in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, where he factors into a robot-themed storyline. His design and name play on well-known robot media, blending toy-like origins with a heroic leadership role among his robotic allies. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Cowboy Bob
text: Cowboy Bob is RV salesman who sells recreational vehicles to the Simpson family, notably at Bob's RV Round-Up. Cowboy Bob is a slick, opportunistic salesman who runs an RV lot and has a knack for spotting an easy mark. He first appears pushing the Simpsons toward an oversized, overpriced RV called The Ultimate Behemoth before settling them for a cheaper model when Homer can't afford it. He pops up again singing alongside Homer, Marge, and Jasper in the snow, showing a lighter, more musical side to his salesman persona. In a later appearance, he tries to con Homer into another RV purchase during a financial pinch and ends up shipping Homer and his kids off to Turkey. Despite working at Bob's RV Round-Up, he's clarified he doesn't actually own the business, brushing off questions about it with a cryptic "long story." Overall, he embodies the stereotypical shady used-vehicle salesman trope, always looking for the next sucker to close a deal with. Voiced by Albert Brooks ("The Call of the Simpsons"); Dan Castellaneta ("Mobile Homer").

title: Annette (The Sweetest Apu)
text: Annette (The Sweetest Apu) is Squishee supplier at the Kwik-E-Mart and Apu's affair partner. Annette is a minor character who worked as the Squishee delivery supplier for the Kwik-E-Mart. She became romantically involved with Apu, leading to a secret affair that was eventually caught on security camera footage. When Homer returned a keg for a deposit, he stumbled upon the affair and it was later revealed to Manjula, causing a major rift in Apu's marriage. In order to reconcile with his wife, Apu ended his relationship with Annette. After her departure, both she and the Squishee product line were replaced at the store by a hobo who delivered a rival drink called Smooshies. Annette herself has no distinct personality traits explored on-screen, existing mainly as a plot device tied to Apu's infidelity storyline. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Halle Berry (character)
text: Halle Berry (character) is Real-life actress and fashion model who appears as herself in cameo/guest appearances in The Simpsons. Halle Berry appears as a fictionalized version of herself within the Simpsons universe, most notably presenting an Oscar for best short film in a way that seems oddly delayed. She's plagued by a recurring nightmare where her teeth fly out of her mouth, a quirky personal detail revealed during her appearance. Beyond her on-screen role, she's referenced multiple times in the show's pop culture jokes, often used as a stand-in for glamour or fame, such as being a hypothetical Santa's delivery costume choice or part of a celebrity fantasy list. Her image also decorates the walls of a local Springfield business, cementing her status as an aspirational celebrity figure in the town. In non-canon material, her name becomes shorthand for someone acting erratically, referencing her real-life award acceptance speech reputation. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: what the Halle Berry?
quotes: what the Halle Berry?

title: Ludwig van Beethoven
text: Ludwig van Beethoven is Real-world historical composer depicted as a minor recurring character/cameo figure in The Simpsons. Ludwig van Beethoven appears in The Simpsons as a fictionalized version of the famous 18th-century composer. He is mostly referenced through busts, cameo appearances, and stories told within the show rather than being a fully developed character. In one tale narrated by Marge, he is shown spending time with Emperor Joseph II, much to the annoyance of a rival composer seeking an audience. He also appears as a ghost alongside Mozart when Bart plays piano, tying him loosely into the show's musical gags. In a non-canon storyline, he even faces off against rapper Tupac Shakur in a music contest set in Heaven, showing the show's tendency to blend historical and pop-culture figures for comedic effect. Overall, his role is more symbolic and referential than central, often used as a shorthand for classical music greatness or as a visual gag via his bust. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Bob Belcher
text: Bob Belcher is Crossover character from Bob's Burgers, husband and father, appearing in non-canon Simpsons crossover segments. Bob Belcher is a crossover figure brought into The Simpsons universe from his own animated show, Bob's Burgers, appearing mainly in non-canon segments like couch gags and crossover specials. He's portrayed as a family man running his own restaurant, with his wife and three children in tow during these guest appearances. In one non-canon segment, his restaurant becomes the setting for a strange encounter when Homer Simpson turns up inside it, leading to a humorous exchange about names and identity involving Bob's daughter Louise. Bob comes across as a mildly exasperated but good-natured proprietor who tolerates the chaos brought by the Simpsons family invading his world. He also appears alongside Homer and Family Guy's Peter Griffin during a multi-show crossover event, situating him within the broader animated sitcom universe. His presence in the show underscores The Simpsons' history of blending with other popular animated sitcoms for special crossover episodes. Voiced by H. Jon Benjamin. Notable quotes: "They couldn't keep him."
quotes: "They couldn't keep him."

title: Louise Belcher
text: Louise Belcher is A crossover character from Bob's Burgers who appears in non-canon Simpsons material as part of the Belcher family. Louise Belcher is one of the Belcher children, best known from Bob's Burgers, who makes non-canonical appearances in Simpsons-related media. She's shown as sharp-tongued and mischievous, quick to offer blunt opinions about the Simpson family, particularly Homer. When Homer sneaks into the Belchers' restaurant, Louise reacts with dry humor, suggesting a swap of names between Homer and her father Bob rather than panicking. She also shows a mix of suspicion and sympathy, noting she'd feel bad for Homer if he were actually trying to rob them, hinting at her streetwise but soft-hearted nature. Louise also appears as a background reference on a poster in Lisa Simpson's bedroom, showing her recognition within the show's fictional universe. She's part of a broader crossover appearance with her whole family during a Simpsons premiere celebration and an anniversary special. Voiced by Kristen Schaal.

title: Black weasel
text: Black weasel is One of Nelson Muntz's two crony bullies at Springfield Elementary (later Shelbyville Elementary). The Black weasel is one of Nelson's two nearly identical bully sidekicks, distinguished from his counterpart only by his darker skin coloring. He shares the same name, "Nelson's Weasel," as the other weasel, and the two are rarely seen apart. After Nelson suffers a humiliating defeat at the hands of Bart, the weasel only sporadically continues to associate with him, suggesting a fickle loyalty typical of schoolyard hierarchies. At some point he transfers to Shelbyville Elementary School alongside the Yellow weasel, showing that even minor bully characters can shift settings within the show's world. The two weasels later reunite with Nelson at a bully summit, hinting that bullying culture persists across school lines. As a background bully character, he has appeared in a large number of episodes over the series' long run, usually without major dialogue or plot focus. Voiced by Jo Ann Harris, Pamela Hayden.

title: James Brown (character)
text: James Brown (character) is Real-world musician who appeared as himself in a guest role on The Simpsons. James Brown appears as a fictionalized version of himself, the legendary singer-songwriter renowned for his decades-long influence on 20th century music. His main appearance comes in an episode where he interacts with the Simpsons family in some capacity, lending his celebrity persona to the show. He's also briefly glimpsed in the afterlife, seated on a cloud in Heaven, during a scene involving Gil Gunderson being cast out to hell. Beyond his on-screen cameo, he's referenced in other episodes and tie-in media, underscoring his status as a pop-culture icon woven into the show's universe. As with many celebrity guest appearances on the series, his role is brief but memorable, capitalizing on his real-world fame rather than developing him as a original character. Voiced by James Brown.

title: Anita
text: Anita is One of The Cool Moms, an old friend group of Marge's; wife of Chris and mother of Erik. Anita is a recurring member of The Cool Moms, the clique of mothers Marge briefly reconnects with. She's shown to be somewhat oblivious to normal social norms, questioning why Marge was cutting up chicken for a meal at The Enchanted Snail when no one else seemed to be eating. Like the rest of the group, she takes part in judging Bart as a bad influence, which leads to friction with Marge. She's also seen getting affectionate with the other moms in a make-out session, hinting at a fluid sexuality among the group. Outside of her mom-clique antics, she's mentioned to have a family that rents a beach house for daily beach trips. She later reappears at a location called Quiet Rivers, though little else is detailed about her life there. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Babe the Blue Ox
text: Babe the Blue Ox is Fictional blue ox belonging to lumberjack Paul Bunyan, appearing in Simpsons folklore-themed episodes. Babe the Blue Ox is a folkloric companion animal tied to Paul Bunyan, appearing mostly as a statue or background figure rather than a speaking character. In one storyline, a statue of Babe stands beside a Paul Bunyan statue at a tourist attraction until Bart Simpson accidentally destroys it during a reckless trolley ride. In a separate tall-tale legend, Babe is shown as a mountain carving brought to life by magical lightning, becoming Paul Bunyan's loyal partner in outsized adventures that inadvertently shape famous American landmarks. In a non-canon Halloween special, Babe becomes a giant living mascot alongside Paul Bunyan, rampaging through Springfield until the town's advertising-fueled monsters lose power. Babe never speaks and functions purely as an oversized sidekick or set piece tied to Bunyan's legend, embodying exaggerated tall-tale humor typical of the show's folklore parodies.

title: Honest Abe
text: Honest Abe is Wrestling alter-ego adopted by Grampa Abraham Simpson. Honest Abe is a wrestling persona taken on by Grampa Simpson, styled after Abraham Lincoln with a brown facial hair wig as part of the costume. He adopted this heroic identity after abandoning his previous, more villainous wrestling character, Glamorous Godfrey, because that heel persona was negatively affecting Bart. As Honest Abe, Grampa transformed Bart's wrestling identity as well, turning him from Beautiful Bart into a new sidekick called Laddie Liberty. Together, the pair used their good-guy personas to team up against Mr. Burns in the ring, ultimately defeating and pinning him. The character represents a redemptive shift for Grampa, trading villainy for a wholesome, patriotic hero role. Honest Abe only appears in a single episode but has also been featured as a skin in a mobile game tie-in. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Daphne Beaumont
text: Daphne Beaumont is Theater critic for the Springfield Shopper, minor recurring character. Daphne Beaumont is a minor recurring figure in Springfield's media scene, working as a theater critic for the local newspaper. She is part of a trio of critics, alongside Jamie Killday and Garth Trelawny, whose harsh judgments end up shaping Homer's own brief career as a restaurant critic. Her influence pushes Homer toward giving unfairly negative reviews to establishments that resemble their own critical circle. She's shown to have a bit of a mob mentality, joining in when Homer becomes the target of public anger. Outside of her critic duties, she's also just an ordinary Springfield resident who enjoys live music, having attended a Green Day concert. Overall, she serves as a background character representing the pretentious, cynical world of professional criticism. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Drew Carey (character)
text: Drew Carey (character) is Real-life celebrity guest character who appears as himself in The Simpsons. Drew Carey appears as a fictionalized version of himself within the Simpsons universe. His main canonical appearance has him introducing Krusty the Clown during a milestone 4000th show, where he playfully jabs at Krusty for allegedly stealing his comedic material over the years. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he shows up to Sherri and Terri's funeral, though his motivation for attending is less about mourning and more about a mix-up, since he mistakenly believed it was a corporate Microsoft event. This gives him a running gag of self-serving or clueless motivations rather than genuine sentimentality. Overall, he's a minor guest character used for a bit of celebrity cameo humor rather than a fleshed-out personality within the show. Voiced by Drew Carey (Himself).

title: Brad (King of the Hill)
text: Brad (King of the Hill) is A minor recurring character, one of two Powersauce advertising representatives who appears in the episode "King of the Hill". Brad works alongside his partner Neil promoting the energy bar company Powersauce. Together they scout out a celebrity to scale the dangerous mountain known as The Murderhorn for a publicity stunt, initially approaching action star Rainier Wolfcastle. When Wolfcastle refuses, Bart's suggestion that Homer take on the climb leads to Brad enthusiastically agreeing to use him instead. He acts as something of a hype man for the stunt, addressing the crowd before Homer's ascent and promising Homer will plant the Powersauce flag at the summit. Brad and Neil also co-host the in-universe Powersauce Newsbreak segment. He's a minor, opportunistic corporate figure whose main function is driving the plot of his featured episode forward through advertising schemes. Voiced by Brendan Fraser.

title: Babysitting receptionist
text: Babysitting receptionist is Minor recurring character who works as a receptionist at Rubber Baby Buggy Bumpers Babysitting Service. The Babysitting Receptionist is a minor, gray-haired background character best known for handling calls at the babysitting service the Simpsons rely on. She has a memorably strict, no-nonsense attitude, most notably banning the Simpson family from using the service after past incidents. Homer manages to work around this by disguising his identity over the phone to secure a babysitter anyway. Beyond her babysitting duties, she pops up in the wider Springfield community, appearing at a town meeting concerning Mr. Burns' massive fine. She also makes a brief non-canon appearance within one of Lisa's dream sequences, adding a touch of surreal humor to her otherwise mundane role. Overall, she serves as a small recurring piece of Springfield's background texture rather than a major character. Voiced by June Foray.

title: Steve Buscemi (character)
text: Steve Buscemi (character) is Real-life celebrity who appears as himself in cameo roles in Springfield. This character is a fictionalized version of actor, director, and writer Steve Buscemi, appearing as himself within the show's universe. He's shown casually strolling through Springfield, joining in on a musical number with Homer as if it were the most normal thing in the world. His brief interactions with the Simpsons family highlight the show's tendency to poke fun at celebrities by placing them in absurd, everyday situations, such as being questioned about his famous movie roles or getting caught up in a dispute with hostile foreigners. He also appears connected to the Springfield entertainment industry, showing up at a table read for a film project. Overall, his role is a lighthearted cameo that leans on his real-world fame and iconic film history for comedic effect. Voiced by Steve Buscemi.

title: Boxcar Bob
text: Boxcar Bob is A hobo who was Homer's first opponent in his brief boxing career. Boxcar Bob is a minor hobo character who appears when Homer decides to try his hand at boxing. He agrees to fight Homer for the prize of a sandwich, showing just how little it takes to motivate him into a brawl. During the match, he punches relentlessly, pausing only briefly to check on his bindle, showing a strange attachment to his few possessions even mid-fight. Despite his aggressive punching, he eventually tires himself out and loses the match to Homer. He later resurfaces in a more sinister context, appearing among the mob attempting to kill the Simpson family. His appearances are brief, but memorable for his gritty hobo persona and comedic single-mindedness during the boxing match. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Brown-Nose Bear
text: Brown-Nose Bear is Minor fictional cartoon character within the Itchy & Scratchy Show universe. Brown-Nose Bear is a cartoon character that exists within the show-within-a-show world of The Itchy & Scratchy Show. He is one of several characters revealed to have been plagiarized by Roger Meyers, Sr., surfacing as evidence during the courtroom battle between Chester J. Lampwick and Roger Meyers, Jr. Alongside other stolen creations like Disgruntled Goat, Flatulent Fox, Rich Uncle Skeleton, and Dinner Dog, his original drawings are presented in court to prove Lampwick's claim of authorship. He is a non-speaking background character with no real personality traits of his own, existing mainly as a piece of the show's meta-commentary on cartoon copyright theft. Beyond his courtroom appearance, he shows up briefly as a parade float and gets a passing mention in a Simpsons book.

title: Sorcerer-intendent Chalmers
text: Sorcerer-intendent Chalmers is A non-canon fantasy-world counterpart of Superintendent Chalmers, serving as sorcerer-intendent to King Quimby. This character is a magical, medieval-style reimagining of Springfield's school superintendent, appearing in a non-canon fantasy episode. He works in service to King Quimby, overseeing matters of sorcery within the kingdom. His main role in the story comes when Lisa is discovered practicing magic, prompting him to arrive alongside fellow sorcerers to escort her away for formal training. He acts more as an authority figure enforcing magical law than as a fully developed personality. The character also appears in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game, tying into the same fantasy-themed storyline. As with many alternate-universe versions of Simpsons characters, he mirrors the personality traits of his real-world counterpart while existing in a whimsical, sorcery-filled setting. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Anthony Bourdain (character)
text: Anthony Bourdain (character) is Celebrity chef who appears as a guest character in a dream sequence involving the Simpson family. Anthony Bourdain is a real-life celebrity chef who makes a surreal cameo appearance within one of Marge's dreams. In this dream, he interacts with Marge, Bart, and Lisa before Homer barges in and begins gorging himself on food. The scene takes a whimsical turn as Bart, Lisa, and Bourdain end up bouncing around on space hoppers while chanting after Homer. Beyond this dream sequence, his presence in the show is minimal, with only a background picture of him appearing in a later episode set inside The Penny Loafer. His role is largely a novelty cameo referencing his real-world fame as a chef and food personality. Voiced by Anthony Bourdain (Himself).

title: Mr. Blackheart
text: Mr. Blackheart is Minor recurring character; an ivory dealer who tries to buy Bart's elephant Stampy. Mr. Blackheart is a shady businessman whose checkered résumé includes whale-hunting, seal-clubbing, and even a stint as president of the FOX network before settling into the ivory trade. His willingness to profit from exploiting animals makes him a fitting, if minor, embodiment of corporate greed in the show. He enters the Simpsons' orbit when Homer, desperate to get rid of the elephant Bart won, agrees to sell Stampy to him for a hefty sum. His deal falls through when Bart frees Stampy before the exchange can be completed. He later makes a brief background appearance during a Trappuccino promotional event in the Simpsons movie, suggesting he remains a fixture in Springfield's world of dubious enterprises. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Aline
text: Aline is Minor recurring character; wife of Cletus Spuckler in a flashback wedding scene. Aline is a minor background character best known for her brief appearance as the bride in a flashback wedding to Cletus. Little is revealed about her personality or background beyond the circumstances of her marriage. The scene plays into the show's running gag of poking fun at the hasty, informal nature of some Springfield unions, particularly involving Cletus's family. She has made only a handful of appearances across the series, mostly in passing or as part of flashback sequences. Her character exists largely as a footnote in Cletus's backstory rather than as a fully developed figure in her own right. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Cain
text: Cain is Biblical figure appearing in a Ned Flanders-made film within the show; son of Adam and Eve, brother of Abel and Kevin. Cain is a minor biblical character who appears in a homemade movie that Ned Flanders films starring his sons after catching them watching an inappropriate ad. In the show's version of the story, he is portrayed as one of the sons of Adam and Eve, alongside his brothers Abel and Kevin. The Simpsons universe adds a twist to the classic tale by giving Cain and Abel a middle brother, Kevin, who feels neglected and manipulates events to frame Cain for Abel's murder. This storyline is referenced by Dr. Hibbert as an extreme example of "middle child syndrome" when diagnosing Lisa. Cain himself doesn't appear as a major character, functioning mostly as a reference point for the show's comedic riffs on sibling rivalry and biblical stories. He's also referenced in a joking threat between Rod and Todd Flanders, showing how the show uses the Cain and Abel story as a shorthand for fraternal conflict. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Maya Angelou
text: Maya Angelou is Real-world author and poet who appears as a minor recurring character in Springfield. Maya Angelou appears as a fictionalized version of the real-life American author and poet within the Simpsons universe. She is portrayed as a respected literary figure, appearing at events like the Festival of Books and as a guest on Krusty's Poetry Korner. Her dialogue tends toward flowery, metaphor-heavy language that pokes fun at highbrow poetic style, especially when answering a mundane question about a bomber with an elaborate poetic response. A recurring joke involves other characters, like Moe, being surprised to learn she is black, highlighting some characters' ignorance. Her image and influence pop up throughout the show, from posters to being referenced in children's skipping rhymes and graduation speeches, cementing her status as a cultural touchstone within the show's universe. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: The ebony fighter awakens, dabbled with the dewy beads of morn. It is a mach-5 child, forever bound to suckle from the shriveled breast of Congress. - Maya Angelou
quotes: The ebony fighter awakens, dabbled with the dewy beads of morn. It is a mach-5 child, forever bound to suckle from the shriveled breast of Congress. - Maya Angelou

title: Boy with bangs
text: Boy with bangs is A minor recurring background student at Springfield Elementary School. The boy with bangs is a nondescript student who frequently appears in the halls and classrooms of Springfield Elementary. He doesn't have a distinct personality explored on the show, functioning mainly as one of the many background children who populate school-related scenes. His most notable individual moment was attending Dylan's birthday party, suggesting he has some level of social involvement with other kids at school. Otherwise, he appears sporadically across many seasons, often unnamed and unremarked upon, as part of the show's large ensemble of recurring extras. His defining physical trait, as his name suggests, is his brown hair styled with bangs.

title: Armando (hairdresser)
text: Armando (hairdresser) is A minor recurring hairdresser in Springfield who styles Marge's hair. Armando is a hairdresser who works at Le Pamperie Hair Salon and later at The Perm Bank, where Marge Simpson is one of his regular customers. He's shown to have a distinctive, if questionable, sense of style, once giving a customer a tall blue hairdo that left her visibly displeased. His most memorable moment comes when Homer sneaks into the salon to secretly take over cutting Marge's hair himself, silently pushing Armando aside so he can try to prove himself as a better husband. Armando doesn't get much dialogue or characterization beyond his profession, functioning mainly as a background figure tied to Springfield Mall's beauty services. Despite his minor role, he's appeared across a couple of episodes as a recognizable recurring face in Springfield's service industry. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Cassandra
text: Cassandra is One of three teenage Wiccans who befriend Lisa Simpson in the forest. Cassandra is a pink-haired teenage witch who, along with her friends Esmeralda and Gwendolyn Nightshadow, practices Wiccan rituals centered on nature and friendship. She and her companions become close with Lisa Simpson, even attempting to recruit her into their coven. Their reputation takes a dark turn when Ned Flanders accuses them of being demonic, leading to their arrest, though they are later acquitted in court. In a dramatic twist tied to their supposed powers, much of Springfield's population goes blind after the girls warn that doubters would be struck blind. When an angry mob hunts them down using archaic witch-hunting logic, Lisa steps in to save them and clarify the misunderstanding. The trio's bond with Lisa highlights themes of tolerance and friendship despite their unconventional lifestyle. Voiced by Neve Campbell.

title: Papa Bear
text: Papa Bear is Father bear character from the fictional "Goldilocks and the Three Bears" story as told within The Simpsons universe. Papa Bear is the patriarch of the bear family featured in the classic fairy tale parodied throughout the show. He appears alongside his wife Mama Bear and son Baby Bear (also called Kid Bear) in Bart's twisted retelling of the story to Maggie, where the family returns home to find an intruder in their beds. The character also shows up as an animatronic figure in a Storytown Village attraction the Simpson family visits, and later as a book-cover image that terrifies a bear-phobic Homer. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, the bears take a much darker turn, violently attacking Goldilocks upon finding her in their home. Overall, Papa Bear functions less as a developed personality and more as a recurring fairy-tale device used for comedic and horror parody purposes within the series. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Hey, look, man—breakfast in bed!
quotes: Hey, look, man—breakfast in bed!

title: Bouncing Battle Baby
text: Bouncing Battle Baby is Maggie Simpson's non-canon superhero alter-ego appearing in Simpsons comics and Tapped Out. Bouncing Battle Baby is the accidental superhero identity Maggie Simpson takes on after being caught in a botched cloning experiment at Professor Frink's lab. She ends up with a mix of powers from her babysitters, Stretch Dude and Clobber Girl, gaining both invulnerability and stretchy rubber-like abilities. As a baby superhero, she's understandably unreliable on missions, needing diaper changes, crying during a robbery, and requiring nap time in the middle of crimefighting. Despite the chaos she causes, she proves surprisingly useful in a climactic showdown, being used as living ammunition in a slingshot to take down a horde of cloned villains. Her arc highlights a comedic take on the idea of an infant superhero, blending typical baby behavior with superhero tropes. Ultimately she's accepted as a genuine member of the makeshift superhero trio.

title: Lando Calrissian
text: Lando Calrissian is Non-canon Star Wars crossover character; an employee at Jabba's Hut Jedi Preschool. Lando Calrissian is a non-canon crossover character based on the Star Wars smuggler-turned-general, appearing in Simpsons Star Wars-themed specials. In this incarnation, he works at a preschool called Jabba's Hut Jedi Preschool, where he is tasked with the mundane job of supervising the Cloud City Nap Room instead of any grand space adventures. He later shows up socially at Moe's Tavern for a Disney+ anniversary celebration, showing that even galactic heroes unwind at Moe's like everyone else in Springfield. He is a non-speaking character, so his personality is conveyed mostly through visual gags rather than dialogue. His appearances are largely cameo-style nods to Star Wars for fans, referencing his classic film counterpart played by Billy Dee Williams. He has also appeared in costume form in at least one regular episode.

title: Charles Montgomery Burns' adoptive father
text: Charles Montgomery Burns' adoptive father is The wealthy billionaire who adopted young Charles "Happy" Burns, taking him from his birth parents. This unnamed billionaire appears only in a flashback as the man who takes in a young Mr. Burns, offering him a life of wealth in place of his impoverished but loving biological family. His arrival in a limousine seals the deal instantly, as young Burns eagerly abandons his parents and even his beloved teddy bear to go with him. The scene is a deliberate homage to the classic film Citizen Kane, mirroring the moment a young Charles Foster Kane is taken away by a wealthy financier. Though he has almost no characterization beyond this single scene, his choice sets in motion Mr. Burns' transformation into the cold, wealth-obsessed tycoon seen throughout the series. His fate is unknown, and he may or may not still be alive. Notable quotes: Happy, would you like to continue living with us, your loving natural parents, or would you rather live with this twisted loveless billionaire? - Mr. Burns' father | Let's roll. - Young Burns
quotes: Happy, would you like to continue living with us, your loving natural parents, or would you rather live with this twisted loveless billionaire? - Mr. Burns' father
Let's roll. - Young Burns

title: Bao mother
text: Bao mother is A crossover character from the Pixar short "Bao," appearing in a Simpsons special. Bao mother is a non-canon character who crossed over from the Pixar short film Bao into a Simpsons special. She is depicted as a mother accompanying her son on a family outing tied to a Mother's Day theme. Her appearance is limited to a single special, and she has no spoken lines, making her a purely visual cameo. As a crossover figure, she exists mainly to nod to Pixar's Bao within the Simpsons universe rather than to serve as a developed character with her own personality or recurring gags. Her role is brief and tied entirely to the event of the Mother's Day trip.

title: Mama Bear
text: Mama Bear is Mother bear character from the Goldilocks and the Three Bears fairy tale as depicted in The Simpsons. Mama Bear is a fictional bear who appears as part of the classic fairy tale Goldilocks and the Three Bears, referenced within The Simpsons universe. She is the wife of Papa Bear and mother of Baby Bear, forming a traditional family unit of anthropomorphic bears. Her most notable appearance comes in a subverted, crude retelling of the story that Bart narrates to Maggie, where the tale takes a darker turn than the traditional version. She also appears as an animatronic figure in a theme park attraction visited by the Simpson family, and is referenced in other episodes as part of bear-related media that frighten Homer. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, the bear family's story turns violent when they discover and attack Goldilocks. Overall, she functions as a background storybook character used for comedic and parodic purposes rather than a fully developed personality. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Prince Charles
text: Prince Charles is Real-world British royal (Prince of Wales) who appears as a minor character in Springfield-related storylines. This character is a fictionalized version of the real-life Prince Charles, depicted as a member of the British royal family alongside his mother, Queen Elizabeth II. He's shown watching Springfield's citizens through hidden surveillance cameras, giving him an odd voyeuristic connection to the town despite never actually visiting it. His mother even compares him to Ralph Wiggum after hearing one of Ralph's nonsensical lines, poking fun at Charles's public image. He also shows up in print media within the show, appearing on a magazine cover and being mentioned as one of Ned Flanders's list of admirable liberal figures. The character serves mostly as a cameo or background reference rather than a fully developed personality, leaning on real-world associations with the royal family for humor. Voiced by Eddie Izzard.

title: Mrs. Borton
text: Mrs. Borton is Minor recurring background character; mother of Wendell Borton and wife of Mr. Borton. Mrs. Borton is a minor figure in the Simpsons universe, known primarily as the mother of classmate Wendell Borton. She appears mostly in the background of school-related scenes, functioning as one of the many unnamed or barely-named parent characters that populate Springfield Elementary's world. Her most notable canonical moment involves picking her son up from school, a small domestic detail that ties her to the show's recurring cast of parents. In non-canon material, she is shown taking Wendell to a children's play area secretly run by mobster Fat Tony, adding a bit of ironic humor typical of the show's comic spin-offs. She has no speaking lines in the show, reinforcing her status as a background character rather than a developed personality. Despite her limited role, she has appeared across numerous episodes and comic issues, making her a familiar if silent presence.

title: Bette
text: Bette is A jewel thief who appears in a heist storyline with Marge and other Springfield women. Bette is a career criminal specializing in jewel theft, first introduced as part of a tight-knit heist crew alongside Erin, Sarah Wiggum, and Lindsey Naegle. Her history is defined by betrayal, since Lindsey double-crossed the group during a robbery, sounding the alarm and escaping with the loot while Bette and Erin took the fall and went to prison. This betrayal fuels her main motivation later on, as she seeks revenge rather than simple profit. She's resourceful and willing to go to extreme lengths, including kidnapping Marge and Sarah, to orchestrate an elaborate scheme against Lindsey. Working undercover as a waiter during a high-society gala shows her willingness to blend in and play the long con. Ultimately she's more of a schemer than a purely violent criminal, preferring manipulation and framing to get even with those who wronged her. Voiced by Natasha Rothwell.

title: Justin Bieber (character)
text: Justin Bieber (character) is Real-life celebrity musician who appears as a guest character in The Simpsons universe. Justin Bieber appears in the show as a version of his real-world pop star persona, popping up in cameo-like roles across several episodes. He's treated as a celebrity so famous that even Lisa reportedly fainted just thinking she spotted him in a crowd. In one appearance, he attempts to join a kids' talent show but gets turned away for being too old. His fame is referenced through incidental details, like his picture hanging in a local business, and his birthplace becoming a piece of trivia when the Simpsons visit Toronto. Overall, he functions less as a developed character and more as a running pop-culture reference to his real celebrity status. Voiced by Justin Bieber (Himself).

title: Andrés Cantor (character)
text: Andrés Cantor (character) is Argentinian sportscaster who guest-appeared in the Simpsons universe. Andrés Cantor is a real-life sportscaster who appears as himself in the show, providing commentary on a World Cup match between Brazil and Luxembourg. His defining running gag is an exaggerated speech quirk where he elongates and accentuates certain words ending in a sound like '-oal,' mimicking the enthusiastic goal-calling style typical of many Latin American sports announcers. This tic causes him to stumble comically over unrelated words like 'control' or 'toll' that merely share that ending sound. He's portrayed as a passionate, energetic broadcaster fully immersed in the excitement of the game. His role is brief but memorable, serving as a parody of the dramatic flair often associated with soccer commentary. Voiced by Andrés Cantor (Himself).

title: Captain Bowditch
text: Captain Bowditch is Sea captain who runs a father-son relationship retreat aboard his ship, appearing as a minor recurring character. Captain Bowditch operates a nautical program designed to mend strained father-son relationships through hard labor and sailor discipline. Marge enrolls Homer and Bart on his ship, and he ends up guiding several other Springfield father-son pairs through similar exercises. He shows genuine investment in his passengers' growth, even promoting Bart to midshipman during his stay. Despite his tough, no-nonsense captain persona, it's revealed that he struggles with alcoholism, which is actually why he took to the sea in the first place. In a non-canon appearance, he's also shown hosting a school field trip aboard a decommissioned WWII vessel, getting kids to do menial shipboard chores. He maintains a stern but ultimately caring demeanor, whether dealing with troubled families or nosy schoolchildren. Voiced by Nick Offerman. Notable quotes: My name is Captain Bowditch. Your wife signed you up for a week at sea, where you'll live like sailors, eat like sailors and use therapeutic techniques to solve father-son conflicts... like sailors.
quotes: My name is Captain Bowditch. Your wife signed you up for a week at sea, where you'll live like sailors, eat like sailors and use therapeutic techniques to solve father-son conflicts... like sailors.

title: Bear Robot
text: Bear Robot is A malfunctioning robot built by Professor Frink for Mr. Burns. The Bear Robot is a mechanical creation of Professor Frink, designed as a substitute companion for Mr. Burns after he lost his beloved teddy bear Bobo. Its intended purpose was simple and affectionate: to hug Burns and perform a little dance for his amusement. Unfortunately, a programming glitch turned this comforting gesture into chaos, causing the robot to violently grab and shake Burns instead of gently embracing him. The malfunction didn't stop there, as the robot proceeded to smash through a wall, leaving destruction in its wake. Despite its brief and disastrous appearance, the Bear Robot has since made non-canon appearances in Simpsons mobile game content.

title: Eduardo Barcelona
text: Eduardo Barcelona is Homer Simpson's former childhood pen pal from Spain, appearing in the episode "YOLO". Eduardo Barcelona, also known as Eddie Miami in English, is a flamboyant Spanish chef who reconnects with Homer as an adult after being his childhood pen pal. He boasts an enormous family, with eight wives and 200 children who have gone on to become artists, doctors, and chefs of their own. Marge arranges for Eduardo to visit in order to lift Homer's spirits and help him relive some of the dreams he once shared as a ten-year-old. He later teams up with a fellow chef to explore a conspiracy theory about counterfeit saffron being used in paella dishes. In a non-canon twist, he is revealed to secretly be the alter ego of the supervillain Paella Man. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Carrot Top
text: Carrot Top is Real-world celebrity cameo appearing as himself in Springfield. Carrot Top is a real-life American stand-up comedian and actor who appears in the Simpsons universe as a version of himself. He shows up as one of the roasters at the Roast of Krusty the Clown, trading barbs alongside other comedians before later attending the funeral of Krusty's father. His comedic reputation extends into other episodes, including a joke revealing that he secretly ghostwrites all of Krusty's material for a talk show segment. He's also referenced as an author, having written a book that Rod Flanders is seen reading, and as a pitchman through an in-universe advertisement for novelty prop bets. Beyond his own appearances, his name has become a bit of a running gag/insult, used by other characters to mockingly nickname someone with orange or carrot-colored hair, such as Lisa in a vegetable costume. He remains a non-speaking, real-world character rather than a fully voiced original Simpsons character.

title: Burly
text: Burly is Fictional mascot character for Burly Paper Towels, object of Marge Simpson's brief infatuation. Burly is the buff, rugged mascot used to advertise Burly Paper Towels, clearly modeled on the real-world Brawny Man. He catches Marge's eye after she accidentally buys the wrong brand, sparking an unexpected crush that leads her to write him a fan letter. Homer and Bart exploit this infatuation as an opportunity for a prank, with Homer posing as the fictitious model "Chad Sexington." The gag culminates in an awkward dinner setup where Barney shows up dressed like a poor imitation of Burly instead of the real deal. Though he doesn't appear as a live character often, Burly's image recurs as a background joke and advertising figure in later episodes. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Fantasize, Marge. Fantasize about Burly.
quotes: Fantasize, Marge. Fantasize about Burly.

title: Catwoman
text: Catwoman is A Batman villain/anti-hero referenced within the Simpsons universe, mostly through pop-culture discussions and costumes. Catwoman appears in the Simpsons world purely as a pop-culture reference to the Batman franchise rather than as an original character with her own storyline. She's brought up in conversations about which actress best portrayed her, with Adam West insisting only certain classic actresses count as the "true" Catwoman. Comic Book Guy fantasizes about her while hallucinating as Spock, listing her among women he'd like to romance. She also shows up as a costume choice for various characters and background fans at conventions like Comicalooza. In a non-canon storyline, Comic Book Guy even requests a Catwoman-costumed celebrity as a substitute Christmas gift. Overall, she functions as a running nod to Batman fandom rather than a developed personality within the show.

title: Tyler Boom
text: Tyler Boom is Minor recurring character; son of Scotty Boom, a barbecue rival of Homer's. Tyler Boom is a mischievous young character best known for his appearance in the episode 'Cue Detective. He's the son of Scotty Boom, and shows a willingness to bend the rules to get what he wants. In a notable act of theft, he took Homer's smoker for his father's benefit. Interestingly, despite helping his dad in competition, he later sabotaged his father's cooking on purpose, revealing that he valued spending time with his dad more than winning. This small but telling detail gives him a bit of emotional depth for a minor character. He also appears briefly in the opening gag sequence of another episode. Voiced by Bobby Moynihan.

title: Timothée Chalamet
text: Timothée Chalamet is A fictionalized version of real-world actor Timothée Chalamet who appears within the Simpsons universe. This version of Timothée Chalamet exists as a celebrity figure within the Simpsons world rather than a member of the main cast. He starred as Muttley in a in-universe film called Wacky Races: Furry Road, working alongside Sideshow Mel who played Dick Dastardly. His casting stirred up enough controversy that Comic Book Guy launched a fan campaign trying to get his co-star recast. He's also apparently attractive enough to inspire questionable life choices, as Marge got a large tattoo of him on her back before eventually having it removed. His presence in the show is brief but pokes fun at celebrity culture and fandom obsession. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Peggy Bundy
text: Peggy Bundy is Fictional character from Married... with Children who appears in crossover clips/episodes within The Simpsons. Peggy Bundy is a crossover character brought into The Simpsons universe from the sitcom Married... with Children, appearing mainly as clips watched by other characters rather than as a true Simpsons cast member. She's portrayed as Al Bundy's wife, frequently pushing for intimacy with him despite his reluctance, a running gag from her original show carried over into her Simpsons appearances. Her scenes are typically shown being viewed by Simpsons characters, such as Ned Flanders laughing at her antics or NASA scientists watching a clip during a space mission. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, she and Al are reimagined as aliens amid a chaotic parody of endless Married... with Children broadcasts. Across her appearances, she remains a comedic, sex-driven counterpart to her exasperated husband, reflecting the same dynamic she had on her home series. Voiced by Pamela Hayden, Maggie Roswell, Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: No, Peg,
quotes: No, Peg,

title: Marlon Brando
text: Marlon Brando is Real-world actor referenced/parodied within the Simpsons universe. Marlon Brando appears in the show as a version of the famous real-life actor, existing within the Simpsons universe as a celebrity referenced by various characters. He is depicted as having voiced the villainous robot John Truckasaurus in a fictional in-universe movie, showing how the show blends real celebrities into its fictional media landscape. He's also tied to a bizarre errand involving Bart delivering hundreds of Big Macs to Brando's private island, playing into jokes about celebrity excess. Milhouse imagines him in a couple of odd daydream sequences, including one about cupcakes, showing how pervasive his cultural image is even among children. Fat Tony also references Brando as someone whose voice and mannerisms are famous enough to be impersonated. Overall, Brando functions less as a character with his own personality and more as a running pop-culture reference point for humor. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Casper the Friendly Ghost
text: Casper the Friendly Ghost is A comic book character referenced within the Simpsons universe, appearing as a fictional-within-fiction figure tied to Bart and Lisa's comic reading habits. Casper the Friendly Ghost exists in the Simpsons world as a beloved comic book character rather than an active participant in the show's events. He's tied into the franchise's fictional comic industry, published by Harry Comics, and his likeness to Richie Rich sparks a funny theory from Bart and Lisa about their true relationship. Casper's cultural presence pops up in odd ways throughout Springfield, from Wendell's school presentation on famous pale figures to Homer's punny comparison of a spicy pepper to the ghost's name. He also appears in a non-canon capacity, including a gravestone gag and a glowing review from Comic Book Guy. Overall, Casper serves as a recurring pop-culture reference point used for jokes rather than a character with direct interactions with the Simpsons family. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Ghost pepper? More like Casper the Friendly Ghost pepper.
quotes: Ghost pepper? More like Casper the Friendly Ghost pepper.

title: Asa (senior)
text: Asa (senior) is A minor resident of the Springfield Retirement Castle. Asa is an elderly background character who lives at the Springfield Retirement Castle. He became a familiar face to Homer after Homer spent time at the facility. Asa is typically seen in the company of fellow residents Hattie and Beatrice, suggesting he is part of a small social circle among the retirees. He is a non-speaking character, so little is known about his personality or backstory beyond his presence in a couple of episodes. His role is largely that of set dressing to flesh out the retirement home's community of elderly residents.

title: Zeph Burns
text: Zeph Burns is One of Mr. Burns' siblings, son of Clifford Burns and Daphne Burns. Zeph 'Buddy' Burns is a minor, non-speaking member of the extended Burns family, known only through print appearances rather than the animated series. He is one of the siblings of Charles Montgomery Burns, alongside George, Cornelia, and Cornelius. Little is known about his personality or life, as he exists mainly as a picture-only character in supplementary Simpsons book material. His inclusion mainly serves to flesh out the sprawling and eccentric family tree of the show's wealthiest and most infamous character, Mr. Burns. Despite his obscurity, he represents the show's tendency to expand background lore through tie-in books rather than televised episodes.

title: Jimmy Apollo
text: Jimmy Apollo is A minor recurring TV football commentator watched by Homer for betting tips. "Smooth" Jimmy Apollo is a cigar-chomping sports pundit who appears on a fictional program called Inside Football Today, offering weekly predictions on NFL matchups. He touts a modest 52% accuracy rate and dramatically presents his featured pick as the "Lock of the Week," complete with an oversized padlock prop. His forecasts are a mixed bag, correctly calling one game while whiffing on another, underscoring his unreliable expertise. Homer treats his tips seriously enough to base gambling decisions on them, which becomes a plot point in one episode. The character is a parody of real-life bookmaker and broadcaster Jimmy "the Greek" Snyder, blending swagger with the inherent uncertainty of sports betting. Despite his brief screen time, he's a memorable one-off caricature voiced by the versatile Phil Hartman. Voiced by Phil Hartman.

title: Aurora
text: Aurora is Non-canon crossover character from Disney's Sleeping Beauty appearing in Simpsons specials. Aurora is a non-canon Disney crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe, based on the classic Sleeping Beauty princess. She appears alongside her mother, Queen Leah, during a Mother's Day outing to a Disney-themed location. Her role is minor and non-speaking, existing mostly as a cameo tying into a larger crossover storyline involving Disney characters. Aurora becomes caught up in a bizarre plot involving copyright disputes between the Grimm brothers and Disney, which leads to a dramatic and unexpected fate. She is ultimately erased from existence by Thanos as part of the fallout from that conflict. Overall, she serves as a background figure in these special crossover episodes rather than a fully developed character.

title: Billy (Homer's Triple Bypass)
text: Billy (Homer's Triple Bypass) is Minor character; son of the owner of Gasso gas station, appearing when Homer brings his car in during a health scare. Billy is a teenage gas station worker who helps run Gasso alongside his father. He appears briefly during Homer's visit to check out a strange noise in his car, which turns out to be a heart problem rather than a mechanical one. Billy is portrayed as naive and a bit slow-witted, especially in his exchange with his father about what to do with an old, broken-down vehicle. His father's blunt remark calling him a "dull boy" reinforces this comedic characterization. Billy's role is small, existing mainly for a single comedic exchange that plays into the episode's darker themes about mortality. He has since made a non-canon appearance in a Simpsons mobile game. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Hey, where's he going? | We're going to sell him to Mr. Nikapopoplus?
quotes: Hey, where's he going?
We're going to sell him to Mr. Nikapopoplus?

title: Señora Bumblebee Man
text: Señora Bumblebee Man is Ex-wife of Bumblebee Man, a minor recurring Springfield resident. Señora Bumblebee Man is a minor character defined almost entirely by her relationship to Bumblebee Man, sharing his distinctive Mexican accent. Her marriage ends after he accidentally destroys their home, leading her to divorce him in a fit of anger. Despite the split, the two are later seen sitting together in church, hinting they may have reconciled. She also turns up in New York City holding hands with another man, suggesting she moved on romantically. In an odd twist, she appears as one of the deceased wives on Ned Flanders' wall within one of Bart's coma dream sequences, tying her briefly into the show's more surreal storytelling. Overall, she functions as a background gag character rather than a fully developed personality. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Jake Boyman
text: Jake Boyman is Alias used by Lisa Simpson to infiltrate the boys' side of Springfield Elementary School. Jake Boyman, nicknamed 'Toilet' after an embarrassing incident with toilet paper, is actually a disguise adopted by Lisa Simpson during a period when Springfield Elementary was segregated by gender. Struggling at first to fit in with the boys and even getting bullied by Nelson, Jake eventually gains acceptance with Bart's help once Bart discovers the truth. In a morally uncomfortable moment, Jake is pushed by Bart into beating up the gentle Ralph Wiggum, which paradoxically boosts Jake's social standing among the school bullies. Jake's academic talents shine through when he wins a math award, leading to a dramatic reveal where Lisa exposes her true identity in front of the whole school, proving that the top math student was a girl all along. The character highlights themes of gender expectations and Lisa's willingness to challenge them through subterfuge. Voiced by Yeardley Smith.

title: C-3PO
text: C-3PO is Crossover character from Star Wars appearing in various Simpsons episodes. C-3PO is the famous droid from Star Wars who makes several cameo and crossover appearances throughout The Simpsons universe. He's most memorably depicted getting badly beaten in a wrestling match against the Cylons, only to be abandoned by his companion R2-D2, leading him to declare his hatred for the other droid. Beyond that dramatic moment, he shows up in more mundane forms, such as a convention costume, a poster cameo, a collectible figure, and even as a subject of debate regarding his supposed romantic relationship with Chewbacca. In non-canon material, he's referenced as a benchmark for combat toughness and becomes the center of a joke about his origin, mistakenly guessed to be Indian before being corrected as English. Overall, C-3PO functions as a recurring pop-culture nod rather than a fully integrated character, appearing in fragments, references, and background gags. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: I hate him! - C-3PO
quotes: I hate him! - C-3PO

title: Barry Bonds
text: Barry Bonds is Real-world former MLB baseball player referenced in the show. Barry Bonds appears in the show as a real-world figure rather than an animated speaking character, showing up mainly as an image or a name-drop rather than through dialogue. He is depicted on the cover of a Sports Illustrated magazine that Principal Skinner sheepishly asks Lisa to return for him, hinting at some awkward backstory involving items mysteriously appearing in his bag. Bonds is also referenced as someone who supposedly knows a mysterious concept called "The Answer," adding a bit of mythic mystery to his cameo. He's further honored by being included on Ned Flanders' list of admirable left-handed people. Since he never speaks on screen, his presence in the show functions more as a pop-culture nod than a character in his own right. Notable quotes: "But when you go, could you return this Sports Illustrated for me? Someone must've put it in my bag. They do that, you know? They're always putting things in my bag." - Principal Skinner
quotes: "But when you go, could you return this Sports Illustrated for me? Someone must've put it in my bag. They do that, you know? They're always putting things in my bag." - Principal Skinner

title: 4-H leader
text: 4-H leader is Minor character; leader of Springfield's 4-H club who oversees Bart's involvement in the organization. The 4-H leader is a gray-haired dairy farmer who runs Cheddarbarrel Farm and also serves as head of Springfield's 4-H chapter. He appears mainly in a practical, no-nonsense role, skipping formalities like initiation oaths in favor of getting straight to work. When Bart joins the club, the leader wastes no time putting him to use operating a combine harvester. He later organizes a cow-raising competition, tasking the club's members with raising cattle over the summer. Little is known about his personal life or personality beyond his dedication to farming and youth agricultural education. He also appears in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out as a generic farmer character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Billy Baldwin
text: Billy Baldwin is One of the four Baldwin brothers, a real-life actor appearing as a character in The Simpsons. Billy Baldwin is depicted as one of the famous Baldwin acting siblings, alongside Alec, Daniel, and Stephen. He is mistaken for his brother Alec by a bewildered Homer Simpson during a chaotic encounter at a getaway house. Billy's plans to perform in a theatrical production of Romeo and Juliet fall apart after he and his brothers get tangled up in a feud with the Sheen-Estevez clan. He mostly exists as a punchline referencing real-world celebrity family dynamics and Hollywood mix-ups rather than as a fully developed character. His appearances are brief, functioning more as a running gag about sibling confusion than as a major storyline. Notable quotes: "Billy Baldwin!" - Homer Simpson
quotes: "Billy Baldwin!" - Homer Simpson

title: Sergio Aragonés (character)
text: Sergio Aragonés (character) is Real-life cartoonist and writer who appears as a non-canon character in Simpsons comics. This character is a fictionalized version of the real cartoonist Sergio Aragonés, appearing in Bongo comic stories rather than the animated show itself. He is depicted as a comic book creator who can be found working at his own table during a Comic-Con style event. When approached by Bart and Lisa for help finding Simpsons Comics, he admits he never leaves his table, yet still manages to sketch something for them based on what he could see from his desk, showing his dedication to his craft even while stationary. His head later makes a cameo appearance in a bizarre setting called Nerdanus XII, reflecting the surreal, self-referential humor common in these non-canon stories. Overall, he serves as a playful nod to real-world comic industry figures within the Simpsons Comics universe.

title: Bildorf
text: Bildorf is President of the Springfield Junipers Golf Club, briefly Bart's employer. Bildorf is a wealthy, self-important golf club president who cares deeply about protecting his club from closure. He's shown to be manipulative, hiring Bart as his caddie specifically to use him as leverage against Marge's petition to shut down the club. He's opportunistic, quickly latching onto Bart's offhand comment to invent a golf-based religion that saves his business and even wins over Mayor Quimby. Despite this cunning, he's also careless with loyalty, casting Bart aside the moment the crisis passes, which backfires spectacularly. His story ends in disgrace when police discover his golf course had secretly become the front for a sex cult. Overall, he's a comedic example of Springfield's absurd blend of greed, hypocrisy, and hidden scandal. Voiced by Stephen Root.

title: Al Bundy
text: Al Bundy is Fictional character from Married... with Children, appearing as a crossover/parody character on The Simpsons. Al Bundy is a crossover character brought over from the sitcom Married... with Children, appearing on The Simpsons whenever characters watch that show within the show. He's depicted as a beleaguered husband stuck in a loveless, joke-filled marriage with his wife Peggy, often the butt of jokes about their nonexistent romantic life. His appearances are mostly meta gags referencing the source show's humor, shown through clips watched by characters like Ned Flanders and even NASA scientists. In a non-canon Halloween segment, he and Peggy are reimagined as aliens, continuing the running joke about their marriage being sexless and strange. Al himself isn't given much personality beyond mirroring his sitcom counterpart's deadpan, weary demeanor. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "No, Peg" —Al Bundy | Peggy then told Al that they hadn't had sex in four years.
quotes: "No, Peg" —Al Bundy
Peggy then told Al that they hadn't had sex in four years.

title: Bruce Baum (character)
text: Bruce Baum (character) is Real-world comedian who appeared as himself in an episode of The Simpsons. Bruce Baum is a real-life stand-up comedian who makes a cameo appearance as himself within the Simpsons universe. He first shows up in "The Last Temptation of Krust," an episode centered on Krusty the Clown's foray into stand-up comedy, fitting given Baum's own background as a performer. He later appears briefly in the opening sequence of "Homer's Adventures Through the Windshield Glass." Because he is a guest-starring version of himself rather than a scripted character, little is known about his personality within the show's continuity. His presence is more of a nod to real-world comedy culture than a fleshed-out storyline. As a recurring but minor real-world figure, he adds a touch of authenticity to the show's satire of the stand-up comedy scene. Voiced by Bruce Baum (Himself).

title: Ronnie Beck
text: Ronnie Beck is A minor recurring child character in Springfield, admired by Bart Simpson for his soapbox derby success. Ronnie Beck is a ten-year-old soapbox derby champion who has won the title three times, making him something of a legend in Bart's eyes. He's talked about with a mix of awe and rivalry, embodying the kind of competitive local fame that captures a kid's imagination. Ronnie doesn't get much screen time himself, appearing mainly as a name dropped in conversation rather than a fully fleshed-out character. His one notable on-screen moment comes when he serves as the trophy presenter after Bart finally wins the Springfield soapbox derby championship, effectively passing the torch. He also shows up briefly in a later opening sequence gag. Overall, Ronnie functions as a benchmark of achievement that motivates Bart's storyline in his featured episode. Voiced by Russi Taylor.

title: Joyce Brothers (character)
text: Joyce Brothers (character) is Real-world psychologist who appeared as herself in a guest role on the show. Joyce Brothers is a real-life celebrity psychologist who makes a cameo appearance in Springfield's fictional universe. She shows up as a guest on the local talk show Smartline to discuss the power plant strike alongside Homer Simpson and Mr. Burns. Ever the professional, she comes prepared with her own microphone rather than relying on the station's equipment. Beyond her television appearance, her image later turns up on a wall of notable figures at the Springfield Speakers Bureau, cementing her status as a recognized public personality within the show's world. Voiced by Herself.

title: Stephanie Brockman
text: Stephanie Brockman is Weatherwoman for Channel 6 News and wife of news anchor Kent Brockman. Stephanie Brockman is a minor recurring character known primarily as the weather lady on Channel 6 News and the spouse of anchorman Kent Brockman. She rarely appears on screen or speaks, existing mostly as a background reference tied to her husband's storylines and his stepdaughter Brittany. Despite her marriage, she was once spotted with Hans Moleman during a Halloween-themed segment, hinting at some marital intrigue. Her name was first dropped by Kent himself, who referenced their union in a moment of dramatic, tabloid-style news commentary. She also appears in a non-canon capacity as a character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. Overall, she functions less as a developed personality and more as a running detail in Kent Brockman's family life. Notable quotes: Not since this reporter's marriage to Stephanie the weather lady has this town been so consumed with rumor and innuendo. — Kent Brockman
quotes: Not since this reporter's marriage to Stephanie the weather lady has this town been so consumed with rumor and innuendo. — Kent Brockman

title: Lionel Budgie
text: Lionel Budgie is A veterinarian in Springfield who mentors Lisa Simpson and treats various animals belonging to the main cast. Dr. Lionel Budgie runs his own veterinary practice, Lionel Budgie, D.V.M., and serves as a recurring authority figure on animal care in Springfield. He takes Lisa Simpson under his wing as an apprentice after she rescues an injured raccoon, showing a willingness to nurture her compassion for animals. He later proves his medical skill by saving Plopper the pig after the animal is attacked by Mr. Burns' hounds. During a town crisis caused by laws prioritizing dogs' welfare above humans, Budgie acts as a voice of reason, warning that unchecked canine dominance would lead to disaster, and he is proven right when the situation turns dangerous. When the town needs guidance to regain control over the feral dogs, he is called upon as the expert to help resolve the chaos. His gray hair and calm, knowledgeable demeanor mark him as a trusted elder figure in Springfield's animal care community. Voiced by Michael York.

title: Bitey
text: Bitey is A minor animal character; an opossum discovered living in the Springfield Monorail train. Bitey is a brown opossum who, along with her four children, made an unexpected home inside a fire extinguisher container aboard the Springfield Monorail. She was discovered by Marge, who was startled to find the animal family living there. Homer, unfazed by the surprise, casually named the largest opossum "Bitey." Bitey has no lines of dialogue and exists purely as a background gag tied to the chaos of the monorail storyline. Despite her minimal role, she has become a memorable one-off character remembered for Homer's offhand naming of her. She has also appeared in non-canon material like The Simpsons: Tapped Out, where she is tied to monorail-themed content. Notable quotes: I call the big one Bitey.|Homer Simpson
quotes: I call the big one Bitey.|Homer Simpson

title: Blob Jitsu
text: Blob Jitsu is A minor fictional character existing within the show's fictional universe, part of the in-universe franchise Ki-Ya Karate Monsters. Blob Jitsu is a slime-based monster character belonging to the fictional Ki-Ya Karate Monsters franchise referenced within The Simpsons universe. His defining trait is his mastery of jujutsu, blending his gooey, formless body with martial arts skill. As a non-speaking character, he exists mostly as background lore or merchandise rather than an active participant in storylines. His most notable real-world presence is as a wall sticker decoration in Comic Book Guy's apartment, reflecting Comic Book Guy's fandom for nerdy pop culture properties. Blob Jitsu doesn't interact directly with the main Simpsons cast, serving instead as a piece of world-building for the show's parody of geek culture franchises.

title: Bowl-O-Rama clerk
text: Bowl-O-Rama clerk is A minor recurring background character who works as a clerk at Barney's Bowlarama. The Bowl-O-Rama clerk is a minor employee character seen working at Barney's Bowlarama, the bowling alley frequented by residents of Springfield. He first appears helping Marge get set up with her bowling equipment after Homer buys her a bowling ball, showing a helpful, service-oriented demeanor. Interestingly, he isn't limited to the bowling alley, as he's also shown working at VHS Village, suggesting he may hold multiple jobs around town or that Springfield's citizens tend to see the same faces in different service roles. He doesn't have much of a distinct personality beyond his role as a background service worker, appearing mainly to facilitate other characters' storylines. Despite his minor status, he has popped up across a handful of early episodes, making him a small but recognizable piece of Springfield's background cast. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Raymond Bird
text: Raymond Bird is A pet homing pigeon adopted by Bart Simpson after being injured. Raymond Bird was a gray and white homing pigeon who crash-landed at the Simpson house with a broken wing, having escaped from his original owner Raphael's massive flock. Lisa tracked down his owner using the identification band on his leg, but Raphael refused to reclaim him, leaving Bart to nurse him back to health. Once healed, Ray chose to stay with the family, and Bart grew attached to him, even using his homing instincts to send secret notes back and forth with Milhouse. Ray's story takes a tragic turn when, just as he's being prepped for a local pigeon race, Santa's Little Helper suddenly kills and eats him. His death leaves Bart devastated and briefly threatens the family dog's place in the household. Despite his short appearance, Ray represents one of the show's darker pet-related storylines, blending sentimental attachment with sudden, comedic tragedy. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Lee Carvallo
text: Lee Carvallo is Fictional video-game golfer featured in the in-universe game 'Lee Carvallo's Putting Challenge' from the episode 'Marge Be Not Proud'. Lee Carvallo is not a flesh-and-blood Springfield resident but a character within a video game that appears in the show. He acts as a stern, instructional golf coach, offering advice on club selection and swing strength to guide players toward a better score. Bart treats his guidance as something to be deliberately ignored, comically sabotaging his own game just to make it more entertaining, though he quickly loses interest. Carvallo also appears in a fantasy sequence in Bart's mind, serving as a voice of reason urging him not to shoplift a video game, in contrast to persuasive cameo appearances by other game characters egging him on. His warning proves prophetic when Bart's theft leads to him getting caught. The character is a gentle parody of real-life golfer Lee Trevino, and his deadpan, monotone presentation makes him a memorable one-off pop culture gag. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Welcome to Lee Carvallo's Putting Challenge. I am Carvallo.
quotes: Welcome to Lee Carvallo's Putting Challenge. I am Carvallo.

title: Princess Bean
text: Princess Bean is Crossover character from Disenchantment appearing as a figure/statue in The Simpsons. Princess Bean, full name Princess Tiabeanie Mariabeanie de la Rochambeau Grunkwitz, is a crossover character brought into The Simpsons universe from the animated series Disenchantment. Rather than appearing as a living, speaking character, she shows up as a collectible statue and figure within Comic Book Guy's apartment, reflecting his fandom for the show. She is depicted alongside her Disenchantment companions Elfo and Luci, emphasizing their bond as a trio. Since she has no dialogue in her Simpsons appearances, she functions purely as a background nod for fans of the crossover. Her presence highlights the show's tendency to reference other animated series through in-universe merchandise and easter eggs.

title: James Caan (character)
text: James Caan (character) is Celebrity guest character playing a fictionalized version of himself who briefly becomes entangled with the Simpsons' Springfield neighbors. James Caan appears in Springfield as a version of himself, mingling with the show's cast in a couple of comedic cameos. He's invited by Bart to attend a party at his treehouse, showing a willingness to hang out with the show's regular characters. His most memorable storyline involves a romance with Brandine Spuckler, which sparks jealousy from her husband Cletus. This leads to a darkly comic homage to Caan's own film history, as Cletus organizes an ambush that mirrors the toll booth assassination of Sonny Corleone, the character Caan played in The Godfather. He's later mentioned as taking an unlikely gig working an espresso machine at a local coffee house, showing the show's habit of placing celebrities in mundane or absurd Springfield jobs.
