text: Clobber Girl is Superhero alter-ego of Lisa Simpson, non-canon character from a Treehouse of Horror segment. Clobber Girl is the super-strong crime-fighting persona Lisa adopts after a freak accident with a portable X-ray machine. She teams up with her brother Bart, who becomes the stretchy Stretch Dude, and together they battle a rotating cast of villains ranging from bank robbers to Nazi Zeppelins. Her greatest test comes against The Collector, the villainous alter-ego of Comic Book Guy, during a parody adventure involving actress Lucy Lawless. Despite her strength, she and Stretch Dude are ultimately outmatched and captured, needing to be rescued rather than saving the day themselves, adding a comedic twist to the superhero parody. The character exists purely as a one-off spoof of superhero tropes rather than a recurring serious identity, though her costume and image have resurfaced in later media like video games and title screen gags. Voiced by Yeardley Smith. Notable quotes: Hold the funeral, poindexter!
quotes: Hold the funeral, poindexter!

title: Dr. Clownius
text: Dr. Clownius is A comic-book supervillain from the Radioactive Man universe, played by Krusty in adaptations of the franchise. Dr. Clownius is a clown-themed villain who appears in Radioactive Man comic adaptations, commanding his own army of clown henchmen. In the movie adaptation, he masterminds a scheme to discredit Radioactive Man by kidnapping Gloria Grand and disguising himself as a legitimate newsman, Dr. Swartzwelder, to spread misinformation on live television. His plot is foiled when Radioactive Man and Fallout Boy intervene, exposing his true identity on air. The role is notably one that Krusty is offered to play instead of his preferred character, Crispy the Clown, highlighting the character's place within the show's meta fictional comic-book universe. In a later, unfinished Radioactive Woman film, Krusty again portrays Dr. Clownius, this time suffering a comedic downfall when a gas turns his own henchmen against him. Overall, the character serves as a recurring, campy antagonist figure tied closely to the show's satirical take on superhero media.

title: Peter D'Abbruzio
text: Peter D'Abbruzio is Keyboard player for the band Sungazer, who recruited Apu as their lead singer. Peter D'Abbruzio is a blond-haired musician who plays keyboard for the rock band Sungazer. After the band's former lead singer Grant LeDavid passed away, Peter helped scout and recruit Apu to take his place, flattering him by claiming he had the perfect "pure Sungazer sound." He proves to be somewhat manipulative and business-minded, pressuring Apu to keep touring even when Apu wanted time off, citing the band's spent money on excess as justification. Peter enforces the strict contract Apu signed, showing little sympathy for his personal struggles. Beyond his role with the band, he's also shown as a fan of local podcasts, appearing in the audience for live recordings. He represents the seedier, exploitative side of the music industry within the show's world. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Harrison Ford
text: Harrison Ford is A real-world celebrity referenced within the Simpsons universe, appearing as himself. Harrison Ford exists as a real-world celebrity mentioned and briefly seen within the world of The Simpsons. He is never given any spoken lines, appearing mostly as a name-drop or in a non-speaking cameo. Comic Book Guy claims a Harrison Ford lookalike gave him a Star Wars-themed bumper sticker, tying Ford to his famous role as Han Solo. He is later shown attending a launch event for The Drederick, arriving in his own personal plane, which hints at his wealth and love of aviation. He's also considered as a potential celebrity endorser for Mr. Burns' brandy, though Burns dismisses him as "too Hollywood." Overall, Ford's presence in the show is minor and used mostly for celebrity name-recognition humor.

title: David Copperfield (character)
text: David Copperfield (character) is Guest character based on the real-life illusionist; appears as himself in the Simpsons universe. David Copperfield appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, a renowned American illusionist. He is depicted as having a history in Broadway theater, having starred in a play called Astonishing Girlfriend. In his main appearance, he joins forces with fellow real-world magicians Penn Jillette, Teller, and Ricky Jay in a plot against a rival magician, The Great Raymondo. This portrayal plays into the show's tradition of blending celebrity cameos with the fictional world of Springfield. His character leans into the mystique and rivalry culture often associated with professional magicians. He remains a minor but memorable guest character tied specifically to the world of stage magic within the series. Voiced by David Copperfield (Himself).

title: Esmeralda
text: Esmeralda is One of three teenage Wiccan girls who befriend Lisa Simpson in the forest. Esmeralda is a teenage witch who, alongside Cassandra and Gwendolyn Nightshadow, practices Wiccan traditions in the woods outside Springfield. She and her friends value nature and companionship, and they quickly bond with Lisa Simpson, even encouraging her to join their coven. Their claims of casting spells lead to trouble when Ned Flanders accuses them of being demonic, resulting in their arrest, though they are later acquitted in court. When a superstitious mob pursues them under outdated 17th-century witchcraft laws, Lisa steps in to defend and rescue them. Esmeralda represents themes of tolerance and misunderstood outsiders within the episode's storyline. She remains a minor, one-episode character whose main significance comes from her friendship with Lisa. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Cheery
text: Cheery is A character from the in-universe cartoon 'The Happy Little Elves', a favorite show of Maggie and Lisa Simpson. Cheery is an animated elf character who appears within The Happy Little Elves, a children's cartoon show watched by the Simpson kids. As the sole female member of the elf group, she stands out with her blonde hair and upbeat, sunny disposition that matches her name. Her image appears frequently as posters and merchandise in the Simpsons household, particularly decorating the bedroom walls of young Maggie and Lisa, showing how ingrained the show is in their childhood. Behind the scenes, Cheery is essentially a parody of Smurfette, mirroring the trope of the single token female in an otherwise all-male cartoon cast. Despite being a minor, in-universe fictional character rather than a full cast member, she has made numerous background appearances across many seasons of The Simpsons. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: Jimmy Fallon (character)
text: Jimmy Fallon (character) is Real-world talk show host who appears as a character in The Simpsons universe, referenced in connection with Homer and pop culture. Jimmy Fallon appears as a version of himself, the well-known American late-night talk show host, occasionally popping up in the Simpsons' world both in canon episodes and in non-canon Treehouse of Horror segments. His name has become a bit of a cultural shorthand within the show, referenced by characters like Lindsey Naegle and Nash Castor almost as a verb or measuring stick for viral fame and media relevance. He's portrayed as recognizable enough that even Grampa expects Bart to know who he is, though Bart's response pokes fun at how random celebrity references can feel to younger generations. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror appearance, he's grouped among a set of celebrities visiting Homer and Marge, where his laughter gets him scolded by Homer for ruining a comedic bit. Overall, his role in the show is more of a running pop-culture reference than a fully fleshed-out character with his own personality traits. Voiced by Matthew Friend.

title: Roberto Dinero
text: Roberto Dinero is A personal injury lawyer who briefly represents Homer Simpson. Roberto Dinero is an attorney working at Personal Liability Attorney, having studied law at Springfield School of Law. His name is a playful pun referencing actor Robert De Niro. He's shown to be ethically flexible, willing to fabricate evidence to win a case, such as drawing fake burn marks on a client to exaggerate an injury. Despite the questionable tactics, he proved successful in court, helping secure a payout from an unrelated party. He appears as a minor, one-off character tied to one of Homer's schemes involving a fast food mishap. His role highlights the show's recurring satire of frivolous lawsuits and shady legal practices. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: W. C. Fields
text: W. C. Fields is Real-world comedian referenced and depicted within the Simpsons universe. W. C. Fields is a real-life comedian, actor, juggler, and writer who appears in the show as a cultural reference rather than a core cast member. His image shows up as a poster in Homer's college dorm room, placed alongside Albert Einstein, reflecting Homer's odd taste in idols. He also appears in-universe within a fictional Itchy & Scratchy cartoon short, where he's depicted pouring dog blood into a wine glass, a dark parody gag typical of the show's satire. Additionally, he's listed among Ned Flanders' list of notable left-handed people, tying him into one of the show's recurring background jokes about famous lefties. His presence in the series is minor and mostly used for comedic or nostalgic effect rather than characterization. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Bill de Blasio (character)
text: Bill de Blasio (character) is Real-life Mayor of New York City who made a cameo appearance in a Simpsons episode. Bill de Blasio appears as a guest cameo playing himself, the Mayor of New York City, during the Simpson family's visit to the city. He's shown letting Grampa ride on his shoulders, joking that from that height Grampa could see all the way to Rhode Island before breaking into laughter. This brief, good-humored appearance plays on the tradition of real-world political figures making cameo appearances in the show. He also shows up in a non-canon special, comedically grouped among other 2020 Democratic presidential candidates performing a can-can dance number. Overall, de Blasio's role is minor and largely a novelty cameo rather than a developed character. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: You could see Rhode Island from here! - Bill de Blasio
quotes: You could see Rhode Island from here! - Bill de Blasio

title: Mrs. Frink
text: Mrs. Frink is Wife of Professor Frink and mother of his son; minor recurring character. Mrs. Frink is a rarely seen character known mainly through mentions by her eccentric scientist husband, Professor Frink. She appears to be a patient and understanding wife, given how she reacts to her husband's bizarre inventions and mishaps. Her most notable on-screen moment comes when a temporarily transformed, more attractive Frink invites her out for a night at the cyclotron, and she happily agrees to join him. Much of her characterization is implied through Frink's anecdotes rather than direct appearances, making her a background figure who nonetheless rounds out the Frink family dynamic. She also appears in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Female interviewer
text: Female interviewer is Minor recurring news reporter in Springfield who appears in a handful of episodes. The female interviewer is a minor recurring news reporter who pops up covering odd local stories in Springfield. She's most notable for chasing down the Bigfoot sighting story, where she unwittingly interviews Marge Simpson about the creature, not realizing it's actually Homer in disguise. Her persistent, straightforward reporting style leads to some unintentionally comedic moments, especially when Marge's answers reveal domestic details about "Bigfoot" rather than anything cryptid-related. She later shows up again to interview Krusty the Clown, suggesting she's a general-purpose reporter for whatever strange or newsworthy events occur in town. She has red hair and no other defining physical or personal traits are given beyond her profession. Voiced by Maggie Roswell. Notable quotes: But that's my husband! | pork chops are his favorite
quotes: But that's my husband!
pork chops are his favorite

title: Deaf girl
text: Deaf girl is A minor recurring character, an eight-year-old deaf student at The Sky's the Limit. The deaf girl is a young student affiliated with The Sky's the Limit, a program noted in the show for its inclusive approach. She gained a bit of attention for playing the lead role in a production of Richard III, reportedly the first time an eight-year-old deaf girl had taken on that part. Beyond her theatrical achievement, she's shown enjoying a fairly ordinary childhood moment, joining other kids in smashing a Shrek pinata at a party. She's a background character with limited screen time, appearing mainly as a small but memorable presence in a couple of episodes. Notably, she is voiced by Kathy Buckley, a hearing-impaired actress, which mirrors the character's own disability in a nod to authentic casting. Voiced by Kathy Buckley.

title: Clint Eastwood
text: Clint Eastwood is Fictionalized depiction of actor Clint Eastwood, appearing as an outlaw character in a parody musical sequence. This version of Clint Eastwood is a parody portrayal of the real-life actor, depicted as the outlaw he played in the film Paint Your Wagon. He rolls into a village with a shabby wagon, and after a local remarks on its poor condition, he casually agrees before breaking into song and dance. The bit plays on his stoic, laconic screen persona, contrasting his tough-guy image with a lighthearted musical number. Outside of this main appearance, he's used as a quick non-canon cameo, popping up as a guest star in a Halloween special's opening. He's also referenced in merchandise as a nod to his iconic 'Man with No Name' role. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: I reckon it could use a... coat of paint.
quotes: I reckon it could use a... coat of paint.

title: Annie Dubinsky
text: Annie Dubinsky is Krusty the Clown's talent agent and former lover, later his producer. Annie Dubinsky is a sharp, tenacious talent agent who discovered Herschel Krustofsky performing at a comedy club and helped shape him into the beloved Krusty the Clown persona. Their professional partnership evolved into a romance, though Krusty eventually abandoned her, leaving her bitter for years afterward. Fate brings her back into contact with the Simpsons and Krusty, and despite their painful history, she chooses to forgive him and resume representing his career. Her ambition and business savvy help revive Krusty's career with new projects, but her demanding, overbearing nature eventually gets her in trouble with network executives. Krusty's loyalty to her, refusing to fire her despite the pressure, shows the strength of their bond. She's also notable for having briefly represented other Springfield entertainers before reconnecting with Krusty. Voiced by Joan Rivers.

title: Corey (teenage idols)
text: Corey (teenage idols) is A running-gag group of fictional teen idol celebrities, all named Corey, referenced in Simpsons universe magazines. Corey isn't a single character but a parody of the late-1980s/early-90s trend of teen heartthrobs sharing the same first name, poking fun at real-life stars like Corey Haim and Corey Feldman. According to Lisa, there are eight different teen idols all named Corey, each appearing on the covers of fictional fan magazines like Teen Scream, Teen Spleen, and Non-Threatening Boys Magazine. They're distinguished mostly by superficial traits like hair color or the presence of sunglasses and glasses, emphasizing how interchangeable and manufactured these celebrities are. None of them have any real personality or dialogue, existing purely as background gags and pieces of set dressing referencing celebrity culture. Their appearances are limited to background magazine covers rather than active roles in any storyline.

title: Tootsie Childs
text: Tootsie Childs is A minor recurring jazz singer in the Springfield community. Tootsie Childs is a jazz singer who pops up at various Springfield social gatherings, showing herself to be a fixture of the local entertainment scene. She performed at Bart's benefit concert and even pushed back when Bart claimed Lisa had the biggest heart among jazz musicians, showing she has some pride in her craft. She's socially active around town, attending birthday parties, complimenting Marge on a charity calendar, and getting swept up in activism by supporting Roy Snyder's cause, even getting arrested at a protest rally. She also paid respects at Albert's funeral, suggesting she's a woman who shows up for her community in good times and bad. Behind the scenes, she is managed by the slick manager of United Parasites, tying her into the show's music industry satire. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: The Edge
text: The Edge is Guest star appearing as himself, a member of the band U2. The Edge is the real-life guitarist of U2 who appears as himself in the world of The Simpsons. He lent his voice to a self-portrayal in a season 9 episode, joining his bandmates in a cameo tied to a Springfield storyline. His appearance is brief, functioning as a celebrity cameo rather than a recurring role. He later appeared again through archive footage reused in a season 13 episode, extending his presence without new voice work. As with most musician cameos on the show, his role leans on his real-world fame rather than an original personality crafted for the series. Voiced by The Edge.

title: Joey Crusher
text: Joey Crusher is One of Mr. Burns' hired goons, used for intimidation and enforcement work. Joey Crusher is one of Mr. Burns' thuggish enforcers, usually paired with his partner Low Blow to carry out the tycoon's dirty work. While Low Blow handles the actual physical violence, Crusher's role tends to be laughing menacingly at the pain inflicted on others, whether it's Homer, Smithers, or even Mr. Burns himself. Despite his intimidating job, he seems to have a surprisingly amicable rapport with Homer, who casually calls him by his first name. This suggests that beneath his goon exterior, he's not entirely without some camaraderie with the people he's sent to threaten. He appears across many seasons as a recurring background enforcer whenever Burns needs someone strong-armed into compliance. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Smilin' Joe Fission
text: Smilin' Joe Fission is Animated mascot character for the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant and Springfield Isotopes. Smilin' Joe Fission is a cheerful cartoon spokesman created to promote nuclear power, first appearing in an educational filmstrip shown to schoolchildren touring the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. He also doubles as the mascot for the town's baseball team, the Springfield Isotopes. Beyond his debut short, he has starred in a series of other bizarre atomic-themed educational films with equally odd titles. A running joke about his character is that he's oddly touchy about being compared to real-life businessman Ross Perot. Merchandise based on him, like a novelty night light, has appeared in in-universe catalogs, reflecting his status as a quirky piece of corporate branding within Springfield's nuclear industry. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Madame Eczema
text: Madame Eczema is Supervillain leader of the group Eczema, and antagonist in the Radioactive Man comic book storyline. Madame Eczema is a comic-book supervillain whose backstory involves tragedy turning to villainy after a severe skin condition disfigured half her face. She uses her hair to hide the affected side and adopted a ruthless, ambitious persona, clawing her way to power within her criminal organization by eliminating her own superiors. She's cunning and manipulative, capable of impersonating other characters to lure her enemies into traps. Her most notable scheme involved exposing a superhero's secret identity and orchestrating an ambush on a team of heroes by posing as an ally. Despite her clever planning, she is ultimately outmaneuvered and defeated when her captives are rescued. She appears exclusively within the Radioactive Man comic book storyline featured in Bongo Comics.

title: Boba Fett
text: Boba Fett is Star Wars bounty hunter character who appears as a crossover/reference figure in The Simpsons. Boba Fett is a crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe from the Star Wars franchise, appearing mainly as a pop-culture reference rather than a fully integrated character. He is referenced by fans within the show, such as Bart, who idolizes him as a cool, badass mercenary, and Comic Book Guy, who uses him as a size comparison for a sinkhole. He also serves as a mascot for a fictional tea shop, showing his embedded status in Springfield's pop culture. In a non-canon Star Wars-themed segment, he takes on his classic villainous role by freezing the Simpson family in carbonite. Homer, ever the skeptic of nerd culture, mocks Boba Fett's look, jokingly calling him a "weirdo" for combining a jetpack and a cape. Overall, Boba Fett's presence highlights the show's frequent parody and homage to Star Wars fandom. Voiced by Chris Edgerly. Notable quotes: Bart said that mercenaries are cool, like Boba Fett. | Homer then said that Boba Fett should pick a lane, calling him a weirdo.
quotes: Bart said that mercenaries are cool, like Boba Fett.
Homer then said that Boba Fett should pick a lane, calling him a weirdo.

title: Ernst
text: Ernst is Recurring performer/entertainer, half of a white tiger act with his partner Gunter, appearing in Springfield and Las Vegas casino settings. Ernst is a flamboyant showman who, alongside his partner Gunter, performs a magic and animal act featuring white tigers, most notably one named Anastasia. The duo is a clear parody of the real-life act Siegfried and Roy, right down to the eerie coincidence of their fictional mauling predating a real incident involving the real performers' tiger. Ernst and Gunter are usually depicted as inseparable, working together at casinos in both Springfield and Las Vegas, and getting entangled in chaotic incidents involving their unpredictable tigers. They pop up repeatedly in the background of Simpsons episodes as recognizable Vegas-style celebrities, attending events like funerals and celebrity parties. Their act's danger becomes a running joke, especially given how often their tiger goes out of control around them or other characters. Ernst himself doesn't have much individual personality outside of this partnership, functioning mostly as one half of the Gunter-and-Ernst duo. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Michael Dukakis
text: Michael Dukakis is Real-world American politician referenced/appearing as a minor character in The Simpsons. Michael Dukakis is depicted in the show as a real-world figure representing his actual history as the former governor of Massachusetts and the Democratic candidate who lost the 1988 presidential election. He's mostly used as a punchline or background reference rather than a fleshed-out character, often invoked as shorthand for liberal political stereotypes. He appears in a recurring joke about Lisa's supposed sympathies, gets referenced through a mall business named after his old campaign, and shows up as a spectral figure in one of Lisa's anxiety dreams alongside other losing Democratic candidates. He also makes a brief non-speaking cameo in a crowd scene. Overall, his presence in the show leans on real-world political history for comedic and satirical effect rather than giving him any real personality or dialogue.

title: Ling Chow
text: Ling Chow is Owner of The Pan-Fried Dragon restaurant in Springfield, married to Sheila Chow. Ling Chow is a minor recurring Springfield business owner who runs a Chinese restaurant, The Pan-Fried Dragon, formerly called The Lonely Dragon. He's shown to be resourceful and a bit shady, once selling Homer an oddly shaped square watermelon from a fruit stand. He's not above confrontation, angrily calling out Moe for stealing his cable television. Perhaps his most memorable trait is putting on an exaggerated, stereotypical persona for customers, enlisting his wife Sheila to play along in order to entertain a very drunk Homer, before unceremoniously dumping him in a dumpster afterward. Overall, he comes across as a savvy, somewhat opportunistic small business owner willing to bend the truth for profit. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Capri Flanders
text: Capri Flanders is Mother of Ned Flanders and grandmother of Rod and Todd Flanders. Capri Flanders, nicknamed 'Kookie,' is the matriarch of the Flanders family and wife of Nedward Flanders Sr. She was once a beatnik in her younger years, a surprising contrast to her son Ned's straight-laced, devout personality. Capri appears only occasionally throughout the series, often in flashbacks or as a mentioned figure rather than a frequent presence. Despite being Ned's mother, she and her husband have shown a curious fondness for Homer Simpson, sometimes seeming to prefer his company to their own son's. She and her husband remain supportive family figures, attending major life events like Ned's wedding to Edna Krabappel. Her name has been inconsistently referenced across episodes, having also been called Mona and Agnes Flanders in different appearances. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: We've tried nothing and we're all out of ideas.
quotes: We've tried nothing and we're all out of ideas.

title: Curious Bear Cub
text: Curious Bear Cub is A fictional character from the in-universe children's show 'The Happy Little Elves', appearing as merchandise/imagery in Lisa Simpson's world. Curious Bear Cub is a small, helpful bear character who exists within the fictional cartoon 'The Happy Little Elves,' a show favored by young fans within the Simpsons universe. She is best known for her role in a special episode where she teams up with Doofy to rescue Bubbles, showcasing her adventurous and loyal nature. Rather than appearing as a fully animated character in most episodes, she typically shows up as a picture, doll, or piece of merchandise decorating Lisa's bedroom. This recurring background presence spans many seasons, reflecting how deeply the Happy Little Elves franchise has embedded itself into the show's world. She has no spoken lines, functioning purely as a nostalgic or decorative touch rather than an active participant in the main plot.

title: Harlan Dondelinger
text: Harlan Dondelinger is Principal of Springfield High School, connected to Homer and Marge's teenage years. Harlan Dondelinger has served as the strict principal of Springfield High School since at least 1974, overseeing Homer and Marge's final year of school. He's remembered as a stern authority figure who frequently butted heads with Homer and Barney Gumble as students. Years later, he publicly embarrassed an adult Homer by revealing at a reunion that he never actually graduated, which sets Homer on a quest to finally earn his diploma. Interestingly, when Homer takes an adult education science class to make up his credits, he finds Dondelinger teaching it, having returned to the classroom after the death of his wife. Despite their history, Dondelinger shows no real grudge against Homer in this setting and ends up passing him. He continues to pop up in the background of Springfield civic and school events over the years. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: FBI agent (Donnie Fatso)
text: FBI agent (Donnie Fatso) is An FBI investigator who pursued Fat Tony and recruited Homer as an informant in the episode "Donnie Fatso". This unnamed federal agent appears when the FBI sets its sights on taking down Fat Tony's mob operation. He recruits Homer Simpson to go undercover, giving him a fake identity and a wig rigged with a hidden camera and microphone. His methods are shown to be manipulative, as he stages a prison fight to help Homer gain the trust of the mafia. He also poses undercover as a prison guard to keep tabs on the operation from the inside. Despite Homer's cooperation and risk, the agent proves cold and ungrateful, refusing even a simple handshake once the case concludes. He is depicted as gray-haired and strictly business, embodying a no-nonsense law enforcement archetype. Voiced by Jon Hamm.

title: Fantastic Dan
text: Fantastic Dan is A minor recurring character who works as a sky-writer pilot for hire. Fantastic Dan is a sky-writing pilot who takes on paying jobs to send aerial messages over Springfield. He apparently once resided inside a Whack-A-Mole booth at a traveling carnival, where he was struck on the head by Nelson. His most notable job came when Apu hired him to write a Valentine's Day message to Manjula, a task that turned dangerous when a jealous Homer physically attacked him mid-flight to stop the delivery. Despite the struggle and a spilled tank of dangerous gas, the message still got through, inadvertently smoothing over romantic troubles for many Springfield couples. He's a background character mostly defined by this one chaotic aerial mission rather than deep characterization. In behind-the-scenes commentary he was jokingly misnamed "Handsome Dan." Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Paul Flart
text: Paul Flart is Fictional movie character within the show, a parody figure appearing in "Replaceable You" and The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Paul Flart is a non-canon character who exists as the titular hero of an in-universe film called Paul Flart: Water Park Cop, itself a joke on the real-world movie Paul Blart: Mall Cop. His brief on-screen history is pure slapstick: he gets stuck on a mast while riding a Segway, has a lost dog poster stapled to his head by a passerby, and is then urinated on by the very dog from the poster. He has no lines of dialogue, fitting his role as a background gag rather than a developed character. He later appears as part of the Splash and Burn content in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. His entire existence is a satirical nod to police-comedy action films.

title: Mr. Dandy
text: Mr. Dandy is Minor recurring Springfield resident, manager of the Candy Most Dandy candy store. Mr. Dandy is a background Springfield townsperson best known for running the candy shop Candy Most Dandy. His most notable moment comes when he catches Bart and his friends vandalizing the statue of Jebediah Springfield, reacting with anger and later joining an angry mob seeking revenge against Bart and Homer. Despite his ordinary appearance, he pops up in various roles across the show, later being seen operating a hotdog stand instead of his candy store. He doesn't have a strong defined personality beyond being an easily provoked, civic-minded townsperson who gets swept up in mob mentality. He's part of the show's large cast of recurring extras who appear in different jobs and settings depisode to episode. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: ClownFace
text: ClownFace is A guest supervillain from the fictional Batman TV show within the Simpsons universe, portrayed by Krusty the Clown. ClownFace is a campy villain from a parody Batman TV show, played by Krusty the Clown, complete with green hair and a garish, Joker-like appearance. He commands three henchmen named Hoo, Hah, and Hee, and his signature scheme involves trapping Batman and Robin on a deadly spinning carousel. He's got a flair for corny wordplay and sarcastic quips, especially when mocking Batman's endless utility-belt gadgets. His TV antics inspire Bart to stage a copycat stunt with Milhouse on the school merry-go-round, which backfires on both the boys and Krusty. Beyond his one televised appearance, ClownFace later shows up as a museum statue and in a mobile game, cementing him as a minor pop-culture footnote in Springfield's fictional superhero lore. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Show our guests to the twirly gates. | What don't you have in that belt!
quotes: Show our guests to the twirly gates.
What don't you have in that belt!

title: Geoffrey Chaucer
text: Geoffrey Chaucer is Historical figure who appears as a ghost in one of Homer's dreams. Geoffrey Chaucer is depicted as the ghost of the real-life English poet, known as the Father of English literature and the first poet buried at Poet's Corner in Westminster Abbey. He appears in a dream Homer has while working on Bart's school project of Westminster Abbey. In this dream sequence, Chaucer offers Homer advice about parenting, encouraging him to keep doing Bart's work for him. His counsel is quickly contradicted by another historical apparition, Anne of Cleves, creating a comedic clash of ghostly opinions in Homer's subconscious. Chaucer's appearance is brief and serves mainly as a whimsical, educational cameo rather than a recurring role. He also appears in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Pip Diddler
text: Pip Diddler is Minor recurring character; emcee-style entertainer on the country-western variety show Ya Hoo!. Pip Diddler is a small-time entertainer best known as a host on the country-western variety program Ya Hoo!. He plays the role of emcee, warming up the crowd and introducing other performers rather than being a headline act himself. His most notable appearance ties him to Lurleen Lumpkin, whom he introduces for a song after enjoying a joke at Homer's expense. Diddler later turns up performing in Branson, Missouri, suggesting he tours the same kind of down-home variety circuit as Lurleen. He also gets a nod later on via a poster advertising him outside a cabaret, hinting that his career persists in the background of Springfield's entertainment scene. Overall he's a background fixture of the Simpsons universe's country-music subplot rather than a character with his own storyline. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Deadpool
text: Deadpool is A Marvel comic book character referenced within The Simpsons universe. Deadpool is not an original Simpsons character but a nod to the real-world Marvel superhero, appearing mainly as a pop-culture reference. Bart Simpson is shown to be a big fan, only willing to watch a movie if Deadpool breaks the fourth wall and talks directly to the camera. This trait becomes a running joke when Bart watches the actual Deadpool film on his phone. In a non-canon story, the aliens Kang and Kodos jokingly compare their spaceship to Comic-Con, imagining Kodos dressed as Harley Quinn and Kang dressed as Deadpool. These brief mentions treat Deadpool as a symbol of geek culture and cosplay rather than giving him any real narrative role. Overall, his presence in the show is limited to lighthearted crossover humor and meta commentary on superhero fandom.

title: Female jockey
text: Female jockey is A minor recurring character, one of the jockeys residing in Jockey Town. The female jockey is a small, background resident of Jockey Town, notable mainly for her pink hair. She appears as part of the group of jockeys who confront Homer about his horse Duncan's winning streak. Joining her fellow jockeys, she sings to express their displeasure over losing races because of Duncan's success. She explains to Homer that Duncan's victories are upsetting the jockey community. Beyond this brief appearance, little else is known about her personality or background, as she functions mainly as part of the jockey ensemble rather than a fully developed individual character. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: She told Homer that Duncan winning races was making them frown.
quotes: She told Homer that Duncan winning races was making them frown.

title: Crazy Iguana Lady
text: Crazy Iguana Lady is A minor non-canon character appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment, a Mayan version of Crazy Cat Lady. The Crazy Iguana Lady is a background character who appeared in an ancient Mayan setting during a Treehouse of Horror Halloween special. She is depicted as mentally unstable, wandering the city of Chichen Itza while yelling nonsensical gibberish. Her defining running gag is throwing iguanas at passersby, echoing the antics of Springfield's own Crazy Cat Lady but with reptiles instead of felines. As a non-canon figure, she exists purely for comedic effect within the Halloween anthology format. She later made an appearance in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Her design and behavior serve as a historical parody, transplanting a familiar Simpsons archetype into an ancient civilization. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Fat cheeked housekeeper
text: Fat cheeked housekeeper is A minor housekeeper working at Mr. Burns' mansion. The fat cheeked housekeeper is a minor background character employed at Mr. Burns' sprawling mansion. Her sole moment of note comes during a musical sequence, where she contributes a single sung line while Mr. Burns performs 'See My Vest.' She has light brown hair and is depicted as an adult woman with a notably round, fat-cheeked face. The character serves as a visual and thematic parody of Nanny from Disney's 101 Dalmatians, fitting into the episode's broader spoof of that film. Beyond her brief singing cameo, she has no other established personality traits or storylines, making her a fleeting but memorable one-off gag character. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Kill two for matching clogs
quotes: Kill two for matching clogs

title: Roz Davis
text: Roz Davis is Homer Simpson's former assistant and a former nuclear safety inspector at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. Roz Davis briefly worked alongside Homer at the power plant before betraying his trust to take his job for herself. She initially came across as warm and complimentary, even comparing Homer's smile to a summer breeze, but this pleasant facade masked a manipulative and domineering streak once she gained power over him. She has a strange aversion to physical touch, which becomes a key plot point when Homer uses this knowledge against her. Despite her harshness toward Homer, she shows a friendlier, generous side at Moe's Tavern, where she happily covers drink tabs for regulars like Lenny and Carl. Her competitive streak surfaces in a flashback showing her dominating a race at Bible camp as a child. Ultimately her cruelty catches up with her when her own actions lead to her being fired by Mr. Burns, and she's forced to admit she underestimated Homer. Voiced by Jane Lynch. Notable quotes: I hate to be touched. Don't tell anyone.
quotes: I hate to be touched. Don't tell anyone.

title: Fortune teller
text: Fortune teller is A minor recurring character who tells fortunes at a Renaissance-fair-like tent, first encountered by Lisa. The fortune teller is a mysterious woman with an apparent knack for predicting the future, encountered by Lisa while she was chasing after the mythical creature Esquilax. Inside her tent, she reveals visions of Lisa's future, including glimpses of her first love. She later reappears reading Moe's fortune, only for the session to be interrupted by Bart speeding by in a bizarre vehicle once owned by Adolf Hitler. Her predictions seem uncannily accurate, correctly identifying details about the whereabouts and behavior of various Simpson family members, though at least one instance suggests she may have cheated by peeking at a name tag. She exists mostly as a plot device to deliver foreshadowing or comic asides rather than as a fully developed character. She has also appeared in non-canon material such as The Simpsons: Tapped Out video game. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Female foodie
text: Female foodie is A minor recurring background character in Springfield, part of a trio of foodies. The female foodie is a blonde-haired background character who shares a passion for food criticism with her companions Amuse Bruce and Fois Garth. She's typically depicted tagging along to review restaurants and food-related events around Springfield, first appearing when the trio sampled Ethiopian cuisine and later checked out a fusion restaurant. Beyond her culinary pursuits, she pops up at a variety of unrelated Springfield gatherings, including movie premieres, podcast recordings, town meetings, and even a taxidermy convention. As a non-speaking character, she never has any dialogue, existing purely as a recurring face in crowd scenes. Her consistent pairing with the other two foodies suggests a tight-knit group dynamic, even though little else about her personality or backstory is explored.

title: Chester (The Winter of His Content)
text: Chester (The Winter of His Content) is A legendary bully who appears at the Bully Summit in Springfield. Chester is a minor character introduced as a bully whose reputation is so extreme that he's rumored to have once wedgied a kid clean in half. He appears at the Bully Summit, a gathering of Springfield's bullies, where he delivers a lengthy speech. His moment in the spotlight is cut short when Wilbur Nurple takes a shot at him using Bart's slingshot, sparking chaos. This incident sets off a large mob that goes hunting for the bullies involved. Beyond his brief canon appearance, Chester also shows up in a non-canon capacity as the Bully Boss in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. He's portrayed as a tough, intimidating teenage figure within Springfield's bully hierarchy. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Mother Dexter
text: Mother Dexter is A minor recurring Springfield resident whose family unofficially adopted Snowball II as a second pet. Mother Dexter is a gentle, grandmotherly figure living in Springfield who unknowingly became a secondary caretaker of the Simpsons' cat, Snowball II. She's the type to bake treats for visiting children, showing a warm and trusting nature even toward strangers. Her most memorable appearance involves being duped by Bart Simpson, who invents an absurd cover story and a nonsensical name for himself just by glancing at her appearance. Despite being fooled, she comes across as harmless and sweet rather than foolish. She later appears briefly in a crowd scene, showing she's an ordinary background citizen of the town who engages in civic events like elections. Overall, she represents the quirky, everyday townsfolk of Springfield who add texture to the show's world without playing a central role in the plot. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Esther
text: Esther is Deceased wife and magician's assistant of The Great Raymondo, a minor character connected to Lisa's storyline. Esther appears only as a memory and hallucination in the show, having passed away before the events depicted. She spent her life as the assistant and wife of the magician known as The Great Raymondo, though the couple never had children. Her presence is felt mainly through Raymondo's longing for her, culminating in a poignant scene where he takes ether to hallucinate her image and dance with her one last time. Esther's character design is a tribute to Bess Houdini, wife of the famous real-world magician Harry Houdini. Beyond her brief appearance, she is referenced again as an image on a poster in a later, non-canon appearance. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Duff Knight
text: Duff Knight is A minor non-canon knight character appearing in the medieval-themed "Springfieldia" universe. Duff Knight is a background figure in the fictional fantasy realm of Springfieldia, a parody setting used in a non-canon Simpsons episode. He appears armored and ready for battle, embodying the stereotypical grim knight archetype of the medieval parody world. His most notable moment comes from a dark, comedic musing on the afterlife, framing it as an endless cycle of violence. Beyond this brief appearance, little is known about his personality or backstory, as he serves mostly as a side character supporting the episode's fantasy setting. He later appears as a character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game, tied to a special in-game event. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: he thought it was an eternity of being slaughtered and slaughtering your enemies.
quotes: he thought it was an eternity of being slaughtered and slaughtering your enemies.

title: Elmo
text: Elmo is Parody crossover character from Sesame Street appearing in various Simpsons episodes. Elmo is a version of the famous Sesame Street puppet who appears in the Simpsons universe in a handful of surreal, often dark cameo appearances. He's been seen chasing Homer alongside Big Bird and Oscar the Grouch, and shows up as a beloved children's toy that Maggie and Moe end up tickling too aggressively. In one of his darker appearances, he's wrongfully imprisoned at the Ronald Reagan Reeducation Center after mistakenly attending the wrong fundraiser, and the ordeal drives him to take his own life. He also turns up in odd hallucinations and misunderstandings, such as Ralph's bizarre dream involving a party with Buzz Lightyear, and Ralph mistaking an actual rat for an Elmo toy. Elmo's brand recognition is further referenced through costumes worn by criminals who rob Moe in New York City. Overall, Elmo functions less as a recurring character with his own arc and more as a running gag referencing his real-world pop culture ubiquity. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: No means no for Elmo!
quotes: No means no for Elmo!

title: Ethan Foley
text: Ethan Foley is A student at the Enriched Learning Center for Gifted Children who briefly interacts with Bart Simpson. Ethan Foley is a minor classmate figure who appears when Bart is temporarily placed in a gifted school. He's part of the clique of intellectually advanced kids who look down on Bart, mocking him for not fitting in with their academic level. Despite the friction, he later shows up as one of Bart's regular fourth-grade classmates, suggesting his role as a gifted student was tied to a specific storyline rather than a permanent status. He doesn't have a strongly defined personality beyond this brief antagonistic role, functioning mostly as background support for the plot about Bart's fake genius status. Ethan represents the general student body Bart has to navigate through in his early elementary years. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Surly Duff
text: Surly Duff is One of the Seven Duffs, mascot costumed characters for Duff Beer, appearing at events like Duff Gardens and Duff Days. Surly Duff is one of the seven mascot characters representing Duff Beer, distinguished as the only one of the group who actually talks. His personality lives up to his name, as he approaches every interaction with cynicism, sarcasm, or outright insults. Despite being a corporate mascot meant to promote Duff responsibly, his true attitude often slips through, such as when he mutters about drinking responsibly only as an afterthought. He's occasionally spotted out of costume duty, whether ogling Marge Simpson after her surgery mishap or mourning the closure of Moe's Tavern. In non-canon material, he even attempted to become Duffman before an injury sidelined him. Surly stands out among the Seven Duffs as one of only four named in their debut appearance, alongside Tipsy, Queasy, and Remorseful. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Drink Duff! | Responsibly
quotes: Drink Duff!
Responsibly

title: Julia Child
text: Julia Child is A real-world celebrity chef who makes brief cameo-like appearances in Simpsons dream sequences and background gags. Julia Child appears in the show not as a full character but as a whimsical reference to the famous American chef. She shows up in one of Marge's dreams, oddly trailing behind Homer as he bounces along on a space hopper. Later, her image resurfaces as one of several celebrity chef photos used in a website's captcha verification screen, which Lisa ends up clicking on. She has no spoken dialogue in either appearance, making her a purely visual cameo. Her inclusion works as a nod to real-world pop culture rather than serving any ongoing storyline. Despite her minimal presence, she is treated as a recurring background reference within the show's universe.

title: Count Dracula (Republican)
text: Count Dracula (Republican) is A member of the Springfield Republican Party, a minor recurring background politician character. Count Dracula is a vampiric member of the Springfield Republican Party who appears mainly at party meetings and gatherings. He seems to hold genuine opinions on political candidates, showing skepticism toward unqualified nominees. Despite his monstrous, undead appearance, he acts as an ordinary, if judgmental, party member among the Republicans. His role in the show is largely as a background gag, blending horror-movie iconography into mundane Springfield politics. He appears sporadically across many seasons, usually in scenes depicting Republican Party functions. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: He thought the other members were crazy for suggesting Ralph be the Republican candidate as Ralph isn't even allowed to use big boy scissors.
quotes: He thought the other members were crazy for suggesting Ralph be the Republican candidate as Ralph isn't even allowed to use big boy scissors.

title: Combo-Rilla
text: Combo-Rilla is A gorilla superhero and member of The Secret Society of Super-Simians, appearing in Radioactive Man comics within the Simpsons universe. Combo-Rilla is a comic-book superhero who belongs to a group of simian heroes called The Secret Society of Super-Simians. He has an explorer-themed costume, giving him a rugged, adventurous look despite his cartoonish origins. He claims to have once been radioactive himself, though this seems more like a boastful aside than a defining trait. He's shown growing impatient with long-winded storytelling, notably rolling his eyes at Radioactive Ape's repeated retelling of his own origin story. Combo-Rilla mostly appears as a background member of the super-simian team rather than a central figure, popping up in group scenes and lending support during team business. His appearances are limited to a couple of in-universe comic issues referenced in the Radioactive Man comic line.

title: The Doctor
text: The Doctor is Crossover character based on the lead character from the British sci-fi show Doctor Who, appearing briefly in Simpsons episodes. The Doctor is a crossover cameo character from Doctor Who who pops up in various Simpsons episodes and media as a nod to the long-running British series. He's depicted with the classic long scarf look associated with the Fourth Doctor, tying his design to a specific era of the source show despite many actors having played the role over the decades. He was among the TV representatives called together when Sideshow Bob threatened to blow up Springfield unless it gave up television, and he later appears as a participant in a British invasion of Springfield during a satirical storyline. He's also referenced in non-canon material, including being trapped in a bag by a Treehouse of Horror villain and appearing as a costume choice at a fan convention. Comic Book Guy even dressed as a mixed version of the character for a costume event. Overall, the Doctor exists purely as a fun nod to Doctor Who fandom rather than a fleshed-out personality within the show.

title: Edwina
text: Edwina is A British woman from Abe Simpson's past, and the mother of his previously unknown daughter Abbey. Edwina is a wartime fling of Abe Simpson's from his time stationed in England during World War II. She and Abe had a brief romance before he was shipped out to D-Day, and unknown to either of them, she was left pregnant. She raised their daughter Abbey alone, with Abe having no clue of her existence for decades. Edwina reenters the story nearly six decades later, tracking Abe down at a London airport just as the Simpson family is about to head home from vacation. Her sudden reappearance forces Abe into an awkward reckoning with his past, ending in him bolting for the plane once he realizes Abbey is his daughter. She's a minor but pivotal figure whose backstory reveals a hidden chapter of Abe's youth. Voiced by Jane Leeves.

title: Tommy Chong (character)
text: Tommy Chong (character) is Comedy actor from Springfield, one half of the comedy duo Cheech and Chong, referenced in comparison to young Homer and Barney. Tommy Chong is a real-life celebrity who appears as himself within the Simpsons universe, working as a comedy actor alongside his longtime partner Cheech Marin. Before turning to comedy, he had a stint as a weatherman for Channel 6 News, until an accidental exposure to police-burned marijuana fumes turned him and Cheech into stoners who eventually became famous for their stand-up act. His and Cheech's laid-back, drug-associated persona became so iconic that Principal Dondelinger nicknamed young Homer and Barney after them when he caught the boys smoking in a school bathroom. Chong briefly split from Cheech to try new material, leading to an odd partnership with Seymour Skinner billed as "Teach and Chong," before he and Cheech eventually reunited for good. He's treated in the show as a cultural touchstone for marijuana humor, even referenced by Marge when she associates cannabis use with the duo's famous image. Voiced by Tommy Chong (Himself).

title: Cupid
text: Cupid is Mythological figure who appears as the Roman god of love, connected to Valentine's Day-themed episodes. Cupid is a whimsical, minor supernatural character who embodies the spirit of romance and Valentine's Day in the show. He tends to appear at dramatic emotional moments, offering cryptic advice about love and relationships to characters like Bart. Despite his celestial status, he's treated with a comedic lack of respect, becoming the target of physical attacks rather than reverence. His appearances are brief but memorable, often used for quick visual gags rather than extended storylines. Ultimately, his fate takes a dark comedic turn when he's killed off in a Valentine's Day-related scene, poking fun at the show's willingness to subvert expectations even with symbolic figures.

title: The Chocobots
text: The Chocobots is Fictional team of superhero characters from the in-universe cartoon 'Mattel and Mars Bar Quick Energy Chocobot Hour'. The Chocobots are a fictional band of chocolate-themed superheroes who star in their own kids' television program within the world of The Simpsons. Their show notably took over the timeslot once held by Kidz Newz, making them a small piece of the show's satire of children's programming and merchandising tie-ins. The group includes members like Almondis Prime, Major Nougat, Nougatron, Gooey, and Cocoa, each apparently modeled after candy or robot motifs. In a non-canon comic story, they attempt to battle the Bumblebee Monster but are defeated when the villain melts them by reflecting sunlight onto them with a giant pair of glasses. During that fight, Nougatron admits fear to Almondis Prime, who dismisses the idea that there's ever a proper time to be afraid. Beyond their brief TV and comic appearances, they've also shown up as collectible robot decorations in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game.

title: Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus ringmaster
text: Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus ringmaster is Ringmaster of the Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus, briefly Krusty the Clown's employer. This gruff circus boss runs the Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus and isn't afraid to fire performers who don't cut it, as he did with Krusty when he first hired him as 'Soggy the Clown.' He's pragmatic and opportunistic, willing to exploit a dangerous stunt for profit and later turn in a wanted fugitive for reward money to save his struggling business. Despite his hard-nosed exterior, he shows a bit of showmanship savvy, quickly recognizing star potential when Krusty accidentally becomes a hit with audiences. Financial troubles clearly weigh on him, as he has to shut the circus down and make tough calls to keep it running. He also seems to value the opinions of his crew, deferring to Scuzzo before making final decisions. Beyond his main appearance, he's been reimagined in non-canon material as a ringmaster for a spooky traveling circus. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Wilson DeFarge
text: Wilson DeFarge is A minor recurring character, a former third-party presidential candidate who appears as a judge in a Springfield event. Wilson DeFarge is a background figure in Springfield known primarily for his political past as a third-party presidential candidate. His most notable role comes when he serves as one of the judges for the Reading Digest essay competition final, an event tied to Lisa's storyline in Washington. He later makes a brief cameo appearance at Homer's art show, showing he remains a recognizable local figure even outside politics. DeFarge doesn't have any spoken lines in the show, fitting into the category of non-speaking characters. His presence is minimal but adds a touch of civic and political flavor to the town's background cast. He hasn't been given much depth beyond his professional roles, making him more of a functional character than a fully developed one.

title: Jack Deforest
text: Jack Deforest is A student at Springfield Elementary School who briefly becomes a romantic interest for Lisa. Jack Deforest is a tough, capable kid at Springfield Elementary who unexpectedly lands the lead role of Rick opposite Lisa's Ilsa in the school's Casablanca production. He proves surprisingly formidable, single-handedly fending off a gang of bullies hired by Bart to sabotage his performance so Milhouse could take over the part. Despite this display of strength, Skinner controversially reinstates Milhouse as the lead, disappointing Lisa given Milhouse's poor acting skills. In a twist, Jack secretly performs the play disguised as Milhouse, delivering a flawless performance without anyone realizing the switch. By the end of the episode, he and Lisa share a moment together on a float, hinting at a budding connection. His name is a nod to actor Humphrey Bogart, whose middle name was Deforest. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Cleopatra
text: Cleopatra is Historical figure (last pharaoh of Ancient Egypt) referenced and portrayed in costume by various Simpsons characters. Cleopatra is not an original Simpsons character but a real historical figure who appears in the show through references, costumes, and depictions rather than as a direct participant in the plot. She is noted as the last pharaoh of Egypt and is remembered for her romantic ties to Julius Caesar and Mark Antony. Within the show's universe, she appears as an image on a wall celebrating famous left-handed people, and as one of several notable women Lisa imagines honoring with statues in her dream house. Various characters take on her likeness for costumes, including Marge during a Treehouse of Horror segment and Miss Hoover at a masquerade ball. Mr. Burns even cites her as one of the authoritative figures he enjoys imitating through costume, underscoring her lasting cultural image as a powerful ruler.

title: Fausto
text: Fausto is A crew member on the fishing boat The Rotting Pelican, later a resident of Springfield and Pin Pals bowling team member. Fausto, nicknamed "Portuguese" Fausto, is a sailor who first appears as one of Homer's shipmates aboard the Rotting Pelican. He's quirky in a low-key way, having built his entire identity around fiddling with his pocket knife until it broke, leaving him searching for a new hobby. He shows a practical, cautious streak, warning against risky decisions like checking baited hooks unnecessarily. After the ship sinks, he survives thanks to a rescue by a Japanese fishing vessel, only to be pursued by immigration officials due to his mysterious past. He later settles in Springfield's Little Europe neighborhood and becomes part of the Pin Pals bowling team, even surviving a helicopter crash that many assumed had killed him. His character is a nod to a figure from a well-known Wes Anderson film, giving him an air of exotic, offbeat charm among Springfield's supporting cast. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Alex Désert. Notable quotes: it's not opposite day
quotes: it's not opposite day

title: Guthrie Frenel
text: Guthrie Frenel is A theatrical director who adapted Lisa and Marge's comic book into a stage musical. Guthrie Frenel is an eccentric theater director known for his erratic mannerisms and unconventional interactions with the world around him. Fiercely committed to his own artistic vision, he refuses to accept input or criticism from anyone, even when adapting someone else's original work. This stubbornness caused friction when he took Lisa and Marge's comic 'Sad Girl' and transformed it into a musical that barely resembled the source material, upsetting Lisa in the process. His inflexibility led to a technical disaster during the show's performance, and he was crushed when critics labeled it one of the worst productions in theater history. Despite this humiliation, he continued to appear in Springfield's cultural scene, attending events like a building launch and a live podcast recording. Voiced by Martin Short.

title: Clip-Clop
text: Clip-Clop is A fake pony given to Lisa Simpson as a Christmas present, appearing in "She of Little Faith". Clip-Clop isn't really a pony at all, but an elaborate prank cooked up by the Simpson family to lure Lisa away from her newfound Buddhist beliefs and back toward the commercialism and traditions of Christianity. Wrapped up as a seemingly innocent gift, the 'pony' is actually Ralph and Milhouse hiding inside a costume made of wrapping paper. The scheme falls apart comically when the boys burst out asking for more sugar, revealing the family's deception. Clip-Clop exists only as a one-episode gag rather than a true recurring character, poking fun at how far the Simpsons will go to manipulate Lisa's beliefs. Despite its brief appearance, the character later resurfaced in a non-canon capacity within the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright, Pamela Hayden.

title: Ginger Flanders
text: Ginger Flanders is Ned Flanders's short-lived Las Vegas wife and ex-stepmother to Rod and Todd. Ginger Flanders is a cocktail waitress from Las Vegas who briefly became part of the Flanders family after a drunken night out. She worked alongside Amber, Homer's own impulsive Vegas bride, at the Nero's Palace restaurant where the two men were drinking. After being abandoned in the desert when their husbands tried to flee, Ginger and Amber eventually tracked the men down in Springfield to try married life for real. Ginger's stint as Ned's wife didn't last, as she found the Flanders household's wholesome habits, like refusing to spike her coffee and flushing her cigarettes, too much to handle. She's a smoker with a taste for vice that clashes comically with Ned's straight-laced lifestyle. Ginger has only appeared in a handful of episodes but is remembered as a strange footnote in Ned Flanders's otherwise devout life. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Crazy Dog Man
text: Crazy Dog Man is A minor eccentric character in Springfield, a male counterpart to the Crazy Cat Lady. Crazy Dog Man is an odd, eccentric figure whose defining trait is his habit of throwing dogs, mirroring the infamous cat-throwing antics of the Crazy Cat Lady. He appears to be a lonely soul until he crosses paths with his female equivalent, sparking an unlikely romantic connection. Their courtship is unconventional, involving flirtation mixed with pet-related chaos rather than typical gestures of affection. Despite the odd nature of their meeting, the two seem to bond over their shared strange behavior, ending their encounter holding hands while their animals fight nearby. He is a rarely seen background character, appearing mainly as a one-off gag rather than a recurring presence in the main storylines. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Frink's Robot Dog
text: Frink's Robot Dog is A robotic dog belonging to Professor Frink, a minor animal character in the show. Frink's Robot Dog is a gray mechanical canine created and owned by the eccentric scientist Professor Frink. It appears as a minor, non-speaking background character, seen being walked by its owner during a moment of citywide panic in Springfield. As a robotic creation, it fits neatly into Frink's established role as the town's resident mad scientist and inventor of odd gadgets. The dog has no dialogue or distinct personality traits shown, functioning more as a quirky visual gag tied to Frink's character than a fully developed character in its own right. It later resurfaced in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, expanding its presence beyond the television series. Overall, it remains a minor recurring curiosity rather than a focal point of any storyline.

title: Doctor Duff
text: Doctor Duff is Fictional mascot character for a Duff Brewery product, appearing only as a picture in the show. Doctor Duff is a minor, picture-only mascot associated with the Duff Brewery, specifically representing Doctor Duff's Health Tonic. He has no speaking lines and exists solely as an image within the show's universe, first appearing on a poster during a brewery tour. Because he never appears as an animated, interactive character, little is known about his personality or backstory beyond his branding purpose. He later shows up again in a non-canon appearance, seen on the wall of Moe's Juicebar within one of Homer's dreams. His inclusion highlights the show's penchant for creating elaborate background advertising and satirical corporate mascots tied to the fictional Duff beer brand.

title: Thistlewick Flanders
text: Thistlewick Flanders is An English relative of Ned Flanders, appearing at a Flanders family reunion. Lord Thistlewick Flanders is a minor, aristocratic member of the extended Flanders clan who hails from England. He appears during the Flanders Family Reunion B.B.Q., an event so exclusively Flanders-only that Homer wasn't invited, much to his annoyance. Despite his refined, lordly demeanor, he is reluctantly coaxed into adopting the family's trademark speech quirks, tacking on "diddly" and "doodly" to his words. His brief appearance highlights the quirky, almost cult-like unity of the Flanders extended family and their shared verbal tics. As a mostly one-off character, he has since resurfaced only in non-canon material like a mobile game. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "Charmed. [nudged by Ned] (sigh) a googely-doogely."
quotes: "Charmed. [nudged by Ned] (sigh) a googely-doogely."

title: Philip J. Fry
text: Philip J. Fry is Crossover character from Futurama; a delivery boy for Planet Express who appears in Simpsons/Futurama crossover episodes. Fry is a delivery boy for Planet Express who shows up in several Simpsons episodes as part of Futurama-themed crossovers. He's often paired with Leela and Bender, getting caught up in time-travel schemes involving the Simpson family, including a mission to prevent Bender from killing Homer in the past. Despite his usual bumbling nature, he manages to be useful in a pinch, such as fixing a broken time portal simply because he could read the English instructions. His appearances tend to be brief cameos or background images rather than starring roles, reflecting his status as a guest character from another show. There's also a fun bit of trivia about how his middle name connects to Matt Groening's own father, tying him thematically to Homer Simpson. Voiced by Billy West.

title: Dimwillie
text: Dimwillie is Mascot character associated with the Springfield business Dimwillie's. Dimwillie is a minor, non-speaking mascot figure tied to the restaurant or business known as Dimwillie's. In the show's main continuity, he's represented only by a statue perched on the roof of the establishment, giving him a background, visual-gag presence rather than an active role in any storyline. He later gained a bit more life in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, where he appears as part of the Food Wars content. Since he has no dialogue and no personality traits described, his character is defined almost entirely by his branding function as a mascot. He remains a trivial, background piece of Springfield's commercial landscape rather than a character interacting with the main cast.

title: Winston Churchill
text: Winston Churchill is Real-world historical figure (former Prime Minister of England) referenced in the Simpsons universe. Winston Churchill appears in the show as a nod to real history rather than as an active character in Springfield's story. He shows up mostly through archival-style footage, photographs, and passing references, such as in a WWII documentary clip and on a captcha screen for 20th-century dictators. His legacy is treated with a mix of reverence and absurdity, being namechecked as calming listening for a pregnant woman alongside Mozart, and later used as a punchline when a character is compared to him. He's also listed among history's notable progressive figures on Ned Flanders' list of laudable lefties. In one non-canon Halloween-episode twist, his image turns up on the cover of a fictional erotic book. Overall, he functions as a recurring cultural touchstone joke rather than a fleshed-out character, never actually speaking in any episode.

title: Queen Elizabeth I
text: Queen Elizabeth I is Historical English monarch depicted in a Simpsons-narrated fictional story, played by Selma Bouvier. Queen Elizabeth I is a real-world historical figure reimagined in a Simpsons segment as a role played by Selma Bouvier within a tale told by Marge. In this fictionalized version, she is pressured to marry so she can produce an heir, and rejects unimpressive suitors before falling for Walter Raleigh after he gifts her tobacco. Her story takes a dramatic turn when she discovers Raleigh's secret romance with her lady-in-waiting, and must simultaneously deal with a Spanish invasion led by one of her spurned suitors. Ever resourceful, she leads her forces to a surprising victory when Raleigh accidentally sets fire to the English fleet, which then defeats the Spanish armada. In the end she proves independent, choosing to remain unmarried and declaring that England itself is enough for her. She's also referenced as a feminist icon admired by Lisa, and her ghost makes a brief appearance elsewhere in the show. Voiced by Julie Kavner. Notable quotes: Finally, Henry's daughter, Elizabeth, became Queen. England's power was never greater, and British actresses always had a role to play when they got to a certain age.
quotes: Finally, Henry's daughter, Elizabeth, became Queen. England's power was never greater, and British actresses always had a role to play when they got to a certain age.

title: Simon Cowell (character)
text: Simon Cowell (character) is Real-life American Idol judge who appears as a guest character in a Season 21 episode alongside Moe. Simon Cowell shows up in Springfield lore as himself, the notoriously blunt American Idol judge, when Moe is brought on as a temporary fellow judge. He tries to offer Moe some genuine advice, admitting that his own constant nastiness has left him lonely and warning Moe not to make the same mistake. True to his reputation, though, he can't help reverting to his harsh, mocking persona on live television, undercutting Moe's attempt at kindness toward a contestant. This betrayal sends Moe into a violent rage, leading to a chaotic scuffle and Moe's banishment from California. Cowell is depicted as sharp-tongued and image-conscious, even blending into the shadows thanks to his dark clothing. He's a one-episode guest character rather than a recurring fixture, tied specifically to the show's satire of American Idol culture. Voiced by Himself.

title: Rodney Dangerfield (character)
text: Rodney Dangerfield (character) is Real-world actor who appears as a character/caricature in The Simpsons. Rodney Dangerfield appears in the show as a version of the real-life American comedian and actor known for his self-deprecating humor. Within the Simpsons universe he shows up as a guest character, most notably in the episode "Bart Gets a 'Z'", with a further appearance in "Clown in the Dumps". He is also referenced in a non-canon context, where Werner Herzog jokes about channeling his comedic persona while performing at a comedy club. His portrayal leans on his real-world reputation as a stand-up comedian and actor. He is depicted as an adult, Jewish celebrity character, and is listed among the show's recurring characters despite his limited appearances. As with other real-world figures who appear on the show, his character is largely a nod to his actual public persona rather than an original creation. Voiced by Maurice LaMarche.

title: Henry K. Duff
text: Henry K. Duff is The original inventor of Duff Beer, a minor background figure in Springfield lore. Henry K. Duff is a shadowy historical figure known only as the creator of Duff Beer, Springfield's beloved brand of alcohol. He never appears as a living character in canon episodes, existing mostly as a name attached to a premium product, the Henry K. Duff Private Reserve. In a non-canon story, he is revisited through an old recording made at his cabin, where he claims to have stumbled upon something terrifying while perfecting his beer recipe. His warning not to read the recipe aloud suggests a man haunted by his own creation, hinting at supernatural undertones to the beer's origins. Ironically, what he believed to be a demonic possession affecting his own family turns out to be nothing more than a hallucinogenic side effect of the brew. This gives him a strange legacy as both an unwitting horror victim and an accidental inventor of a mind-altering substance.

title: Marie Curie
text: Marie Curie is Real-world historical physicist and chemist referenced/depicted in The Simpsons as a symbol of scientific achievement. Marie Curie appears in the show not as an active character but as a historical figure invoked to represent scientific brilliance and sacrifice. Lisa frequently references her as an inspiration, comparing her family's situation to Curie and her husband Pierre, and later citing her as the epitome of scientific passion during a power plant visit. She appears as an image or statue in various settings meant to honor accomplished women, including Lisa's imagined dream house gallery and a diorama of notable women in history. Her legacy is also tied to a darkly comedic aside about her death from radiation poisoning, which Bart turns into an exaggerated fantasy involving giant radioactive Curies destroying a Japanese city. Overall, she serves as a recurring symbol of intellectual achievement and feminist historical pride within Lisa's worldview, appearing mostly through pictures, mentions, and homages rather than direct involvement in the plot.

title: Fake Lisa Simpson
text: Fake Lisa Simpson is A recast replacement for Lisa Simpson in an in-universe parody spin-off, also appearing as a minor background character. Fake Lisa Simpson is a strange conjectural character who exists mainly as a joke about television spin-offs gone wrong. In a non-canon segment, the Simpson family got their own variety show, but the actual Lisa refused to participate, so producers quietly swapped her out for an older, more conventionally attractive model without telling anyone. This is a direct parody of a real-life incident from The Brady Bunch Hour. Outside of that gag, the same blonde-haired woman shows up in the actual show's continuity in small background roles, once as one of stunt daredevil Lance Murdock's assistants in Las Vegas, and later as an attendee at Amber Simpson's funeral. She has no dialogue or personality traits established, functioning purely as a visual cameo and running gag about her uncanny resemblance to Lisa. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Female mail carrier
text: Female mail carrier is Recurring background character who delivers mail to the Simpson family and other Springfield residents. The female mail carrier is one of the minor recurring figures who service the Simpson household at 742 Evergreen Terrace. She's shown to have a fair amount of patience, particularly when dealing with Bart's impatience over a mail-order item he's anxiously awaiting. Beyond her delivery duties, she occasionally gets pulled into the family's antics, such as stepping in to stop Homer from petty vandalism involving a neighbor's mailbox. Despite her limited screen time, she's appeared across several episodes spanning different seasons, functioning as a recognizable piece of Springfield's everyday background life. Her role is largely functional rather than comedic, though her presence often triggers jokes from other characters. Voiced by Maggie Roswell / Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Uh-oh, the femail man. | Female carrier, Bart.
quotes: Uh-oh, the femail man.
Female carrier, Bart.

title: Dawn
text: Dawn is Minor recurring character; a fling of Kirk Van Houten from his separation period with Luann. Dawn is a minor character best known for her brief romantic history with Kirk Van Houten during one of his splits from Luann. She resurfaces to cause trouble when the Simpson family tries to sell a painting originally bought from the Van Houtens, claiming Kirk had stolen it from her while they were involved as friends with benefits. Her revelation creates marital tension for Kirk and Luann, since Kirk had claimed he never dated anyone during their separation. Beyond this scandal, Dawn appears as a background figure, later spotted in the crowd at one of Springfield's podcast events. She functions mainly as a plot device to stir up drama in the Van Houtens' rocky relationship rather than as a fully developed character. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Evil Queen
text: Evil Queen is Antagonist from a story told by Lisa, based on the Disney Evil Queen character. The Evil Queen is a villainous character who appears within a fairy-tale story narrated by Lisa, drawing directly on the Disney version of the character from Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. She is consumed by vanity and jealousy, obsessed with being told she is the fairest of all, and reacts murderously when she learns Snow White surpasses her in beauty. She relies on trickery, disguising herself as an old woman to deceive her stepdaughter into eating a poisoned apple. Despite her cruelty, she is ultimately undone by the forces of nature she underestimates, meeting a violent end at the hands of woodland animals. In non-canon crossover appearances, she is depicted alongside other Disney villains, showing a more comedic, self-aware side, even protesting her portrayal as an unfair stereotype of stepmothers. She also appears in holiday-themed specials engaging in stereotypically witchy activities like brewing poison and selling apples. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Maxwell Flinch
text: Maxwell Flinch is An injury lawyer occasionally hired by Homer Simpson to sue people after accidents. Maxwell Flinch is a recurring injury lawyer known for advertising his services to Springfield residents looking to sue someone after an accident. He first appeared when Homer hired him to sue Mr. Burns following a workplace injury, only for Homer to have a last-minute change of heart and throw the case. Despite this setback, Flinch shows a somewhat sensitive side, feeling overlooked and unappreciated in his profession, which prompts Homer to stage another injury just to give him a case. He later returns to defend Homer in a more serious matter involving Gil Gunderson, cleverly exploiting the jurors' love of dogs to win a not-guilty verdict.
