His court tactics end up influencing actual legislation in Springfield, showing his surprising ability to sway public policy through simple courtroom manipulation. Flinch is bald and comes across as a stereotypical ambulance-chasing lawyer, ready to jump on any opportunity for a lawsuit. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Emma (Separate Vocations)
text: Emma (Separate Vocations) is A robot at the National Testing Center in Proctorville, Iowa, that appears in the episode "Separate Vocations". Emma is a peculiar robotic machine tasked with correcting standardized tests at a testing facility far from Springfield. She is minded by an elderly attendant who prods her with a broom whenever she malfunctions or stalls, suggesting she is old and somewhat unreliable technology. Her one notable moment in the show comes when she is overwhelmed while grading Bart Simpson's test, ultimately breaking apart from the strain. This小 mishap plays into the episode's themes of standardized testing and Bart's knack for causing chaos in bureaucratic systems. Emma has no dialogue or personality of her own, functioning purely as a plot device and a bit of background comedy. She later reappears in a non-canon capacity as a building in The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Chilton Danes
text: Chilton Danes is A minor recurring background character in Springfield, known as a wealthy socialite. Chilton Danes is a well-off gadabout who pops up in various minor jobs and social settings around Springfield. He's shown serving as a judge for a prestigious essay contest, working retail at a jewelry store, and later staffing a skateboard shop. Despite his wealth, he seems to drift between odd jobs and appears frequently at upscale gatherings and parties, suggesting a life of leisure interspersed with occasional employment. He is a non-speaking character, existing mostly as a background presence rather than a driver of plot. His appearances span several classic-era episodes, making him a recognizable if minor fixture of the show's world.

title: Bill Cipher
text: Bill Cipher is A crossover demon character appearing briefly in The Simpsons, taken on by Loki as one of his forms. Bill Cipher is a demonic entity who crosses over from the animated series Gravity Falls into the world of The Simpsons. In his appearance, he manifests as one of the many forms taken by Loki from Norse mythology. His main act of mischief in the show involves convincing the Simpson family to invest in cryptocurrency, playing into his trickster, deal-making nature. As a guest character, he doesn't have an extensive ongoing role but serves as a fun nod to fans of both shows. His inclusion highlights The Simpsons' tradition of incorporating pop-culture crossovers and guest villains for comedic effect. Voiced by Alex Hirsch.

title: Cleatus the Football Robot
text: Cleatus the Football Robot is Fox Sports mascot robot who appears as a crossover character in The Simpsons. Cleatus the Football Robot is a real-world Fox Sports mascot that crosses over into the Simpsons universe. He appears when Homer, desperate for his imagined vision of Stradivarius Cain to return, knocks himself on the head repeatedly until Cleatus shows up instead. Homer treats the robot's arrival as his last hope, and the robot responds by dancing. The twist reveals that Cain had actually been hiding inside the Cleatus costume all along. Beyond this gag appearance, Cleatus also shows up in non-canon specials and in The Simpsons: Tapped Out as a mascot character. He is a non-speaking character with no distinct personality beyond his mascot antics.

title: Faith Crowley
text: Faith Crowley is Patriotism editor of Reading Digest magazine, appearing in the episode where Lisa's family visits Washington. Faith Crowley is a minor recurring character who works as the patriotism editor for Reading Digest magazine. She oversees a youth essay competition that brings Lisa Simpson and her family to Washington, D.C. Faith acts as a welcoming host to the finalists, introducing Lisa to her fellow competitors with a sense of professional pride in the contest. Her patience is tested by Homer, whose obliviousness and constant questions, such as asking what each letter in "VIP" stands for, clearly irritate her. Despite this, she remains composed enough to preside over the final ceremony, announcing the judges and presenting the award to the eventual winner. She serves mainly as a background authority figure representing the bureaucratic, patriotic pageantry of the competition. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Randall Curtis
text: Randall Curtis is Creator of the fictional Cosmic Wars film series, a one-episode character in the Simpsons universe. Randall Curtis is a filmmaker best known for creating the Cosmic Wars movie franchise, a clear stand-in for George Lucas and his Star Wars empire. He runs his business out of the Cosmic Wars Ranch, a satirical nod to Skywalker Ranch, and seems out of touch with what made his own films great in the first place, leaning too heavily on flashy CGI. When confronted by young critics Bart and Lisa about the disappointing quality of his latest movie, he initially brushes them off with a generic form letter before meeting them face to face. Their blunt feedback actually resonates with him, prompting him to try to reconnect with his creative roots. Unfortunately, his attempt at a nostalgic journey is cut short in a chaotic, humiliating encounter with a very drunk Homer and Marge. He's a mostly one-off character used to poke fun at blockbuster franchise fatigue and out-of-touch Hollywood creators. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Dr. Foster
text: Dr. Foster is Ned Flanders' childhood psychologist who treated him for anger management. Dr. Foster is the therapist who worked with a young Ned Flanders to help him suppress his anger, a treatment that famously backfired years later when Ned finally snapped. He reappears periodically in Springfield, showing signs of aging and vanity, such as getting Botox and adopting a toupee over time. Beyond his history with Ned, he takes on other odd psychological duties in town, including leading the search effort for a missing, allegedly insane Marge Simpson and overseeing therapy sessions for recovering alcoholic cowboys. His name is a nod to the classic English nursery rhyme 'Doctor Foster.' Though a minor, recurring figure, he's tied to one of the show's most memorable Ned Flanders episodes. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: First Prime Minister of Australia
text: First Prime Minister of Australia is Minor background character; a statue depicting Australia's first Prime Minister seen by Lisa and Marge during their trip to Australia. This character exists only as a statue glimpsed at the Cultural Centre during the Simpson family's visit to Australia. He has no dialogue and no real personality of his own, functioning purely as a piece of background scenery that helps establish the setting. The wiki notes he is based on the real historical figure Edmund Barton, Australia's actual first Prime Minister. Amusingly, the fan community treats him as an Australian mirror image of Springfield's own petty criminal Snake, tying into the joke that Australia was originally founded as a British penal colony. Beyond his brief appearance as a statue, he later shows up as a purchasable decoration in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Dennis the Menace (character)
text: Dennis the Menace (character) is A crossover character/comic strip figure referenced within The Simpsons universe, often compared to Bart. Dennis Mitchell, better known as Dennis the Menace, is a famous troublemaker who exists as a pop-culture reference point within the Simpsons universe rather than a regular cast member. He's frequently name-dropped as a comparison for Bart, since both are iconic childhood mischief-makers. Sideshow Bob even calls Bart "that century's Dennis the Menace" while hunting him down, underscoring the parallel between the two characters. He also appears in more direct ways, showing up on a book cover and even physically present on a school playground in one crossover-style episode. His presence in the show is largely as a nod to the classic comic strip and its legacy rather than an active participant in Springfield's storylines. Notable quotes: "that century's Dennis the Menace" - Sideshow Bob (referring to Bart)
quotes: "that century's Dennis the Menace" - Sideshow Bob (referring to Bart)

title: Dalmatian puppies
text: Dalmatian puppies is Non-canon crossover characters from the 101 Dalmatians franchise appearing in Simpsons specials. These are the litter of dalmatian puppies belonging to Pongo and Perdita, brought into the Simpsons universe as crossover characters from the 101 Dalmatians franchise. They don't speak, instead appearing in background or gag-driven moments across various holiday specials. In one appearance they're shown watching Lady and the Tramp on television, tying them further into the Disney animated world. They also join their parents on a family outing to Disney Playground Planet during a Mother's Day themed special. In a more chaotic cameo, they are seen being worn as a coat by the villainous Cruella de Vil before escaping and running off. Their appearances are purely visual gags rather than developed storylines, marking them as non-canon novelty characters.

title: Harriet K. Duff
text: Harriet K. Duff is CEO of Duff Beer, a minor recurring character in the Simpsons universe. Harriet K. Duff is a corporate executive who runs Duff Beer, the beloved brewery central to Springfield's drinking culture. She's shown taking her role seriously, presiding over board meetings that decide the company's future direction, including business decisions about the brand's iconic mascot. Her connection to Springfield's elite is further shown through her inclusion in an exclusive social circle tied to Mr. Burns. As a relatively new character introduced later in the show's run, she represents the business side of Duff Beer rather than its consumption, offering a rare glimpse into the corporate structure behind Springfield's favorite beverage. Little is known about her personal life or personality beyond her professional dealings. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Terry Delegeane (character)
text: Terry Delegeane (character) is Non-canon comic book character based on real-life Bongo Comics writer/editor. Terry Delegeane is a non-canon, real-world-inspired character appearing in Simpsons comic book stories that poke fun at the making of the comics themselves. He is depicted as a writer and editor working for Bongo Comics, appearing alongside fellow editor Bill Morrison. In one story, he is humorously shown in a maximum-security prison as part of a joke about the strict approval process for Simpsons Comics. He also appears representing Bongo Comics at the Springfield Comic-Con, where the booth's poor placement next to the restrooms causes attendees to overlook it. His appearances are limited to meta, behind-the-scenes style comic stories rather than the main show continuity.

title: Erin (Uncut Femmes)
text: Erin (Uncut Femmes) is A jewel thief and member of a criminal gang featured in a couple of Simpsons episodes. Erin is a recurring criminal character who runs in the same circles as Bette, Sarah Wiggum, and Lindsey Naegle. She's a seasoned jewel thief, comfortable with heists, disguises, and long-term schemes for revenge. After being betrayed and arrested due to a double-cross during an earlier robbery, she holds a grudge that eventually drives her back into crime. Erin is resourceful and willing to go undercover, even posing as catering staff to pull off an elaborate diamond theft. Her partnership with Bette is central to her characterization, as the two consistently work as a duo in both their criminal past and their later scheme. Ultimately she's defined by loyalty to her partner and a taste for elaborate revenge plots against those who wronged her. Voiced by Tiya Sircar.

title: Duncan
text: Duncan is A racehorse adopted by the Simpson family, appearing in the episode "Saddlesore Galactica". Duncan is a horse the Simpsons rescue after his career as an abused diving-horse attraction at the State Fair is shut down for animal cruelty. Bart convinces the family to take him in, and Homer initially tries to make him useful by testing him out in football before settling on horse racing. Duncan starts out timid and easily intimidated, losing his first race out of fear, but a pep talk from Bart helps him gain confidence. After a flashy makeover, he's rebranded as the aggressive, swaggering "Furious D," who wins races by intimidating and attacking other horses. His success eventually draws the ire of rival jockeys, leading to a race-fixing conspiracy that Bart and Homer thwart. Duncan's arc is essentially an underdog story of transformation from a nervous, mistreated animal into a fierce and confident champion who ultimately retires happily as a stud. Voiced by Jim Cummings. Notable quotes: He's the bad boy of racing. He's got attitude and bad-itude, so show him some latitude and you'll win his gratitude. Only in America!
quotes: He's the bad boy of racing. He's got attitude and bad-itude, so show him some latitude and you'll win his gratitude. Only in America!

title: Bob Denver (character)
text: Bob Denver (character) is Real-life American actor who appears as himself in a Simpsons episode. Bob Denver appears as a fictionalized version of himself, playing off his famous role as Gilligan from Gilligan's Island. He shows up during a Naval Reserve tour that Homer and Marge attend, where he addresses the annoying habit fans have of greeting him with his character's catchphrase and swatting him with a hat. Despite his plea for the joke to stop, he gets irritated when the crowd laughs at his complaint instead of taking it seriously. Homer, missing the point entirely, plans to do the very thing Denver just complained about. In a non-canon Halloween appearance, he's shown trapped in a villain's lair alongside other captured celebrities. His role in the show is a brief celebrity cameo that pokes fun at his typecasting from his most iconic television role. Voiced by Bob Denver.

title: Dickie
text: Dickie is Minor recurring character, a retail clerk who worked at Halloween Headquarters. Dickie is a minor character who works retail jobs around Springfield, first appearing as an employee at a Halloween store alongside his friend Lem. After Homer gets him and his coworkers fired, Dickie takes part in a revenge scheme against Homer, which ultimately lands him in trouble with the police. Despite this run-in with the law, Chief Wiggum offers him a lighter path forward, hinting that he isn't seen as a hardened criminal. He later shows up as an audience member at one of Kent Brockman's public podcast recordings, suggesting he's just an ordinary Springfield resident who pops up in the background of larger stories. In a fantasy sequence imagined by Marge, Dickie appears as an inmate in the asylum-like Darkham Asylum, playing into a comic-book parody storyline, and is broken out by parody versions of Homer and Marge. Overall, Dickie functions as a recurring background character used for quick gags and cameo appearances rather than deep characterization. Voiced by Blake Anderson.

title: Barney Fife
text: Barney Fife is Crossover character from The Andy Griffith Show who has appeared briefly in The Simpsons. Barney Fife is a nervous, easily-flustered deputy sheriff borrowed from The Andy Griffith Show and inserted into The Simpsons universe as a crossover gag. He's shown as somewhat clueless and jumpy, most notably when he's baffled and unsettled by Charles Bronson's violent replacement of Andy Griffith. He later appears having a strange, almost eerie conversation with Chief Wiggum through the television. Beyond his brief speaking appearances, his image pops up as a background nod on the walls of Springfield locations. Since original actor Don Knotts had retired and couldn't reprise the role, Dana Gould stepped in to voice him for the show. Voiced by Dana Gould. Notable quotes: Where's Otis? — Barney Fife | I gotta go. — Barney Fife
quotes: Where's Otis? — Barney Fife
I gotta go. — Barney Fife

title: Dragon of Springfieldia
text: Dragon of Springfieldia is A non-canon fantasy creature appearing in the Game of Thrones-parody segment "The Serfsons," commanded by Rainier Wolfcastle. This fire-breathing dragon is depicted as the last of its kind in the fantasy kingdom of Springfieldia. It serves as a weapon of mass destruction, ridden into battle by Wolfcastle's character to crush a peasant uprising against the ruling nobility. Its fiery breath is tied directly to the magic sustaining the entire kingdom, making it far more important than a simple monster. After being killed in a clever act of self-sacrifice, its death nearly causes all magic to vanish, until Homer's serf counterpart revives it by relighting a fire in its mouth. Once resurrected, it immediately reverts to destructive form, torching the village. It has no lines, functioning purely as a visual and plot device within the parody segment.

title: Captain Flag
text: Captain Flag is An elderly professional wrestler who appears in the episode "Gorgeous Grampa". Captain Flag is a veteran wrestler who teams up with Half-Mast for a tag-team match against the villainous duo of Gorgeous Godfrey and Beautiful Bart. Little is known about his personality since he is a non-speaking character, but he represents the classic aging wrestler archetype within the show's wrestling storyline. His match becomes a backdrop for a lesson learned by Grampa and Bart about winning fairly rather than resorting to cheating. Outside of the main show, Captain Flag also appears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, tied to its wrestling content. He remains a minor, recurring figure rather than a central character in the Simpsons universe.

title: Santa Claus (The Fight Before Christmas)
text: Santa Claus (The Fight Before Christmas) is A fictional Santa Claus who appears in a Simpsons Christmas episode, portrayed within the show by Krusty the Clown. This version of Santa Claus, also called Kris Kringle, is depicted as a weary, run-down figure operating out of a shabby office rather than a magical workshop. He tells Bart that the company behind his toy operation, Claus Co., has gone broke, and even claims to be eating his own reindeer to survive. His pitiful act convinces Bart to leave without his requested dirt bike, but it's later revealed to be a ruse, since Santa is secretly quite wealthy. The character plays into a cynical, comedic twist on the beloved holiday icon, exposing him as a fraud in this particular story. Notably, within the show's meta-narrative, this Santa is revealed to be portrayed by Krusty the Clown, adding another layer of showbiz satire to the character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Larry Fine
text: Larry Fine is One of The Three Stooges, appearing as a cartoon parody/cameo character in The Simpsons universe. Larry Fine is a caricatured version of the real-life Three Stooges member, appearing briefly within the show's fictional world rather than as a regular cast member. He's depicted as the beleaguered middle man of the trio, often caught between Moe's aggression and Curly's antics. In his main appearance, he tries to reason with Moe about Curly's lack of health insurance, only to become the target of Moe's slapping himself. His portrayal leans into classic slapstick comedy, poking fun at the real Three Stooges' dynamic. Larry mostly shows up as a background reference or visual gag, such as his face appearing in the sky or his skeleton and brain being shown in unrelated contexts. He is treated as a deceased celebrity figure within the show's universe, referenced for comedic nostalgia rather than plot importance. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Farrah Fawcett
text: Farrah Fawcett is Real-world actress referenced/depicted in background gags throughout the show, not an actual character in the Simpsons universe. Farrah Fawcett-Majors-O'Neal-Varney is a non-speaking background reference to the real actress Farrah Fawcett, best known for Charlie's Angels. She appears mostly as posters, drawings, or pictures scattered throughout various episodes rather than as an actual interacting character. Her name is a running joke combining her real-life marriages and relationships with a nod to actor Jim Varney of the Ernest movies. She's tied to a few recurring gags, including her own parody cereal brand and a hair salon joke about her iconic hairstyle. Bart even imagines her appearing on a futuristic game show alongside other celebrities in one of his fame-fueled fantasies. Overall, she functions as a piece of pop-culture set dressing rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: The Collider
text: The Collider is A villain character from the fictional Radioactive Man film franchise within The Simpsons universe. The Collider is a movie villain created for the film Radioactive Man Re-Rises, serving as the antagonist to the superhero Radioactive Man. He became notable in the show through a tie-in action figure sold as a Krusty Burger Laffy Meal toy, which Milhouse owned. The toy itself was a running joke, as it bluntly and unnecessarily spoiled the plot of its own movie by announcing twist details through pre-recorded phrases. This absurd bit of merchandising satire pokes fun at movie tie-in toys and franchise marketing. Despite being a minor, non-recurring character in the main storyline, The Collider later appeared as a playable superhero/villain figure in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: I turn out to be a good guy | I die, but come back to life after the credits
quotes: I turn out to be a good guy
I die, but come back to life after the credits

title: Scott Christian
text: Scott Christian is Weekend news anchor and fill-in reporter for Channel 6 News in Springfield. Scott Christian is a secondary news personality at Channel 6, stepping in for lead anchor Kent Brockman while also covering field stories around Springfield. Despite his plain, buttoned-down on-air persona, he secretly enjoys mingling with the town's celebrities at parties. He's a member of the shadowy Stonecutters fraternal order, showing he has ties beyond just journalism. He's also shown a willingness to take public stances, having signed a petition against medicinal marijuana. One recurring quirk associated with him is his inconsistent hair color, appearing with black hair most of the time but sometimes sporting a strikingly different orange hue. He has appeared covering major Springfield events, including reporting for FOX during the manhunt for Homer Simpson after Mr. Burns' shooting. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: E-mail
text: E-mail is A minor student at Springfield Elementary School and member of the Superfriends club (a group of nerdy kids). E-mail is a red-haired eight-year-old who belongs to the Superfriends, a clique of academically-minded kids that includes Database, Cosine, Ham, and Report Card. He first appears welcoming Bart Simpson into their group after Bart becomes famous for discovering a comet, taking part in the club's tradition of giving new members nicknames by dubbing Bart 'Cosmos.' When the danger of the comet becomes clear, E-mail joins the rest of the group on a frantic trip to the Springfield Observatory to warn the astronomers. Like his fellow Superfriends, he's defined more by his role in the group than by strong individual character traits, functioning as background support for Lisa and Bart's storylines. A later appearance suggests he may have transferred to a Montessori school. He has made numerous brief background appearances across many later seasons, comics, and books despite his minor role. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Trevor Denman (character)
text: Trevor Denman (character) is Real-world sportscaster who appears as himself commentating on horse races involving Duncan and Bart. Trevor Denman is a real-life sportscaster who appears in the show as himself, providing race commentary for the horse races featuring Duncan and Bart. He's portrayed as a professional broadcaster who narrates the action with excitement and detail, giving viewers a play-by-play of the racetrack events. His most memorable moment comes during the climactic final race, where he grows alarmed at Duncan's increasingly aggressive and human-like behavior toward the jockeys. Fearing a chaotic uprising akin to a 'planet of the horses' scenario, he abandons his booth in a panic. This brief but comedic appearance plays on the absurdity of the episode's horse-related plot escalating into something surreal. As a guest-starring real-world character, his role is limited to this single storyline before he vanishes from the narrative. Voiced by Trevor Denman (himself).

title: Della
text: Della is Secretary at Lionel Hutz's law firm, I Can't Believe It's a Law Firm!. Della is the perpetually distracted secretary working for the bumbling lawyer Lionel Hutz. She seems far more interested in reading magazines like Popular Secretary than in actually doing her job, often barely registering the presence of clients like Homer Simpson. Her one notable task during Homer's visit to the office was relaying a nonsensical message about the Supreme Court calling, which she delivered with obvious uncertainty. This running gag underscores the general incompetence and shoddiness of Hutz's law practice. She has made brief background appearances in other episodes, including once riding a subway train in New York. Her name is likely a nod to Della Street, the secretary of fictional lawyer Perry Mason. Voiced by Doris Grau. Notable quotes: Calls? ... Oh, calls. The Supreme Court called again. They need your help on some freedom thing.|Della
quotes: Calls? ... Oh, calls. The Supreme Court called again. They need your help on some freedom thing.|Della

title: Billie Eilish (character)
text: Billie Eilish (character) is Real-life musician who appears as herself in a Simpsons special, briefly bonding with Lisa. Billie Eilish appears as a fictionalized version of herself who crosses paths with Lisa Simpson after hearing her play saxophone under a bridge. Impressed by the young girl's musical talent, she impulsively fires her entire backing orchestra so she can record with Lisa instead, showing a spontaneous and generous side to her personality. Beyond music, she shares a quieter, more personal moment with Lisa, lying on top of her car to talk about their families, hinting at a reflective and down-to-earth demeanor beneath her celebrity persona. A recurring quirk associated with her character is that she changes her hair color so often that her recording studio keeps a daily sign announcing its current shade. She's also shown attending a glitzy premiere in the show's non-canon material, reinforcing her status as a real-world celebrity guest star woven into the Simpsons universe. Voiced by Herself.

title: Mr. Fantastic
text: Mr. Fantastic is A Marvel superhero (member of the Fantastic Four) referenced within The Simpsons universe, mainly through comics and costumes worn by other characters. Mr. Fantastic isn't a true Simpsons character but a Marvel superhero who appears as a pop-culture reference within the show. He's part of the Fantastic Four and married to the Invisible Woman. Rather than appearing as himself in the main continuity, his presence is felt through other characters imitating him, such as Chief Wiggum dressing up in his Future Foundation outfit and Carl wearing his costume during a superhero-themed pub crawl. In a non-canon Halloween segment, Bart even takes on the role of Mr. Fantastic when Lisa magically transforms the family into the Fantastic Four. He is a non-speaking character, existing mostly as a costume or comic reference rather than a fully realized personality within the show.

title: Arthur Fortune
text: Arthur Fortune is Billionaire owner of the Fortune Megastore department store chain; a minor recurring Springfield character. Arthur Fortune is a flamboyant, larger-than-life billionaire businessman known for his eccentric stunts and extravagant lifestyle. He's built a massive retail empire with over a hundred store locations, and he loves showing off his wealth in flashy, playful ways, such as tossing free cash to crowds simply because he has more money than he needs. His reputation includes outlandish personal feats like sledding down Mount Everest and physically overpowering a boxing legend, painting him as a daring adventurer as much as a mogul. Despite his cheerful showmanship, he's not above joining an angry mob against Homer Simpson when the town turns hostile. He's widely seen as a parody of real-world billionaire entrepreneurs known for their bold public personas. Beyond his TV appearances, he has also shown up in Simpsons mobile game content. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Chett Englebrick
text: Chett Englebrick is Founder and president of the Mixed Martial Arts Ultimate Punch, Kick and Choke Championship; one-time antagonist to Marge Simpson. Chett Englebrick runs a scrappy mixed martial arts league built around brutal punching, kicking, and choking matches. When Marge Simpson tries to shut his championship down for good, he responds by challenging her to fight him personally, betting the future of his organization on the outcome. Despite being an experienced fighter who only takes on opponents his own size, he underestimates Marge and ends up losing the bout, forcing him to give up the championship. He's a minor one-episode antagonist whose defeat becomes a memorable moment for Marge as an unlikely fighter. His brief legacy lives on mainly through a callback image used in a later couch gag. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Laney Fontaine
text: Laney Fontaine is A Broadway performer who had a brief romantic fling with Moe Szyslak. Laney Fontaine is a gray-haired Broadway entertainer skilled in comedy, dance, singing, and acting. Moe caught her show after scoring free tickets and ended up taking her home, though their tryst fizzled quickly once his bar's sorry state was revealed. Despite that rocky start, the two apparently kept seeing each other for a while afterward. Their eventual breakup became fodder for her art, as she wrote a scathing Broadway play about splitting from Moe that ended up winning her a Tony Award. She's also popped up as an audience member at a podcast recording and even appeared in one of Bart's surreal coma-dream visions. Behind the scenes, her name nods to real-life acting duo Lunt and Fontanne, while her mannerisms are modeled after actress Elaine Stritch. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Dowager
text: Dowager is A minor recurring wealthy elderly woman living in Springfield, mother of the débutante. The dowager is a wealthy, elderly Springfield socialite who appears in the background of various high-society events. She is the mother of the débutante and is married to an unnamed husband. Known for her refined status, she once kindly fed a steak to Santa's Little Helper and She's the Fastest. She also appeared among the crowd when Mr. Burns introduced his grandson Larry, an encounter that turned sour when Larry insulted her daughter. She later showed up as a potential investor at a Springfield Nuclear Power Plant event, reflecting her recurring role as a stock high-society extra in Springfield's elite circles. In supplementary material, she has been mistaken for another wealthy Springfield woman, Mrs. Vanderbilt. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Michigan J. Frog
text: Michigan J. Frog is Crossover cartoon character appearing briefly in The Simpsons, originally the mascot of the Warner Brothers Network. Michigan J. Frog is a Looney Tunes character borrowed for a cameo appearance on The Simpsons, tying into his real-world role as the mascot for the Warner Brothers Network. In his appearance, he performs his signature singing and dancing routine across the network logo, only to walk off looking annoyed once the performance ends, hinting that he resents the job he's forced to do. He later shows up again as a video Bart watches on a tablet, suggesting his fame persists as a piece of pop culture media within the show's universe. He doesn't have an ongoing storyline or personality development beyond these brief gags, functioning mainly as a nostalgic nod to classic animation for viewers. His inclusion highlights The Simpsons' frequent use of crossover cameos referencing other famous cartoons. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Estonian dwarf
text: Estonian dwarf is A recurring minor background character; a dwarf actor and stuntman from Estonia who appears in various guises throughout the show. The Estonian dwarf is a small-statured actor and stuntman who takes on a variety of odd jobs around Springfield. He hails from Estonia and seems willing to take almost any role, from impersonating a child to standing in for a costumed mascot. His most memorable job involved being disguised as Lisa Simpson as part of one of Mr. Burns' elaborate schemes, during which he shared bits of Estonian culture. He also suffered physical comedy at the hands of Homer, who mistook his costumed performance for a real threat. As a stuntman, he's been used as a body double for child actors in dangerous scenes, highlighting the show's running gag of exploitative and absurd behind-the-scenes showbiz practices. He is a smoker and adult, though little else is known about his personal life. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta (normal voice), Yeardley Smith (Lisa voice).

title: Fernando
text: Fernando is A recurring minor character who works as a commercial airline pilot, often flying routes to Brazil. Fernando is a commercial pilot best known for flying routes between Springfield and Rio de Janeiro. He has a signature catchphrase about the weather in Rio that he repeats every time the plane approaches the city, much to the annoyance of his co-pilot and romantic partner, who nonetheless credits that very joke as the reason he fell for him. His piloting skills are questionable at best, as he's shown crashing a plane directly into the Simpson family's house on one occasion. He later reappears flying for Air Brasilia, where he takes offense at Marge's attempts to learn Portuguese during a flight. Despite his limited screen time, he's a recognizable recurring background character tied to the show's occasional international travel plots. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: The local temperature in Rio de Janiero is hot, hot, hot with a 100% chance of passion
quotes: The local temperature in Rio de Janiero is hot, hot, hot with a 100% chance of passion

title: Frankie (Mommie Beerest)
text: Frankie (Mommie Beerest) is Health Department inspector and childhood friend of Moe Szyslak. Frankie was a lifelong friend of Moe Szyslak, their bond forged in a rough childhood where their fathers encouraged them to fight each other for entertainment. As an adult, he became a health inspector who routinely visited Moe's Tavern, though his inspections were a sham since he turned a blind eye to violations to keep the bar open. His real motivation was avoiding his unhappy marriage rather than any professional diligence. His negligence and fondness for the bar ultimately proved fatal, as he died on the job after eating one of Moe's infamous pickled eggs. His death led to a much stricter replacement inspector taking over, exposing just how lax Frankie had been. He later made a brief supernatural appearance as a ghost in one of Bart's dreams. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Ned Flandish
text: Ned Flandish is Puritan captain of the Mayflower, a Ned Flanders-inspired character appearing in a story told by Lisa. Ned Flandish is a stern, rule-bound Puritan sea captain who commands the Mayflower in a tale spun by Lisa, serving as an obvious historical stand-in for Ned Flanders. He is rigidly opposed to anything he sees as sinful, banning alcohol, colorful clothing, dreaming, and even poetry aboard his ship. His piety is played for comedic irony when he accidentally composes a poem and punishes himself with self-flagellation and salt. Despite his severity, he shows a reflective, guilt-ridden side once the Mayflower reaches the New World, expressing genuine regret over the suffering Europeans would later inflict on Native Americans. His arc blends slapstick religious satire with a surprisingly somber acknowledgment of historical injustice. The character also appears as a Thanksgiving-themed skin in The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Gertie Feesh
text: Gertie Feesh is Organ player at the First Church of Springfield and at Springfield War Memorial Stadium. Gertie Feesh is a minor recurring background character best known as the church organist who accompanies Reverend Lovejoy's services. She's also sometimes credited under other names like Helen or Martha. Her gags tend to involve the organ itself, whether that's collapsing from exhaustion after an overly long hymn or reacting badly to being replaced by modern technology. She's largely a silent, functional presence in Springfield's religious and civic life, popping up for decades of episodes without ever taking center stage. Despite her minimal characterization, she's persisted as a fixture of Springfield's background cast since the early seasons. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Devin (You Won't Believe What This Episode Is About – Act Three Will Shock You!)
keys: devin (you won't believe what this episode is about – act three will shock you!)
text: Devin (You Won't Believe What This Episode Is About – Act Three Will Shock You!) is Lenny Leonard's pet dog, a minor recurring animal character. Devin is the black and white dog belonging to Lenny, acquired after Lenny gave up on finding human companionship. He's a mostly background character who appears at the Springfield Dog Park, where an attempt to socialize with Santa's Little Helper goes poorly. Devin is timid, retreating to Lenny after being snarled at rather than standing his ground. Despite the rocky first meeting, Devin later appears alongside Lenny in a more amusing bonding moment, both wearing sunglasses in a show of dog-owner solidarity. He has no lines, functioning purely as a visual gag and extension of Lenny's characterization as someone who has substituted pet ownership for human relationships.

title: Wilma Flintstone
text: Wilma Flintstone is Crossover character from The Flintstones, referenced in The Simpsons as a pop-culture allusion. Wilma Flintstone is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed figure from the classic animated series The Flintstones, used sparingly as a running gag and pop-culture reference within the show. She never actually appears as a live character interacting with the Simpsons cast, but instead shows up through mentions, costumes, and background props. Notably, Mr. Burns mistakenly calls Marge and Maggie by the names Wilma and Pebbles after Mr. Smithers plays a prank on him. Her image also turns up on a novelty phone, as a museum model of a Flintstone-themed car, and as a costume worn by other characters at a masquerade ball. In non-canon material, she appears again through costume references and even as a background figure in a Treehouse of Horror segment. Overall, she functions purely as a nostalgic nod rather than a fleshed-out character within the Simpsons universe.

title: Ethereal Beings
text: Ethereal Beings is Non-canon alien species that Springfield residents encounter through a black hole in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Ethereal Beings are a species of white and light blue aliens hailing from an unnamed rocky planet. They first appear when Springfield residents discover them on the other side of a black hole that had been used as a garbage dump, comically mistaking the townspeople's trash for gifts. This first contact establishes them as a naive, easily pleased race rather than a hostile threat. They later show up in other non-canon contexts, including a futuristic presidential debate audience and as captives in an extraterrestrial zoo on Rigel 7. Their appearances are scattered across Halloween specials, mobile game content, and other bonus material, marking them as a minor recurring novelty species rather than a core part of the show's continuity. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Tress MacNeille.

title: Carnage Destructicus
text: Carnage Destructicus is A transforming robot antagonist from a non-canon Treehouse of Horror parody segment. Carnage Destructicus is a giant transforming robot who appears in a Treehouse of Horror parody of robot-battle blockbuster films. He is depicted as a heavily armed war machine, outfitted with missiles and machine guns, built for large-scale destruction rather than personality-driven storytelling. In the story, he squares off against rival robots, including a sedan-based bot and a robot called Bestimus Muchos, in a spoof of Transformers-style combat. Being a non-canon character, he exists purely within this parody episode and later resurfaces as a collectible figure in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. He has no deep characterization beyond his role as a combat robot, functioning mainly as a visual and action-oriented gag rather than a fleshed-out personality. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Mr. Dirt
text: Mr. Dirt is Villain from a video-game-within-the-show, main antagonist of the fictional 'Big Super Happy Fun Fun Game'. Mr. Dirt is a non-canon villain who exists only within the fictional video game featured in The Simpsons Game. He mocks and challenges Homer and Lisa, boasting that they cannot possibly overcome the three Sparklemon creatures he has unleashed. His confidence proves misplaced, since once the Sparklemon are captured and used to release Mr. Sparkle, his power collapses entirely. In a twist revealing his true nature, he transforms back into Milhouse after losing his powers, only to be set upon by the very Sparklemon he created. He later reappears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. His design and concept are clearly inspired by The King of All Cosmos from Katamari Damacy. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Dr. Evil
text: Dr. Evil is A costume worn by Comic Book Guy, based on the villain from the Austin Powers film series. Dr. Evil isn't actually a character native to The Simpsons universe, but rather a reference to the parody villain from the Austin Powers movies. He appears only because Comic Book Guy dresses up as him for a costume event called Bond Parody Con. Alongside this costume, Comic Book Guy also dons a companion outfit resembling Mini-Me. Since this is purely a costume appearance rather than an actual character in the show's continuity, Dr. Evil has no dialogue, personality traits, or voice actor within the Simpsons canon. His inclusion is essentially an homage to the source film franchise, used as a one-off visual gag tied to Comic Book Guy's love of pop culture costuming. He is categorized as a non-speaking, recurring crossover character within the Simpsons comic universe.

title: Nedward Flanders, Sr.
text: Nedward Flanders, Sr. is Ned Flanders' beatnik father and grandfather of Rod and Todd Flanders. Nedward Flanders, Sr., also called Nedsel "Daddio" Flanders, is depicted as an old-school beatnik poet, contrasting sharply with his square, uptight son Ned. He and his wife Capri struggled to control young Ned's difficult behavior, eventually seeking help from Dr. Foster. There are hints he may have had a military background, possibly referenced as "Commander Flanders" during World War II. He and Capri appear only occasionally in Ned's adult life, notably attending Ned and Edna Krabappel's wedding as the sole guests besides the grandsons. In a later visit to Ned's house, the elder Flanders couple seemed to enjoy Homer's company more than their own son's, adding an awkward comedic touch to their family dynamic. His hip, jazzy speech pattern and disapproval of squareness serve as a running personality trait whenever he appears. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Oh, man! Ned spilled ink all over my poems! He's a real flat tire. I mean a cube, man. He's putting us on the train to Squaresville, Mona. | Homer, you met my parents,

title: The Detonator
text: The Detonator is A professional gamer hired to tutor Bart Simpson's e-sports team; minor recurring character. The Detonator, whose real name is Jason, is a hoodie-and-beard-sporting video game expert known for his walkthrough videos and commentary. He was brought in by Homer to coach Bart's team in the game Conflict of Enemies, narrating even mundane moments like bathroom breaks. His confidence crumbled after a poorly timed pee break got his character killed, causing him to dramatically quit gaming, burn his signature hoodie and beard, and take a job at his uncle's tile store. Despite this retirement, he later resurfaced as a recognized internet personality at a social media gathering, and was still making walkthrough videos afterward. He comes across as a self-serious, slightly dramatic figure who treats gaming commentary as a professional calling. Voiced by Chris Edgerly.

title: Dexter Colt
text: Dexter Colt is A private detective hired by Homer to investigate Lisa, later revealed as a corrupt and dangerous con man. Dexter Colt is a sleazy private investigator styled after classic noir detectives like Philip Marlowe. He's hired by Homer to dig up dirt on Lisa's interests, using unscrupulous methods like locker raids, blackmail, and bribery to get results. His greed becomes apparent when he padds his expense report to an outrageous degree, sparking a falling out with Homer. Beyond his shady business practices, Colt turns out to be a genuinely dangerous criminal, willing to frame Lisa for a crime and even resort to violence, including shooting Homer and threatening him with a human cannonball. He is eventually outwitted and defeated by Lisa using a simple laser pointer, leading to his arrest. He later resurfaces working for Mr. Burns, showing his detective services are available to the show's other unscrupulous characters as well. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Dixie Chicks (characters)
text: Dixie Chicks (characters) is Real-life American country/folk band appearing as recurring celebrity guest characters in Springfield. The Dixie Chicks appear as themselves in several episodes, popping up as celebrity guests and cameo figures within Springfield's world. They've performed at Krusty's holiday special and were spotted among famous detainees at the Ronald Reagan Reeducation Center. In one storyline, shady manager Royce Lumpkin steals a song from his own daughter Lurleen, turns it into a patriotic anthem called "America's Back," and has the band perform it, unaware of its true origin. When they later learn the truth about the theft during a recording session at White Trash Records, the trio doesn't hesitate to retaliate, smashing their instruments over Royce in fury. This portrayal plays up their real-world reputation for outspokenness and no-nonsense attitude. Their appearances are brief but tie them into the recurring Lumpkin family drama subplot.

title: Remorseful Duff
text: Remorseful Duff is One of the Seven Duffs, mascot costume characters for Duff Beer. Remorseful Duff is one of the seven costumed mascots representing Duff Beer, appearing at promotional locations like Duff Gardens. He is part of a group clearly parodying the Seven Dwarfs from Disney's Snow White, each embodying a different mood or personality trait as his name suggests. Remorseful was among the first four of the Duffs to actually be named on-screen, alongside Tipsy, Surly, and Queasy, giving him slightly more recognition than some of the other Duffs. Beyond his brief debut, he mostly exists as background mascot material, showing up on posters, statues, and merchandise rather than having any real personality-driven storyline. His appearances are largely non-speaking and promotional in nature, fitting his role as a corporate mascot rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: El Margo
text: El Margo is A graffiti alias used by Marge Simpson before Bart's "El Barto". El Margo isn't a separate character but a secret piece of Marge Simpson's past, revealing a rebellious streak she rarely shows as an adult housewife. As a student at Springfield Middle School, she tagged her nickname onto a teacher's shirt, only to second-guess herself over the grammar of the phrase. This nitpicky correction, changing the tag to "La Marga," is a small but telling gag about Marge's perfectionism even in acts of youthful rebellion. The alias predates and possibly inspired Bart's own graffiti tag, "El Barto," tying mother and son together through a shared mischievous history. In a non-canon comic story, the concept resurfaces when a de-aging incident turns Marge into a child again, prompting her to spray a variant tag, "El Margeo," on the family fence.

title: City worker
text: City worker is Recurring minor Springfield background character who appears in various city/town-related jobs. The City worker is a minor recurring figure in Springfield who seems to pop up in nearly every branch of municipal employment. He's been seen operating records at the Hall of Records, performing in a civic play, administering a realtor's licensing exam, and running a pet shop for helper animals. His jobs tend to bring him into odd, brief interactions with Homer Simpson, whether guiding him toward an emotional family revelation or dealing with his mishandling of a helper monkey. Despite the variety of roles, he maintains a calm, procedural demeanor typical of a city bureaucrat. He even had a personal life outside of work, having once been involved with Mrs. Muntz. His many jobs make him something of a running gag about the interchangeable nature of Springfield's civic employees. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Tom Clancy (character)
text: Tom Clancy (character) is Real-world author who appears as a guest character in The Simpsons. Tom Clancy appears as a fictionalized version of himself in the show, popping up at literary events and in phone calls involving Springfield residents. He's shown as a good-natured but sometimes awkward celebrity guest, getting interrupted mid-answer at a book panel and being talked into an endorsement he initially resists. His famous techno-thriller novels, especially the fictional 'Op-Center' series, become running gags referenced by multiple characters, from Homer to Santa Claus. Interestingly, his books are also used as a punchline in prison settings, where inmates supposedly use them as blunt weapons. Despite his fame, characters like Sideshow Bob have expressed distaste for his work, adding a bit of irony to his literary reputation within the show. Voiced by Hank Azaria (also voiced by himself). Notable quotes: If you're hunting for a good read this October, Marge Simpson's book is a clear and present danger to your free time
quotes: If you're hunting for a good read this October, Marge Simpson's book is a clear and present danger to your free time

title: Disgruntled Goat
text: Disgruntled Goat is Minor cartoon character within the show-within-a-show Itchy & Scratchy universe. Disgruntled Goat is a background character created for the fictional Itchy & Scratchy Show franchise within The Simpsons universe. He never speaks and mainly exists as merchandise, appearing as a doll sold at the Itchy & Scratchy Land gift shop alongside other minor characters like Uncle Ant and Klu Klux Clam. His origins are tied to the show's dark satire of cartoon copyright theft, as he is revealed to be one of the many characters Roger Meyers, Sr. allegedly stole from the down-on-his-luck cartoonist Chester J. Lampwick. Despite his minimal presence, he has shown up in various forms across the franchise, including a parade float, toy figurines, and even mobile game merchandise in The Simpsons: Tapped Out. He represents the show's recurring gag of expanding the Itchy & Scratchy universe with obscure, forgettable spin-off characters.

title: Funeral home salesman
text: Funeral home salesman is A minor recurring salesman who works at the funeral home (and later Casket City) interacting with the Simpson family. This slick, opportunistic salesman specializes in upselling grieving or unsuspecting customers on funeral and burial services. When the Simpson family visits with a free autopsy coupon, he eagerly pitches extras like a coffin, tombstone, and anti-stink spray. He has a knack for dressing up death with luxury, offering deluxe cemetery plots, unused virgin graves, self-cleaning monuments, and even a weeping widow service for those who want to travel to the afterlife in style. His pitch is laced with faux-spiritual justification, claiming that God favors those who spend big on their final send-off. He later resurfaces at Casket City, continuing his morbid sales career by luring Grampa Simpson into a casket shop, much to Grampa's horror. Overall, he represents a recurring gag of dark comedic commercialism surrounding death in the show. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: He says that God prefers people who travel in style.
quotes: He says that God prefers people who travel in style.

title: Joe Frazier (character)
text: Joe Frazier (character) is Real-world boxer appearing as himself in cameo roles in The Simpsons. Joe Frazier is a guest-starring cameo character based on the real-life professional boxer of the same name. In his first appearance, he presents Homer Simpson with the inaugural Montgomery Burns Award for Outstanding Achievement in the Field of Excellence. He later turns up in a television advertisement for the Smoke Damage Outlet Store, where customers are invited to meet him at the entrance. His presence in that ad is a nod to his famous nickname, 'Smokin' Joe,' which he wryly acknowledges is the only reason he agreed to appear. As with many real-world guest appearances on the show, his role is brief and used mainly for a topical joke rather than deep characterization. He has no known relatives or ongoing storyline within the Simpsons universe. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: "I'm only here because I'm nicknamed 'Smokin' Joe'."
quotes: "I'm only here because I'm nicknamed 'Smokin' Joe'."

title: Devil
text: Devil is The ruler of Hell in the show's non-canon/fantasy segments, appearing mainly in Halloween specials. The Devil, also called Satan, presides over Hell in various non-canon Simpsons stories and specials. He tends to show up whenever a character dies or dreams their way into the underworld, often reacting with amusement rather than menace. He's shown giving Homer noogies in Hell and casually threatening to wake up John Wayne if Homer gets too loud. In another skit he bosses God around, demanding coffee, revealing an oddly casual dynamic between the two. He even auditioned to play Mr. Burns in an in-universe film, showing a comedic, almost showbiz side to his character. Overall he's portrayed less as a terrifying figure and more as a recurring gag rooted in dark, absurdist humor. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Idris Elba. Notable quotes: The Devil told him to be quiet or he'd wake up John Wayne.
quotes: The Devil told him to be quiet or he'd wake up John Wayne.

title: Pope Francis
text: Pope Francis is Real-world head of the Catholic Church who appears as a minor recurring character in the show. Pope Francis appears in the series as a real-world celebrity cameo rather than a fully developed fictional character. He is depicted through references like his real Twitter account, which Bart shows to Lisa, and through a brief physical appearance attempting to enter Springfield before being comically thwarted by a collapsing bridge. He's later seen hitchhiking, and his image even shows up as part of a religious-themed captcha test online. As a non-speaking character in the show, his role is mostly symbolic or background, tied to real-world events and internet culture rather than storylines within Springfield. His inclusion reflects the show's habit of referencing current real-world figures for topical humor. Notable quotes: Honor thy father + check out this epic votive candle fail!
quotes: Honor thy father + check out this epic votive candle fail!

title: Annie Crawford
text: Annie Crawford is FBI Special Agent who investigates Homer in the episode "Homerland". Annie Crawford is an FBI Special Agent brought in by Lisa to investigate Homer's strange behavior. She struggles with bipolar disorder, relying on medication that frequently causes vivid hallucinations, sometimes blurring the line between her fantasies and reality. Despite her unstable mental state, she proves to be a surprisingly capable field agent, able to infiltrate places covertly and physically overpower Homer when needed. Her interrogation tactics are unconventional, ranging from torture to seduction, whatever gets results. There's a hint of attraction between her and Homer after he compliments her looks. She is a clear parody of Carrie Mathison from the show Homeland, mirroring that character's mix of professional skill and personal instability. Voiced by Kristen Wiig.

title: Shepard Fairey (character)
text: Shepard Fairey (character) is Real-world artist appearing as himself; an undercover cop who interacts with Bart Simpson. Shepard Fairey appears as a fictionalized version of himself, blending his real-world identity as a famous street artist with a surprising twist as an undercover police officer. He initially praises Bart's street art alongside other real-world artists, encouraging him to pursue a gallery show. His friendly demeanor masks his true purpose, as he later reveals his police role to arrest Bart for graffiti. The character plays on Fairey's real history with iconic works like the Obama "Hope" poster and his OBEY branding, using them ironically given his in-show role as a law enforcer. This twist highlights the show's tendency to blend celebrity cameos with satirical commentary on authority and rebellion. He is a one-episode guest character with a memorable, ironic punchline about his own artwork. Voiced by Shepard Fairey (Himself). Notable quotes: Hey, don't be so surprised. I spent twenty years putting up posters that said "obey".
quotes: Hey, don't be so surprised. I spent twenty years putting up posters that said "obey".

title: Flip Flop
text: Flip Flop is A minor recurring clown character at Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus. Flip Flop is a background clown who performs with the Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus, distinguished mainly by the flip flops he wears. He was one of several clowns introduced to Krusty by Scuzzo, and he could be seen assisting around the circus and taking part in its shows before eventually departing Springfield by train with the rest of the troupe. Despite his minor role, he has left a small mark on Springfield culture, appearing as part of a trivia team at Moe's Tavern and even inspiring a doll owned by Maggie Simpson. He is a non-speaking character, existing mostly as a visual gag and recurring background presence rather than a fully developed personality.

title: The Chipmunks
text: The Chipmunks is A fictional animated virtual band referenced within the Simpsons universe, parodying the real-life Alvin and the Chipmunks franchise. The Chipmunks exist as a pop-culture fixture within the Simpsons world rather than a fully realized set of characters. They're mentioned in passing by Homer, who owns their greatest hits album and references them in conversation, showing how deeply embedded they are in Springfield's media landscape. Their fictional film franchise, produced by Ginormous Pictures, gets a nod when its third installment is advertised on a poster. In non-canon material, the joke escalates absurdly, with Krusty releasing a cover album of their songs and Homer owning a bizarre bootleg recording blending them with the Beatles and the Monkees. The group never appears as actual characters on screen, functioning purely as a background reference and running gag about pop music parody. Their presence highlights the show's habit of building out a deep, silly extended universe of fictional media brands.

title: Patrick Ewing
text: Patrick Ewing is Real-world basketball player who appears as himself in guest cameo roles in the show. Patrick Ewing appears in The Simpsons as a fictionalized version of the real-life NBA star. His first appearance has him serving as a genie at Krusty's nondenominational holiday funfest, a bizarre and comedic role for a professional athlete. He later shows up as himself during a book signing for his book Tall Tales, where a devoted fan named Mike Wegman has him sign his own daughter, who was named Patrick Ewing Wegman in his honor. Ewing doesn't speak in his appearances, functioning purely as a cameo character tied to real-world basketball fame. His inclusion plays on the show's frequent use of celebrity cameos for comedic effect, especially through absurd juxtapositions like a famous athlete moonlighting as a genie.

title: Gene "No Helmet" Dupree
text: Gene "No Helmet" Dupree is A demolition derby driver who briefly interacts with Homer. No Helmet Dupree is a gruff, bald, mustachioed demolition derby driver whose nickname suggests a reckless disregard for safety. He first appears when Homer accidentally backs his car into a lamppost that Dupree claims is the mayor's favorite, using the mishap as leverage to buy Homer's damaged car for $500. Homer's odd response of spitting a pickled egg at him hints at the show's typical absurd humor surrounding their encounter. Later, Dupree resurfaces at the Springfield Demolition Derby, now driving the very car he bought from Homer, facing off against an opponent named Car-ack Obama. The outcome of that derby battle is left unresolved. His character is minor but memorable for his colorful nickname and his role in the demolition derby subplot. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Micky Dolenz
text: Micky Dolenz is Real-world musician (former member of The Monkees) referenced in The Simpsons. Micky Dolenz appears in the show as a real-world figure tied to his fame as a member of The Monkees rather than as an active character. He's depicted only through a lunchbox and a flashback, showing how deeply the band's pop culture footprint had reached even into Marge's childhood. The reference plays on the era's skepticism toward manufactured pop bands, with a schoolgirl mocking Marge for liking a group accused of not writing their own songs or playing their own instruments. He later shows up in a more literal cameo tied to the Monkeemobile at a car museum. As a non-speaking, picture-only character, his role is purely nostalgic and visual rather than narrative-driven.

title: Esme Delacroix
text: Esme Delacroix is A romance novelist who inspires Marge Simpson to write her own book. Esme Delacroix is a successful and prolific author of romance novels, best known for her long-running 'Scoundrel' series. She studied at Yale University before becoming a celebrated publisher and writer. Marge Simpson encounters her at Bookaccino's reading aloud from her book, and is inspired to try writing herself. Esme comes across as a bit detached and self-absorbed, relying heavily on an assistant to even summarize the books sent to her rather than reading them personally. Despite this, she proves supportive of Marge's efforts, offering feedback and helping her secure endorsements from other famous authors for her manuscript. Her career and mannerisms poke fun at the formulaic, mass-produced nature of romance novel publishing. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Esme told Marge that it was the best book her assistant had ever summarized to her.
quotes: Esme told Marge that it was the best book her assistant had ever summarized to her.

title: The Flying Giuseppe
text: The Flying Giuseppe is A human cannonball performer at a traveling circus, briefly used as a weapon against Homer. The Flying Giuseppe is a circus performer whose act involves being fired out of a cannon. He becomes entangled in the Simpsons' story when the villainous Dexter Colt, who had sold off animals freed from a medical research facility, uses him as a literal projectile weapon against Homer and Lisa. Despite the absurd danger of his profession, Giuseppe seems almost cheerfully oblivious to the pain involved, initially believing being launched into Homer somehow helped his aching back. His brief appearance doubles as a callback gag, reaffirming Homer's oddly durable body from his stint as a human cannonball substitute in a prior episode. He's a one-off character whose humor stems from the ridiculousness of his job and his nonchalant reaction to physical punishment. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Ooh! I think that fixed my back! [stretches, hears a loud crack] Oh, no, no. It's much worse.
quotes: Ooh! I think that fixed my back! [stretches, hears a loud crack] Oh, no, no. It's much worse.

title: Dumlee
text: Dumlee is A pawnbroker at Frank Needy & Sons who appears in a minor role dealing with Homer. Dumlee runs a pawn shop where Homer tries to sell off a wheelbarrow of trophies. He's businesslike and a bit mercenary, willing to charge Homer just to dispose of junk. His shop happens to have Homer's father's old pocket watch for sale, having been pawned by Milhouse after a falling out with Bart. Dumlee's negotiating style oddly backfires when Homer haggles the price upward rather than down, showing him to be somewhat passive in trade dealings. As a character, he's essentially a one-scene figure created to parody a well-known reality TV pawnbroker. His presence highlights the show's habit of spoofing real-world pop culture figures through minor guest-starring roles. Voiced by Brian Posehn.

title: DMV manageress
text: DMV manageress is Manageress of the Springfield Department of Motor Vehicles. The DMV manageress is a minor recurring official who oversees operations at Springfield's DMV. She has authority over promotions and discipline, as shown when she both rewarded and nearly punished Patty and Selma Bouvier for smoking in a government building. She has a sharp tongue, notably comparing Homer Simpson unfavorably to Hitler after he took the blame for the twins' misconduct. Beyond her workplace duties, she occasionally appears in the wider Springfield community, such as attending Patty's wedding and showing up to support a local political campaign. Despite her limited screen time, she serves as a recurring bureaucratic figure tied closely to the Bouvier sisters' storylines. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: "worse than Hitler"
quotes: "worse than Hitler"

title: Desmond
text: Desmond is A former employee at Well + Good, a marijuana dispensary in Springfield. Desmond is a knowledgeable employee at the cannabis shop Well + Good, valued for his expertise in cannabinoids and modern delivery methods. He's the one who welcomes Marge to the business after she unknowingly applies for a job there, working alongside Lauren and Drederick Tatum to bring her on board. Desmond is easygoing and enthusiastic about the product, though not always the most effective salesman, as shown when he fails to convince a bewildered Otto to buy anything. He enjoys indulging in the merchandise himself, getting high and dancing with Lauren during an event at The Drederick. When the venue burns down and marijuana is re-criminalized in the state, Desmond's job at Well + Good comes to an end. He later turns up as an audience member at one of Tabitha Shingle's podcast recordings. Voiced by Billy Porter.

title: Queasy Duff
text: Queasy Duff is One of the Seven Duffs, costumed mascots representing Duff Beer. Queasy Duff is one of the seven costumed mascots created to promote Duff Beer, appearing in parks like Duff Gardens as part of a group parody of the Seven Dwarfs. He was one of only four of the Duffs actually named when they first appeared in the show, alongside Tipsy, Surly, and Remorseful. Beyond his role as a walking advertisement, little else is known about his personality, since he mainly exists as a background gag rather than a fleshed-out character. He has popped up outside the main show in non-canon media, including a poster in Moe's Tavern in a Simpsons video game and as a topiary decoration in a mobile game. His name follows the group's theme of humorous, dwarf-like nicknames tied to physical or emotional states.

title: Geena Davis
text: Geena Davis is Real-life actress who appears as herself in cameo/reference roles within the Simpsons universe. Geena Davis appears in the show as a fictionalized version of the real-world actress, known for her work in film, writing, producing, and modeling. Within the Simpsons universe, she's portrayed as an exceptionally accomplished figure, being both an Olympic-level archer and a member of the high-IQ society Mensa. She's referenced as a celebrity whose film work Marge enjoys watching, and she's held up as an example of excellence when Lisa is welcomed into Mensa alongside other notable geniuses. The character also appears in fictional in-show media, including a short-lived sitcom and an internet project bearing her name. Her role is largely as a background celebrity reference rather than a fully developed character with her own storyline. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Princess Diana
text: Princess Diana is Real-world British royal referenced and briefly appearing in The Simpsons. Princess Diana appears in the show mostly as a cultural touchstone and running joke rather than a fleshed-out character. Characters frequently reference her in passing, from tabloid-style questions about her personal life to nostalgic or morbid jokes about her death. Her image and legacy are used as shorthand for fame, tragedy, and royal glamour, appearing in everything from Halloween costumes to internet captcha tests. She actually appears on-screen only once, as a hologram performer at the Simpson family's house. The character reflects the show's habit of using real-world celebrities and historical figures as background cultural references. Her death is treated with the show's typical mix of dark humor and pop-culture commentary. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Daria
text: Daria is A minor recurring character who was briefly Barney Gumble's girlfriend. Daria is a minor background character best known for her short-lived romance with Barney Gumble. The two became a couple after Barney won a bet on a dog race at Springfield Downs, giving him enough money to impress her. She appears sporadically throughout the first season in various Springfield settings, including the Department of Motor Vehicles and a party at the Simpsons' house. She even tried out for a local theater production directed by Llewellyn Sinclair. Daria has no spoken lines in the show, making her a purely visual presence rather than a vocal one. Her appearances are brief and she fades from the show without further explanation after her early season one cameos.

title: Ms. Dubinsky
text: Ms. Dubinsky is A teacher at Springfield Elementary School who runs the school debate team. Ms. Dubinsky is a minor faculty member at Springfield Elementary School best known for overseeing the debate team. She appears briefly to recruit Lisa Simpson, pitching the activity as a practical alternative to other extracurriculars since it requires no equipment or funding, a subtle nod to budget cuts affecting the school. She's a brunette, and the show notes this hair color happens to be common among the debate team members, a small running joke about the group's makeup. Beyond her recruitment pitch, little else is shown of her personality or history, as she mostly serves as a background figure tied to one specific storyline. Her presence is largely functional, existing to nudge Lisa toward a new after-school pursuit rather than to develop as a character in her own right. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Little Dot
text: Little Dot is A comic book character referenced within the Simpsons universe, not an actual member of the main cast. Little Dot is a fictional comic character that exists within the world of the Simpsons rather than being a true character in the show itself. She's depicted as a comic book heroine associated with a dot motif, published under the fictional Harry Comics banner. Bart considers ripping off her concept when trying to invent his own superhero, showing the show's tendency to poke fun at comic book culture and originality (or lack thereof). Marge dryly remarks on the character's love of dots, adding a bit of comedic commentary on the simplicity of some comic characters. She appears on the cover of the in-universe comic 'Death of Casper' and shows up in a few other background or costume appearances throughout the series' run. Notable quotes: that little girl sure loved dots
quotes: that little girl sure loved dots

title: Niles Crane
text: Niles Crane is A crossover character from the TV series Frasier who appears in Simpsons comic material. Niles Crane is a fussy, intellectual psychiatrist best known from the sitcom Frasier, brought into the Simpsons universe through a comic crossover. He is the brother of Frasier Crane and the ex-husband of the notoriously wealthy and elusive Maris Crane. In his one noted appearance, Bart and Homer watch a Frasier episode in which Niles admits to his brother that he lets their father intimidate him because their father owns a handgun, giving a glimpse of his anxious, self-aware personality. The character's inclusion is largely a meta joke: he is voiced by David Hyde Pierce, who also lends his voice to Cecil Terwilliger, the brother of Sideshow Bob in the actual Simpsons show. This creates a layered in-joke, since Sideshow Bob is voiced by Kelsey Grammer, the actor who plays Niles' brother Frasier on Frasier. Niles himself remains a minor, largely trivia-based figure within the Simpsons franchise rather than a fully developed character.

title: Flash Gibbon
text: Flash Gibbon is A gibbon superhero and member of The Secret Society of Super-Simians, appearing in Radioactive Man comic stories. Flash Gibbon is a comic-book superhero and primate member of the Secret Society of Super-Simians, a group of super-powered apes who appear in the Radioactive Man comics within the Simpsons universe. He wears a space suit and helmet as part of his superhero attire. During a society meeting, he shows a somewhat dismissive attitude toward Radioactive Man, telling him to sit and have a drink, and later expresses annoyance at having to hear his origin story repeated. He is also seen alongside Radioactive Ape when Fallout Boy calls looking for Radioactive Man. His name is a playful nod to the classic science-fiction hero Flash Gordon. He remains a minor, background figure within the larger super-simian superhero parody universe.

title: The Flash
text: The Flash is DC Comics superhero referenced within the Simpsons universe, often used as a costume inspiration for Comic Book Guy. The Flash is not an original Simpsons character but a real-world DC Comics superhero famous for his super speed, who exists as a pop-culture reference within the show. He's mostly brought up in conversations about comics and speed, such as debates over whether the Springfield Monorail or Superman could outrun him. His most direct appearance comes when Comic Book Guy dresses up as him to compete in the Springfield Marathon, embodying his obsessive fandom for superhero lore. The character also shows up on comic book covers and in Comic Book Guy's various costume changes at conventions, reinforcing his status as a running gag tied to comic culture rather than an active participant in Simpsons stories. Even a parody version, Hot Flash, exists within the show's fictional superhero universe. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: No one can outrun The Flash! | Eh, sure, why not?
quotes: No one can outrun The Flash!
Eh, sure, why not?

title: Erin (Summer of 4 Ft. 2)
text: Erin (Summer of 4 Ft. 2) is A summer vacationer who befriends Lisa Simpson at the beach town of Little Pwagmattasquarmsettport. Erin is a laid-back teenage girl Lisa meets while on vacation, quickly bonding with her over a shared appreciation for doing nothing in particular. She's easygoing and a bit too cool for typical kid antics, dismissing Bart's skateboard tricks and comparing him to a classic troublemaker character. Despite her aloof exterior, she shows genuine warmth toward Lisa, exchanging handmade friendship tokens and defending her once Bart tries to expose Lisa's nerdy side. Erin values authenticity over image, ultimately proving that her friendship with Lisa wasn't shallow. She's later humorously categorized as the embodiment of teenage indifference in an in-universe guide to elementary school archetypes. Voiced by Christina Ricci. Notable quotes: It doesn't matter who she was, she couldn't fake the kind of good person she is.
quotes: It doesn't matter who she was, she couldn't fake the kind of good person she is.

title: Doug (camera man)
text: Doug (camera man) is A recurring background cameraman who films various events and TV shows in Springfield. Doug is a minor recurring character who works as a cameraman for local Springfield productions. He's best known for his deadpan attitude, especially when tasked with the impossible job of pixelating out inappropriate content. He has a history of letting Bart hang around his room, which led to Bart smoking a joint under his supervision. Doug's work has taken him behind the scenes of shows like Mother Flippers and Sneakers, as well as covering local news events like Springfield's dog-friendly law announcement. He's a low-key, blue-collar type character who pops up whenever the show needs a camera crew. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: There aren't enough pixels in the world
quotes: There aren't enough pixels in the world

title: Evil shopkeeper
text: Evil shopkeeper is Minor recurring character; owner of the House of Evil shop that sells cursed objects. The evil shopkeeper runs the House of Evil, a shady store specializing in objects that carry sinister curses. He first appeared warning Homer about the dangers of the items he purchased for Bart's birthday, delivering ominous warnings with a flair for dramatic understatement. Despite his eerie demeanor, he maintains a strange sense of customer service, even offering complimentary frogurt to paying customers. He later makes a brief appearance attending Cregg Demon's magic show, suggesting some connection to the world of magic and the supernatural. His character is designed as a spoof of Mr. Wing from the film Gremlins, reflecting the show's love of horror movie parody. Though rarely seen, he remains a memorable figure from the Treehouse of Horror universe. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Take this object, but beware, it carries a terrible curse!
quotes: Take this object, but beware, it carries a terrible curse!

title: Dr. Crab's robot
text: Dr. Crab's robot is Giant robot villain created by Dr. Crab, appearing in Radioactive Man comic stories. This towering robot is the creation of the mad scientist Dr. Crab, built with the specific purpose of destroying the superhero Radioactive Man. It first appears rampaging through Zenith City, drawing the attention of reporter Gloria Grand, who ends up gaining superpowers after deflecting the robot's isotropic ray back onto herself. The robot manages to overpower Radioactive Man himself, grabbing him and nearly finishing him off before the newly empowered Gloria Grand intervenes and takes it down.
