It exists purely as a mechanical menace with no personality beyond its programmed hostility, serving as a plot device to kickstart Gloria Grand's transformation into a radioactive heroine. The robot's rampage also becomes a photo opportunity for photographer Sheldon Phillips, though he loses his camera in the chaos. It has since become a recurring element referenced across multiple Radioactive Man comic issues.

title: Freddy Freeman
text: Freddy Freeman is Bassist for the band Sungazer, a minor recurring character. Freddy Freeman is a gray-haired bassist who plays in the rock band Sungazer. He was part of the group's decision to recruit Apu as their new lead singer after the death of their previous frontman, Grant LeDavid. When Apu later tried to leave the band, Freddy sternly reminded him of the binding contract he'd signed for a lengthy world tour. He's a minor figure mostly defined by his role within the band's business dealings rather than a strong individual personality. He later appeared briefly in the audience at one of Tabitha Shingle's live podcast recordings, showing he circulates in the same entertainment circles as other minor Springfield celebrities. Overall, Freddy serves as a background figure who helps tie together storylines involving Apu's music career. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Fred (Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire)
keys: fred (simpsons roasting on an open fire)
text: Fred (Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire) is A minor acquaintance of Homer Simpson who appears in the background of a few early episodes. Fred is a minor, non-speaking character who exists on the periphery of Homer Simpson's social circle. Little is known about his personality or background since he never utters a line of dialogue in any of his appearances. He is most notable for attending the Springfield Elementary School Christmas show, placing him in the very first episode of the series. Beyond that brief appearance, he shows up again in a couple of early first-season episodes without adding much to the plot. His gray hair suggests he is an adult, though no other physical or biographical details are given. Fred remains a background fixture of Springfield rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: Cora (Mothers and Other Strangers)
text: Cora (Mothers and Other Strangers) is Minor recurring character; a waitress who briefly interacted with Grampa and Homer during a road trip. Cora is a blonde waitress working at the Latter Days Inn diner, encountered during one of Grampa and Homer's misadventures. She shows a flirtatious side, taking an interest in Grampa Abe and hoping to start dating him. Abe, ever pragmatic and jaded about relationships, brushes off the idea by jokingly suggesting they skip straight to the breakup instead of going through the dating process. Cora's role is brief and comedic, existing mainly as a one-off gag character within a road trip storyline. She later reappears in a minor capacity in a Springfield diner scene tied to Homer's traffic-related heroics. Overall, she serves as a small supporting piece in episodes centered on Simpson family antics rather than having significant development herself. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Abe said that since he was with Homer, they would skip the dates and go straight to the part where they broke up.
quotes: Abe said that since he was with Homer, they would skip the dates and go straight to the part where they broke up.

title: Fyvush Finkel (character)
text: Fyvush Finkel (character) is Real-life actor who appears as himself in a guest role on The Simpsons. This character is a self-parody appearance by actor Fyvush Finkel, playing himself within the show's universe. His main claim to fame in this world is portraying Krusty the Clown in a lurid, tell-all TV movie about the clown's troubled life. The bit leans into exaggerated show-biz scandal tropes, with Finkel recounting a stint in rehab and a history of substance abuse, despite having several prestigious awards to his name. The gag is further heightened by a farcical subplot involving a disastrous marriage to Mia Farrow. Adding to the comedic confusion, he mixes up the names of two characters meant to be his sons in the film. Overall, his appearance is a brief, satirical cameo rather than a recurring dramatic role. Voiced by Fyvush Finkel.

title: Blanche DuBois
text: Blanche DuBois is Fictional character from Tennessee Williams' 'A Streetcar Named Desire', portrayed by Marge Simpson in the musical 'Oh, Streetcar!'. Blanche DuBois is a literary character originating outside The Simpsons universe, brought into the show through a community theater production. She is a faded Southern belle and former English teacher whose life has fallen into decline, a role Marge unexpectedly wins in a local musical adaptation. The part has history within Springfield's amateur theater scene, having previously been played by Ned Flanders due to his all-boys school background. The character also appears via the classic 1951 film adaptation, which Milhouse's class watches and which inspires Milhouse's admiration for Marlon Brando. Blanche's storyline serves mainly as a vehicle for Marge's brief brush with local stardom and for referencing classic American theater and film within the show's universe. Voiced by Julie Kavner. Notable quotes: ♪ I thought my life would be a Mardi Gras. A never-ending party, ha! I'm a faded Southern dame without a dime. ♪
quotes: ♪ I thought my life would be a Mardi Gras. A never-ending party, ha! I'm a faded Southern dame without a dime. ♪

title: Count Fudge-ula
text: Count Fudge-ula is Cereal mascot character appearing in The Simpsons universe. Count Fudge-ula is the vampire-themed mascot for a sugary breakfast cereal, clearly designed as a spoof of the real-world Count Chocula, who himself riffs on Count Dracula. His backstory carries a darkly comic edge: years of eating his own sugary cereal caused him to lose all his teeth, forcing him to wear dentures. Despite this consequence, he remains stubbornly devoted to his sugar habit and still craves more. As a mascot rather than a member of the main cast, he mostly exists as background satire of cereal advertising and health issues tied to sugary foods. He appears briefly across a couple of episodes, including a Treehouse of Horror segment fitting his vampiric design. His character leans entirely on parody rather than deep personality development. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Dia-Betty
text: Dia-Betty is Cletus Spuckler's overweight, diabetic cousin from the Spuckler family. Dia-Betty is a minor recurring member of the sprawling Spuckler clan, defined almost entirely by her diabetes and her contradictory habits of exercising while simultaneously eating cake. She has an unhealthy obsession with sugary and bizarre foods, going so far as to ask Cletus for a piece of his baby to put in her coffee. Despite her health problems, she remains active in community affairs, joining Marge's lawsuit-related mob against the Motherloving Sugar Corp. and later joining the angry townsfolk who turned on Homer during the dome crisis. She's also shown as being fiercely proud and vocal about her size, becoming a member of the "Big is Beautiful" group and attending their protests and functions. Her name is a straightforward pun on the word 'diabetic.' She largely appears as a background gag character rather than a focus of any storyline. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Just bring them to a window so I can pinch 'em.
quotes: Just bring them to a window so I can pinch 'em.

title: Evan Conover
text: Evan Conover is US State Department official who handles the Bart-Australia diplomatic incident. Evan Conover is a government bureaucrat working in the State Department's Undersecretary for International Protocol office, specifically within the oddly specific 'Brat and Punk Division.' He is sent to the Simpson household to address the diplomatic fallout after Bart's prank phone call rings up a huge bill and insults Australia. During a briefing, he accidentally reveals a slide referencing a secret contingency plan involving Cuba, then swallows the film to destroy the evidence, hinting at a shady, secretive side to his job. He accompanies the family to Australia to smooth things over, but ultimately betrays their trust by allowing Bart to receive a harsher punishment than promised. His brief appearance paints him as an unreliable, slippery government functionary more concerned with international politics than fairness to the family he's supposed to help. Voiced by Phil Hartman.

title: Mr. Costington
text: Mr. Costington is Owner/chairman of Costington's department store and Springfield Mall, a recurring employer of Springfield residents. Mr. Costington is the gray-haired businessman who runs the Costington's department store chain and owns Springfield Mall. He's portrayed as generally kind-hearted toward his employees, though he occasionally shows a callous or insensitive side. Over the years he's given work to several familiar Springfield faces, including Homer in a variety of odd jobs, along with Gil and the Yes Guy. His signature bit involves theatrically drawn-out hiring and firing announcements, delivered with a sing-song flourish. He's also been glimpsed mingling in Republican political circles, hinting at his status among Springfield's elite. Notably, he's one of the rare Simpsons characters drawn with visible eyebrows. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: You're firee-e-e-ed! | You're hiree-e-e-ed!
quotes: You're firee-e-e-ed!
You're hiree-e-e-ed!

title: Hillary Clinton
text: Hillary Clinton is Real-world political figure appearing in The Simpsons as Bill Clinton's wife and a former First Lady/presidential candidate. Hillary Clinton appears in the show as a caricature of her real-world political persona, tied closely to her marriage with Bill Clinton. She's portrayed as politically ambitious, notably pushing Bill to campaign for her during a presidential run. Her fictional appearances range from cameos in fictional media within the show, like being cast as a running mate in an Itchy & Scratchy cartoon, to being confused with Marge Simpson due to a physical resemblance when Marge wears a pantsuit. She's also referenced through her real-life authorship of a book that shows up as a prop. In non-canon material, she's depicted in more absurd, exaggerated political satire involving other real politicians. Overall she functions as a recurring background reference to real-world politics rather than a core cast member. Voiced by Tress MacNeille, Carolyn Omine.

title: Nick Delacourt
text: Nick Delacourt is Drummer for the band Sungazer, minor character connected to Apu's storyline. Nick Delacourt is a minor musician character who plays drums for the band Sungazer. He becomes relevant to the plot when Sungazer's former lead singer, Grant LeDavid, passes away, prompting the band to seek out Apu as a replacement. Nick is the bandmate who breaks the news of LeDavid's death to the band Covercraft. He doesn't have much of an independent personality explored on the show, functioning mainly as a supporting figure in the music-industry subplot involving Apu. Beyond his appearance in the episode "Covercraft," he also appears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Matthew Sweet.

title: Michael D'Amico
text: Michael D'Amico is Son of mobster Fat Tony, a quiet Springfield Elementary student uninterested in the family's criminal business. Michael D'Amico is the young son of mafia boss Fat Tony and his late wife Anna Maria. Unlike his intimidating father, Michael is soft-spoken and largely silent around others, leading classmates like Sherri and Terri to view him as strange and withdrawn. His true passion lies in cooking rather than crime, and he has shown real talent as a chef. When his father was hospitalized after an attack by rival gangsters, Michael was given the chance to take control of the family business but declined, preferring to let others step in. Despite his reluctance to embrace mob life outright, he still proved capable of ruthless action, secretly poisoning the rival gang that hurt his father. The character is designed as a clear homage to Michael Corleone from The Godfather, mirroring that character's conflicted relationship with his own crime-family legacy. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Tom Cruise
text: Tom Cruise is Real-life actor referenced as a celebrity figure within the Simpsons universe. Tom Cruise appears in Springfield lore only as a celebrity name-dropped or pictured rather than as a speaking character. He's invoked during Marge's Kwik-E-Mart trial when the blue-haired lawyer uses him to gauge jury bias, and Apu imagines him alongside ex-wife Nicole Kidman in a magazine fantasy about assimilating into American culture. He's also listed among Ned Flanders' surprisingly left-leaning celebrities, showing the show's tendency to poke fun at real-world political assumptions. Principal Skinner even cobbles together a cheap Halloween costume based on Cruise's iconic look from 'Risky Business.' In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, his blockbuster 'Edge of Tomorrow' is mocked by Comic Book Guy as an example of star-driven box office failure. Interestingly, the show once hoped to cast Cruise himself to voice an unrelated character named Tom, but he never came through, leading to Phil Hartman taking the role instead.

title: Arthur Crandall
text: Arthur Crandall is A children's entertainer and ventriloquist who briefly rivaled Krusty the Clown for popularity in Springfield. Arthur Crandall is the human puppeteer behind the wooden dummy Gabbo, whose show caused a sudden ratings collapse for Krusty the Clown. His fame was short-lived, as a public scandal involving Gabbo cursing at children brought his career crashing down once Krusty made his comeback. Years later, he's shown to have fallen far from his peak, performing tired casino gigs with a visibly worn-out Gabbo. Despite once being professional rivals with Krusty, he seems to maintain friendly ties with other Springfield entertainers, such as attending Sideshow Mel's birthday party. He's also seen as part of the town's collective panic during the environmental disaster caused by Homer, showing he's just another ordinary resident when not performing. Overall, Crandall represents a classic show-business cautionary tale of fleeting stardom and inevitable decline. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Leonardo DiCaprio
text: Leonardo DiCaprio is Real-world celebrity (actor and film producer) who appears as himself in cameo-style roles in the show. Leonardo DiCaprio appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, popping up in odd, celebrity-cameo situations rather than as a regular cast member. He's shown having an awkward encounter with Lily after she moves to America, starring in an animated series called Cookie Castle, and even turning up as a face on a chef-themed captcha screen that Lisa encounters online. He's also portrayed as socially conscious, joining Sting in writing angry letters to Mr. Burns to stop him from turning a nature preserve into a golf course. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he meets a grim fate as part of a celebrity killing spree orchestrated by Kang and Kodos. Overall, his appearances lean on his real-life fame and persona for quick jokes and pop-culture references rather than any deep characterization. Voiced by Chris Edgerly.

title: Chip Davis
text: Chip Davis is A minor recurring Springfield resident known for holding many odd jobs, whose funeral becomes a major town event. Chip Davis was a beloved but oddly obscure figure in Springfield, dubbed 'Springfield's Most Beloved Character That You Never Saw.' Despite his low profile, he held an astonishing number of jobs over the years, from working at the nuclear plant to being a Duffman actor, a sideshow performer, and a proofreader for the town's sign. His death drew an enormous outpouring of grief, with even national celebrities attending his funeral, and Homer likened him to an honorary member of the Simpson family. Chip was also a published author, having written Hans Moleman's biography, and he offered emotional support to Bumblebee Man after a tragic loss. Even in death, he was remembered for a handful of quirky personal regrets involving local landmarks and achievements. His memorial plaque humorously listed his bizarre career history, reinforcing the running gag of his mysterious ubiquity in town life. Notable quotes: People called him the sixth Simpson. Not sure why.
quotes: People called him the sixth Simpson. Not sure why.

title: Fleetwood Mac
text: Fleetwood Mac is Real-world British-American rock band referenced and briefly appearing in The Simpsons universe. Fleetwood Mac exists in the Simpsons world as the real rock band, mentioned and occasionally depicted rather than voiced by a specific actor. Their music and imagery pop up as background references, such as Homer and Marge name-dropping them alongside Disco Duck while reminiscing about their old 8-track collection. Band members Mick Fleetwood and Stevie Nicks make a non-speaking cameo appearance walking around Springfield Heights, posed to mirror the famous cover art of their album Rumours. Their song "Don't Stop" gets needle-drop treatment twice, once as Bart's soundtrack while joyriding in a stolen army tank, and again when the Fleet-A-Pita van pulls up to the power plant. A mock documentary about Nostradamus even jokes that the seer predicted the band's real-life breakup, complete with a shot of the Rumours album cover. Overall, they function as a pop-culture easter egg rather than a fleshed-out character with personality or dialogue.

title: Señor Ding-Dong
text: Señor Ding-Dong is A minor recurring Mexican character who owns a doorbell store and appears occasionally in Springfield. Señor Ding-Dong is an oddball figure defined almost entirely by the bell perpetually perched atop his head. He runs a novelty shop specializing in doorbells, and his first appearance has him personally intervening to silence one of his own products after it becomes an endless nuisance for Marge. He speaks with a strange, almost philosophical air about his own existence, hinting that he was originally nothing more than a promotional gimmick before becoming something greater. Despite his eccentricity, he's resourceful enough to talk Chief Wiggum out of shooting the offending doorbell. He later turns up as an unexpected member of a local bowling team and is seen among a crowd of Mexican townsfolk enjoying a slapstick stunt show. His mysterious background and simple sight-gag design have made him a recurring but always background presence in Springfield. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: He told Marge that he was once just a promotional item but had since become "so much more".
quotes: He told Marge that he was once just a promotional item but had since become "so much more".

title: Calvin Coolidge
text: Calvin Coolidge is Real-world historical figure (30th U.S. President) referenced in the Simpsons universe. Calvin Coolidge is a real-world historical figure who appears only tangentially in the Simpsons universe, mostly as a background reference rather than an active character. He is depicted through a picture and a mention rather than any spoken dialogue, reflecting his status as a non-speaking character in the show. His presence is tied to Grampa Simpson's fondness for old-fashioned Americana, as seen through a nostalgic poster referencing Coolidge's presidency. He also appears briefly in an educational context when Superintendent Chalmers shows Bart historical figures, just before Bart's fixation shifts to Theodore Roosevelt. Coolidge's inclusion works mainly as a subtle historical joke rather than a fleshed-out character within the show's world. Notable quotes: I've got to be honest, Monty. I've never dated anyone who knew Calvin Coolidge.
quotes: I've got to be honest, Monty. I've never dated anyone who knew Calvin Coolidge.

title: Mason Fairbanks
text: Mason Fairbanks is A treasure hunter and former lifeguard who was briefly believed to be Homer Simpson's biological father. Mason Fairbanks is an elderly adventurer with a taste for underwater treasure hunting and a past as a lifeguard. He enters the Simpson family's life when Homer discovers old love letters he wrote to Mona Simpson and becomes convinced Fairbanks is his real father. Despite the awkward circumstances, he forms a genuine, warm bond with Homer, Bart, and Lisa, and a paternity test seems to confirm the connection. He proves heroic when he rescues Homer from a sinking submarine during a celebratory treasure hunt gone wrong. It's later revealed that Grampa had secretly rigged the paternity test, meaning Fairbanks was never actually Homer's biological father, though the friendship they built remained meaningful. He later appears at Mona's funeral, showing his continued connection to the Simpson family even after the paternity revelation. Voiced by Michael York.

title: Elliott
text: Elliott is Minor character appearing in a parody segment referencing E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, mentioned in "A Star Is Burns". Elliott is a barely-there character whose sole notable moment comes in a parody sequence spoofing E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial. In this scene, Mr. Burns takes on the role of E.T., leaving Elliott behind before departing in a spaceship. He has no dialogue, fitting his status as a non-speaking character, and his appearance is largely a vehicle for the film reference rather than any personal characterization. He also appears briefly in a non-canon capacity at Springfield Elementary School. Overall, Elliott exists less as a fleshed-out character and more as a nostalgic nod for fans of the classic film he's based on.

title: John Dillinger
text: John Dillinger is Real-life American bank robber referenced and briefly depicted in The Simpsons, notably as a member of the Jury of the Damned. John Dillinger is not an original Simpsons character but a historical figure incorporated into the show's mythology. He's mentioned as a point of comparison for criminal behavior, most memorably when Chief Wiggum cites his origin story while discussing Marge's crime spree. Homer also imagines him socializing in the afterlife alongside other infamous or celebrity figures like Ty Cobb and Joseph Stalin. Beyond these mentions, Dillinger appears in a non-speaking capacity as one of the members of the Jury of the Damned in a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment. He's also listed among Ned Flanders' collection of infamous historical 'lefties.' Overall, he functions as a background cultural reference rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: Malfunctioning Eddie
text: Malfunctioning Eddie is A minor non-canon robot character appearing in Simpsons/Futurama crossover comics. Malfunctioning Eddie is a background robot character who appears in a Simpsons-Futurama crossover comic storyline. As his name suggests, he is prone to breaking down, and his defining moment comes when he malfunctions and explodes while conversing with Gil during the chaos of Springfield's citizens being teleported to New New York. He has no deep characterization beyond this brief, comedic role, existing mainly as a bit of sci-fi slapstick within the crossover narrative. His gray hair suggests an older or worn design, fitting his glitchy, unreliable nature. He is considered non-canon within the main Simpsons continuity, tying him specifically to the Bongo comics universe.

title: Hubert J. Farnsworth
text: Hubert J. Farnsworth is Futurama scientist/professor who crossed over into The Simpsons universe, distant ancestor of Philip J. Fry. Professor Farnsworth is an elderly, eccentric scientist from the Futurama universe who appears in a Simpsons crossover episode. He's shown to be logically driven, quickly dismissing the idea of time machines in favor of quantum-entangled singularities, and willing to consider drastic solutions like killing a Simpson family member to solve a genetic crisis. Despite his scientific bravado, he has moments of despair, briefly giving up when a means of returning home seems lost. He works alongside Professor Frink and Lisa Simpson to solve the New New York creature problem, eventually helping devise a plan to contain the monsters. His appearances outside the crossover are mostly cameos, such as on a museum exhibit banner and a convention poster referencing Futurama. He also shows up as one of several bodies Homer could hypothetically possess in a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment. Voiced by Billy West.

title: French Fry
text: French Fry is A MyTuber who co-hosts a gaming commentary series with Astrid. French Fry is a blonde-haired MyTube personality best known for co-hosting the online series Let's Talk Boblox! With Astrid and French Fry alongside her partner Astrid. Together they cover in-game happenings within the virtual world of Boblox, providing commentary for their subscribers. She appeared on-screen covering a school rivalry storyline that played out inside the game, reacting to events alongside Astrid. French Fry shows a curious, slightly whimsical side, wondering aloud about odd everyday questions unrelated to the game. She and Astrid also invite their audience to engage by sharing their own theories, suggesting an interactive, community-driven persona. She is a minor recurring character introduced in the show's later seasons. Voiced by Grey DeLisle. Notable quotes: French Fry asked why candy canes were only for Christmas
quotes: French Fry asked why candy canes were only for Christmas

title: Cat Deeley (character)
text: Cat Deeley (character) is A celebrity TV presenter who appears as herself in The Simpsons. Cat Deeley is a guest-star character based on the real-life British television presenter of the same name. In the show's universe, she hosts a reality competition series called So You Think You Can Duff?, tying her into the town of Springfield's fondness for beer-related media. She later appears in a non-canon capacity, attending a glitzy premiere event for a season finale of The Simpsons itself, poking fun at the show's own meta-awareness. As a guest character, she doesn't have an extensive personal history or running gags within the main canon, functioning mostly as a cameo tied to specific episode plots. Her presence highlights the show's frequent use of real celebrities voicing fictionalized versions of themselves. Voiced by Cat Deeley (Herself).

title: Frosty the Hit Man (character)
text: Frosty the Hit Man (character) is A fictional video game character/hit man appearing within a game-within-the-show, featured in the episode "White Christmas Blues". Frosty the Hit Man is a violent, snowman-themed assassin who exists as the protagonist of an in-universe video game rather than a true member of the Simpsons cast. Within his game, he hunts down and kills a bizarre mix of holiday-related figures, blending dark comedy with Christmas imagery. His rampage culminates in a symbolic act of destroying a rack of Endless Christmas Specials, suggesting a satire on overplayed holiday programming. He is a non-speaking character, letting his actions rather than dialogue define him. The character also crosses over into the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, reinforcing his status as a meta, game-based figure rather than a standard resident of Springfield.

title: Principal Finch
text: Principal Finch is Principal of a magnet school in the Springfield school district, rival of Principal Skinner. Principal Finch is a minor recurring character who leads a magnet school within the Springfield school district. He's shown to be quick-witted, cracking a joke at a fellow principal's expense during a district meeting that goes over well with his peers. His biggest moment comes when Superintendent Chalmers selects him to be his plus one for a trip to an educational conference in Cincinnati, a slight that clearly bothers Principal Skinner. Finch never actually makes it to the conference, however, since he falls ill from food poisoning right before the trip. It's later revealed that Skinner sabotaged him by secretly contaminating his food with black mold, allowing Skinner to take his place. Finch's role highlights the petty rivalries among Springfield's school administrators. Voiced by Hannibal Buress.

title: Lord Evilton
text: Lord Evilton is Fictional dark wizard villain from the in-universe Angelica Button book series. Lord Evilton is a fictional antagonist within the Simpsons' parody book franchise Angelica Button, written by the fictional author T.R Francis. He serves as a dark, menacing wizard figure who denies the existence of another character, Malicious Krubb, and has the young heroine Angelica banished to a place called Mount Krushmore as punishment. His design and role are clearly modeled after Harry Potter's most infamous villains, blending traits of both a fearsome dark lord and a sinister, brooding authority figure. Beyond his appearances in the books, he crosses into the show's main continuity when Homer dons an Evilton costume in an attempt to frighten Bart. Though he never appears as a 'real' character interacting with the Simpsons family directly, his cultural presence within the show mirrors how deeply the fictional book series has permeated Springfield life. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Count Dracula (monster)
text: Count Dracula (monster) is Vampire monster from Transylvania who appears in various Treehouse of Horror segments. Count Dracula is a classic vampire figure who occasionally crosses paths with the Simpson family in the show's non-canon Halloween specials. He is married to Countess Dracula and is the father of Edmund, tying him into a small vampire family unit. In one appearance he haunts a mountain lodge alongside other classic monsters, and in another he's mocked as an outdated monster who gets kicked out of a party by the monsters' wives. His most significant storyline involves traveling with Homer to find his runaway son Edmund and Lisa, where he attempts to turn Lisa or Homer into a vampire, only to be foiled by Homer's unhealthy cholesterol levels. Despite his menacing vampire nature, he's often portrayed comically and ineffectually within the show's parody horror segments. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Carmen Electra (character)
text: Carmen Electra (character) is Guest celebrity character appearing as herself, a TV host/actress who becomes entangled with Homer and Marge. Carmen Electra appears as a fictionalized version of herself, playing a television personality who co-hosts a reality show and later stars in a melodramatic series. She's shown as willing to go to elaborate, ethically dubious lengths for entertainment, orchestrating an elaborate hoax involving Homer and Marge that nearly gets Homer executed for a staged murder. Despite being the perpetrator of a cruel prank, she ends up as the butt of a different joke when Homer, lecturing her about exploiting people for ratings, can't stop staring at her chest. In her second appearance, she plays an actress in a fictional in-universe show called Boobs, again leaning into her sex-symbol image while trying to be seen as a serious performer. The character plays on Electra's real-life persona as a glamorous television host, blending self-parody with her cameo role in the Simpsons universe. Voiced by Carmen Electra. Notable quotes: Homer? My face is up here. | I've made my choice
quotes: Homer? My face is up here.
I've made my choice

title: Miles Davis
text: Miles Davis is Real-world jazz musician referenced in the Simpsons universe, particularly as a favorite of Lisa Simpson. Miles Davis appears in the show not as a character but as a real-world musical icon whose work resonates within the Simpson family's world. His album Birth of the Cool is treasured by Lisa, symbolizing her sophisticated taste in music compared to the rest of her family. Homer once tries to use this album to bond with Lisa, hoping to prove he understands her interests better than she thinks. Bart and Milhouse are also shown listening to a compilation of his music, showing his influence crosses generational and character lines. He also appears as one of Lisa's educational flashcards on jazz legends, reinforcing his status as a legendary figure in her personal pantheon of musical greats. Miles Davis never physically appears as an animated character but is referenced through album art and mentions.

title: Millard Fillmore
text: Millard Fillmore is Real-world 13th President of the United States, referenced/depicted in various Simpsons episodes. Millard Fillmore is not really a character in the traditional sense but a recurring historical reference within the show, standing in for the real-life 13th U.S. President. He's most memorably brought to life in a school pageant, where a student named Richard portrays him during a Presidents' Day event. Over the years, the show uses him as a punchline or trivia nod, from Krusty joking about his supposed drinking habit to Springfield Elementary cutting him from the curriculum to save money. He also appears as an animatronic figure more than once, whether taking driver's license photos at the DMV or automating machinery at the Duff Brewery, poking fun at how obscure and forgotten some presidents become. His image even shows up in a book Superintendent Chalmers uses to spark Bart's interest in presidential history. Overall, Fillmore functions as a running gag about historical obscurity rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: Dash Dingo
text: Dash Dingo is Fictional video game character and mascot for the Dingo Junction clothing store, referenced within the Simpsons universe. Dash Dingo is a fictional video game hero who exists within the world of the Simpsons, serving both as a game protagonist and a store mascot. He's a parody of Crash Bandicoot, complete with exaggerated Australian stereotypes in his hat, clothing, and speech. Lisa Simpson becomes unexpectedly obsessed with his game after staying home sick, playing it for three straight days despite initially dismissing it. His in-game villain mimics the evil laugh of Crash Bandicoot's antagonist, Dr. Neo Cortex, adding to the parody. Beyond the games, Dash Dingo's likeness also promotes Dingo Junction, a clothing store found in Springfield Mall. He later appears in non-canon media, including mobile and crossover games. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: The Fossil Fuel Four
text: The Fossil Fuel Four is A supervillain group from the Radioactive Man comic-within-the-show universe, serving as antagonists. The Fossil Fuel Four are a team of four villains—The Fracker, Charcoal Briquette, Petroleus Rex, and Old King Coal—each themed after a different type of fossil fuel. They exist within the fictional superhero universe of Radioactive Man, appearing as a coordinated group rather than solo villains. Their defining moment is attacking a nuclear power plant and successfully killing the hero Radioactive Man, a rare instance of a Simpsons universe villain group actually defeating the protagonist they target. The group's concept is a parody of Marvel's Frightful Four, translated into an environmental/energy-industry gimmick. They later appeared as action figures, reinforcing their status as merchandise-style comic book villains within the show's fictional media landscape.

title: Cowboy accountant
text: Cowboy accountant is The Rich Texan's personal accountant, who assists with his financial and legal paperwork. The cowboy accountant is a minor background figure who handles the financial dealings of the wealthy Rich Texan. He's brought in to help draft paperwork so the Rich Texan can make a tax write-off donation to Marge and Lisa, ultimately leading to the creation of a charitable foundation in Lisa's name. He appears businesslike but also shares in a small celebratory moment with his employer using office tools like a stapler and calculator. Later, he's called upon again to notarize documents converting the foundation's building into a homeless shelter. He fits into the show's tradition of quirky one-off professionals tied to the eccentric, oil-rich Texan stereotype character. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Frink Jr.
text: Frink Jr. is Minor recurring character; son of Professor Frink and grandson of Jonathan Frink, Sr.. Frink Jr. is a minor member of the Frink family, resembling his father with thick glasses, and also sporting braces. He is a non-speaking character who appears only briefly in the show's canon, notably during a mishap with a remote-controlled toy plane. In non-canon material, he joins his father in battle during a robot competition against Bart and Homer. He has also appeared as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Little else is known about his personality since he never speaks on screen.

title: Deuce
text: Deuce is Hot dog vendor and former owner of Deuce's Caboose Chili Dogs, with a nostalgic connection to Homer. Deuce is an elderly hot dog stand owner who ran Deuce's Caboose Chili Dogs for years in Springfield. When Homer was a child waiting outside during his parents' marriage counseling sessions, Deuce took pity on him and gave him free chili dogs, forming an affectionate bond and nicknaming him his little H-Dog. As Homer grew older he forgot about Deuce, but years later, when healthy food trends took over Springfield's restaurants, Homer rediscovered Deuce's greasy stand and their friendship was rekindled. Deuce initially claims not to remember Homer, masking guilt over feeling he couldn't be the father figure Homer needed. He proves fiercely protective when Homer's life is endangered, revealing his true attachment. Ultimately warm-hearted and self-deprecating about his own worth as a mentor, Deuce represents a minor but touching figure from Homer's childhood. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: little H-Dog
quotes: little H-Dog

title: The Fracker
text: The Fracker is Supervillain enemy of Radioactive Man and member of The Fossil Fuel Four. The Fracker is a fictional supervillain who appears within the Radioactive Man comic-book-within-a-show universe. He is one of four antagonists making up The Fossil Fuel Four, a team themed around environmentally destructive energy practices. His weapon of choice is a pipe capable of blasting polluted water into the ground, a clear nod to real-world fracking controversies. He is notable for dealing the killing blow to Radioactive Man during a battle at the Zenith City nuclear power plant, marking him as a particularly significant and lethal member of his villain team. Beyond the comics, his cultural presence extends into merchandise, appearing as an action figure and even as a collectible figure in Comic Book Guy's apartment. He also appears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Dumbo
text: Dumbo is A flying elephant character appearing in The Simpsons, based on the Disney character of the same name. Dumbo is a gray flying elephant who appears in a handful of Simpsons episodes and specials, often as a nod to the classic Disney film he originates from. He's the son of Mrs. Jumbo, and in one story Homer even names an elephant at a circus after him by tossing a peanut at it. Lisa also imagines him as a symbol of good things about America, and he's shown following jazz legend Louis Armstrong to Canada in search of legal weed. In non-canon material, he's depicted in a bizarre alternate cartoon as a Nazi elephant that destroys London, and he later joins his mother on a Mother's Day family outing. Dumbo doesn't speak in his appearances, functioning purely as a visual crossover gag referencing Disney.

title: Elfo
text: Elfo is A crossover character from the animated series Disenchantment, appearing only as a figure/statue in The Simpsons. Elfo is not actually a native Simpsons character but a half-elf from the unrelated Matt Groening series Disenchantment. His presence in The Simpsons universe is limited to a brief crossover nod rather than any actual storyline or dialogue. He first shows up as part of a statue depicting himself alongside Princess Bean and Luci, owned by Comic Book Guy. Later, a smaller figure of Elfo is seen displayed in Comic Book Guy's apartment. Because he never speaks or interacts with any Simpsons characters, he functions purely as an Easter egg for fans of Groening's other shows. There's no indication of personality, backstory, or running gags within this context, since he's essentially a background collectible item in the world of Springfield.

title: Desert park ranger
text: Desert park ranger is A park ranger who oversees Springfield Desert State Park, appearing during a school field trip. The desert park ranger is a minor employee tasked with guiding visitors through Springfield Desert State Park. He appeared when Springfield Elementary took a field trip to the park, showing the kids around the desert landscape. In a strange and comedic moment, a rock climber mistook him for part of the terrain and attempted to climb him. He later appeared in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Little else is known about his personality or background, as his role is largely limited to this single episode appearance. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Gulliver Dark
text: Gulliver Dark is A minor recurring lounge singer performing at Springfield venues. Gulliver Dark is a smooth-voiced lounge entertainer who pops up performing at a couple of Springfield's nightlife spots. He's first seen crooning at the Sapphire Lounge, where his singing is interrupted by Homer's unexpected heartfelt speech about respecting women. The moment apparently strikes a nerve with Dark, who is emotionally shaken enough to phone his own mother in tears. He later resurfaces as the singer backing Tito Puente's band at Chez Guevara, suggesting he's a steady fixture of the local music scene. The character originated as a recurring sketch figure on The Tracey Ullman Show before making his way into the main series. Overall, he's a background performer whose brief moments add flavor to Springfield's bar and lounge culture rather than a character with deep development. Voiced by Sam McMurray ("Homer's Night Out"); George Balmeseda ("Who Shot Mr. Burns? (Part Two)").

title: Kelly Clarkson
text: Kelly Clarkson is Real-world celebrity referenced in The Simpsons, appearing only as a picture/background element. Kelly Clarkson appears in The Simpsons universe strictly as a real-world figure depicted through photographs rather than as an active character. She is glimpsed in a picture during Simon Cowell's audition footage for American Idol, tying into the show's parody of that talent competition. Separately, Krusty the Clown once performed at a party held at her house, where the walls were decorated with numerous photos of her. Since she never speaks or physically interacts with the cast, she functions purely as a cameo reference acknowledging her fame as a singer and television personality. Her presence is a nod to pop culture rather than a developed storyline, fitting the show's tradition of incorporating celebrity likenesses in background gags.

title: George Clooney
text: George Clooney is Real-life celebrity referenced and briefly depicted in The Simpsons. George Clooney appears in the show as himself, a famous movie star whose celebrity status is frequently name-dropped by various characters. He's often used as a benchmark for fame and success, such as when a studio head laments failing to live up to him, or when other characters compare him to their own dubious liquor endorsement deals. Gary Coleman name-drops him as reason to skip Christmas with the Simpsons, showing how his fame outranks even other celebrities in-universe. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he meets a gruesome end at the hands of a killer Homer Simpson, dying in wet cement outside Grauman's Chinese Theatre. He also makes a cameo as a guest star in another Halloween episode's opening sequence. Overall, Clooney functions less as a character with personality and more as a running punchline about celebrity culture and branding.

title: Darwin Fish
text: Darwin Fish is A prehistoric fish accidentally killed by Homer Simpson during a time-travel mishap in the "Treehouse of Horror V" segment "Time and Punishment". Darwin Fish is a minor, non-canon creature that exists solely as a plot device in one of Homer's chaotic time-travel misadventures. While journeying through the prehistoric era, Homer carelessly steps on the fish, killing it and unknowingly setting off a chain reaction that drastically alters the present-day world upon his return. The fish itself has no dialogue or personality, serving purely as a symbol of how the smallest actions in the past can have massive butterfly-effect consequences. Its name is a playful nod to Charles Darwin and the theory of evolution, fitting the segment's time-travel comedy theme. Despite its brief and silent appearance, Darwin Fish later resurfaced as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, gaining a small extended life beyond its original one-scene role.

title: Amber Duffman
text: Amber Duffman is Estranged daughter of Duffman, an artist who later opens a cannabis business. Amber Duffman is the long-lost daughter of the beer-mascot Duffman, whose relationship with her father soured after her mother left him once he took on his flamboyant persona. Growing up resentful, she swore off ever speaking to him again by the time she finished high school. Years later, Homer and other concerned fathers pushed Duffman to attempt reconciliation, leading to an awkward and nearly disastrous reunion at her apartment party. Despite the rocky start, the two mend their relationship after Duffman reveals he kept a childhood drawing she made of them together, prompting him to abandon his Duffman persona for good. Amber later channels her artistic talents into opening a cannabis-themed business, ironically employing her father as its new mascot, "Puffman." She's left stunned by the revelation that she might not be Duffman's only estranged child. Voiced by Aubrey Plaza.

title: Alex DeLarge
text: Alex DeLarge is A costume Bart wears on Halloween, based on the character Alex DeLarge from the novel and film 'A Clockwork Orange'. Alex DeLarge isn't an original Simpsons character but a reference to the infamous protagonist of Anthony Burgess's novel and Stanley Kubrick's film adaptation, A Clockwork Orange. In the show, this identity appears only as a Halloween costume worn by Bart Simpson during a wraparound segment. The costume later reappears during a musical number in a holiday special. Because it's simply an outfit Bart puts on rather than a character with his own dialogue or arc, there's no unique personality attached to it within the Simpsons universe. The reference has also been echoed or parodied in a handful of other episodes, showing the show's fondness for nodding to the classic film. It also inspired a virtual costume item, Clockwork Bart, in a Simpsons mobile game. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Danger Dog
text: Danger Dog is Fictional superhero character within the Simpsons universe, from an in-show cartoon called Danger Dog. Danger Dog is a superhero character created by fictional cartoonist Geoff Jenkins, existing as a show-within-the-show in the Simpsons universe. He's romantically involved with Sarah Jessica Barker and has an ongoing rivalry with his arch-enemy, Molly Ringworm. His adventures are set in Michigan, giving his world a specific, if oddly mundane, backdrop for a superhero franchise. The character is clearly a spoof blending elements of classic animated heroes like Danger Mouse and Underdog. His popularity within the show is evidenced by fans dressing up as him at the fictional convention Bi-Mon-Sci-Fi-Con. Outside the main continuity, he also appears as a collectible character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Count Four Count
text: Count Four Count is A jazz musician who appears in Springfield's jazz scene, connected to Bart and Lisa. Count Four Count is a minor jazz musician who circulates through Springfield's jazz clubs. He first appears watching Bart play drums at Jazzy Goodtime's before joining him onstage alongside Skinny Palmer and Marbles Le Marquez. He's also part of the crowd at The Jazz Hole, where he's one of many musicians Lisa knows personally. His running gag involves a bit of comedic obliviousness, reacting emotionally to Lisa's frustration before realizing he doesn't even know what the issue is. Like several other patrons of the club, he gets caught up in a shared lottery ticket loss. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he performs onstage during one of the show's surreal body-swap gags. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: Count Four Count jumped out of his chair and agreed, before he asked what they were upset about.
quotes: Count Four Count jumped out of his chair and agreed, before he asked what they were upset about.

title: Sleazy Duff
text: Sleazy Duff is One of the Seven Duffs, mascot characters for Duff Beer. Sleazy Duff is one of the Seven Duffs, a group of costumed mascots created for Duff Beer as a parody of the Seven Dwarfs from Disney's Snow White. He appears as a costumed character at promotional locations like Duff Gardens and Duff Days. His notable moment involves handing out pink elephant balloons at the exit of a Duff Days event, a nod to classic drunken hallucination imagery associated with beer. Unlike some human characters, he has never been voiced or shown without the costume, keeping his true nature a mystery. He also makes minor non-canon appearances, such as on a rotating poster in Moe's Tavern in a video game, and as a topiary in a mobile game.

title: Experimental Ant Colony
text: Experimental Ant Colony is A NASA-owned ant farm that ends up loose aboard the space shuttle Corvair in a Homer-caused mishap. The Experimental Ant Colony is not a character in the traditional sense but a science experiment that becomes an unlikely source of chaos during Homer's trip to space. NASA had set up the ant farm as part of its research aboard the Corvair shuttle. Things go wrong when Homer, unable to resist eating smuggled potato chips in zero gravity, sends the snacks floating through the cabin. While chasing the drifting chips, he crashes into the ant colony's container, breaking it open and releasing the ants throughout the shuttle. The incident becomes one of the memorably absurd consequences of Homer's presence on a serious space mission, playing into the show's running gag of him inadvertently sabotaging important events through simple gluttony and clumsiness. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta, Nancy Cartwright.

title: Demogorgon
text: Demogorgon is Monster creature appearing in parody segments of The Simpsons, based on the Stranger Things villain. The Demogorgon is a monstrous creature that first appeared within the show-within-a-show Odder Stuff, a parody of Stranger Things. It is depicted as a dangerous predator that hunts and devours people, including background characters like Lenny and Carl. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, an entire dimension called the Over Under is populated by these creatures, tying into Mr. Burns' portal experiments. The Demogorgons are shown to be somewhat rule-bound, only attacking if their prey moves or speaks, which Milhouse learns the hard way. Despite their menace, they are ultimately dispatched fairly easily by Homer using a flamethrower and by Lisa using psychic powers. The creature serves mainly as a comedic horror parody rather than a recurring dramatic threat. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Lara Croft
text: Lara Croft is A crossover character (based on the video game heroine) who appears in Homer's dream in a Simpsons comic. Lara Croft appears as a fictional archaeologist who crosses over into Homer's dream world in a Bongo comic story. She's drawn to Homer's brazen disregard for social norms, comparing it to legendary golden Siamese mummies, and offers him cryptic wisdom about controlling his own destiny. Despite her adventurous, no-nonsense demeanor, she refuses to help Homer cheat at a video game, showing she has some ethical limits even in a dream. Her appearance is a playful nod to the famous Tomb Raider video game franchise. Beyond the dream sequence, she also inspires a costume worn by another character, Cloris Clane, at a sci-fi convention. Overall, Lara Croft functions as a one-off fantastical cameo rather than a recurring presence in Homer's real life. Notable quotes: his casual disregard for the mutually-agreed upon rules of society draws her to him, like the legend of the golden Siamese mummies | he is master of his own fate
quotes: his casual disregard for the mutually-agreed upon rules of society draws her to him, like the legend of the golden Siamese mummies
he is master of his own fate

title: Grandma Flanders
text: Grandma Flanders is Grandmother of Ned Flanders, who briefly lived with the Flanders family. Grandma Flanders is an elderly, somewhat frail member of the Flanders clan who appears mainly in flashback sequences. She's shown to be a bit forgetful or confused, mistaking Ned for someone named Joe and asking a startled young Bart for help with her sums. Despite her fragile health, she was still trusted to babysit the Flanders and Simpson kids together. Her near-death experience after hearing Bart curse, followed by her eventual actual death from Ned's overly enthusiastic hymn-singing, plays into the show's dark comic streak. She's ultimately a minor but memorable example of the show's tendency to treat mortality with absurdist humor. She is deceased by the time later episodes reference her. Voiced by Yeardley Smith. Notable quotes: Hello, Joe.|Grandma Flanders | Can you help me with my sums?
quotes: Hello, Joe.|Grandma Flanders
Can you help me with my sums?

title: Cinderella
text: Cinderella is Crossover Disney princess character referenced and appearing in The Simpsons. Cinderella is the classic Disney princess who occasionally crosses over into the world of The Simpsons, mostly through references and cameo appearances rather than a starring role. She's mentioned as the subject of a bedtime story read by Eddie and Lou, and her tale of servitude to a cruel stepmother is later used by Bart as a manipulative tool to turn Ned's kids against Edna. In non-canon specials tied to Disney+ promotions, she appears as a background figure at Disney-themed events, interacting briefly with Lisa and other characters like Snow White and Jiminy Cricket. She's depicted as kind and helpful, aiding Lisa when she stumbles, but also somewhat clumsy, nearly stepping on tiny characters. Her presence in the show is largely symbolic, representing Disney's broader ownership and integration with the Simpsons universe rather than developing as an independent character with her own arc. Notable quotes: And Cinderella had the most beautiful gown at the ball, with eight satin petticoats, each more delicate than the last.
quotes: And Cinderella had the most beautiful gown at the ball, with eight satin petticoats, each more delicate than the last.

title: Aretha Franklin
text: Aretha Franklin is Real-world singer referenced/imagined in a Simpsons episode, not a core cast member. Aretha Franklin appears in The Simpsons as a nod to her real-life legacy as an American singer, songwriter, pianist, and civil rights activist. She shows up as a figure Lisa imagines when thinking about the positive aspects of America. In the same storyline, she is depicted following Louis Armstrong to Canada in pursuit of legal marijuana, a humorous aside rather than a deep characterization. She also appears as a picture on a wall dedicated to famous left-handed people. As a non-speaking character, she has no dialogue and functions purely as a background or cameo reference rather than an active participant in the plot.

title: Snoop Dogg (character)
text: Snoop Dogg (character) is Real-life rapper appearing as himself in a guest role on The Simpsons. Snoop Dogg appears as a fictionalized version of himself within the Simpsons universe, referenced first as a comparison point in a guessing game between Mr. Burns and Smithers. He later shows up in a more direct capacity, performing a musical diss aimed at a character named Jay G over a stolen handyman. His appearance culminates in a hologram performance where he delivers a pointed remark to Mr. Burns, Homer, and Bart about being outsmarted. As a celebrity cameo character, his role leans on his real-world persona as a rapper and performer rather than any deep original characterization. He's treated as a pop-culture reference rather than a fully developed member of the Simpsons cast. Voiced by Snoop Dogg (Himself). Notable quotes: flipped the script
quotes: flipped the script

title: Ernie (Muppet)
text: Ernie (Muppet) is A crossover character from Sesame Street referenced and appearing occasionally in The Simpsons. Ernie is the famous Muppet character from Sesame Street who occasionally crosses over into the world of The Simpsons, usually alongside his companion Bert. He's referenced in conversation, appears in hallucinations, and shows up as a costume choice or a picture in other characters' rooms, reflecting his status as a beloved pop-culture icon. Marge invokes his and Bert's wholesome image to criticize a raunchier show for children. Various Simpsons characters, including Lou, Eddie, Lenny, and Carl, show admiration for the pair through costumes and decor. In one bizarre anecdote, even Krusty the Bear is said to owe gambling debts to Bert and Ernie, adding a comedic criminal underworld twist to their family-friendly image. Overall, Ernie functions as a nostalgic nod to Sesame Street rather than a fully developed character within the Simpsons universe. Notable quotes: Bert and Ernie left it to your imagination.
quotes: Bert and Ernie left it to your imagination.

title: Demon technician
text: Demon technician is A minor demon working in Hell's Ironic Punishment Division. The demon technician is a low-level worker in Hell tasked with administering punishments in the Ironic Punishment Division. He appears briefly when Homer is sent to Hell before his trial over a soul-selling deal with Flanders the Devil. His job involves force-feeding Homer an endless supply of donuts as a fitting punishment for his gluttony. The technician seems more accustomed to victims breaking quickly, as shown by his confusion when Homer doesn't lose his mind the way a previous victim did. This small moment highlights Homer's legendary appetite even in the face of infernal punishment. The character is non-canon and appears only briefly, existing mainly as a background figure in one of the show's Halloween specials. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Citizen Solar
text: Citizen Solar is A superhero ally of Radioactive Man within the show's fictional comic universe. Citizen Solar is a solar-powered superhero who teams up with Radioactive Man during times of crisis. He works alongside his own sidekick, Wind Lad, forming part of the extended superhero circle within the Radioactive Man comics. His powers are tied directly to sunlight, making him surprisingly vulnerable on cloudy days, which becomes a notable weakness when his abilities fail him at a critical moment. Despite being a hero, this dependency on weather conditions gives him a somewhat comedic, fragile edge compared to more traditional superheroes. He's popular enough in-universe to have a collectible figure, seen displayed in Comic Book Guy's apartment. Beyond the comics, he has also appeared as a character and action figure in various other media tied to the franchise. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Handsome Dan
text: Handsome Dan is The mascot bulldog of Yale University, appearing in episodes involving the Simpsons and Yale. Handsome Dan is the real-life bulldog mascot of Yale University, depicted in the show as being consulted alongside various Yale sports teams on university decisions. He has a quirky, mischievous streak, once hugging Mr. Burns uninvited and then pretending to urinate on him. He appears in Lisa's Yale-related storylines, both when she is accepted and in a dream sequence where she is rejected, in which he dances with Mr. Burns. Unlike many animal characters on the show, Handsome Dan is based on an actual bulldog who serves as Yale's real mascot rather than a person in a costume. He's a minor, comedic recurring presence tied specifically to Yale-centric plots. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: The Entangler
text: The Entangler is Marge Simpson's superhero alter ego who battled Bartman. The Entangler is a non-canon comic book persona taken on by Marge Simpson after being exposed to a nuclear explosion. Her signature power is the ability to control her famously tall hair, using it as both a weapon and tool in combat. She appears as one of several superheroes who face off against Bartman, Bart Simpson's own crime-fighting alter ego. Her costume includes a belt that doubles as her iconic string of pearls, blending her everyday identity with her superhero look. The character exists purely within Bongo Comics' superhero-parody storylines rather than the animated series. She represents a playful twist on Marge's usual domestic role, transforming her into an action-oriented figure. Notable quotes: There is no Mrs. Simpson, only The Entangler!
quotes: There is no Mrs. Simpson, only The Entangler!

title: Tom Colicchio (character)
text: Tom Colicchio (character) is Celebrity chef who appears in Marge's fantasies and food-related storylines. Tom Colicchio is a real-world celebrity chef who makes surreal cameo appearances in Marge's imagination. In one daydream, he judges her cooking on a parody cooking show and rewards her with a brand new kitchen, which he then bizarrely transforms into. He later resurfaces in another of Marge's dreams during a storyline about her food blog, this time riding a space hopper and bouncing after Homer. His appearances are brief and dreamlike rather than grounded in the show's normal reality, functioning as comedic exaggerations of Marge's anxieties about cooking and her family's opinions of her food. Colicchio himself doesn't have much personality development beyond serving as a whimsical guest-star cameo tied to food-centric episodes. Voiced by Himself.

title: The Collector
text: The Collector is Non-canon supervillain alter-ego of Comic Book Guy, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Collector is a comic-styled supervillain who serves as the arch-enemy of the parody heroes Stretch Dude and Clobber Girl. True to his name, he has an obsessive urge to collect things, extending even to capturing people rather than mere objects. His scheme involves trying to force Xena into marriage while attempting to permanently seal his superhero foes inside blocks of lucite. He meets his end in a fittingly theatrical fashion, striking a dramatic pose referencing an actor from Battlestar Galactica as he perishes. As a non-canon character, he exists purely within the Treehouse of Horror universe and later spin-off media rather than the show's main continuity. His visual gimmick of the frozen dramatic pose became enough of a signature that it was reused as a joke in an unrelated video game. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Coward
text: Coward is A minor recurring student at Springfield Elementary who joins Bart's makeshift army. The Coward is an unnamed classmate of Bart's whose defining trait, as his nickname suggests, is his timidity. He's quick to cheer for Bart when he stands up to Nelson, but just as quick to flee when things get dangerous. When Bart forms his own army to take down Nelson and his gang, the Coward signs up, but his nerve fails him during a training exercise involving a barking guard dog. His fear leads to a brief conflict with Bart, who slaps him out of frustration, only for Grampa to intervene and scold Bart for mistreating his troops. Despite his jitters, the Coward ultimately takes part in the final battle against Nelson's weasels and shares in the army's victory. He later shows up again as one of the kids eager to see Bart's scandalous photo of Homer dancing with Princess Kashmir. In the original script, he's simply credited as "SMALL BOY." Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Darcy
text: Darcy is A teenage girl from North Haverbrook who briefly became Bart Simpson's fiancée. Darcy is a young girl whose whirlwind romance with Bart nearly ended in a teenage marriage. She was easily convinced by one of Bart's absurd lies about his age, showing a somewhat naive and trusting side. When she found herself pregnant, she pushed for marriage mainly out of fear of her parents' reaction rather than genuine devotion to Bart. Despite the chaos of the situation, she showed real gratitude when Bart chivalrously offered to marry her to protect her reputation. The situation is resolved when her mother reveals her own pregnancy, allowing the family to disguise Darcy's baby as a sibling instead. Darcy and Bart part on friendly terms, and she has since made brief reappearances in later episodes, including a moment implying she may have had a child with Jimbo Jones. Voiced by Natalie Portman.

title: Zane Furlong
text: Zane Furlong is Former Collaborative Educational Outreacher at Springfield STEM Academy, later a Postmates delivery man. Zane Furlong is a tech-savvy educator who briefly ran the experimental Springfield STEM Academy, where lessons were dictated by a data-driven algorithm rather than traditional teaching. He comes across as trendy and well-meaning, insisting every child is gifted while gamifying discipline and instruction. His career day appearance rattles Homer with a blunt prediction about job automation, showcasing his tendency to deliver unsettling truths in a chipper, corporate tone. When Bart and Lisa uncover a flaw in the school's algorithm, Zane proves surprisingly heroic, rescuing them as the server room self-destructs. After the school's destruction, he's forced into gig work as a Postmates courier, a comedic downgrade from his tech-education career. He later resurfaces as an audience member at a podcast recording, suggesting he remains a minor recurring presence in Springfield life. Voiced by Zach Woods.

title: Mrs. Clark
text: Mrs. Clark is Mother of Lewis Clark and minor recurring resident of Springfield. Mrs. Clark is a background parent figure in Springfield, best known as the mother of Lewis and wife of Mr. Clark. She tends to appear in group settings like church, school meetings, and restaurants rather than having a distinct personality of her own. As a non-speaking character, she's mostly seen rather than heard, quietly existing in the periphery of larger community scenes. She has been shown among concerned parents at Springfield Elementary School, suggesting some involvement in her son's upbringing. In one appearance, she and her husband were implied to be considering having another child. In a non-canon storyline, it was revealed that her marriage to Mr. Clark was ending in divorce.

title: Erin (soldier)
text: Erin (soldier) is Ex-soldier and one-time lover of Krusty the Clown, mother of Sophie. Erin is a former soldier who had a brief but memorable fling with Krusty the Clown during the Gulf War while he was performing on a USO tour. That one night resulted in the birth of her daughter, Sophie. Her military career was derailed when Krusty interfered with her mission to assassinate Saddam Hussein, tackling her at the crucial moment because Saddam was part of his comedy act. The failed mission left her deeply embittered toward clowns, leading her to decorate her home with disturbing artwork depicting clowns being tortured and killed. In non-canon material, she later appears disapproving of her daughter Sophie's marriage to Jimbo. Erin's story ties her permanently, if reluctantly, to Krusty's chaotic personal life. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Dotty
text: Dotty is Homer Simpson's assistant during his brief stint as the Power Plant's 'Accounts Man'. Dotty is a minor employee at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant who serves as Homer's assistant during his short-lived promotion to the role of Accounts Man. She's notable mostly for her quirky habit of referring to Homer and Marge by informal nicknames rather than their full names. Her role is limited to supporting Homer's workplace storyline, giving a glimpse of office life outside his usual position at the plant. Dotty doesn't have much development beyond this single appearance, functioning as a background character who adds a touch of workplace color to the episode. She later reappears briefly via archive footage in a later episode. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: She referred to Homer and Marge as "Mr. S" and "Mrs. S".
quotes: She referred to Homer and Marge as "Mr. S" and "Mrs. S".

title: Edmund
text: Edmund is A vampire love interest of Lisa Simpson, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment as a parody of Twilight's Edward Cullen. Edmund is a centuries-old vampire disguised as a new student at Springfield Elementary who becomes romantically involved with Lisa Simpson. He displays superhuman strength and speed, using his powers to repeatedly save Lisa from being hit by out-of-control vehicles before revealing his true vampiric nature to her. His father, Count Dracula, joins him for an awkward dinner at the Simpsons' home, leading to embarrassment that pushes Edmund and Lisa to run off together. He ultimately wants Lisa to become a vampire and live forever as an eight-year-old, but she has second thoughts once she learns what eternal childhood really means. When Edmund tries to force the transformation on her, Homer intervenes, and ironically his cholesterol-laden blood proves fatal to both Edmund and Dracula. The character is a direct spoof of Edward Cullen from the Twilight franchise, right down to casting a British genre-film heartthrob (Daniel Radcliffe) in the role. Voiced by Daniel Radcliffe.

title: Dorothy
text: Dorothy is A minor recurring senior character residing at the Springfield Retirement Castle. Dorothy is an elderly woman confined to a wheelchair who lives at the Springfield Retirement Castle alongside other background senior characters. She has no significant personality traits explored in the show, functioning mainly as part of the retirement home's background cast. Her most notable moment comes from a mix-up where Grampa Simpson briefly confuses her with Jacqueline Bouvier. She appears sporadically across several episodes, often in minor or cameo roles, reinforcing the show's habit of populating the retirement castle with a variety of elderly extras. Dorothy doesn't drive any major plotlines herself but adds to the texture of the Retirement Castle setting. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Erik
text: Erik is A 5th-grade student at Springfield Elementary School and one of Bart's former playmates. Erik is a fifth-grader at Springfield Elementary whose scuffle with Bart during a dodgeball game sparks a full-blown rivalry between the fourth and fifth grades. The conflict takes an unexpected turn when Bart notices Erik has a matching scar on his hand, hinting at a shared past. It turns out their mothers, including Marge, once belonged to a clique called The Cool Moms who arranged playdates for their kids, making Erik one of Bart's old childhood friends. Once the moms reunite, so do their children, with Erik and the other kids egging Bart on to do risky and reckless stunts. Bart eventually works to break up the reunited group of kids, undoing the childhood connection. Erik's role is largely tied to this single storyline about rekindled friendships and peer pressure among the school kids. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Charlie (Oh Brother, Where Bart Thou?)
text: Charlie (Oh Brother, Where Bart Thou?) is A young orphan boy briefly adopted by Bart Simpson as a pretend younger brother. Charlie is an orphan from the Springfield Orphanage who impulsively follows Bart home after Bart is denied the chance to adopt a little brother. He quickly becomes Bart's partner in mischief, sharing his love of pranks and troublemaking, which makes the two an instant match. Despite this bond, Charlie's youth becomes apparent when he panics during a scary movie, showing he isn't quite as tough as Bart. He also proves surprisingly clever, using his innocent appearance to disarm Chief Wiggum and swipe his pepper spray during an escape attempt. After a chaotic series of adventures with Bart and a tense standoff with Lisa, Charlie is ultimately returned to the orphanage. He is later adopted by a family with six daughters, ending his brief but memorable stint as Bart's unofficial brother. Notably, he holds the distinction of being the only Simpsons character voiced by a child actor. Voiced by Jordan Nagai.

title: Disapproving squirrel
text: Disapproving squirrel is A one-time cartoon character within The Itchy & Scratchy Show, created as a parody response to Marge Simpson's protest. The disapproving squirrel is a satirical character created by the fictional Itchy & Scratchy production team as a direct jab at Marge Simpson, after she led a protest against the show's violent content. Visually and behaviorally modeled after Marge, the squirrel attempts to play the role of a moral voice, scolding Itchy and Scratchy for their violence. Her appearance in the cartoon is brief and ends in over-the-top gory slapstick, undercutting her disapproving message entirely. The joke lands as an in-universe mockery of Marge's activism, with Homer completely missing the reference while Marge is visibly irritated by it. Despite only appearing once, the character became a memorable example of the show's meta-commentary on censorship and parody. Voiced by Julie Kavner. Notable quotes: Don't do that! Don't do that! Hey! Don't DO that!
quotes: Don't do that! Don't do that! Hey! Don't DO that!

title: Poppin' Fresh
text: Poppin' Fresh is Non-speaking mascot character (based on the Pillsbury Doughboy) referenced in various Simpsons episodes. Poppin' Fresh is a background/mascot figure modeled after the real-world Pillsbury Doughboy, appearing mostly as a visual gag or hallucination rather than a fleshed-out character. He first shows up as a plush toy Homer clutches as a child in a flashback with his mother, Mona Simpson. Later, he becomes central to a comedic mix-up when an ether-addled Mr. Burns hallucinates Homer as Poppin' Fresh and unknowingly writes him a bowling team sponsorship check made out to the doughboy. This leads to an absurd investigation by Smithers using facial-matching technology to determine who impersonated the mascot. Poppin' Fresh also gets a mention as Clancy Wiggum's pet nickname for his wife Sarah, and appears in a list of "Famous Pale People" in a school presentation. He never speaks and exists purely as a running visual joke tied to mistaken identity and background pop-culture references. Notable quotes: to my pal, Poppin' Fresh
quotes: to my pal, Poppin' Fresh

title: Flint Drywall
text: Flint Drywall is A minor recurring fireman who appears after responding to emergencies at the Simpson family's house. Flint Drywall is a fireman shown responding to a fire at the Simpson home, one of many blazes caused by Homer's carelessness. He engages in some deadpan banter with a colleague named Gus about statistics on fires caused by birthday candles, showing a dry, matter-of-fact demeanor typical of background emergency responders in the show. He also reveals the surprising frequency of the fire department's visits to the Simpsons' house, highlighting the family's chaotic home life. In a non-canon appearance, he shows a more whimsical side, delighting in a fire hydrant turned into a chocolate fountain and eagerly using his helmet to collect the treat. Overall, he serves as a minor comedic figure emphasizing the Simpsons' accident-prone household. Voiced by Harry Shearer, Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Homer told him that one of those times, he accidentally dialed 9-1-1, so he set the house on fire so there would be a point in calling.
quotes: Homer told him that one of those times, he accidentally dialed 9-1-1, so he set the house on fire so there would be a point in calling.

title: Clyde (Pac-Man)
text: Clyde (Pac-Man) is Ghost character from the classic arcade game Pac-Man, appearing as a video game reference/crossover in The Simpsons. Clyde is one of the four ghosts from the classic arcade game Pac-Man, making cameo appearances within The Simpsons universe as a piece of video game pop culture. He first appears on screen when Mr. Burns is playing Ms. Pac-Man in his office. Later, he and the other ghosts show up dancing at the televised wedding of Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man during a fictional Super Bowl broadcast. He also appears alongside Pac-Man when the game is displayed on a screen after Homer disrupts a gaming World Championship by cutting the power. Beyond his in-show appearances, Clyde is also depicted on the cover art of the album Pacman Fever, referenced in supplementary Simpsons material. As a non-speaking character, he never has any dialogue and exists purely as a nostalgic nod to classic video games.

title: Fruit Bat Man
text: Fruit Bat Man is Superhero alter ego of Mr. Burns, a Batman parody. Fruit Bat Man is the costumed persona Mr. Burns adopts after buying up an entire comic book store and deciding to live out his childhood fantasy of being a superhero. Despite his frail, elderly body, his light weight lets him fly, and he relies heavily on his loyal butler Smithers to stage-manage his crime-fighting career behind the scenes. Much of his early heroics turn out to be rigged, with Smithers secretly paying off petty criminals like Snake and Apu so Burns can "win" without real danger. When a genuine crime arises involving Bart being framed by Groundskeeper Willie, Fruit Bat Man is forced into an authentic act of heroism and actually brings the culprit to justice. He later gains Smithers as an official sidekick and even considers recruiting Homer, then working as Duffman, for the role. In non-canon material he's shown teaming up with other aging heroes as a member of a group called The Dependables. The character is a clear parody of Batman, right down to his wealthy alter ego and self-styled crime-fighting mythology. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Walt Disney
text: Walt Disney is Real-world animator and entrepreneur referenced and parodied within the Simpsons universe. Walt Disney appears in the show mostly as a cultural reference point rather than an active character. He's cited by Dr. Hibbert as sharing an 'evil gene' with infamous figures like Adolf Hitler, which pokes fun at conspiracy theories surrounding him. Homer's confusion about Disney once being President highlights the show's running gag of Homer's ignorance of history. In non-canon material, he's depicted in a much stranger light, including a statue on an alien planet and a preserved, talking head kept by Mr. Burns, riffing on the popular urban legend that Disney's body was cryogenically frozen. This head gag is a direct homage to the head-in-a-jar humor from Futurama. Overall, Disney functions as a satirical touchstone for corporate legacy, media conspiracy, and old-Hollywood mythology. Notable quotes: Hey! What about me?
quotes: Hey! What about me?

title: Aiden Freemont
text: Aiden Freemont is A third-grade student at Springfield Elementary School.
