Aiden Freemont is a minor background student at Springfield Elementary School, appearing among the sea of children who populate the show's classroom scenes. He is a non-speaking character, existing mostly as a face in the crowd rather than a figure with any real personality traits explored on screen. His inclusion is largely a visual cameo, appearing in a picture and in an opening sequence gag rather than through active participation in an episode's plot. As such, he represents the show's tendency to fill out its world with named but undeveloped extras. There are no known relatives, defining quirks, or catchphrases attached to him.

title: Circe
text: Circe is A mythological sorceress parody appearing in the Odyssey segment of "Tales from the Public Domain". Circe is a mystical sorceress who rules over her own island, encountered by Odysseus and his crew during their journey home. She's outwardly hospitable, welcoming visitors with drink, but her hospitality hides a dark trick, since anyone who drinks from her cauldron is transformed into a pig. Despite this seemingly villainous act, she tries to warn and help Odysseus, giving him directions home to Ithaca and cautioning him about the dangerous path ahead through the Underworld. She's characterized by a calm, knowing demeanor even as chaos unfolds around her, including Odysseus obliviously eating his own transformed crew. In the non-canon segment "Greek to Me," she's shown with family ties, being the sister of Medusa and later attending Medusa's wedding to Polydectes. Her role blends dark comedy with mythological homage, tying into the show's parody of classic literature. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: You must first go through Hades, crossing the River Styx.
quotes: You must first go through Hades, crossing the River Styx.

title: Bill Cosby
text: Bill Cosby is Real-world celebrity comedian who appears as a minor recurring character in Springfield's pop culture references. Bill Cosby appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, referenced mainly through his real-world career as a comedian, author, and television personality. He's brought up in conversations about fame and success, such as when Homer considers him as an example of someone who got rich from an unlikely skill. His sitcom and talk show both make appearances or get mentioned within the Simpsons universe, blurring the line between the real Cosby and the show's world. He and his family are even shown competing for a spot on a reality TV series, though they lose out to the Simpsons themselves. Cosby's book on fatherhood becomes a recurring prop, first given to Homer as a gift and later seen being burned. Overall, he functions as a running pop-culture cameo rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Salvador Dalí
text: Salvador Dalí is Real-world Spanish painter referenced/depicted as a minor character in The Simpsons. Salvador Dalí appears in the show as a nod to the real-life surrealist artist rather than as a fully developed character. He is mentioned by Comic Book Guy during a song about cultural experiences, and briefly shown appearing at the end of that number. He also makes a silent appearance during a segment of the Krusty the Clown show. In another instance, a Dalí-themed balloon is featured in a parade celebrating highbrow artists in Capital City. He has no spoken lines in any of his appearances, functioning purely as a background or visual reference to real-world art culture.

title: Big Daddy
text: Big Daddy is Non-canon Cajun crime lord who appears in a Chief Wiggum spin-off segment, antagonist to Chief Wiggum and Ralph. Big Daddy is an extremely overweight Cajun crime boss who operates outside the normal Simpsons continuity, existing within a fictional spin-off show. His schemes are elaborate and oddly whimsical, including sending a fake alligator threat to Chief Wiggum and kidnapping Ralph, only to bond with the boy by teaching him to play the spoons. He has a taste for stolen luxury, using a pilfered governor's mansion as his personal hideout. In a later comic strip appearance, he's shown employing zombie-inducing gumbo to trick people into redecorating his estate, revealing a vain streak about his interior design. His downfall in that story comes when his own insults provoke Principal Skinner into shoving him out a window. Despite his menace, he tends to escape consequences, slipping away from the authorities each time. Voiced by Gailard Sartain.

title: Collette (Flaming Moe's)
text: Collette (Flaming Moe's) is A waitress hired by Moe at Flaming Moe's, appearing in the episode "Flaming Moe's". Collette is a minor character introduced during the brief glory days of Moe's rebranded bar, Flaming Moe's. She's sharp enough to figure out that Moe stole his famous cocktail recipe from Homer, and she uses that knowledge to push Moe toward doing the right thing by splitting the profits. Her relationship with Moe takes a personal turn after they sleep together, which only strengthens her resolve to get Homer his due credit. She vanishes from the story once Homer's drunken outburst spoils the big recipe sale, with Moe later giving a vague and unconvincing explanation for her disappearance. The character is essentially a sitcom homage, modeled after Diane Chambers from Cheers, mirroring that show's famous will-they-won't-not-they dynamic between two bar employees. Interestingly, she was originally voiced by a different actress before being redubbed for the final episode. Voiced by Jo Ann Harris.

title: Eliza
text: Eliza is A minor rival character to Lisa Simpson, an eight-year-old second grade student. Eliza is a young rival of Lisa's who appears alongside her brother Lester in a single episode. The pair unexpectedly outshine Bart and Lisa by saving the Itchy and Scratchy Studios before they can, earning gratitude from both Apu and Krusty for unrelated favors. Their success leaves Bart uneasy, hinting at a running gag where background or minor characters overshadow the main kids without explanation. Eliza doesn't speak in her appearance, fitting into the show's tradition of silent background characters who still get named and referenced. Interestingly, she shares her name with Lisa's ancestor Eliza Simpson, though this seems to be a coincidental nod rather than a connection. A lookalike character also appears earlier in the series' history, though it's likely unintentional since Eliza hadn't been created yet at that point.

title: Rosalind Franklin
text: Rosalind Franklin is Real-world historical scientist referenced/pictured in the show, not an active Simpsons character. Rosalind Franklin appears in the Simpsons universe purely as a historical reference rather than an active character. She was a real English chemist and X-ray crystallographer famed for her contributions to discovering the structure of DNA. In the show, Lisa cites her as an example of the Matilda effect, the phenomenon where female scientists are overlooked in favor of male colleagues, alongside Lise Meitner and Jocelyn Bell Burnell. She also turns up as a picture in Lori Spivak's house, underscoring her status as an inspirational figure rather than a speaking character. Since she never appears in person or speaks any dialogue, she functions more as an educational nod to real-world science history than a traditional Simpsons character.

title: Sigmund Freud
text: Sigmund Freud is Real-world historical figure referenced in the Simpsons universe as a famous psychoanalyst. Sigmund Freud appears in the show as a real-world historical figure rather than a fictional character created for the series. He is referenced as the founder of psychoanalysis, whose theories about childhood shaping the subconscious mind come up in discussions between characters like Ian and Bart. Homer also brings up Freud's name when trying to psychoanalyze Bart's fixation on Grampa's watch. Freud's image appears as a picture in at least one episode and he shows up briefly in a couch gag and a hallucination sequence. He functions mostly as a cultural touchstone the show uses for humor about psychology and self-analysis rather than as an active character in the plot. Notable quotes: Dr. Marvin Monroe is transmitted live from the home of Sigmund Freud, Vienna.
quotes: Dr. Marvin Monroe is transmitted live from the home of Sigmund Freud, Vienna.

title: Freedom
text: Freedom is A falcon owned by the character Diggs, associated with Bart Simpson. Freedom is a gray and white falcon belonging to Diggs, introduced through his role in the Springfield Elementary Falconry Club. He comes to Bart's aid by swooping in to attack Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney when they were bullying him, sparking a bond between Bart and the bird. Bart grows fond of watching Freedom fly and perform tricks, and even takes on caretaking duties when Diggs is hospitalized. Freedom's story concludes on a note of literal freedom, as Diggs releases him along with other falcons during a falconry contest rather than keeping them competitively confined. As a non-speaking animal character, Freedom's role is more symbolic and plot-driven than comedic, tied closely to themes of loyalty and liberation.

title: Cyborg Bart
text: Cyborg Bart is A non-canon cyborg version of Bart Simpson from a Treehouse of Horror segment. Cyborg Bart is the vengeful, mechanically-enhanced form Bart takes after being abandoned by his family in the woods. After falling into a coma from a failed roof-to-pool jump, Bart is replaced at home by a more obedient robotic boy named David, sparking jealousy and rivalry once Bart wakes up. Rather than resolve the tension fairly, Homer dumps Bart in the woods, leading him to scavenge parts from a group of defunct robots to rebuild himself as a cyborg. Driven by anger over being discarded, he returns home seeking violent revenge on both his robotic replacement and his father. His storyline plays into the show's Halloween tradition of dark, exaggerated parodies of family dysfunction. He later appeared as a collectible character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: There should be a law against abandoning your child!
quotes: There should be a law against abandoning your child!

title: Coltrane
text: Coltrane is The Simpson family's fourth cat, adopted by Lisa. Coltrane was a short-lived pet cat adopted by Lisa Simpson to replace the recently deceased Snowball III. He was named after jazz saxophonist John Coltrane, a fact that convinced Lisa to take him home despite her initial hesitation about getting another cat. Tragically, his time with the family was extremely brief, as playing his namesake's music apparently drove him to leap out a window to his death almost immediately after arriving. He was notable for being one of the few white-furred cats in the family's long line of pets, and he bore a passing resemblance to Bart. His death led to yet another of Lisa's memorial services, continuing the show's running gag of the family's cats meeting untimely ends. He later made a brief non-speaking cameo as a ghost in one of Bart's dream sequences. Notable quotes: We'll always have the ride home from the animal shelter.
quotes: We'll always have the ride home from the animal shelter.

title: Christmas Ape (character)
text: Christmas Ape (character) is A fictional ape character who exists within the Simpsons universe as the star of various in-universe movies and merchandise. Christmas Ape is a fictional simian celebrity within the Simpsons' pop-culture landscape, best known as the subject of the Troy McClure-directed film and later a holiday-themed movie called Christmas Ape's Miracle On Ice starring Valerie Bertinelli. His branding extends beyond film into novelty items, including a Christmas-themed audio album of ape-inspired holiday songs. He's more of a merchandising and media phenomenon than an active character, existing mostly through references to his fictional movies and collectibles rather than direct appearances. In one notable moment, Homer stumbles upon a physical version of Christmas Ape at the Bi-Mon-Sci-Fi Convention, discovering him having a tea party with baby Maggie in the daycare room. This quirky, unexpected scene highlights the character's whimsical, background presence in the show's expansive fictional universe of parody media and toys.

title: Fantastic Four
text: Fantastic Four is A superhero team referenced/parodied within the Simpsons universe, portrayed through costumes and magical transformations by main characters. The Fantastic Four aren't a distinct group of characters but rather a recurring costume/role-play concept that Springfield residents adopt. In one instance, Homer, Carl, Lenny, and Barney dress up as the team's members during a superhero-themed pub crawl, with Homer taking on The Thing's persona. In a non-canon Halloween segment, Lisa uses a magic stopwatch to transform her own family into the team, casting Homer as The Thing, Marge as the Human Torch, Bart as Mr. Fantastic, and Maggie as Invisible Woman. The joke largely relies on mixing and matching which family member gets which power, playing off their personalities. It's less about the Fantastic Four themselves and more a vehicle for costume gags and family dynamics in a superhero parody setting.

title: Chinnos
text: Chinnos is A supervillain from the fictional "Vindicators" superhero movie franchise within the Simpsons universe. Chinnos is a cosmic-level villain who serves as the primary antagonist of the in-universe film Vindicators: Crystal War. He seeks to acquire the Doomsday app so he can reshape the world into what he considers a utopia, even if that means turning everyone into crystal. Despite being seemingly defeated by having his head blown off by Airshot, he casually restores himself using an app on his phone, showing a blend of menace and absurd, tech-savvy resourcefulness. He later resurfaces in a virtual reality simulation built for Bart, trying to manipulate the boy into revealing movie spoilers in exchange for superpowers. Ultimately he's thwarted by Bart's cleverness with a slingshot and the combined might of the Vindicators. As a blatant parody of Marvel's Thanos, Chinnos embodies over-the-top blockbuster villainy with a satirical edge. Voiced by Kevin Feige.

title: Eczema
text: Eczema is A secret evil society within the Radioactive Man comic universe, led by Madame Eczema, serving as recurring villains against Radioactive Man and the Superior Squad. Eczema is a shadowy criminal organization that appears in the Radioactive Man comic book storylines referenced throughout The Simpsons universe. The group is ruled by the ruthless Madame Eczema, who clawed her way to leadership by eliminating those above her in the ranks. Eczema's schemes include exposing Radioactive Man's secret identity to the public and orchestrating an elaborate fake seance as a trap to capture the Superior Squad. Their plots tend to escalate toward dramatic, televised showdowns, though they are ultimately foiled when heroes intervene. The organization also employs dangerous agents like Eczematous-Prime to carry out assassinations. Eczema represents a persistent, comic-book style threat that ties together several chapters of the in-universe Radioactive Man mythology.

title: Dino
text: Dino is A crossover character from The Flintstones who appears in various forms within The Simpsons universe. Dino is not an original Simpsons character but a nod to the classic animated dinosaur pet owned by Fred Flintstone. Within the Simpsons world, he shows up only as an image or reference rather than a fully animated participant, appearing on items like Bart's Flintstone Phone and Homer's Flintstones-themed map. He's a purely visual crossover gag referencing the beloved prehistoric cartoon family. Dino has no dialogue and never physically interacts with the main Simpsons cast, existing solely as an Easter egg for fans of classic animation. In one darkly comedic touch, a stone age flashback even shows Fred Flintstone carrying Dino's dead body, playing on the show's willingness to twist nostalgic references for humor.

title: Cletus (I Married Marge)
text: Cletus (I Married Marge) is Minor one-off character, husband of Aline, appearing in a flashback in "I Married Marge". Cletus is a minor background character defined by his rough, working-class habits, notably drinking beer and smoking cigarettes. He appears briefly in a flashback centered on his wedding to Aline, officiated by Milford A. Alexander at Shotgun Pete's. His demeanor is laconic and unbothered, responding to his own wedding vows with a single casual word. Beyond his wedding appearance, he shows up in the background of a parenting class, suggesting he and Aline may have started a family. The character's name was later reused by the show's writers for the more prominent "slack-jawed yokel" character Cletus Spuckler, though the two are unrelated. Overall, this Cletus exists mostly as a quick visual gag and a piece of Simpsons trivia regarding character naming. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "yup"
quotes: "yup"

title: Mr. Fisk
text: Mr. Fisk is Minor recurring character; father of Eugene Fisk. Mr. Fisk is a minor Springfield resident best known as the father of Eugene Fisk. He appears to hold conservative, old-fashioned values, seeming uncomfortable with rowdier adult behavior. This is shown at his son's bachelor party, where he and Eugene alone are put off by the drinking, smoking, and arrival of a bellydancer. He's the type of dad who treasures small sentimental gestures, such as receiving a baseball glove as a Father's Day gift. He also makes brief public appearances around town, such as attending a children's miniature golf tournament. Overall, he's a background character whose few moments emphasize his prim, disapproving nature amid Springfield's chaos. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: "We're in Hell."
quotes: "We're in Hell."

title: Easter Bunny
text: Easter Bunny is A minor holiday-themed background character associated with Easter in the Simpsons universe. The Easter Bunny is a fictional rabbit figure tied to the Easter holiday, mostly appearing in background gags, mentions, and non-canon material rather than as a fleshed-out character. In the show's canon, Homer once took on the role of the Easter Bunny for the mayor's egg roll, and there was even a fictional in-universe Christmas movie about the character. In non-canon material, the character shows up in odder contexts, such as being part of a church collection, getting into a midair fight with the Leprechaun, or being impersonated by Bart while chased by chicks. A running joke acknowledges that, unlike some other holiday icons in the show, the Easter Bunny is explicitly stated not to be real. The character never speaks and functions purely as a recurring visual or referential gag rather than a developed personality.

title: CJ
text: CJ is A minor character who appears as a pro bidder on the in-universe TV show Storage Battles, watched by Homer. CJ is a minor, in-universe television personality rather than a member of the core cast. He works as a professional bidder on the fictional reality show Storage Battles, which Homer is shown watching on TV. There's little characterization beyond his role on this show-within-a-show, making him more of a background gag than a developed character. He later resurfaces as a collectible figure in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, tied to an auction-themed event. His appearances are limited to a single episode and the game, giving him a very small footprint in the franchise overall. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Database's mother
text: Database's mother is Mother of Database, a minor recurring character in the Simpsons universe. Database's mother is a minor, non-speaking background character known mainly through her connection to her son, Database. She has brown hair and appears to be a fairly ordinary parent within the show's extended universe of side characters. Her most notable moment involves attending a family outing, the Bounce-A-Thon, alongside her husband and son, suggesting she's a supportive and present parent. Beyond this, little else is revealed about her personality or role, as she functions largely as a background presence rather than a driver of storylines. She appears across multiple later-season episodes, indicating she's part of the show's ongoing rotation of recurring, low-profile characters.

title: Cregg Demon
text: Cregg Demon is A minor recurring magician character who briefly ran for Parliament in Canada. Cregg Demon is a flashy, self-promoting stage magician whose gaudy showmanship and appearance earn scorn from the more traditional Great Raymondo. His signature stunt involves supposedly descending into Hell to retrieve a woman, whose phone number he then has tattooed on himself and his audience. He later manipulates Lisa Simpson through his own son in order to learn the secret behind Houdini's famous milk can escape trick, which nearly gets him killed when rival magicians sabotage his equipment. After being rescued, he dramatically announces he's quitting magic to pursue politics in Canada, but this proves short-lived since he's later spotted performing again on a cruise ship. He's essentially a parody of real-life illusionist Criss Angel, right down to his over-the-top catchphrase branding. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Harlan Ellison (character)
text: Harlan Ellison (character) is Real-life author and screenwriter who appeared as himself in a guest role on The Simpsons. Harlan Ellison appears as a fictionalized version of himself, the famous real-world speculative fiction writer. He is shown waiting in line at the Android's Dungeon for a new comic book release, where he gets into a confrontation with Milhouse. His reputation as a writer is referenced later when Comic Book Guy cites one of his stories as an example of an 'imaginary story,' implying Ellison penned it deliberately to get himself fired from a writing job. This nod plays on Ellison's real history of clashing with studios and editors. He is a minor recurring character rather than a core member of the Simpsons universe, existing mainly as a cameo tied to comic book culture in Springfield. Voiced by Harlan Ellison.

title: Freddy (student)
text: Freddy (student) is A minor recurring student at Springfield Elementary School and classmate of Bart Simpson. Freddy is a background kid who attends Springfield Elementary and appears in Bart's class across many episodes. He's mostly known for small, incidental moments rather than a defined personality, such as being the one who received a copy of an embarrassing photo of Homer, which he passed along and caused a chain of trouble for the family. His design is inconsistent from appearance to appearance, with his skin color oddly shifting between yellow and brown in different episodes. Fans have speculated he might have a twin sister, since a similar-looking girl sits next to him in one episode and is also part of Bart's class. Despite his minimal role, he has shown up repeatedly throughout the show's run as well as in Simpsons comics and books. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Mr. Clark
text: Mr. Clark is Father of Lewis Clark, husband of Mrs. Clark, and a minor recurring parent/staff member connected to Springfield Elementary School. Mr. Clark is a background parent figure in Springfield, best known as the father of Bart's occasional friend Lewis. He's been shown attending church and various family outings with his wife, suggesting a fairly ordinary domestic life. He appears to have some connection to Springfield Elementary, having been spotted in the teachers' lounge and collecting students' cell phones, though it's unclear if teaching is his main profession. He also reportedly works security, once guarding celebrity James Corden from an angry public. Mr. Clark is a non-speaking character, existing mostly on the sidelines of episodes as a recurring but minor presence. In a non-canon storyline, his marriage was rumored to be ending, adding a bit of unexpected drama to his otherwise unremarkable background role.

title: Duff Cowboy
text: Duff Cowboy is A giant advertising mascot for Duff Beer that briefly comes to life in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Duff Cowboy is a towering neon billboard mascot for Duff Beer that exists in the non-canon Treehouse of Horror universe. He springs to life during a bizarre ionic disturbance caused after Homer steals a giant donut from atop the Lard Lad Donuts sign, which somehow animates the town's advertising icons. At first the massive cowboy figure delights onlookers with his sheer scale, but he quickly turns dangerous, smashing bystanders with his oversized neon beer bottle prop. He becomes one of several rampaging mascots that plunge Springfield into chaos alongside other animated advertisements. Like the rest of the living billboards, he is ultimately defeated not through force but by the town simply losing interest and ignoring him, which drains his power and causes him to collapse. He has no spoken lines, functioning purely as a visual horror-comedy threat in the segment.

title: Cap'n Crunch
text: Cap'n Crunch is Cereal mascot character who appears in Homer's imagination and various Simpsons media. Cap'n Crunch is a fictional cereal mascot who exists mostly as a figure of Homer's imagination and pop culture references within the show. He's depicted as a gruff, authoritative figure, fitting for Homer's fantasy of him as a great military leader dispensing crunchy wisdom. His appearances are brief and often played for comedic effect, tying into Homer's obsession with cereal and junk food. In one grim twist, he meets a violent end at Bart's hands within a video game called Cereal Killer, poking fun at his own mascot status. Despite being a background gag character, he's been referenced or imagined enough times to be considered a recurring bit in the show's universe. His fictional status is listed as deceased, likely tied to his death in the video game scenario. Voiced by Maurice LaMarche. Notable quotes: "Stay crunchy in milk," Cap'n Crunch
quotes: "Stay crunchy in milk," Cap'n Crunch

title: Cookie (Dude, Where's My Ranch?)
text: Cookie (Dude, Where's My Ranch?) is An elderly rancher and employee at the Lazy I Ranch who interacts with the Simpson family during their stay. Cookie is an aging ranch hand the Simpsons encounter during a family trip to the Lazy I Ranch. He's a bit odd and old-fashioned, offering Marge one of his own teeth as a greeting instead of a normal handshake. Despite his eccentricities, he shows a domestic side by cooking a meal for the family to share at a picnic. He's also shown to be capable of rougher, rural tasks, such as preparing to kill a chicken he'd tied up, which unsettles young onlookers. Cookie enthusiastically joins in on the ranch's farewell dance despite tiring himself out, and ends up sharing sleeping quarters with the Simpsons, leading to a minor mix-up when Lisa tries to use his bunk. Interestingly, he shares his appearance and voice with an unrelated one-off character, the last registered Democrat, from an earlier episode. Voiced by Karl Wiedergott.

title: Cheery Red Tomatoes
text: Cheery Red Tomatoes is A women's social club in Springfield that Marge Simpson briefly joins. The Cheery Red Tomatoes are a Springfield women's society clearly modeled on the real-world Red Hat Society, complete with age-based dress codes for members. Led by Tammy, the group provides a social outlet for women, including Marge Simpson, who joins after being shunned by her usual friends. Their activities take an unexpectedly criminal turn when they pull off a heist targeting Mr. Burns' Faberge eggs, after which the group disbands and its members scatter. Agnes Skinner is also among its members, alongside several unnamed women rounding out the group. The club later gets a strange afterlife cameo, appearing among the portraits of Ned Flanders' deceased wives in one of Bart's coma dreams.

title: Database's father
text: Database's father is Minor recurring background character; father of Database, a Springfield Elementary student. Database's father is a minor, largely background figure known mainly through his connection to his son. He joined Ned Flanders and other Springfield fathers on a road trip in Flanders' RV to retrieve their sons from Shelbyville. He later appeared alongside his son at a school fundraising event called Drowning in Debt for Springfield Elementary. He has no recorded dialogue, functioning purely as a non-speaking character. Little else is known about his personality or life beyond these brief appearances. His presence mostly serves to round out the ensemble of Springfield parents.

title: T. R. Francis
text: T. R. Francis is Fictional author credited with the Angelica Button fantasy book series, popular in Springfield. T. R. Francis is presented to the public as the celebrated author behind the massively popular Angelica Button fantasy novels, a series adored by both kids and grown-ups in Springfield. She serves as a sly parody of J.K. Rowling, mirroring the real-world phenomenon of Harry Potter. When Lisa finally corners her at the Duff Center Arena, the truth comes out: T. R. Francis is not a real writer at all, just a hired actress used to put a face on the book jackets. In reality, the Angelica Button stories are churned out collectively by executives in corporate board meetings, exposing the commercialized, ghostwritten nature of the franchise. Notably, her depicted appearance is inconsistent between episodes, appearing as an old woman in one and a different actress in another, highlighting the show's own joke about the character's fabricated identity. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Donna
text: Donna is A minor student character at Springfield Elementary School. Donna is a background student at Springfield Elementary known for her rebellious streak and pink hair. She hangs out with fellow troublemaker Tammy, and the two are shown smoking cigarettes in the school's bathroom reserved for bad girls. Donna and Tammy try to rope Lisa Simpson into their mischief, both by suggesting a prank on Principal Skinner and by offering her a cigarette, though Lisa ultimately declines their company in favor of her own antics. She later appears among the student body during Science Week, laughing along with her classmates at Bart's infamous Buttzilla prank. Overall, Donna serves as one of the show's many minor delinquent schoolkids who add flavor to Springfield Elementary's student body without playing a central role in the plot. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Countess Dracula
text: Countess Dracula is Non-canon vampire character, wife of Count Dracula, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment. Countess Dracula is a minor, non-canon monster character who exists within the horror-themed universe of the show's Halloween specials. She is introduced as the spouse of Count Dracula, and her only notable moment comes from catching her husband flirting with other women at a party. Enraged by his infidelity, she retaliates by attacking him, showing a jealous and vengeful streak fitting her vampiric nature. Beyond this brief appearance, she has little characterization and is mostly referenced rather than featured. She later appears as a collectible character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, grouped among other vampire-themed characters. Her presence in the show's canon is otherwise limited to a passing mention in a later episode. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Guy Fieri
text: Guy Fieri is Real-world celebrity chef who appears as a caricature/cameo in The Simpsons universe. Guy Fieri is depicted in the show as the real-life restaurateur, author, and television personality he is in reality, appearing mostly in surreal or exaggerated contexts rather than as a grounded character. He first shows up in one of Marge's dreams, comically bouncing on top of fellow chef Paul Prudhomme while trailing after Homer. Later he's portrayed as part of the wealthy inner circle that Mr. Burns assembles around Persephone Odair, suggesting his status as a celebrity businessman. He's also used as a punchline reference point, with Marge comparing a lost-seeming Ned Flanders to Guy Fieri stripped of his 'bold flavors.' As a non-speaking recurring character, he functions purely as a cameo/reference rather than a fleshed-out personality within the show.

title: Ned Flanders I
text: Ned Flanders I is Non-canon ancestor of Ned Flanders; a corrupt sheriff of Springfield in a past-set flashback storyline. Ned Flanders I was the grandfather of the modern-day Ned Flanders, presented as a lawman with a stern moral code learned from nuns at an orphanage. Despite his tough talk about earning goodness the hard way, he turns out to be deeply corrupt, taking bribes from the Szyslak Brothers and indulging in gambling and drugs behind his badge. His story spirals into violence when a mob deal goes wrong, leading him to kill one gangster over hidden money and later die accidentally by falling onto another man's knife. The stolen money he hid remains lost for decades until his grandson unknowingly recovers it and donates it to an orphanage in his name, ironically restoring his reputation. He serves as a dark, noir-style twist on the Flanders family history, showing a hypocritical contrast to Ned's own wholesome nature. Voiced by Timothy Olyphant. Notable quotes: "death to pigs, except you, man!" | "the harder the good, the better the man."
quotes: "death to pigs, except you, man!"
"the harder the good, the better the man."

title: Morgan Freeman
text: Morgan Freeman is Real-life actor, director, and narrator who appears as a celebrity guest character in The Simpsons. Morgan Freeman appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, often used for his iconic deep narrating voice. He is portrayed voicing over dramatic moments, such as praising Homer's apology as one of the greatest of all time. Other characters reference him as a cultural shorthand for gravitas, comparing an imaginary friend's comforting presence to his role in Driving Miss Daisy, and even joking that God's voice sounds like his. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he meets a gruesome fate as part of a macabre celebrity death display. In another non-canon appearance, he acts as an ominous warning figure, cautioning a documentary narrator against narrating a penguin segment due to a supposed curse linked to Happy Feet. Across his appearances, he's treated as a legendary, almost mythic voice of authority and doom. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Doe-Eyed Boys
text: Doe-Eyed Boys is A fictional Australian boy band appearing in an episode of The Simpsons. The Doe-Eyed Boys are a manufactured Australian boy band consisting of four members named Bindi, Boz, McQuarrie, and Wadonga. Like many fictional pop acts in the show's universe, they are portrayed as not actually singing or performing live, poking fun at manufactured pop stardom. Their claim to fame in the show is performing the song "LV U 4 Ever" at a concert attended by Homer, Lisa, and the Jambowski siblings. A running joke connects them to a broader conspiracy theory involving hidden subliminal messaging, tying them to other fictional boy bands like the Party Posse through the recurring "Yvan Eht Nioj" gag. They also make a non-canon appearance as a poster on Lisa's bedroom wall, suggesting she was a fan of theirs as a teenager.

title: Guillermo del Toro (character)
text: Guillermo del Toro (character) is Real-world filmmaker who appears as himself in a guest appearance on the show. Guillermo del Toro appears as a fictionalized version of himself, the famous Mexican filmmaker, author, actor, and former special effects makeup artist. He is enlisted by Mr. Burns to produce a short film intended to help Burns escape legal trouble. True to his real-life reputation, the film he creates centers on his passion for monsters, though he also weaves in praise for Burns himself, ultimately succeeding in its persuasive goal. He is later referenced as having contributed to the design of Moe Szyslak for an in-universe show. His appearances are brief and cameo-like, playing on his real-world creative persona rather than establishing him as a recurring personality within Springfield. Voiced by Guillermo del Toro (Himself).

title: Larry Davis
text: Larry Davis is Lead singer of the band The Larry Davis Experience, a recurring minor character in Springfield. Larry Davis fronts a local band called The Larry Davis Experience, appearing occasionally as a musical performer in Springfield's background scene. He's a fairly minor, easily forgettable figure who pops up at various events without much development to his personality beyond his role as a performer. His most memorable moment comes from a party where he jokingly hypes up his band's connection to a member of a famous act. Despite his limited screen time, he's appeared across many episodes since the show's first season, cementing him as a recurring but low-key part of the show's world. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: OK, everybody, who likes the Doobie Brothers? 'Cause we've got one of them.
quotes: OK, everybody, who likes the Doobie Brothers? 'Cause we've got one of them.

title: Fritz
text: Fritz is One of the German businessmen who briefly bought the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. Fritz is a minor recurring character who, alongside Hans and Horst, purchased the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant from Mr. Burns in an attempt to run it more efficiently. He and his partners quickly discovered that maintaining the plant was far more costly and dangerous than anticipated, leading them to sell it back to Burns. Fritz has a dismissive attitude toward American culture, notably criticizing American beer as inferior to what he's used to. Years later he appears to have taken a job at a geriatric medical center alongside Hans, suggesting a shift away from the energy business. A continuity quirk sees his hair color change between appearances, which fans debate as either an animation error or an intentional dye job. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Elsa
text: Elsa is Crossover character from Disney's Frozen, appearing in various Simpsons costumes, fantasies, and Disney-related crossover episodes. Elsa is the former queen and princess from Disney's Frozen who appears in The Simpsons purely as a crossover figure rather than a fully developed character in her own right. She never speaks in her appearances, instead showing up as a costume worn by other characters like Patty, or as a role played by Janey in one of Principal Skinner's fantasies. Lisa also dons an Elsa costume in a couch gag, tying into her recurring desire to be a princess. Elsa's more 'real' appearances come in Disney-branded specials, where she uses her ice magic at a Disney+ anniversary party and joins her family, including her mother Queen Iduna and sister Anna, on a Mother's Day outing. A statue of her also appears outside a castle Lisa visits while chasing her princess dreams. Overall, Elsa functions as a fun nod to Disney fandom rather than a character with her own arc on the show.

title: Frankenscratchy
text: Frankenscratchy is A cartoon-within-the-show character; Scratchy's Frankenstein's Monster persona in an Itchy & Scratchy Show episode. Frankenscratchy is a version of Scratchy cast as Frankenstein's Monster within the cartoon-within-a-cartoon world of The Itchy & Scratchy Show. He was stitched together from spare body parts by the sadistic Mad Doctor Itchy, who treats his own creation less like a companion and more like a punching bag. Despite the violence inflicted upon him, Frankenscratchy retains the same gentle, shy, and friendly demeanor that defines Scratchy in his other roles. His storyline is a direct parody of the classic 1931 Frankenstein film, complete with a lightning-powered resurrection and an ill-fated encounter with a little girl by a lake. He later appears as a collectible character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out video game during a Treehouse of Horror event. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: David (Treehouse of Horror XVI)
text: David (Treehouse of Horror XVI) is A robot boy purchased by Homer and Marge as a replacement son for Bart in a Treehouse of Horror segment. David is a non-canon android child created by the fictional retailer Boys R Us, bought by Homer and Marge while Bart was lying in a coma. Designed to be the perfect son, he behaves impeccably and comes equipped with handy extra features, like turning old clothing into toys. His good behavior quickly makes him more appealing to the Simpsons than the real Bart, creating tension once Bart wakes up. Feeling threatened by his mechanical replacement, Bart ultimately destroys David to eliminate the competition. The character is a parody homage to the robotic boy from the film A.I. Artificial Intelligence. His appearance is limited to a segment of Treehouse of Horror XVI, plus a brief cameo in a later opening sequence. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Elvis Costello (character)
text: Elvis Costello (character) is Real-world English musician who appears as himself, running an instrument shack at a rock camp Homer attends. Elvis Costello appears as a fictionalized version of himself, working as the manager of his own instrument shack at The Rolling Stones' Rock N' Roll Fantasy Camp. He tries to keep order among aspiring musicians by suggesting some play bass instead of guitar, an idea that goes over poorly with Homer. He later takes part in a charity concert alongside other rock stars, where Homer's antics cause chaos and even a fire. Despite the mishap, Costello is gracious enough to apologize to Homer afterward and invite him to perform again, showing a good-natured side beneath his rockstar exterior. He's also referenced elsewhere as being considered one of the 'cutest vegetarians' by Lisa, and is the subject of a running mix-up where Homer confuses him with comedian Lou Costello. Voiced by Elvis Costello (himself).

title: Colette (A Serious Flanders)
text: Colette (A Serious Flanders) is Non-canon villain from "A Serious Flanders"; a debt collector working for Costas Becker and wife of Seamus. Colette is a ruthless debt collector who works alongside her husband Seamus for the criminal Costas Becker. She is shown to be violent and impulsive, willing to destroy property and kill without hesitation to get results. Despite her hard exterior, she has a softer side, enjoying simple pleasures like cooking and watching the show Property Brothers. Her relationship with Seamus is turbulent, swinging between deep affection and violent arguments, often over their lack of vacations and constant work. This volatile marriage ultimately leads to their darkly comedic demise. Colette's story serves as a subplot in the non-canon special "A Serious Flanders," adding dark humor to the show's crime narrative. Voiced by Jessica Paré.

title: Dwight Diddlehopper
text: Dwight Diddlehopper is A bank-robbing criminal who takes Marge Simpson hostage during a heist and subsequent escape. Dwight Diddlehopper is a desperate, volatile criminal whose crime spree becomes personal after he strikes up a brief conversation with Marge in a bank line just before robbing it. His abandonment issues surface when he forces Marge to take him to the theme park where his mother left him as a child, revealing a more tragic, wounded side beneath his violent behavior. Despite his menace, he shows a flash of heroism by saving Chief Wiggum during a chaotic amusement park confrontation. He's also unpredictable and emotionally erratic, swinging between threats of violence and moments of surprising tenderness, like the sentimental soap carving he gives Marge. His exaggerated bulging eyes are a visual gag referencing his voice actor Steve Buscemi. Beyond his main appearance, he later shows up as a background reference in an imagined alternate storyline involving Homer and Marge. Voiced by Steve Buscemi.

title: Dick Cheney
text: Dick Cheney is Real-world politician (46th U.S. Vice President) who appears as a recurring caricature character in the show. Dick Cheney is depicted as a sinister, power-obsessed figure living in a heavily fortified, laser-guarded compound. He briefly employs Smithers after Mr. Burns is thought to be dead, using him for odd, cruel tasks like pulling wings off bees out of boredom. He expresses an unsettling hope for terrorist attacks so he can stay informed, and manipulates Smithers with fear of being seen as letting Al Qaeda win before erasing his memory. His legacy is mocked through an animatronic in a Vice Presidents hall and a musical about his life, as well as a comic book pitting him against a superhero. Even Mr. Burns regards him as a nearly immortal, unsettling figure. Overall, he's portrayed as a darkly comic symbol of political menace and dry humor about real-world politics. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Cheney then said that if Smithers left, he would feel that Al Qaeda had won. | Mr. Burns said that nobody lives forever, except Dick Cheney.
quotes: Cheney then said that if Smithers left, he would feel that Al Qaeda had won.
Mr. Burns said that nobody lives forever, except Dick Cheney.

title: Eve
text: Eve is Biblical figure referenced/appearing in various Simpsons episodes and dream sequences; wife of Adam and mother of Cain and Abel. Eve is a biblical character occasionally referenced or depicted in The Simpsons, usually in throwaway jokes, dream sequences, or background art rather than as a regular presence. She's portrayed as the first woman, created from Adam's rib, and mother to Cain and Abel. Various characters bring her up in offhand comments, such as Bart's joke about bookkeeping or Rev. Lovejoy's comparison of his marriage to Adam and Eve's. In one of Marge's dreams, she plays a more active role, being tempted by a serpent into eating a forbidden apple and later getting caught trying to sneak back into Eden with Adam's help. She doesn't have a consistent personality across appearances since she's mostly used as a symbolic or joke reference rather than a fleshed-out character. Her most notable non-canon appearance is in the parody of the Garden of Eden story. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: Humpty Dumpty
text: Humpty Dumpty is Nursery rhyme character occasionally referenced or depicted in Springfield media and attractions. Humpty Dumpty is the classic egg-shaped nursery rhyme figure who famously falls from a wall and can't be repaired, and in the Simpsons universe he pops up mostly as a background reference rather than a fully realized character. He appears as a decorative figure at Storytown Village and as scenery in a non-canon Itchy & Scratchy miniature golf game. Bart twists his story into a corporate motivational lesson about staying focused to avoid falling off the wall. He's also invoked humorously in conversations, such as when Homer is compared to him or reimagined as a grotesque cracked-egg alter ego. In a non-canon short, he gets a full comedic treatment, recklessly rocking on a wall despite warnings before deliberately leaping off, leading to a dark joke about eating him. Overall, he functions as a recurring pop-culture in-joke and cameo rather than a personality-driven character. Notable quotes: He could see Heaven if he leaned back, Humpty Dumpty said, and started rocking. | Humpty Dumpty then threw himself off the wall, saying that he could fly. | Lenny said to tell them to bring the bacon.
quotes: He could see Heaven if he leaned back, Humpty Dumpty said, and started rocking.
Humpty Dumpty then threw himself off the wall, saying that he could fly.
Lenny said to tell them to bring the bacon.

title: Mrs. Claus
text: Mrs. Claus is Wife of Santa Claus, a minor holiday-themed character in the Simpsons universe. Mrs. Claus is a rarely seen figure tied to the Simpsons' Christmas mythology, existing mostly as a passing reference rather than an active character. She's mentioned when Homer, disguised as a mall Santa, jokes about her sisters overstaying their visit, hinting at some domestic tension in the Claus household. In non-canon material, she's depicted in a cheeky pinup-style painting by a young Abe Simpson on the side of Santa's sleigh, giving her a mischievous, playful edge outside the main continuity. She also appears as a character within The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game during holiday events. Overall, she serves as a lighthearted nod to the classic Santa Claus mythos rather than a fully developed personality within the show. Notable quotes: "Naughty or Nice"
quotes: "Naughty or Nice"

title: Estelle
text: Estelle is A minor student at Springfield High School in 1974, briefly connected to Barney Gumble. Estelle is a background character from Springfield High School's class of 1974, appearing only in a flashback context. She shares a detention session with a young Barney Gumble, who works up the nerve to ask her to the prom. Rather than accepting, she rebuffs him with a sharp, dismissive remark, showing little patience or interest in him. Estelle doesn't have much development beyond this single interaction, existing mainly as a footnote in Barney's teenage romantic failures. Her brief appearance underscores the show's frequent gag of Barney's bad luck with women even before his adult struggles with alcoholism and love. Voiced by Maggie Roswell. Notable quotes: Hi, Estelle? Will you go to the prom with me? | I wouldn't go to the prom with you if you were {{Ch|Elliott Gould}}.
quotes: Hi, Estelle? Will you go to the prom with me?
I wouldn't go to the prom with you if you were {{Ch|Elliott Gould}}.

title: Frankie the Squealer
text: Frankie the Squealer is Low-level member of the Springfield Mafia and associate of Fat Tony. Frankie the Squealer is a small-time Mafia associate whose defining trait is his complete inability to keep secrets. He blabs about Mafia business because doing so makes him feel important, despite the fact that his loose lips constantly land him in trouble. He's repeatedly beaten, kidnapped, and mistreated by enforcers Legs and Louie as punishment for his indiscretion, yet the Springfield Mafia keeps him around anyway. In one dream sequence, his ghost appears to Bart Simpson seeking help to move on to the afterlife, asking Bart to take violent action against several other mobsters. He's a recurring, mostly comic background figure representing the Mafia's own dysfunction and incompetence. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Matt Dillon (Gunsmoke)
text: Matt Dillon (Gunsmoke) is Non-canon parody character; U.S. Marshal of Dodge City and the main character of the show-within-a-show "Gunsmoke", appearing in a Simpsons opening sequence parody. Matt Dillon is a spoof of the iconic lawman from the classic western series Gunsmoke, brought into The Simpsons universe as part of a parody opening sequence. He appears as a stoic, duty-bound marshal facing off in a classic western showdown. His only real function in the show is to be gunned down in a fast draw, referencing and mocking the record-breaking nature of the Gunsmoke franchise. The gag plays on Simpsons' own longevity by having this fictional lawman lose his own long-standing record. He's treated as non-canon, existing purely as a meta joke about television history rather than a real Springfield resident. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Can't let you do it, can't let you break my record.
quotes: Can't let you do it, can't let you break my record.

title: Cooder
text: Cooder is A carnival worker (carny) and father of Spud, who briefly caused chaos for the Simpson family. Cooder is a grizzled, gray-haired carny who travels the fairground circuit running games like ring toss alongside his son Spud. He's crafty and manipulative, willing to exploit a situation to his own advantage, as shown when he and Spud manage to trick the Simpsons out of their own home. Despite his shady dealings, he eventually gets outwitted himself when the Simpsons cheat their way back into their house. Cooder has a bizarre physical party trick involving making a cigarette travel through his body and emerge from unusual places, and he can also pop out his own eye. He appears sporadically across the show's run, usually in carnival or fair settings, showing he never really leaves the carny lifestyle behind. The character was designed to resemble former Simpsons showrunner David Mirkin. Voiced by Jim Varney.

title: Dennis Franz (character)
text: Dennis Franz (character) is Real-world actor who appears as himself in a Simpsons-universe TV movie, playing Homer Simpson. Dennis Franz is a real actor, famous for playing Detective Andy Sipowicz on NYPD Blue, who appears in the Simpsons universe as himself. He is cast to portray Homer Simpson in a tabloid TV movie dramatizing the babysitter sexual harassment scandal that engulfs Homer. His performance leans into exaggerated melodrama, showing Homer as a reckless, menacing driver who terrorizes a babysitter. The bit is a parody of sensationalist true-crime reenactment shows rather than a serious character study. Beyond this main appearance, his likeness turns up as a framed photo in a couple of other episodes, tying him loosely into the show's background scenery of celebrity references. He has no ongoing personality traits within the show beyond this single satirical portrayal. Voiced by Dennis Franz. Notable quotes: "If you keep it up, I'll yell so loud the whole country will hear!"
quotes: "If you keep it up, I'll yell so loud the whole country will hear!"

title: Courtney (The Incredible Lightness of Being a Baby)
keys: courtney (the incredible lightness of being a baby)
text: Courtney (The Incredible Lightness of Being a Baby) is Mother of Hudson; an acquaintance of Marge Simpson met through a playdate for their babies. Courtney is a wealthy, image-conscious mother who first crosses paths with the Simpsons when her son Hudson takes a liking to Maggie at the park. She arranges a playdate with Marge but quickly reveals herself to be judgmental and overbearing, grilling Marge with invasive questions about vaccinations, allergies, and even sexual history. Courtney is quick to criticize other parenting styles, taking issue with Maggie's pacifier habit and her hairstyle, which strains her budding friendship with Marge. Her snobbish, high-society lifestyle is exemplified by her extravagant home, complete with a floor salvaged from an old Venetian church and reassembled by a famous elderly architect. Despite the friction, she and Marge eventually manage to set aside their differences for the sake of their children's happiness. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Brother Faith
text: Brother Faith is A traveling faith healer who runs a revival show and appears occasionally in Springfield. Brother Faith is a charismatic traveling preacher who claims to have healing powers, performing at revival meetings in Springfield. He notably assisted in freeing Homer from a bucket stuck on his head, and in doing so identified a supposed gift in Bart, inadvertently launching the boy's brief career as a faith healer. Beyond his live shows, he also hosts his own religious television program, which has attracted at least one dedicated viewer in Ned Flanders. His public persona blends showmanship with religious healing, and his broadcasts feature dramatic, almost miraculous demonstrations mixed with questionable outcomes for his followers. He has also been seen attending community events, showing he's a recognized figure within Springfield's social and religious circles. Voiced by Don Cheadle.

title: Ted Flanders
text: Ted Flanders is Ned Flanders' cousin who briefly moved into the house next door to the Simpsons. Ted Flanders is a minor member of the extended Flanders family who takes up residence at 740 Evergreen Terrace after the previous occupant, Sideshow Bob posing as Walt Warren, gets arrested. He is the cousin of Ned Flanders and father to daughters Bonnie and Connie. What stands out most about Ted is how closely he mirrors Ned, sharing both his cousin's distinctive appearance and his folksy manner of speaking. His introduction plays on the show's tendency to explore the Flanders extended family and their quirky uniformity. Ted has only appeared in one episode, making him a very minor recurring character, though he has also shown up in the mobile game Tapped Out. Little else about his personality or job is detailed beyond his resemblance to Ned. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Chris (Moms I'd Like to Forget)
text: Chris (Moms I'd Like to Forget) is Minor recurring character; husband of one of The Cool Moms. Chris is a background father figure connected to the group known as The Cool Moms, married to Anita and father to Erik. He comes across as somewhat irritable about the social obligations tied to his wife's friend group, showing little patience for spending time with the other husbands. His main character trait is a kind of weary reluctance toward forced socializing, which he expresses bluntly rather than politely. Beyond his brief appearance at a gathering of the moms and their families, he later turns up at Quiet Rivers, suggesting some ongoing connection to the community. Overall, Chris is a minor, largely functional character used to round out the ensemble of parents in the show's background. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Emil
text: Emil is A minor recurring resident of the Springfield Retirement Castle. Emil is an elderly background character who lives at the Springfield Retirement Castle. He's one of the many seniors Homer becomes acquainted with during his time visiting the facility. Emil is typically seen in the company of another resident named Hester. As a non-speaking character, he has no distinct personality traits or memorable dialogue, existing mainly as part of the retirement home's ensemble cast. He has appeared briefly across several episodes spanning multiple seasons, usually in group scenes with other elderly residents. In a non-canon appearance, he was shown among the other seniors during a musical number about financial hardship.

title: Ellen DeGeneres (character)
text: Ellen DeGeneres (character) is Real-world celebrity guest character based on comedian and talk show host Ellen DeGeneres, who appears in cameo roles in the Simpsons universe. This character is a fictionalized version of the real Ellen DeGeneres, appearing periodically as a celebrity cameo within the show. She's first introduced meeting the Simpson family in Hollywood alongside her girlfriend Anne Heche, grounding her early appearance in a real-life relationship of the actress. Later she pops up as a judge on American Idol, where she's portrayed as delightfully scatterbrained, veering off into a rambling tangent about a classic rock song, nuts, and a comic strip before abruptly breaking into dance. Her image and presence recur in small ways throughout the series, such as a photo hanging in a restaurant or a spotting in the Oscars audience. She's also referenced by Marge as an example of a public figure whose beloved image could be shattered by hidden, less flattering truths coming to light. Overall, she serves as a quick pop-culture nod rather than a deeply developed character. Voiced by Maggie Roswell (later voiced by Ellen DeGeneres herself).

title: Zooey Deschanel (character)
text: Zooey Deschanel (character) is A non-canon guest appearance by actress Zooey Deschanel, playing herself in a Simpsons special. This version of Zooey Deschanel is a non-canon cameo appearance where the real-life actress plays herself. She appears at a Fox event where Homer clumsily trips her in order to steal her dinner plate, leaving her sprawled on the floor. Confused and looking for someone to blame, she is misdirected by Homer toward Rupert Murdoch instead. She later shows up in a promotional capacity, welcoming the Simpson family to the Fox Sports studio. Her role is brief and comedic, existing mainly as a celebrity cameo rather than a developed character. Voiced by Herself.

title: Edgy Duff
text: Edgy Duff is One of the Seven Duffs, mascot characters for Duff Beer. Edgy Duff is one of the Seven Duffs, a group of costumed mascots created for Duff Beer, clearly modeled as a parody of the Seven Dwarfs from Snow White. He never actually appears on-screen in the show itself, existing mainly as a background reference tied to Duff Gardens and promotional material. Edgy's presence is largely limited to non-canon media, such as a poster in Moe's Tavern in The Simpsons: Hit & Run and topiary decorations in The Simpsons: Tapped Out. As a mascot character, he has no distinct personality traits explored in canon, serving instead as part of a joke about corporate branding mimicking beloved children's media. His name, like the other Duffs, plays on both the Duff Beer branding and dwarf-naming conventions.

title: Little Debbie Dimples
text: Little Debbie Dimples is A minor clown character and colleague of Krusty the Clown. Little Debbie Dimples is a veteran television clown who, like her peers, struggles with the declining popularity of clowning in the modern era. She's known for a trademark pout meant to convey cuteness, though performing it now causes her physical discomfort due to age. Despite her fading relevance, she remains a source of wisdom within the clown community, offering Krusty the idea to start a clowning school to train a new generation of performers. She's cryptic and slow to share her insights, eventually revealing that timing is the most essential skill in comedy. Her appearances are brief but pivotal, positioning her as a mentor figure among the show's clown ensemble. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: the most important thing in comedy was timing
quotes: the most important thing in comedy was timing

title: Clyde
text: Clyde is Minor recurring Springfield resident, war veteran and owner of Tire Fire Souvenirs. Clyde is a gruff, elderly war veteran who runs a small souvenir stand called Tire Fire Souvenirs, built around the Springfield Tire Yard. He's fiercely protective of his livelihood, going so far as chaining himself to a gate to stop bulldozers from destroying the tire yard when Marge Simpson tried to fulfill her mayoral campaign promise. He's touchy about his military past, taking offense easily when casual phrases accidentally remind him of painful wartime memories from his service in Vietnam. Despite his combative streak, he reveals a softer side, noting that his souvenir sales helped put his son through medical school. Clyde also tends to show up in the background of civic unrest, appearing at contentious town meetings and riots around Springfield Elementary School. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "Thank Yu" was his friend who stepped on a land mine in the Battle of One Pun Too Many.
quotes: "Thank Yu" was his friend who stepped on a land mine in the Battle of One Pun Too Many.

title: Ezekiel
text: Ezekiel is A minor recurring student character at Springfield Elementary School, classmate of Bart. Ezekiel is a background student who appears briefly during Bart's fourth-grade years, notable mainly for his religious upbringing. He and his classmate Ishmael are excused from watching a sex-ed film in class due to their parents' religious wishes, highlighting his family's strict faith-based values. Later, when Bart is expelled from Springfield Elementary and transferred to Springfield Christian School, Ezekiel turns up there too, sharing a class with him once again. He is a non-speaking character, existing mostly as a quiet presence rather than a driver of plot or comedy. His name is a nod to the biblical prophet Ezekiel from the Book of Ezekiel, reinforcing his character's religious associations. Beyond these two appearances, little else is known about his personality or family life.

title: Cruella de Vil
text: Cruella de Vil is Crossover villain character from Disney's One Hundred and One Dalmatians, appearing in non-canon Simpsons specials. Cruella de Vil is a crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe through several Disney+ themed specials, retaining her classic villainous personality from her original franchise. She is depicted as cruel and eccentric, notably wearing animal fur as clothing and even attempting to make one out of Santa's Little Helper's puppies. Her villainous nature is played for both comedy and menace, such as when she recklessly burns down a bouncy castle full of children just to make a point. She's shown mingling with other famous animated villains, including Scar, suggesting a broader Disney Villain community within the Simpsons' non-canon specials. Despite her menace, the tone around her is often satirical, poking fun at her over-the-top wickedness. She also appears as a distant, whimsical addition to the extended Simpsons family tree in a Halloween special. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Don Vittorio DiMaggio
text: Don Vittorio DiMaggio is Godfather of the Springfield Mafia, ranking above Fat Tony. Don Vittorio DiMaggio is the elderly, white-haired head of the Springfield crime family, holding authority even over Fat Tony. He speaks with an exaggerated old-world Italian gangster charm, often delivering dramatic, theatrical lines about honor and gratitude. His main appearance comes in "Homie the Clown," where he nearly has Homer and Krusty killed after mistaking Homer for the real Krusty, only relenting when the two perform a death-defying tricycle stunt together. Despite his menacing role as a mob boss, he's also shown participating in lighter town events, such as attempting to help build the world's tallest human pyramid. He later joins an angry mob against Homer during the town's environmental crisis in The Simpsons Movie. His design and mannerisms are modeled after classic Italian-American character actors, giving him a nostalgic, old-Hollywood gangster feel. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Grazie, grazie. You have brought great joy to this old Italian stereotype. | Yes, I am. I know it, I am.
quotes: Grazie, grazie. You have brought great joy to this old Italian stereotype.
Yes, I am. I know it, I am.

title: District attorney
text: District attorney is Springfield's district attorney, a recurring legal official who prosecutes major criminal cases in the show. The district attorney is a gruff, older man who carries himself with more competence and seriousness than most other lawyers in Springfield. He's a no-nonsense prosecutor who takes his job seriously, most memorably leading the case against Krusty the Clown for the Kwik-E-Mart robbery. His sharp questioning during that trial famously exposed Krusty's inability to read. He later reappears in other high-profile Springfield legal and political proceedings, including Bart's murder trial and a congressional hearing about evacuating the town from an incoming comet. His design was reportedly inspired by real-life defense attorney Clarence Darrow. Though a minor recurring character, he consistently represents the more competent, authoritative side of Springfield's otherwise chaotic justice system. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: French chef
text: French chef is A minor antagonist chef who conspired with other restaurant owners to kill Homer Simpson. The French Chef is a restaurateur who runs a stand called The French Confection, a nod to the film 'The French Connection'. After Homer's harsh restaurant reviews threaten to ruin local businesses, he joins a group of angry chefs plotting revenge. He devises a poisoned chocolate éclair as the murder weapon, only for the plan to be foiled by Bart, Marge, and Lisa. Despite being caught by Lou and Eddie, he manages to slip away from custody. He later resurfaces innocently making omelettes at a gathering, showing he escaped any real consequences for the plot. His role highlights the show's recurring gag of exaggerated, cartoonish villainy among minor side characters. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Fatov
text: Fatov is A fictional imaginary mascot created by Bart Simpson, appearing as a minor gag character. Fatov is a fabricated Olympic mascot invented by Bart Simpson during the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics storyline. Bart creates the character not through official channels but by literally cutting up a piece of Homer's driver's license photo and modifying it into a makeshift pin. He then uses this crude creation to swindle a collectible pin salesman, trading it for Lisa's pearls. The joke centers on the salesman being oddly enchanted by the fake pin, leading to an absurd romantic fantasy about the 'real' Fatov that parodies Dr. Zhivago. Fatov himself has no dialogue and exists purely as a running joke about Bart's scheming and the absurdity of Olympic mascot culture. He later reappears in a non-canon capacity in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. Notable quotes: the Russian spirit of sloth and alcoholism
quotes: the Russian spirit of sloth and alcoholism

title: Frankenstein's Monster
text: Frankenstein's Monster is A recurring monster character in The Simpsons, based on Mary Shelley's classic creature, appearing mainly in Halloween-themed and costume contexts. Frankenstein's Monster is depicted as the classic reanimated creature from Geneva, Switzerland, drawing on Mary Shelley's novel and the iconic Boris Karloff film portrayal. He's married to a fellow monster, Julienstein, and their relationship provides some comedic tension, including a jealous outburst when he flirts with another woman at a party. He's often used as a Halloween costume choice by other characters rather than appearing as himself, though he has shown up in non-canon Treehouse of Horror stories interacting with other classic monsters like the Werewolf and Count Dracula. In one odd bit of trivia, he even played basketball in a spoof film against the Harlem Globetrotters, scoring a basket that was controversially ruled a penalty. Guillermo del Toro has cited him as one of his favorite classic movie monsters. Overall, he functions as a background pop-culture reference rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Harry Shearer.

title: Dave (I, (Annoyed Grunt)-bot)
text: Dave (I, (Annoyed Grunt)-bot) is An announcer for the fictional Robot Rumble TV show within The Simpsons universe. Dave is a minor, non-canon character who works as a commentator for the robot fighting show Robot Rumble, pairing up with a co-announcer named Steve. He appears during the episode where Bart competes with his robot Chief Knock-A-Homer, providing color commentary on the matches. He seems to have a dry, slightly humorless demeanor, appearing annoyed at one of his co-announcer's puns during a fight. He's also shown to be knowledgeable about the technicalities of Robot Rumble's rules, correcting his partner about human eligibility in the competition. Dave's name wasn't actually revealed in the TV episode itself, but rather through tie-in content in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Overall, he functions as a background character whose main purpose is to add broadcast-style narration to the robot battles. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Der Zip Zorp
text: Der Zip Zorp is Minor recurring character; a celebrity musician who appears as a judge and audience member in various Springfield events. Der Zip Zorp is a best-selling electronica artist known around Springfield as a minor celebrity figure. He frequently pops up in judging roles for local talent competitions, lending an air of odd, techno-flavored authority to events like reality shows. He's also shown attending or performing at other entertainment happenings, suggesting he's a fixture of the town's pop culture scene. Despite his recurring appearances, he remains a background character with no dialogue, functioning more as a visual gag or cameo than a fleshed-out personality. His name and aesthetic evoke a quirky, robotic or alien-inspired electronica persona typical of the show's absurdist humor.

title: Grant Connor
text: Grant Connor is A professional hunter living in Springfield Forest who appears in the episode "The Fat and the Furriest". Grant Connor is a rugged, no-nonsense hunter who makes his home in a wooden hut deep in Springfield Forest. He has a habit of killing nearly any animal he encounters and repurposing their remains into furniture and household items, such as a chair made from a lion and tiger or a footstool crafted from a baby hippo. His diet is equally unusual, ranging from butterflies to eagles shot out of the sky and turned into sandwiches. Grant plays a key role in escalating the story of Homer's bear encounter by filming Homer fleeing in fear and sending the footage to Kent Brockman's show. He later rigs a tracking device onto the bear, and when Homer tries to lead it to safety, Grant is among those ready to shoot it, assuming it's dangerous. His character embodies an exaggerated, comedic take on backwoods hunting culture. Voiced by Charles Napier.

title: Ms. Coco
text: Ms. Coco is Clown and former history teacher at the Herschel Krustofsky School for the Clowning Arts. Ms. Coco is a minor educator figure in the world of professional clowning, teaching History 101 at the School for the Clowning Arts. She quizzes her students on obscure clown trivia, such as the origins of the double-winged neck ruff and the identity of America's first female clown. Her class becomes notable mainly because Bart Simpson, usually indifferent to schoolwork, surprises everyone by actively engaging and correctly answering her questions. She appears to be knowledgeable and precise about clown history, reinforcing the show's parody of academic institutions by applying serious teaching methods to absurd subject matter. Beyond her classroom scene, she has also appeared in a non-canon capacity within The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Delbert Fornby
text: Delbert Fornby is A minor recurring character; a landowner and artist living in the Springfield Desert State Park. Delbert Fornby is a gruff, reclusive artist and landowner who lives out in the Springfield Desert State Park with his wife. He values his privacy and property, reacting with hostility when Martin wanders onto his land while chasing a butterfly. Despite being an artist known for metal sculptures, he shows a fierce independence and distrust of government interference, famously refusing a large grant from the National Endowment for the Arts and destroying his own artwork rather than accept it. He later appears among a group of elderly Springfield residents seeking more of the medication MusBeNy from Hotenhoffer Pharmaceuticals, suggesting he is elderly himself. Overall, he's a minor but memorable side character defined by his short temper and anti-establishment attitude. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Chucky
text: Chucky is Crossover character from the Child's Play horror film franchise appearing in The Simpsons. Chucky is the murderous doll from the Child's Play movie series, brought into The Simpsons universe as a crossover figure rather than an original character. In his appearances he acts as a violent threat, attacking Wayne Slater with a knife during a training sequence before being overpowered. He's also referenced as one of many infamous villains invoked by Mr. Burns, appearing as a shadow puppet during a musical number. Beyond these brief cameos, he's shown lurking around a school playground, adding to his creepy, out-of-place presence in the show's world. He never speaks in any of his appearances, relying purely on his sinister reputation from the horror films he originates from.

title: Lilly Ellison
text: Lilly Ellison is A minor recurring student character at Springfield Elementary School. Lilly Ellison is a young girl who attends Springfield Elementary School in the third grade, appearing mostly in the background of various episodes. She's a non-speaking character, so little is known about her personality or distinct traits beyond her status as a classmate among the school's many students. In a non-canon appearance, she was shown in the audience for the final episode of a Krusty the Clown show, suggesting she's a fan of the character like many other Springfield children. Overall, she serves as one of the many faces populating the elementary school setting rather than a character with a developed storyline.

title: Clark
text: Clark is An orderly at the Springfield Retirement Castle who interacts with Abraham Simpson. Clark is a minor staff member working as an orderly at the Springfield Retirement Castle. He appears to be sensitive and easily hurt by harsh words, as shown when a simple insult from a cranky resident brings him to tears. Despite being an authority figure who can throw out unruly patients, he shows a surprisingly emotional and vulnerable side, seeking comfort from a coworker after being insulted. His brief appearance highlights the sometimes contentious relationship between the retirement home staff and its elderly residents. Clark's role is largely functional, serving as a foil for Abraham Simpson's cantankerous personality in a single episode. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: I wish I was a fish tank... then I could filter out your nasty words.
quotes: I wish I was a fish tank... then I could filter out your nasty words.

title: E.T.
text: E.T. is A crossover/parody character based on the film alien E.T., referenced or briefly appearing throughout various Simpsons episodes. E.T. is not an original Simpsons character but a nod to the beloved movie alien, popping up as a running pop-culture reference rather than a fully developed figure. He's invoked in political speeches, stand-up comedy bits, and moments of alien paranoia, always tied to his famous catchphrase about phoning home. The show plays with his image in different forms, from an animatronic likeness to a Halloween costume to a hallucinated vision Homer has after a head injury. Reverend Lovejoy even compares him to a religious savior figure, fondly recalling his on-screen resurrection. Bart is dressed as him during an audition, and characters use chocolate-coated peanut butter candies as an homage to his fondness for Reese's Pieces. Overall, E.T. functions as a nostalgic touchstone the show returns to for quick jokes and cultural callbacks. Notable quotes: As E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial said, we 'phoned home' with a message of hope. | I pity the fool that don't phone home! | E.T. phone Homer Simpson
quotes: As E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial said, we 'phoned home' with a message of hope.
I pity the fool that don't phone home!
E.T. phone Homer Simpson

title: Duff Beer advertiser
text: Duff Beer advertiser is Minor recurring character; the on-screen narrator/actor featured in Duff Beer television commercials seen throughout the series. This character is essentially a recurring piece of in-universe advertising rather than a fully developed personality. He appears as the pitchman in a Duff Beer commercial, narrating the ad and finishing by holding up a bottle for the audience. The commercial itself becomes a small plot device, as it airs during Loaftime and successfully tempts Homer into grabbing a beer. Because the ad is reused as background material, the same footage of him resurfaces later on Channel 6 in another episode. He has no personal storyline of his own beyond being the face of Duff's advertising within the show. Voiced by Sam McMurray.

title: CONRAD
text: CONRAD is A sentient app created by Lisa Simpson to predict social media consequences, appearing in "The Girl Code".
