She later appears pregnant with Snake's child, and the two eventually marry, cementing their on-again, off-again romance. However, a later appearance on a dating show suggests the couple eventually split. Her dynamic with Snake provides a recurring source of dramatic and comedic subplots involving crime, jealousy, and domestic instability. Voiced by Julia Louis-Dreyfus.

title: Hugh Hefner (character)
text: Hugh Hefner (character) is Guest celebrity character based on the real-life founder of Playboy magazine, who interacts with Bart and Homer. Hugh Hefner appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, the famous publisher of Playboy magazine. He is portrayed as living a glamorous, laid-back lifestyle at his mansion, typically lounging around in his signature red robe. He has a whimsical side, revealed by a hidden laboratory in his home, and shows a willingness to help out when Bart comes calling for a favor involving Krusty's comeback special. He even joins in with some lighthearted musical fun using wine glasses. Later, he's shown surrounded by Playboy bunnies at his mansion when Homer and Bart visit after Homer's Angry Dad film becomes a hit. As a recurring guest-star character, his appearances are brief but tied to memorable pop-culture crossover moments in the show. Voiced by Himself.

title: Hermes
text: Hermes is Greek mythological messenger god who appears in a non-canon Simpsons comic story, portrayed by Bart. Hermes is depicted here not as an original Simpsons character but as the mythological messenger of the gods, reimagined with Bart taking on his role in a comic adventure. In this retelling, he becomes tangled up in the myth of Hercules, helping the demigod handle the many strange creatures he must capture during his famous labors. Rather than dealing with them directly, Hermes cleverly calls in the Grecian SPCA, reasoning that the unlicensed and potentially rabid animals should be handled by professionals. The character is portrayed with blue hair and exists purely within a fantastical, non-canon storyline rather than Springfield's main continuity. His appearances are largely limited to costume references and a single Bongo comics story blending Simpsons humor with Greek mythology.

title: Grogu
text: Grogu is Crossover character from The Mandalorian referenced/appearing in Simpsons specials and episodes. Grogu, better known to fans as Baby Yoda, is a crossover character borrowed from The Mandalorian who pops up in a handful of Simpsons references rather than as a true cast member. In the actual show, he's mostly a pop-culture touchstone Marge invokes while trying to teach Maggie sign language, and his merchandise-fueled fame is joked about via a themed changing station at a fan convention. In non-canon specials, he becomes an actual physical presence, riding along with Homer, getting fussed over by Maggie, and even attending a Star Wars-themed daycare where Maggie causes mischief by stealing his pod. He's a silent, infant-like character whose humor comes entirely from his cultural ubiquity and cuteness rather than any dialogue or personality of his own. Grogu never speaks in these appearances, fitting his non-speaking status in the source material as well.

title: Kamala
text: Kamala is A Rigellian alien, daughter of Kang, who briefly romances Bart in a Treehouse of Horror segment. Kamala is a non-canon alien character from the planet Rigel VII, introduced as part of a one-off Treehouse of Horror parody. She rescues Bart after he becomes trapped in a banana plant, and the two quickly fall in love and mate, leading to her pregnancy. Her family, including her father Kang and uncle Kodos, escort her to see the Rigellian queen to obtain a substance called Hillarium to aid in childbirth, only for the encounter to erupt into conflict with human forces. Despite the violence, Kamala remains pragmatic, noting that peaceful negotiation could have avoided the battle entirely. She serves primarily as a spoof of Neytiri from the film Avatar, mirroring that character's interspecies romance plot. Kamala later appears as a collectible alien character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Kamala said that if they had just asked, they would have given them Hillarium.
quotes: Kamala said that if they had just asked, they would have given them Hillarium.

title: Iron Lung
text: Iron Lung is Superhero alter ego of Hans Moleman, member of The Dependables. Iron Lung is the non-canon superhero identity adopted by the elderly, accident-prone Hans Moleman. He joins The Dependables, a ragtag superhero team, stepping in when Fruit Bat Man is taken captive by The Abominable Dr. Lenny. As with many of Moleman's ventures, the character leans on the joke of an unlikely, frail figure taking on a heroic role. The name and concept parody Marvel Comics' Iron Man, poking fun at the idea of a feeble old man donning a tech-based superhero persona. He is a non-speaking character who appears primarily as a background gag rather than a fleshed-out figure. His inclusion reflects the show's tendency to spoof superhero tropes through its most unassuming citizens.

title: Great daughter
text: Great daughter is Minor one-off character; a young girl seen at Mr. Burns' company picnic in an early episode. The great daughter is a minor character who appears with her family—father, mother, and brother—at a company picnic hosted by Mr. Burns. She briefly looks down on Homer, feeling sorry for what she perceives as his sad life, unaware that her own family is deeply unhappy. Despite outward appearances of normalcy, her family is secretly seeking help at a family therapy center. When the Simpsons inadvertently cause a citywide power drain that affects the therapy center, her family flees in a panic. She serves mainly as a background figure highlighting the irony that even seemingly put-together families have their own hidden dysfunctions. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Galactic senator
text: Galactic senator is Fictional character within the show-within-a-show Cosmic Wars: The Gathering Shadow, parodying Star Wars. The galactic senator is a minor fictional character appearing in the Simpsons' in-universe parody film series Cosmic Wars: The Gathering Shadow. He's depicted presiding over a senate roll call when the proceedings are interrupted by an AT-AT walker bursting in to propose an amendment to a Space Bill. Unfazed by the chaos, he calmly instructs the intruder to wait its turn before resuming his roll call, playing into the joke of bureaucratic indifference amid absurd sci-fi spectacle. The character is a direct parody of Chancellor Palpatine, also known as Darth Sidious, from the actual Star Wars films. His appearance is brief, existing mainly as a background gag rather than a fully developed character within the show's fictional universe. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: The Iron Yuppie
text: The Iron Yuppie is A minor professional wrestler seen in the Simpsons universe. The Iron Yuppie is a professional wrestler who appears briefly during a brutal Texas Death Match at the Springfield Grapplarium. His opponent in this match is Dr. Hillbilly, and the stakes are unusually high, with the losing wrestler set to be unmasked and killed. The character doesn't speak, leaving his true nature as a hero or villain ambiguous. Homer Simpson expresses a mild dislike for him, hoping he loses simply because of his perceived arrogance. Beyond this one scene, little else is revealed about his personality or background. He later reappears as part of the wrestling roster in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Surly Joe
text: Surly Joe is Minor recurring character; owner and worker of a foundation repair company who occasionally interacts with the Simpson family. Surly Joe is a gruff construction worker who runs his own business, Surly Joe's Foundation Repair. He's called upon whenever the Simpsons' house suffers structural damage, showing up to assess and quote repairs. He once attempted to charge Homer an exorbitant fee to fix cracks caused by a car crash, only for Homer to opt for a cheaper cosmetic fix instead. Beyond home repairs, he's shown to have a bit of an adventurous streak, participating in a record-breaking human pyramid stunt. He's a minor but recognizable background character, identified as a smoker and an adult in the show's background lore. His name reflects his no-nonsense, ill-tempered demeanor. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Hypnotoad
text: Hypnotoad is A crossover character from Futurama who appears in The Simpsons universe as a hypnotic toad. The Hypnotoad is a strange, glowing-eyed toad whose stare has the power to hypnotize anyone who looks at it. Originally a character from Futurama, it crosses over into The Simpsons' world during a time-travel adventure to the future. Its signature gag is putting people into a trance simply by appearing on a screen, leading to comedic drooling and mindless staring from its victims. The creature doesn't speak and mostly appears silently in the background or as a tool used by other characters like Leela. It has shown up in both canon episodes involving future New New York and in a non-canon Halloween special where it hypnotizes Lisa in a bizarre alternate world.

title: Girl scout
text: Girl scout is A minor recurring background character in Springfield who sells Girl Scout cookies. This nameless brown-haired girl scout pops up occasionally as a background gag character in Springfield. Her defining trait is her dogged persistence in selling cookies door-to-door, even when it leads to awkward or unfortunate situations. She appeared within Barney Gumble's film-festival movie in a mix-up scene, and later became the victim of a pie-throwing prank when Homer, disguised as the Pie Man, hit her in the face to protect his secret identity while she was trying to sell cookies at Burns' manor. She has no deep backstory or personality beyond being a stock kid character used for quick comedic moments. Her appearances are brief and scattered across a few episodes rather than being a major storyline. Overall, she serves as a minor running joke about the ubiquity and misfortune of door-to-door cookie sales in Springfield. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Groot
text: Groot is A Marvel superhero referenced within the Simpsons universe, often appearing as a costume or cameo rather than a core cast member. Groot is a tree-like Marvel superhero who appears in the Simpsons universe mainly through costumes, cameos, and references rather than as a fully developed character. He's tied to his famous catchphrase, which various Springfield residents repeat while dressed as him at conventions like Bi-Mon-Sci-Fi-Con and Comicalooza. Several background characters, including Steve Fishbein and Stan, don Groot costumes for different occasions, showing how deeply Marvel fandom has permeated Springfield culture. In non-canon material, Groot even blends into the show's own mythology, such as Bart's treehouse being depicted as him or the Living Treehouse reacting to his on-screen appearance. He also shows up in family-friendly contexts, like a Mother's Day trip involving Baby Groot. Overall, Groot functions as a recurring pop-culture gag rather than a character with his own storyline. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: I am Groot. | I am Steve Fishbein.
quotes: I am Groot.
I am Steve Fishbein.

title: Rob Halford (character)
text: Rob Halford (character) is Real-world musician who guest-starred as himself in a Simpsons episode. Rob Halford is a fictionalized version of the real English singer, famous as the frontman of the heavy metal band Judas Priest. In his sole notable appearance, he and his bandmates use their music as a tool of intimidation, performing for the Simpson family in an attempt to force them out of the Consulate of Sweden. His inclusion plays on his real-life reputation as a metal icon, using his intense stage persona for comedic effect within the show's plot. Unlike many recurring characters, he exists mainly as a cameo tied to a single storyline rather than an ongoing presence. His appearance highlights the show's tradition of blending real celebrities into absurd, exaggerated scenarios. He is credited simply as playing himself, reinforcing the meta joke of a real musician participating in a cartoon world. Voiced by Rob Halford (himself).

title: Hellroads principals
text: Hellroads principals is Conjoined faculty members of Hellroads school in Hell, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Hellroads principals are a bizarre, physically joined pair of unnamed men who run the infernal school Hellroads, located in Hell itself. Their voices and appearances are clearly modeled on Springfield Elementary's Principal Skinner and Superintendent Chalmers, suggesting a demonic mirror of the familiar duo. They enforce strict rules, such as skinning Beelzebart Simpson for lacking a Hell pass, showing a petty, bureaucratic cruelty typical of authority figures in the Treehouse of Horror universe. During a graduation ceremony, they deliver a pompous prepared speech quoting Webster's dictionary, only to reveal the actual Noah Webster chained up as a punished prisoner. Their irrational grudge over a minor spelling preference underscores their absurd, tyrannical nature. Ultimately they name Beelzebart the class's morbidly punny "mal-edictorian," fitting the show's penchant for wordplay even in its non-canon horror segments. Voiced by Harry Shearer, Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: You changed the 'R-E' to 'E-R' in 'theater.' I hate that!
quotes: You changed the 'R-E' to 'E-R' in 'theater.' I hate that!

title: Jennifer Garner (character)
text: Jennifer Garner (character) is Real-life actress who appears as a guest-starring cameo character in The Simpsons. Jennifer Garner is a celebrity guest character based on the real actress, known for playing Sydney Bristow in the TV series Alias. In her canon appearance, she takes part in a chaotic Nobel Prize ceremony alongside Dudley Herschbach, presenting the Science award to Professor Frink, and remains oddly upbeat even as things spiral into madness. She also shows up in a non-canon capacity as a magazine cover subject, prompting Homer to muse about her preference for family life over Hollywood glamour. Homer's confusion between her and her television alter-ego becomes a running joke, as he refers to her simply as "Alias" rather than by her real name. Her appearances are brief and cameo-based, existing mostly to poke fun at celebrity culture and Homer's pop-culture obliviousness. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: Then I fell asleep. When I woke up, Letterman was talking to Alias.
quotes: Then I fell asleep. When I woke up, Letterman was talking to Alias.

title: Headmaster Greystash
text: Headmaster Greystash is Fictional headmaster character within the in-universe 'Angelica Button' book series (a Harry Potter parody). Headmaster Greystash is a fictional wizard character from the Angelica Button books that Lisa Simpson reads, serving as a clear parody of Albus Dumbledore. His most notable trait is an absurdly long mustache that stretches several feet on each side and is imbued with magical properties. In the original story he meets a grim fate, killed by an evil wizard, but Homer improvises a more triumphant ending when reading to Lisa, giving his mustache super-strength via a can of spinach so he can defeat his enemy. Beyond the books, his likeness has become popular enough for fans to dress as him at conventions like Comicalooza and Cartoon Con. Despite being a character within a story rather than a member of Springfield's main cast, he has appeared in mobile game content as well. Interestingly, his design was modeled after Homer Simpson himself. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Stewie Griffin
text: Stewie Griffin is Crossover character from Family Guy; infant son of Lois and Peter Griffin who appears in non-canon Simpsons crossover episodes. Stewie is the diabolical baby of the Griffin family from Family Guy, brought into the Simpsons universe through various non-canon crossovers. He quickly latches onto Bart as a role model, mimicking his skateboarding, slingshot use, and wardrobe, but his admiration curdles into obsessive and violent behavior. True to his usual characterization, he shows a twisted, murderous streak, kidnapping and torturing anyone who wrongs or annoys Bart, including Nelson and Apu. His attempt at humor badly misfires when he makes a prank call to Moe with disturbing results, showing his skewed sense of what's funny. Ultimately his friendship with Bart collapses when Bart deems him too unstable to be around. Despite the fallout, Stewie's fixation lingers, leading him to comically insist he'll stop thinking about Bart. He also turns up in other bizarre non-canon scenarios, including as a mutant creature and as a figure used to access a secret room in the Android's Dungeon. Voiced by Seth MacFarlane, Chris Edgerly. Notable quotes: I took Apu. | I Will Not Think About Bart Anymore.
quotes: I took Apu.
I Will Not Think About Bart Anymore.

title: Alvarine Gurney
text: Alvarine Gurney is Jacqueline Bouvier's mother and Marge Simpson's great-grandmother. Alvarine Gurney is a minor, deceased member of the Bouvier family tree, appearing mainly in flashbacks and family history references. She was known for disapproving of the men her daughter and granddaughter chose to marry, showing a critical streak common among the Bouvier women. Despite never smoking, she had an unusually raspy voice, a quirky trait that set her apart. Her poor eyesight led to a clumsy moment feeding baby Marge, repeatedly missing her mouth with the spoon during the classic airplane-feeding game. She is also tied to a family mystery involving a supposed Civil War figurine that turned out to be nothing more than an old liquor bottle. Overall, she exists mostly as a background figure fleshing out Marge's maternal lineage. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: Queen Gautama
text: Queen Gautama is Non-canon queen character, mother of Siddmartha Gautama, appearing in a Simpsons Bible-parody segment and mobile game. Queen Gautama is a minor, non-canon royal character introduced as part of a parody of the Buddha origin story in the show's anthology-style segment 'My Way or the Highway to Heaven.' She is depicted as a well-meaning but out-of-touch parent, attempting to please her child with extravagant gifts rather than understanding what would truly make them happy. Alongside her husband, King Gautama, she represents a satirical take on royal or overindulgent parenting. Her character also extends beyond the show into 'The Simpsons: Tapped Out,' where she appears as part of the Springfield Enlightened questline. She has no significant character arc beyond her family relationships and her brief comedic appearance tied to a failed attempt at parental generosity. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: Girl with a ponytail
text: Girl with a ponytail is An unnamed background student in Lisa Simpson's class at Springfield Elementary. The girl with a ponytail is one of the many nameless children who populate Lisa's classroom and the halls of Springfield Elementary. She's easily identified by the ponytail she wears, though her hair color is notoriously inconsistent, shifting between white and blonde depending on the episode due to her status as a minor background character. She has appeared since the show's very first season, often lingering in crowd shots or classroom scenes without ever being given a line of dialogue. One notable moment of inclusion came when she was invited to a sleepover at the Simpsons' house. She also shows up in the classic opening sequence near the broken-down school bus. Despite her frequent appearances across many seasons, she remains entirely undeveloped as a character, existing purely as set dressing for Lisa's world.

title: Curly Howard
text: Curly Howard is Real-world comedian and member of the Three Stooges, referenced/appearing as a minor pop-culture figure in the Simpsons universe. Curly Howard appears in the show as a nod to the real-life Three Stooges comedian, referred to in one episode as 'Curly Four' to acknowledge that the character had been recast multiple times over the Stooges' history, most notably replaced by Shemp Howard. His appearances are mostly brief and non-verbal, including a face in the sky, a brain in a jar, and bones in a box, reflecting his role as background comedic trivia rather than an active character. A newspaper headline references his on-again feud with Shemp, playing into the running joke about their sibling rivalry within the Stooges. Bumblebee Man's mistaken belief in his own invincibility, comparing himself to Curly, humorously underscores Curly's reputation for being seemingly indestructible despite his frequent slapstick death gags. In a non-canon Halloween segment, Bart and Lisa also reference both Curly and Shemp as running jokes about annoying noises. Overall, Curly functions as a recurring pop-culture reference rather than a fleshed-out character with his own personality within the show. Notable quotes: Curly to Shemp: You're Out! | Please, Bart, I've seen your stupid Shemp. | Yeah, I've seen your Curly too.
quotes: Curly to Shemp: You're Out!
Please, Bart, I've seen your stupid Shemp.
Yeah, I've seen your Curly too.

title: Ice cream lady
text: Ice cream lady is Minor recurring background character who works as a waitress in Springfield. The ice cream lady is a minor recurring worker seen serving customers at Phineas Q. Butterfat's ice cream parlor and Izzy's Deli. She's portrayed as an obese woman who can be easily flattered, as shown when Bart Simpson manipulates her with a backhanded compliment to get a bigger dessert. Despite her small role, she has popped up in a handful of episodes over the years, including participating in a wacky town-wide record attempt. She doesn't have much personality development beyond these brief comedic appearances, functioning mostly as background color in Springfield's food service world. Voiced by Doris Grau. Notable quotes: "You know, I was just wondering how someone who works at an ice cream store keeps such a trim figure."
quotes: "You know, I was just wondering how someone who works at an ice cream store keeps such a trim figure."

title: Buddy Hodges
text: Buddy Hodges is Former child actor who played Fallout Boy in the Radioactive Man TV show. Buddy Hodges was the child actor who once played Fallout Boy, the sidekick character in the Radioactive Man television series. Years later, he made a living appearing at comic book conventions and answering fan questions about his old role, seemingly trading on nostalgia. He shared a mysterious close bond with Dirk Richter, the actor who portrayed Radioactive Man, and became defensive of him when fans pried into his life. As an adult, his acting career shifted away from superhero fare, landing a part as Rum Tum Tugger in a touring production of Cats. He also had a rather self-important encounter with Comic Book Guy, casually asking him to fetch a drink while he flirted with another convention attendee. Overall, he's a minor but memorable example of a washed-up child star clinging to his brief brush with fame. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Dirk Richter was a beautiful man... Can't you little vultures leave him alone?!
quotes: Dirk Richter was a beautiful man... Can't you little vultures leave him alone?!

title: Gamera
text: Gamera is A Japanese movie monster who appears briefly in Simpsons fantasy/parody sequences. Gamera is a giant turtle-like kaiju borrowed from Japanese monster movies who makes cameo appearances in The Simpsons. He first shows up in a nightmarish daydream imagined by Lisa, in which she is banished to a monster-infested island after failing gym class, alongside other famous movie monsters. Later, he appears again during the family's trip to Tokyo, joining Godzilla, Rodan, and Mothra in an attack on their departing airplane. Gamera has no dialogue and functions purely as a visual gag referencing classic kaiju films rather than as a developed character. His inclusion highlights the show's frequent parody of Japanese pop culture and monster movie tropes.

title: Frida Kahlo
text: Frida Kahlo is Historical/real-world Mexican painter who appears as a character in Simpsons canon, notably in a Rockefeller Center art dispute segment. Frida Kahlo appears as a fictionalized version of the real-life painter within a Simpsons segment about art and capitalism. She is depicted as fiercely principled, resentful of her husband Diego Rivera's willingness to work for wealthy capitalists like John D. Rockefeller Jr., and she channels her frustration into deeply personal, emotionally raw paintings. Her artistic honesty ultimately earns Diego's respect, leading to a darkly comic exchange about mutual infidelity in their marriage. Beyond this storyline, she's referenced as an inspirational figure in Lisa Simpson's life, appearing in Lisa's imagined artist gallery, in a book Lisa reads, and as a Halloween costume Lisa wears. She's also invoked humorously by Mr. Burns, who claims to own a portrait made with a brush from her eyebrow hair. Overall, she functions as a symbol of artistic integrity and feminist inspiration within the show's universe. Voiced by Yeardley Smith, Julie Kavner. Notable quotes: he underestimated her and she was a genius | painted by Diego Rivera's great-nephew with a brush made of hair from Frida Kahlo's eyebrows
quotes: he underestimated her and she was a genius
painted by Diego Rivera's great-nephew with a brush made of hair from Frida Kahlo's eyebrows

title: Greyhound puppies (first litter)
text: Greyhound puppies (first litter) is Litter of 25 puppies born to Santa's Little Helper and She's the Fastest, owned by the Simpson family and later Mr. Burns. This litter of 25 puppies was born quickly in the Simpsons' kitchen, with each pup quickly earning its own bowl and a mischievous streak. They caused chaos around the house, from shredding Bart's socks to swiping potato chips from Homer and forcing Marge to put the whole family in flea collars. After the puppies embarrassed Homer in front of the IRS, the Army, and Reverend Lovejoy, the family tried to give them away, only for the greedy Mr. Burns to kidnap the entire litter. Burns had sinister plans to turn the puppies into a novelty tuxedo, foiled when Bart and Lisa intervened and a puppy resembling Rory Calhoun (dubbed Little Monty) softened his resolve. In the end, the puppies became champion racing dogs, ironically making Burns a fortune. Their story stands as one of the more elaborate side-plots involving the Simpsons' pets, blending family sitcom humor with over-the-top Burns villainy. Voiced by Frank Welker.

title: The Godfather (character)
text: The Godfather (character) is Head of the Springfield Mafia, ranking above even Fat Tony. The Godfather is the top authority within the Springfield Mafia, wielding more power than even Fat Tony, who answers to him. He appeared as a stand-in leader for the mob during a period when Joe Mantegna had not yet returned to voice Fat Tony, making him a temporary but important fixture in the show's criminal underworld storylines. Despite his fearsome title, he's shown with a somewhat particular, almost fussy demeanor, as seen in his complaint about a poorly made drink. His presence highlights the show's recurring satire of organized crime tropes and hierarchy. He appears sporadically across a handful of episodes and specials, reinforcing his role as a background authority figure rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Phil Hartman. Notable quotes: What did I do to deserve this flavorless Manhattan?
quotes: What did I do to deserve this flavorless Manhattan?

title: Rosey Grier (character)
text: Rosey Grier (character) is Real-world guest character; a Christian minister and former football player who appears at the Super Bowl. Rosey Grier appears as a fictionalized version of himself, blending his real-life identity as a former NFL player with his post-football career as a Christian minister. In the show, he operates a portable chapel at the Super Bowl for fans who don't want to miss church while attending the game. He's portrayed as earnest and devout, leading a congregation in prayer even amid the chaos of the big game. His storyline ties into Ned Flanders' anxiety about missing church, showing Grier's chapel as a solution for football fans with a guilty conscience. The character is a one-episode cameo rooted in real-world sports and religious culture rather than a recurring fictional role. His inclusion highlights the show's tendency to use real athletes and celebrities as themselves in humorous, faith-adjacent scenarios. Voiced by Rosey Grier (Himself).

title: Claude Kane II
text: Claude Kane II is Fictional nuclear physicist and father of Claude Kane III (the superhero Radioactive Man), appearing in the Radioactive Man comic-book stories within the Simpsons universe. Claude Kane II is a brilliant but emotionally distant scientist whose life is entangled with his son's secret superhero identity as Radioactive Man. He repeatedly finds himself in danger due to his scientific work, whether as a hostage during a lab heist, a victim of sabotage and fire, or a target tied to ransom demands from villains. His devotion to his missing wife, Camellia Kane, drives a long personal quest that uncovers the sinister experiments of Dr. Crab. Despite his intelligence and wealth, he struggles with fatherhood, admitting he loves his son but views him as a disappointment for not living up to his expectations. He is often saved by Radioactive Man, unaware for much of the story that the hero is actually his own son. His arc blends personal tragedy, mad-science plotlines, and strained family drama typical of the Radioactive Man comic parody. Notable quotes: He later told Gloria that he loved his son, but considered him a disappointment as he expected great things from him.
quotes: He later told Gloria that he loved his son, but considered him a disappointment as he expected great things from him.

title: Larry King (character)
text: Larry King (character) is Real-world radio and television host who appears as himself in cameo roles throughout the show. Larry King appears in the Simpsons universe as a version of himself, popping up in odd, often surreal contexts rather than as a consistent character with his own storyline. He's referenced as a soothing voice Homer turns to for comfort, such as listening to him read the Bible on tape, and as someone associated with mental health crises, being on speed dial at a mental hospital. He's also used as a punchline for shallow media, with Lisa comparing a lowbrow newspaper to a mix of trivia and Larry King. He occasionally takes on more active roles, such as moderating a mayoral debate and being portrayed by Grampa in a fictionalized account of the first Olympics. His name is also invoked as a vague threat or an off-screen figure Death is dealing with, reinforcing his role as a running cultural reference rather than a fleshed-out character. Voiced by Larry King (Himself). Notable quotes: "flimsy hodgepodge of pie graphs, factoids and Larry King"
quotes: "flimsy hodgepodge of pie graphs, factoids and Larry King"

title: Mr. Kidney Punch
text: Mr. Kidney Punch is A supervillain from the Radioactive Man comic book series within The Simpsons universe, and a member of the Threatening Threesome. Mr. Kidney Punch is a minor comic-book supervillain who exists as one of Radioactive Man's many recurring foes. He is part of a trio of villains known as the Threatening Threesome, though little else is defined about his personality or backstory. He appears repeatedly across Bongo comic issues, usually as a defeated adversary rather than a serious threat. He has crashed a wedding, been used as a holographic illusion to torment Radioactive Man, and been shown battling another hero, Purple Badge of Courage, in Zenith City Park. His appearances suggest he is a stock antagonist rather than a deeply developed character, existing mainly to be beaten by the heroes of the comic-within-a-show.

title: Hattie
text: Hattie is A minor recurring resident of the Springfield Retirement Castle. Hattie is one of the elderly residents living at the Springfield Retirement Castle. She's a background figure whom Homer comes to recognize over his time visiting the facility. She's often seen in the company of fellow seniors Asa and Beatrice, suggesting she's part of a small social circle among the retirement home's inhabitants. Hattie doesn't have any spoken lines in her appearances, existing purely as a visual presence in the retirement castle scenes. She represents the recurring cast of elderly extras that populate the show's depiction of the retirement home setting.

title: Tom Hamilton (character)
text: Tom Hamilton (character) is Real-world musician (bassist of Aerosmith) who appears as himself in guest cameo appearances. Tom Hamilton is depicted in the show as a real-world guest character, appearing as himself alongside the rest of Aerosmith. He is portrayed performing music at Moe's Tavern with his bandmates. He also shows up in a flashback attending a Grammy Awards party alongside the Be Sharps. As with other real musician cameos on the show, he doesn't have an extensive personality arc, serving mainly as a nod to his real identity as Aerosmith's bassist. His appearances are brief and tied directly to his band's presence in Springfield lore. Voiced by Tom Hamilton (Himself).

title: Hansel (Treehouse of Horror XXXI)
text: Hansel (Treehouse of Horror XXXI) is Fairy tale character from Hansel & Gretel, referenced/appearing in various Simpsons episodes. Hansel is one half of the famous fairy tale duo, appearing alongside his sister Gretel in a Treehouse of Horror segment where the pair are held captive by Mr. Burns and Waylon Smithers. In a darkly comic twist, Burns reveals he prefers his captives "stringy and tough" rather than fattened up, subverting the original story's premise. Beyond his non-canon horror appearance, Hansel is mostly referenced within the show as a storybook figure, appearing on a book cover Homer reads to a young Lisa and Maggie, and mentioned in passing by Homer while looking through a View-Master. The character has also been reimagined in other non-canon contexts, including a retelling of Grimms' Fairy Tales where Bart plays his role. Overall, Hansel functions less as a developed character and more as a recurring nod to classic fairy tale lore woven into the Simpsons universe. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Boy, that Hasnel sure can eat.|Homer Simpson
quotes: Boy, that Hasnel sure can eat.|Homer Simpson

title: The Joker
text: The Joker is A minor background character in Springfield, based on Batman's iconic villain. The Joker is a green-haired figure who occasionally pops up in the background of Springfield, more as a nod to the famous Batman villain than a fully developed character. He's a non-speaking presence, appearing in crowds or referenced in passing rather than driving any plot himself. He once stood in line hoping to claim Beatrice Simmons' inheritance when Grampa Simpson offered it up for grabs. Mr. Burns name-drops him during a musical number listing off villains, complete with a shadow cameo. He's also been the subject of a playful mash-up idea combining him with dancer/choreographer Bob Fosse. Beyond the show itself, he's shown up in tie-in media like comics, a theme park ride exhibit, and even as a costume choice for Kearney in a mobile game.

title: Killer Toupée
text: Killer Toupée is Non-canon horror movie monster from a Treehouse of Horror segment; Snake's sentient toupée. The Killer Toupée is a bizarre, murderous wig that was once Snake's hair, transplanted onto Homer's head after Snake's execution. Once attached, it secretly takes control of Homer's body at night, using him as a vessel to hunt down and kill those who witnessed Snake's fatal 'third strike.' Its presence turns mild-mannered Homer into an unwitting killer, creating a darkly comedic parody of classic slasher and body-possession horror films. Even after being torn off, the toupée retains a life of its own, crawling and attacking on its own accord before finally being gunned down by the police. Its death scene deliberately echoes the demise of the doll Chucky from the Child's Play franchise, fitting the parody-heavy tone of the Treehouse of Horror series. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Hot Stuff (character)
text: Hot Stuff (character) is A comic book character (parody of Hot Stuff the Little Devil) who appears in The Simpsons universe. Hot Stuff is a devilish comic book protagonist referenced within the Simpsons universe as the star of his own titular comic series. He appears on the cover of a comic called Death of Casper, published by the in-universe company Harry Comics. In a non-canon segment, he is depicted as a resident of a hellish afterlife known as 'Super Hell,' reserved for characters from poorly regarded comics. When Bart Simpson frees him, Hot Stuff pushes back on the notion that he's especially evil, instead explaining his punishment is tied to the low quality of his comic book appearances. He even produces an old issue from 1940 as evidence of his long, lackluster history. The character serves as a comedic jab at outdated or campy children's comics rather than a fully developed personality within the show. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "that evil" | he was being punished for how lame his comics were
quotes: "that evil"
he was being punished for how lame his comics were

title: Homer (Greek)
text: Homer (Greek) is The ancient Greek poet credited with writing the Iliad and the Odyssey, referenced within the Simpsons universe. This is a version of the legendary blind poet Homer, existing in the Simpsons universe both as a historical/literary figure and as a non-canon comedic character. In canon, his epic works are simply referenced as books read by children or seen in a school library. In the non-canon material, however, he's portrayed as a fraud who fakes blindness to seem more authentic, an idea he apparently borrowed from his friend Oedipus. He works as a sort of tour guide for children, droning on about the Iliad and Odyssey until he's exposed and forced to entertain kids with actual mythological stories instead. He's also shown clashing creatively with the fabulist Aesop, rudely interrupting his storytelling to punch up the narrative for a younger demographic. Eventually his and Aesop's storytelling gigs get replaced by an infomercial, poking fun at commercialization of culture. Notable quotes: Oh, oh, Homer Simpson. Oh, no, I thought you were talking about, uh, Homer the blind poet who wrote "The Iliad" and "The Odyssey" there, yeah.
quotes: Oh, oh, Homer Simpson. Oh, no, I thought you were talking about, uh, Homer the blind poet who wrote "The Iliad" and "The Odyssey" there, yeah.

title: Kaa
text: Kaa is Non-canon crossover character; a Disney villain (from The Jungle Book) appearing in Simpsons specials set in Disney Villain Land. Kaa is a snake villain borrowed from Disney's The Jungle Book, appearing in the Simpsons universe as part of a group of Disney villains. He is depicted as manipulative and menacing, using hypnotic and musical persuasion to lure Lisa into joining the villains' club. His snake-like nature is played up through both charm and physical threat, as he is shown crushing Homer in his coils while hypnotizing him. Kaa also participates in a group villain song number, blending into the ensemble of Disney antagonists. In another appearance, he emerges in a surprising transformation twist involving Tiana and a cursed frog. Overall, he serves as a non-canon crossover figure used for comedic and thematic Disney parody purposes rather than as a developed character. Voiced by Dawnn Lewis.

title: Ganesha
text: Ganesha is A Hindu deity honored by Apu Nahasapeemapetilon, appearing mainly as a statue or image in his shop and apartment. Ganesha is not a living character in the traditional sense but a recurring symbol of Apu's Hindu faith throughout the series. He most often appears as a small statue that Apu keeps in his apartment or at the Kwik-E-Mart, quietly reinforcing Apu's cultural background without ever speaking or taking direct action in the plot. The character resurfaces in odd, comedic contexts, such as a pun-based game called "Ganesh-Gnop" and a keychain trinket, showing how the show often works religious references into throwaway jokes. Apu's devotion is further highlighted when he sculpts an image of Ganesha out of dryer lint, a humorous but sincere gesture of reverence. Ganesha's image has also shown up in unexpected places like a candle during a town fire, underscoring how deeply embedded the icon is in Springfield's background details. As a non-speaking, non-canon-adjacent figure, Ganesha functions purely as a visual motif tied to Apu's identity and Hindu practices rather than as an active character in the show's storylines.

title: Ruhollah Khomeini
text: Ruhollah Khomeini is Real-world historical figure (Iranian ayatollah) referenced/depicted in background imagery in the show. Ruhollah Khomeini appears in the show not as an active character but as an image, most notably printed on a mocking T-shirt that becomes a minor plot point involving Homer and Marge. He is a non-speaking, picture-only presence, existing purely as a visual reference to real-world history rather than a personality within the Simpsons universe. His image also turns up on a souvenir shot glass owned by Moe, tied to the Iran hostage crisis. The joke around him hinges on Homer's confused and outdated grasp of Middle Eastern politics, using Khomeini's name to riff on other invented ayatollahs. He's also referenced in a Simpsons tie-in book as part of a satirical political costume line. Overall, he functions as a background gag rather than a true character with development or dialogue.

title: Glamorous Godfrey
text: Glamorous Godfrey is Abraham Simpson's wrestling alter ego, a heel wrestler persona used by Grampa Simpson. Glamorous Godfrey was the villainous wrestling persona adopted by Grampa Simpson back in the 1950s, designed to make audiences despise him through cheating and theatrical showmanship. He wrestled opponents like Baby Face Palooka and Olaf Johannsen, but the constant hatred from fans eventually bled into his real life, prompting him to quit and bury the persona in a storage locker. Decades later, Homer accidentally rediscovers the gear after winning the locker at auction, leading Mr. Burns to identify Grampa as the once-famous heel and convince him to return to the ring. The persona later inspires Bart to create his own heel character, Beautiful Bart, showing how the villainous act can be both entertaining and corrupting. Ultimately, Grampa retires Glamorous Godfrey for good after seeing the negative influence the heel gimmick has on his grandson, transforming into the heroic Honest Abe instead. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Glamorous Godfrey was the most famous wrestler in the world!
quotes: Glamorous Godfrey was the most famous wrestler in the world!

title: Ian (very tall man)
text: Ian (very tall man) is Minor recurring Springfield resident known for his extreme height. Ian is a background character instantly recognizable for his towering, lanky frame and glasses. His unusual height has made him the subject of jokes among Springfield residents, though he's shown he can dish it out too, once humiliating Nelson after being laughed at. He pops up in a variety of odd situations, from riding a bus to New York to attempting a world-record human pyramid and playing a Pokémon Go-style game in a cemetery. He even has trouble finding clothes that fit, shopping at a specialty store for oversized or lanky men. Interestingly, his height isn't consistent across appearances, sometimes dwarfing everyone around him and other times appearing only slightly taller than average. The character is a visual caricature of actual Simpsons writer Ian Maxtone-Graham. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Tom Gammill (character)
text: Tom Gammill (character) is Minor recurring child character, son of Mr. Gammill, an employee at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. Tom Gammill is a young boy best known for accidentally causing his father to lose his job at the power plant. He innocently mentioned skipping a Little League game to attend one of Mr. Burns's picnics, an offhand remark that led to disastrous consequences for his father. Despite this incident, the family seems to bounce back, as his father is later shown still employed by Burns at a company gathering. Tom's family unit occasionally appears together in background roles, including as extras in a movie production. He's a minor background character whose few appearances tie into larger stories involving other Simpsons characters rather than standing on his own. The character's name is a nod to a real-life writer and producer who worked on the show. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Oliver Hardy
text: Oliver Hardy is A minor recurring character based on real-life comic actor Oliver Hardy, appearing as part of the Laurel and Hardy duo in the Simpsons universe. Oliver Hardy is depicted in the show as the fictionalized version of the real comedian famous for the Laurel and Hardy duo, particularly known for his portly build. His appearances are brief and scattered across different episodes, often in flashbacks or surreal contexts rather than as a fully developed character. He's shown in one instance handcuffed to his partner Stan Laurel at a blacksmith's shop, and in another memory sequence disembarking from a train alongside him. In a more chaotic scenario, the duo is responsible for nearly dropping a piano onto Homer and Maggie from a balcony. He also appears as part of a drug-induced hallucination experienced by Homer and Ned, cementing his role as a pop-culture reference rather than a standalone personality within the show. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Jimmy (The City of New York vs. Homer Simpson)
keys: jimmy (the city of new york vs. homer simpson)
text: Jimmy (The City of New York vs. Homer Simpson) is A minor recurring New York carriage driver who briefly interacts with the Simpson family. Jimmy is a carriage driver working in New York City, best known for giving Marge and her three children a horse-drawn tour around Central Park. He's a minor, one-off type character whose role is largely functional rather than comedic, serving as a small piece of local color during the family's New York excursion. He later resurfaces years later outside the Springfield Court House, where he offers a ride to a laughed-out-of-court Jeeves. Despite his limited screen time, he has appeared in more than one episode, making him a low-key recurring background character rather than a single-appearance extra. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Kim Jong-il
text: Kim Jong-il is Real-world North Korean leader depicted as a minor recurring character in the show. Kim Jong-il appears as a caricature of the real-life North Korean leader within the Simpsons universe. He is portrayed as an authoritarian figure associated with missile launches and propaganda, fitting the show's satirical take on real-world dictators. His depictions include a musical made about his life, which he watched after having a captured writer forced to create it. He's also referenced as one of several authoritarian figures that Mr. Burns enjoys impersonating, highlighting the show's recurring gag of comparing Burns to infamous real-world tyrants. Kim Jong-il's appearances are brief and mostly played for background jokes or satire rather than deep characterization. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Green sweater boy
text: Green sweater boy is A minor student character at Springfield Elementary School. The green sweater boy is a background student at Springfield Elementary, identifiable mainly by his distinctive green sweater and red pants. He is a black character with black hair, and little else about his personality or backstory is known since he does not speak. He first appeared in a Treehouse of Horror segment before showing up as a recurring background figure in later seasons. As a non-speaking character, his role is largely limited to appearing in classroom or school-related scenes without any significant plot involvement.

title: Isabel Gutierrez
text: Isabel Gutierrez is A second-grade classmate of Lisa Simpson at Springfield Elementary School. Isabel Gutierrez is a bright young student who first bonds with Lisa Simpson over a shared love of learning, only to discover their political views couldn't be more different. As a staunch Republican facing off against Lisa's Democratic leanings, their friendship is tested when they run against each other for class president. Despite the political rivalry, the two girls ultimately choose their friendship over ideology. She's later shown to be intelligent enough to join the gifted program at Springfield STEM Academy, suggesting she's one of the more academically talented kids at school. She also appears among a crowd of Mexican citizens enjoying Bumblebee Man's show. In a non-canon glimpse of the future, her political rivalry with Lisa escalates into a full presidential debate moderated by Anderson Cooper. Voiced by Eva Longoria.

title: Sean Hannity
text: Sean Hannity is Real-world political commentator caricatured as a minor character in The Simpsons. Sean Hannity appears as a caricature of himself, the real-life conservative talk show host, author, and pundit. In his canon appearance, he's depicted on a book cover being menaced by a knife-wielding Bill O'Reilly, poking fun at rivalries among conservative media figures. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he hosts a Fox News parody called Tox News, ranting about culture war grievances like light bulb regulations. His rant escalates into absurd territory, wondering aloud whether the government will next come after truck testicles or Mrs. Butterworth's bosom. The character is used purely for satire, exaggerating his on-air persona as an outrage-driven commentator. He has no real relationships or personality development within the show beyond this parody role. Notable quotes: He then asked if they'd come for peoples truck testicles or Mrs. Butterworth's "ample bosom" next.
quotes: He then asked if they'd come for peoples truck testicles or Mrs. Butterworth's "ample bosom" next.

title: Huell Howser (character)
text: Huell Howser (character) is A real-world television personality who appears as himself in a show-within-the-show watched by the Simpsons. Huell Howser is a real-life TV personality who shows up in the Simpsons universe as the host of a fictional program called Under the Wrapper. He's depicted as cheerfully enthusiastic and easily impressed, reacting with wide-eyed wonder even to unsettling information. His segment involves touring a gumdrop factory, where his upbeat commentary clashes with the increasingly gruesome details the manufacturer reveals. This tonal mismatch becomes a joke at his expense, as his naive fascination contrasts with Homer and Lisa's growing horror. Howser only appears briefly, functioning as a parody of overly cheery local TV hosts covering mundane subjects. His role is minor but memorable, appearing again later in a background cameo and getting a passing mention in another special. Voiced by Huell Howser (Himself). Notable quotes: "amazing"
quotes: "amazing"

title: Cornelia Hernandez
text: Cornelia Hernandez is Extended relative of Mr. Burns; sister of Charles Montgomery Burns and daughter of Daphne and Clifford Burns. Cornelia Hernandez is a minor member of the sprawling Burns family tree, born to Daphne and Clifford Burns. She is one of several siblings that include the infamous nuclear plant owner Charles Montgomery Burns, as well as George, Zeph, and Cornelius Burns. After marrying Sancho Hernandez, she took his surname and became a mother to their daughter, Pepita. Cornelia exists only as a background/genealogical figure, appearing without any dialogue in the books that reference her. She has no established personality traits since she has never been shown speaking or acting in any storyline, functioning purely as a piece of the extended Burns family lore.

title: Julius Hibbert's father
text: Julius Hibbert's father is Father of Dr. Julius Hibbert, appearing after being moved out of the Springfield Retirement Castle. This elderly, gray-haired man is Dr. Hibbert's father, briefly introduced when the Springfield Retirement Castle is shut down and Hibbert must bring him home. He is blunt and a bit cantankerous, unafraid to tell his accomplished son that he considers him a disappointment despite his medical career. He has a running fondness for the cheap fortified wine Ripple, treating it almost like a beloved family member. His sharp, comedic jabs at his son provide a brief but memorable glimpse into the Hibbert family dynamic. Outside of his single canonical appearance, he also shows up in a non-canon mobile game. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: Without Ripple, I never would have had you. Ripple is your real Daddy.
quotes: Without Ripple, I never would have had you. Ripple is your real Daddy.

title: Hamburglar
text: Hamburglar is Minor crossover character based on the McDonald's mascot, appearing briefly in Springfield media. The Hamburglar is a non-canon crossover figure lifted from McDonald's advertising and dropped into the Simpsons universe for a quick gag. He's best known as the star of his own in-universe comic book, the Hamburglar Adventure Comic. His fate gets a dark comedic touch when Kent Brockman reports his death, revealing he was survived by his longtime companion Mayor McCheese. He later shows up as part of a smear campaign photo used against Mayor Quimby, suggesting a scandalous association. In a surreal non-canon short, he even turns up hiding in Donald Trump's hair. Overall he's a background novelty character rather than a fully developed personality, existing mostly as a nod to real-world fast food branding.

title: Jiminy Cricket
text: Jiminy Cricket is A crossover reference character from Disney's Pinocchio, mentioned or referenced in various Simpsons media. Jiminy Cricket is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed reference to the famous conscience-figure from Disney's Pinocchio. He appears mainly as a punchline or pop-culture touchstone rather than a fleshed-out character in the show itself. His name is invoked as an exclamation by Apu when discovering shockingly expired ham at the Kwik-E-Mart. In a bizarre non-canon twist, Mr. Burns is shown to have literally sealed his own conscience, in the form of Jiminy Cricket, inside amber. He also turns up as an odd link in one of Homer's absurd six-degrees-of-separation chains connecting him to Aerosmith. In another non-canon appearance, he's nearly crushed alongside Ant-Man by Cinderella, underscoring his role purely as a whimsical crossover cameo. Notable quotes: "Jiminy Cricket!"
quotes: "Jiminy Cricket!"

title: Hans (Burns Verkaufen der Kraftwerk)
text: Hans (Burns Verkaufen der Kraftwerk) is One of the German businessmen who briefly purchased the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant from Mr. Burns. Hans is a minor recurring character who, alongside Horst and Fritz, represents a trio of German investors that took control of the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. His tenure as an owner is short-lived, as he and his partners quickly discover the plant is too costly and dangerous to manage, prompting them to sell it back to Mr. Burns. In later appearances, he seems to have moved on to a job at the Center for Geriatric Medicine alongside Fritz. He also shares a taste for eccentric conspiracy theories with Horst, at one point investigating claims about Angela Merkel's birthplace. Hans mostly appears in background or cameo roles rather than driving major storylines, functioning as a running gag tied to German stereotypes and business satire. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Joshua and Amber's mother
text: Joshua and Amber's mother is Minor recurring character; mother of Joshua and Amber, married to a Springfield Nuclear Power Plant employee, and an acquaintance of Marge Simpson. This unnamed woman is best known as the proud parent of two overachieving kids, footballer Joshua and theater star Amber. She traditionally settled sibling rivalry by comparing their report cards, until the year both children earned straight As, leaving her without a tiebreaker. Her husband works at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, connecting her family loosely to the show's central workplace. She appears as part of Springfield's social fabric, attending a company picnic hosted by Mr. Burns where she let loose after drinking spiked punch. That event led to an unlikely bonding moment with Marge Simpson, culminating in the two women singing together. Her recurring background appearances across several episodes mark her as a familiar, if minor, fixture of the town. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Headless Horseman
text: Headless Horseman is Non-canon Halloween-episode character based on the classic Legend of Sleepy Hollow figure. The Headless Horseman is a spooky, folklore-inspired figure who pops up mainly in the show's Halloween specials rather than the main continuity. In one segment, Krusty the Clown takes on the role, gleefully carrying his own severed, laughing head before flinging it at the screen, which splatters the show's title in blood and ends with his signature groan. In a more canon-adjacent moment, Homer is seen casually clinking beer mugs with the Horseman in Sleepy Hollow, New York, while belting out a tune, treating the legendary spook as just another drinking buddy. This mix of horror imagery and absurd comedy fits the show's tradition of playfully mocking classic scary stories. The character has no real personality of his own beyond being a vessel for gags and cameo appearances, existing purely for shock or laughs rather than any ongoing storyline. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Hudson
text: Hudson is A baby who is Maggie Simpson's love interest and friend. Hudson is a blond-haired baby who becomes Maggie Simpson's romantic interest after a chance encounter at a playground. He first catches Maggie's attention by heroically pulling her out of the way of a rolling baby on a slide, sparking an instant infatuation. Their relationship plays out like a tiny romance, complete with playground make-believe games, a wistful separation, and a dramatic train chase where they exchange a pacifier kiss instead of a real one. Despite obstacles like mismatched playdates and their mothers' clashing parenting styles, Hudson and Maggie's bond persists, culminating in a sweet moment where Maggie carries him over the threshold of a playhouse. As a baby, Hudson is non-speaking, expressing his affection and heroics through actions rather than words. He also appears in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Jockeys
text: Jockeys is A secretive group of racehorse jockeys who live together in Jockey Town, encountered by Homer and Bart in "Saddlesore Galactica". The Jockeys are a small, insular community of horse racers who reside in a hidden settlement called Jockey Town. They come across as clannish and intimidating, banding together to protect their turf whenever an outsider's horse threatens their dominance on the track. When Homer's horse Duncan, reinvented as "Furious D," starts winning races, the jockeys grow furious and resort to musical intimidation and outright threats to force Homer into throwing a race. Their culture is portrayed as strange and almost cult-like, complete with secret panels, group songs, and cannibalistic threats. Despite their menacing behavior, they are ultimately outwitted and humiliated by Homer's family. The group is noted to draw inspiration from the Munchkins of The Wizard of Oz and the Oompa-Loompas of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta, Hank Azaria, Nancy Cartwright, Harry Shearer, Tress MacNeille.

title: Warren G. Harding
text: Warren G. Harding is Real-world 29th President of the United States, referenced as a historical figure within the Simpsons universe. Warren G. Harding appears in the show not as a living character but as a historical footnote, showing up mainly in pictures and offhand references. His portrait gets defaced with a drawn-on moustache by Milhouse during the kids' takeover of Springfield Elementary. He's also invoked by Lisa as a piece of trivia to needle Bart, name-dropping his wife Florence Harding. Bart briefly encounters his image in a book before becoming fixated on Theodore Roosevelt instead. In one of the show's more surreal moments, a fictional monument called the Warren Harding Memorial Through-hole is used by Homer to lead townsfolk to Springfield Mesa. Overall, he functions as a minor bit of presidential trivia and background gag material rather than an active character.

title: Jenny (The Good, the Sad, and the Drugly)
keys: jenny (the good, the sad, and the drugly)
text: Jenny (The Good, the Sad, and the Drugly) is One of Bart Simpson's girlfriends, a devout Christian girl he met while she was volunteering. Jenny is an eleven-year-old girl who caught Bart's attention while volunteering at the Springfield Retirement Castle. She is devoutly Christian, even praying to God during school hours, which sets her apart from Bart's usual crowd. Initially charmed, she believed Bart to be a genuinely kind person, but her opinion soured once she learned the truth about his mischievous nature. Their brief romance ended in a breakup, leaving lingering tension between them. When Bart later tried to reconnect with her, she made it clear she wanted nothing to do with him, rebuffing him harshly before shutting the door. She is also notably related to Sister Belle, an activist nun, who is her aunt. Voiced by Anne Hathaway. Notable quotes: eat my shorts
quotes: eat my shorts

title: LeBron James (character)
text: LeBron James (character) is Real-world basketball star who appears as himself in guest spots on The Simpsons. LeBron James appears as a fictionalized version of himself who gets roped into Homer's antics. He seeks out Homer's help after his celebration dances fail to impress audiences, becoming one of several athletes Homer coaches. His larger-than-life athleticism plays for laughs, such as when he hogs the salad at a family dinner and leaps onto a light fixture before crashing back down. Despite being a wealthy superstar with a massive contract, he's portrayed as easily delighted by simple pleasures like a home-cooked omelet. He's also referenced in later episodes as a benchmark for greatness in debates about sports legends. In a non-canon appearance, he even shows up at a glitzy premiere event. Voiced by LeBron James.

title: Thomas Jefferson
text: Thomas Jefferson is Historical U.S. President appearing in dream sequences, memorials, and historical stories within the show. Thomas Jefferson appears in The Simpsons as a recurring historical figure, often depicted as a statue, animatronic, or dream character rather than a living presence in the main story. He is portrayed as somewhat bitter and lonely, lamenting that his monument is overshadowed by the more popular Lincoln Memorial despite his major accomplishments. His appearances tend to be brief and comedic, poking fun at how historical figures are remembered or forgotten. In one story, he is shown as impatient and short-tempered, insulting Lewis and Clark for taking too long on their expedition. He also appears as a talking statue who longs for visitors, giving the show a chance to blend educational history with self-deprecating humor about neglected legacies. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: No one ever comes to see me. I don't blame them. I never did anything important-- just the Declaration of Independence, the Louisiana Purchase, the dumbwaiter...
quotes: No one ever comes to see me. I don't blame them. I never did anything important-- just the Declaration of Independence, the Louisiana Purchase, the dumbwaiter...

title: Kim Jong-un
text: Kim Jong-un is Real-world North Korean supreme leader referenced/appearing in minor Simpsons cameos and gags. Kim Jong-un is a caricatured version of the real-world North Korean leader who appears in a handful of minor, mostly non-canon Simpsons gags. He's depicted as a touchy, easily angered dictator, shown reacting furiously when a guard drops an ice cube on his head during a parody of the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge. He's referenced in political jokes, including being pictured in a smear campaign against Mayor Quimby and being humorously linked to a stray ICBM strike near North Korea. The character is largely used as a punchline for real-world political satire rather than a fleshed-out figure in Springfield's world. He has no confirmed voice actor and rarely speaks on screen.

title: Inky
text: Inky is One of the ghost characters from the Pac-Man arcade game, referenced within The Simpsons universe. Inky is a video-game ghost from the classic Pac-Man franchise who makes several cameo appearances within the world of The Simpsons rather than being an original character. He first shows up on Mr. Burns's Ms. Pac-Man arcade screen, and later appears at the fictional wedding of Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man during a Super Bowl broadcast, dancing along with the other ghosts. Inky's image also turns up printed on an arcade cabinet during a chaotic scene, and again on-screen during a blackout at a gaming championship. He even appears on the cover of an in-universe album called Pacman Fever. As a non-speaking crossover character, Inky exists purely as a nod to classic gaming nostalgia rather than having any real personality or dialogue in the show.

title: G.I. Joe
text: G.I. Joe is Minor character; soldier and ex-husband of Stacy Lovell, creator of Malibu Stacy. G.I. Joe is a gruff military man best known as the estranged husband of toy designer Stacy Lovell. He appears only briefly, showing up at her mansion in an attempt to win her back after their divorce. When she rejects him, his soldierly demeanor turns menacing, and he storms off after making a violent threat toward her home. His name is also used as a generic nickname for a U.S. Marine during the Simpson family's trip to Australia, showing how the character's identity blurs with the real-world toy line he's based on. Beyond this, he has no ongoing presence in the show, appearing mainly as a one-off gag tied to the Malibu Stacy doll storyline. His design and name are a clear parody of Hasbro's G.I. Joe action figure franchise. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Hermione Granger
text: Hermione Granger is Harry Potter character referenced/crossed over in The Simpsons universe. Hermione Granger appears in The Simpsons as a nod to the famous Harry Potter book series, functioning as a crossover reference rather than an original character with her own storyline. She is depicted as an English Muggle-born witch, staying true to her source material. Within the show, she is regarded as an admirable figure, notably appearing on Lisa's imagined wall of great women alongside other influential female icons like Joan of Arc and Harriet Tubman. Lisa also pays tribute to her by dressing up as Hermione for a Halloween event at school. Hermione has no spoken lines in her appearances, existing purely as a visual and thematic reference. Her inclusion highlights her cultural status as a symbol of intelligence and bravery, fitting for Lisa's admiration.

title: Magic Johnson (character)
text: Magic Johnson (character) is Real-life basketball player who makes a guest appearance in Springfield, interacting with Homer. Magic Johnson appears as himself, a celebrated NBA star for the Los Angeles Lakers, in a cameo tied to one of Homer's accidental triumphs. He calls Homer to offer congratulations after Homer inadvertently averts a nuclear disaster, showing a friendly and generous side. Despite nursing a painful bad ankle, he insists on playing anyway, revealing a tough, dedicated athlete's mentality. He also offers a bit of philosophical insight, warning that people who succeed through luck rather than genuine skill will eventually be revealed as frauds. In a lighthearted running gag, he later mimics one of Homer's clumsy mishaps by sliding after a slam dunk near cheerleaders, jokingly calling it 'pulling a Homer.' His appearance is brief but memorable, blending celebrity cameo humor with a wink at Homer's reputation for stumbling into accidental heroism. Voiced by Magic Johnson. Notable quotes: he pulled a Homer.
quotes: he pulled a Homer.

title: Bob Iger
text: Bob Iger is Real-world media executive depicted in non-canon Simpsons specials. Bob Iger appears in the show as a real-world figure, referenced rather than featured as a true story character, reflecting his status as Chairman and former CEO of The Walt Disney Company. His presence is largely symbolic, existing mostly as background decoration or a nod to Disney's ownership of the franchise. He is non-speaking and non-canon, appearing only in special episodes tied to Disney-related promotions or crossovers. One notable gag involves Mickey Mouse humorously parking in his designated spot, poking fun at corporate hierarchy. Overall, his inclusion serves as a meta joke about Disney's real-world connection to The Simpsons rather than developing him as an actual character in the show's universe.

title: Ernest Hemingway
text: Ernest Hemingway is Real-world author referenced and depicted as a historical figure within the Simpsons universe. Ernest Hemingway appears in the Simpsons world primarily as a literary legend rather than a living character, mostly shown through pictures, mentions, and brief appearances. He is best known in-universe as the author of 'A Farewell to Arms,' a book whose author photo has popped up more than once. His legacy intertwines with the show's characters in odd ways, such as being cited as a grim example when discussing suicide, or being linked to Lisa's romantic troubles through the ghosts of his ex-wives. He's also tied to Cuba lore, referenced when the Simpsons visit Havana and read about his historic house. In one flashback, even Mr. Burns claims to have met him personally, sketching his portrait. Despite his fame, Hemingway himself never really speaks on the show, appearing instead as a symbol of literary greatness and troubled personal life.

title: Hug-A-Bull
text: Hug-A-Bull is A costumed bull mascot at the Kissimmee St. Nick Theme Park and Resort. Hug-A-Bull is a minor recurring character who works as a mascot at a Simpsons-universe theme park. True to his name, his whole gimmick revolves around offering hugs to park guests, though he's oddly insistent on legal technicalities about who can initiate physical contact. He appeared willing to comfort even a frustrated Homer during a family vacation mishap. Later he turns up in a different seasonal setting, this time stationed beside a sign warning visitors not to hug him, a funny reversal of his usual purpose. He doesn't have much personality beyond his mascot role, but he serves as a quick punchline about theme park absurdity and liability culture. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Hug-A-Bull told Bart that legally, Bart had to initiate the hug.
quotes: Hug-A-Bull told Bart that legally, Bart had to initiate the hug.

title: Jub-Jub
text: Jub-Jub is Selma Bouvier's pet iguana, a recurring animal character in the Simpson/Bouvier family. Jub-Jub is a green iguana who originally belonged to Aunt Gladys before passing through the hands of Jacqueline Bouvier and eventually settling in as Selma's beloved pet. He has a morbid streak, showing a persistent fascination with eating dead or motionless things, including once nearly munching on Selma's foot when it fell asleep. He's also fond of snacking on roaches, reinforcing his creepy-crawly appetite. Selma has darkly joked that Jub-Jub will eventually eat her remains after she dies, a nod to an old urban legend. As a non-speaking animal character, Jub-Jub never talks but has appeared across many seasons and various Simpsons media as a quiet fixture of the Bouvier household. His quirky name was reportedly coined by writer Conan O'Brien, who used to blurt it out randomly in the writers' room.

title: Kevin (Stealing First Base)
text: Kevin (Stealing First Base) is A blind 4th-grade student at Springfield Elementary and an unlikely friend of Nelson Muntz. Kevin is a young, blind classmate of Nelson Muntz who becomes an unexpected companion after Nelson realizes his disability. Despite his blindness, Kevin isn't entirely helpless or innocent, as shown when he provokes Nelson by touching his face and calling him ugly. He has a mischievous streak, famously tricking Nelson into thinking he'd regained his sight before revealing it was a joke. Nelson, in turn, takes on a protective role over him once the truth about his blindness is known, defending him from other threats. Kevin's design is notably similar to another minor Springfield Elementary student named Kyle, suggesting a reused character model. He appears in a handful of episodes as a background or side character tied mainly to Nelson's storyline. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: Ha Ha!
quotes: Ha Ha!

title: The General
text: The General is An Air Force general who runs a covert program using children in combat simulations, appearing in Bart's storyline. The General is a stern military officer who oversees a secretive Air Force program at an asylum, recruiting children believed to be sociopathic to participate in what they think are shooting simulations. He appears calculating and manipulative, willing to use kids for real combat missions under the guise of training exercises. When Bart Simpson, sent to the asylum after a prank, excels at the simulation, the General reveals the disturbing truth that it was not a simulation at all. His willingness to deceive children into committing real violence highlights his morally dubious and cold approach to his duties. Ultimately, his program rejects Bart once it becomes clear the boy has a conscience and isn't a true sociopath, showing the General's specific interest in emotionally detached recruits. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Gaston
text: Gaston is Non-canon crossover character from Beauty and the Beast appearing in Simpsons Disney+ specials. Gaston is a crossover guest character imported from Disney's Beauty and the Beast rather than an original Simpsons creation. He appears in a handful of special Disney+ crossover episodes, existing mainly as a background or cameo figure rather than a fully developed character. He's shown attending a party at Moe's Tavern celebrating Disney+'s anniversary, mingling with the Simpsons cast by dancing with Marge, and joining a group of Disney villains in song during a holiday special. He has no dialogue in these appearances, functioning purely as a visual nod to Disney fans. His inclusion highlights the increasingly frequent blending of Simpsons and Disney properties following the studio's acquisition of the franchise.

title: Frank Grimes, Jr.
text: Frank Grimes, Jr. is Illegitimate son of Frank Grimes and a would-be assassin of Homer Simpson. Frank Grimes, Jr., known as Junior, is the secret offspring of Frank Grimes and an unnamed prostitute, born from his father's fondness for hookers. Consumed by hatred for Homer Simpson, whom he blames for driving his father insane and causing his death, he orchestrates a string of murder attempts against him. Like his father before him, Junior grows increasingly enraged the longer he spends around Homer, mirroring the elder Grimes' slow descent into fury. He manages to keep his identity hidden while working as Homer's mechanic, only exposing his true motive once he's cornered. His scheme ultimately falls apart, and he is hauled off by the Springfield Police, vowing that he must still kill Homer. In a non-canon story, he later resurfaces as a mysterious masked prisoner tied to one of Mr. Burns' secret schemes. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: He said that he must kill Homer.
quotes: He said that he must kill Homer.

title: Garfield
text: Garfield is Real-world comic strip cat referenced and parodied within The Simpsons universe. Garfield is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover reference to the famous newspaper comic strip cat created by Jim Davis. Within the show, he's treated as a well-known pop culture figure that the citizens of Springfield are familiar with, often invoked in jokes about lasagna and laziness. Various characters reference him in different contexts, from Milhouse owning Garfield binders to Krusty using Garfield cartoons to avoid laughing on the job. He even appears in a fictional Itchy & Scratchy parody episode called "The Garfield Assassination." Garfield's cultural ubiquity is used as running gag material, with characters like Fat Tony and Colonel Hapablap referencing his known love of lasagna and hatred of Mondays. In a non-canon Halloween special, his grave was even shown in the Springfield Cemetery. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: faster than Garfield finds lasagna
quotes: faster than Garfield finds lasagna

title: Hosey the Bear
text: Hosey the Bear is A fire safety mascot bear who appears at Springfield Elementary's fire safety fair and as a talking statue at Mt. Useful Visitors Center. Hosey the Bear is a costumed mascot character whose job is to teach children about fire safety. He appears in at least two forms: a life-size costume that interacts with kids like Ralph Wiggum, and an interactive talking statue at a visitors center that poses a rhetorical question about preventing forest fires. In a humorous twist, when someone presses the button to answer that question, the statue reveals it's actually referring to itself rather than the visitor. Ralph Wiggum mistakes Hosey for Santa Claus during a photo session, rambling about wanting a bike and a monkey. When Hosey earnestly asks if Ralph plans to start any fires, Ralph's oddly matter-of-fact reply hints at unsafe habits at home. Overall, Hosey serves as a minor comedic mascot figure used to satirize public safety campaigns and childhood innocence. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: At my house we call them Uh-Oh's.
quotes: At my house we call them Uh-Oh's.

title: Gandalf the Grey
text: Gandalf the Grey is Non-canon parody character appearing in a Lord of the Rings-themed Simpsons comic, member of the Fellowship of the Ring. Gandalf the Grey shows up in a comic-book parody of The Lord of the Rings after the Simpson family gets pulled into Middle Earth by Saruman. He's portrayed as a wise but easily exasperated wizard, quickly worn down by Bart's constant pestering about how to destroy the One Ring. Despite the epic stakes of battling Sauron's forces, he ends up on the receiving end of Homer's trademark clumsiness, first getting knocked over mid-fight and later getting accidentally shoved off a ledge after Homer defeats the Balrog. In a laid-back moment amid the chaos, he's shown sharing some of Middle Earth's finest smoke with Frodo Baggins following the deaths of Legolas and Gimli. Beyond his main comic appearance, the character is referenced or parodied a few more times, including as a Halloween costume and in cover art.
