His backstory is a darkly comic mix of family trauma and Cold War absurdity: he was once his brother Marvin's test subject for a bed-wetting cure gone horribly wrong, and he later picked up his tattooing skills through a botched CIA scheme targeting Fidel Castro. A running gag involves his questionable professionalism, from nearly tattooing a curse word onto Bart's arm to holding an infamous record for the most misspelled tattoos ever inked. He's also had his heart literally and figuratively broken by a woman named Tattoo Annie. Despite his shady trade, he pops up in ordinary Springfield life, from parenting classes to record-breaking human pyramids to visiting a son in juvenile detention. His scruffy appearance hides a odd secret: even his beard is a tattoo. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Get in the chair.|Mervin Monroe|Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire
quotes: Get in the chair.|Mervin Monroe|Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire

title: Neil
text: Neil is Minor recurring character; an advertiser for the energy bar brand Powersauce who appears in Homer's extreme sports storyline. Neil is a marketing man for Powersauce, working alongside his partner Brad to promote the energy bar brand through stunts and media appearances. Together they approach action star Rainier Wolfcastle to climb the treacherous Murderhorn as a publicity stunt, but when Wolfcastle refuses, Bart volunteers Homer instead, setting off one of Homer's daring adventures. Neil and Brad also serve as hosts of the in-universe Powersauce Newsbreak segment, giving him a recognizable media presence within Springfield. He shows up in a handful of other episodes as a background or cameo character, including at a garden party hosted by Trent Steele. In non-canon material, he's also glimpsed at the Springfield Country Club during an unusual incident involving Dr. Zoidberg saving Mr. Burns' life. Overall, Neil functions as a background businessman whose main claim to fame is kickstarting one of Homer's more absurd extreme-sports escapades. Voiced by Steven Weber.

title: McBabe
text: McBabe is A fictional character within the show's parody action film series, McBain, portrayed by actress Clara Hosenfrauen. McBabe is a glamorous action-movie love interest who appears alongside the fictional hero McBain in his string of over-the-top film adventures. She's the classic tough-but-alluring sidekick, quick with a flirtatious quip after McBain dispatches a room full of enemies. Her chemistry with McBain leans heavily on genre clichés, mixing violence with romance in true parody-action style. Beyond her single on-screen scene, she's referenced as having starred in multiple McBain films, cementing her as a recurring fixture of the fictional franchise rather than a one-off character. She embodies the show's affectionate mockery of 1980s action-movie tropes. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: You certainly broke up that meeting.
quotes: You certainly broke up that meeting.

title: Lady Milhouse
text: Lady Milhouse is Milhouse Van Houten's in-game character persona from the fictional MMORPG Earthland Realms. Lady Milhouse is the alter ego Milhouse plays while immersed in the online game Earthland Realms, serving as an assistant to the Shadow Knight character. The persona came about after a spell turned the character into a lady, a transformation that was supposed to be temporary. Bart, who plays the Shadow Knight, promises to undo the spell but never actually gets around to it, leaving Milhouse stuck in the role. The character has blue hair and exists purely within the game's fictional fantasy setting rather than in the show's real world. She later reappears as a collectible character skin in The Simpsons: Tapped Out, tying her non-canon presence to the mobile game universe. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Barry Mackleberry
text: Barry Mackleberry is Homer's former supervisor at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant and father of Sherri and Terri. Barry Mackleberry is a minor recurring figure at the power plant, best known as the man who once fired Homer following a workplace disaster. He is the husband of Jerri Mackleberry and father of twins Sherri and Terri, tying him to two of Lisa and Bart's classmates. His appearance has been inconsistent over the show's history, having been mistakenly colored brown in his debut before later appearing with lighter skin, and his surname wasn't confirmed until many seasons after his first appearance. In a non-canon video game depiction, his marriage is portrayed as having fallen apart due to a shared crush with his wife on newsman Kent Brockman. Despite his behind-the-scenes inconsistencies, he has persisted as a background character across many seasons of the show. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Brody McKenna
text: Brody McKenna is Federal prosecutor, father of Nikki McKenna and husband of Madison McKenna; minor recurring character in Springfield. Brody McKenna is a stern, litigious federal prosecutor who appears as a minor recurring figure in Springfield. He is best known for his overprotective reaction after Bart Simpson kissed his daughter Nikki, leading him and his wife to press legal charges against Springfield Elementary School. This incident resulted in the school implementing a controversial no-touch policy, showing how far he's willing to go to protect his daughter's interests. Outside of his role as a concerned father, he's shown living a fairly ordinary suburban life, such as attending a Cheech and Chong concert with his wife. He doesn't have much of a defined personality beyond his protective and legally-minded nature, functioning mostly as a plot device tied to his family's storylines. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mr. McIntyre
text: Mr. McIntyre is Guidance counselor at Springfield High School, appearing in a flashback involving young Homer. Mr. McIntyre is a minor background figure at Springfield High School who serves as its guidance counselor. He's shown giving advice to a teenage Homer, who came to him confused about his feelings for Marge. Rather than offering deep emotional insight, McIntyre suggests the practical solution of finding common ground with her. He also nudges Homer toward his future career path by handing him a brochure for the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, foreshadowing Homer's eventual job. His appearances are limited to flashback sequences, making him a small but historically important piece of the Simpsons' backstory. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Minnie Mouse
text: Minnie Mouse is Disney character who appears as a crossover cameo in The Simpsons, married to Mickey Mouse. Minnie Mouse is a guest crossover character from the Disney universe rather than a native Simpsons character. She is Mickey Mouse's wife and appears only in a non-speaking capacity within the show. In one non-canon moment she is seen dancing with Bart, and she later appears alongside Mickey at the close of a musical number. Her only other mention comes from a story told by Grampa, in which a character's voice is compared to hers while wearing jodhpurs. She has no dialogue and functions purely as a nostalgic cameo rather than a developed personality within the series.

title: Hannibal Lecter
text: Hannibal Lecter is Parody crossover character; a mental patient at New Bedlam Rest Home who briefly appears near Homer during his stay there. This version of Hannibal Lecter is a nod to the famous cannibalistic psychiatrist from Thomas Harris's novels and their film adaptations. In the show, he's confined to New Bedlam Rest Home for the Emotionally Interesting, kept restrained in a straitjacket and muzzle for obvious safety reasons. He's glimpsed in the background during Homer's tour of the asylum, once strapped to a hand truck and once sipping a drink through a straw at lunch, muzzle and all. His only real moment of dialogue comes during an audition for a Mr. Burns film, where he creepily slithers while saying a single word, a wink to his iconic line about eating liver with fava beans and a nice Chianti. He's less a developed character than a quick, dark visual gag referencing his cinematic counterpart, played on screen by Anthony Hopkins. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: "excellent"
quotes: "excellent"

title: Ben Matlock
text: Ben Matlock is Fictional defense attorney from the TV series Matlock, beloved by Springfield's senior citizens, who makes a rare in-person cameo appearance. Ben Matlock exists within the Simpsons universe as the title character of the elderly citizens' favorite TV show, a courtroom drama that seniors like Grampa and Jasper obsess over constantly. His popularity with Springfield's retirees is so great that a highway is renamed the Matlock Expressway purely to win their votes in a mayoral election. When he actually visits Springfield in person, his adoring elderly fans nearly kill him with their over-enthusiastic greeting, tugging at his hair and causing chaos that ends with him being hospitalized. He's treated as a genuine celebrity by the town's older residents, to the point where poetry readings and casual conversation frequently circle back to him. Ironically, younger characters like Bart have to remind confused seniors that he's not a real person. Even in the afterlife, in a non-canon segment, Jasper is shown still watching Matlock reruns in Hell.

title: Evan Marriott (character)
text: Evan Marriott (character) is Real-life celebrity guest character who appears as himself in The Simpsons. Evan Marriott appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, playing off his real-world fame as the star of the reality dating show Joe Millionaire. His cameo pokes fun at his public persona, particularly the show's twist where he deceived a potential bride about his wealth. In one episode, a promotional clip for his series becomes a brief comedic prop when Homer eats it, only to spit it out upon learning it's a FOX promo. In another appearance, he's shown starring in a stage adaptation of The Cherry Orchard, where a joke is made tying back to his reality TV persona of hiding the truth from a woman. His role is minor and largely a satirical nod to early-2000s reality television culture rather than a substantial character arc. He exists mostly as a one-off pop culture reference rather than a recurring personality with deep characterization. Voiced by Evan Marriott (Himself).

title: Ms. Melon
text: Ms. Melon is Teacher at the Enriched Learning Center for Gifted Children, briefly Bart's instructor. Ms. Melon runs a classroom for gifted students, using a hands-off teaching style that lets kids explore topics at their own pace. This approach works well for her naturally bright pupils but proves disastrous for Bart, who ends up there after cheating on Martin Prince's IQ test. Lacking real aptitude for the advanced material, especially chemistry, Bart's presence under her loose supervision leads to chaos. Outside the classroom, she pops up occasionally around Springfield, including family outings, showing she has a life beyond the gifted program. She's depicted as a mild, background recurring character rather than a dominant personality, most notable for the contrast her teaching method creates with Bart's usual struggles at Springfield Elementary. Voiced by Marcia Wallace.

title: Stan Lee (character)
text: Stan Lee (character) is Real-life comic book legend who appears as himself in guest cameos, tied closely to Comic Book Guy's storyline. Stan Lee appears in the show as a guest-starring version of himself, tied mostly to the world of comics and Comic Book Guy. He shows up in odd, surreal situations, from acting erratically while playing with action figures to appearing as a hallucinated vision offering advice. Despite his age, he's portrayed as spry and a bit stubborn, insisting he can do what he wants at 90 years old. He plays a significant real role in Comic Book Guy's life, eventually officiating his wedding to Kumiko. Beyond his direct appearances, he's frequently referenced through photos, quotes, and even a Halloween costume, showing his pervasive influence on Springfield's comic-book culture. He is also mentioned in various non-canon spinoff materials tied to the show's expanded universe. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: With great power there must also come great responsibility
quotes: With great power there must also come great responsibility

title: Anton Lubchenko
text: Anton Lubchenko is A football player for Springfield University who appears in a homecoming episode with Homer and Marge. Anton Lubchenko is a college football star recruited to Springfield University seemingly for his athletic talent alone, with little regard for his academics. He hints at being a foreign athlete brought in under the label of an "All-American," though he's cut off before elaborating. During a homecoming game, he suffers a leg injury caused by Homer's poorly made float, only to be comically "healed" by Bart, who is posing as a faith healer. In a bizarre climax, his injured leg detaches and still manages to score the winning goal, turning the leg itself into an unlikely hero while Anton is rushed off in an ambulance. His storyline pokes fun at the exploitative nature of college sports, especially when it's revealed his supposed academic major is fake. Despite his brief appearance, he leaves an absurd and memorable mark on Springfield University's football legacy. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Uma Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Uma Nahasapeemapetilon is One of Apu and Manjula's octuplet babies, a minor recurring character in the Simpsons universe. Uma is one of the eight Nahasapeemapetilon children born after Manjula took fertility drugs. As an infant, she has no distinct personality of her own beyond being one of the octuplets, who are generally treated as a single unit throughout the show. Her introduction ties into the storyline of Apu and Manjula struggling to cope with suddenly having eight children at once. This overwhelming responsibility leads them to place the babies in a display exhibit at the Springfield Zoo, a decision they come to regret. Uma's main claim to notability is being rescued alongside her siblings when Apu and Homer break the octuplets out of the zoo. She has continued to make background appearances in the Simpsons universe across many later episodes, comics, and other media as part of the growing Nahasapeemapetilon family. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Chuck Liddell (character)
text: Chuck Liddell (character) is Real-world mixed martial artist who appeared as himself in a guest role on The Simpsons. Chuck Liddell appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, the real-life mixed martial arts fighter. He shows up in Springfield in connection with the world of MMA, lending his real-world reputation and physical presence to the episode's storyline. As with many celebrity cameos on the show, his character trades on the audience's familiarity with his actual career rather than an original personality crafted for the series. He is a minor, recurring guest character rather than a core member of the Springfield cast. His inclusion reflects the show's frequent practice of having real athletes voice themselves for a touch of authenticity and humor. Voiced by Chuck Liddell (himself).

title: Zack Morris
text: Zack Morris is A college student and minor character who appears in a Simpsons comic story, based on the Saved by the Bell character. Zack Morris is a crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe from the sitcom Saved by the Bell. In his appearance, he's depicted as a college student who gets tutored by Homer at the Old Springfield Library, alongside fellow Bell characters Screech and Jessie Spano. This tutoring session happens because Homer mistakenly believes it's Opposite Day and thinks that makes him smart enough to teach. Zack's image also shows up on the cover of a Nostalgi-Con magazine, tying him to nostalgic pop-culture references within the comics. Notably, his name is misspelled as "Zach" in the story itself, a small trivia quirk noted by fans. As a recurring but minor figure, he mostly serves as a nod to 90s sitcom nostalgia rather than having deep characterization within the Simpsons canon.

title: Melric
text: Melric is A minor non-canon character from the medieval-themed "The Serfsons" episode, owner of a shop called Melric's Melnibones. Melric is a shopkeeper from the fictional realm of Springfieldia, appearing in the fantasy-parody episode "The Serfsons." He runs a store called Melric's Melnibones, a name that pays homage to Michael Moorcock's classic Elric of Melniboné sword-and-sorcery stories. When the townsfolk rise up against the tyrannical Lord Montgomery, Melric joins the rebellion and storms the castle alongside his fellow citizens. Unfortunately, his heroic effort is cut short when he is killed by the Dragon of Springfieldia. He later reappears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, tied to the Warmfyre-themed content. As a non-canon character, his story exists outside the show's main continuity. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Kool-Aid Man
text: Kool-Aid Man is Fictional mascot character for Kool-Aid who makes brief appearances/references in The Simpsons. The Kool-Aid Man is a pitcher-shaped mascot character who appears in a handful of surreal or fantastical moments throughout the show rather than as a regular cast member. He's depicted as part of the backdrop of Americatown, standing alongside other iconic American figures like Uncle Sam and Elvis Presley. He also shows up in one of Homer's odd childhood fantasies, where Homer imagines drinking Kool-Aid straight from him. In another strange twist, a museum exhibit combines him with Jesus Christ into a piece called "Kool-Aid Jesus," poking fun at commercialism and religious imagery. In a non-canon crossover appearance, he bursts through a courthouse wall in classic fashion, though he mistakenly ends up in the wrong Springfield. Overall, he functions as a pop-culture cameo used for quick visual gags rather than a developed character. Voiced by Seth MacFarlane.

title: Mrs. Norton
text: Mrs. Norton is Librarian at the Springfield Public Library, occasionally seen at Springfield University and Elementary School. Mrs. Norton is a minor recurring background character who works as a librarian in Springfield, primarily seen at the Springfield Public Library. She maintains a friendly rapport with Lisa Simpson, who visits the library for various pursuits including helping Bart improve his mini golf skills. Despite her generally amiable nature, she is not above enforcing library rules, most memorably when she scolds Homer for treating the library like a convenience store. Her role occasionally extends beyond the public library, as she has also been shown working at Springfield University's library. She appeared among the staff of Springfield Elementary during the fallout of Mr. Burns' oil-draining scheme, showing she has ties to the town's educational institutions more broadly. Overall, she serves as a stock authority figure representing Springfield's library system across multiple locations. Voiced by Maggie Roswell. Notable quotes: This is not a Kwik-E-Mart!
quotes: This is not a Kwik-E-Mart!

title: Maitre D'
text: Maitre D' is A minor recurring waiter character at the Chez Paree restaurant. The Maitre D' is a background service worker best known for his appearance at the upscale Chez Paree restaurant. He is the one who seats Homer and Marge Simpson and assists Homer in the peculiar task of picking out a live lobster for dinner. Beyond his signature restaurant role, he has also turned up in other settings, including the exclusive Millionaire's Club and even in a dream sequence during one of the Treehouse of Horror specials. He doesn't have a deep personality explored on the show, functioning mostly as a recurring bit of set dressing for Springfield's fancier locales. His presence across a few episodes has been enough to earn him a small but consistent place among the show's recurring minor characters. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Krusty the Clown fan
text: Krusty the Clown fan is An unnamed second-grade student at Springfield Elementary who is a devoted fan of Krusty the Clown. This minor background character is one of the many nameless kids populating Miss Hoover's second grade classroom. His defining trait is his enthusiasm for Krusty the Clown, to the point of owning fan merchandise and seeking autographs. His brief moment of fame comes from a joke about generational ignorance, since he treasures a book of jokes about a pop duo he knows nothing about. He appears only briefly across a handful of episodes, functioning as a one-off gag character rather than a recurring personality. Like many Springfield Elementary students, he exists mostly as part of the classroom background, popping up for a quick comedic beat before disappearing. His humor stems from the irony of being devoted to a joke book referencing something outdated or unfamiliar to him. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Nathaniel
text: Nathaniel is Minor recurring character, an employee at the Candy Shoppe in Barnacle Bay. Nathaniel works at the Candy Shoppe in the quirky town of Barnacle Bay. He and his coworkers are unaccustomed to seeing outsiders, reacting with surprise when the Simpson family visits as tourists. He's eager to please customers, even offering to caramelize body parts on request, which leads to Homer suffering when his arm gets the treatment. Beyond his candy shop duties, Nathaniel also helps out with other town chores, such as repairing the local carousel. A darker running joke reveals that he and his fellow employees squander their earnings on drugs, hinting at the seedier underbelly of the seemingly quaint seaside town. He remains a minor, one-episode character whose main purpose is to add local color to Barnacle Bay. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Man in dinner jacket
text: Man in dinner jacket is A minor recurring character, one of the Lost Souls aboard the Ship of Lost Souls encountered by Homer Simpson. The man in dinner jacket is a mysterious, world-weary wanderer who sails the seven seas aboard the Ship of Lost Souls, a vessel crewed by people trying to escape their troubled pasts. He speaks in cryptic, existential terms, claiming he and his companions are nobody, going nowhere, and may not even truly exist, giving him an air of melancholy and philosophical detachment. Despite this brooding persona, his own tragic backstory turns out to be comically trivial, undercutting the group's serious tone with absurdist humor. He reacts with genuine shock upon hearing Homer's darker confession, showing that even the Lost Souls have limits to what they consider acceptable. Visually and tonally, he is designed as a spoof of classic film actor Peter Lorre, reinforcing the noir-ish, dramatic atmosphere of his scenes. He appears only briefly across a couple of animated shorts, functioning mainly as a device for absurd humor rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: that they were no one, that they were sailing nowhere, and that he didn't even know if they existed
quotes: that they were no one, that they were sailing nowhere, and that he didn't even know if they existed

title: Sun Moon
text: Sun Moon is A Korean girl who competes as a finalist in the Spellympics spelling competition. Sun Moon is a minor recurring character who represents Korea as one of the three finalists in the Spellympics. Her defining moment comes when she is given a trick sound-alike word challenge, revealing the rigged and unfair nature of the competition's judging. No matter which word she chose to spell, she was destined to be disqualified, showing the deceptive tactics used by the contest's organizer. Beyond her appearance at the Spellympics, she has a brief cameo in a later episode, seen waiting in a customs line while traveling through Cuba. She has black hair and is depicted as a studious, competitive child. Her character exists mainly to serve the plot of the spelling competition storyline rather than to showcase deep personality traits. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Kwik-E-Mart CEO
text: Kwik-E-Mart CEO is The Indian guru-like head of the entire Kwik-E-Mart franchise (and Ohio's Stop-O-Mart), appearing in the episode "Homer and Apu". This character is portrayed as a wise, serene guru who presides over the Kwik-E-Mart empire from a remote Himalayan headquarters, spending his time sitting cross-legged and sipping a Squishee. He is treated with reverence, being described as "benevolent" and all-knowing, though notably he doesn't know the combination to the store's safe. His authority is absolute within the franchise, as he is the only one able to reinstate Apu after his firing. He allows visitors a strict limit of three questions, a rule that becomes a running joke when Homer wastes the opportunity on repetitive, pointless questions instead of letting Apu ask something meaningful. Despite the disruption, he remains polite and unbothered, calmly dismissing his guests afterward. In non-canon material, he also appears in comics offering guidance to Apu regarding a corporate rival store, and shows up in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Are you really the Head of the Kwik-E-Mart? | He is the benevolent, enlightened president and C.E.O. of Kwik-E-Mart, and in Ohio, Stop-O-Mart.
quotes: Are you really the Head of the Kwik-E-Mart?
He is the benevolent, enlightened president and C.E.O. of Kwik-E-Mart, and in Ohio, Stop-O-Mart.

title: Paul Newman (character)
text: Paul Newman (character) is Real-life actor Paul Newman appears as himself, serving as the mascot for Newman's Own Salad Dressing in the Simpsons universe. Paul Newman is a rare instance of a real celebrity appearing as a semi-fictionalized version of himself within the show's world, tied to his real product, Newman's Own Salad Dressing. He's referenced humorously when a farmer blames him for potential harm to popcorn production after a radioactive gas leak damages crops. In his one physical appearance, he speaks directly from a salad dressing bottle to dissuade Homer from a bad idea, delivering a witty and dismissive line reminiscent of a Hollywood legend brushing off a lesser rival. The character is a lighthearted nod to Newman's real-life philanthropic food brand and his reputation in Hollywood. His most poignant appearance came posthumously, when the show paid tribute to him following his death shortly before an episode aired. Overall, he's a minor but memorable cameo character used for comedic celebrity self-parody. Voiced by Paul Newman (Himself). Notable quotes: Homer, I'll tell you what I told Redford. "It ain't gonna happen."
quotes: Homer, I'll tell you what I told Redford. "It ain't gonna happen."

title: Michael Clarke Duncan-type
text: Michael Clarke Duncan-type is A recurring inmate (later guard) at Springfield Penitentiary, designed to resemble Michael Clarke Duncan's character from The Green Mile. This unnamed prisoner is visually modeled on actor Michael Clarke Duncan, complete with a bald head and imposing presence reminiscent of John Coffey from The Green Mile. Despite his gentle, almost tender interactions with his pet mouse Mr. Jingles, he has a violent streak, at one point attempting to strangle Homer. He shares a strange redemptive bond with Mr. Burns during Burns' stint in prison, later trying to spread that same reform to Fat Tony. Eventually promoted from inmate to guard, he plays a small role in exposing Sideshow Bob's return to Springfield. He later cycles back into prisoner status, taking part in a highway cleanup detail and helping search for a missing Bart. The character's voice has switched between two actors across his appearances, adding a bit of behind-the-scenes trivia to his low-key recurring presence. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: Give me your hands, boss.
quotes: Give me your hands, boss.

title: Lord Montgomery
text: Lord Montgomery is Non-canon medieval lord and owner of the Springfieldia Human Power Plant, appearing in the fantasy-parody segment "The Serfsons". Lord Montgomery is a feudal ruler and clear stand-in for Mr. Burns, presiding over a grim power plant where subjects are forced into pointless, exhausting labor. He is cruel and dismissive toward those beneath him, refusing Homer's request for a pay advance without a second thought. His method of generating power is absurd and cartoonishly villainous, turning the suffering of his workers into a magic powder that grants him small, useless wings. His selfishness and disregard for his people eventually provoke an uprising, as the citizens of Springfieldia storm his castle in rebellion. Like many parody characters in the show's non-canon segments, he exists mainly as a fantastical mirror of a familiar Simpsons figure, exaggerated for comedic effect. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: John Legend (character)
text: John Legend (character) is Celebrity guest character who appears as himself to help persuade Springfield residents. John Legend appears as a fictionalized version of himself within the Simpsons universe, brought in by Marge through his wife Chrissy Teigen to help sway public opinion in Springfield. He uses his musical talent, singing a persuasive song while playing piano to convince the townspeople to fund a new STEM school. His appearance highlights his celebrity status and busy lifestyle, as he and Chrissy quickly move on to a promotional event for their joint perfume line. Even in a brief cameo, he's shown as accommodating, agreeing to Homer's odd request for a song justifying skipping jury duty. The character leans on Legend's real-world fame and musical career rather than an original personality, serving mainly as a guest-star novelty. He's also noted to have made a non-canon appearance at a Simpsons season finale premiere. Voiced by Himself.

title: Mr. Met
text: Mr. Met is Real-life mascot of the New York Mets referenced within the show. Mr. Met is a non-speaking, minor background reference rather than a true character in the Simpsons universe. He appears only through a photograph that Mary Spuckler owns of herself with the mascot. Later, he's referenced again in a more absurd context when a therapy app called Nutz sells CBD gummies shaped like various gods, with Mr. Met being one of the designs. His inclusion is purely a pop-culture nod tying the show's world to real-world sports iconography rather than a developed character with personality or dialogue.

title: Mom (Futurama)
text: Mom (Futurama) is Crossover character from Futurama; owner and CEO of MomCorp who appears in Simpsons/Futurama crossover comics and the episode "Simpsorama". Mom, whose real name is Carol, is the ruthless and scheming head of the powerful MomCorp corporation from the Futurama universe. She crosses paths with the Simpsons cast during a bizarre interdimensional mix-up that sends the people of Springfield to New New York. Cunning and opportunistic, she buys Mr. Burns during a slavery auction and the two strike up an unlikely romance built on mutual greed and cruelty. She delights in chaos, watching gleefully as her city is destroyed by rampaging book characters. After Burns returns to his own universe, Mom keeps a lock of his hair to secretly clone him, hinting at future villainous schemes. Her personality mixes corporate ambition with a flair for dramatic, gloating villainy. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: it'll be brutal, it'll be vicious, it'll be...excellent!
quotes: it'll be brutal, it'll be vicious, it'll be...excellent!

title: Nigel (Moho House)
text: Nigel (Moho House) is Mr. Burns' old boarding school friend who briefly schemes to break up Homer and Marge. Nigel is a wealthy, cynical Englishman from Mr. Burns' school days who no longer believes true love can last. To prove his point, he wagers Burns that he can split up Homer and Marge, resorting to manipulation like blackmailing Homer into drinking and exploiting Moe's crush on Marge by funding a fancy new bar for him. His scheme ultimately collapses when Homer and Marge's marriage proves too strong to break. Off the clock, Nigel's own love life is a mess, as his wife Rosa is carrying on with their tennis instructor, which fuels his bitterness about romance. Ironically, his admiration for Burns and Smithers' loyal partnership inspires a side bet and an unexpected kiss with Smithers out of gratitude. He's a minor but memorable recurring figure known for his conniving nature and surprisingly candid relationship drama. Voiced by Michael York.

title: Martin's grandmother
text: Martin's grandmother is Grandmother of Martin Prince, a minor recurring character at Springfield Elementary. Martin's grandmother is an elderly woman who appears on occasions like Grandparents Day at Springfield Elementary. She comes across as a bit demanding and easily offended, particularly when she felt slighted by her grandson's lack of attentiveness. Her jealousy was sparked when she saw how warmly Bart treated Agnes Skinner while pretending to be her grandson, leading her to scold Martin for not offering her his sweater when she was cold. She is a minor background character who has made a handful of appearances across several episodes. In a non-canon segment, she was depicted among a group of elderly citizens during a musical number. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Cheech Marin (character)
text: Cheech Marin (character) is Real-life comedian and actor who appears as himself, one half of the comedy duo Cheech and Chong, with a minor recurring presence in Springfield lore. Richard "Cheech" Marin is depicted as a Springfield native who started out as a weather man before marijuana fumes from a police bonfire turned him and his partner Tommy Chong into stoners-turned-comedians. He and Chong became a legendary comedy act, eventually performing at the Springfield Clamphitheater, where a falling out led to a temporary breakup and Homer briefly filling in as "Cheech and Chunk." Homer's stint reveals a running gag that Cheech is more interested in cultured pursuits like museums than nonstop partying, subverting expectations of his stoner image. The duo eventually reconcile and reunite, ditching their temporary replacement partners. Cheech's name has become shorthand in Springfield culture for marijuana use, invoked by both Principal Dondelinger scolding young troublemakers and Marge referencing him when discussing weed sales. He's also noted for having played King Arthur in a fictional in-universe film, showing his side career as an actor beyond stand-up comedy. Voiced by Cheech Marin (Himself).

title: Mimi
text: Mimi is Minor recurring character; a retired food critic and ex-wife of the Lifeways editor. Mimi is a former newspaper food critic whose career came to an end when her ex-husband, the Lifeways editor, replaced her with Homer Simpson. She doesn't take the transition gracefully, showing her critical streak even at her own retirement party by complaining about the food served there. This suggests she's someone who can't turn off her professional judgment even in personal, celebratory settings. Beyond her career woes, she's also shown to be civically engaged, appearing among a crowd of PBS supporters tracking down Homer for a pledge he owed the station. Her brief appearances paint her as a sharp-tongued, opinionated woman defined largely by her past profession and her messy divorce. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Leopold
text: Leopold is Assistant superintendent under Gary Chalmers at Springfield Elementary School. Leopold is a large, gruff, and intimidating man who works as Gary Chalmers' assistant superintendent. He has a memorable trick of terrifying students by acting like a fearsome disciplinarian before revealing a much friendlier purpose for his visit, such as introducing a substitute teacher. This bait-and-switch routine has been used more than once, showing off his flair for dramatic, unsettling humor followed by a sudden shift to politeness. Despite his scary demeanor, he is ultimately a functionary who supports the school's administration rather than a true villain. He also appeared among school officials during a major ceremonial event tied to the school's oil well. Notably, he is one of the rare characters on the show drawn with visible eyebrows. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Willy Loman
text: Willy Loman is A recurring fictional character from the play Death of a Salesman, referenced and parodied within The Simpsons universe. Willy Loman is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed figure from Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman, who appears whenever the show parodies that play. He's portrayed by different actors across episodes, including a Chinese stage actor and even Krusty the Clown in a rewritten version of the play. His most famous line reflects his weary, philosophical view of being a salesman and how people use others up like fruit before discarding them. In a non-canon storyline, he's reimagined as a jaded, dark-humored door-to-door salesman friend of Ned Flanders, unbothered by the fact that the trampolines he sells can cause death, treating it as just part of the sales game. This version of Willy is cynical and blackly comic, embodying the exhausted, morally flexible salesman archetype. Across his appearances, Willy Loman mainly functions as a running theatrical joke and pop-culture nod rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: You can't just eat the orange and throw the peel away -- a man's not a piece of fruit! | Boys, you see what I was talking about? The greatest things can happen.
quotes: You can't just eat the orange and throw the peel away -- a man's not a piece of fruit!
Boys, you see what I was talking about? The greatest things can happen.

title: Lumpy
text: Lumpy is The pet snake belonging to Springfield Elementary School. Lumpy is a green boa constrictor kept as the school pet at Springfield Elementary. Unlike a typical classroom pet, Lumpy has an unsettling habit of eating students, a fact so accepted by the school that its charter explicitly absolves teachers of responsibility if the snake devours Milhouse Van Houten. This dark running gag frames Lumpy less as a cuddly mascot and more as an ever-present low-level threat lurking in the classroom. He appears only briefly in the show's canon, mostly referenced rather than shown in action. In non-canon material, his appetite is expanded upon, with mentions that he may have eaten other animals and even students. Lumpy never speaks and functions purely as a background source of morbid humor about the school's questionable safety standards.

title: Kliff
text: Kliff is Car salesman and owner of Kliff's Kar Chalet, minor recurring character encountered by the Simpson family. Kliff is a shady used-car dealer running Kliff's Kar Chalet in Springfield. He appears when the Simpsons, having received charity money after townspeople mistakenly believed they'd been robbed on Christmas, come to his lot to buy a new car. He's an opportunistic and dishonest salesman, inflating the price of the car Homer wants and tacking on unnecessary overpriced extras like undercoating to squeeze more money out of them. When Bart, feeling guilty about spending charity money, tries to speak up and suggest donating it instead, Kliff repeatedly jabs him with a pen to silence him, showing his impatience and willingness to bully customers to close a sale. He's a minor but memorably sleazy figure representing the show's recurring theme of Springfield's greedy local business owners taking advantage of the Simpsons. Kliff later reappears in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Angus MacGyver
text: Angus MacGyver is Fictional TV secret agent character, the object of Patty and Selma Bouvier's obsessive fandom. Angus MacGyver is the title character of an in-universe TV show called MacGyver, a secret agent known for improvising gadgets out of everyday objects to defeat villains. He exists primarily as a running gag tied to the intense, longtime fandom of Patty and Selma, who idolize him to an almost obsessive degree. References to him pop up whenever the sisters are stressed, comforted, or reminiscing, often as a coping mechanism or punchline about their spinsterhood and eccentric obsessions. The real-world actor who played him, Richard Dean Anderson, even appears in the show and gets pulled into a bizarre kidnapping plot by the sisters, who force him to reenact MacGyver-style escapes for their own amusement. The joke escalates when Anderson becomes so enamored with escaping that he becomes an annoyance right back to his captors, flipping the power dynamic. His likeness has also been recreated in odd, low-budget ways, including a toenail-clipping-and-hair-wax sculpture Patty and Selma constructed of him. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: MacGyver was a show about a secret agent who used inventions made of everyday objects to defeat bad guys. | He's hugging us. What do we do? | Just close your eyes and think of MacGyver.
quotes: MacGyver was a show about a secret agent who used inventions made of everyday objects to defeat bad guys.
He's hugging us. What do we do?
Just close your eyes and think of MacGyver.

title: Linda McCartney (character)
text: Linda McCartney (character) is Real-world musician who appears as herself alongside her husband Paul McCartney in a guest cameo. Linda McCartney is a real-world musician who appeared as a guest character alongside her husband Paul in the Simpsons universe. She and Paul are found relaxing on Apu Nahasapeemapetilon's secret rooftop garden, a hidden spot he reveals to Lisa. Her appearance ties into the episode's vegetarian theme, as Paul famously encourages Lisa's dietary choice. She has no dialogue-driven personality traits noted beyond being present as herself, functioning more as a celebrity cameo than a fleshed-out character. Her role is brief but memorable, tied to one of the show's most famous celebrity guest spots. She also appears fleetingly in a later opening sequence gag. Voiced by Herself.

title: Nichelle Nichols (character)
text: Nichelle Nichols (character) is Guest character voiced by herself, an actress famous for Star Trek who visits Comic Book Guy's shop. Nichelle Nichols appears in the show as a fictionalized version of herself, playing on her real-life fame as a Star Trek actress. In her cameo, she visits Comic Book Guy at The Android's Dungeon & Baseball Card Shop, presumably as a special guest appearance for fans. Unfortunately, the meeting doesn't go as planned, since Comic Book Guy embarrasses himself by having pie smeared on his face during the encounter. This brief, comedic mishap becomes the extent of her interaction on the show. She also appears briefly in an opening sequence gag in another episode. Her role is minor but adds a touch of real-world celebrity crossover typical of the show's humor. Voiced by Nichelle Nichols (Herself).

title: Princess Leia
text: Princess Leia is Star Wars character referenced and parodied within The Simpsons universe. Princess Leia is not a native Simpsons character but a recurring pop-culture reference to the famous Star Wars heroine. She's invoked whenever the show wants to riff on Star Wars, whether through posters, costumes, or offhand comparisons. Homer once flatters Marge by likening her beauty to Leia's, while Lisa experiments with Leia's iconic hairstyle during a phase of trying new looks. The character becomes a running gag through parody appearances, such as a version in the Cosmic Wars Ranch and Ralph Wiggum's clueless costume choice for a school event meant to honor inspirational women. Other townsfolk, like the Lovejoys, also cosplay as Leia and Luke Skywalker for a masquerade, showing how deeply Star Wars imagery has embedded itself into Springfield culture. She even appears as an entry in one of Lisa's geeky reference charts, cementing her status as a beloved nerd-culture icon within the show. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: I'm a Star Wars. — Ralph Wiggum
quotes: I'm a Star Wars. — Ralph Wiggum

title: Mob lawyer
text: Mob lawyer is A lawyer who represents members of the Springfield Mafia. The mob lawyer is a legal representative called upon by the Springfield Mafia when trouble arises. He's shown to be methodical, bringing along his own rate clock to charge by the minute even when hastily summoned from home. He speaks slowly and deliberately, seemingly more interested in billing time than urgency, and jumps to assume his clients are guilty of serious crimes like murder. When faced with a case that doesn't fit his expectations, such as Fat Tony's innocent pickpocketing charge, he becomes annoyed and unhelpful, quickly giving up and leaving. Despite his unhelpfulness, he manages to escape any violent retaliation from the mob thanks to Fat Tony's mercy. Voiced by Bob Odenkirk.

title: Fred Mertz
text: Fred Mertz is Fictional character from I Love Lucy who appears as a parody/crossover figure in The Simpsons. Fred Mertz is a crossover character borrowed from the classic sitcom I Love Lucy, appearing in The Simpsons as a nod to that show. He is portrayed as the landlord and best friend of Ricky and Lucy Ricardo, married to Ethel Mertz. His inclusion is mostly a background gag, referenced when Homer and Marge are mistaken for Fred and Ethel at a themed hotel, and later heard through a TV broadcast that Lisa catches snippets of. He even shows up alongside the Simpson family during their trip to Cuba, interacting with Ricky Ricardo about smuggling into a cigar store. The character leans on nostalgia and meta-humor, with a line about Ricky and Lucy replayed later as a recurring audio gag in the closing credits. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: George Meyer (character)
text: George Meyer (character) is A former writer for The Itchy & Scratchy Show, based on real-life Simpsons writer George Meyer. George Meyer is a cartoon version of one of the real Simpsons' longtime writers, depicted as a staffer on the in-universe Itchy & Scratchy Show. He loses his job when Roger Meyers Jr. cleans house and hires Abraham Simpson instead, leaving Meyer among the unemployed. He briefly resurfaces at a crisis meeting for the ailing show, where his sharp, skeptical wit gets him in trouble with a network executive pushing corporate buzzwords, and he's promptly fired again. After that he drifts through unemployment, collecting social security checks and wandering Springfield. He's also the target of an odd rumor, appearing on a list of people alleged to be gay. In a non-canon alternate universe, he even hosts his own late-night talk show, a playful nod to his real-world career as a comedy writer. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: "proactive" and "paradigm" are just buzzwords that dumb people use to sound important.
quotes: "proactive" and "paradigm" are just buzzwords that dumb people use to sound important.

title: Cleric Marge
text: Cleric Marge is Marge Simpson's in-game avatar in the online role-playing game Earthland Realms. Cleric Marge is the persona Marge Simpson adopts when she becomes engrossed in the online game Earthland Realms. She starts out dutifully completing quests given by the portly wizard, gradually leveling up and exploring the game's world. Her story takes a personal turn when she learns that the villainous Shadow Knight terrorizing the realm is secretly controlled by her own son, Bart. Determined and a bit mischievous, she trails the Shadow Knight and humiliates him publicly before trashing his prized trophy room with a whimsical Hello Kitty expansion pack. This act of digital vandalism leads to her in-game death at the Shadow Knight's hands, though he later revives her. Ultimately, Cleric Marge's story ends when Marge retires the character, replacing her with Warrior Marge to seek revenge after Bart's character is killed. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: Oyster Lucy
text: Oyster Lucy is A minor novelty item in the Simpsons universe—a hand-painted oyster shell crafted by Moe to resemble Lucille Ball. Oyster Lucy is one of Moe's quirky handicraft creations, a painted oyster shell designed to look like classic sitcom star Lucille Ball. Moe sells this odd trinket at his stall during the Springfield Swap Meet, showcasing his knack for bizarre, low-effort artistry. Despite being an inanimate object, the character gets a brief moment of personified humor when voiced with a fittingly theatrical line referencing Lucille Ball's real-life husband, Desi Arnaz's TV counterpart. The joke plays on the absurdity of merchandise culture and Moe's eccentric side hustles. It's a small, one-off gag rather than a recurring storyline, appearing only in a single episode and later reappearing as a nod in a mobile game. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Oh, Mr. Mooney, I just gotta meet Bob Cummings! — Moe as Oyster Lucy, Homer's Barbershop Quartet
quotes: Oh, Mr. Mooney, I just gotta meet Bob Cummings! — Moe as Oyster Lucy, Homer's Barbershop Quartet

title: Nell Nicholson
text: Nell Nicholson is A background student at Springfield Elementary School. Nell Nicholson is a minor, non-speaking student who appears in the background at Springfield Elementary School, typically shown alongside other children. She's easily identified by the headband she always wears, though beyond that her design is inconsistent since she's a low-priority background character. In earlier seasons she was drawn with an exaggerated overbite and oversized teeth, and animators have occasionally colored her hair and skin to match other students like Sherri and Terri Mackleberry. Her name went unknown to viewers for years until it was finally revealed in a book shown in the episode "Woo-Hoo Dunnit?". Despite her lack of dialogue, she has appeared consistently across many seasons of the show as part of the school crowd.

title: Lucy Lawless (character)
text: Lucy Lawless (character) is Guest-starring celebrity character based on the real actress, known for playing Xena, who appears in a Treehouse of Horror segment. Lucy Lawless appears as a fictionalized version of herself, most memorably in a Treehouse of Horror parody where she's mistaken for her famous alter ego Xena. She's good-humored about the confusion, repeatedly insisting she isn't actually Xena even while displaying warrior-like combat skills. Her most notable canon appearance involves being kidnapped by a supervillain using a giant magnet to attract her metal costume, only to free herself and help rescue her would-be rescuers. She's also referenced as an object of fanboy admiration, with Comic Book Guy recalling meeting her fondly and even requesting her as a substitute delivery person in a letter to Santa. Kent Brockman invokes her name sarcastically while dressed as Superman during an unrelated mix-up. Overall she serves as a running injoke about her Xena fame overshadowing her own identity within the show's universe. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: I'll ask the questions here, Lucy Lawless! | And let me tell you, like her character Xena, she can hit quite hard.
quotes: I'll ask the questions here, Lucy Lawless!
And let me tell you, like her character Xena, she can hit quite hard.

title: Little Lulu (character)
text: Little Lulu (character) is A comic-book character appearing on the cover of a Little Lulu comic seen within The Simpsons universe. Little Lulu, whose full name is Lulu Moppet, is the titular star of the fictional comic book Little Lulu that appears within Springfield. She's a picture-only character, meaning she never speaks or takes real action in the show, only being seen depicted on comic covers. Her presence is essentially an in-universe nod to the real-world classic comic strip of the same name. In a bit of non-canon fun, a parody Italian version of her comic reimagines her as a grown-up divorce lawyer. Otherwise, she has no direct interaction with the main Simpsons cast and exists purely as background flavor referencing pop culture.

title: Lady (dog)
text: Lady (dog) is Crossover character from Disney's Lady and the Tramp, referenced within The Simpsons. Lady is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover appearance borrowed from the Disney film Lady and the Tramp. Her presence in the show is limited to brief homages rather than an active role in the story. The famous spaghetti dinner scene from her film is echoed in a Simpsons episode during a dramatic moment involving Bart. She also appears indirectly when Santa's Little Helper watches her original movie streaming on a parody service. In a non-canon special, she's glimpsed again as background entertainment for other characters. Overall, Lady functions as a nostalgic nod to classic animation rather than a developed character within the Simpsons universe.

title: Malibu Stacy actress
text: Malibu Stacy actress is A minor performer who appeared in the musical stage show Malibu Stacy: The Musical alongside Waylon Smithers, Jr.. This blonde-haired actress is a minor, one-scene character known only through her role as a performer in a stage production celebrating the famous Malibu Stacy doll line. She shares the stage with Smithers, sitting atop a giant replica of Stacy's Corvette surrounded by oversized toy accessories. Together they perform a duet number as part of the show. Her only other appearance is a background cameo, glimpsed on a promotional poster hanging in Smithers' office. Little else is known about her personality or background, as she exists purely as a theatrical prop character to satirize commercial tie-in entertainment. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Corey Masterson
text: Corey Masterson is A teenage pop idol/entertainer within the Simpsons universe, popular with young girls including Lisa. Corey Masterson is a fictional teen idol who exists as a pop-culture figure within the show's universe, akin to a boy-band heartthrob adored by adolescent girls. Lisa Simpson was among his devoted fans, going so far as to call a fan hotline dedicated to him, which resulted in a spike in the family's phone bill. He appears mostly in the background of the show, showing up on posters, magazines, and merchandise rather than in major speaking roles. Despite his minor presence, his fame within the show is treated as a running joke about celebrity obsession among young fans. He's part of a broader group of teen idols referenced throughout the series. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Herman Millwood
text: Herman Millwood is Owner of the company that manufactures the Aerochair; briefly involved in producing an Angry Dad movie with Bart. Herman Millwood is a businessman best known for creating and selling the Aerochair. As a child he had a passion for building chairs, though his father discouraged him from ever actually sitting on them, an odd quirk that hints at his lifelong obsession with furniture design over practicality. As an adult, he acquires the rights to Angry Dad after BetterThanTV.com defaults on payments for a large order of Aerochairs, and he also seizes several other failed online cartoons as compensation. Seeing an opportunity in a Hollywood devoid of fresh ideas, he proposes turning Angry Dad into a feature film and personally works alongside Bart to get it made. He comes across as a shrewd, opportunistic entrepreneur who leverages debt and business savvy to break into the entertainment industry. His character appears to be a parody of the real-world furniture company Herman Miller and its famous Aeron chair. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Willie Nelson (character)
text: Willie Nelson (character) is Real-life musician cameo character with a recurring presence and history in Springfield. Willie Nelson appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, tied loosely to Springfield through a former house he once owned there. He's referenced or shown in a variety of odd contexts, from a swimming feat mentioned by police to his old home becoming Krusty's Clown College. His music has a lasting presence in town, notably filling the jukebox at Moe's Tavern after he paid a bar tab with old records. In a non-canon storyline, he's shown as a close friend of Doctor Hibbert who helps stage an award show to reconcile the Simpson family, revealing a quirky detail about a finicky comb machine he owns. Nelson is generally portrayed as an easygoing, beloved cultural icon whose peace-and-love philosophy and eccentric charm echo his real-world persona. Voiced by Willie Nelson (Himself); Dan Castellaneta.

title: Little Lotta
text: Little Lotta is A comic book character appearing within the Simpsons universe, featured on a fictional comic cover in the show. Little Lotta is a minor, picture-only character who exists within the fictional comic book world referenced in The Simpsons. She appears on the cover of a comic titled 'Death of Casper,' published by the in-universe company Harry Comics. She has blonde hair and no other defined personality traits or dialogue in the show. Her presence is largely a nod to classic comic book characters, blending real-world comic history with the show's satirical take on collectibles and nerd culture. She is mentioned in passing in other episodes tied to comic book fandom, reinforcing her status as an easter-egg style reference rather than a fully developed character.

title: Lisafer
text: Lisafer is Non-canon Hell persona of Lisa Simpson, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment. Lisafer is an alternate, demonic version of Lisa Simpson that emerges after she is transported to Hell. Rather than being tormented, she turns the tables on the mean girl demons who mock her appearance by mocking them right back, which unexpectedly makes her popular. Her rise to popularity is treated as a supernatural sign, causing it to snow in Hell. Eventually she discovers a portal that allows her to escape the underworld, which happens to lead directly into Mr. Burns' office. The character is a one-off gag rooted in the 'it's cold in Hell' idiom, blending Lisa's usual assertiveness with a darker, edgier twist. She later appears as a collectible skin in The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Yeardley Smith.

title: Poison Lenny
text: Poison Lenny is A minor villain from a Batman-parody story told by Bart, appearing in Gotham City. Poison Lenny exists only within a fantastical story spun by Bart, in which he takes on the role of Bartman fighting crime in Gotham City. He is one of several villains Bartman confronts while searching for the man who killed his parents. Despite being treated as a villain, Poison Lenny protests that he is not actually a criminal but simply a transvestite, a distinction that does him no good. The police shoot him regardless, making his appearance brief and darkly comic. The character is a clear visual and conceptual parody of the comic book villain Poison Ivy, specifically referencing Uma Thurman's portrayal in the film Batman & Robin. His inclusion highlights the absurd, exaggerated nature of Bart's imagined superhero narrative. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: he wasn't a villain, he was a transvestite.
quotes: he wasn't a villain, he was a transvestite.

title: Mulan
text: Mulan is Non-canon crossover character from the Mulan franchise appearing in Disney+ themed Simpsons specials. Mulan is a guest crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe as part of Disney-themed specials celebrating Disney+. She appears alongside her mother, Fa Li, suggesting a family-oriented cameo role rather than a deeply developed character. Her appearances are largely non-speaking, functioning more as a nostalgic nod to Disney fans than as an active participant in Simpsons storylines. She shows up in festive or celebratory contexts, such as an anniversary party and a Mother's Day outing, as well as during a chaotic pop-culture event involving Thanos. Overall, she exists within the show's non-canon universe purely as a background or cameo presence tied to Disney branding.

title: Helen Mirren
text: Helen Mirren is Real-world English actress who appears as a celebrity cameo character in The Simpsons. Helen Mirren appears as a fictionalized version of herself within the Simpsons universe, mingling with other celebrities in cameo-style appearances. She's portrayed as somewhat oblivious to her surroundings, missing cues and not quite understanding the context of things happening around her, such as failing to hear a request at a bar or being confused about the purpose of an interview. She was even considered as a potential new mascot for Duff Beer, standing alongside other whimsical candidates. In a non-canon Halloween special, she meets a gruesome fate as part of a spelled-out horror title gag. Overall, she serves as a lighthearted celebrity guest character rather than a fully developed personality within the show. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Ms. Mouse
text: Ms. Mouse is Minor cartoon character within the Itchy & Scratchy Show, a fictional cartoon-within-a-cartoon in The Simpsons universe. Ms. Mouse is a background character appearing in the ultra-violent cartoon show that Bart and Lisa watch, Itchy & Scratchy. She appears alongside Itchy during one of his sadistic pranks on Scratchy, lounging with him in a hot tub while he enjoys the fruits of his latest scheme. She has no dialogue and exists purely as a visual gag prop within the cartoon's twisted slapstick violence. Her role is fleeting, serving mostly to underscore Itchy's smug enjoyment of tormenting Scratchy. She later resurfaces as a collectible character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, expanding her presence beyond her single television appearance.

title: Morbo
text: Morbo is Alien news reporter from Futurama who appears in a crossover episode with The Simpsons. Morbo is an extraterrestrial newscaster best known from Futurama, who crosses over into the Simpsons universe during a special team-up episode. He works alongside his co-anchor Linda van Schoonhoven delivering news bulletins, including reports on strange occurrences like the New New York creatures. Though not a native Simpsons character, his appearance highlights the show's willingness to blend universes through animated crossover events. Fans have embraced him enough to dress as him at conventions, showing his popularity beyond his home series. His gruff, alien news-anchor persona and deadpan delivery of bizarre stories are part of his enduring appeal. Voiced by Maurice LaMarche.

title: Harpo Marx
text: Harpo Marx is Real-world comedian and member of the Marx Brothers, appearing as a fictionalized character in Simpsons episodes. Harpo Marx is depicted in the show as a fictionalized version of the famous silent comedian from the real-life Marx Brothers act. He appears alongside his brothers Groucho and Chico in various cameo and dream sequences rather than as a regular cast member. True to his real persona, he's a non-speaking character who communicates through physical comedy and antics. He's shown getting into a mishap involving Zeppo that the brothers agree to cover up, appearing in a bizarre Itchy and Scratchy parody where he swaps his tongue with a dog's, and dancing with Chico in the afterlife setting of Jewish Heaven. He's also referenced posthumously as one of the notable deceased left-leaning celebrities in Ned Flanders' book. Overall, he serves as a nostalgic pop-culture cameo rather than a developed character within the main story.

title: Stella Kowalski
text: Stella Kowalski is Fictional character from Tennessee Williams' "A Streetcar Named Desire" who appears within a Simpsons episode as a musical role. Stella Kowalski isn't an original Simpsons character but rather a role from the classic play A Streetcar Named Desire, referenced and parodied within the show. In the episode "A Streetcar Named Marge," the character is portrayed by Helen Lovejoy in a local musical adaptation called Oh, Streetcar!, staged at the Springfield Community Center and directed by Llewellyn Sinclair. She later resurfaces in "What Animated Women Want" when Springfield Elementary's fourth graders watch the 1951 film version during a special Movie Day, prompting Milhouse to recall a memorable scene from it. Stella herself has no independent personality within the Simpsons universe, existing only as a reference point for the show's ongoing homage to the source material. Her main significance lies in being married to Stanley Kowalski within the original story, and in providing an opportunity for the show to poke fun at community theater and classic film culture. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Rachel Maddow (character)
text: Rachel Maddow (character) is Real-life TV host who appears as herself, former colleague of Kent Brockman at Channel 6 News. Rachel Maddow appears in the show as a fictionalized version of herself, tying into her real-world career as a television news host. In the show's canon, she once worked alongside Kent Brockman at Channel 6 News before moving on to cover bigger national stories. She returns to Springfield for a colleague's funeral, using the opportunity to nudge Kent toward a bigger career opportunity in national news. Outside of canon, she's shown attending a glitzy movie premiere and hosting a parody news program where she makes a pointed political joke. Her role is largely a cameo/guest appearance rather than a fleshed-out recurring character, poking fun at cable news culture and journalism in general. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: far-light crazies need to check their watt privilege
quotes: far-light crazies need to check their watt privilege

title: Duff McShark
text: Duff McShark is A Great White Shark who becomes the mascot for Duff Beer, replacing Santa's Little Helper's alter ego Suds McDuff. Duff McShark is an animal character introduced when a real shark attacked Homer during a staged rescue scheme meant to win Duffman his old mascot job back. Instead of eating Homer, the shark bit into a giant Duff Beer keg and got hilariously drunk, floating ashore intoxicated in front of a delighted crowd. The Duff Company, always eager to capitalize on anything that sells beer, decided a drunken shark was even better publicity than a heroic dog or a buff mascot, so they hired him on the spot. He represents the show's running gag of corporations shamelessly exploiting absurd situations for marketing, and his sudden shift from a dangerous predator to a beloved party animal is treated as an obvious punchline. He mostly appears as a minor mascot figure tied to Duff Beer's promotional antics rather than as a character with deep personality traits. Voiced by John Kassir. Notable quotes: He's gone from predator to partier! - Sideshow Mel
quotes: He's gone from predator to partier! - Sideshow Mel

title: Nabendu Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Nabendu Nahasapeemapetilon is One of Apu and Manjula Nahasapeemapetilon's octuplet babies. Nabendu is one of the eight babies born to Apu and Manjula after she took fertility drugs to conceive. As an infant, he has no distinct personality traits of his own, being one of an indistinguishable set of octuplets rather than a fully developed character. His main claim to fame is being part of the chaotic 'Octopia' storyline, in which the overwhelmed Kwik-E-Mart clerk and his wife struggled to cope with raising eight children simultaneously. Unable to manage, his parents placed the octuplets on public display at the Springfield City Zoo as a novelty exhibit. Displeased with this arrangement, Apu and Homer ultimately staged a rescue to break the babies out of the zoo. Since his debut, Nabendu has continued to appear as a background character in numerous episodes, comics, and other Simpsons media. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: King Kong (character)
text: King Kong (character) is A fictional giant ape/monster referenced within the Simpsons universe, appearing as pictures, posters, and merchandise rather than as an active character. King Kong exists in the Simpsons world as a famous monster icon rather than a character who actually interacts with the cast. He's depicted in various background appearances, such as a photo in a research book and a poster in someone's office, showing his cultural status as a legendary giant ape. He's even acknowledged by real-world figures like Guillermo del Toro and Peter Jackson within the show's universe, tying him to actual film history. King Kong also appears as physical memorabilia, including a tower replica sold at auction. He has no dialogue and never physically appears as a living, moving character, making him more of a recurring visual reference and pop-culture nod than a true character. His son, Son of Kong, is noted as his only listed relative.

title: Peter Lewis
text: Peter Lewis is Fictional nerdy student-turned-physicist, the main character of the in-universe film "Gladys the Groovy Mule," portrayed by Troy McClure. Peter Lewis is a socially awkward student desperate to be accepted by his popular, jock-dominated peers, including rivals like Bash Flashman. Rejected from the football team for not fitting the part, he's assigned to care for the school's talking mule mascot, Gladys, who takes him under her wing and teaches him how to be cool. Their adventures take them from a jazz club confrontation with Soviet agents trying to recruit Peter for Khrushchev, to a triumphant football comeback where Gladys herself helps win the big game. His heroics catch the attention of Richard Nixon, who recruits him to work on a bomb test at Los Alamos, an event that darkly claims the lives of his old tormentors. Peter's arc is a mix of nerd-makes-good wish fulfillment and Cold War satire, ending with a toast to his unlikely mentor, Gladys. As a character existing entirely within a parody film shown on the show, he embodies The Simpsons' penchant for spoofing mid-century Americana and B-movie tropes.

title: Milhouse (Lemon of Troy)
text: Milhouse (Lemon of Troy) is A boy from Shelbyville who serves as the doppelgänger of Springfield's Milhouse Van Houten, appearing in "Lemon of Troy". This Milhouse is Shelbyville's near-identical counterpart to Springfield's own Milhouse Van Houten, sharing the same blue hair, big nose, similar voice, and fondness for the word 'radical.' Unlike his Springfield twin, he doesn't wear glasses or have prominent eyebrows. Despite being ordered by the Shelbyville gang leader to attack any Springfield kids found in town, he couldn't bring himself to harm his counterpart, likely due to the strange bond of sharing the same name. His brief appearance highlights the show's running joke that Shelbyville is an eerie mirror image of Springfield, populated by analogues of familiar characters. He later shows up in a non-canon comic story at the Speed-E-Mart. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Jay North (character)
text: Jay North (character) is Real-life actor who appears as himself, best known for playing Dennis the Menace. Jay North is a guest appearance by the real actor famous for portraying Dennis the Menace in the classic TV show. In his cameo, he shows up at Greaser's Cafe, where he reminisces to Bart about his acting days, including a memorable storyline where he stepped on Mr. Wilson's flowerbed across a two-part episode. He seems eager to share his nostalgic showbiz stories and clearly takes pride in his old nickname as television's mischievous kid. However, Bart is unimpressed by his reputation as 'America's Badboy,' highlighting a generational gap in what counts as rebellious. His appearance plays on the joke of former child stars trying to relive their glory days to an audience that no longer cares. Voiced by Himself.

title: Lee Majors
text: Lee Majors is Fictionalized version of the real actor, appearing in a Marge fantasy sequence. Lee Majors is a fictionalized appearance of the real-life actor best known for starring in The Six Million Dollar Man. In the show, he appears only within a daydream that Marge has about the future. She imagines that once Bart graduates from Harvard, she leaves her family behind to run off with Majors, and the two fly away together. Because this is purely a fantasy sequence, Majors doesn't interact with the Simpsons family in reality. His inclusion plays on his pop-culture status as a classic action-hero heartthrob. He also has a minor mention via a DVD cover appearance in another episode. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Joseph Monsarno
text: Joseph Monsarno is Founder of the Monsarno Research Campus, depicted only as a statue in the show. Joseph Monsarno is a minor, non-speaking figure whose only presence in the show is a statue erected in his honor at the Monsarno Research Campus. He doesn't have any actual dialogue or active role in the story, existing purely as a background detail within the corporate facility he founded. His statue becomes the target of a bit of typical Homer mischief when the Simpson family visits the campus. Beyond this brief comedic moment, nothing else is revealed about his personality, history, or fate. He remains a mostly forgotten background character, more of a prop than a personality.

title: Mr. Mitchell
text: Mr. Mitchell is Minor recurring character who briefly adopted Santa's Little Helper. Mr. Mitchell is a blind resident of Springfield who briefly becomes the owner of Santa's Little Helper after Bart gives the dog away, renaming him Sprinkles. He initially resists returning the dog when Bart tries to reclaim him, even calling the police, but ultimately gives him back after recognizing the bond between Bart and the dog. He carries medicinal marijuana for his condition, claiming that without it he could go blind entirely. Beyond his central appearance, he pops up in small roles across several episodes, including a human pyramid attempt, a Phish concert supporting medical marijuana legalization, and a news report. He also has a guide dog that Lisa mistakenly adopts during one of her animal-rescuing sprees. Notably, the role was originally recorded by John Turturro before being redubbed by Dan Castellaneta after a script dispute. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: could go blinder
quotes: could go blinder

title: Groucho Marx
text: Groucho Marx is Real-world comedian (of The Marx Brothers) referenced and appearing in dream sequences in The Simpsons. Groucho Marx is depicted as a real-world historical figure who occasionally crosses paths with the Simpsons universe, most notably appearing in one of Bart's dreams alongside his brothers Harpo and Chico. He's treated as a legendary wit, with other characters referencing his famous quips and even stealing his jokes. Dick Cavett recalls a dinner with Groucho when comparing Homer's rude behavior to him, which sets off a comedic threat from Homer. Elsewhere, he's shown enjoying an afterlife of dancing in Jewish Heaven, tying into the show's recurring gags about celebrity heaven. Martin Prince quotes one of his signature lines almost verbatim, showing his enduring cultural influence within the show. Groucho never has a major speaking role but is used as a nostalgic pop-culture reference point. Notable quotes: "You wouldn't want to belong to any club that would have me for a member!"
quotes: "You wouldn't want to belong to any club that would have me for a member!"

title: Marty McFly
text: Marty McFly is Crossover character from the Back to the Future franchise who appears in non-canon segments of The Simpsons. Marty McFly is a guest character brought into The Simpsons universe from his own film series, most notably losing his skateboard to Bart while fleeing a hypnotized mob. Despite his famous time-traveling exploits in his home franchise, in this crossover he's reduced to being roughed up by Biff Tannen's gang after Bart borrows his ride. In a non-canon future vision experienced by Chief Wiggum, Marty appears as a doting father on hoverboards with a cloned daughter, enjoying futuristic treats like space ice cream. That same segment finds him victimized again, this time by Snake Jailbird, who steals the bitcoins Marty was saving for his daughter's college fund. He also makes a brief cameo alongside Doc Brown in a couch gag, tying him further into the show's tradition of referencing pop culture icons. Overall, Marty serves as a running joke about being an unlucky bystander dragged into Springfield's chaos.

title: Noodles
text: Noodles is A minor background clown character in the Simpsons universe, associated with Krusty's entourage. Noodles is a minor, non-speaking clown character who appears in the background of a few episodes. He's identified by his orange hair and clown attire, fitting into the show's recurring stable of Krusty-adjacent performers. His most notable moment involves handing out champagne at a promotional store opening, and later getting caught up in a chaotic escape from Krusty's car when Bart commandeers a tank and threatens to run it over. Beyond these brief appearances, little else is known about his personality or background since he never speaks on screen. He represents the kind of throwaway side character that populates Springfield's larger clown community.

title: Cheesy McMayor
text: Cheesy McMayor is Mascot for an unnamed hamburger restaurant on Springfield's Fast-Food Boulevard, a parody of McDonald's Mayor McCheese. Cheesy McMayor is a burger-headed mascot representing one of the many fast-food establishments along Fast-Food Boulevard. He's portrayed as an emotionally fragile character, prone to crying and being easily consoled or dismissed by others, most notably during a town meeting after his restaurant district was destroyed. Despite being a man in costume, he's treated with a strange mix of sympathy and casual cruelty by the citizens of Springfield, including being eaten by fellow mascots and appearing in Homer's dream only to be devoured again. He's also shown to have a side career as a member of a bowling team called the Are They Reals. In a strange historical twist, he even appears in an old photograph tied to Napoleon III's France, suggesting a bizarre, undefined presence across different eras. Overall, Cheesy McMayor serves as a running gag figure representing the show's love of absurd, throwaway mascot characters. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: I told myself I'd stay strong. | There, there, Cheesy McMayor. No one likes weepy meat. | I can't stand to see a grown burger cry!
quotes: I told myself I'd stay strong.
There, there, Cheesy McMayor. No one likes weepy meat.
I can't stand to see a grown burger cry!

title: Mike (Moms I'd Like to Forget)
text: Mike (Moms I'd Like to Forget) is Husband of one of The Cool Moms, and father to Tyler. Mike is a minor recurring character who is married to Connie, one of the members of The Cool Moms, and is father to a son named Tyler. He's less than thrilled about the social obligations that come with his wife's friend group, particularly having to spend time with the other husbands. His annoyance at being dragged back into these gatherings suggests a mild, resigned exasperation with suburban social life. He was later seen at Quiet Rivers, hinting at some continued connection to the community's goings-on. Mike doesn't have much of a defined personality beyond his reluctant participation in these family and social duties. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: The Mighty Smiter
text: The Mighty Smiter is Superhero alter-ego of Waylon Smithers, Jr., appearing in Simpsons comic book stories.
