The Mighty Smiter is a Thor-inspired superhero identity assumed by Waylon Smithers after a nuclear plant explosion grants superpowers to the citizens of Springfield. Decked out in Viking-style armor and a flowing blond wig attached to his helmet, he wields a giant executive washroom key named Kjohler as both a weapon and a means of flight. His heroic debut is undercut by comic mishaps, including being knocked out of the sky by Radioactive Man and having his helmet knocked off to reveal his true gray hair beneath the wig. He battles a group of mutated, long-armed power plant workers dubbed the "Fission Division," though he struggles to defeat them on his own. Later, after losing and regaining his powers, he joins the other empowered Springfieldians to help stop the villain Sinister Van Dalus. The character is essentially a parody of Marvel's Thor, right down to Kjohler standing in for the mystical hammer Mjolnir.

title: Man in the Iron Mask
text: Man in the Iron Mask is A minor fictional-within-fiction hero character who appears in Simpsons parody segments, imprisoned at Château d'If. The Man in the Iron Mask is a background character used in two of the show's parody sequences rather than a true member of the main cast. In one storyline, based loosely on 'The Man in the Iron Mask' and Zorro tales, he duels Zorro after the Three Musketeers are defeated, and is promised that King Arthur will be restored to the throne. In another appearance drawing from The Count of Monte Cristo, he is held captive in the infamous Château d'If prison. There he confides to his guard, Carl, that he is actually the rightful king of France, only to comically realize too late that no one else heard his confession. His masked, mysterious persona and his tie to swashbuckling adventure stories make him a fun one-off homage to classic literary and film heroes. He has no continuing relationships or ongoing role beyond these brief comedic cameos. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta, Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: The Man in the Iron Mask then asked if anyone heard him admit it, before he realized nobody did.
quotes: The Man in the Iron Mask then asked if anyone heard him admit it, before he realized nobody did.

title: Medbot
text: Medbot is A minor robotic character appearing in a future-set episode of The Simpsons. Medbot is a medical robot that appears in a flash-forward storyline set in the show's future timeline. Its main function shown is scanning an unborn baby, giving it a practical, clinical role rather than a comedic or emotional one. Despite being a background device, it becomes part of a quirky, absurd moment when characters use it for an unrelated purpose. Medbot fits into the show's tradition of imagining quirky futuristic technology used by the Simpson family. It has since been referenced in the mobile game tie-in, extending its presence beyond the original episode. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Please do not make a sound.
quotes: Please do not make a sound.

title: Ralph Nader
text: Ralph Nader is Real-world political activist depicted as a minor recurring character and member of the Springfield Republican Party in the show. This character is based on the real-life political activist, author, lecturer, and attorney Ralph Nader. In the show, he appears as an eager member of the Springfield Republican Party, always ready to volunteer for schemes even when not needed. He's also referenced as a symbolic figure of political idealism, appearing as a shadowy figure among a list of villains in one musical number, and as a poster and voting choice representing alternative political leadership in other episodes. His appearances are largely brief cameos or references rather than substantial storylines, poking fun at his real-world reputation as a perennial third-party presidential candidate. He's portrayed as harmless and overeager rather than menacing, despite being lumped in with villains in one instance. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Lloyd (Homer Goes to Prep School)
text: Lloyd (Homer Goes to Prep School) is Doomsday prepper who recruits Homer into his survivalist group. Lloyd is the leader of a small community of doomsday preppers who believe society's collapse is imminent. He convinces Homer that the end is near and that joining his secretive group will make him superior to unprepared outsiders. Paranoid and secretive by nature, he insists Homer keep their plans hidden from everyone else. When Homer accidentally triggers an EMP, Lloyd welcomes the Simpson family into his underground retreat, only for tensions to rise once Homer realizes the group has no intention of helping anyone left outside. His storyline plays on survivalist stereotypes, ultimately being undercut when he and his fellow preppers discover the outside world never actually fell apart. Voiced by Tom Waits.

title: Rich Moore (character)
text: Rich Moore (character) is A real-world animator/director who appears as a recurring background cameo character in Springfield. Rich Moore is a background character based on the real-life director of the same name, popping up in various Springfield crowd scenes rather than playing an active role in the plot. He's been spotted gambling at Plato's Republic Casino, delivering children's letters to Santa Claus at the Court House, and attending the ill-fated inauguration of the Springfield Monorail, where he later tumbles off the Escalator to Nowhere. He also turned up as one of the escaped convicts in Sideshow Bob's mocking campaign advertisement. In a less flattering appearance, he joined the crowd that jeered at Bart after he was wrongly blamed for stealing the church's collection money. A non-canon deleted scene additionally casts him as an animator on The Itchy & Scratchy Show who researched real cats and mice to make the cartoon characters more believable.

title: Maleficent
text: Maleficent is Crossover Disney villain character appearing in non-canon Simpsons Disney+ specials. Maleficent is the classic Disney villain from Sleeping Beauty, imported into the Simpsons universe as part of various Disney crossover specials. She appears as a gatekeeper figure at a Disney+ anniversary party, strictly enforcing the guest list and turning away Homer for not being on it, only for him to sneak in anyway. She's also shown among other famous Disney villains at a themed villain attraction and joins them in a group musical number. Her presence ties into a running gag of the Burns family being linked to various fictional and Disney characters through an elaborate family tree. Overall, she serves less as a developed character and more as a nostalgic cameo representing Disney's ownership of the franchise. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Manny
text: Manny is One of three giant advertising mascots for the fictional Zip Boys company in Springfield. Manny is a background fixture of Springfield rather than a true character, existing mainly as a piece of advertising signage seen around town. He's part of a trio of oversized mascot figures for the Zip Boys, alongside Joe and Mack, typically appearing as a billboard or sign rather than an active participant in the plot. In a non-canon Halloween special, he and his fellow mascots are brought to life by a mysterious ionic disturbance after Homer disturbs a giant donut display, leading to a rampage through the city before the mascots lose their power once townsfolk stop paying attention to them. Outside of that supernatural episode, Manny never speaks and simply shows up as a static image advertising his company. He's essentially a piece of set dressing and a parody reference to a real-world mascot figure, giving him a niche but recognizable presence among Springfield's fictional brand icons.

title: Mountain man
text: Mountain man is A resident of the Outlands who first meets the Simpson family after they are exiled from Springfield. The mountain man is a gruff, isolationist settler living in the Outlands, wary of outsiders at first encounter. He initially threatens Homer at gunpoint before softening once he learns the Simpsons have been cast out of Springfield, a fate he sympathizes with deeply. Despite his rough exterior, he shows a protective, almost paternal concern for the family, warning them about dangers like coyotes snatching babies. He plays a key role in welcoming the Simpsons into the Outlands community, acting as an informal guide to their new lifestyle. However, his commitment to isolation from civilization is absolute, and when Springfield's influence begins creeping into the Outlands, he abandons the settlement rather than live near modern conveniences like medical care. This reflects his core trait as a fiercely independent frontier survivalist who values solitude over comfort. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: get back where you belong. | when God shuts a door, he opens a window
quotes: get back where you belong.
when God shuts a door, he opens a window

title: Stanley Kowalski
text: Stanley Kowalski is Fictional character from the play/musical "A Streetcar Named Desire"/"Oh, Streetcar!" that appears within The Simpsons universe. Stanley Kowalski is a fictional character originating from A Streetcar Named Desire, portrayed within the show's fictional world in two different adaptations. In the musical parody Oh, Streetcar!, he is famously played by Ned Flanders, directed by Llewellyn Sinclair at the Springfield Community Center. He is married to Stella Kowalski and is the brother-in-law of Blanche DuBois. The character is also referenced through the original film, in which Marlon Brando's portrayal influences Milhouse's behavior after he watches it. Stanley himself doesn't appear as an active character in Simpsons continuity so much as a role performed by other characters, making him a meta/crossover figure tied to the show's parody of the classic Tennessee Williams work. His job is listed as a factory parts salesman, fitting the blue-collar nature of the original character. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Moira
text: Moira is A minor character appearing within a black-and-white film shown in the show, married to Mick. Moira is a fictional character who exists within a stylized black-and-white film segment featured in the show. She and her husband Mick are depicted as a sophisticated detective couple who had just solved a case involving the poisoning of copper barons. Their storyline follows a lighthearted anniversary outing that goes awry when their dog Aster steals a valuable jewel from a restaurant. Moira's calm, indulgent attitude toward her husband and pet is evident when she tells Mick to simply let their dog do as he pleases. The character serves as a parody of Nora Charles from the classic mystery film series The Thin Man, fitting into the show's tradition of referencing old Hollywood film tropes. She appears only briefly, mainly functioning as part of a nostalgic film pastiche rather than a core Simpsons cast member. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: LadyBot
text: LadyBot is A robot companion created by Professor Frink, later cloned for use by Bourbon Verlander. LadyBot is a robotic creation of Professor Frink, originally built as a Valentine's Day companion who shared a tender moment with him as he sang a classic love song. Her existence takes a strange turn when a second robot appears, revealed to be her robot mother, leaving even Frink puzzled about his own invention. Multiple clones of LadyBot, dubbed 'Sally May,' become part of a bizarre scheme by Bourbon Verlander, who wants them educated to pass as human so they can qualify for student loans and secure taxpayer money. Despite being tutored by a group of real-world experts, the clones become too human-like, taking offense at being mocked and ultimately self-destructing. In another appearance, a LadyBot shows up pregnant with Frink's child at a STEM conference, adding to the running gag of her unusual and often absurd robotic existence. Overall, LadyBot serves as a vehicle for the show's satire on technology, education, and human-robot relationships. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Low Blow
text: Low Blow is One of Mr. Burns' hired goons, partnered with Crusher. Low Blow is a bald, muscular enforcer employed by Mr. Burns to carry out intimidation and physical dirty work. He operates as part of a duo with his partner Crusher, with Low Blow typically serving as the muscle who delivers the actual blows while Crusher provides the menacing laughter. Their dynamic is almost comedic in its division of labor, with Homer at one point confused about which of them is the 'pain guy' and which is the 'laugh guy.' Burns frequently deploys the pair to escort or threaten Homer and others on his behalf, using them as tools of coercion rather than reasoning. Despite his tough exterior, Low Blow is essentially a background thug used for quick physical gags rather than a fully developed character. He has appeared across several seasons and even in Simpsons comic spinoffs, cementing his role as a recurring minor henchman figure. Voiced by Hank Azaria, Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Homer asked Low Blow if he was the pain guy or the laugh guy, and Low Blow hit Homer, causing Crusher to laugh.
quotes: Homer asked Low Blow if he was the pain guy or the laugh guy, and Low Blow hit Homer, causing Crusher to laugh.

title: Lost Souls
text: Lost Souls is A group of minor characters who sail aboard The Ship of Lost Souls. The Lost Souls are a mysterious band of seafarers who wander the ocean aboard The Ship of Lost Souls, each trying to escape and forget a tragic chapter of their past. Their defining ritual is gathering to share their sorrowful personal stories with one another. When Homer joined them after fleeing the hospital to avoid donating a kidney to his father, the group welcomed him into their storytelling circle. However, Homer's tale proved so disturbing that the group reacted with horror and threw him overboard. They later reappear briefly when Homer nearly collides with their ship while trying to pilot his own vessel. The group includes distinct individuals such as a British Raj man, a Caribbean outcast, a man in a dinner jacket, a sad-looking Frenchman, and a woman in a wedding dress.

title: Ebenezer McGrew
text: Ebenezer McGrew is A Scrooge-parody character appearing in the animated short "Mr. McGrew's Christmas Carol" within the show. Ebenezer McGrew is an elderly, wealthy, and selfish figure who serves as the show's parody of Ebenezer Scrooge and Mr. Magoo. He's comically oblivious, at one point speaking to his stovepipe oven while mistaking it for a pregnant woman, and even sticking his head inside it. He treats his employee Bob Cratchett harshly, forcing him to work on Christmas despite the holiday. His selfishness extends to his personal life, valuing money over love, which nearly costs him his engagement. Like his literary counterpart, he is visited by ghostly spirits who try to show him the consequences of his greed, including a chilling glimpse of his own grave. He later reappears in a non-canon capacity in a Simpsons mobile game. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Joe Mantegna (character)
text: Joe Mantegna (character) is Fictionalized version of real-life actor Joe Mantegna who appears within the Simpsons universe, portraying Fat Tony in an in-universe film. This character is a self-referential depiction of actor Joe Mantegna appearing as himself within the Simpsons world. In the story, he takes on the role of Fat Tony for a biopic dramatizing Bart Simpson's murder trial, even though the film inaccurately portrays Bart as guilty. His performance casts Fat Tony as a reluctant accomplice rather than a mastermind. The role is notable enough in-universe that Chief Wiggum references Mantegna's connection to Fat Tony when cataloguing the Springfield Mafia's known associates. It's a playful meta moment where the show blurs the line between real-world celebrity and its own fictional crime drama. Voiced by Joe Mantegna (Himself).

title: Senator Mendoza
text: Senator Mendoza is Fictional villain within the Simpsons universe's movie-within-a-show, serving as archenemy to the action hero McBain. Senator Mendoza is the corrupt politician antagonist featured in the in-universe McBain film series. Publicly a respected senator, he secretly operates a drug cartel, making him a target for the two-fisted action hero McBain once evidence of his crimes surfaces. He is a scheming and violent figure, orchestrating an assassination attempt on McBain using a fake waiter, and later setting an absurd trap involving a rigged shrimp. His villainy catches up with him when McBain guns down his boardroom staff and tosses Mendoza out a window, where he dies in a gas truck explosion. Beyond the films, the actor who played Mendoza shows up in other unrelated contexts, such as performing with an orchestra and attending a school science fair, blurring the line between the fictional character and his in-universe performer. He also appears in a non-canon capacity within The Simpsons: Tapped Out game. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Lama
text: Lama is A Buddhist religious leader in Springfield who appears among a group of clergy in a golf-club subplot. The Lama is a minor recurring figure representing the Buddhist faith among Springfield's religious leaders. He first appears when Marge recruits him and other clergy to expose the golf club's First Church of the Blessed Mulligan as a fake religion. Instead of denouncing it, the Lama and his fellow religious leaders end up embracing the golf club as legitimate, even joining it themselves once they're offered a discounted group membership, showing a willingness to go along with convenience over principle. This gives him a small comedic role highlighting the show's satire of organized religion and consumerism. He later reappears in a more serious context, standing alongside other religious leaders at the scene of a mine cave-in, suggesting he serves as part of Springfield's ensemble of faith representatives called upon in times of crisis. Overall, the Lama is a background character used mainly for quick jokes about religious institutions rather than for deep characterization. Voiced by James Sie.

title: Mighty oak leader
text: Mighty oak leader is A non-canon tree monster leader who appears in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The mighty oak leader is a sentient tree brought to life during a supernatural uprising against humanity. Positioning himself as the head of a tree revolution, he rallies his fellow trees with a fiery speech about long-standing mistreatment by people, framing their retaliation as a twisted celebration of Arbor Day. His menace is played for dark comedy, as he invades a familiar Springfield location and threatens a beloved local shop owner with a gruesome fate. Despite his brief appearance, he embodies the classic Treehouse of Horror blend of parody and violence, turning a wholesome holiday into a source of terror. As a non-canon character, he exists purely within the show's Halloween special universe and later game tie-ins. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "he'd make a fine beanbag chair"
quotes: "he'd make a fine beanbag chair"

title: Lisa Leslie (character)
text: Lisa Leslie (character) is Real-life WNBA basketball player who appeared as herself in a Springfield basketball game episode. Lisa Leslie appears as a guest character based on her real identity as a professional basketball player. In her appearance, she is shown as sharp-witted and a stickler for proper grammar, correcting Bart Simpson's casual slang during a game. She maintains a professional, no-nonsense demeanor with fans, even while participating in a lighthearted halftime charity shot event with Ned Flanders. Despite her serious side, she shows good sportsmanship, thanking fans for supporting women's basketball. The character also nods to Leslie's real-life height of six-foot-five, which is referenced admiringly by Lisa Simpson. She later appears in a non-canon capacity attending a premiere event in Los Angeles. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: Look, that's Lisa Leslie! She showed little girls everywhere that they can grow up to be six-foot-five! | I think you mean I have game. Try to speak correctly. | Yes, I will depart, lest your bad grammar rub off on me.
quotes: Look, that's Lisa Leslie! She showed little girls everywhere that they can grow up to be six-foot-five!

title: George Lucas
text: George Lucas is Real-world film director (Star Wars, Indiana Jones) who appears as a non-canon character in Simpsons comics/episodes. George Lucas appears in the Simpsons universe as a fictionalized version of himself, the famous director of Star Wars and Indiana Jones. He's depicted as somewhat thin-skinned about criticism of his later Star Wars films, getting into a testy exchange with Nelson Muntz over bootlegging and quality complaints. His inclusion often serves as a meta joke about real-world reactions to the Star Wars prequels. He's also shown as part of a broader community of film directors who share a common fear of internet mockery, appearing among peers celebrating Comic Book Guy's death. Overall he functions less as a developed character and more as a cameo used for pop-culture satire and in-jokes about his own filmography. Notable quotes: As a filmmaker, I really wish you wouldn't do that! - George Lucas | As a film watcher, your last two movies sucked, Lucas, so shut up before I pound ya! - Nelson Muntz
quotes: As a filmmaker, I really wish you wouldn't do that! - George Lucas

title: Wheels McGrath
text: Wheels McGrath is Retired air force member and old friend of Abraham Simpson, appearing in a Cuba-set episode. Wheels McGrath is an elderly former air force man with a shady past, having hijacked a plane back in the 1970s. He crosses paths with Abraham Simpson at a bar in Cuba, and the two elderly men bond over shared history, eventually turning the stolen aircraft into an impromptu nightclub. His criminal history catches up to him when a CIA agent infiltrates his operation to reclaim the plane. McGrath is portrayed as a grizzled, somewhat roguish senior citizen still living off past exploits. He represents the show's recurring theme of Abe's colorful, often disreputable old acquaintances resurfacing. Despite his outlaw background, he comes across as affable enough to strike up a genuine friendship with Abe. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Marvin the Martian
text: Marvin the Martian is A crossover alien character who briefly appears in a police lineup in Springfield. Marvin the Martian is a guest alien character borrowed from the Looney Tunes universe, appearing in Springfield when FBI agents investigate an alien sighting reported by Homer. He is included in a lineup of famous fictional aliens alongside Gort, Chewbacca, ALF, and a Rigellian, and he is visibly annoyed at being made a suspect. To avoid copyright issues, his design is shown slightly discolored from his original appearance. His signature line from Looney Tunes carries over as his catchphrase in this appearance. Beyond this brief cameo, he later shows up as a playable character in a fighting video game referenced within the show. He has no deeper connection to the main Simpsons cast beyond these two appearances. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: This makes me very angry.|Marvin the Martian|The Springfield Files
quotes: This makes me very angry.|Marvin the Martian|The Springfield Files

title: Cyndi Lauper (character)
text: Cyndi Lauper (character) is Real-world celebrity guest character; singer who appears in Springfield. Cyndi Lauper appears in the show as a fictionalized version of herself, the real-life American pop singer. Her main appearance involves performing the national anthem before a Springfield Isotopes baseball game, only for the crowd to comically try to leave immediately afterward, forgetting the game was about to start. She later shows up again via a look-alike performer singing a satirical song alongside other celebrity impersonators. Her role is brief and cameo-like, existing mostly as a nod to her real-world fame rather than a developed character with personality traits or running gags. She has no family ties or ongoing storylines within the show's main cast. Voiced by Herself.

title: Brian McGee
text: Brian McGee is A fake identity used by Homer Simpson to buy beer underage. Brian McGee isn't a real person, but a fabricated identity Homer Simpson used as a teenager to purchase alcohol before he was of legal age. The fake ID listed a birthdate of August 2, 1948, and gave Homer's alias red hair. The gag centers on how obviously fake the ID was, since the person pictured on it looked nothing like Homer, yet the cashier sold him the six-pack of Duff Beer anyway. This small bit of backstory appears only briefly, tied to a flashback about Homer's youth and his early relationship with alcohol. Brian McGee has no dialogue or independent characterization, existing purely as a prop within Homer's history rather than a character in his own right.

title: Joe Namath (character)
text: Joe Namath (character) is Celebrity guest character, a real-life professional football player who appears in cameo roles in the Simpsons universe. Joe Namath appears as a fictionalized version of himself, popping up sporadically to interact with the Simpson family. He's remembered by Abe as a flashy, sideburned football star from Super Bowl III, someone Abe considers less manly than Johnny Unitas but who represents changing times to Mona. His most notable appearance has him showing up conveniently outside Bart's house with car trouble, seemingly poised to share football wisdom before getting distracted and driving off before revealing anything useful. He's obsessed with warning people about the dangers of vapor lock, treating it as a matter of great importance despite it being a minor and obscure car issue. This running gag becomes self-aware when he breaks the fourth wall to lecture the audience directly about it. Later continuity nods reference lasting effects of old football injuries and memorabilia bearing his signature, cementing him as a recurring but minor celebrity cameo character. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: there's nothing funny about vapor lock | It's the third most common cause of car stallings.
quotes: there's nothing funny about vapor lock
It's the third most common cause of car stallings.

title: Maxine Lombard
text: Maxine Lombard is Democratic assemblywoman and speaker of Springfield's state assembly, love interest of Mr. Burns. Maxine Lombard is a politician who enters Springfield after Lisa writes to her about illegal fracking happening near the Simpsons' home. Despite shutting down Mr. Burns' fracking operation and being his political opposite, she ends up falling for him and the two begin a secret romantic affair. Their relationship is defined by a mix of professional rivalry and genuine attraction, with Burns famously describing their dynamic as enemies by day and lovers by night. When their scheme to seize Evergreen Terrace's gas rights collapses, Burns breaks things off with her out of anger, and she retaliates by transforming his mansion into a progressive-themed community center. The two eventually reconcile after Burns admits his mistake, showing that beneath her political persona she's capable of both petty revenge and genuine affection. She later makes a minor appearance in the audience of a podcast recording, suggesting she remains a recurring figure in Springfield's civic life. Voiced by Jane Fonda. Notable quotes: "recycling center, slash Native American history museum, slash condor sanctuary"
quotes: "recycling center, slash Native American history museum, slash condor sanctuary"

title: Jared Kushner
text: Jared Kushner is Non-canon parody character; senior adviser to Donald Trump in Simpsons political shorts. Jared Kushner appears as a background figure in a handful of non-canon Simpsons shorts satirizing the Trump White House. He's portrayed as a loyal, somewhat robotic aide who follows Trump around attending to menial tasks, such as bringing him toothpaste and a toothbrush. In one bizarre scene, he's shown strangling fellow adviser Steve Bannon while oddly fixating on keeping his suit unwrinkled. He later turns up hanging from the ceiling alongside Bannon and Kellyanne Conway, another surreal gag typical of these specials. Overall, he serves as a minor comedic prop used to lampoon the chaotic and absurd atmosphere of the Trump administration rather than as a fully developed character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Mowgli
text: Mowgli is Non-canon crossover character from Disney's The Jungle Book, appearing in Simpsons specials. Mowgli is a guest character brought over from Disney's The Jungle Book for a crossover appearance in a Simpsons special. He shows up at Moe's Tavern as part of a celebration marking Disney+'s second anniversary, mingling among a crowd of other Disney characters. In a later special, he's briefly seen waiting in line to visit Homer, who is dressed up as Santa Claus. He has no dialogue in either appearance, functioning purely as a background cameo rather than a character with development. His presence is a nod to Disney's ownership of the franchise and a fun easter egg for fans of both properties.

title: Michael (Warrin' Priests: Part One)
text: Michael (Warrin' Priests: Part One) is Member of the First Church of Springfield choir and church council. Michael is a minor but active figure within Springfield's church community, serving both in the choir and on the church council. He's shown to be a bit reckless behind the wheel, once driving erratically and crossing a double yellow line while rushing the choir to a service, which drew the attention of the police. When Reverend Lovejoy began losing his voice, Michael stepped up to announce a replacement speaker, showing he takes some initiative in church affairs. He later played a role in the council's decision to remove Lovejoy from his position in favor of a new reverend, Bode Wright. Michael continued to be present during the fallout of that decision, including attending a tense town meeting after Bode's controversial actions came to light. Overall, he represents the everyday churchgoers of Springfield who get swept up in the drama surrounding their religious leadership. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson.

title: Michelin Man
text: Michelin Man is Real-world tyre company mascot referenced/appearing briefly in The Simpsons. The Michelin Man is a non-speaking, picture-only character based on the real-life advertising mascot for the Michelin tyre company. He never appears as a fully animated character but shows up through references, images, and a costume within the show. His name is notably one that Homer's friends are forbidden from calling him, playing into a running gag about nicknames. He also turns up as an image in a pamphlet about Michigan and is cited by Wendell Borton as one of the "Famous Pale People" in a school presentation. As a recurring but minor pop-culture reference, he represents the show's frequent nods to real-world branding and iconography rather than being an active participant in the plot.

title: Melvin (G.I. (Annoyed Grunt))
text: Melvin (G.I. (Annoyed Grunt)) is A minor recurring senior citizen residing at the Springfield Retirement Castle. Melvin is an elderly, gray-haired resident of the Springfield Retirement Castle, appearing as a background figure among the show's many nameless or barely-named seniors. He is noted for being confused and disoriented, as seen when he struggles to understand a simple game of bingo at the retirement home. His only real distinguishing trait comes from a story Abraham Simpson tells Homer, revealing that Melvin has a son who plays banjo and personalizes his songs by including the names of the seniors during visits. Melvin himself never speaks on screen, fitting into the show's tradition of silent, incidental elderly characters. He represents the quiet, often overlooked residents who populate the retirement home's halls. His appearances are brief, serving mostly as background color for scenes set among Springfield's senior citizens.

title: Michael (And Maggie Makes Three)
text: Michael (And Maggie Makes Three) is Fictional main character of the in-universe TV show "Knightboat", watched by the Simpson family. Michael exists only within the world of The Simpsons as the star of a fictional television series called Knightboat. He's a clear parody of Michael Knight, the character David Hasselhoff played on Knight Rider, transplanting that action-hero formula onto a boat instead of a car. The family, including Bart, Lisa, and Homer, are shown watching an episode of his show together, treating it as an unremarkable part of their television diet. Michael himself doesn't have much personality beyond being a stand-in for cheesy '80s action TV, existing purely as a joke about the show-within-a-show format. He's a minor, background gag character rather than someone with any real development. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Nascar Dad
text: Nascar Dad is Minor recurring background character in Springfield. Nascar Dad is a minor, non-speaking resident of Springfield whose name pokes fun at the stereotypical demographic term for auto-racing enthusiast fathers. He tends to pop up in small, incidental moments rather than driving any major storylines. He was almost the buyer of Homer's old car before Homer intervened, and he later took part in a focus group sampling Moe's homemade bourbon. He's also been shown sharing a dinner with Ruth Powers, hinting at some social life outside these odd cameos. In one episode he's depicted as one of several men pictured on a wall of people who have dated and left Nelson, adding a bit of comedic mystery to his background. Overall, he functions as a recurring extra used for quick visual gags and background continuity rather than characterization.

title: Lester
text: Lester is A young rival of Bart Simpson who appeared in "The Day the Violence Died". Lester is a minor recurring kid character who serves as a sort of foil to Bart Simpson. Along with his sister Eliza, he manages to outdo Bart and Lisa by rescuing Itchy and Scratchy Studios before them, earning gratitude from both Apu and Krusty for resolving their personal troubles. His and Eliza's success even gets commemorated with a dedicated cartoon episode, overshadowing Bart and Lisa's efforts. Bart finds the situation unsettling, hinting at an odd rivalry or unease about Lester's presence. Lester doesn't have much individual personality beyond being an overachieving double to Bart, fitting into the show's occasional use of doppelgänger-style side characters. He's a blond ten-year-old student who appears only briefly but leaves Bart visibly bothered by his existence. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Kyoto
text: Kyoto is A minor recurring artist character connected to Homer's brief career as an artist. Kyoto is a female artist who appeared during the period when Homer briefly became part of the art world. She was among the new circle of artistic friends Homer made at that time, alongside Gunter and Cecil Hampstead. Little else is known about her personality or background, as she is a non-speaking character. Her role is largely visual, representing the eccentric art crowd Homer temporarily associated with. Kyoto has made a couple of appearances in the show, tied specifically to storylines about Homer's art career.

title: Lois Lane
text: Lois Lane is DC Comics character (Superman's love interest/wife) referenced within the Simpsons universe as a comic book character. Lois Lane is a crossover character borrowed from DC Comics who appears mainly as comic book merchandise and pop-culture references within the Simpsons world. She's best known as Superman's romantic interest, though the show plays with this by having her married to him in odd, exaggerated scenarios, including a triple marriage with Lana Lang and Xena in a non-canon German comic parody. Homer isn't particularly impressed by her, openly stating he prefers Wonder Woman. Lisa, on the other hand, is a fan, having collected Lois Lane comics and even given her a spot on a geeky list of favorites. She's more of a running reference and collectible figure than an active character, often represented by dolls or images rather than direct appearances. Notable quotes: I like pink very much, Lois
quotes: I like pink very much, Lois

title: Sandeep Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Sandeep Nahasapeemapetilon is One of Apu and Manjula's octuplet children, the first-born of the Nahasapeemapetilon family. Sandeep is one of the eight babies born to Apu and Manjula after she took fertility drugs, making him the eldest of the octuplets. Overwhelmed by the demands of raising eight infants at once, his parents initially placed him and his siblings in a display nursery at the Springfield Zoo called 'Octopia.' There, Sandeep was cast in the role of the comedic performer nicknamed 'Punchline' during the zoo's baby show. Unhappy with having their children exhibited like zoo animals, Apu and Homer eventually staged a breakout to rescue the babies. As an infant character, Sandeep has little individual personality of his own beyond his stage persona and his status as the firstborn among his siblings. He has appeared as a background character across many later seasons, comics, and other Simpsons media. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Freddy Krueger
text: Freddy Krueger is Crossover horror character from A Nightmare on Elm Street who appears as a non-canon guest villain in The Simpsons' Treehouse of Horror episodes. Freddy Krueger is a guest appearance from the Nightmare on Elm Street franchise, brought into the Simpsons universe primarily for Halloween-themed segments. He shows up as one of several classic movie monsters unleashed when Homer is freed from a cellar, joining the likes of Jason Voorhees, Count Dracula, the Mummy, the Wolfman, and Pinhead, though he's initially more interested in finishing his meal than menacing anyone. He also makes a cameo in a couch gag, sitting alongside Jason Voorhees on the Simpsons' couch waiting for the family to show up. In a memorable parody, Groundskeeper Willie takes on a Krueger-like persona, complete with a matching backstory as a school janitor. A look-alike of Freddy even shows up singing in a musical number in one episode. Overall, he functions as a fun horror-icon cameo rather than a fully developed character within the show's continuity. Voiced by Robert Englund.

title: Cowardly Lion
text: Cowardly Lion is A crossover character from The Wizard of Oz referenced within The Simpsons universe. The Cowardly Lion is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed figure from The Wizard of Oz, appearing mainly as a visual reference or costume within the show. He's brought up in conversation when Homer misremembers the character's defining trait, mixing up his lack of courage with having no heart, only to be corrected by Carl. This mix-up becomes part of a larger comedic exchange involving other Oz characters like the Scarecrow and Tin Man. The character himself doesn't speak on the show and functions more as a pop-culture touchstone than a fleshed-out figure. In one non-canon future scenario, someone auditions for a Wizard of Oz production dressed as the Lion. Overall, he's a minor, non-speaking recurring reference rather than a true member of the Simpsons cast.

title: James Lipton (character)
text: James Lipton (character) is Talk show host of Inside the Actor's Studio who has appeared interviewing Simpsons characters and celebrities. James Lipton is a real-world talk show host who appears as himself within the Simpsons universe, running his celebrity interview program. He's portrayed as unfailingly polite and professional, maintaining his composure even in absurd or dangerous situations. During one memorable interview, he was accidentally shot by a guest who got too into character, yet he responded with unwavering graciousness rather than panic. He later hosted a reunion special for a fictional show's cast, attempting to dig into gossip about a character's hairstyle, only to be met with resistance from one guest and an oversharing confession from another. His image has also popped up as background decor in at least one Simpsons location, cementing his status as a recognizable pop-culture figure within the show's world. Voiced by James Lipton (Himself). Notable quotes: It was a pleasure to eat your lead, good sir! | everyone in the cast - including the dog.
quotes: It was a pleasure to eat your lead, good sir!
everyone in the cast - including the dog.

title: Fox Mulder
text: Fox Mulder is FBI Special Agent from The X-Files who guest-stars investigating Homer's alleged alien sighting. Fox Mulder is a crossover character brought in from The X-Files to investigate a supposed alien encounter in Springfield. He is a firm believer in UFOs and government conspiracies, contrasting with his more skeptical partner Dana Scully. During his visit, he subjects Homer to bizarre tests and follow-up investigations, showing a dry, deadpan sense of humor even in absurd situations. Unlike Scully, who quickly dismisses Homer's story once evidence seems unconvincing, Mulder stubbornly lingers in the forest musing about the universe's mysteries long after everyone else has given up. He has made minor non-canon and background appearances since, including as a fundraiser phone operator and a framed picture in a restaurant. His most quoted line pokes fun at his conspiratorial, misinformation-spreading reputation. Voiced by David Duchovny. Notable quotes: His jiggling is almost hypnotic. | I would never lie. I willfully participate in a campaign of misinformation
quotes: His jiggling is almost hypnotic.
I would never lie. I willfully participate in a campaign of misinformation

title: Meredith Milgram
text: Meredith Milgram is Former principal of Springfield Elementary School, predecessor to Principal Skinner. Meredith Milgram is a minor, elderly character who once served as principal of Springfield Elementary before Seymour Skinner took over the role. She resurfaces years later when a distinctive piece of paper with blue rings leads Skinner to recognize her old stationery. Curious about the connection, Skinner brings along a group of students, including Bart, Milhouse, Nelson, Ralph, and Otto, to track her down. It turns out she has taken on an unofficial mentoring role, teaching Lisa cursive handwriting, a skill seemingly forgotten in modern curriculum. Milgram doesn't have much of a defined personality beyond this brief appearance, functioning mainly as a nostalgic nod to the school's history and a plot device connecting past and present staff at Springfield Elementary. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Gwendolyn Nightshadow
text: Gwendolyn Nightshadow is Teenage Wiccan who befriends Lisa Simpson in the episode "Rednecks and Broomsticks". Gwendolyn Nightshadow, real name Stacy Deathsatan, is one of three teenage witches who practice Wicca in the woods outside Springfield. Alongside her fellow Wiccans Cassandra and Esmeralda, she values nature and friendship, and the trio quickly bond with Lisa Simpson, even trying to recruit her into their beliefs. When Ned Flanders becomes suspicious that the girls are dangerous or demonic, they end up arrested, only to be acquitted in court. Their claim of magical power seems to manifest when much of Springfield's population mysteriously goes blind after they curse their doubters. Despite being cleared legally, they become the target of a superstitious mob that judges them by outdated witch-hunting standards, and Lisa ultimately steps in to save them. The experience cements a strong bond between Lisa and the Wiccans, who tell her she makes them feel accepted. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Luigi (video game character)
text: Luigi (video game character) is A crossover video game character (Nintendo's Luigi) who appears occasionally in Simpsons episodes. Luigi is a parody appearance of the famous Nintendo plumber character, brought into the Simpsons universe as a crossover cameo. He is depicted as Mario's younger brother, often shown tagging along beside him rather than taking center stage. In his first appearance, he is one of several video game icons who tempt Bart into shoplifting a video game, standing in contrast to the more moral Lee Carvallo. He later shows up in a more mundane, comedic moment, snapping a photo of Mario with Homer after the brothers step off an Italian tour bus. Luigi also appears as part of a dream sequence involving fictional sibling duos. A non-canon gnome-like version of him appears in a video game tie-in alongside other Nintendo characters. Overall, he functions as a fun nod to gaming culture rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Noid
text: Noid is A parade balloon character and advertising mascot for Domino's Pizza appearing in Springfield. The Noid is a promotional mascot for Domino's Pizza who appears as a parade balloon during Springfield's Thanksgiving Day festivities. He later shows up in a more direct advertising capacity when the First Church of Springfield accepts corporate sponsorship to pay for repairs after a rocket accident. In that appearance, he is introduced by Reverend Lovejoy to give a sermon-like pitch on pizza before being cut off. The character is mostly a background gag referencing real-world Domino's advertising campaigns rather than a fleshed-out personality. In a non-canon appearance, he humorously joins in stabbing Little Caesar in a Julius Caesar-style parody. Overall, the Noid functions as a satirical nod to corporate branding creeping into Springfield life. Notable quotes: Avoid the Noid! He ruins pizzas! | Et tu, Noidus?
quotes: Avoid the Noid! He ruins pizzas!
Et tu, Noidus?

title: Nibbler
text: Nibbler is A Futurama character (Nibblonian) appearing as a crossover pet in a Simpsons/Futurama crossover episode. Nibbler is a small, black alien creature belonging to Leela, originating from the Futurama universe. He appears when the Simpsons family finds themselves transported into the future, where they encounter him at Planet Express headquarters. In a bit of gross-out slapstick humor typical of his species' odd biology, he gets chased by strange creatures, eats one, and then experiences a bizarre digestive mishap that leads to further chaos. His inclusion serves mainly as a nod to fans of Futurama during this crossover story. Despite his mischievous circumstances, he's mostly a background gag character rather than a major player in the plot. His presence highlights the whimsical blending of the two animated universes. Voiced by Frank Welker.

title: Trevor McBride
text: Trevor McBride is Springfield High School student and football quarterback who appears in a Shauna-related storyline. Trevor McBride is the star quarterback at Springfield High School, known for throwing a pool party after being impressed by Shauna's band audition. He uses the promise of admission via beer to get high schoolers to his house, revealing a somewhat manipulative or opportunistic streak. When his stash of alcohol is stolen by his friend Johnny Joe, the party spirals out of control once the beer arrives anyway, showing how little control Trevor actually has over the chaos he sets in motion. He and Shauna abandon Lisa during the party, leaving her to fend for herself, which hints at a callous or careless attitude toward other students. His parents' absence, off doing an escape room in another town, sets the stage for the unsupervised party gag. Trevor is a minor but memorable recurring character tied closely to teenage party culture at the school. Voiced by Chris Redd.

title: Magnesium Man
text: Magnesium Man is A fictional superhero and member of the Vindicators within the Simpsons universe's franchise. Magnesium Man is a member of the superhero team the Vindicators, appearing primarily in the in-universe film franchise Vindicators: Crystal War. He's a clear parody of Iron Man, decked out in a powered suit with flight and laser abilities. His personality leans toward wisecracking bravado, often using humor and distraction tactics during battle to give his teammates an edge. He plays a notable role in bridging the fictional and 'real' worlds when he pulls Bart into a virtual reality version of the Vindicators' universe to stop him from spoiling the sequel. Beyond the films, his likeness shows up in merchandise and fan culture, including costumes, figures, and pajamas owned by Comic Book Guy. As a non-canon extension, he also appears as a playable character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: aww, what's the matter? Bad head day?
quotes: aww, what's the matter? Bad head day?

title: Medicine woman
text: Medicine woman is An Inuit healer who helps Homer reach a life-changing epiphany in The Simpsons Movie. The medicine woman is a mysterious Inuit healer encountered by Homer during his stint in the Alaskan wilderness. Known for her strikingly large breasts, she earns the nickname "boob lady" from Homer, who can't help but focus on that feature even in serious moments. She acts as a spiritual guide, forcing Homer through a vision-inducing throat-singing ritual so he can confront his flaws and realize he must save Springfield. Beyond her mystical role, she also has a practical side, later tracking Homer down to collect payment he owes her for her services. Her recurring gag involves blending spiritual wisdom with comic absurdity, appearing in visions at convenient moments to nudge Homer in the right direction. She also appears in a non-canon capacity, scolding Bart for skateboarding in a couch gag-style opening sequence. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Homer calls her "boob lady" after thanking her for helping him reach his epiphany. | Marge asks who she is, Homer replies that she was his "therapist".
quotes: Homer calls her "boob lady" after thanking her for helping him reach his epiphany.
Marge asks who she is, Homer replies that she was his "therapist".

title: Chief Knocka-Homer
text: Chief Knocka-Homer is A fighting robot built and secretly piloted by Homer Simpson to compete on the TV show Robot Rumble. Chief Knocka-Homer is a homemade combat robot that Homer Simpson constructs in an attempt to impress his son Bart and win glory on the television competition Robot Rumble. Unable to build a true autonomous robot, Homer instead hides inside the machine himself, pedaling a tricycle and manipulating the arms directly while pretending a decorative remote control operates it. To keep himself fighting at full intensity, Homer rigs the remote to shock his own backside, turning self-inflicted pain into a bizarre competitive advantage. The robot racks up a string of victories against other contestants before facing its toughest challenge in the advanced machine Killhammad Aieee, built by Professor Frink and his son. That climactic battle exposes Homer's secret and nearly gets him killed, but it also earns him newfound respect from Bart once the truth comes out. Visually, Chief Knocka-Homer resembles an oversized mailbox on wheels, topped with a war bonnet and armed with a hammer and grappling hooks capable of stealing enemies' weapons. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Audrey McConnell
text: Audrey McConnell is A teacher at Springfield Elementary School who once taught Bart and Lisa. Audrey McConnell is one of the lesser-seen faculty members at Springfield Elementary, initially introduced as a third grade teacher before apparently moving up to teach fourth grade. Unlike her more jaded colleagues, she comes across as upbeat, self-assured, and generally competent, at least until things go wrong, such as a botched buddy-system exercise. She harbors some petty disdain for fellow teachers Edna Krabappel and Miss Hoover, subtly mocking their personal habits of smoking and drinking whenever they come up in conversation. Outside of the classroom, she's shown participating in ordinary Springfield life, appearing at the Town Square during the Trappuccino chaos, socializing at Ned and Edna's wedding party, and attending a Sungazer concert. She mostly appears as a background recurring character rather than a focus of any major storyline. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Lincoln squirrel
text: Lincoln squirrel is A minor animal character in Springfield, a squirrel that briefly gained fame for resembling President Abraham Lincoln. The Lincoln squirrel is a quirky one-off gag character whose sole claim to fame is its uncanny resemblance to President Abraham Lincoln. Its discovery was notable enough to land it on the front page of the Springfield Shopper newspaper. Tragically, its brief brush with local celebrity ended when Kent Brockman reported its assassination on Channel 6 News, mirroring the fate of the president it resembled. The character never speaks or interacts directly with the main cast, existing only as a background visual joke. It appears exclusively as a picture-only character, reinforcing its role as a throwaway piece of Simpsons trivia rather than a developed character.

title: Ahura Mazda
text: Ahura Mazda is A minor deity from Zoroastrianism who briefly appears in the show's depiction of Heaven. Ahura Mazda is a divine figure representing the god of Zoroastrianism, making a brief comedic cameo in the show's ever-expanding pantheon of deities. He's portrayed as a bit of a drunk, stumbling into a scene with a wine goblet in hand. His appearance comes during a debate between God and the Tetragrammaton about Krusty's religious identity, where Mazda is consulted despite his questionable sobriety. Rather than offering wisdom, he simply calls out God's own drinking habits before passing out. He later shows up in a non-canon episode set in Heaven, existing as part of the show's running gag of mixing together deities from various world religions. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Oh, and like you're not!
quotes: Oh, and like you're not!

title: Muk Mu
text: Muk Mu is A minor recurring character; a huge basketball player nicknamed "The Human North Pole" who appears in Springfield-related sports events. Muk Mu is an enormous, imposing basketball player whose towering size earns him the nickname "The Human North Pole." Hailing from the Ketchikan, Alaska area, he becomes a rallying figure for the townspeople when Mr. Burns threatens to send him back home after Lisa's protest against a new stadium. Despite his gentle appearance, which leads Lisa to see him as a kind and loving soul, Muk Mu secretly enjoys a much darker pastime—killing whales for fun. He later shows up in an unrelated context as a judge on a talent competition, introduced with NBA star status and a peace sign greeting. His brief, gruff dialogue and stark contrast between public image and private nature make him a memorable one-off character used mostly for comedic effect. Voiced by Karl Wiedergott / Chris Edgerly. Notable quotes: Please don't take our freak! | Tuqurunga aghloonik.
quotes: Please don't take our freak!
Tuqurunga aghloonik.

title: Ed McMahon (character)
text: Ed McMahon (character) is Real-world celebrity (Johnny Carson's longtime TV announcer/sidekick) who appears as himself in guest cameos on The Simpsons. Ed McMahon appears as himself, drawing on his real-life fame as Johnny Carson's booming, laugh-happy sidekick on The Tonight Show. In the show's canon, he's referenced as a legendary drinker and toady, with Homer even claiming to have studied his sycophantic, hard-drinking skills under him. Smithers reveres him enough to include him among history's great toadies for his role as Carson's chuckling second banana. He also lends his name and voice to real-world tie-in material like forewords and books referenced within the Simpsons universe. In non-canon Treehouse of Horror segments, he shows a darker comedic side, hosting a fictional gruesome execution show while keeping his classic showman catchphrases intact. His signature laugh and iconic introductions are treated as running gags whenever he appears. Voiced by Ed McMahon. Notable quotes: Heeeeere's Snake! | Hi-yooooo!
quotes: Heeeeere's Snake!
Hi-yooooo!

title: Los Souvenir Jacquitos leader
text: Los Souvenir Jacquitos leader is Leader of the elderly Mexican-American gang Los Souvenir Jacquitos, recurring minor character connected to Grampa Simpson's storylines. This character leads a group of elderly men known as Los Souvenir Jacquitos, easily identified by his Planet Hollywood jacket. He has a recurring connection to Grampa Simpson, whether racing him, thanking him for smuggling prescription drugs, or training him to become a matador for Springfield's repurposed stadium. His group tends to show up at major town events, from concerts to meetings about local issues. He and his fellow gang members have also been swept up in bizarre town mishaps, including a drug-related incident that caused elderly residents' eyes to fall out. Despite his minor role, he appears across many episodes, often as part of a comedic backdrop involving Springfield's senior citizens. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Milhoose
text: Milhoose is Milhouse Van Houten's Canadian counterpart, met by Bart during a trip to Vancouver. Milhoose is essentially a mirror image of Milhouse, right down to the raspy voice, love of glasses, and a crush on Lisa. The key differences are cosmetic and cultural: he has brown hair instead of blue, wears rectangular-lensed glasses instead of round ones, and speaks with an exaggerated Canadian accent full of 'oot' and 'eh'-style phrasing. He befriended Bart quickly when Bart visited Vancouver for the Olympics, bonding over snowboarding and inviting Lisa along. Like his American counterpart, he initially fancies Lisa, but his interest cools once he witnesses her over-the-top obsession with collecting Olympic pins. He also has an unfortunate run-in with the intimidating Canadian Nelson, who punches him. Milhoose exists mainly as a one-off joke exaggerating Canadian stereotypes through a familiar Simpsons character template. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: Your sister's hotter than a Calgary brushfire. Mind if I ask her oot? | She is as loonie as a one-dollar coin.
quotes: Your sister's hotter than a Calgary brushfire. Mind if I ask her oot?
She is as loonie as a one-dollar coin.

title: Seth MacFarlane (character)
text: Seth MacFarlane (character) is A minor, real-world character depicted as a federal courthouse sketch artist in the Simpsons universe. This version of Seth MacFarlane appears as a courthouse sketch artist working within the federal court system, a nod to the real MacFarlane's role as an animator and filmmaker. He is drawn into the story after Krusty commits treason by selling secrets to North Korea, landing his case in federal court rather than under Marge's more skilled artistic eye. Unlike Marge, whose courtroom sketches are praised for being realistic and moving, MacFarlane's work is comically poor, producing a caricature of Krusty that resembles Stewie Griffin. The character serves as a meta joke referencing MacFarlane's own animated series, Family Guy, blending real-world persona with in-universe absurdity. He also shows up in non-canon material, including a courtroom crossover appearance and a bit involving Milhouse and his father imitating him imitating Frank Sinatra.

title: Cooper Manning (character)
text: Cooper Manning (character) is Real-world guest character; brother of Eli Manning and Peyton Manning, appearing in a dream sequence with Bart. Cooper Manning is a real-life figure who appears as a fictionalized version of himself in a dream sequence experienced by Bart Simpson. As the eldest of the Manning brothers, he tries to assert his authority and share his own athletic accomplishments, contrasting himself with his more famous NFL siblings. His attempt at bragging backfires comically when his younger brothers mock him and physically exclude him from their game. The scene plays on sibling rivalry, with Cooper cast as the overlooked older brother despite his own achievements. His appearance is brief, limited to a comedic cameo rather than an ongoing role in the show. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: "squirt"
quotes: "squirt"

title: Sir Loves-A-Lot
text: Sir Loves-A-Lot is A talking teddy bear toy sold as a Love Day gift, briefly owned by Homer Simpson. Sir Loves-A-Lot is a novelty toy from the Simpsons universe, designed as a plush teddy bear clad in medieval knight garb, complete with a heart emblem, a sword, and heart-shaped balloons. His gimmick is a saccharine, robotic voice that repeats affectionate declarations, making him a parody of overly sentimental holiday merchandise. He became a minor source of disappointment for Homer, who received him as a Love Day gift but had secretly wanted a different, similarly themed bear. The character's arc quickly turns dark and comedic when he's discarded and ends up buried in Springfield's trash, an image used for satirical effect regarding waste and consumerism. He later resurfaces as discount merchandise, reinforcing his status as a forgotten, low-value product. Despite his brief appearances, he's remembered as a quirky one-off gag character tied to the show's holiday-episode humor. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: I'm Sir Loves-A-Lot, the bear who loves to love!
quotes: I'm Sir Loves-A-Lot, the bear who loves to love!

title: Pahasatira Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Pahasatira Nahasapeemapetilon is Daughter of Sanjay Nahasapeemapetilon and niece of Apu; minor recurring student at Springfield Elementary. Pahasatira is a young member of the sprawling Nahasapeemapetilon family, part of the extended household connected to Apu's relatives. She's shown as a participant in local events, most notably competing in a beauty pageant where her singing is only appreciated by her own family members, hinting at a running gag about her questionable talent being overlooked by everyone outside her immediate circle. She also plays a small role as an informant, revealing a scandalous secret about two Springfield Elementary staff members to her father and uncle. Her ambitions extend to entertainment, as she later tries out for a televised talent competition. Despite limited screen time, she represents another branch of the ever-expanding Nahasapeemapetilon family tree that recurs throughout the series. Voiced by Yeardley Smith, Pamela Hayden, Nancy Cartwright (Singing).

title: Courtney Love
text: Courtney Love is Real-world singer-songwriter referenced/appearing as a minor character in the show. Courtney Love appears in the Simpsons universe as a version of her real-life self, a musician whose image and persona are referenced rather than deeply explored. She's shown as a minor celebrity figure whose cereal box appearance draws Lisa's disapproval, hinting at the show's satire of celebrity marketing. In another instance, Otto Mann mistakes a recording of an NPR commentator for one of Love's notoriously rambling sound checks, poking fun at her reputation for erratic public behavior. She has no dialogue in her canonical appearance, functioning more as a background pop-culture reference than an active character. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, she meets a comedic apocalyptic fate, being launched into the sun along with other doomed figures. Overall, she serves as a quick cultural nod rather than a fleshed-out character within the show.

title: Libby
text: Libby is A minor superhero character from the Radioactive Man comic universe within The Simpsons. Libby is a feminist superhero who appears as an ally, and occasional critic, of Radioactive Man within the show's comic-book-within-a-show mythology. Her design features a Venus symbol on her costume and visible underarm hair, both intentional nods to the women's liberation movement. She has black hair and is depicted as a non-speaking, picture-only character across her appearances. Libby first appeared in a Treehouse of Horror Halloween special as part of a Radioactive Man comic cover where she was shown scolding the titular hero. Since her introduction, she has mostly shown up as a background image in various episodes and title screens rather than taking an active speaking role. Her character exists mainly as a satirical wink at superhero comic tropes and feminist iconography.

title: Lainie Leonard
text: Lainie Leonard is Lenny Leonard's sister, a minor recurring character. Lainie Leonard is a background figure known mainly through her connection to her brother Lenny. She has a peculiar Valentine's Day arrangement with Carl, who dates her while Lenny dates Carl's sister, apparently because both men enjoy dating someone who resembles their best friend. She joined the guys on a boating trip aboard the Something's Fishy, a vessel co-owned by Homer, Lenny, and Carl. Lainie doesn't have much individual characterization beyond these connections, functioning more as an extension of the running joke about Lenny and Carl's close friendship. She remains a rarely seen but recurring part of the show's extended universe of side characters. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Mike (Homer's Night Out)
text: Mike (Homer's Night Out) is Minor recurring character; father of Freddy's classmate, appearing in early Simpsons episodes. Mike is a minor background character introduced in the show's first season. He is known primarily as the father of a child named Freddy, tying him loosely to the school-parent community of Springfield. His most notable action was passing along a photo of Homer with Princess Kashmir to his friend Al, which contributed to the fallout of Homer's misadventure at a bachelor party. Beyond this brief moment of relevance, Mike mostly appears in cameo roles in later episodes, blending into crowd scenes without much individual characterization. He has no strong personality traits or catchphrases established in canon, functioning more as a background fixture than a fully developed character. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Norman
text: Norman is Sideshow Mel's deceased father. Norman is a minor, rarely-seen character known only as the father of Sideshow Mel. He appears primarily in mentions rather than on-screen scenes, with his most notable appearance being in a Bongo comic book story exploring Mel's origins. By the time of the show's later continuity, Norman has passed away, and his funeral is referenced as something Mel had to attend. Little is revealed about his personality or history beyond his familial connection to Mel, making him more of a background detail used to flesh out Sideshow Mel's backstory than a fully developed character. He exists mostly as a footnote mentioned in a handful of episodes.

title: Marge robots
text: Marge robots is A group of robotic replicas of Marge Simpson built by Artie Ziff, appearing in the episode "Hail to the Teeth". The Marge robots are a series of mechanical creations built by Artie Ziff in a misguided attempt to recreate the woman he loves, Marge Simpson. Each version comes with its own comedic malfunction or flaw, from lacking basic kindness to actively trying to kill him, highlighting how far off he is from capturing the real Marge. Artie's obsession culminates in a fake wedding to one of the robots, staged purely to make Marge jealous, though it backfires into a moment of genuine emotional low for him. After Marge convinces him to use his talents for good, the robots seem to reject the idea of romantic servitude entirely, flying away the moment Artie suggests making one his bride. The group also doubles as a visual gag, with several designs referencing other pop culture robots like the Terminator and Bender from Futurama. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: C. W. McAllister
text: C. W. McAllister is A mountaineer who attempted to climb The Murderhorn alongside Abraham Simpson. C. W. McAllister is a minor, deceased character whose tragic fate is revealed in the episode "King of the Hill." He and Abe Simpson nearly reached the summit of The Murderhorn together before running out of supplies. Contrary to Abe's self-serving version of events, it was actually Abe who bit McAllister's arm and stole his oxygen, leaving McAllister to freeze to death alone on the mountain. His frozen body later serves an unexpectedly practical purpose when Homer discovers it and uses it as a makeshift sled to slide down the mountain to safety. McAllister is a largely silent, background character whose backstory adds a darkly comic and grim twist to Abe's boastful mountaineering tale. Notable quotes: I have mountaineered to the utmost, but the peak is unclimbable. Worse still, that treacherous skunk Abe Simpson stole my oxygen and tried to eat my left arm.
quotes: I have mountaineered to the utmost, but the peak is unclimbable. Worse still, that treacherous skunk Abe Simpson stole my oxygen and tried to eat my left arm.

title: Loki (Norse mythology)
text: Loki (Norse mythology) is Norse mythological god of mischief who appears in a Simpsons comic story and later in an episode involving the Simpson family. Loki is depicted as the trickster deity of Norse legend, first shown up in a tale Grampa spins for Bart and Lisa. He later crosses over into the main show's continuity, confronting the Simpson family directly and revealing a much darker, manipulative side. His scheme involves stripping away Marge's faith in human goodness, treating her belief as something he can literally steal. He toys with the idea of ancient laws and rituals, only to casually admit he was making them up, showing his love of deception. Loki also claims kinship with a host of other trickster figures from world mythology and fiction, suggesting he is really one archetype wearing many masks. This connects him to a broader multiverse of trickster gods within the show's mythology-themed stories. Voiced by Alan Cumming. Notable quotes: "My victory is complete!" | "It is what the old laws demand." | "There are no old laws."
quotes: "My victory is complete!"
"It is what the old laws demand."
"There are no old laws."

title: Monkey paw seller
text: Monkey paw seller is A minor vendor character who sells a cursed monkey paw to Homer in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The monkey paw seller is a merchant hailing from Marrakesh, Morocco, best known for his brief but memorable appearance in one of Homer's nightmarish fantasies. He deals in mysterious, potentially dangerous items, most notably the titular monkey paw, and dutifully warns customers of the misfortune it may bring before selling it anyway. Beyond his mystical wares, he oddly claims a political past, having once served as president of Algeria. In a separate, non-Treehouse-of-Horror continuity, he also plays a small but pivotal role by providing Homer and Barney Gumble with a gadget called the Placefinder 9000 to help them locate a buried stash of beer in ancient Egypt. He's a quirky, background character who blends the exotic and the absurd, fitting into the show's love of surreal one-off side characters. His stall's exact location becomes a point of comic confusion for Homer when Marge asks about the paw's origin. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mr. Lacoste
text: Mr. Lacoste is A snooty French waiter at Springfield's upscale restaurant, the Gilded Truffle, who appears in a memorable episode involving Freddy Quimby. Mr. Lacoste is a proud, easily-offended French waiter known for his exaggerated accent and pretentious demeanor. He becomes central to a courtroom farce after falsely accusing Freddy Quimby of assault when he actually just clumsily knocked himself out in a kitchen while refusing to repeat the word 'chowder.' His insistence that he is not a bumbling, Clouseau-like figure is immediately undercut when he stumbles and falls out a window into a passing truck full of rat traps, providing one of the show's classic slapstick moments. Despite this humiliating incident, he continues working as a waiter at various fancy restaurants throughout Springfield. His name humorously echoes the real-world Lacoste apparel brand, though the show never draws direct attention to this connection. He's a minor but memorable recurring background character who pops up in numerous episodes. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mr. McGreg
text: Mr. McGreg is A former patient of Dr. Nick Riviera who appears briefly in the Simpsons universe. Mr. McGreg is a minor, oddball character notable for a bizarre physical mix-up: he has a leg where an arm should be and an arm where a leg should be. He is a former patient of the incompetent Dr. Nick Riviera, who treats his strange condition with total nonchalance, as though it were perfectly normal. Their interaction plays into the show's running gag about Dr. Nick's questionable medical skills and lack of concern for his patients' bizarre outcomes. Mr. McGreg is a background curiosity rather than a developed character, appearing mainly for a quick visual joke. He later shows up in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, tied to the Cirque du Springfield content. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: King Mitothin
text: King Mitothin is A former king of the noncanon fantasy realm Springfieldia, appearing only as a statue in "The Serfsons". King Mitothin is a minor, noncanon figure from the medieval-fantasy parody episode "The Serfsons." He is never seen alive, existing only as a commemorative statue erected in his honor within the kingdom of Springfieldia. His statue plays a small but practical role during a castle battle, serving as cover for townspeople trying to avoid the fighting. Beyond this, nothing is known of his reign, personality, or fate, since he is deceased before the story begins. His grand epithet, "the Statue-Worthy," is the only hint at how he was regarded by his subjects. He also appears as a purchasable decoration in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Ray Magini
text: Ray Magini is A roofer who becomes an unlikely friend of Homer Simpson. Ray Magini is a roofer Homer strikes up a friendship with, though for most of their time together no one else seems able to see or believe in him, leading the town to think Homer has lost his mind. His name is a clever anagram for "imaginary," hinting at the mystery surrounding whether he's real. Eventually he reveals himself to the townspeople, proving he's an actual person and not just a figment of Homer's imagination, with various characters having comically specific reasons for having missed him earlier. Despite his profession, he doesn't seem particularly skilled or well-trained as a roofer, and he's also shown picking up odd work stacking shelves in hardware stores. He later resurfaces as part of an angry mob chasing Homer during the Trappuccino incident in the movie. Fittingly, he was designed to look and sound like his voice actor, Ray Romano. Voiced by Ray Romano.

title: Krav-Ma Golem
text: Krav-Ma Golem is A fictional character from the in-universe show "Ki-Ya Karate Monsters", referenced within The Simpsons. Krav-Ma Golem is a minor character existing within the show-within-a-show Ki-Ya Karate Monsters. As his name suggests, he is a Golem warrior who has trained in the martial art of Krav Maga, giving him a samurai-like fighting persona. He doesn't actually speak or appear as a fully active character in the main Simpsons continuity; instead, his presence is mostly limited to a wall sticker seen in Comic Book Guy's apartment, showing his popularity as a piece of merchandise among fans of the fictional franchise. Interestingly, his design closely mirrors that of another character called the Male Golem, suggesting a reused or homage-based aesthetic within the show's animation. Because he never speaks on screen, he is classified as a non-speaking character despite technically recurring across a couple of episodes.

title: Megan Matheson
text: Megan Matheson is A billionaire tech mogul and one-off antagonist who appears in a Springfield art-heist storyline. Megan Matheson is a wealthy tech tycoon introduced during an auction subplot involving a valuable painting called The Poetess. She outbids Mr. Burns to win the artwork, only for it to vanish before delivery, prompting an investigation by the detective Manacek. Confident and a bit flirtatious, she deflects suspicion by pointing fingers at Burns while also revealing she's in a committed relationship with a former Miss Denmark who researches malaria-curing mosquitoes. Beneath her polished exterior lies a criminal mastermind: she orchestrates the theft herself using twin stand-ins for security guards, motivated by a need to fund her girlfriend's scientific research. When cornered, she resorts to violence, pulling a gun on Manacek before being subdued. She later reappears briefly as an audience member at a podcast recording, showing she remains part of Springfield's social scene despite her criminal past. Voiced by Cecily Strong. Notable quotes: "If her girlfriend invented a cure for commitment, she should let him know."
quotes: "If her girlfriend invented a cure for commitment, she should let him know."

title: Dalai Lama
text: Dalai Lama is Real-world spiritual leader who appears as a minor character/guest figure in Springfield. The Dalai Lama appears in the show as a fictionalized version of the real Tibetan Buddhist spiritual leader. He is depicted as a bald, dignified figure who lends his presence to Springfield civic life, notably serving as a guest speaker at the Springfield Town Hall. His image has also popped up in unexpected places, such as a captcha screen on a fictional website, showing the show's tendency to insert real-world celebrities into mundane or absurd Springfield settings. He is mentioned in passing in other episodes before making an actual appearance. The character carries an air of calm authority befitting his real-life religious status, used mostly for background cultural flavor rather than deep characterization. He also appears in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out as part of the "Enlightened" character group. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mayan gods
text: Mayan gods is Non-canon deities from ancient Mayan civilization who appear in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Mayan gods are a group of ancient deities depicted as bringing about the end of the world on the predicted date of the 13th Baktun in 2012. In their brief appearance, they are shown wreaking havoc across the globe, obliterating famous landmarks in a spectacular display of destruction. Their rampage spans multiple continents, striking symbolic structures like the Great Wall of China, Big Ben, and the Eiffel Tower, before turning their attention to American icons including Mount Rushmore and Springfield itself. They exist purely as a apocalyptic joke tied to the real-world 2012 doomsday prophecy associated with the Mayan calendar. Beyond their destructive cameo, the gods later resurfaced as collectible characters in a mobile game tie-in. They have no individualized personalities or dialogue, functioning instead as a faceless force of cataclysmic destruction for comedic effect.

title: Mixed Martial Medusa
text: Mixed Martial Medusa is A fictional monster character within the show's in-universe cartoon Ki-Ya Karate Monsters. Mixed Martial Medusa is a fictional character existing within the show-within-a-show Ki-Ya Karate Monsters, appearing as a monstrous parody figure rather than a member of the main Simpsons cast. She reimagines the mythological Medusa with green snake-like hair, blended with the modern combat sport of mixed martial arts, giving her a fierce, gladiatorial persona.
