As a non-speaking character, she conveys her identity purely through her design and fighting theme rather than dialogue. She briefly appeared in the animated series before being adapted into a collectible character for the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, tied to a Treehouse of Horror event. Her role is largely visual and thematic, serving as one of many bizarre monster-themed characters that populate the show's fictional cartoons and game tie-ins.

title: Lauren
text: Lauren is Former employee at Well + Good, a minor recurring Springfield character. Lauren is a young employee at the marijuana dispensary Well + Good, notable mainly for being hired for her looks rather than any particular skill. She's friendly and a bit ditzy, greeting Marge warmly and complimenting her hair despite wearing her own nametag upside down without noticing. Lauren helps talk Marge into staying at the company alongside her coworkers Desmond and Drederick Tatum. She's shown to enjoy the perks of working around marijuana, getting high and dancing at a company party. After the business shuts down following a fire and a change in local drug laws, she pops up in the background at a couple of Springfield podcast recordings, suggesting she's still around town even without her old job. Voiced by Chelsea Peretti.

title: Andrew Lloyd Webber
text: Andrew Lloyd Webber is Real-world composer of musical theater who appears as a guest character in Springfield. Andrew Lloyd Webber appears as a fictionalized version of the famous English musical theater composer. He helps out at Expressions, assisting Lisa and Elaine Stritch with making wallets one Friday morning. He later shows up at an auction at Gavelby's Auction House, bidding on a rare bottle of wine once owned by Napoleon Bonaparte, opening the bidding at a cool one million dollars. During this scene, Smithers jokes about him being an unusually straight wine collector, and he chats with Robert Parker about funding his purchase through his music career earnings. He's also referenced by Sideshow Bob during a prison performance of Les Misérables, where Bob invokes his name in horror at a bad rendition of a famous song, only to be corrected that Webber didn't even write that particular musical and is still alive. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: the most surprisingly straight wine collector in the world. | Andrew Lloyd Webber must be spinning in his grave.
quotes: the most surprisingly straight wine collector in the world.
Andrew Lloyd Webber must be spinning in his grave.

title: Thelonious Monk
text: Thelonious Monk is Real-world jazz musician referenced in The Simpsons universe, tied to Lisa and Bleeding Gums Murphy. Thelonious Monk appears in the show as a nod to the real-life jazz legend rather than as a fully developed character. He's shown as a figure from jazz history, having once played alongside Bleeding Gums Murphy at Minton's Playhouse, cementing his place in the show's jazz mythology. His image also pops up as a bebop musician on a captcha screen that Lisa interacts with, tying him to her love of jazz. In a non-canon comic story, he takes on a more whimsical role, joining the Jazz Squad to help Mayor Quimby solve Springfield's problems with unruly dogs by calming them with his piano playing. Overall, he functions as a background homage to real jazz history within the Simpsons universe rather than a recurring personality.

title: Lyle McCarthy
text: Lyle McCarthy is Celebrity fitness trainer hired to get Homer in shape for the Everyman film. Lyle McCarthy is a high-profile personal trainer known for whipping celebrities into shape. He's brought in to transform Homer's physique for his role as Everyman, putting him through an intense diet and exercise regimen that actually works. Despite his professionalism, Lyle has a flighty, in-demand quality, frequently abandoning clients mid-project to move on to bigger names. His dramatic rooftop exit, gliding away on a jacket-parachute, highlights his flair for theatrical showmanship. Once he leaves, his clients like Homer tend to backslide immediately, underscoring how much his personal attention mattered. Lyle's client list name-drops real Hollywood stars, cementing his status as an elite, sought-after trainer to the famous. Voiced by Seth Rogen.

title: Maurice
text: Maurice is A donkey owned by César and Ugolín, the French family who host Bart during his exchange trip in "The Crepes of Wrath". Maurice is a black donkey belonging to the French winemakers César and Ugolín. He appears briefly during Bart's foreign exchange storyline, serving as a small but pointed symbol of how poorly Bart is treated by his hosts. Notably, Maurice is given more comfort than Bart, sleeping on a bed of hay while the boy is forced to sleep on a bare floor. He is a non-speaking animal character with no real personality traits beyond this contrast, existing mainly as a background detail in the episode. Maurice has since made minor non-canon appearances in comics and mobile games tied to the franchise.

title: Newshound
text: Newshound is A dog living at the Channel 6 News studios, appearing as a minor recurring character. Newshound is exactly what his name suggests: a canine mascot tied to the Channel 6 newsroom. He's notable for his distinctive lazy eye, which gives him a quirky, off-kilter appearance. Despite being a non-speaking animal character, he's treated as a legitimate member of the station's staff, having supposedly earned an impressive haul of Emmy Awards over the years. His award record is played for absurdist humor, since he's just a dog wandering the studio. In the mobile game Tapped Out, he becomes part of a job assignment where Arnie Pye takes him for a walk, reinforcing his status as a beloved station pet rather than any kind of anchor or reporter.

title: Ludacris (character)
text: Ludacris (character) is Real-world rapper who appeared as himself in an in-universe educational dental film watched by Lisa. Ludacris appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, starring in a cheesy educational dental hygiene film called Menace Tooth Society. In it, he plays a toothpaste tube character named Luda-Crest who battles various dental ailments like tooth decay, gum disease, and plaque with the help of a toothbrush and floss. The film is paired with a rap song meant to make dental care fun and memorable for kids. A running joke is that the film was only meant to be shown once, in Canada, but the Springfield Dental Complex used it without his permission, poking fun at licensing shortcuts and cheap local businesses. His appearance is a brief celebrity cameo rather than a recurring storyline, existing mainly as background media consumed by Lisa during a dentist visit. Voiced by Ludacris.

title: Veronica Lodge
text: Veronica Lodge is A character from Archie Comics who appears as a crossover reference in The Simpsons. Veronica Lodge is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover figure borrowed from the Archie Comics universe. Within the show, her presence is limited to a background appearance, notably featured on the cover of a parody comic titled Itchy and Veronica. She has no direct interactions or storyline within Springfield itself, functioning purely as an easter-egg reference for fans familiar with Archie Comics. Her inclusion ties into the show's history of referencing other comic and pop culture franchises. She also appears connected to a broader crossover event involving the villain Plasmo, who found himself in the Archie Comics universe after fleeing the All-Creation Legion of Villainy. Overall, Veronica serves as a nod to outside media rather than a developed character in the Simpsons' own continuity.

title: Leprechaun
text: Leprechaun is A recurring minor supernatural character, an Irish faerie who appears sporadically throughout the series. The Leprechaun is a mischievous, solitary faerie tied to Irish folklore, complete with the classic pot of gold and Saint Patrick's Day associations. He pops up in odd, unconnected moments across Springfield rather than having one consistent storyline, at times acting as a bad influence by serving as Ralph Wiggum's imaginary friend who urges him toward destructive behavior. He's shown participating in a St. Patrick's Day musical number, marching in a parade, attacking Homer and Bart, and even brawling with a rival orange-haired Northern Irish version of himself. He also holds a spot on the bowling team known as the Are They Reals. In non-canon material, he's depicted marrying a Gypsy character in a wedding officiated by Yoda, and in the comics he schemes against Ralph by posing as a kid seeking a role model, only for his plans to fall apart. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Mathemagician
text: Mathemagician is A minor recurring character who performs mathematically-themed magic tricks at children's birthday parties. The Mathemagician is a novelty entertainer hired to perform math-based magic tricks for kids' parties, notably appearing at Martin's birthday celebration. Despite his flashy showman persona and confident presentation, he secretly struggles with basic division, undercutting his supposed mathematical mastery. His visual design is a nod to Bill Gates, giving him a nerdy tech-mogul look paired with a carnival performer's flair. Though his screen time is brief, he's become a small piece of Simpsons trivia due to his oddly specific profession and his hidden ineptitude at the very subject he performs tricks about. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Now, prepare to marvel at the mysteries of the universe as I make this remainder disappear.
quotes: Now, prepare to marvel at the mysteries of the universe as I make this remainder disappear.

title: Donkey Kong
text: Donkey Kong is Crossover video game character (based on Nintendo's Donkey Kong) who appears in various non-canon and background cameos throughout the show. Donkey Kong is a barrel-throwing gorilla imported from the world of Nintendo who pops up repeatedly as a background or cameo character in Springfield. He's one of the video game characters who tempts Bart into stealing a game, and he's later shown as a washed-up arcade attraction who proves he's still relevant by hurling a barrel at a heckling patron. He appears alongside Mario in multiple gags, usually recreating his classic barrel-throwing shtick from the original arcade game, and even gets referenced as a metaphor for persistence in unrelated storylines like Grampa's romantic history. In a non-canon appearance in The Simpsons Game, he takes on a villainous role by kidnapping Professor Frink, forcing Bart and Lisa to chase him through Mario-style pipes before he's defeated in a fight parodying the Terminator films. Overall, he functions less as a developed character and more as a recurring pop-culture cameo and running gag tied to classic video game references. Voiced by Harry Shearer, Hank Azaria.

title: John Lennon
text: John Lennon is Real-world musician and Beatles member who appears as a character in various Simpsons episodes. John Lennon is depicted in the show as the famous co-founder of The Beatles, appearing in flashbacks, dream sequences, and wax museum exhibits across Springfield lore. He's shown having crossed paths with Krusty the Clown in the 1960s and even co-hosting Krusty's show with his wife Yoko Ono. The show plays on his real-life assassination, noting he's the only Beatle who never got to voice himself on the series since he died years before it aired. Various non-canon and alternate-continuity stories reimagine his history, including a comic strip where Homer and Abe are mistaken for the band. In a Treehouse of Horror segment, he appears riding the Yellow Submarine as part of a surreal, undead spectacle. Overall, he functions less as a recurring personality and more as a pop-culture reference point tied to Beatles nostalgia and parody. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: All we are saying...is let's eat some brains!
quotes: All we are saying...is let's eat some brains!

title: Isaac Newton
text: Isaac Newton is Real-world historical physicist who appears as a recurring reference/cameo character in The Simpsons. This version of Isaac Newton is a fictionalized depiction of the famous real-world physicist and mathematician, used mostly for comedic cameos rather than as a fleshed-out character. He first shows up in one of Homer's dreams, standing in for a guardian angel, though Homer fails to recognize him and he morphs into Colonel Klink instead. In another gag, Professor Frink's malfunctioning time machine only manages to bring back Newton's disembodied leg, which chases Frink around kicking him. He's also referenced by Lisa as an example of a smart person historically bullied, alongside Galileo, and turns up as a nude character in a fictional British romcom, a smashed bust in Frink's lab, and in various background pictures celebrating scientists and left-handed people. Overall, he functions as a recurring visual and verbal joke tied to genius, science, and historical trivia rather than a character with his own arc. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Noah (Bible)
text: Noah (Bible) is Biblical figure referenced and parodied within The Simpsons, portrayed by various characters in in-universe media. Noah is the ark-building figure from the Bible who appears in several parodies and reenactments throughout the show rather than as a consistent character. He's most memorably portrayed by Troy McClure in a movie-within-the-show, where he constantly questions God's bizarre instructions, including a requirement to gather stink beetles for the ark. Homer later takes on the role of Noah during a Super Bowl halftime show retelling of the flood story. Barney also gets involved with the character, awkwardly auditioning for a stage role as Noah despite the character not even being in the production, only to later appear as Noah anyway. In a non-canon storybook version told by Bart, Noah is drawn to look exactly like Ned Flanders, poking fun at the town's resident religious figure. Across these appearances, Noah functions less as a defined personality and more as a vehicle for satirizing biblical stories and religious media adaptations. Voiced by Phil Hartman, Dan Castellaneta.

title: Pria Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Pria Nahasapeemapetilon is One of the octuplet children of Apu and Manjula Nahasapeemapetilon. Pria is one of the eight babies born to Apu and Manjula after Manjula's use of fertility drugs led to an unexpectedly large family. As an infant, she has no distinct personality traits explored beyond being one of the octuplets, but her existence drives a memorable storyline about the challenges of sudden, overwhelming parenthood. Unable to cope with raising eight children at once, her parents temporarily placed her and her siblings in a zoo exhibit called 'Octopia,' turning the babies into an unwitting tourist attraction. This situation upset Apu and Manjula, prompting Apu and Homer to rescue the children from the zoo. Since her introduction, Pria has continued to appear as part of the octuplet group in numerous background and crowd appearances across many seasons. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Leo (The Old Man and the Key)
keys: leo (the old man and the key)
text: Leo (The Old Man and the Key) is A minor recurring senior citizen character in Springfield. Leo is an elderly man briefly seen taking driving license lessons at the Springfield Community Center alongside his wife. He appears as a background senior character across several episodes without ever speaking, making him one of the show's many non-speaking extras. Little is known about his personality or background beyond his marital status and his attempt to renew his driving skills later in life. His recurring appearances suggest he's a regular fixture among Springfield's senior citizen community. Despite his lack of dialogue, he's been included in multiple episodes over the years, giving him a small but consistent presence in the show's expansive background cast.

title: Ravencrow Neversmiles
text: Ravencrow Neversmiles is Alter ego adopted by Lisa Simpson during a brief goth phase. Ravencrow Neversmiles is not a separate character but a persona Lisa Simpson invents while searching for a new sense of identity. She embraces a dark, brooding goth aesthetic complete with a suitably dramatic name to match. The identity is short-lived, existing mainly as an experiment in self-reinvention rather than a lasting personality shift. She later resurfaces briefly in a non-canon future vision shown in one of the show's holiday-themed flash-forwards. The character also appears as a collectible skin in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, further cementing her as a fun, minor side note in Lisa's ever-evolving search for who she is. Voiced by Yeardley Smith.

title: Walter Mondale
text: Walter Mondale is Real-world former U.S. Vice President referenced sporadically throughout the show. Walter Mondale is a real-life politician who appears in the Simpsons universe mostly as a background reference rather than an active character. He's tied to a newspaper headline that ran the day Lisa was born, and later a naval vessel bearing his name rescues the Simpson family during a diplomatic crisis in Australia. His likeness also crops up in odd places, like a portrait in a speakers' bureau and an animatronic figure at a theme park's Hall of Vice Presidents. He even appears as a ghostly figure in one of Lisa's nightmares, grouped with fellow unsuccessful Democratic presidential candidates. Overall, Mondale functions as a running historical/political easter egg rather than a fleshed-out character with personality traits of his own. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Garth Motherloving
text: Garth Motherloving is CEO of the Motherloving Sweets and Sugar Company, a recurring antagonist in Marge-focused sugar-industry plots. Garth Motherloving is a ruthless sugar tycoon who built his fortune by lacing nearly every product in Springfield with sugar, seemingly without concern for public health. He is unapologetically greedy and combative, mocking suggestions to reduce sugar content and even joking about renaming himself after Hitler rather than compromise. When challenged in court by Marge, he resorts to threats and bribery rather than admit wrongdoing, revealing a corrupt, win-at-all-costs mentality. Despite his defeat in the sugar-smuggling scheme, he remains a recurring figure tied to Springfield's food industry and later reappears at public events, showing he keeps his business interests active. He tends to be sarcastic and dismissive when confronted, using humor and menace interchangeably to get his way. Voiced by Ben Stiller, Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: I'm not up on the current slang, but do the kids still say, get the hell out of my office? | That'll boost sales!
quotes: I'm not up on the current slang, but do the kids still say, get the hell out of my office?
That'll boost sales!

title: Spike Lee
text: Spike Lee is Real-life film director who appears as a fictionalized cameo character in various Simpsons episodes. Spike Lee shows up mostly as a background or mentioned figure rather than a fully developed character in the show. He's imagined by Bart as a panelist on a futuristic version of Match Game alongside other celebrities, and his name pops up in throwaway gags, like a video store's adult section or a Toronto Raptors comparison made by Krusty. The show also nods to his real-world cultural significance, tying him to the late-1980s rise of Afrocentric media influence and his film Do the Right Thing. He's noted as someone Ned Flanders would consider one of the "laudable lefties." In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he meets a grim fate by being sent into the sun to be destroyed. Overall, he functions as a celebrity cameo used for quick references and satire rather than a recurring storyline character.

title: Male jockey 1
text: Male jockey 1 is An unnamed jockey from Jockey Town who appears in a minor role during Homer's horse-racing storyline. This character is one of the many secretive jockeys who inhabit the hidden community known as Jockey Town. He first meets Homer at the racetrack, skeptically questioning whether Homer's mule, Duncan, is fit to compete. He and his fellow jockey Bill mock Duncan's flashy makeover into 'Furious D,' showing a teasing, insecure streak common among the jockeys. Later, he plays a key role in luring Homer into the jockeys' secret underground world, revealing the bitter truth that jockeys are social outcasts rather than the glamorous figures of legend. He participates in the group musical number demanding that Duncan lose an upcoming race, then helps forcibly remove Homer from their hideout. Despite kicking Homer out, he sneaks back to warn him that the threat was serious, hinting at a slightly more conflicted or sympathetic side beneath his gruff jockey persona. Visually, he is notable for changing hair color and outfit between scenes, a small continuity quirk fans have noted. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: He told Homer that the stories of jockeys owning car dealerships and marrying beauty queens was all a lie as no woman would want them because they're freaks.
quotes: He told Homer that the stories of jockeys owning car dealerships and marrying beauty queens was all a lie as no woman would want them because they're freaks.

title: Golda Meir
text: Golda Meir is Real-world Israeli politician who appears as a character in afterlife/dream sequences and a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment. Golda Meir appears in the show as a representation of the real former Israeli Prime Minister, showing up in depictions of Jewish Heaven alongside other historical and fictional deceased figures. She is a non-speaking character, appearing mostly in brief cameo-like scenes rather than having an active role in the plot. In one dream sequence she is seen conversing with Hyman Krustofsky, tying her into the show's recurring afterlife imagery. She also appears as a recognizable historical face used in a dictator-identification captcha on a parody tech website. In a non-canon Halloween segment, she takes on a more active, comedic role, attacking Homer with a Star of David-shaped weapon that humorously references her Jewish identity. Overall she functions as a cameo/reference character rather than a fully developed personality within the show.

title: Lisa the Conjuror
text: Lisa the Conjuror is Lisa Simpson's superhero alter-ego in the non-canon Bongo comics. Lisa the Conjuror is a comic-exclusive persona adopted by Lisa Simpson after she discovers Bartman's secret identity and steps in to help fight crime while Bart is injured. Wielding mysterious psychic powers tied to a magic crystal ball, she teams up with her baby sister Maggie, who becomes the sidekick known as the Great Maggeena. Together they patrol Springfield, battling the supervillain Canker and his henchmen, and ultimately help uncover that Lenny Leonard is the mastermind behind the villain's schemes. The character shows Lisa's cleverness and resourcefulness, as she and Maggeena use quick thinking (like jamming giant novelty teeth with a rattle) to escape a deadly trap. She embodies a lighthearted, non-canon superhero parody within the Bartman comic storyline, blending Lisa's intelligence with whimsical psychic-themed heroics.

title: Roger Meyers, Sr.
text: Roger Meyers, Sr. is Founder of Itchy & Scratchy Studios, father of Roger Meyers, Jr., and creator of The Itchy & Scratchy Show cartoons. Roger Meyers, Sr. is the late founder of the animation studio behind The Itchy & Scratchy Show, having produced the first Itchy cartoon, Steamboat Itchy, back in 1928. His legacy is complicated by a controversial propaganda-style film, Nazi Supermen Are Our Superiors, which drew public criticism, though he also produced more artistic musical works like Scratchtasia and Pinitchio. After his death, his son Roger Meyers, Jr. inherited control of the studio. A major twist to his legacy is the revelation that he never actually created Itchy, but stole the character from another animator, Chester J. Lampwick. He's essentially a satirical stand-in for Walt Disney, right down to the rumors of antisemitism reflected in his fictional propaganda cartoon. Meyers appears only in flashback or historical context, as he is deceased for the entirety of the show's present-day storyline.

title: H. P. Lovecraft
text: H. P. Lovecraft is Non-canon real-world author character appearing briefly in a Treehouse of Horror segment. H. P. Lovecraft appears as a non-canon, non-speaking cameo based on the real-life horror author of the same name. He is depicted casually sharing coffee with the fictional cosmic entity Cthulhu, a nod to Lovecraft's own literary creation. His appearance is brief, occurring only in the opening sequence of a Treehouse of Horror episode, and he has no dialogue or developed personality shown on screen. He later appears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. His role is essentially a quick homage to horror fiction rather than a fleshed-out Simpsons character. As a real-world figure inserted into the show's Halloween tradition, he exists purely as an Easter egg for fans of classic horror literature.

title: DJ Kwanzaa
text: DJ Kwanzaa is Minor recurring character, a member of the Rolling 80 gang who appears in the episode "Angry Dad: The Movie". DJ Kwanzaa is a bald member of the Rolling 80 crew who has a brief but memorable encounter with Homer and Marge. He rolls up in his car after spotting the couple tampering with the Watts Towers, ready to confront them. His attitude shifts once he recognizes Homer as the voice behind Angry Dad, showing a mix of street toughness and genuine fan excitement. He's surprised Homer isn't off celebrating at the Oscars given his fame, and even coins the phrase that Homer's been "Oscar blocked." Ultimately he proves helpful rather than threatening, offering the pair a ride to the awards ceremony. He's a one-off character used mainly for a comedic cameo tied to Homer's brief brush with animated stardom. Voiced by J. B. Smoove. Notable quotes: he has been Oscar blocked
quotes: he has been Oscar blocked

title: Jack Nicholson
text: Jack Nicholson is Real-life celebrity caricature appearing as a member of the Stonecutters world council and The Ancient Mystic Society of No Homers. Jack Nicholson appears in the show as a fictionalized version of the famous actor and filmmaker, tied into Springfield's secretive fraternal organizations. He's referenced as a benchmark of skill when Homer struggles at mini-golf, implying his legendary status even in trivial pursuits. When Homer becomes the Stonecutters' chosen one and starts doing good deeds, Jack turns against him, wanting him dead, showing a darker, antagonistic side tied to his real-world reputation for intense roles. A lookalike of his also shows up among other celebrity impersonators singing in a group number. The character leans on his real-life fame, particularly his iconic role in a horror film, which the show references and parodies. Homer's confusion between him and a famous golfer adds a comedic layer to his portrayal. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Ms. Mancuso-Gluckman
text: Ms. Mancuso-Gluckman is A grief counselor at Discount Grief Counselor who has counseled members of the Simpson family. Ms. Mancuso-Gluckman is a professional grief counselor who works at a low-budget practice called Discount Grief Counselor. In her canon appearance, she calmly listens as Homer derails a session meant to help him and Marge, instead ranting about destination weddings. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, she attempts to comfort a grieving Lisa after several of her friends die, offering to be her best friend. Her role is largely that of a background professional figure used for comedic effect, absorbing the family's overblown emotional dramas. Ironically, her attempt at kindness in the Halloween special leads to her own sudden and absurd death, a classic dark-comedy twist typical of the Treehouse of Horror episodes. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Mack
text: Mack is One of three mascots for the Zip Boys, a Springfield company advertised on signs and billboards. Mack is a background advertising mascot in Springfield, appearing as one third of the Zip Boys trio alongside Joe and Manny. He exists mostly as a static image on signs and billboards rather than as an active character, and he never speaks throughout his appearances. His most notable moment comes in a non-canon Halloween segment, where he and his fellow mascots are brought to life by a strange ionic disturbance and rampage through the town as giant, animate figures with oversized heads. The chaos only ends once the townspeople stop paying attention to the mascots, draining their power and causing them to collapse. Beyond that horror-themed cameo, Mack's image simply turns up in the background of unrelated storylines, such as on a church sponsorship sign and a roadside billboard. He is essentially a visual parody of a real-world auto parts mascot rather than a fleshed-out personality.

title: Ninja from the Black Lagoon
text: Ninja from the Black Lagoon is A fictional monster character from the in-universe show "Ki-Ya Karate Monsters", referenced in The Simpsons. Ninja from the Black Lagoon is a fictional character that exists within the show-within-a-show Ki-Ya Karate Monsters, watched by characters in The Simpsons universe. He is designed as a mashup of two classic monster archetypes, combining the aquatic menace of the Creature from the Black Lagoon with the stealthy skills of a ninja. He doesn't speak or interact directly with the main cast, instead appearing as a piece of background merchandise, specifically a wall sticker in Comic Book Guy's apartment, which fits his nerdy collector persona. His presence is mostly a nod to pop culture parody rather than a driver of plot. He later appeared in mobile game merchandise for The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Overall, he functions as a minor easter-egg style character rather than a fully realized personality.

title: Lenore
text: Lenore is Deceased wife of the narrator in Edgar Allan Poe's "The Raven", referenced in a Treehouse of Horror segment. Lenore is a non-canon character adapted from Edgar Allan Poe's poem "The Raven," appearing in the Simpsons' Halloween anthology segment based on that work. She herself does not actively appear or speak, existing mainly as a memory that haunts her grieving husband, the poem's narrator. Her death drives the narrator into madness, a plot point that gets humorously reenacted when Homer imagines himself in the narrator's role. In that fantasy, Marge stands in for Lenore, tying the classic literary tragedy into the show's own family dynamic. Lenore's presence in the show is brief and symbolic, appearing only in a picture and later as a bust in a later Treehouse of Horror short. She has no dialogue and functions purely as a background figure tied to the horror-poetry parody.

title: Chico Marx
text: Chico Marx is Real-world comedian/actor (one of the Marx Brothers) who appears as a fictionalized character in Simpsons dream/fantasy sequences. Chico Marx is depicted as a version of the famous real-life comedian and member of the Marx Brothers, appearing in surreal or dream-like segments rather than as a regular Springfield resident. He's shown alongside his brothers Harpo and Groucho, maintaining the classic Marx Brothers dynamic of scheming and comedic misdirection. In one appearance, he takes charge of damage control after an incident involving Zeppo, insisting the group keep their story consistent. He's later seen enjoying a carefree afterlife in Jewish Heaven, dancing with Harpo to a live orchestra. Despite his limited screen time, he embodies the same quick-witted, slightly conniving persona associated with the real Chico Marx. His appearances tie into the show's frequent homages to classic Hollywood and comedy legends. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Los Souvenir Jacquitos
text: Los Souvenir Jacquitos is A recurring group of elderly Springfield residents who wear pop-culture-themed jackets. Los Souvenir Jacquitos are a clique of senior citizens identifiable by their matching souvenir jackets emblazoned with various pop-culture references. Led by their own designated leader, they appear as a tight-knit unit throughout several episodes, often engaging in reckless or comedic senior-citizen antics alongside Grampa Simpson. They've taken part in a dangerous death race, attended a Green Day concert, and shown up at civic meetings about Lake Springfield. Their misadventures have included a bizarre incident where their eyes fell out from a flower-based drug, and one member reportedly had a romantic entanglement with Mrs. Muntz. The group serves as a running background gag representing Springfield's eccentric elderly population, popping up in unexpected and often absurd situations across the show's run.

title: Sandy Koufax
text: Sandy Koufax is Real-world retired baseball pitcher referenced within the Simpsons universe. Sandy Koufax appears in the show as a real-world legend rather than an active character, mostly cropping up in conversation among Springfield residents. He's remembered for his famous refusal to pitch on Yom Kippur, a fact that other characters bring up when comparing sports performances or religious devotion. Comic Book Guy idolized him as a child, treasuring a signed baseball that became tied to a bittersweet memory involving his father. He's also honored on a Jewish Walk of Fame and included on a list of notable left-handed people. Koufax never actually speaks or physically appears as an active participant in any story; he exists purely as a legendary name invoked by other characters like Homer, Grampa, and Krusty.

title: Harold Mitchell
text: Harold Mitchell is A supporting character in the play "A Streetcar Named Desire" as adapted within the Simpsons universe. Harold "Mitch" Mitchell isn't a resident of Springfield at all, but rather a fictional character within a fictional play referenced in the show. He originates from Tennessee Williams' famous drama "A Streetcar Named Desire," and appears in the Simpsons universe as a role performed by Lionel Hutz in the local musical parody "Oh! Streetcar." This theatrical production, directed by the eccentric Llewellyn Sinclair, becomes a memorable episode plot involving Marge Simpson. Mitch also exists on the periphery of Springfield's pop culture as portrayed by Karl Malden in the 1951 film version, which gets screened for schoolchildren during a "Movie Day" at Springfield Elementary. As a character-within-a-character, Mitch himself has no independent personality traits in the show—his relevance comes from being a vehicle for jokes about community theater and film adaptations. Voiced by Phil Hartman. Notable quotes: Lionel Hutz, attorney at law. I'm filing a class-action suit against the director on behalf of everyone who was cut from the play. I also play Mitch.
quotes: Lionel Hutz, attorney at law. I'm filing a class-action suit against the director on behalf of everyone who was cut from the play. I also play Mitch.

title: Little Miss Muffet
text: Little Miss Muffet is Minor background figure based on the English nursery rhyme character, appearing as a decorative statue in the Simpsons universe. Little Miss Muffet is not a living character in the show but a static figure themed after the classic nursery rhyme. She appears as part of the whimsical decor at Storytown Village, standing near a spider prop at the park's entrance. Her figure has no dialogue or personality of her own, existing purely as background scenery. After the park's decline, her damaged effigy lingers at the entrance even after the location is repurposed into Praiseland. She's a small nod to classic children's rhymes woven into the show's satirical settings rather than a character with any narrative arc.

title: Jay Leno (character)
text: Jay Leno (character) is Real-life comedian and talk show host who appears as a recurring guest-starring celebrity in Springfield. Jay Leno appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, popping up in various contexts around Springfield rather than as a core member of the cast. He's shown hosting late-night television, booking acts like Krusty the Clown for his show, and even literally crashing into other characters' vehicles while making puns about his own name. The character leans heavily on Leno's real-world reputation as a car and vehicle enthusiast, which Bart references when comparing himself to Leno's love of collecting. His image also turns up as background décor in places like Springfield Sardi's and The Penny Loafer, reinforcing his status as an omnipresent celebrity figure in the show's universe. Leno is portrayed as quick with topical jokes, often riffing on current events such as political and environmental controversies. He's also included on a satirical list of notable left-leaning celebrities compiled by Ned Flanders. Overall, he functions as a running pop-culture cameo rather than a developed character with an ongoing storyline. Voiced by Jay Leno (Himself); Dan Castellaneta.

title: Mrs. Long
text: Mrs. Long is A minor recurring Springfield resident and acquaintance of Marge Simpson, married to a Power Plant employee. Mrs. Long is a background townsperson whose husband works at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant alongside Homer. She's most notable for her brief friendship with Marge, bonding over shared parenting duties and a company picnic. Like many of Springfield's minor citizens, she pops up at town gatherings and local hotspots, from Moe's Tavern to civic meetings about Mr. Burns' fine money. She's typically depicted as an unassuming mother blending into the crowd rather than driving any storylines herself. Her recurring presence at communal events highlights the tight-knit, everyone-knows-everyone nature of Springfield. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Jay Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Jay Nahasapeemapetilon is Apu Nahasapeemapetilon's nephew and Sanjay Nahasapeemapetilon's son; a Kwik-E-Mart clerk. Jamshed, later known as Jay, is a member of the extended Nahasapeemapetilon family who first appears as a child left to mind the Kwik-E-Mart. Even as a kid he shows a willingness to take drastic action, brandishing a shotgun to scare off troublemakers Jimbo, Dolph, and Kearney. As he grows older he becomes notable for aging more dramatically on screen than any other Simpsons character, going from toddler to young adult. After attending college, symbolized by his Wharton-branded sweater, he returns to Springfield with a more modern, millennial persona and a shortened, less ethnically marked name. He eventually takes over majority ownership of the Kwik-E-Mart from his father Sanjay, rebranding it into the trendier Quick & Fresh. His arc reflects generational change and assimilation within the Nahasapeemapetilon family business. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright; Utkarsh Ambudkar.

title: Peyton Manning (character)
text: Peyton Manning (character) is Real-life NFL quarterback who appears as himself in a Bart dream sequence and other guest spots. Peyton Manning is a real-world football player who crosses into Simpsons canon as a guest character, appearing alongside his brothers Eli and Cooper Manning. He first shows up in a dream Bart has, where the brothers share a warm moment tossing a football together, with Eli suggesting that sibling bonding means more than winning a Super Bowl. Homer later seeks him out for a second opinion on retirement after getting advice from Andrew Luck, showing Peyton's role as a trusted authority figure on football life. In non-canon material, he and Eli host a podcast where they interview Homer, extending his presence beyond the main show into spin-off media. He's also referenced visually, with his picture appearing on a wall at Springfield Elementary. Overall, Peyton serves as a lighthearted cameo tied to real NFL culture rather than a deeply characterized figure within the show's fictional world. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: "Perfect spiral" - Peyton Manning
quotes: "Perfect spiral" - Peyton Manning

title: Master sushi chef
text: Master sushi chef is Japanese chef at The Happy Sumo, the sushi restaurant frequented by the Simpsons. The master sushi chef is the top-tier cook at The Happy Sumo, renowned for being the only staff member skilled enough to safely prepare the poisonous fish fugu. He oversees his assistant Toshiro, whom he treats with condescension, enjoying moments where he can prove his superior technique and make Toshiro feel inferior. Despite his self-importance, his arrogance is somewhat justified given his genuine mastery of a dangerous culinary skill. He is also shown to be self-absorbed, prioritizing his personal romantic pursuits over his professional duties, notably choosing to continue a tryst with Edna Krabappel instead of returning to the kitchen when needed. This mix of vanity, skill, and comic unreliability makes him a minor but memorable figure tied to one of the show's more infamous food-related storylines involving Homer eating poisoned fugu. Voiced by Sab Shimono.

title: Moldy
text: Moldy is The oldest member of The Happy Little Elves, a fictional children's TV show group within The Simpsons universe. Moldy is a character within the show-within-a-show The Happy Little Elves, a program watched by the Simpson children. As the eldest of the elf group, he takes on a leadership role among his fellow elves. He is best known for his part in helping save Christmas, tying his appearances to holiday-themed episodes. Moldy is a minor, background element used mostly for background humor rather than a fully developed personality. He appears briefly across a couple of episodes and a video game, functioning as part of the show's meta-commentary on children's television. Despite his small role, he has enough presence to be considered a recurring character in the Simpsons universe. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Alfred E. Neuman
text: Alfred E. Neuman is Mascot for Mad magazine appearing as a crossover reference within The Simpsons universe. Alfred E. Neuman is the iconic, gap-toothed mascot of Mad magazine, brought into the Simpsons universe as a recurring visual gag and crossover reference. His image appears in various forms throughout the show, including on magazine covers, as a tattoo, and even as a giant decoration atop the Mad Magazine Headquarters building. He doesn't have much of a personal storyline, functioning more as an easter egg for fans familiar with Mad magazine's branding. In one notable bit, Otto uses an Alfred E. Neuman model kit as a cover story to buy glue for unrelated purposes, only to discard it afterward. The character's presence highlights the show's frequent nods to other media and pop culture icons rather than serving as a fully developed personality within Springfield. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Loch Ness Monster
text: Loch Ness Monster is A legendary creature from Loch Ness captured by Mr. Burns and later employed at his Las Vegas casino. The Loch Ness Monster, affectionately called Nessie, is a purple cryptid whose existence Mr. Burns sets out to prove for the sake of fame. After Professor Frink drains the loch, Burns, Homer, and Willie track down the creature, leading to an off-screen skirmish in which Nessie reportedly swallows Burns whole before he somehow subdues her. Rather than being hostile, Nessie turns out to be surprisingly affectionate, showing fondness toward both Homer and Burns. She initially enjoys being exhibited as a mysterious wonder of the world, though the flashing photography during her display upsets Burns enough to ruin the event. Ultimately, Burns finds her a more fitting role as a doorman at one of his Las Vegas casinos. She's a non-speaking character, existing more as a novelty and running gag about cryptid folklore than as a dialogue-driven figure.

title: Howie Long (character)
text: Howie Long (character) is Real-world NFL on FOX analyst who appears in Simpsons promotional shorts. Howie Long appears as a fictionalized version of himself, playing his real-life role as an NFL on FOX analyst. In a promotional short, he interacts with Homer and Bart during a broadcast, showing a good-natured willingness to let Bart send a shoutout to his family and friends on air. When Bart's greeting turns into a joke at someone else's expense, prompting Homer to strangle him, Howie finds the chaos amusing rather than off-putting. He later shows up again as part of a Fox Sports panel interviewing the Simpson family for a Super Bowl promo. His role is brief and lighthearted, existing mainly to bridge the show's world with real NFL on FOX programming. Voiced by Himself.

title: Lion-O
text: Lion-O is A crossover character referenced as a costume worn by Comic Book Guy, not an original Simpsons character. Lion-O is not actually a native character of The Simpsons universe, but rather the protagonist of the ThunderCats franchise who appears in the show only as a costume reference. Comic Book Guy dons a Lion-O costume for Halloween in 1986, showcasing his fandom for pop culture properties beyond comics. The character has no dialogue or personality development within the Simpsons continuity itself, existing purely as a nod to ThunderCats fans and a way to highlight Comic Book Guy's nerdy interests. As a non-speaking crossover character, Lion-O serves as a background gag rather than a fleshed-out figure in the show's world.

title: Mayan Marge
text: Mayan Marge is Non-canon Mayan counterpart of Marge Simpson, wife of Mayan Homer. Mayan Marge is a non-canon alternate version of Marge Simpson, appearing as part of an ancient Mayan civilization in a Treehouse of Horror segment. She is married to Mayan Homer, who has been chosen as a sacrifice. Rather than accept this fate passively, she shows a cunning streak by manipulating a Mayan priest into becoming the sacrifice instead, saving her husband. This brief appearance highlights a craftier, more scheming side to the character compared to her mainstream counterpart. She later appeared as an unlockable costume/skin in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, reflecting the show's tendency to reuse Halloween-special designs in merchandise and games. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: David Letterman (character)
text: David Letterman (character) is Real-world talk show host who appears/is referenced in The Simpsons universe. David Letterman appears as a fictionalized version of himself, tied into the show's running gags about celebrity culture and media. He's referenced when Homer's exploits become fodder for late-night ridicule, most notably during Homer's infamous sex scandal. His late-night show pops up in the background of channel-surfing scenes, showing how deeply he's woven into the Simpsons' media landscape. He's also honored as a supposed liberal icon on one of Ned Flanders' lists, poking fun at the perception of late-night hosts. In non-canon material, he's portrayed as easily annoyed by unexpected celebrity intrusions, such as the Simpson family barging onto his set. He also becomes an unwitting punchline when Homer shouts his name for no clear reason, only to be casually greeted by Grampa as if they were old acquaintances. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Hi, David, I'm Grampa.
quotes: Hi, David, I'm Grampa.

title: M'nthster
text: M'nthster is Non-canon monster character, son of Cthulhu, appearing in The Simpsons universe. M'nthster is a tentacled monster creature who exists as the offspring of the Lovecraftian entity Cthulhu. He appears briefly in a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, where he interacts with Bart Simpson by scooping him up with his tentacles while Bart skateboards through Springfield. As a non-speaking character, he has no dialogue and is defined mostly by his monstrous design and eldritch heritage. He later became part of the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, categorized among the game's Eldritch Horrors. His role is minor and largely visual, serving as a nod to horror and cosmic monster tropes within the show's Halloween tradition.

title: Daisy McGunnan
text: Daisy McGunnan is A minor bounty hunter character in the Simpsons universe. Daisy McGunnan is depicted as one of several bounty hunters operating alongside characters like Ned Flanders, known for being more dangerous than her peers. She appears briefly in the show's canon, mentioned as an alternative to Ned when he considers quitting his bounty hunting duties. Her character is non-speaking in her canonical appearance, giving her an air of mystery and menace. In the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, she gets more development as part of the Breakout Bounty content. Her design and concept are inspired by the character Cherry Darling from the 2007 film Planet Terror, giving her a grindhouse, action-heroine aesthetic. Overall, she serves as a minor but memorable addition to the show's rotating cast of eccentric side characters.

title: Museum lady
text: Museum lady is Minor recurring background character who works as a cashier at the Springfield Natural History Museum. The Museum lady is a minor recurring figure best known for her job collecting donations at the Springfield Natural History Museum. She's a background presence who pops up in various civic and public settings around Springfield, suggesting she's just a regular townsperson who gets around. She served on the jury during Marge's shoplifting trial and attended a town hall meeting about how to spend Mr. Burns' settlement money. She's also been spotted at the mall, on television, and even waiting in line at the World Trade Center's observation deck during a family trip to New York. Her role is largely non-speaking or minor dialogue, existing mostly as one of Springfield's many recognizable extras. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Noah's mother
text: Noah's mother is Minor recurring character; mother of Noah, a classmate of Bart's friend group. Noah's mother is an intensely overbearing 'helicopter parent' who micromanages her son's life to an extreme degree. She drills Noah with rigid academic exercises, such as forcing him to recite state capitals in alphabetical order on command, which leaves him visibly frightened of her. Her parenting style is portrayed as controlling and anxiety-inducing rather than nurturing. She also has an unnamed daughter, suggesting her strict approach may extend to her whole household. In one encounter, she becomes irritated with Marge simply for giving her children milk and cookies, highlighting how her uptight nature clashes with more relaxed parenting styles. She appears mainly as a side character used to satirize overprotective parenting trends. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Mayor Quimby's body guards
text: Mayor Quimby's body guards is The security detail assigned to protect Mayor Quimby of Springfield. These are the anonymous, interchangeable bodyguards tasked with keeping Mayor Quimby safe from harm. Despite the seriousness of their duty, they're often depicted as comically negligent, getting distracted by trivial things like watching clouds while the mayor faces actual danger. Their incompetence has occasionally led to them being sacked, with Homer once stepping in as a temporary replacement. In one odd moment, one bodyguard is handed a baby by Quimby, who claims it isn't really his despite Cookie Kwan's insistence, and is told to raise it himself. The bodyguard's only reaction is to put sunglasses on the infant and smile, showing the same nonchalant, unbothered attitude that defines the group. They serve as recurring background muscle in Quimby-related storylines across many seasons. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Eartha Kitt (character)
text: Eartha Kitt (character) is Real-world singer/actress who appears as a celebrity character in The Simpsons, briefly married to Krusty. Eartha Kitt appears in the show as a fictionalized version of herself, drawing on her real-life fame as a singer, actress, and cabaret star. Her main claim to fame within the Simpsons universe is a bizarrely short-lived marriage to Krusty the Clown, which lasted only six hours before ending in her utter contempt for him. This past marriage becomes a plot device when Bart and Milhouse use footage of her scathing comments to try to sabotage Krusty's wedding to Princess Penelope. She's also referenced as one of the actresses considered a "true" Catwoman, tying her into the show's love of classic pop-culture trivia. Beyond her spoken appearance, her image turns up as background decor in at least one Springfield location, and she's briefly seen in an opening sequence gag. Overall she functions as a one-off celebrity cameo rather than a recurring presence, remembered mainly for the Krusty marriage joke. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: "cat-astrophe"
quotes: "cat-astrophe"

title: Sashi Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Sashi Nahasapeemapetilon is One of Apu and Manjula's octuplets, a minor recurring baby character in the Nahasapeemapetilon family. Sashi is one of the eight children born to Apu and Manjula after Manjula's fertility treatments unexpectedly produced octuplets. As a baby, she has no distinct personality traits explored individually, since she's typically portrayed as part of the collective octuplet group rather than as a standalone character. Her main claim to fame comes from the chaotic circumstances of her birth, which overwhelmed her parents and led to a memorable storyline. Unable to handle raising eight infants at once, Apu and Manjula temporarily housed the octuplets at the Springfield City Zoo, where they were put on public display as an attraction. This arrangement upset the family, prompting Apu and Homer to rescue the babies from the zoo. Since her introduction, Sashi has appeared as a background character across many later seasons, comics, and other Simpsons media. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Gheet Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Gheet Nahasapeemapetilon is Baby son of Apu and Manjula, one of the Nahasapeemapetilon octuplets. Gheet is one of the eight Nahasapeemapetilon babies born after Manjula took fertility drugs. Overwhelmed by raising eight infants at once, his parents Apu and Manjula were persuaded to place the octuplets on display at the Springfield City Zoo in a show called Octopia, where Gheet was cast as the villainous character known as The Baron. He is reportedly Manjula's favorite of the eight siblings, giving him a slightly special status among the octuplets. His notable misadventures include being accidentally left behind at Moe's Tavern by his parents. Despite being an infant with no spoken lines, he has made numerous background and cameo appearances throughout the show's later seasons, comics, and other Simpsons media. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Lenny Kravitz (character)
text: Lenny Kravitz (character) is Real-world musician who appears as a guest character at the Rolling Stones' Rock N' Roll Fantasy Camp. Lenny Kravitz appears as a fictionalized version of himself in the Simpsons universe, working as a mentor at a rock star fantasy camp. He runs a fashion-advice booth called the Thread Shed, offering guidance on stage attire to aspiring musicians like Apu. He's portrayed as good-natured but part of a group of rock stars who briefly turn hostile toward Homer after a chaotic on-stage incident at a charity concert. Despite the conflict, he's willing to make amends, apologizing to Homer and inviting him back to perform, showing a forgiving and easygoing personality. His character leans into the running gag of real musicians popping up in unusual, exaggerated cameo roles within the show. Voiced by Himself.

title: Joey Kramer (character)
text: Joey Kramer (character) is Real-life celebrity guest character; drummer of Aerosmith who appears in cameo roles at Moe's Tavern and elsewhere. Joey Kramer appears as himself, the real-world drummer of the rock band Aerosmith, making cameo appearances in Springfield. He first shows up performing with his bandmates at Moe's Tavern, bringing a bit of real celebrity spectacle to the local bar scene. He's also glimpsed among the crowd at a Grammy Awards party attended by the Be Sharps, tying him into one of the show's classic musical storylines. In a later appearance, he has an amusing exchange with Ned Flanders, mistaking him for another drummer associated with Aerosmith. As a real-world guest character, he doesn't have much personality development beyond his musician persona, serving mainly as a nod to Aerosmith fans and a source of celebrity cameo humor. Voiced by Joey Kramer.

title: Murderpuss
text: Murderpuss is A non-canon fighting robot entered into Robot Rumble by Reverend Timothy Lovejoy, Jr. and his daughter Jessica. Murderpuss is a robotic combatant built for the destruction-derby style contest Robot Rumble, owned and entered by Reverend Lovejoy and his daughter Jessica. Roughly the size and shape of a hot water heater, it moves on three wheels and is armed with eight boxing glove fists meant to batter opponents into submission. Despite its aggressive design and intimidating name, Murderpuss proves unsuccessful in combat, losing decisively when its remote control is destroyed by a rival machine. Its brief appearance ties it to the Lovejoy family's competitive side project rather than any ongoing storyline, making it a minor one-off gag robot in the Simpsons universe. It later resurfaces as a collectible robot decoration in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Lifeways editor
text: Lifeways editor is Editor of the Lifeways section of the Springfield Shopper newspaper. The Lifeways editor is a minor recurring figure at the Springfield Shopper who oversees the paper's lifestyle content. He's the one responsible for giving Homer a shot as a food critic, a decision that leads to plenty of chaos. He's shown to have a short temper and a sarcastic streak, unimpressed by bad ideas pitched to him. Beyond his newsroom duties, he's been seen joining an angry mob against Homer during the Springfield dome crisis, showing he's not above public outrage when the town turns on someone. He's also just an ordinary Springfield resident who turns up in crowd scenes, such as in the audience for a talent show. His personal life includes a failed marriage to a woman named Mimi. Voiced by Ed Asner. Notable quotes: This is a joke right? I mean this is the stupidest thing I've ever read.
quotes: This is a joke right? I mean this is the stupidest thing I've ever read.

title: 'N Sync (characters)
text: 'N Sync (characters) is Guest-starring boy band who appear in an episode featuring the Party Posse. 'N Sync is a real-life boy band who make a guest appearance in the Simpsons universe, portrayed as friendly rivals or supporters of the fictional group the Party Posse. They show up to praise the Party Posse's performance, bring them a gift basket, and quickly rush off because their outfits have become outdated. Later they take on a more heroic role, arriving aboard a naval vessel to try to stop a disgruntled sailor from blowing up the Mad Magazine building. Their attempt to defuse the crisis through song and dance ultimately fails, showing them to be well-meaning but not always effective. In a comedic twist ending, the other band members forcibly enlist J.C. Chasez into the Navy against his wishes, poking fun at his real-world public image.

title: Marguerite (Treehouse of Horror XXIV)
text: Marguerite (Treehouse of Horror XXIV) is A circus performer who briefly marries Moe Szyslak in a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment. Marguerite is a sideshow performer with the Burnsum and Bailey Circus, distinguished by having one blue eye and one pale brown eye, which she considers her own kind of 'freakishness.' She shows compassion by standing up for the other circus freaks and treating them with dignity despite the ringmaster's mistreatment. Her kindness extends to Moe Szyslak, whom she kisses and later agrees to marry after being manipulated by the jealous Strong Man, who wants her emerald ring and plots to kill Moe. Despite being caught in a scheme not of her own making, Marguerite proves sharp-eyed and protective, catching the Strong Man in the act of poisoning Moe's drink and intervening to stop him. She appears only in the non-canon Treehouse of Horror XXIV segment 'Freaks no Geeks' and later in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: McGriff the Crime Dog
text: McGriff the Crime Dog is Mascot for the Springfield Police Department, appearing as a hand puppet in a minor Marge Simpson scene. McGriff the Crime Dog is a minor, non-speaking character who exists as the mascot of the Springfield Police Department. He is depicted as a brown dog, most notably appearing in puppet form when Marge uses him to deflect a serious conversation with Lisa. The character is a clear parody of the real-world McGruff the Crime Dog, a well-known anti-crime mascot. Beyond his brief live-action-style cameo, McGriff has little personality of his own, functioning mainly as a background gag. He later resurfaces in the non-canon mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. A separate, unrelated parody dog mascot named Bite Back appears elsewhere in the show, but is explicitly not the same character as McGriff.

title: Valley Mercer
text: Valley Mercer is A background student at Springfield Elementary School, part of Lisa's second-grade class. Valley Mercer is a minor recurring background character who has appeared in numerous episodes since her debut in season seven. She is a second grader at Springfield Elementary and is typically recognizable by the single-pearl necklace she wears. Interestingly, in some of her earliest appearances she was drawn without this necklace and had blonde hair instead of her usual brown. She is a non-speaking character, existing mostly in crowd scenes and classroom shots rather than having any dialogue or major plot involvement. Her name remained a mystery to viewers for years until it was finally revealed in a book shown in the episode "Woo-Hoo Dunnit?". Despite her long-running presence on the show, little else is known about her personality or backstory.

title: Jack LaLanne (character)
text: Jack LaLanne (character) is Real-world celebrity guest character; fitness icon who appears in Springfield to perform a heroic rescue. Jack LaLanne appears as a real-life motivational speaker and nutrition expert who pops up during a crisis at the Springfield Retirement Castle. When the elderly residents are stranded on a sinking boat after Mr. Burns' yacht plows through it, LaLanne steps forward from the panicked crowd to take charge of the rescue. True to his no-nonsense fitness persona, he grips a rope in his teeth and dives into the water to tow the survivors to safety himself. Even when the boat breaks apart mid-rescue, he stays calm and determined, continuing to haul the front portion back to shore. His brief appearance plays on his real-world reputation for extraordinary physical feats and stamina well into old age. He also appears in a cameo during an opening sequence gag in a later episode. Voiced by Himself.

title: Bette Midler (character)
text: Bette Midler (character) is Celebrity guest character; real-life singer who appeared as herself performing with Krusty on his comeback special. Bette Midler appears as a fictionalized version of herself who gets roped into helping revive Krusty's career. She's first encountered by Bart and Lisa while she's out picking up litter along a roadside, an encounter that turns chaotic when Snake Jailbird tosses trash at her car and she retaliates by throwing it right back, sending the vehicle off the road. Despite this rocky introduction, she agrees to lend her star power to the Krusty Comeback Special, teaming up with Krusty for a heartfelt duet of 'Wind Beneath My Wings.' Beyond this main appearance, she mostly shows up as background material, her image or archive clips popping up on walls and in montages across the show's run, referencing her brief but memorable connection to Springfield. In one non-canon appearance, she even attends a glitzy movie premiere in Los Angeles. Her role is largely that of a celebrity cameo rather than a recurring personality with deep characterization. Voiced by Bette Midler.

title: Michelle Kwan (character)
text: Michelle Kwan (character) is Real-life figure skater who appears as a celebrity guest character in the Simpsons universe. Michelle Kwan appears as a fictionalized version of herself, a celebrity athlete who gets pulled into Springfield's chaotic sports-related storylines. She's shown signing up for Homer Simpson's ill-fated Showboating Academy, where Milhouse fanboys over her before being stunned that she can actually talk. Her competitive intensity is played for dark comedy when she violently retaliates against a judge for docking her score, turning the moment into a gruesome visual gag. She later gets swept into Homer's absurd Super Bowl halftime spectacle, working alongside other athletes to move a giant ark. In a non-canon Halloween appearance, she's depicted among an elite group of humans selected to evacuate to Mars, underscoring her status as a celebrated public figure even in apocalyptic scenarios. Voiced by Herself.

title: Rupert Murdoch (character)
text: Rupert Murdoch (character) is Real-life media mogul and owner of FOX, appearing as a recurring guest character in The Simpsons. Rupert Murdoch appears as an exaggerated, self-parodying version of the real media tycoon who owns FOX and numerous other companies. He's portrayed as ruthless and money-obsessed, whether he's serving time in prison for an unspecified crime, kicking ordinary Springfield residents out of his Super Bowl executive box, or gleefully inflating his own net worth with spray paint at Billionaire Camp. His greed is a running joke, exemplified by his gratitude when Bart's small pledge donation supposedly saves his entire network. He also has ties to Mr. Burns's circle of wealthy elites, showing up among Burns's rich associates on multiple occasions. Despite his villainous billionaire persona, he's treated as more of a comedic caricature of corporate excess than a genuine antagonist. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta (also voices himself in some appearances). Notable quotes: "billionaire tyrant" | "saved my network"
quotes: "billionaire tyrant"
"saved my network"

title: Sadruddin Mabaradad
text: Sadruddin Mabaradad is A minor recurring character who is a Hindu priest and yoga TV show host in the Simpsons universe. Sadruddin Mahbaradad is a gray-haired Hindu priest known primarily for hosting his own television program focused on yoga instruction. He appears briefly as part of the show's background pantheon of oddball TV personalities that populate Springfield's media landscape. A biography about him, with a slightly different spelling of his name, is referenced as existing within the show's universe, adding a layer of in-universe media to his character. The discrepancy between the spelling of his name and the title of his biography has led to speculation about which came first, the character or the book. He is a minor figure who has not appeared frequently, but his yoga program and religious occupation give him a distinct niche among Springfield's colorful side characters. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Scrooge McDuck
text: Scrooge McDuck is Crossover cameo character from Disney appearing in The Simpsons universe. Scrooge McDuck is a wealthy cartoon duck who crosses over from Disney's universe into the world of The Simpsons. He's referenced as an emblem of extreme wealth, notably in a magazine headline joking about his inability to swim in a pool of Bitcoin instead of his usual gold coins. He makes a background appearance at a holiday gathering on Mammon Street, fitting his association with money and affluent settings. In a non-canon musical sequence, he's grouped among other rich CEOs satirizing class disparity. Scrooge doesn't speak in any of his appearances, functioning purely as a visual cameo and cultural reference to wealth. His inclusion highlights the show's penchant for blending pop culture and corporate satire.

title: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon's mother
text: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon's mother is Apu Nahasapeemapetilon's unnamed mother, a minor recurring character connected to the Nahasapeemapetilon family. Apu's mother travels from her home country to Springfield to ensure her son follows through on an arranged marriage to Manjula. She is strict and determined about tradition, refusing to let Apu escape his obligation even after he schemes with Homer to fake a marriage to Marge in order to dodge the wedding. Her anger upon discovering the ruse ultimately pushes the situation forward until Apu genuinely falls for Manjula, allowing her to return home satisfied. She's shown to have a lighter, more communal side as well, participating in a Springfield world record attempt for the tallest human pyramid. Though she appears in only a couple of episodes, she plays a key role in the storyline that leads to Apu and Manjula's marriage. Voiced by Andrea Martin.

title: Marco
text: Marco is A waiter at The Gilded Truffle restaurant, a minor recurring character in the Simpsons universe. Marco is a fine-dining waiter who serves the Simpson family after Homer's lucky football bet nets them a fancy meal. He plays along good-naturedly with Homer's terrible jokes, feigning polite amusement even when the humor clearly falls flat. His restaurant offers absurdly upscale, over-the-top menu items that highlight the show's satire of high-end dining culture. Marco appears only briefly across a couple of episodes, functioning mainly as a background gag character rather than a fully developed personality. Despite his limited screen time, he leaves an impression through his deadpan delivery and exaggerated culinary descriptions. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Bring us your finest food you got stuffed with your second finest. | Excellent, sir... lobster stuffed with tacos.
quotes: Bring us your finest food you got stuffed with your second finest.
Excellent, sir... lobster stuffed with tacos.

title: Laa-Laa
text: Laa-Laa is A crossover character from the children's show Teletubbies who occasionally appears within the Simpsons universe. Laa-Laa is one of the four Teletubbies who occasionally pops up on television screens within the Simpsons' world, reflecting the show's fondness for parodying pop culture. She's a non-speaking character, existing mainly as background entertainment that the Simpson children watch, most notably Bart, Lisa, and Maggie. In one memorable and rather bizarre appearance, Laa-Laa joins the other Teletubbies in chasing Homer as part of an angry mob after a financial mishap, shooting lasers from her antenna. She and her fellow Teletubbies have also served as an opening act for a fictional pop star's concert. In a non-canon segment, the Simpson family cosplays as the Teletubbies, with Bart taking on the role of Laa-Laa. Overall, she functions as a running pop-culture gag rather than a fully developed character.

title: Molloy
text: Molloy is A cat burglar and elderly resident of Springfield Retirement Castle who appears as a criminal antagonist in one episode. Molloy is an aging but cunning thief who poses as a harmless senior citizen while secretly running an elaborate crime spree across Springfield. He steals a wide variety of items from townspeople, ranging from sentimental keepsakes to the world's largest cubic zirconia, showing his lack of discrimination in targets. After being caught and arrested, he proves his cleverness once again by orchestrating an elaborate hoax treasure hunt to distract the town, using the chaos to break out of prison. His backstory suggests a long, seasoned career as a burglar rather than a one-time criminal act. The character is a nod to classic gentleman-thief archetypes in cinema, specifically modeled after a famous jewel thief character from a 1960s film. Even after his escape, his legacy lingers, as he becomes a suspect again when one of his most famous stolen items resurfaces missing. Voiced by Sam Neill.

title: Mayo Clinic doctor
text: Mayo Clinic doctor is A minor recurring doctor at the Mayo Clinic who has treated Mr. Burns. This unnamed physician appears as a background figure representing the famous Mayo Clinic in the world of Springfield. He is best known for diagnosing Mr. Burns with an extraordinary collection of ailments, discovering that the elderly tycoon somehow has every known disease along with several never seen before, yet remains alive because the conditions offset one another. Beyond his medical duties, he has also served in civic roles, sitting on a jury for a notable court case involving Homer Simpson. He appears sporadically across several episodes, functioning as a stock authority figure rather than a fully developed character. His gray hair and clinical demeanor mark him as a typical background medical professional in the show's recurring cast of doctors. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Anoop Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Anoop Nahasapeemapetilon is One of Apu and Manjula's octuplet children, part of the Nahasapeemapetilon family. Anoop is one of the eight babies born to Apu and Manjula after she took fertility drugs to conceive. Overwhelmed by the demands of raising octuplets, his parents initially struggle before the babies end up displayed as a novelty attraction at the Springfield City Zoo. Anoop is given the nickname 'Animal' and specifically portrays a rocker character during the zoo's 'Octopia' show. He and his siblings are eventually rescued from the zoo exhibit by Apu and Homer. As an infant, Anoop has no distinct personality traits beyond his assigned zoo persona, and he mainly appears as part of the octuplet group in later episodes and media. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Robert E. Lee
text: Robert E. Lee is Historical figure referenced in The Simpsons, the Confederate General-in-Chief during the American Civil War. Robert E. Lee is not a regular character but a real-world historical figure whose legacy appears in passing references throughout the show. He is mentioned during a chaotic reenactment of the American Revolution that Homer accidentally becomes part of, where an actor invokes his name while arguing about handling a prisoner. His statue also appears in a framed picture of Market Street Park hanging in the Hibbert house. Lee's presence in the series is mostly symbolic, tying into small moments of historical parody rather than any direct interaction with the main cast. He also appears in the non-canon comic 'Springfield: Year Zero' and in a dialogue cameo within The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game.

title: Mary Lincoln
text: Mary Lincoln is Historical figure appearing in a Homer fantasy sequence; wife of Abraham Lincoln and First Lady of the United States. Mary Lincoln appears only within one of Homer's imagined historical daydreams, where she sits beside her husband at the theater on the night Homer saves him from John Wilkes Booth. She has no real personality development, functioning mainly as a background figure to support Lincoln's story rather than a character in her own right. She's later referenced again when Homer struggles to recall her name while looking through a set of First Lady-themed collectible pine cones. In a non-canon short, she appears in an alternate version of the assassination scene, reacting affectionately to a time-traveling Professor Frink after he thwarts Booth's attack. Interestingly, her likeness reportedly inspired the design of Mr. Burns' ancestor, Jeannette Burns. Overall she exists as a historical cameo rather than a fleshed-out Simpsons character.

title: Margarita
text: Margarita is A fictional soap opera character within the show-within-a-show 'Search for the Sun', watched by Simpsons characters. Margarita is a melodramatic character from the fictional soap opera Search for the Sun, which several Simpsons characters watch throughout the series. Her storylines are packed with classic soap opera tropes, including secret pregnancies, forbidden romances, and love triangles. She has an affair with a man named Jack despite being married to someone else, and separately becomes entangled with her boss Avery Devereaux after he fires her mid-flirtation. Her scenes are often interrupted by news broadcasts or other events, poking fun at the melodrama and unpredictability of daytime television. Beyond her in-show soap appearances, the actress portraying her is also glimpsed among the chaotic crowd at the Do What You Feel Festival, blurring the line between the fictional actress and her soap persona. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Millicent
text: Millicent is Horse trainer who runs The Grateful Gelding Stables, minor recurring character. Millicent is the gray-haired proprietor of a stable who sold Homer a pony for Lisa when he was trying to win back her affection. This purchase forced Homer to take a second job at the Kwik-E-Mart to cover the costs. She's a minor recurring figure who has popped up in the background of Springfield life, including once being spotted dining with Mr. Largo at Luigi's restaurant. Visually, the character was designed to resemble actress Katharine Hepburn. Millicent has also appeared in tie-in media such as The Simpsons: Tapped Out, where she has dialogue tied to a Wild West-themed content update. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Professor Lombardo
text: Professor Lombardo is Art teacher at Springfield Community College who taught Marge painting. Professor Lombardo is a quirky art instructor known for his oddly balanced critiques, always following a harsh remark with an unexpectedly kind one. He tends to praise almost any artwork, even mundane things like a janitor's painted sign, yet struggles to accept compliments directed at himself. His interactions with Marge suggest a subtle, bashful attraction, hinted at when he removes his sunglasses in her presence. Beyond the classroom, he has shown up in unexpected settings, including participating in an attempt to build the world's tallest human pyramid. Lombardo's blend of pretentious artspeak and backhanded encouragement makes him a memorably eccentric side character in Springfield's academic scene. Voiced by Jon Lovitz. Notable quotes: "The man was a fool!" | "But you must admire his strong convictions."
quotes: "The man was a fool!"
"But you must admire his strong convictions."

title: Minotaur
text: Minotaur is A mythological creature appearing in a Simpsons comic book dream sequence. The Minotaur is a figure from Greek mythology who appears in a Simpsons comic story rather than the animated series proper. He shows up within a dream that Milhouse has, in which Icarus and Daedalus are imprisoned by King Minos for keeping the secret of a labyrinth they built. The Minotaur is said to dwell within that very labyrinth, tying the dream narrative back to classic Greek myth. As a crossover character rooted in mythology rather than Springfield's usual cast, he serves as a fantastical element within Milhouse's imagination. He has no dialogue or personality traits described beyond his mythological role.

title: Ilsa Lund
text: Ilsa Lund is Parody character appearing in a Simpsons episode's fictional alternate ending of the film Casablanca, portrayed within the show's universe.
