Ilsa Lund is a parody version of the classic film character from Casablanca, appearing in a surreal alternate ending sequence within the show. In this bizarre reimagining, she dramatically parachutes down onto a piano, crushing Hitler in the process, before happily marrying Rick Blaine as a cheering crowd watches them leave a church. The character exists purely as a one-off homage to the famous movie, blending old Hollywood romance with typical Simpsons absurdity. She also appears in a separate episode as part of a school play poster, referencing Casablanca once again, this time with Lisa Simpson taking on the role of Ilsa in a student production. Ilsa herself has no independent personality traits beyond this cinematic homage, since she's essentially a device for movie-parody humor rather than a recurring character. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Menthol Moose
text: Menthol Moose is Fictional advertising mascot for Laramie Cigarettes, appearing in Springfield-related events. Menthol Moose is a cartoon moose used as the promotional face of Laramie Cigarettes within the show's world. He appears on parade floats and advertisements, often tied to civic events like the Springfield Founders Festival Parade. His design and purpose parody real-world tobacco mascots, poking fun at how cigarette companies used friendly, animal-based branding to appeal to audiences. Menthol Moose doesn't have a personality of his own since he's essentially a walking billboard, appearing in ads and posters rather than as a speaking character. His recurring presence in the background of various episodes serves as a satirical nod to advertising culture in Springfield.

title: Nasreen
text: Nasreen is Minor character; a stall owner at Towne Centre at Springfielde Glenne who briefly interacts with Ned and Lisa. Nasreen is a minor, one-off character who runs a small makeup stall in a shopping center. Her stall shares a rotating display with Ned Flanders' Leftorium Express, leading to an amusing mix-up when Ned spins the display around to reveal her business instead of his own. She comes across as pushy and short-tempered, attempting to push a cream product on Lisa Simpson. When Lisa turns down her sales pitch, Nasreen reacts with visible frustration and irritation rather than politeness. Despite the tense exchange, she simply asks to be spun back around, suggesting she quickly moves on rather than dwelling on the rejection. She has since made a small appearance in mobile game media tied to the show. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Chester Lampwick
text: Chester Lampwick is Original creator of the cartoon character Itchy, later a wealthy recurring guest character. Chester J. Lampwick is an elderly cartoonist who claims to have drawn the very first Itchy cartoon back in 1919, only to have the idea stolen from him by Roger Meyers Sr. without payment. He spent decades as a destitute bum nursing his grudge until Bart Simpson helped him sue the Itchy and Scratchy studio, winning an enormous settlement that made him instantly rich. Despite his newfound wealth, extravagant gold house, and rocket car, he remains stubborn and disinterested in further business ventures, brushing off pleas for help with blunt refusals. He also harbors a long-standing feud with Abe Simpson over a decades-old broken deal involving a chicken coop paint job and bad corn muffins. The character is a clear parody of real-life animator Ub Iwerks, whose creative contributions were similarly overshadowed and exploited by a more famous collaborator. Lampwick has made small later appearances, including in a mob scene and a human pyramid attempt. Voiced by Kirk Douglas. Notable quotes: I don't need anymore money. I'm not greedy, as long as I've got my health, my millions of dollars, my gold house, and my rocket car; I don't need anything else. | Not interested.
quotes: I don't need anymore money. I'm not greedy, as long as I've got my health, my millions of dollars, my gold house, and my rocket car; I don't need anything else.
Not interested.

title: Karl Malden
text: Karl Malden is Real-world actor referenced within the Simpsons universe, depicted via his film role in A Streetcar Named Desire. Karl Malden appears in the show as a representation of the real actor known for playing Mitch in A Streetcar Named Desire. His appearance comes up when Springfield Elementary's fourth grade class watches the film during a special Movie Day screening. The scene becomes a point of classroom debate, with young Martin Prince offering his own opinion on the film's romantic dynamics. Nelson Muntz, ever the class heckler, uses the moment to poke fun at Malden's on-screen appearance with a blunt nickname. This brief cameo highlights how the show often weaves real-world film and pop culture references into everyday Springfield life. Voiced by Maurice LaMarche. Notable quotes: "Potato Nose." - Nelson Muntz
quotes: "Potato Nose." - Nelson Muntz

title: Marilyn Monroe
text: Marilyn Monroe is Real-world actress referenced/appearing in minor cameos and mentions within the Simpsons universe. Marilyn Monroe appears in the Simpsons universe not as a regular character but as a real-world cultural reference woven into various gags and background details. She shows up in one of Homer's absurd daydreams, is the subject of a joking inquiry from John F. Kennedy and his brothers, and appears as a background picture in multiple unrelated scenes. She's also listed among notable left-leaning figures on one of Ned Flanders' lists, tying her into the show's habit of name-dropping historical celebrities. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, she is humorously linked to a fictional Simpsons character in a surreal aside. Overall, she functions as a nostalgic pop-culture Easter egg rather than a fleshed-out character with her own personality within the show.

title: Eli Manning (character)
text: Eli Manning (character) is Real-life NFL football player who appeared as himself in a dream sequence involving Bart. Eli Manning is a real-world football player who makes a cameo appearance in a dream Bart has, alongside his brothers Peyton and Cooper Manning. In the dream, he reflects on the simple joy of playing catch with his siblings, valuing it above even winning a Super Bowl. He shows a bit of sibling rivalry by teasingly calling Cooper a "squirt" despite Cooper being the eldest brother. He and Peyton then gang up on Cooper in a playful game of keep-away with a football. Outside of the show's canon, he also appears alongside Peyton interviewing Homer on a podcast in a non-canon special. His role is brief and lighthearted, existing mainly as a celebrity cameo rather than a developed character. Voiced by Himself. Notable quotes: Eli said that winning a Super Bowl didn't compare to just chucking a ball with his brother.
quotes: Eli said that winning a Super Bowl didn't compare to just chucking a ball with his brother.

title: James Madison
text: James Madison is Historical figure and 4th President of the United States, referenced and depicted in The Simpsons universe. James Madison is portrayed in the show as a minor historical reference rather than a fleshed-out character, standing in as a symbol of overlooked or 'little' historical figures. He's noted for his real-world claim to fame as the shortest U.S. president, a fun-fact detail the show includes for trivia value. His image appears in a book shown to Bart, tying him briefly into Bart's fascination with presidential history before Theodore Roosevelt takes over his interest. In one notable appearance, a look-alike actor playing Madison shows up in what Homer believes is a dream, urging him not to endorse Ted Nugent for office. This turns out to be a ruse orchestrated by the Simpson family rather than a supernatural or dream sequence, adding a comedic twist to his otherwise dignified historical persona. Overall, Madison functions as a running device for jokes about obscure history and political satire rather than a recurring personality. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Larry Newell
text: Larry Newell is A Shelbyvillian snowboarder who competes against Bart Simpson in a comic book story. Larry Newell is a young snowboarder from Springfield's rival town, Shelbyville, who appears in Bongo comic book stories rather than the animated series. He represents his town in a high-stakes downhill snowboarding race against Bart Simpson, with the outcome deciding which town wins the overall games. Despite his unassuming, dorky look, Larry proves to be a cunning and underhanded competitor, willing to cheat to secure victory. His defining moment comes when he sabotages Bart's equipment before the race, showing he's more concerned with winning than fair play. Ultimately his scheme backfires when Mr. Burns steps in to finish the race in Bart's place and defeats him anyway.

title: Mothra
text: Mothra is A giant moth movie-monster from Japanese kaiju films, appearing as a crossover creature in Simpsons fantasy/parody sequences. Mothra is a fictional kaiju borrowed from the Godzilla film franchise, appearing in The Simpsons purely as a background monster in exaggerated fantasy or parody sequences. She first shows up in Lisa's daydream about being exiled to a ridiculous 'Monster Island' after failing gym class, alongside other famous giant monsters. Later, she is depicted attacking the Simpson family's airplane as they leave Tokyo, teaming up with Godzilla, Rodan, and Gamera. She has no dialogue and no real personality of her own, functioning instead as a nod to classic Japanese monster movies. Guillermo del Toro even name-drops her as one of his favorite movie monsters in another appearance. Overall, Mothra exists as a fun homage to kaiju cinema rather than a fully developed character.

title: Sam Monroe
text: Sam Monroe is A girl who became Lisa Simpson's close friend after they met on the school bus. Sam Monroe is a young girl introduced as a kindred spirit to Lisa, someone who shares her love of music and her feeling of being different from those around her. She plays clarinet and generously lets Lisa borrow one of her saxophones, quickly bonding with her over their shared interests. Sam's family is portrayed as warm and different from the Simpsons, which draws Lisa in and eventually leads her into a web of lies as she tries to impress Sam and her father. Despite the deception spiraling out of control, Sam and her family prove forgiving once the truth comes out, showing a kind and understanding nature. She continues to pop up in Lisa's life afterward, appearing in a school play and attending the gifted program at Springfield STEM Academy, showing she remains a recurring presence in Lisa's social circle. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Karl Marx
text: Karl Marx is Real-world philosopher depicted as a minor recurring background character in The Simpsons. Karl Marx appears in the show as a fictionalized version of the real German philosopher famous for founding Marxism. He is a non-speaking character used mostly for brief visual gags and cameo appearances rather than any substantial storyline. In one instance he shows up in an illustration tied to a satirical political song, pictured embracing Barack Obama. In another appearance, set in the afterlife, he is shown dancing alongside Groucho Marx of the Marx Brothers at an orchestra performance in a heavenly setting for Jewish characters. His inclusion plays on the coincidental shared surname with the comedic Marx Brothers. Overall, he functions as a background reference joke tied to his real-world political legacy rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: Wally Kogen
text: Wally Kogen is A travel agent who arranges a trip to the Super Bowl for Homer Simpson and his friends. Wally Kogen is the none-too-savvy operator of Springfield Travel Agency, first crossing paths with Homer through a pyramid scheme and again at a tire shop. He's remarkably gullible, easily talked into buying unnecessary products and services, including a bogus 'Road King Package' from a tire salesman. His naivety extends to purchasing what turn out to be counterfeit Super Bowl tickets printed on crackers, which sets off the main plot involving Homer and his pals. Despite his poor judgment, he has some useful connections, notably being acquainted with country star Dolly Parton, who helps bail him and his friends out of a jailhouse jam. He later makes a brief appearance during a scene in The Simpsons Movie. Voiced by Fred Willard.

title: Father Mike
text: Father Mike is A minor recurring priest character in Springfield. Father Mike is a background priest character who appeared briefly in the Simpsons universe. He is best remembered for one striking moment where he advanced menacingly toward Bart, Milhouse, Nelson, and Ralph, suggesting an unexpectedly intimidating side for a clergyman. He is a non-speaking character, so his personality is conveyed entirely through action rather than dialogue. The character serves as a reference to Father Fitzgibbon from the film Going My Way. Father Mike appears only sparingly in the show, marking him as one of Springfield's many minor adult townsfolk.

title: Leroy "Shakey" McGee
text: Leroy "Shakey" McGee is Minor recurring character; a former archery bronze medalist who appears at Springfield sporting ceremonies. Leroy "Shakey" McGee is an elderly former archer with a claim to two Olympic bronze medals from the 1920 and 1930 Games. He's best known for his ceremonial role of lighting the torch and brazier at the Montgomery Burns Winter Games and the Montgomery Burns Games using a flaming arrow shot from mid-field. True to his nickname, his aim is unreliable, and on both occasions he missed the target entirely, accidentally setting fire to Mayor Quimby's bag instead. Because of his shaky performance, organizers eventually had to resort to using a simple match to light the flame. Despite his failures, he remains a recurring fixture at these Springfield athletic events. He originates from the Simpsons comic book series rather than the television show.

title: Arthur Miller
text: Arthur Miller is Real-world American playwright who appears as a fictionalized character/ghost in The Simpsons. Arthur Miller appears in The Simpsons as a fictionalized version of the real-life playwright, often invoked as a symbol of high-brow literary achievement. He shows up in a dream sequence honoring great Americans, humbly considering himself unworthy next to Lisa Simpson. His name is also used as a shorthand for prestige, such as when Ned Flanders compares himself unfavorably to him. Later, his ghost appears alongside other literary and pop-culture spirits like William Shakespeare and Krusty the Clown's humor, showing a somewhat prideful streak when he boasts about being America's greatest playwright. This leads to a sarcastic jab from Shakespeare, poking fun at Miller's self-importance. Overall, he's used as a recurring cultural reference rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Arthur Miller then said that he was America's greatest playwright, to which Shakespeare sarcastically responded, "Exactly."
quotes: Arthur Miller then said that he was America's greatest playwright, to which Shakespeare sarcastically responded, "Exactly."

title: KITT
text: KITT is Crossover character from Knight Rider who briefly appears as a talking car in a home movie made for Homer. KITT is the crime-fighting talking car from the TV series Knight Rider, brought into the Simpsons universe as a crossover cameo. He appears in a heartfelt video the Simpson family assembles to cheer up a depressed Homer, complete with a supposed surprise invitation from KITT himself. Unfortunately, the tape catches fire mid-announcement, leaving Homer none the wiser and even more distressed. Beyond that scene, KITT is referenced as an exhibit in a museum dedicated to talking objects and is name-dropped during one of Homer's rambling six-degrees-of-separation stories linking celebrities to Scrappy-Doo. The show later spoofs the character's concept with its own parody vehicle, Knightboat. Voiced by William Daniels.

title: Poonam Nahasapeemapetilon
text: Poonam Nahasapeemapetilon is One of the Nahasapeemapetilon octuplets, daughter of Apu and Manjula. Poonam is one of the eight babies born to Apu and Manjula after fertility drugs led to a surprise octuplet pregnancy. Overwhelmed by parenting eight infants at once, her parents ended up placing her and her siblings on public display at the Springfield City Zoo in a show called Octopia, where she performed under the stage name Dazzle as a dancer, though she wasn't especially well received by audiences. She and her siblings were eventually rescued from the zoo life when Apu and Homer broke them out. In a moment of patriotic panic, her name was briefly changed to Apple Pie McGillicutty when Springfield rebranded itself as Libertyville. As an infant character, she's mostly defined by being part of the octuplet group rather than having a distinct individual personality. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: Mommy.
quotes: Mommy.

title: Royce McCutcheon
text: Royce McCutcheon is A minor character who is a salesman appearing at a franchise expo in the show. Royce McCutcheon is a slick, overconfident salesman who shows up pitching his business franchise to prospective buyers. He relies on flashy, over-the-top promises rather than substance, assuring people that partnering with him means instant credibility and wild success. His pitch escalates into an absurd claim about reaching the moon and profiting from lunar inhabitants, highlighting his willingness to say anything to close a deal. Though he only appears briefly in the show's canon, his catchphrase-like sales pitch was later reused in a mobile game to celebrate player milestones. He embodies a broad parody of overzealous, exaggerating salesmen often seen in get-rich-quick pitches. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: That's the miracle of Level 50! You're on a rocket ride to the moon!
quotes: That's the miracle of Level 50! You're on a rocket ride to the moon!

title: Bill McCloskey
text: Bill McCloskey is A player for the Springfield Isotopes baseball team. Bill McCloskey is a recurring minor character who plays for the Springfield Isotopes, Springfield's local baseball team. He's portrayed as a fairly average, unremarkable athlete, once described on air as a "mediocre slugger," despite hitting a memorable game-winning grand slam. His interactions with the Simpson kids highlight the team's often lackluster performance, as seen when he casually admits he'll just "try" to win games before botching a routine practice throw. Milhouse regards him with more respect, labeling him the team's cleanup hitter. Beyond his playing days, McCloskey also lends his experience to a baseball instructional video, showing a slightly more authoritative side to his character. Overall, he serves as a recurring background figure tied to Springfield's sports culture and the town's beloved but hapless Isotopes. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Gonna try,
quotes: Gonna try,

title: Markery
text: Markery is Non-canon twin brother of Marge Serfson (a parody version of Marge Simpson) in the Game of Thrones-themed segment "The Serfsons". Markery is a fantasy-world counterpart of Marge Simpson, appearing as her identical twin brother, distinguished mainly by his beard. He comes across as calm, supportive, and a bit smug, especially when reminding Marge and Homer that he was always the better romantic option. His presence causes friction with Homer, who reacts jealously and tells him to back off. Despite the tension, Markery proves to be a loyal ally, joining the effort to storm Lord Montgomery's Castle to save Lisa. He embodies patient confidence, using proverbial wisdom to needle Homer without losing his cool. As a one-off parody character, his role is brief but memorable within the non-canon "Serfsons" storyline. Voiced by Nikolaj Coster-Waldau. Notable quotes: Good things come to those who wait.
quotes: Good things come to those who wait.

title: Knightboat (character)
text: Knightboat (character) is A crime-solving boat from a fictional TV show within the Simpsons universe. Knightboat is a talking boat and the star of its own in-universe TV series, watched by characters like Michael. It patrols waterways chasing down criminals, most memorably starfish poachers, always conveniently finding a river or water feature to pursue them along. The show is a clear parody of Knight Rider, swapping out the sentient car KITT for a sentient boat. Knightboat's world plays into the Simpsons' tradition of absurd, low-effort in-universe media that mirrors real pop culture with a silly twist. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mayor of Albuquerque
text: Mayor of Albuquerque is Minor recurring character; a political figure who attempts to lure sports teams away from Springfield. The Mayor of Albuquerque is a minor political figure defined almost entirely by his ambition to bring professional sports to his city. He first appears attempting to purchase the Springfield Isotopes from owner Howard K. Duff VIII, only to have the sale scuttled by furious Springfield residents. Undeterred, he sets his sights on stealing another team altogether, showing a stubborn and somewhat clueless determination that doesn't let details like a team's actual sport get in his way. His inflated self-importance is played for laughs, as he speaks of himself and his office with grandiose authority despite governing a relatively minor city. Overall he serves as a one-note comic antagonist tied to the show's recurring baseball-related storylines. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: "They'll play what I tell 'em to play, for I am the Mayor of Albuquerque!"
quotes: "They'll play what I tell 'em to play, for I am the Mayor of Albuquerque!"

title: Eddie Murphy
text: Eddie Murphy is Real-world celebrity referenced and occasionally appearing in the Simpsons universe. Eddie Murphy appears in the Simpsons universe as a version of the real-life American actor and comedian, mentioned or depicted in a handful of episodes rather than being a regular cast member. He's referenced as a cultural touchstone, from Dr. Hibbert citing his career pivot to Dr. Dolittle as justification for Krusty's political run, to being name-dropped as one of Krusty's listed music interests online. He's shown mingling with other celebrities like Steven Spielberg and James L. Brooks at the restaurant Morton's, and even lends his "voice" within the show's fictional world to a playing card character, the Jack of Clubs. A running gag involves his name being used as a punchline about awkward racial comments, referenced in the fictional book Caucasian Brittleness. Overall, Eddie Murphy functions as one of many real celebrities woven into Springfield's world for satire and cameo-style humor. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: If Eddie Murphy can go on to do Dr. Dolittle, I suppose we can make this work. | Sure, why not? | But I love Eddie Murphy
quotes: If Eddie Murphy can go on to do Dr. Dolittle, I suppose we can make this work.
Sure, why not?
But I love Eddie Murphy

title: Phil McGraw (character)
text: Phil McGraw (character) is Real-life television personality and psychologist who appears as himself in cameo and mentioned roles in the Simpsons universe. Dr. Phil McGraw appears as a fictionalized version of the real-world talk show psychologist, popping up mostly through references and mentions rather than substantial appearances. His self-help persona is referenced when characters cite his book or joke about his tendency for emotional confrontations, such as Bart warning Rest Stop Spuckler not to get overly therapeutic with him. He's associated with wealth and celebrity, reportedly owning a mansion in Affluence Acres, and is treated as a legitimate self-improvement resource by characters like Opal and Homer. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he attempts an intervention to curb Homer's overeating, only to become a victim of it himself when Homer devours him after imagining him as a talking piece of fudge. Overall, he serves as a pop-culture cameo representing real-world self-help culture within the show's satirical lens. Voiced by Himself.

title: Ming the Merciless
text: Ming the Merciless is A crossover supervillain character appearing in a Simpsons comic story. Ming the Merciless is a villainous figure borrowed from the classic Flash Gordon comics, television series, and films, adapted into the Simpsons universe as a non-speaking character. He is depicted as bald with a distinctive black mustache and beard, fitting his role as a menacing antagonist. In the Simpsons continuity, he is tied to a fictional film starring Stradivarius Cain, blending pop culture parody with the show's love of referencing classic media. He also appears in a wartime setting, present at Adolf Hitler's palace during a comic story where Grampa Simpson infiltrates by hiding in a crate to fight the Nazis. His inclusion highlights the show's tendency to mix historical satire with campy science-fiction villain tropes. As a recurring but silent character, his presence is more symbolic and comedic than central to any storyline.

title: Male jockey 2
text: Male jockey 2 is A minor jockey character living in Jockey Town, appearing in a Simpsons episode. Male jockey 2 is one of the many small jockeys residing in the peculiar community known as Jockey Town, introduced during Homer's brief career as a jockey. He takes part in a group musical number alongside his fellow jockeys, warning Homer through song about the fate of Duncan the horse. Beyond his role in this scene, little else is known about his personality or background, as he functions mainly as part of the jockey ensemble rather than as an individual character. His brief appearance ties him to the show's tradition of quirky, background side-characters who exist within Springfield's odder subcultures. He later appears fleetingly again in archive footage in a later episode, reinforcing his status as a background figure rather than a recurring individual presence. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Lovebots
text: Lovebots is Robot companions purchased by Patty and Selma in a future-set episode. The Lovebots are robots designed and programmed to fall in love with their owners. Patty and Selma each buy one, hoping for companionship, but things don't go as planned when Selma's Lovebot rejects her despite its programming. Instead of staying loyal to their respective owners, Selma's Lovebot runs off with Patty's Lovebot, creating an ironic twist on the idea of manufactured love. The characters are a non-canon concept, appearing in a future-set special and later expanded upon in a mobile game, where the female bot is given the name P.A.M.E.L.A. Their design draws inspiration from advanced android characters in a well-known science fiction film about artificial intelligence. Voiced by Hank Azaria (male).

title: Mexican Duffman
text: Mexican Duffman is Mexican counterpart of Duffman, a minor character in the Duff Beer promotional world. Mexican Duffman is essentially a regional twist on the iconic Duff Beer mascot, appearing as Duffman's counterpart representing Mexico. He shares the same enthusiastic promotional spirit, expressed through his signature exclamation. Despite his minor role, he's notable enough to be considered Duffman's best friend, showing a camaraderie between the international Duff mascots. His brief appearances tie him into the broader Duff Beer advertising universe, and he's even been managed alongside other minor celebrities by a shady industry figure. Like other single-purpose gag characters, his humor derives from being a simple cultural riff on an already absurd original character. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Oh, la!
quotes: Oh, la!

title: Lisa Lionheart
text: Lisa Lionheart is A doll created by Lisa Simpson and Stacy Lovell as an alternative to Malibu Stacy. Lisa Lionheart is a doll Lisa Simpson designs in hopes of giving young girls a smarter, more empowering role model than the vapid Malibu Stacy line. Despite generating initial excitement among children and even adult collectors, the doll's launch is doomed when a rolling display of newly-hatted Malibu Stacy dolls diverts the crowd before they ever reach Lisa Lionheart. This mirrors a recurring theme in the show where Lisa's idealistic, socially conscious projects clash with mainstream consumer culture and ultimately fail commercially. The doll later resurfaces as a forgotten relic sold off during a neighborhood rummage sale, underscoring its short-lived legacy. Though fictional within the show, Lisa Lionheart also appears as a collectible item in Simpsons video games, extending its presence beyond the original episode. Voiced by Yeardley Smith. Notable quotes: I want it, I want it, I want it!
quotes: I want it, I want it, I want it!

title: Lorne Michaels
text: Lorne Michaels is Real-world celebrity (SNL producer) who appears as a minor recurring character in Springfield. Lorne Michaels appears as a fictionalized version of the real television producer and comedian known for creating Saturday Night Live. In the show, he's portrayed as a recognizable celebrity figure that other characters are eager to meet or reference, though he's often brushed off or ignored by the Simpsons family. He's shown to have connections to Springfield's celebrity culture, including a star on the Jewish Walk of Fame. A running gag involves his name being invoked in letters or interviews as a mark of prestige. Notably, the character carries a bit of real-life irony, since his voice actor Harry Shearer has publicly acknowledged a mutual dislike between the two stemming from Shearer's early SNL days. Despite his fame, Lorne is treated somewhat dismissively on-screen, most memorably when Homer (as Max Power) coldly ignores him at a party. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: "Lorne, why me? I mean, I did just star in my first movie with Marvelous Marvin Hagler and Tova Borgnine" - Krusty | "where the hell do you get off?" - Tim Meadows, in a letter to Lorne Michaels
quotes: "Lorne, why me? I mean, I did just star in my first movie with Marvelous Marvin Hagler and Tova Borgnine" - Krusty
"where the hell do you get off?" - Tim Meadows, in a letter to Lorne Michaels

title: Meathook
text: Meathook is A rival biker gang leader of the Hell's Satans (Bakersfield chapter), recurring antagonist to Homer. Meathook is a tough, intimidating biker who leads the Bakersfield chapter of the Hell's Satans gang. He first clashes with Homer when the latter forms his own rival biker gang, escalating into a kidnapping of Marge that forces Homer into a direct confrontation to win her back. Despite his rough exterior, Meathook shows up in various odd contexts around Springfield, from political rallies to concerts to bar brawls, suggesting he's a recurring fixture in the town's seedier underbelly. He later gets tangled in a legal dispute after fighting with Snake Jailbird, only to be outmaneuvered by Homer's unconventional lawyering. Meathook embodies the classic biker tough-guy trope, often popping up as muscle or menace in stories involving Springfield's criminal or fringe elements. Voiced by John Goodman.

title: Mickey Mantle
text: Mickey Mantle is Real-world baseball legend referenced within the show, appearing as a collectible card/picture and cultural touchstone rather than an active character. Mickey Mantle appears in the Simpsons universe mainly as a piece of memorabilia and a cultural reference point rather than a physical character. His baseball card becomes a bargaining chip when Bart trades it away to help Milhouse impress a girl, showing how even legendary status can be treated as a casual trading commodity by the kids of Springfield. He's also invoked as a symbol of flawed heroism, with Marge comparing her own cheating to Mantle's imperfect but beloved legacy. Elsewhere, his name is used for comedic effect in an old-timey endorsement joke, tying him to a bygone era of celebrity product pitches. In a non-canon couch gag, his card is anthropomorphized, sarcastically commenting on its own preserved condition before being discarded and eventually trapped in the couch dimension. Overall, Mantle functions less as a character and more as a running nostalgic reference for baseball history and flawed idols. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Lisa told her then that she doesn't want Mickey Mantle, she wants her mom. | Homer told the card that it was the greatest treasure of his youth. | the Mickey Mantle card told Homer that he was now part of the couch
quotes: Lisa told her then that she doesn't want Mickey Mantle, she wants her mom.
Homer told the card that it was the greatest treasure of his youth.
the Mickey Mantle card told Homer that he was now part of the couch

title: Madison McKenna
text: Madison McKenna is Mother of Nikki McKenna and wife of Brody McKenna; a minor recurring character. Madison McKenna is a stern, no-nonsense attorney who appears as an overprotective parent in the Simpsons universe. She becomes furious when Bart Simpson kisses her daughter Nikki, and rather than letting the matter go, she and her husband take legal action against Springfield Elementary School. Her lawsuit results in the school implementing a strict no-touch policy, showcasing her litigious and uptight personality. Outside of her role as an aggrieved parent, she is shown living an ordinary suburban life, such as attending a Cheech and Chong concert with her husband. She functions mostly as a background/recurring character whose defining trait is her rigid, easily-offended demeanor. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: The Monkees
text: The Monkees is Real-world American pop band referenced within the Simpsons universe. The Monkees are a real-world band that appears in Simpsons lore mostly through references and memorabilia rather than direct appearances. Marge owned a childhood lunchbox featuring the group, which led to a painful realization that they didn't write their own songs or play their own instruments. Dr. Zweig later reframed this for her, suggesting the band's true significance was cultural rebellion rather than musicianship. Their car, the Monkeemobile, shows up as an exhibit at the Hollywood Auto Museum, tying them to Springfield's world of pop culture memorabilia. They're also the subject of a misunderstanding when Homer mistakes talk of monkeys in the treehouse for a Monkees reunion, only to be let down by the truth. Overall, the band functions as a nostalgic pop-culture touchstone rather than an active presence in the show. Notable quotes: The Monkees weren't about music, Marge. They were about rebellion, about political and social upheaval.
quotes: The Monkees weren't about music, Marge. They were about rebellion, about political and social upheaval.

title: Mav (The Changing of the Guardian)
text: Mav (The Changing of the Guardian) is Professional surfer chosen along with his wife Portia as potential guardians for Bart, Lisa, and Maggie. Mav is a laid-back professional surfer who, together with his wife Portia, was selected by Homer and Marge as a backup guardian for their children in case anything ever happened to them. He embodies a carefree, beach-bum persona typical of surfer culture, seemingly more interested in waves and casual living than parenting responsibilities. In a later appearance, he unwittingly picks up Bart's washed-off temporary tattoo from the ocean and claims it as his own, proudly showing it off to a fellow surfer. This small moment highlights his easygoing, somewhat oblivious nature. Despite his minor role, Mav represents an alternative, unconventional path the Simpson kids' lives could have taken had their parents' guardianship plans ever come into play. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mesmerino
text: Mesmerino is A minor recurring hypnotist character who works at a Springfield restaurant. Mesmerino is a professional hypnotist plying his trade at a local Springfield eatery. His most notable act involved hypnotizing Homer Simpson into believing he was a twelve-year-old boy, which led to Homer unexpectedly recalling a disturbing memory of discovering a dead body. Beyond his stage act, he briefly appears as part of an angry mob that turns on Homer after he is blamed for endangering the town. He's a background character with little personal depth, existing mainly as a plot device tied to a single memorable gag. His name and image have also popped up in other media, including a poster reference and a mobile game appearance, suggesting he has a small but recognizable niche in Simpsons lore. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Learned pervert
text: Learned pervert is A minor recurring resident of Springfield known for his intellectual take on erotica and his tendency to show up at odd sexually-charged events. The learned pervert is exactly what his name suggests: a well-read Springfield resident with a scholarly justification for his lecherous interests. He first drew attention at a town meeting by defending erotic art in classical works, disturbing everyone present except Moe, who seemed intrigued. He later turned up at Mayor Quimby's bizarre chess-themed orgy, playing the role of a bishop. His penchant for combining literature and lust continued when he started a so-called book club with Miss Hoover and Professor Pocket Pool during a flight. Eventually, his luck ran out when an FBI profiler caught him during an undercover sting operation targeting a habitual airplane groper known as SeatMiser. He's a recurring background character used mostly for one-off gags about Springfield's eccentric adult population. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: There was no classical art without the erotic.
quotes: There was no classical art without the erotic.

title: Maggie's daughter
text: Maggie's daughter is Non-canon future daughter of Maggie Simpson, part of the Simpson family's speculative future generation. Maggie's daughter is a non-canon, future version character introduced in a flash-forward episode, born to a grown-up Maggie Simpson. She was born during a taxi ride gone hospital-bound, and the reveal of her father's identity was cut off before it could be shared, leaving her parentage a mystery. She appears briefly in later flash-forward material, including archive footage and a Thanksgiving gathering following Homer's death. As an infant, she has no dialogue and little personality shown, existing mainly as a plot device to explore the Simpson family's speculative future. Her connection to another possible future daughter of Maggie's, Maggie Jr. from a different non-canon future timeline, remains unconfirmed, adding to the ambiguous nature of the various 'future' Simpsons continuities.

title: Michael Nesmith
text: Michael Nesmith is Real-world musician referenced as a former member of The Monkees, appearing briefly in the show. Michael Nesmith appears in the Simpsons universe as a real-world reference tied to his actual identity as a member of The Monkees. His mention arises from a childhood memory of Marge's, involving a lunchbox decorated with the band and a schoolmate's claim that the Monkees didn't play their own instruments or write their own songs, and that even Nesmith's iconic hat wasn't genuine. This revelation is played for comedic effect, causing young Marge visible distress. He later appears in picture form as part of the Monkeemobile displayed at a car museum. Nesmith himself does not speak or interact directly with characters, functioning purely as a background pop-culture nod. His presence in the show is limited to flashback and visual cameo appearances rather than any active role in the plot. Notable quotes: "that's not even Michael Nesmith's real hat"
quotes: "that's not even Michael Nesmith's real hat"

title: Gabe Kotter
text: Gabe Kotter is Fictional TV teacher from the show-within-the-show Welcome Back, Kotter, referenced within The Simpsons universe. Gabe Kotter is not a native Simpsons character but rather the protagonist of the in-universe television series Welcome Back, Kotter, which a young Homer once watched. He is remembered for a specific classroom anecdote about his uncle being the family's 'halfback,' a pun that gets an approving laugh from his students on the show. Beyond this brief flashback appearance, Kotter's presence in the Simpsons universe is largely symbolic, showing up as a framed picture on a wall honoring great educators at a clown-themed school. His characterization is essentially a nostalgic nod to the real 1970s sitcom rather than a fleshed-out original personality within the Simpsons world. He appears sparingly, functioning more as a pop-culture reference than a recurring player in Springfield life. Voiced by Chris Edgerly. Notable quotes: If you gave him a sandwich, he'd give you half back.
quotes: If you gave him a sandwich, he'd give you half back.

title: Bill Morrison (character)
text: Bill Morrison (character) is Non-canon comic book artist and writer appearing in Bongo Comics meta-stories. Bill Morrison, nicknamed Bongo Bill, is a real-world-inspired, non-canon character who represents the comic book side of the Simpsons franchise. He appears in behind-the-scenes style comic stories that poke fun at the production of Simpsons Comics, including a bit where he's depicted in a maximum-security prison to comically illustrate the approval process for the comics. He also shows up as a staff member at the Springfield Comic-Con, where his booth is humorously overlooked by attendees due to its unfortunate placement next to the restrooms. In another story, he serves as a narrator of sorts, introducing and commenting on the chapters of a comic tale. Overall, he's a lighthearted, self-referential character used mainly for meta humor about the comic book industry rather than for personality-driven storytelling.

title: Yutaka Nakamura
text: Yutaka Nakamura is Father of Kumiko Albertson, who initially opposes her relationship with Comic Book Guy. Yutaka Nakamura is a traditional, protective father who travels to Springfield in search of his daughter Kumiko. He clashes with Homer after a misunderstanding leads him to whisk Kumiko away from Comic Book Guy. Haunted by guilt over a failed double-suicide pact with his late wife, he is visited by her ghost throughout his story, reflecting his unresolved grief. During a drunken, hallucinatory episode, he confronts a supernatural figure called No-Face, only to discover it's a manifestation of himself, forcing him to face his own flaws. This realization softens him, and he ultimately blesses his daughter's marriage. He appears to settle into Springfield afterward, showing up for civic events like the unveiling of the town's new anthem. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Laddie
text: Laddie is A collie briefly owned by Bart Simpson, later a police and guide dog. Laddie is an extraordinarily talented collie that Bart impulsively orders from a catalog using a fraudulently obtained credit card. Trained to perform household chores, use a flushing toilet, and even present fruit as a welcome gift, he quickly becomes beloved by the entire Simpson family. His arrival causes trouble for Santa's Little Helper, who is mistakenly taken to the pound in Laddie's place when the family can't pay for him. Guilt eventually drives Bart to give Laddie up to the police force so he can get Santa's Little Helper back. Laddie goes on to serve as both a police dog and a guide dog for blind individuals, and later even takes part in a canine uprising in Springfield. He is essentially a loving parody of the classic TV dog Lassie. Voiced by Frank Welker.

title: Libido (character)
text: Libido (character) is A personified aspect of Lisa Simpson's mind, representing her inner desires. Libido is not a real person but a personification that exists within Lisa Simpson's imagination. She emerged after Lisa read her mother's romance novel and began reflecting on it, causing her mind to split into distinct personified traits: Libido, Jealousy, Honesty, and Conscience. Libido is depicted as being confined, seemingly representing a repressed or restrained part of Lisa's psyche. She attempts to break free from this confinement, showing a rebellious or eager nature. However, Conscience keeps her in check, reminding her that freedom will only come once Lisa reaches the age of sixteen. This brief but memorable mental sequence gave a whimsical, symbolic glimpse into Lisa's inner emotional development. Voiced by Yeardley Smith.

title: Multi-eyed squirrel
text: Multi-eyed squirrel is Mutant creature featured in The Simpsons Movie, encountered by Bart and Ned Flanders. This creature is a bizarre mutation of an ordinary squirrel, transformed after Homer's careless dumping of pig waste turns Lake Springfield into a toxic mess. Its most striking trait is its grotesque appearance, sporting dozens of eyes ringed entirely around its head along with fanged teeth and chipmunk-like fur patterns. It briefly becomes a symbol of environmental disaster in Springfield, tying into an in-universe prophecy about a beast with a thousand eyes, though it falls comically short of that number. After being discovered during a hike, it's captured by government authorities and shown off to a real-world political figure in a satirical cameo. The character also lives on in merchandise and a brief cartoon cameo in a later season's opening sequence, cementing its status as a memorable one-off monster from the franchise's feature film. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: The Mulk
text: The Mulk is Fictional comic-book superhero within the Simpsons universe, a parody character rather than a main cast member. The Mulk is a green-skinned superhero who exists as an in-universe parody of Marvel's Hulk. He stars in his own comic book series, The Formidable Mulk, which is sold at The Android's Dungeon comic shop. His most notable exploit involves brawling on the side of Catholic St. Patrick's Day celebrants against a rival named The Thung, seemingly because his green coloring aligns him with that side. This clash lands him in legal trouble, as he is later put on trial for the violence he caused. Like many of Springfield's fictional pop-culture creations, he serves as background world-building and comic-shop humor rather than a character with deep personality traits shown on screen. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Buzz Lightyear
text: Buzz Lightyear is Crossover character from Pixar's Toy Story appearing briefly in The Simpsons universe. Buzz Lightyear is the famous space ranger toy from Toy Story, imported into the Simpsons' world as a fun crossover cameo rather than a true series regular. He shows up mainly in dream sequences and hallucinations, reflecting how deeply embedded he is in pop culture imagination within the show. In one instance, Ralph fantasizes about him partying with Elmo, while in another, a drug-fueled vision has Homer and Ned picturing themselves as Buzz and his usual partner Sheriff Woody. In a non-canon special, he appears at Moe's Tavern celebrating a Disney+ anniversary, getting into a physical mishap during an arm-wrestling match with The Mandalorian. His appearances are brief and whimsical, existing purely for nostalgic or comedic effect rather than any deep characterization. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Mario
text: Mario is Crossover video game character (Nintendo's Mario) who appears in cameo roles throughout the show. Mario is the famous Nintendo plumber who pops up occasionally in Springfield as a crossover gag rather than a true member of the cast. He first shows up as one of several video game icons egging Bart on to steal a game from Try-N-Save, standing apart from Lee Carvallo who tries to talk him out of it. In another encounter, Mario's attempt to get a photo with Homer turns sour when Homer starts hurling barrels at him, recreating the classic Donkey Kong arcade gameplay. He's frequently paired with his brother Luigi, appearing alongside him in Bart's dream at Bro-Land and in other cameo spots. Mario is also shown doing plumbing work at Hudson's house and gets referenced by Grampa as a comparison point for falling for Agnes Skinner. A non-canon gnome-like version of him also appears in The Simpsons Game alongside other Nintendo characters. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta, Hank Azaria.

title: Jack Larson
text: Jack Larson is President of Laramie Cigarettes, a minor recurring businessman character in Springfield. Jack Larson is a minor recurring figure known primarily for his corporate role heading Laramie Cigarettes. He appears when a shipment of his company's product is stolen, showing visible distaste at having to address the resulting public commotion. Beyond that incident, he also lends his image to advertising, appearing as a spokesperson for a beauty pageant sponsored by his cigarette brand. He's a background businessman used mostly to tie together Springfield's ongoing product-placement gags and its criminal underworld. His appearances are brief, functioning more as a plot device than a fully fleshed-out personality. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: John Madden (character)
text: John Madden (character) is Real-life football sportscaster who appears as himself in guest cameo roles. John Madden appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, drawing on his real-world fame as a football player turned television sportscaster. He is depicted alongside fellow commentator Pat Summerall, providing play-by-play commentary during a Super Bowl broadcast. His presence in Springfield extends beyond the booth, as a statue of him is later shown standing outside the E4 electronics store, a nod to the popular Madden NFL video game franchise that bears his name. He has also appeared briefly in an opening sequence gag. As a recurring guest-star cameo, Madden's role is limited but tied closely to his real-life persona as a beloved sports broadcasting icon. Voiced by Himself.

title: Leo (cameraman)
text: Leo (cameraman) is A spotlight operator working on The Krusty the Clown Show. Leo is a minor recurring crew member on the Krusty the Clown Show, responsible for operating the spotlight. He comes across as cynical and unimpressed with the quality of the program he works on, openly criticizing both Sideshow Bob's jokes and the show itself. His deadpan honesty tends to annoy those around him, particularly Sideshow Bob. There's some ambiguity around his identity, as Bart at one point calls him by a different name, Louie, leaving it unclear whether one of the names is a nickname or if they're actually two different but similar-looking characters. Despite his small role, Leo has appeared across several episodes spanning many seasons. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: soon, you'll be Napoleon Blown-apart
quotes: soon, you'll be Napoleon Blown-apart

title: Lonnie
text: Lonnie is Minor background character, a crossover figure connected to the Spuckler family tree. Lonnie is an obscure, non-speaking character whose existence in the Simpsons universe is essentially a nod to the film Deliverance. He's depicted as a branch on the Spuckler family tree, tying him loosely to the show's hillbilly clan. Because he originates from a live-action movie reference rather than an original creation, he has no dialogue or personality traits shown on screen. His inclusion is largely a background joke for attentive viewers who recognize the Deliverance reference. He appears fleetingly, first shown in a family tree graphic and later referenced in a picture cameo.

title: Daisy May Moses
text: Daisy May Moses is A crossover character from The Beverly Hillbillies who appears/is referenced in The Simpsons. Daisy May Moses, better known as Granny, is the elderly matriarch from The Beverly Hillbillies who crosses over into the Simpsons universe in a few brief gags. She's portrayed as sharp-tongued and no-nonsense, quick to respond to her grandson Jethro's antics with dry remarks. Her appearances are mostly nods to classic television rather than substantial storylines, showing up in a mentioned crossword clue, a background statue, and a risqué deleted Halloween segment. In the deleted scene, she becomes the target of Professor Frink's clothes-removing ray, which ties her humorously into a Simpsons plot about misused technology. Overall she functions as a nostalgic pop-culture reference rather than a fleshed-out character within the Simpsons' own world. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Granny then said that she wasn't going to cook them.
quotes: Granny then said that she wasn't going to cook them.

title: Moe-looking Satan
text: Moe-looking Satan is A demonic ruler of Hell who appears in a Treehouse of Horror segment, resembling Moe Szyslak. This version of Satan looks strikingly like Moe Szyslak and rules over Hell. He has a history of trying to claim souls from the Simpson family, once attempting to take Patty and Selma during a séance, which led Marge to strike a bargain trading one of her future children for her sisters' safety. Years later he returns to collect on that deal, targeting baby Maggie and unleashing supernatural chaos on the Simpsons' home. When Homer attempts to renegotiate the terms, the demon reveals himself to have bizarre and uncomfortable demands. He's portrayed as a manipulative dealmaker with a strange, unsettling sense of humor. The character exists purely in non-canon Halloween lore and mobile game material rather than the show's main continuity. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Timothy Lovejoy, Sr.
text: Timothy Lovejoy, Sr. is Father of Reverend Timothy Lovejoy and grandfather of Jessica Lovejoy. Timothy Lovejoy, Sr. is an elderly, balding member of the extended Lovejoy family, best known as the father of Springfield's local reverend. He appears as a minor, non-speaking character, having been glimpsed enjoying a visit to the burlesque establishment La Maison Derrière. His presence suggests a mischievous or hypocritical streak within the pious Lovejoy lineage, given the contrast between his son's religious position and his own choice of leisure activity. He has made only brief appearances in the series, including archive footage and a flashback scene, reinforcing his status as a background character rather than a central figure. Little else is known about his personality or history beyond this single notable moment.

title: Duke Mitchell
text: Duke Mitchell is Eco-terrorist antagonist from a McBain comic story. Duke Mitchell is a minor villain who appears in the Bongo comics rather than the animated series. He's an eco-terrorist whose questionable environmental methods draw the attention of action hero McBain. When McBain finds a recyclable can improperly discarded, he traces the offense back to Duke and confronts him about it. Duke seems genuinely confused about what McBain wants from him, unaware of the seriousness with which McBain treats environmental crimes. True to McBain's over-the-top action style, the confrontation ends explosively when McBain blows up Duke's boat, though Duke manages to escape by jumping overboard. He exists mainly as a one-off foil to showcase McBain's exaggerated sense of justice.

title: Leaky Pants
text: Leaky Pants is A minor clown character and former colleague of Krusty the Clown, later working as a restaurant employee. Leaky Pants is a former television clown who gave up his showbiz career and now works as an employee at Mussel & Flanks restaurant. His unusual name becomes fodder for one of Krusty's typically mean-spirited jokes about his birth. He appears on a wall of clowns who quit the entertainment business, which irritates Krusty when he spots it. Despite his low profile, Krusty still sees value in his comedic material, going so far as to offer a large sum of money to buy it outright. When Leaky Pants refuses the offer, Krusty reveals his ruthless side by threatening to simply steal the material instead. Beyond his brief live-action appearance, he also exists as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: Krusty said that when Leaky Pants' mother's water broke, it was seltzer.
quotes: Krusty said that when Leaky Pants' mother's water broke, it was seltzer.

title: Ms. Myles
text: Ms. Myles is First grade teacher at Springfield Elementary School who taught a young Lisa Simpson. Ms. Myles is a minor, non-canon character who appears in a flashback as Lisa Simpson's first grade teacher. She has grey hair, fitting the archetype of an older, somewhat oblivious educator. Her most notable moment comes when she announces a student's birthday in class, unaware that it is also Lisa's birthday, leading to an emotional moment for Lisa. Rather than showing sympathy, she simply sends the upset Lisa off to see Principal Skinner, highlighting a somewhat detached or procedural approach to handling students' feelings. She has no other significant characterization beyond this brief but memorable classroom scene. Voiced by Valerie Harper.

title: Milhouse's dog
text: Milhouse's dog is Pet dog owned by Milhouse Van Houten. This unnamed Shih Tzu is Milhouse's loyal but frequently mishandled pet. She first appears being walked by Milhouse right after Lisa Simpson breaks up with Nelson Muntz, and gets accidentally choked on her leash when Milhouse jumps for joy. She's later entered into the Ugly Dog Contest at the Springfield Pet Fair, where Krusty jokes that she resembles his ex-wife. The dog and Milhouse have a habit of licking tongues together, prompting Milhouse to try using Bart's makeshift 'Cootie Shot' as a precaution, though it was never completed. She has no lines and functions mostly as a background gag tied to Milhouse's quirky, awkward home life.

title: Mid-Atlantic woman
text: Mid-Atlantic woman is Minor recurring background character; a woman briefly considered as a potential guardian for the Simpson children. The Mid-Atlantic woman is an unnamed, minor character defined mainly by her regional origin rather than any deep personality traits. She appears alongside her boyfriend Keith, first seen walking near the sea when Homer and Marge were scouting possible guardians for their children. Marge quickly rules her out upon realizing she hails from the Mid-Atlantic region, the same area where the gritty series 'The Wire' was filmed, prompting an immediate exit. She later reappears in a separate episode, once again spending time with Keith by the waterfront. Her role is essentially a one-off gag rooted in geographic stereotyping rather than any ongoing storyline. She has no known name, job, or distinct backstory beyond these two brief appearances. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: The Mandalorian
text: The Mandalorian is Star Wars crossover character (bounty hunter) who appears in non-canon Simpsons specials. The Mandalorian, also known as Din Djarin, is a crossover character brought into the Simpsons universe from the Star Wars franchise. His first appearance is only as a cardboard standee at the Comic Book Guy's store, which gets destroyed during a scuffle. In later non-canon specials, he shows up in person at Moe's Tavern for a Disney+ anniversary party, where he engages in an arm-wrestling match with Buzz Lightyear and tears his opponent's arm clean off. He's also shown caring for his companion Grogu, dropping him off at a daycare run in connection with Mon Mothma, and briefly gets tangled up with baby Maggie Simpson, even drawing his darksaber when she wanders into Grogu's pod. True to his on-screen persona, he remains stoic and armored throughout, mostly communicating in short, matter-of-fact lines. He ultimately informs Homer that Maggie has drifted off into space, staying true to his role as an outsider bemusedly swept into Simpsons chaos. Notable quotes: Maggie had gone into space.
quotes: Maggie had gone into space.

title: Magmo
text: Magmo is Comic-book supervillain who appears in a Radioactive Man comic Bart reads. Magmo is a fictional lava creature that emerges from underground during a comic-book storyline read by Bart. He bursts forth from a drilling site near Zenith High School after scientists accidentally unearth him, causing chaos and rampaging into the city. He serves as a one-off villain for Radioactive Man and his sidekick Fallout Boy to battle, showcasing typical superhero-comic antics within the Simpsons universe. Magmo doesn't speak or have a developed personality beyond being a destructive molten menace. He's eventually subdued through clever use of asbestos insulation rather than brute force, then discarded back into the hole he came from. As a non-canon character existing only within an in-universe comic, Magmo's appearances are limited to Bongo comics and a video game.

title: Martha (librarian)
text: Martha (librarian) is Librarian at the Springfield Public Library and later Springfield Elementary School. Martha is a minor recurring librarian character who assists patrons of Springfield's library system, first helping Lisa research her family history. She later transitions to working at Springfield Elementary School, where she deals with the school's eccentric students. She's shown to have a dry, observational sense of humor, particularly when commenting on Ralph Wiggum's unusual habits with books. The wikitext notes she was hinted to be a lesbian in one of her appearances. Despite her limited screen time, she leaves a warm impression, even wanting to hug Homer and Marge after a small victory with Ralph. Her character design was later recycled for another background character, Judy, at a nursing home. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Rita LaFleur
text: Rita LaFleur is Former restaurant singer and old flame/eventual wife of Abraham Simpson. Rita LaFleur was a nightclub singer who once performed at a restaurant where a young Abraham Simpson worked alongside Marvin Hamlisch. The two fell deeply in love, but Abe ultimately chose not to run off with her to Europe, worried that his infant son Homer might get hurt by a dangerous electrical socket back home. Decades later, Abe's memories of Rita resurface when he escapes the Springfield Retirement Castle, prompting Homer and Marge to dig into his past. Her gray hair in old age contrasts with the youthful brown-haired image fans see of her earlier years. Rita eventually reunites with and marries Abe, tying up a decades-old romantic loose end. She's a minor but poignant addition to the show's exploration of Grampa Simpson's backstory. Voiced by Anika Noni Rose.

title: Lyla
text: Lyla is Mr. Burns' cousin and long-lost love interest. Lyla is a relative of Mr. Burns whom he met and fell in love with while in Paris, only to be rejected when she deemed him too evil a man to marry. Decades later, Burns becomes nostalgic for her and has his aide Dexter Colt track her down, discovering she had become a Buddhist nun living a life of quiet devotion. She reunites with Burns at The Peak Inn, revealing she had been saving herself for him all along, suggesting she may have regretted turning him down. Tragically, before their romance can be rekindled, she dies, and her body eerily disintegrates into dust when Burns tries to revive her with a kiss. Her story is a bittersweet, gothic tale of lost love and missed chances within the Burns family history. She later appears in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Darth Maul
text: Darth Maul is A Star Wars villain who appears in The Simpsons as a crossover/reference character rather than a core cast member. Darth Maul is the iconic Sith Lord from Star Wars, appearing in The Simpsons universe purely as a pop-culture reference rather than a fully realized character. He's never actually seen speaking or acting on his own; instead, his image and likeness show up in merchandise and costumes throughout the show. A LEGO version of him graces the cover of a toy catalog, and his face appears on the packaging of a novelty double-edged lightsaber. Comic Book Guy pays homage to him by dressing as the character for a convention. In a non-canon short, a man named Gerald Samson cosplays as Darth Maul and engages in a mock lightsaber battle with baby Maggie, even using the Force to bring a cabinet down on her. Overall, Maul functions as a nostalgic nod to Star Wars fandom within the show rather than a story-driving figure.

title: Cyrus Manley
text: Cyrus Manley is Fictional character within a book ('The Harpooned Heart') referenced in the episode 'Diatribe of a Mad Housewife', inspired by Ned Flanders. Cyrus Manley exists as a character inside a story Marge writes, rather than as a member of the actual Simpsons universe. He is romantically involved with Temperance Barrows, a woman unhappily married to the abusive Captain Mordecai. His storyline plays out as a tragic romance, since his affair with Temperance leads to a violent end at Mordecai's hands. Notably, the character is explicitly designed as a fictionalized stand-in for Ned Flanders, suggesting a satirical or wish-fulfillment angle to Marge's writing. Beyond his brief but dramatic literary appearance, Cyrus also shows up in non-canon media like The Simpsons: Tapped Out. His entire existence is confined to a story-within-a-story, making him a uniquely meta character in the show's lore. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: The Mirror Maidens
text: The Mirror Maidens is Non-canon superhero alter-egos of Sherri and Terri from The Simpsons comics. The Mirror Maidens are the superhero personas adopted by twins Sherri and Terri after a nuclear explosion grants them special abilities. Their signature power comes from a magic jump rope, which fuels their heroics in the Bongo comics universe. Visually and thematically, their costumes and rope are modeled after Wonder Woman, giving them a classic superheroine look. As a non-canon duo, they exist purely within the comic book continuity rather than the animated series. Their appearances are limited to a couple of specific comic storylines, marking them as a niche but fun addition to the Simpsons superhero parody lineup.

title: Mayan Homer
text: Mayan Homer is A non-canon Mayan version of Homer Simpson, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror opening sequence. Mayan Homer is a parody variant of Homer set in an ancient Mayan civilization, appearing briefly as part of a Treehouse of Horror opening gag. He is selected as a sacrificial victim, continuing the show's tradition of placing familiar characters into odd historical or mythological scenarios. True to Homer's typical luck, he manages to avoid his grim fate entirely thanks to his wife's quick thinking. His wife, Mayan Marge, distracts the priest meant to prepare him for sacrifice, leading to the priest being sacrificed in his place instead. This twist plays on the recurring theme of Homer narrowly escaping disaster through sheer fortune rather than his own effort. Beyond his one-off animated appearance, the character was also adapted into a collectible costume/skin in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Ally McBeal
text: Ally McBeal is A crossover character/parody referencing the fictional lawyer from the TV series "Ally McBeal", appearing briefly in the Simpsons universe. Ally McBeal is a minor, non-speaking crossover character based on the title character of the television legal drama of the same name, originally played by Calista Flockhart. In the Simpsons universe, she is depicted as a lawyer working in Boston. She is referenced in a joke advertisement for a Lance Murdock toy figure, which humorously implies she causes a violent traction accident involving the stunt daredevil. She also makes a brief cameo appearance in a crowd scene during a parade for the Boston Americans. Her inclusion is purely a nod to the real-world TV series rather than a fleshed-out character with personality traits within the show. She has no dialogue and exists mainly as an Easter egg for fans of pop culture crossovers.

title: The Mad Hatter
text: The Mad Hatter is A minor character based on the Mad Hatter from Alice in Wonderland, appearing in a vision in Lisa's imagination. The Mad Hatter is a non-speaking character lifted from the classic story Alice in Wonderland, appearing within Lisa's imagination rather than as a 'real' Simpsons character. He shows up in a surreal vision where Alice warns Lisa that going to the library is a trap, urging her instead to keep acting cool. In this same vision, the Hatter takes a more menacing turn, pointing a gun at Lisa's head. Aside from this dream sequence, he also appears as an illustration in a pop-up storybook that Lisa and Maggie read together. His only other connection to the show is a nod in the form of Krusty's costume in a Krusty Burger commercial. As a background/fantasy figure, he has no dialogue and exists purely as a reference to the source material.

title: Myra
text: Myra is School secretary at Springfield Elementary and administrative assistant to Principal Skinner. Myra is the harried secretary who keeps Principal Skinner's office running, dealing with paperwork, keys, and unruly students. She has a soft spot for Bart, who chats with her and even brings her flowers when he's sent to the office, and she in turn keeps him updated on her rocky personal life. Her long-term boyfriend Frank strings her along with excuses about a pending divorce that never seems to finalize, leaving their relationship perpetually troubled. Despite her friendliness with Bart, she's not above holding a grudge, refusing to help him avoid punishment after he ruins her breakfast. She appears to eventually move on from Frank, later being spotted with Superintendent Chalmers at a comedy show. Her casual attitude toward her job is shown when she carelessly tosses an important key into a bin full of miscellaneous keys. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: Forget it! This used to be a Croissan'wich. Now it's a ham and cheese car crash.
quotes: Forget it! This used to be a Croissan'wich. Now it's a ham and cheese car crash.

title: Les Moore
text: Les Moore is Greyhound breeder and original owner of Santa's Little Helper. Les Moore runs the No Kill Kennel and bred greyhounds for racing, including Santa's Little Helper's mother, She Biscuit. He's a callous businessman at heart, having abandoned Santa's Little Helper when the dog lost a race, only to resurface later to reclaim him once the dog became valuable as a beer mascot. His willingness to exploit animals for profit makes him an unsympathetic figure, and he's frequently on the receiving end of the Simpson family's anger, getting slapped multiple times across his appearances. Despite his gruff exterior, he shows a rare moment of emotion when he realizes Santa's Little Helper still longs for his mother. Overall, he serves as a minor recurring antagonist tied to the backstory of the family dog. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Moog
text: Moog is Non-canon alternate version of Moe Szyslak, former gang leader of the Glugs and later a bartender in a Clockwork Orange-style parody segment. Moog is a parody incarnation of Moe, cast as the leader of a violent London street gang called the Glugs in a Treehouse of Horror segment spoofing A Clockwork Orange. His criminal days ended when a member's romantic entanglement caused the gang to break apart, leading to Moog being humiliated and literally dropped onto the Shard by rival enforcers. He settled into a quieter life running a bar until nostalgia and a fresh act of aggression from a new generation of thugs pushed him to reassemble his old crew for one final heist. That last job goes chaotic and disastrous when the gang tries to crash Mr. Burns' debauched party and gets overwhelmed. Despite the beating he takes, Moog ends the story oddly content with how things turned out. His name is a playful blend referencing both Moe and the slang term for gang members from the film he parodies. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: "Home Invasion."
quotes: "Home Invasion."

title: New New York creatures
text: New New York creatures is Mutant monsters accidentally created by Bart Simpson in a Futurama/Simpsons crossover episode. These creatures originated from a bizarre mishap when Bart's booger-filled sandwich in a time capsule mixed with Milhouse's lucky rabbit foot, spawning a mutant rabbit-like being. That single creature multiplied into millions, wreaking havoc on the futuristic New New York a thousand years later. Strangely, they eventually evolved to resemble tiny green versions of Bart himself, even repeating his classic catchphrases and pranks. Their rampage becomes a problem for Bart, Lisa, and the Planet Express crew, who must figure out how to stop the chaos their past selves accidentally set in motion. The solution involves trapping the horde and jettisoning them into space, where they meet an unceremonious end as alien cuisine. They serve as a comedic link between the two animated universes, embodying Bart's mischievous legacy taken to an absurd extreme. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Neytiri
text: Neytiri is A fictional Na'vi princess from Avatar who appears as a crossover character in The Simpsons. Neytiri is a crossover character borrowed from the film Avatar, appearing in The Simpsons universe rather than as a traditional cast member. She is referenced as one of Bart's romantic conquests, appearing in his "Little Black eBook" of pictures, suggesting he had some kind of electronic relationship with her. She also shows up as a costume at the Bi-Mon-Sci-Fi-Con convention, worn by an attendee who flees in panic during Chief Wiggum's dream-fueled rampage. Her presence highlights the show's frequent pop-culture parody style, blending real-world film references into Springfield's oddball events. Neytiri herself has no independent personality within the show, functioning purely as a nod to Avatar fans.

title: Man with the braces
text: Man with the braces is A minor recurring TV host character who appears on the reality show Frame Up and later a house-swapping program. The man with the braces is a background TV personality who first shows up hosting the staged reality series Frame Up. He plays a key role in a scripted crime segment, pretending to steal a necklace so that Homer and Marge look guilty when they try to blame an unseen third party. His brief, mysterious appearance becomes a running joke, since Homer and Marge's frantic accusations about him only make them seem more suspicious. Once the twist is revealed, he casually admits he's just an actor hired for the show, deflating the mystery around him. He later resurfaces as the host of a different program centered on families swapping houses. The character is essentially a parody of the elusive 'one-armed man' figure from The Fugitive, used as a device to comment on how flimsy reality TV twists can be. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: It was the man with the braces! | some actor they hired
quotes: It was the man with the braces!
some actor they hired

title: Shelbyville Manhattan
text: Shelbyville Manhattan is Founder of Shelbyville and former partner of Jebediah Springfield. Shelbyville Manhattan is a figure from Springfield's founding lore, known primarily through the historical account recounted by Abraham Simpson. He once traveled alongside Jebediah Springfield as part of the same settling party, but the two had starkly different visions for their new community. Shelbyville's defining trait is his enthusiastic approval of cousin marriage, which he saw as the very point of their expedition, putting him at odds with Springfield's more restrictive ideals. This fundamental disagreement caused an irreconcilable split, leading Shelbyville to break away and found his own town bearing his name. He exists mostly as a legendary, deceased ancestor figure rather than an active character, appearing in flashbacks, museum dioramas, and non-canon media like games. His legacy lives on as the namesake and symbolic founder of Springfield's eternal rival city, Shelbyville. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Larry H. Lawyer, Jr.
text: Larry H. Lawyer, Jr. is A personal injury lawyer in Springfield who occasionally represents members of the main cast. Larry H. Lawyer, Jr. is a fast-talking personal injury attorney who thrives on ambulance-chasing opportunities around Springfield. He represented Homer in a lawsuit against the First Church of Springfield after Homer broke his leg falling into a hole, and he even helped the notoriously reckless Dr. Nick Riviera win a hefty settlement despite Nick's own negligence. His willingness to pounce on any potential case is highlighted when he overhears Bart complaining about a misleading comic book coupon and immediately offers his legal services. Larry's slick, opportunistic persona is modeled after a real-life California personal injury lawyer known for flashy advertising. A subtle joke about his character comes from his license plate, which references a famous number from the Alien film franchise. Overall, he serves as a satirical jab at the exaggerated, publicity-hungry stereotype of personal injury lawyers. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Slip and fall? Can't go back to work? I will work for you!
quotes: Slip and fall? Can't go back to work? I will work for you!

title: Judge Muntz
text: Judge Muntz is Nelson Muntz's grandfather, a judge in Springfield. Judge Muntz is an elderly member of the Muntz family, serving as Nelson's paternal grandfather and the father of Mr. Muntz. He holds a position of authority as a judge, and by 1996 he had reportedly sentenced forty-seven people to death, hinting at a stern and no-nonsense approach to his profession. Despite his intimidating career, he takes part in more lighthearted family activities, such as attending grandparents day events at Springfield Elementary School. He appears to be an active presence in Nelson's life, showing up more than once for school functions. His character adds a bit of generational depth and backstory to the otherwise rough-edged Muntz family. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Jill Munroe
text: Jill Munroe is A crossover character from Charlie's Angels who appears briefly within the Simpsons universe. Jill Munroe is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed figure from the real-world TV show Charlie's Angels, originally played by Farrah Fawcett. Within the show's universe, she exists mainly as a piece of pop culture that the Simpsons characters interact with rather than a true resident of Springfield. She's first referenced when Homer and Barney watch an episode of Charlie's Angels featuring a mission to Hawaii. Later, her likeness turns up as a collectible doll owned by Comic Book Guy, showing her status as a nostalgic icon. In a non-canon special, Troy McClure encounters an exhibit dedicated to Charlie's Angels, including Jill alongside fellow Angels Sabrina Duncan and Kelly Garrett. Overall, her role is a nod to classic television rather than an active part of the Simpsons cast. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Cloris Mozelle
text: Cloris Mozelle is Minor recurring character, a cast member on the country-western variety show Ya Hoo!. Cloris Mozelle is a minor figure in the Simpsons universe known primarily for her distinctive fashion sense. She appears as a performer on the fictional television program Ya Hoo!, a country-western-themed variety show within the show's world. Her defining trait is her fondness for large, flower-adorned hats, which serve as her visual signature.
