She shows up at the Simpson household believing it to be Moe's own bachelor pad, only to find the family still home and Mr. Burns causing chaos. Her charm comes into play when she manages to defuse Burns' anger at Homer with nothing more than a hug and a kiss, showing her to be a calming, good-natured presence amid the sitcom's usual chaos. She joins in on a group Christmas song with the family, and shares a comedic, slightly risqué moment with Moe involving a misplaced kiss. Beyond this main appearance, she's referenced in archive footage and mentioned in passing in another episode, and non-canonically appears attending a fictional Simpsons premiere. The character leans on the novelty of Perry appearing as herself in a puppet-parody segment mocking The Muppets. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: That wasn't my belly button. | I didn't tell you to stop.
quotes: That wasn't my belly button.
I didn't tell you to stop.

title: Retirement Castle administrator
text: Retirement Castle administrator is Recurring minor character who manages the Springfield Retirement Castle. This administrator runs the Springfield Retirement Castle with a clear focus on profit rather than the wellbeing of the elderly residents. He appears in several episodes handling mundane duties like announcing family visits, decorating for holidays, and hosting a poetry reading night for the seniors. His most notable moment of self-interest comes when he pressures Abe Simpson to spend Bea Simmons' inheritance money on the retirement home rather than elsewhere. Even during lighter events like the seniors' poetry night, he shows a bit of exasperation with the residents, particularly when their contributions become repetitive. Overall, he's a background figure representing the mildly exploitative, bureaucratic side of elder care in Springfield. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Rusty the Clown
text: Rusty the Clown is A minor clown character depicted as a balloon in a Springfield parade. Rusty the Clown is a minor, non-speaking character who appears as one of the balloon figures in Springfield's Thanksgiving Parade. He has red hair and no notable personality traits are given, as he is essentially a background prop rather than an active character. Bart is shown to dislike the Rusty the Clown balloon during its appearance. Aside from his brief cameo in the parade sequence, he has no further role in the show's continuity. Rusty later appears as a purchasable balloon decoration in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, reinforcing his status as a background/collectible item rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: Pita
text: Pita is Minor non-canon character who briefly appears in a Treehouse of Horror segment parodying The Hunger Games. Pita is a young boy who takes part in a dystopian battle dome competition, appearing alongside his companion Peta in a Treehouse of Horror segment parodying The Hunger Games. He and Peta meet Lisa Simpson, who quickly warms up to the pair, suggesting he has a likable or charming demeanor. Unfortunately, his time on screen is cut short when Homish falls from the sky and crushes both him and Peta to death. His name and role are a direct play on the Hunger Games character Peeta Mellark. Beyond this brief and darkly comedic appearance, little else is known about his personality or background. He also appears as a character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: John S.
text: John S. is Minor recurring character, husband of Gloria S., who attended a marriage counseling retreat with Homer and Marge. John S. is a bitter, sharp-tongued husband whose marriage to Gloria S. is defined by constant bickering. He appears at a marriage retreat run by Reverend Lovejoy, where his relationship with his wife mirrors the volatile dynamic of Homer and Marge's own troubles. Despite the hostility, he and Gloria manage to reconcile by the end of their appearance together. He resurfaces briefly in later episodes as a background figure, once enjoying a night out at a club and later attending a town meeting about spending Mr. Burns' fortune. His characterization is explicitly modeled after a famous fictional battling couple from classic theater. Overall, John serves as a minor comedic parallel to the show's central marriage, illustrating that even the most contentious relationships can find moments of tenderness. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "Queen of the Harpies"
quotes: "Queen of the Harpies"

title: Sideshow Raheem
text: Sideshow Raheem is One of Krusty the Clown's former sidekicks, predecessor to Sideshow Bob. Sideshow Raheem, born Russell Mason and also known as Raheem Banjoko, served as Krusty the Clown's assistant before Sideshow Bob took the role. He is depicted as a devout Muslim and had an intimidating presence, so much so that Krusty avoided using him as a comedic target. He has made background appearances at various Springfield events, including Krusty's fake funeral and an all-black church service. He also joined the angry mob chasing Homer during the town's environmental crisis. His long-standing recognition among Springfield's community earned him a spot on the Springfield Wall of Fame. Despite his minor role, he's a recurring background character with a distinct personal history noted in supplementary materials like The Krusty Book. Voiced by Michael Carrington. Notable quotes: "an angry young man." - Krusty describing Sideshow Raheem
quotes: "an angry young man." - Krusty describing Sideshow Raheem

title: The Scarlet Whimpernel
text: The Scarlet Whimpernel is Non-canon superhero alter-ego of Milhouse Van Houten from the Bongo comics. The Scarlet Whimpernel is the costumed identity Milhouse Van Houten adopts after being exposed to a nuclear explosion that grants him powers. His main ability is dubbed a 'super whine,' a comedic nod to Milhouse's typically whiny personality translated into a superpower. Initially he tries to be a solitary crime-fighter, embracing the lone-hero trope common in superhero stories. However, his resolve to work alone doesn't last, as he eventually succumbs to loneliness and seeks companionship. The character's name is a playful parody of the classic adventure story 'The Scarlet Pimpernel,' tying into the comic's larger satire of superhero genre conventions. He appears exclusively in Bongo comic issues rather than the TV series, marking him as part of the extended, non-canon Simpsons universe.

title: Mary-Kate Olsen (character)
text: Mary-Kate Olsen (character) is Real-life actress who appears as herself in a guest role on The Simpsons. Mary-Kate Olsen is depicted as a celebrity guest appearance alongside her twin sister Ashley in the show's universe. The pair are shown narrating an audiobook together, taking turns reading sections and cueing each other to continue. Their real-world fame as a young celebrity author duo is referenced through a fictional book of theirs that Milhouse becomes obsessed with. The joke built around her character centers on the twins' close bond and shared identity, to the point that Milhouse jokes about feeling like an unofficial third member of their duo. Beyond these brief appearances, she doesn't have much independent characterization, functioning mainly as a pop-culture cameo. Voiced by Herself.

title: Isabel Sanford (character)
text: Isabel Sanford (character) is A real-life American actress who appeared as herself in a cameo on the show. This character is a self-portrayal of actress Isabel Sanford, best known for playing Weezie on The Jeffersons. In her appearance, she serves as a commentator at an exhibit inside the Museum of Television and TV, guiding an audience through its exhibits. She jokingly notes that visitors won't find a Michaelangelo there, though they might spot other celebrities like Michael Landon or Beverly D'Angelo. In a playful, self-aware moment, she breaks the fourth wall to comment on the storytelling structure of the episode itself, remarking on how audiences enjoy a satisfying ending. She also references her famous TV husband, George Jefferson, tying her cameo back to her most iconic role. Voiced by Isabel Sanford. Notable quotes: She's the beloved Weezie from The Jeffersons. | They won't see a Michaelangelo, but they might see a Michael Landon or Beverly D'Angelo. | They all love George Jefferson and want him to come home.
quotes: She's the beloved Weezie from The Jeffersons.
They won't see a Michaelangelo, but they might see a Michael Landon or Beverly D'Angelo.
They all love George Jefferson and want him to come home.

title: Sarcastic doorman
text: Sarcastic doorman is Minor recurring character; doorman at Club Zipless who briefly interacts with Marge and Raphael. The sarcastic doorman is a minor background character who works the entrance of Club Zipless. As his name suggests, his defining trait is a dry, mocking sense of humor, which he displays when Marge shows up looking for Homer and he jokes about her disheveled, witch-like appearance. This snarky comment draws the ire of Raphael, who confronts him over the remark. Beyond this brief exchange, little else is known about his personality or background, as he appears only fleetingly in the show. He serves mainly as a one-off source of comic relief tied to a specific club setting rather than a fully developed character. His appearances are limited to a couple of episodes from the show's twenty-second season era. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: O.J. Simpson
text: O.J. Simpson is Real-life former football player and actor referenced/parodied within the show, notably in a South Park episode-within-an-episode. This version of O.J. Simpson is a caricature of the real-life athlete and actor, best known in the show's universe for his infamous murder trial and later criminal conviction. His main appearance comes via a fictional South Park episode watched by Bart and Milhouse, where he goes on a violent stabbing spree before mockingly declaring he'll search for the 'real killer.' Beyond that, he's mostly referenced in passing dialogue, often as a grim punchline about scandal, guilt, or financial ruin. Other characters invoke his name as shorthand for infamy, such as comparing a city's bankruptcy to his own downfall. He never appears as an active character in Springfield itself, existing instead as a running cultural reference and dark joke about celebrity crime. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: "Really broke or O.J. Simpson broke?"
quotes: "Really broke or O.J. Simpson broke?"

title: Ranger (Mountain of Madness)
text: Ranger (Mountain of Madness) is A park ranger stationed at Mt. Useful who assists the Simpson family during their mountain retreat. This ranger works at Mt. Useful, a once-popular attraction that has fallen on hard times due to budget cutbacks. He's practical and somewhat weary, openly admitting to Marge that the mountain isn't much fun anymore. When Marge loses track of Bart and Lisa, he uses a chairlift to scan the mountainside and quickly locates the missing kids. He also plays a key role in the rescue of Homer and Mr. Burns, who become trapped in a snowed-in cabin, though his blunt instructions to prepare for handling frozen corpses reveal a dark sense of humor amid the crisis. In a later appearance, he comes to Lisa's aid when she's attacked by deer that turn out to be more savage than expected, escorting her safely back to the visitors center. Overall, he serves as a helpful but overworked authority figure representing the show's satire of underfunded public services. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Scar
text: Scar is Crossover Disney villain character (from The Lion King) appearing in non-canon Simpsons specials. Scar is the villainous lion from Disney's The Lion King, making crossover appearances in non-canon Simpsons specials tied to Disney+ promotions. He shows up as a background character rather than a driving force in the plot, fitting in among other Disney villains. His appearances lean on his established reputation as an antagonist rather than developing new personality traits within the Simpsons universe. He's depicted attending a party at Moe's Tavern, mingling with fellow villain Cruella de Vil, and later joining a gathering of Disney villains at a themed location. He also takes part in a group musical number alongside other villains. Notably, he has no voice actor credited and no spoken lines in these appearances, functioning purely as a visual cameo.

title: Sad-looking Frenchman
text: Sad-looking Frenchman is A minor character among the Lost Souls, a group of melancholy wanderers aboard the Ship of Lost Souls. The Sad-looking Frenchman is one of the world-weary Lost Souls who drift the seas endlessly, each burdened by regret from their past. He's quick to judge others' moral failings, expressing outrage at Dinkley's cruelty toward the man in dinner jacket, yet he himself has a shady past involving stealing an accordion from a blind monkey. When Homer confesses to abandoning his father instead of donating a kidney, the Frenchman is disgusted enough to help throw him overboard. His hypocrisy—condemning Homer's misdeed while having committed his own theft—adds a darkly comic edge to his otherwise gloomy demeanor. He appears only briefly in the animated shorts era of the show, embodying the tragicomic tone of the Lost Souls' seafaring existence. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: Homer disgusted him, even though he had stolen his accordion from a blind monkey.
quotes: Homer disgusted him, even though he had stolen his accordion from a blind monkey.

title: General Sherman
text: General Sherman is A legendary giant catfish that lives in Catfish Lake, featured in a Simpsons episode. General Sherman is an enormous, legendary catfish said to weigh five hundred pounds and be over a century old, residing in Catfish Lake. His fame is kept alive by the local worm man, who spins an exaggerated tale of the fish to customers at a nearby service station, complete with a blurry photo reminiscent of the classic Loch Ness Monster hoax image. Homer accidentally hooks the fish while trying to return a stranger's fishing pole, leading to a wild struggle that pulls him off the pier and across the lake. After finally subduing the fish, Homer faces a moment of reckoning when Marge sees the catch as proof of his selfish priorities during their marriage retreat, prompting him to release General Sherman back into the water. The encounter later gets folded into local folklore, transforming Homer into a mythical giant in the worm man's retelling. In a subtle, near-cut gag, the fish even winks at the camera during Homer and Marge's reconciliation, a moment Matt Groening reportedly disliked. Notable quotes: They say he's five hundred pounds of bottom-dwelling fury, don't you know. No one knows how old he is, but if you ask me, and most people do, he's a hundred years if he's a day. | Well, one fella came close [to catching General Sherman]. Went by the name of Homer. Seven feet tall he was, with arms like tree trunks. His eyes were like steel, cold, hard. Had a shock of hair, red like the fires of Hell ...
quotes: They say he's five hundred pounds of bottom-dwelling fury, don't you know. No one knows how old he is, but if you ask me, and most people do, he's a hundred years if he's a day.

Well, one fella came close [to catching General Sherman]. Went by the name of Homer. Seven feet tall he was, with arms like tree trunks. His eyes were like steel, cold, hard. Had a shock of hair, red like the fires of Hell ...

title: The Patriarch
text: The Patriarch is Minor character; boss of The Parson, appeared briefly in the Springfield religious community. The Patriarch is a minor religious authority figure who oversees The Parson and appears to hold some level of influence over local church affairs. He is shown checking in on Reverend Lovejoy's performance, revealing a somewhat demanding or results-driven attitude toward conversions and church attendance. His brief appearance highlights the humorous, bureaucratic side of Springfield's religious institutions, treating soul-saving like a quota-based job. Despite his authoritative position, the exchange with Lovejoy underscores the show's frequent satire of organized religion. He has not appeared frequently, making him a obscure one-episode character tied to a single storyline. His design and demeanor suggest a stern, no-nonsense personality fitting his supervisory role. Voiced by Kevin Michael Richardson. Notable quotes: "negative six."
quotes: "negative six."

title: Prudence
text: Prudence is A minor recurring resident of the Springfield Retirement Castle. Prudence is an elderly woman living out her retirement at the Springfield Retirement Castle. She's a background figure who Homer comes to recognize after spending enough time visiting the facility. She's often seen in the company of fellow resident Lemuel, suggesting some kind of companionship among the retirement home's residents. Visually, she bears a strong resemblance to another elderly character, Bea Simmons, which has led to some confusion between the two. Prudence doesn't speak in her appearances, existing mainly as part of the retirement home's ensemble of elderly background characters. She has popped up in a handful of episodes over the years, always in her role as a quiet fixture of the Retirement Castle setting.

title: The Rambler
text: The Rambler is Superhero alter ego of Abraham Simpson, member of The Dependables. The Rambler is the costumed superhero identity taken on by Grampa Abraham Simpson within the non-canon superhero universe of the show. He joins the ranks of The Dependables, a group assembled to fill in after other heroes are taken out of action. His recruitment comes about specifically because Fruit Bat Man is captured by the villain known as The Abominable Dr. Lenny, creating a need for reinforcements. True to his name and to Grampa's usual persona, his so-called superpower is simply being able to bore people, likely through his trademark rambling stories rather than any real combat ability. As a character, he serves as a comedic parody of the archetypal all-powerful hero, specifically referencing Superman. His appearance is limited mostly to a single episode and the mobile game Tapped Out, keeping him a minor, novelty addition to the extended Simpsons superhero cast. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Cyrus Simpson
text: Cyrus Simpson is Abraham Simpson's older brother, a non-canon WWII Navy pilot character. Cyrus Simpson is Grampa Abe Simpson's long-lost older brother, introduced in a non-canon Christmas special. He served alongside Abe as a Navy pilot during World War II, sharing his brother's superstitious streak through a treasured musical pocket watch he considered his good luck charm. After being shot down by enemy planes and presumed dead, he actually survived and washed up in Tahiti, where he settled down permanently. His idea of settling down was extreme, as he ended up marrying fifteen different wives instead of returning home to reconnect with Abe. He's portrayed as easygoing and content with his tropical island life, insisting on the technicality that having many wives is different from just having a lot of casual relationships. Since he never appears outside this one special and is absent from any official Simpson family trees, he's treated as a non-canon relative. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Cyrus said that he had wives, not girlfriends.
quotes: Cyrus said that he had wives, not girlfriends.

title: Persuasive man
text: Persuasive man is A minor recurring Springfield resident hired for his supposed persuasive skills. The persuasive man is a minor character whose defining trait is his reputation for being highly persuasive, though this label is largely ironic given his actual track record. Homer once enlisted him to convince Sideshow Bob to leave Springfield, sending him armed with a gun to negotiate at The Aristocrat. Despite his supposed talent for persuasion, he was unable to talk Bob into leaving, undermining the very premise of his role. He later resurfaces in a more civic capacity, attending one of Lisa's town meetings concerning Lake Springfield. Overall, he functions as a background gag character, appearing briefly to serve a specific plot purpose rather than having a developed personality or ongoing storyline. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Robotic Richard Simmons
text: Robotic Richard Simmons is A malfunctioning robotic double of fitness guru Richard Simmons, used as a security/scare device by Mr. Burns; appears in a deleted scene from a Season 5 episode. This character is a mechanical stand-in for real-life fitness personality Richard Simmons, built with the same curly hair and released by Smithers at Mr. Burns' command to frighten off intruders like Homer. It blasts disco music and dances wildly, quickly spiraling out of control and alarming Burns, Smithers, and Bart, who fear it might turn violent. Even after being shot in the head, it regenerates in a nod to the shapeshifting villain from the Terminator films, continuing its frantic booty-shaking routine. The gag escalates until the robot literally explodes, sending its head flying down the driveway. Though filmed for an episode, the scene never made it to air due to a poor reaction during the table reading, and instead surfaced later as archive footage in a retrospective special. Ironically, the real Richard Simmons wanted to appear on the show but backed out once he learned he'd only be voicing this robotic counterpart. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: His ass is gonna blow!
quotes: His ass is gonna blow!

title: Fred Rogers
text: Fred Rogers is Real-world children's television host who appears as a caricatured guest character in The Simpsons. This is a fictionalized version of the beloved real-life PBS television host, author, and producer known for his gentle, sweater-wearing persona. In the show, his wholesome image is subverted for comedic effect, most notably when he's shown joining an angry mob out for Homer's blood. Another gag reveals a secret videotape of him taping his show while intoxicated, arguing about his signature cardigan. Bart even claims the mild-mannered host secretly used crude language like "get bent." His trademark red sweater becomes a punchline elsewhere, referenced when other characters try to emulate his calm, folksy style. Overall, he's used as a one-off cameo/reference character rather than a recurring cast member, poking fun at the contrast between his gentle public image and the show's exaggerated antics. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: It's a beautiful day... to kick your ass!
quotes: It's a beautiful day... to kick your ass!

title: Deion Overstreet
text: Deion Overstreet is Running back for the San Antonio Cow Skulls who appears in a football-themed episode with the Simpsons. Deion Overstreet is a professional football player who visits the Simpsons household to purchase the rights to Homer's goofy dance for $1,000, intending to use it as a touchdown celebration. He's frustrated that his usual celebrations aren't flashy enough to make the highlight reels, so he ends up hiring Homer as a personal choreographer for new celebratory moves. His storyline touches on themes of showmanship and spectacle in professional sports, as he later performs a range of exaggerated celebrations after scoring, including one requested by a sick child. The character is a clear parody of real-life NFL star Deion Sanders, both in name and his flashy persona. He's a minor, one-episode character whose antics tie into Homer's brief side career as a dance consultant. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Antoine Tex O'Hara
text: Antoine Tex O'Hara is Former owner of the Springfield Isotopes baseball team. Antoine Tex O'Hara is a minor recurring figure known primarily as the man who once ran the Springfield Isotopes. He's the one who spotted Homer's crowd-pleasing dance moves during a losing game and decided to make him the team's mascot, later even loaning him out to the Capital City Capitals to boost a fading rival mascot's act. Beyond baseball, he pops up as an ordinary Springfield resident, joining the crowd hoping to see Michael Jackson and later taking part in a mass attempt to build the world's tallest human pyramid. He's a background character rather than a driver of major plots, mostly defined by his connection to Homer's brief stint as a baseball mascot. His ownership of the Isotopes is later superseded in continuity when the Duff Corporation's Howard K. Duff is named as the team's owner. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Ramona
text: Ramona is A minor recurring character, wife of Ben, who appears in the Simpsons universe. Ramona is a minor character known primarily through her marriage to Ben, making her first appearance in the episode "Dangers on a Train." She also shows up briefly in the opening sequence gag of "Homer's Adventures Through the Windshield Glass." Beyond her family connection, little else is detailed about her personality or habits in the show. She falls into the category of adult recurring characters voiced by a guest star. Her role appears limited to supporting appearances rather than a major storyline of her own. As with many one-off spouses in the series, she exists mostly to add background depth to her husband's character. Voiced by Lisa Lampanelli.

title: Rumbleina
text: Rumbleina is A minor professional wrestler character who appears briefly in the Simpsons universe. Rumbleina is a female professional wrestler best known for her chaotic on-screen wedding to fellow wrestler Dr. Bonebreak, held live in the ring for television audiences. The marriage quickly fell apart, escalating into a physical brawl where she notably used a fire extinguisher as a weapon against her new husband. She appears to be a parody of wrestling personality Miss Elizabeth, mirroring the real-life relationship between Elizabeth and 'Macho Man' Randy Savage, whom Dr. Bonebreak seems to be based on. Rumbleina is a non-speaking character, existing mainly as a visual gag tied to professional wrestling culture. She later appears in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out as part of a wrestling-themed content set. Overall, she represents a brief but memorable parody of over-the-top wrestling drama and celebrity relationships.

title: Big Shirtless Ron
text: Big Shirtless Ron is A minor cast member on the fictional country-western variety show Ya Hoo!. Big Shirtless Ron is a background performer on the in-universe program Ya Hoo!, notable chiefly for one distinguishing feature: he never wears a shirt. He doesn't speak in his appearances, functioning purely as a visual gag tied to the show's country-western aesthetic. His presence is mostly incidental, appearing as part of the cast during a segment featuring the fictional variety program. He later shows up again in a more subtle way, as his image appears on a poster outside a nightclub, suggesting he has some minor level of fame or recognition within the show's universe. Despite his limited screen time, his oddly specific name and single defining trait have made him a memorable piece of Simpsons trivia. He remains a non-speaking, recurring background character rather than a fully developed one.

title: Phil (reporter)
text: Phil (reporter) is Minor recurring television reporter in Springfield. Phil is a minor television news reporter who appears in the early days of Springfield's local news coverage. He's best known for covering Bart's heroics at Chupo's Candy Store, giving him a small moment in the spotlight. His career takes a downward turn over time, as he gets demoted to operating a boom microphone before being fired altogether. Phil essentially served as a placeholder newsman before the show settled on more permanent reporter characters. Once Scott Christian and Kent Brockman were established as the show's go-to news personalities, Phil's role was phased out, though he still popped up in a background cameo afterward. In one of his appearances, his voice was noted to sound quite similar to Kent Brockman's. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Richard's father
text: Richard's father is Minor recurring background character; father of Richard, a classmate of Bart. Richard's father is a minor, largely background figure known mainly through his familial connection to his son Richard. He has gray hair and no notable occupation is given in the source material. He is depicted as a non-speaking character, appearing silently in various episodes without any dialogue. One of his few documented actions was attending the Bounce-A-Thon event alongside his wife and son. Beyond this brief family outing, little else is known about his personality or habits, as he mostly exists as set dressing in crowd or family scenes throughout the show's later seasons.

title: Radioactive Dog
text: Radioactive Dog is Radioactive Man's dog sidekick in the in-universe Radioactive Man comic books. Radioactive Dog, nicknamed Glowy, is a comic-book companion to the superhero Radioactive Man within the Simpsons universe's fictional comics. He wasn't always a dog—he started life as an ordinary turtle given as a birthday gift, until a stray blast from an atomic weapon test mutated him into a canine. Because his intended owner, Bug Boy, turned out to be allergic to dogs, Radioactive Man kept him instead, and the loyal pet became a recurring fixture in the hero's adventures. Glowy shows bravery beyond his size, once biting the villainous Larva Girl to rescue a hostage during a superhero wedding gone wrong. An alternate Substitute Earth version of the character also exists, belonging to Radioactive Boy, who meets a tragic end after being crushed while helping battle the monster Nega-Pneumatica. His death is treated with unexpected pathos, as Radioactive Man comforts the grieving Radioactive Boy afterward.

title: Maria Quimby
text: Maria Quimby is Ex-wife of action star Rainier Wolfcastle and member of the extended Quimby family. Maria Shriver-Kennedy Quimby is a minor recurring character best known as the former spouse of movie star Rainier Wolfcastle. She appeared as his wife when their wedding was infamously photographed by paparazzi Homer, leading to tension over Wolfcastle's promise not to seek revenge. Her name and background are a clear parody of the real-life Kennedy family, mirroring how Wolfcastle himself spoofs Arnold Schwarzenegger. She is specifically modeled after journalist Maria Shriver, drawing on Shriver's own real-life divorce from Schwarzenegger for the joke. Beyond her connection to Wolfcastle, she has made a handful of brief appearances across the show's run, including a Treehouse of Horror parody segment and an appearance as an ancestor in a flashback episode. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: he had promised a day without revenge
quotes: he had promised a day without revenge

title: Stark Richdale
text: Stark Richdale is Motivational teacher of the extension class "Successmanship 101" who inspires Homer to become CEO. Stark Richdale is a flamboyant self-help guru who runs a night class aimed at teaching people to be aggressive and confident in order to succeed in business. He wrote a book called Megatronics, The 48 Tips to Corporate Success, and preaches that life is easy for those willing to take it by force. He flaunts his wealth with an absurdly jewel-encrusted watch that no longer functions and a rare Bentley he claims was given to him alongside Steven Spielberg. His teachings directly inspire Homer to seize control of his career, briefly making him CEO of the power plant. Despite his showy, over-the-top demeanor, he appears only sporadically afterward, popping up in background cameos like the Trappuccino incident and a town meeting about Mr. Burns. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Now, life is hard, am I right? Wrong! Life is easy! You suck!
quotes: Now, life is hard, am I right? Wrong! Life is easy! You suck!

title: Ross Perot
text: Ross Perot is Real-world businessman and third-party presidential candidate who appears/is referenced as a minor character in the show. Ross Perot appears in The Simpsons as a real-world figure referenced in connection with American politics and pop culture. He's mentioned as the subject of most of Bart's ghostwritten biography during Bart's brief fame as the "I Didn't Do It Boy," showing how tangential and absurd his inclusion in the show's universe can be. He shows up in background gags, like an old campaign T-shirt owned by the Hibberts, and is even chosen by Ralph Wiggum as a write-in vote for a school club leader. In a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment, he's portrayed as an alien-adjacent bystander furious about the two-party system, punching a hole through his own hat in frustration. He's also comedically dispatched in fictional media within the show, such as being killed off in an in-universe McBain movie. Overall, Perot functions less as a developed character and more as a recurring satirical reference point for American politics.

title: Nancy Reagan
text: Nancy Reagan is Real-world First Lady of the United States, wife of Ronald Reagan, depicted as a background/mentioned figure in the show. Nancy Reagan appears in the show as a real-world historical figure rather than a fleshed-out character, never given any dialogue of her own. She is first seen as a background figure alongside her husband Ronald Reagan watching The Be Sharps perform at a Liberty Weekend concert. Her name is later invoked as an insult when Bart and Lisa mock Sideshow Bob by likening him and Birch Barlow to "Ronnie and his Nancy." She's also the subject of a running mix-up gag when Krusty confuses her with Betty Ford while interviewing Gerald Ford. A humorous nod to real history appears when Marge's photo album includes a picture of Nancy sitting on Mr. T's lap, referencing an actual 1983 White House photograph. The show later acknowledged her real death in 2016 within the wiki's behind-the-scenes notes.

title: Wolfgang Puck (character)
text: Wolfgang Puck (character) is Real-life celebrity chef who makes cameo appearances in the Simpsons universe. Wolfgang Puck appears as a fictionalized version of himself, the famous Austrian chef and restaurateur, popping up in Springfield in a handful of odd cameo roles. He once ran a gourmet food booth at a school fair, offering bizarre high-end twists on ordinary snacks like wasabi-portobello Rice Krispies squares. His enthusiasm for culinary innovation is played for laughs, especially when he excitedly embraces Marge's much simpler M&M Rice Krispies idea as a potential internet business. He drives around in a novelty vehicle called the Puckmobile, reinforcing his over-the-top celebrity persona. Beyond his live appearance, he's referenced as a recognizable chef icon, showing up in Marge's dream and as a captcha image on a parody website. Despite his fame, other characters like Lunchlady Dora don't rank him as their favorite, poking fun at his celebrity status among more down-to-earth tastes. Voiced by Wolfgang Puck (Himself).

title: Mike Scioscia (character)
text: Mike Scioscia (character) is Real-life MLB player/manager who appears as a member of the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant softball team. Mike Scioscia is a real-world baseball figure who crosses into Springfield lore after Waylon Smithers recruits him to join the power plant's softball team while he's out hunting. He takes the plant job mainly for the appeal of working with big machinery, finding it a welcome change from the pressures of professional baseball. Despite being hired purely to play softball, his eagerness to actually work at the plant lands him in the hospital with radiation poisoning. Oddly, the radiation exposure doesn't ruin him—it seemingly grants him mysterious "super-management powers" that later help him guide the Los Angeles Angels to a World Series win, along with a bizarre side effect of being able to demagnetize credit cards. He later shows up in a non-canon capacity attending a premiere in Los Angeles, reinforcing his role as a celebrity cameo character rather than a core member of the cast. Voiced by Himself.

title: Dan Rather (character)
text: Dan Rather (character) is Real-world journalist appearing as himself in cameo roles within the Simpsons universe. Dan Rather appears in the show as a fictionalized version of himself, playing the part of a veteran television news anchor. He's shown interacting with other real and fictional journalists, including bantering with Tom Brokaw and teasing Kent Brockman by swiping his microphone. His most substantial role comes during election coverage in Springfield, where he serves as a debate commentator after the town's primary schedule causes chaos. He also turns up at a support group for former news anchors, offering Kent Brockman some world-weary wisdom about the rarity of honest journalism. Overall, he functions as a minor recurring guest cameo representing real broadcast news culture rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Himself.

title: Mr. Rhenquist
text: Mr. Rhenquist is Father of Francine Rhenquist, a minor recurring character. Mr. Rhenquist is a minor character best known as the father of the aggressive bully Francine Rhenquist. He appeared alongside his wife helping to contain their daughter, showing a somewhat casual attitude toward her violent behavior. His brief role in the show centers on a single notable incident involving Francine's participation in a science event that went awry. Despite limited screen time, he has recurred sporadically across several later seasons. He is portrayed as a mild-mannered, background figure with little characterization beyond his parental role. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: Mr. Rhenquist said that Francine was going to sleep well that night.
quotes: Mr. Rhenquist said that Francine was going to sleep well that night.

title: Tom Petty (character)
text: Tom Petty (character) is Real-world musician who appeared as himself in guest episodes of The Simpsons. Tom Petty appears as a fictionalized version of himself, teaching a songwriting workshop at a rock camp attended by Homer. He initially insists on the importance of thoughtful lyrics, but caves to audience demand for mindless rock anthems, poking fun at his own artistic image. During a charity concert, he and other musicians turn on Homer after being annoyed with him, leading to a chaotic fire that costs Petty a toe. Despite the mayhem, he's shown to be gracious, apologizing to Homer afterward and inviting him back to perform. He later shows up as a face on a website's musician-themed captcha test. In a non-canon dream sequence, he's depicted as a guitar-carrying angel, reflecting his real-life passing. Voiced by Tom Petty (Himself).

title: Bill O'Reilly
text: Bill O'Reilly is Real-world American political commentator and author who appears as a picture-only/non-speaking character in The Simpsons. Bill O'Reilly is depicted in the show purely as a real-world media personality rather than a speaking character. He is shown on the covers of several satirical books, including 'Killing Hannity' alongside Sean Hannity and 'The O'Reilly Factor for Kids,' poking fun at his prolific non-fiction and children's book output. His likeness appears in a Treehouse of Horror segment and in a background gag during a live episode segment, where Lisa references a parking spot bearing his name. In later specials tied to Donald Trump, additional fictional O'Reilly books are name-dropped as being owned by Trump, continuing the running joke about his endless bibliography. Since he never appears as an active participant in the plot, he functions mainly as a topical cameo and satire on media pundits. His presence is entirely non-canon and limited to visual gags and passing mentions.

title: Nutcracker
text: Nutcracker is A mall employee costumed as a Christmas Nutcracker character, appearing in "I Won't Be Home for Christmas". The Nutcracker is a costumed mall worker who embodies one of the many festive characters roaming Towne Centre at Springfielde Glenne during the holidays. He first appears waking Homer up after he'd fallen asleep on a mall bench, revealing a more mundane, tired employee underneath the whimsical costume. Despite the initial gruffness of telling Homer the mall is closed and he needs to leave, the Nutcracker shows some compassion when Homer explains he's away from his family for Christmas, inviting him to an employees-only party. He's later grouped with other whimsical mall mascots described as the "magical creatures of the mall," hinting at a larger ensemble of holiday-themed characters working behind the scenes. The character plays on the contrast between childlike Christmas wonder and the weary reality of retail work during the holiday season. He also appears as a collectible character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Al Roker (character)
text: Al Roker (character) is Real-life celebrity (TV weatherman) who appears as himself in cameo roles in Springfield. Al Roker is a real-world television personality who makes a brief cameo appearance in Springfield, playing himself. He's recognized around town enough that characters like Carl reference him casually, comparing his bald appearance to other characters. His most notable interaction comes when Bart tries to get his autograph, only to try to sell it back to him, prompting Roker to offer to buy it himself. Beyond his direct appearance, his image and name pop up in the background of the show as a running gag, appearing on posters and book covers referencing bald black celebrities. He's more of a recurring background/cameo figure than a fully developed character, existing mostly for quick jokes tied to his real-life fame. Voiced by Al Roker (Himself).

title: Ribhead
text: Ribhead is A minor recurring hippie character who follows the Ribwich burger around the country. The Ribhead is part of a wandering band of hippies devoted to tracking down the limited-time Ribwich sandwich wherever it's sold. He first appears when Homer learns the Ribwich is only available temporarily, and the Ribhead invites him to join their traveling group in pursuit of the burger. He turns up again in San Francisco on the very last day the Ribwich is offered, showing his commitment to the cause. Later, he's spotted attending a Cheech and Chong concert, fitting his laid-back, counterculture persona. His look, complete with graying, balding hair, fits the aging-hippie stereotype. Overall he's a minor background character used for comic flavor rather than any deep storyline. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Abraham Simpson I
text: Abraham Simpson I is Ancestor of the Simpson family; son of Mabel and Virgil Simpson, and great-grandfather of Abraham "Grampa" Simpson. Abraham Simpson I is a historical ancestor within the Simpson family lineage, born to Mabel and Virgil Simpson shortly after their escape from slaveholders with the help of Abraham Lincoln. He was named in honor of Lincoln, who had given the family his own hat as a token of the encounter. Physically, he bore a strong resemblance to his descendant Bart Simpson, though with messier hair. He is noted as the likely namesake for his great-grandson, Grampa Simpson. According to family legend, he may have been the ancestor who accidentally invented the Simpson & Son Revitalizing Tonic while searching for a cheap substitute for holy water. He appears only briefly on-screen and has no recorded dialogue, existing mostly as a piece of family backstory rather than an active character.

title: Jack Ruby
text: Jack Ruby is Real-world historical figure referenced in Simpsons episodes; killer of Lee Harvey Oswald. Jack Ruby is not an original Simpsons character but a real historical figure who is referenced a few times in the show. He appears as a subject of parody when Itchy and Scratchy recreate the famous Oswald shooting in a cartoon directed by Oliver Stone. He's also the punchline of a joke where Homer misunderstands his identity, thinking 'Jack Ruby' is a valuable jewel rather than a person. Additionally, his infamous image is used in a mock campaign video during Krusty the Clown's congressional run, with Krusty's face superimposed over the photograph. His presence in the show is entirely tied to historical parody and dark comedic references rather than any ongoing storyline.

title: Rowan Priddis
text: Rowan Priddis is Cruise entertainment director aboard the Royalty Valhalla cruise ship featured in a Simpsons episode. Rowan Priddis is the relentlessly upbeat entertainment director for the Royalty Valhalla cruise line, whose job is to ensure every passenger has a good time. He's a constant presence over the ship's intercom, hyping up activities and attractions in his announcements. His musical number about savoring the moment inadvertently sparks Bart's obsession with never wanting the cruise to end. After a virus outbreak disrupts the voyage, he adapts his announcements to warn passengers away from a spa turned cult and to describe an unappetizing dinner menu of seagull, barnacles, and jellyfish. He also takes on a judicial role by presiding over the ship's makeshift Fun Court. Overall, he represents the forced cheerfulness and absurd bureaucracy of cruise ship culture within the episode's satire. Voiced by Steve Coogan.

title: Burt Reynolds
text: Burt Reynolds is Real-world actor and comedian referenced/appearing as a minor character in the Simpsons universe. Burt Reynolds appears as a fictionalized version of himself within the Simpsons world, mostly referenced by other characters rather than playing a major role. He is tied to the idea of a lavish, masculine lifestyle, as seen when Chuck Garabedian encourages the Flanders family to live like him despite their modest income. His larger-than-life persona is played for laughs, such as when Springfield's fire trucks are commandeered to film his fictional movie "Fireball and Mudflap" during an actual emergency. He's also the subject of odd trivia, including having been the first male centerfold in Cosmopolitan and playing Gator McKlusky in White Lightning. Memorabilia like one of his mustaches even shows up as a bar decoration, underscoring his celebrity status in Springfield's pop culture landscape. He mostly exists as a punchline and pop-culture reference point rather than a fully developed character. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Paul Simon
text: Paul Simon is Real-world singer-songwriter referenced/appearing as a minor character in The Simpsons. Paul Simon appears as a real-world celebrity cameo tied to his fame as half of the duo Simon & Garfunkel. He briefly shows up as a contestant on Krusty's Li'l Starmaker, only to be disqualified once the judges realize he's an adult impersonating a child contestant. Beyond this appearance, he's mostly referenced in jokes and comparisons made by other characters, such as Principal Skinner likening hose nozzles to the duo's harmony, or Homer invoking Simon's reconciliation with Art Garfunkel as an example for feuding friends to follow. He's also imagined by Homer and Ned during a drug-induced hallucination as one of history's famous pairs. Despite his recurring mentions, Paul Simon remains a non-speaking character whose role is more about cultural reference than personality or dialogue. He's also noted as being included on Ned Flanders' list of admirable liberal figures.

title: Don Pardo (character)
text: Don Pardo (character) is Real-world celebrity guest character who appears via voice-over cameo in the show. Don Pardo is a real-life radio and television announcer who makes brief cameo appearances in the show purely through voice-over. His most notable moment comes when Moe complains about how exhausting doing a voice-over is, prompting Pardo's voice to reply that he's paid far more than Moe could imagine. He also turns up as a voice heard through a cellphone, tied to Mary Spuckler's claim to fame on Saturday Night Live. Pardo never appears visually in the show, existing only as a disembodied voice referencing his real-world career as an announcer. His cameos serve as quick, self-referential jokes about show business and payment for voice work rather than developing any storyline. As a recurring but minor real-world character, he's used sparingly for comedic effect tied to his actual profession. Voiced by Don Pardo (Himself). Notable quotes: he made more than Moe could possibly imagine
quotes: he made more than Moe could possibly imagine

title: Sedan bot
text: Sedan bot is Non-canon transformer robot version of Homer's car, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Sedan Bot is a one-off, non-canon character that started out as Homer's ordinary pink sedan before being transformed by a toy Bart bought at a Malibu Stacy store. Once activated, it becomes a fully autonomous robot, ejecting its driver through a hole in the back and moving and speaking on its own. It exists purely as a spoof of the Transformers franchise, specifically mimicking Optimus Prime in design and role. Its main claim to fame in the show's mythology is a battle against the Geo Metro bot during the segment's chaotic robot-uprising storyline. Beyond this brief Treehouse of Horror appearance, the Sedan Bot also shows up as a collectible decoration in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. It has no dialogue attributed to it and no ongoing relationships or personality traits beyond its robotic combat role.

title: The Scarlet Floozy
text: The Scarlet Floozy is Comic-book supervillain from the Radioactive Man comics, member of the Threatening Threesome and enemy of Radioactive Man. The Scarlet Floozy is a red-haired villainess who appears exclusively in the Bongo comics tied to the Radioactive Man mythos. As part of the Threatening Threesome, she regularly clashes with the superhero Radioactive Man and his allies. Despite her criminal ways, she harbors a soft spot for Radioactive Man, even expressing regret over her villainous life when she learns he is getting married to someone else. She's shown to be capable in combat, using captives as leverage, though she isn't always successful, having been bested by Weasel Woman during a wedding brawl. Her appearances tie her closely to the ongoing soap-opera-like drama and battles within the Radioactive Man comic universe.

title: Scarlett O'Hara
text: Scarlett O'Hara is Fictional character from Gone with the Wind who appears in a parody clip shown within The Simpsons. Scarlett O'Hara is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover figure lifted from the classic film Gone with the Wind, appearing only in brief clips within the show. She is depicted alongside her husband Rhett Butler in a heavily edited, senior-friendly version of the movie screened at the Springfield Retirement Castle. In that altered version, the film's tone is changed so that the couple appears to reconcile happily, contrasting with the original bittersweet ending. She also shows up in a separate romantic movie montage featuring famous on-screen kisses, tying her image to a moment involving Bart and Nikki McKenna. Her role in the show is purely as a nostalgic pop-culture reference rather than a developed character with her own personality or running gags. She exists in the Simpsons universe strictly through these two brief cinematic cameos. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Scuzzo
text: Scuzzo is A minor recurring clown character in the Simpsons universe, associated with Krusty the Clown and the circus world. Scuzzo is a working clown who spends time both in Krusty's orbit and among Springfield's wider clown community. He once served as the right-hand man to the ringmaster at Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus, where he showed Krusty around, fired him after a disastrous debut, and later praised him after a triumphant performance. Despite this brief camaraderie, Scuzzo held a grudge against Krusty for abandoning circus clowning for television, branding him a traitor to real clowns. He's shown to be part of Springfield's broader clown social scene, participating in a trivia team at Moe's Tavern and gossiping about clowns who left TV work at a restaurant gathering. Scuzzo also has ties to the business side of clowning, having been managed at one point by a shady talent manager. He's regarded within the show's universe as one among a group of notably unfunny or lesser clowns. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: He didn't need to worry about him, as he was voted America's least funny clown in Laff Ways. | Scuzzo told Krusty that his act was the bravest act he had ever seen. | Scuzzo told Krusty that he was a TV clown and a traitor to their kind before getting on the train as it pulled away.
quotes: He didn't need to worry about him, as he was voted America's least funny clown in Laff Ways.
Scuzzo told Krusty that his act was the bravest act he had ever seen.
Scuzzo told Krusty that he was a TV clown and a traitor to their kind before getting on the train as it pulled away.

title: Sandra (Game Done Changed)
text: Sandra (Game Done Changed) is Principal of the Limitless Frontier Horizons school, appearing in an episode involving Springfield Elementary. Sandra serves as the nominal principal of the Limitless Frontier Horizons school, a progressive institution where students supposedly direct their own education. She comes across as somewhat ineffectual, deflecting Principal Skinner and Bart's concerns about a feud between their schools rather than addressing them directly. Her attempt to redirect the conversation toward a mundane school fundraiser highlights her avoidance of real authority. The twist in her story is that she isn't actually in charge at all—her colleague Truth-Anne holds the real power. Ultimately, she loses her job over trying to turn a chaotic incident into a teaching moment, though she seems oddly unbothered by her own firing. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Sam Simon (character)
text: Sam Simon (character) is A minor character who worked as a writer for The Itchy & Scratchy Show, based on the real-life Simpsons executive producer of the same name. Sam Simon is depicted as one of the many staff writers toiling under Roger Meyers, Jr. on The Itchy & Scratchy Show. Like his fellow writers, he finds himself out of a job when Meyers abruptly fires the entire writing staff to bring in Abraham Simpson instead. In a separate non-canon appearance, he's portrayed as an executive producer of The Simpsons itself, sporting long nails and long white hair, with a design clearly inspired by the eccentric recluse Howard Hughes. The character doesn't speak on screen, making him a background/cameo figure rather than a major player. A special tribute version of the character was later created by the show's publicity artists to honor the real Sam Simon after his passing, underscoring the character's meta connection to one of the show's actual co-creators.

title: Patricia
text: Patricia is A wealthy Springfield socialite and member of the country club social circle, acquainted with Marge Simpson. Patricia is a well-to-do member of Springfield's upper-crust social scene, first encountering Marge after being introduced by Evelyn Peters at the Springfield Glen Country Club. She's married to a man named Wif, and the couple employs a housekeeper named Iris to manage their household affairs. Despite their wealth, Patricia and Wif once caused a chaotic mess trying to microwave soup themselves late at night rather than disturb Iris, showing a mix of consideration and domestic helplessness. She shares the snobbish attitude common among her social circle, such as agreeing that arguing with retail staff is pointless when mail order shopping is available. Patricia appears frequently as a background fixture at Springfield's high-society gatherings and parties, representing the recurring cast of affluent townsfolk who orbit around Marge's social life. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Irish Pete
text: Irish Pete is A minor recurring elderly Springfield resident of Irish descent. Irish Pete is an older townsperson known for his thick Irish brogue and his good-natured tolerance of Springfield's odd traditions. He appears during Whacking Day, confirming the holiday's dark origins as an excuse to beat up the Irish, yet he shrugs it off as harmless fun. He's shown to be a community-minded citizen, taking part in a neighborhood watch meeting, and sentimental at heart, tearing up during Barney's debut performance with The Be Sharps. His name itself is a small running joke, playing on the term for Irish peat. In a non-canon appearance, he shows a bit of gullibility, misunderstanding a costume reference and believing it revealed a person's father he claimed to have gone to school with. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: 'Tis true! I took many a lump, but 'twas all in good fun.
quotes: 'Tis true! I took many a lump, but 'twas all in good fun.

title: Rasputin the Friendly Russian
text: Rasputin the Friendly Russian is Minor recurring character; a professional wrestler in the Springfield universe who appeared in a televised wrestling match. Rasputin the Friendly Russian is a professional wrestler who competes for World Class Wrestling. Formerly billed as the villainous 'Mad Russian,' he rebranded himself as a friendly figure once the Soviet Union collapsed, softening his image to match the changing political climate. His most notable moment came in a hyped bout against Professor Werner von Brawn, where he dominated early on before losing to an underhanded wrench shot to the head. His name is a playful nod to the real historical mystic Grigori Rasputin, and his redemption arc echoes real-life wrestling gimmick shifts tied to Cold War politics. He has no spoken lines in his appearance, making him a background novelty character rather than a developed personality. Beyond his single televised episode appearance, he later resurfaced as a character in The Simpsons: Tapped Out video game.

title: Ricky Ricardo
text: Ricky Ricardo is Cuban bandleader character from the sitcom I Love Lucy, appearing as a crossover figure in The Simpsons. Ricky Ricardo is a crossover character brought into The Simpsons from the classic sitcom I Love Lucy, where he is portrayed as the Cuban husband of Lucy. In the show, he first appears in an episode that Homer and Bart are watching on television, with the volume loud enough for Lisa to overhear a conversation involving him slapping Lucy. Later, he takes on a more active role, appearing alongside the Simpson family during their voyage to Cuba aboard The Che Gue-Ferry. During this trip, he shows a bit of pride and sharpness, bluntly correcting Homer and boasting about Cubans' ability to pronounce difficult words like 'psychiatrist.' He also gets pulled into a comedic mix-up involving Fred Mertz and disguised women trying to sneak into a cigar store, which he resolves by offering to simply give them cigars. His appearances lean on nostalgia and gentle parody of his original sitcom persona rather than deep characterization within the Simpsons universe. Voiced by Karl Wiedergott, Chris Edgerly.

title: Mike Scully (character)
text: Mike Scully (character) is A real-world producer and writer of The Simpsons who appears as a background character within the show itself. Mike Scully is a self-referential character based on the actual Simpsons producer and writer of the same name. He appears as a non-speaking background figure in a handful of episodes rather than as a developed personality. He was once named on Kent Brockman's infamous list of people suspected of being gay. During a chaotic rhino escape from the zoo, he was shown fleeing the scene with his wife and children. He's also glimpsed waiting in a bathroom line at a concert. In the non-canon 138th Episode Spectacular, his contributions to the show were acknowledged alongside other production staff at Matt Groening's request.

title: Joan Rivers (character)
text: Joan Rivers (character) is Real-world celebrity caricature appearing as a minor recurring character in Springfield. Joan Rivers appears as a fictionalized version of the real-life comedian and actress, mostly through TV appearances and background cameos rather than direct interaction with the main cast. She's portrayed as a sharp-tongued insult comic, famously mocking Chief Wiggum on her talk show to the point he shoots his television in frustration. Her presence in Springfield lore extends beyond life, as she's later shown residing in Jewish Heaven, chatting with figures like King David. She's also honored with a star on the Jewish Walk of Fame, cementing her status among Springfield's Jewish celebrities. Her recurring gag involves being referenced or briefly glimpsed on television screens throughout multiple episodes, often for comedic effect tied to her comedic persona. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Pac-Man (character)
text: Pac-Man (character) is Crossover video game character from the classic arcade game, referenced/appearing in various Simpsons episodes. Pac-Man is the famous yellow arcade icon who occasionally pops up in Springfield in various nods to classic gaming culture. He's shown married to Ms. Pac-Man in a nostalgic Super Bowl halftime clip Homer watches, complete with the ghosts dancing along. His likeness turns up on novelty items like Comic Book Guy's pun-filled t-shirt, and Homer references him both in song (belting out a line from "Pac-Man Fever") and in his own confused train of thought, like mistaking an insult from Mr. Burns as being about the arcade machine beside him. He even becomes a costume for Homer during a Christmas-themed couch gag, comically "eating" his family until the invincibility power-up wears off at just the wrong moment. Beyond direct appearances, Pac-Man's design and fame get spoofed through parody games like Pac-Rat and Prac-Man within the show's universe. Overall, he's less a character with personality and more a recurring pop-culture touchstone the show returns to for jokes and references.

title: Mabel Simpson
text: Mabel Simpson is Great-great-great-grandmother of Homer Simpson, ancestor featured in a flashback episode. Mabel Simpson is an ancestral figure in the Simpson family tree, first seen married to Hiram Simpson before her life took a dramatic turn. She proves to be brave and defiant, standing up to Colonel Burns with a shotgun to protect Virgil, an escaped slave her daughter Eliza had taken in. Loyal to her convictions over her marriage, she ultimately leaves Hiram, divorces him, and flees north to Canada with Virgil despite the danger of being pursued as fugitives. Her journey includes a notable encounter with Abraham Lincoln, who helps her disguise herself. She resettles in Canada, marries Virgil, and the couple has a son, Abraham, continuing the Simpson family line. Her story highlights themes of courage and sacrifice within the family's history. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

title: Robin
text: Robin is Superhero sidekick to Batman, appearing as a background/parody character in Simpsons universe references to DC Comics. Robin, also known as Dick Grayson, is the classic superhero sidekick to Batman, appearing in Springfield lore mostly through references, costumes, and cameos rather than a fully developed character. He's shown alongside Batman in the Batmobile at the Hollywood Auto Museum, and his likeness turns up repeatedly at fan conventions like Comicalooza and Cartoon Con, where people dress up as him. The running gag around Robin tends to involve other characters cosplaying as him, such as Krusty the Clown's sidekick Mr. Teeny donning the costume for a masquerade ball, or Comic Book Guy briefly dressing as Robin during his death-recreation record attempt. He also appears in a hallucination sequence when Homer and Ned imagine themselves as famous superhero duos after taking a mind-altering substance. Overall, Robin functions less as an active character and more as a recurring pop-culture reference and costume motif throughout the series. Voiced by Karl Wiedergott, Burt Ward.

title: Sheila Redfield
text: Sheila Redfield is Daughter of Augustus Redfield and board member of RedStar; briefly befriends Lisa Simpson as part of a corporate scheme. Sheila Redfield is one of Augustus Redfield's children and a calculating member of the RedStar board of directors. Alongside her brothers Colby and Mav, she conspires to remove her father as CEO, believing he is too old to lead the company. To manipulate the situation, she feigns friendship with Lisa Simpson, taking her horseback riding and to the Lincoln Center in an effort to win over Grampa Simpson's vote. Her scheming ultimately backfires when Gus reveals he anticipated the betrayal, leading to her and her siblings being ousted from the company. She's portrayed as ambitious, manipulative, and willing to use personal relationships for corporate gain. The character is a clear parody of Siobhan "Shiv" Roy from the TV series Succession. Voiced by Krysten Ritter.

title: Merl Reagle (character)
text: Merl Reagle (character) is Real-world crossword constructor who appears as a guest character helping Homer reconcile with Lisa. Merl Reagle is a real-life crossword puzzle constructor who appears as himself in a special guest role on the show. He gets pulled into the Simpson family drama when Homer, desperate to apologize to Lisa after betting against her in a crossword championship, enlists Merl's professional skills to secretly embed an apology in a New York Times puzzle. Working alongside fellow real-world crossword editor Will Shortz, Merl helps craft a diagonal hidden message reading Lisa's forgiveness back into existence. He shows up unexpectedly in the Simpsons' living room once the plan succeeds, taking credit for constructing the clever puzzle. His appearance is brief but memorable, blending real-world puzzle culture with the show's fictional universe. He mostly serves the plot rather than displaying an extensive personality of his own. Voiced by Merl Reagle (Himself).

title: Patches
text: Patches is A minor recurring orphan character in Springfield, brother of Poor Violet. Patches is a poor orphan boy who lives with his sister, Poor Violet, in Springfield, surviving on scraps of charity and vitamin money. His nickname comes from his skill at sewing patches and his tendency to scratch the irritation from nettle stings, giving him a slightly comedic, ragged Dickensian air. He and his sister are often used as pitiable figures to tug at the town's heartstrings, most notably when they became unwitting symbols in the Praiseland scandal involving Ned Flanders and Homer. Despite their impoverished circumstances, the two children are resourceful and resilient, though they are frequently swept up in the schemes and mishaps of the adults around them. Visually and thematically, Patches is designed to evoke Tiny Tim from Charles Dickens' 'A Christmas Carol,' reinforcing his role as a symbol of Springfield's overlooked poor. Voiced by Pamela Hayden. Notable quotes: Two walls are not enough!
quotes: Two walls are not enough!

title: Seamus (A Serious Flanders)
text: Seamus (A Serious Flanders) is Debt collector and associate of Costas Becker in the non-canon "A Serious Flanders" storyline; husband of Colette. Seamus is a hired enforcer who works alongside his wife Colette collecting debts for the criminal Costas Becker. He's shown to be capable of violence, helping execute and dispose of a target without hesitation, but he also has a domestic side, caring for Colette by running her baths and cooking with her. Their relationship is strained by stress over never taking a vacation, leading to a heated argument that escalates into a literal fight to the death. Ironically, after they reconcile, an accident triggered by their earlier chaos ends up killing them both. Seamus's blunder of losing an address leads to the mistaken kidnapping of Homer instead of Ned Flanders, driving much of the story's comedy. He ultimately meets a darkly comedic end, crushed alongside his wife in a freak accident caused by a fire and a falling bathtub. Voiced by Chris O'Dowd.

title: Sergeant Sausage
text: Sergeant Sausage is Homer Simpson's imaginary friend, appearing in a non-canon Treehouse of Horror segment. Sergeant Sausage is a bizarre figment of Homer's imagination, conjured up as a sort of protector when Homer finds himself in mortal danger. He appears to be a tough, soldier-like character who springs into action to physically defend Homer, though his combat skills prove no match for a determined foe. His most memorable trait is his indestructibility despite seeming to meet a gruesome end, since being imaginary means he technically cannot die. This leads to an absurd, darkly comic exchange with Homer after his apparent demise. As a non-canon character, he exists purely for comedic effect within a Halloween-themed episode. He later resurfaces as part of a mobile game tie-in, cementing his place as a minor but memorable oddity in Homer's fantastical mind. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: get back in the microwave.
quotes: get back in the microwave.

title: Ralph-O-Cop
text: Ralph-O-Cop is A robot competitor in the Robot Rumble fighting show, built and owned by Chief Wiggum and his son Ralph. Ralph-O-Cop is a homemade battle robot entered into the Robot Rumble competition by Chief Wiggum and Ralph Wiggum. Its design reflects its creators' quirky sensibilities, rolling on tank treads, sporting a police cap, and displaying a picture of Ralph as its face. Armed with a single outstretched arm holding a gun, it takes an aggressive approach in its featured battle, opening fire on its opponent right away. Despite its initial advantage, the robot ultimately loses when its own weapon is turned against it. The character is a parody nod to RoboCop and later appears as an unlockable robot in The Simpsons: Tapped Out mobile game. Notable quotes: Well, if you wanna see a mailbox shoot a boy, that's about as close as you're gonna get.
quotes: Well, if you wanna see a mailbox shoot a boy, that's about as close as you're gonna get.

title: Richie Sakai
text: Richie Sakai is Minor recurring Springfield resident, an anesthesiologist and amateur musician. Richie Sakai is a background Springfield character who works as an anesthesiologist by profession but also has a passion for music. He's been seen enjoying a night out at Moe's Tavern, listening to Homer's tall tales, and later showed off his singing chops at a karaoke bar dedicated to his wife, Pattie. He's civically engaged enough to attend a town hall meeting about spending Mr. Burns' settlement money, and he even turned up in a satirical campaign ad for the villainous Sideshow Bob. Beyond his vocal talents, he's also skilled with the vibraphone, cementing his place among Springfield's jazz musician crowd. The character is a bit of an inside joke, being modeled after and named for the show's real-life producer Richard Sakai. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Nuclear inspectors
text: Nuclear inspectors is State and federal officials who inspect the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant for safety and competence violations. The nuclear inspectors are recurring background officials who appear whenever the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant comes under scrutiny, either from the state government or the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Their role is largely functional rather than comedic in personality, serving as the mechanism by which Mr. Burns's negligence and Homer's incompetence get exposed. State inspectors triggered a costly overhaul of the plant after the discovery of a mutated three-eyed fish, indirectly pushing Burns into a failed run for governor. Federal inspectors later arrive with a specialized simulator van to test employee competence, inadvertently exposing Homer's total unfitness for his job despite Smithers's attempts to hide him. Their strict, matter-of-fact demeanor and unwillingness to be bribed or intimidated highlight the show's satire of bureaucratic oversight clashing with Burns's corner-cutting management style. Ultimately their findings force real consequences, such as Homer being sent back to college for nuclear physics training. Voiced by Harry Shearer, Maggie Roswell, Hank Azaria.

title: Bamm-Bamm Rubble
text: Bamm-Bamm Rubble is Crossover cartoon character from The Flintstones appearing briefly in The Simpsons. Bamm-Bamm Rubble is a character borrowed from the classic animated series The Flintstones, appearing in The Simpsons only as a background or picture reference rather than a fully animated presence. He is depicted as the young son of Barney and Betty Rubble, tying him to the Flintstones' family dynamic. His appearances in The Simpsons are brief cameo-like nods to the source cartoon rather than storyline-driven moments. He shows up first on a novelty phone belonging to Bart, referencing the Flintstones theme. Later, he's pictured on a Flintstones-themed map used by Homer, shown carrying his father Barney. He has no dialogue and functions purely as a visual crossover gag rather than an active character in the Simpsons universe.

title: Red Dragon
text: Red Dragon is A hallucinated dragon figure that appears to Homer during his trip to China. The Red Dragon is a large, fiery-colored dragon that exists only within one of Homer's bizarre hallucinations. It appears alongside a White Dragon and a Yellow Dragon during Homer's visit to China, reacting dramatically when Homer offends the White Dragon by offering only a single peanut. The Red Dragon expresses its displeasure through song, mocking Homer's stinginess in a whimsical musical number. It later resurfaces as the Simpsons prepare to leave China, delivering an ominous farewell song that turns oddly apocalyptic. Despite its menacing appearance and dark warnings, the character is played for comic absurdity rather than genuine threat, fitting into the episode's surreal dream-logic tone. It has no interactions with the show's world beyond this single hallucinatory sequence. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: American jerks are going home. Now we sleep for a thousand years. When we wake the world will end.
quotes: American jerks are going home. Now we sleep for a thousand years. When we wake the world will end.

title: Sadgasm
text: Sadgasm is A fictional GRUNGE band formed by Homer Simpson in the 1990s, featuring Lenny, Carl, and Lou. Sadgasm started out as an R&B group, but Homer overhauled its sound after a jealous fit over seeing Marge with one of her university professors. He rebranded the act as a grunge band under the tongue-in-cheek genre name GRUNGE, standing for Guitar Rock Utilizing Nihilist Grunge Energy. The band debuted at Springfield University and produced a handful of memorable tracks, including a music video parody. Their career came to an abrupt end amid rumors of Homer's supposed drug problem, which was actually just an undiagnosed diabetes issue from excessive frappuccino consumption. The group serves as a parody of grunge-era rock bands and adds another layer to Homer's history of ridiculous side projects. It later resurfaced as a pop-culture reference, appearing as imagery within an in-universe website category.

title: Ray Patterson
text: Ray Patterson is Springfield's long-serving sanitation commissioner, elected sixteen years in a row, and Homer's rival in "Trash of the Titans". Ray Patterson is the hard-working, no-nonsense sanitation commissioner of Springfield, a rare example of a genuinely competent and sane public official in the show's world. His long, successful tenure is threatened when Homer decides to run against him on a wave of unrealistic promises, and Ray grows increasingly frustrated by how easily the town is swayed by empty rhetoric over his solid record. Despite the political rivalry, he tries to remain civil, though Homer's antics and the public's mockery eventually push him to lash out at the town's fickle judgment. After losing the election, he is proven right when Homer's mismanagement causes a literal garbage catastrophe, but Ray refuses to simply forgive and forget, spitefully declining reinstatement to let Springfield stew in the mess it created. He's noted for sharing similarities with Frank Grimes, particularly his diligence and disdain for Homer's incompetence. Ray later makes a brief non-speaking appearance during the events of the EPA dome crisis. Voiced by Steve Martin. Notable quotes: "nonsensical ravings of a loudmouthed malcontent" | "this sleazy lunatic"
quotes: "nonsensical ravings of a loudmouthed malcontent"
"this sleazy lunatic"

title: Al Simmons
text: Al Simmons is A minor executive at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant. Al Simmons is a background employee at the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, rarely seen but occasionally mentioned or glimpsed in early episodes. He's part of the plant's management, though little is known about his personality or day-to-day duties. His most notable appearance involves receiving a scandalous photo of Homer and Princess Kashmir from his friend Mike, tying him briefly into one of Homer's more embarrassing moments. He also shows up as an attendee at the ill-fated first ride of the Springfield Monorail. Overall, Al functions as a recurring but minor background character used to populate the plant's workforce and Springfield's crowd scenes. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Pelé
text: Pelé is Real-world Brazilian soccer legend who appears as a guest character in the Simpsons universe. Pelé is depicted as himself, the famous Brazilian football star, making a special appearance in Springfield. He speaks before an exhibition soccer match between Mexico and Portugal that the Simpson family attends. Beyond his live-action-style cameo, his fame permeates the show's world in smaller ways, such as being referenced in a comic book alongside Radioactive Man and being named on a list of notable left-handed people compiled by Ned Flanders. He's also humorously tied into the show's fictional media, having voiced a character in an in-universe cartoon short. As a real-world figure inserted into the show, his role is more about cultural cachet and cameo appeal than ongoing storylines. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Dave Schultz (character)
text: Dave Schultz (character) is Former hockey player who appears as a coach at Top Goon Academy in a minor guest role. Dave Schultz is a real-world hockey player who makes a cameo appearance as himself, playing a goon instructor at Top Goon Academy. Known by the nickname "The Hammer," he is introduced to students under that moniker but takes a moment to clarify his full given name. He serves as one of the coaches training students, including Nelson Muntz, in the rough style of goon hockey. His appearance is brief and largely functions as a nod to real hockey history and culture. He has no deep characterization beyond this cameo role, existing mainly as a novelty guest character. Voiced by Himself.

title: Pigboy
text: Pigboy is Non-canon superhero alter-ego of Chief Clancy Wiggum from the Bongo comics. Pigboy is the superpowered persona taken on by Clancy Wiggum after he's exposed to a nuclear explosion in the Bongo comic universe. Also referred to as Piggum, he exists purely within the non-canon comic storylines rather than the television series. His superhero identity ties into a larger group of transformed Springfield residents who gain abilities in similar circumstances. As a comic-exclusive character, Pigboy allows Wiggum's typically bumbling, donut-loving persona to be reimagined in a more action-oriented, superhero context.
