He appears across a handful of interconnected comic arcs that explore alternate, exaggerated versions of Springfield's citizens.

title: Fung Pang-Li
text: Fung Pang-Li is A minor recurring character; a tall Chinese WNBA basketball player who appears in Springfield. Fung Pang-Li is a towering professional basketball player who briefly catches Bart's eye during a WNBA game due to her impressive height. Bart gives her the joking nickname "Janine Giraffalo," playing on her stature, which prompts Marge to warn him against pursuing romantic interest in someone so much older and taller than him. Homer even fantasizes about what married life would be like with someone of her height. She is a non-speaking character, existing mostly as a visual gag about her extreme height compared to the Simpsons family. Later, she makes another appearance among a group of sports celebrities gathered to celebrate Bart's victory in a school race, standing alongside other athletes like Muk Mu and Drederick Tatum. Her role is minor but memorable as part of the show's tradition of including exaggerated celebrity athlete cameos.

title: Ray Romano (character)
text: Ray Romano (character) is A fictionalized version of real-life actor and comedian Ray Romano who appears in a Simpsons episode. This character is a caricature of actor and comedian Ray Romano, depicted within the show's fictional universe. He is remembered for a role he played in his youth, appearing as a referee in an obscure film pairing the Harlem Globetrotters with a Frankenstein and Mummy monster mash-up. The joke around him centers on a television broadcast of that old film being abruptly cut short right after the first commercial break, due to Romano taking legal action to block the movie from airing. This gag pokes fun at the litigious side of Hollywood personalities and the odd, forgotten projects actors sometimes have in their past. He only appears briefly, tied to a single episode's storyline, making him a minor one-off reference rather than a recurring presence. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Percival
text: Percival is White tiger owned by boxer Drederick Tatum. Percival is a white tiger belonging to Drederick Tatum, appearing as a non-speaking recurring character. He was featured on a reality show called The Problem Is You, which explored his relationship with Tatum. During a season finale reunion taping, Percival inadvertently caused a fatal accident by untying a rope that held up the show's sign, which then fell and killed Sadie Krustofsky. He later accompanied Tatum to the Springfield Brawliseum, showing his role as a constant companion to the boxer. As an animal character, Percival doesn't speak but factors into the show's storylines through his actions.

title: Rabbi (Daddicus Finch)
text: Rabbi (Daddicus Finch) is An unnamed rabbi at Temple Beth Springfield who officiates religious ceremonies in Springfield. This nameless rabbi serves as the spiritual leader of Temple Beth Springfield and turns up whenever the show needs a Jewish ceremony officiated. He has a son attending school in Superintendent Chalmers' district, which gives Chalmers leverage over him. His most memorable trait is a tendency toward long-winded storytelling, as seen when he dragged out a joke during a bat mitzvah until the impatient crowd and Chalmers forced him to rush the punchline. Beyond that comic mishap, he's shown officiating other significant events, including a robotic wedding and a dockside ceremony, establishing him as Springfield's go-to religious figure for Jewish ceremonies. He's a minor recurring background character rather than a fully developed personality. Voiced by Jon Lovitz.

title: Pyro
text: Pyro is American Gladiator and stuntman; romantic interest of Luann Van Houten. Chase, better known by his stage name Pyro, is a tough, muscular American Gladiator who becomes romantically involved with Luann after her divorce from Kirk Van Houten. He's known for his seemingly indestructible toughness, famously letting Bart smash a chair over his head without flinching. His on-and-off relationship with Luann causes tension with Kirk, even though Pyro surprisingly defends Kirk when Homer attacks him. He's later betrayed when Luann cheats on him with his own best friend, Gyro. Pyro also tries his luck at becoming the new Duffman, nearly succeeding until a disqualifying tattoo advertising a rival Ogdenville beer is discovered. His name is a playful nod to real-life American Gladiator Nitro (Danny Lee Clark). Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Philadelphia Flyers
text: Philadelphia Flyers is Real-world ice hockey team that makes a non-canon appearance as members of the Jury of the Damned. The Philadelphia Flyers appear in the Simpsons universe primarily as a joke referencing their real-life reputation for tough, physical hockey in the 1970s. In a Halloween special, the 1976 starting lineup is hand-picked by Devil Flanders to sit on the Jury of the Damned, and they end up being the only jury members who actually manage to scare the Simpsons family. Outside of this non-canon appearance, the team is also thanked in the credits for their contribution to the in-universe film The Poke of Zorro. They are treated as a background sports reference rather than developed characters, with no individual players given personality or dialogue.

title: Prospector
text: Prospector is Minor recurring character; an alcoholic cowboy who appears at the John Ford Center for Alcoholic Cowboys. The Prospector is a grizzled cowboy character whose defining obsession is gold, to the point that it seems to be the only thing he can focus on. He struggles with alcoholism, which lands him at a rehabilitation center specifically for cowboys with the same problem. During a meeting there, he admits his drinking became so bad that he lost sight of what truly matters to him: gold. His excitement over the subject is so overwhelming that he breaks into an impromptu dance while raving about nuggets as big as a fist. Visually and vocally, he's modeled after classic Western actor Walter Brennan, giving him an old-timey, grizzled cowboy persona. Outside the show's canon, he reappears in The Simpsons: Tapped Out as an Old West character, where it's revealed his real name is John. Voiced by Karl Wiedergott. Notable quotes: He said that he was drinking so much that he forgot what life was about: gold.
quotes: He said that he was drinking so much that he forgot what life was about: gold.

title: Rose Quimby
text: Rose Quimby is Matriarch of the Quimby family; mother of Mayor Joe Quimby. Rose Quimby, also known by the alias Daisy Quimby, is the elderly matriarch behind Springfield's political Quimby dynasty. She is mostly a background figure, mentioned or briefly glimpsed rather than a major presence in the show. Her family status mirrors real-world political matriarchs, as the Quimbys are designed as a parody of the Kennedy family, with Rose standing in for Rose Kennedy specifically. She appeared at the wedding of Rainier Wolfcastle and Maria Shriver-Kennedy Quimby, tying her into the show's satirical take on political dynasties. In a deleted scene from an earlier season, she was introduced to Bart Simpson at her grandson Freddy's birthday party under the name Daisy. Her rare appearances and dual naming add a layer of mystery and running gag to her character, fitting for a matriarch who is more legend than presence. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Rachel (Moms I'd Like to Forget)
text: Rachel (Moms I'd Like to Forget) is One of The Cool Moms, a group of Marge's old friends from her youth. Rachel is a member of The Cool Moms, a clique of Marge's former friends who reunite in her adult life. She is married to Andy and has a son named Ross. When the group gets back together, Rachel joins the others at the Simpsons' home and later at a restaurant called The Enchanted Snail, eager to relive old times. She challenges Marge's devotion to motherhood, questioning whether she can be happy without an identity beyond her children. After Marge leaves the group, Rachel is shown getting more intimate with the other moms, hinting at her bisexuality. She later reappears at a location called Quiet Rivers, suggesting she remains part of the recurring social circle even after the initial storyline. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Jack Pickleson
text: Jack Pickleson is A Krustyland mascot character appearing in the background of the show. Jack Pickleson is a minor, non-speaking mascot character who works at Krustyland, Krusty the Clown's theme park. He is designed as a visual parody of actor Jack Nicholson, likely riffing on Nicholson's look and persona in mascot form. He first appears among the costumed characters at Krusty Fest, and later shows up at a gathering for corporate spokescharacters. Since he never speaks, his humor comes entirely from his appearance and the joke of him existing as a Nicholson-themed park mascot. He remains a background/recurring figure rather than a character with any deeper storyline.

title: Sarah (student)
text: Sarah (student) is A student at Springfield Elementary School and minor recurring bully character. Sarah is one of the many background schoolchildren at Springfield Elementary who occasionally steps into the spotlight to torment Lisa Simpson. She's part of the crowd of kids who mock Lisa for being smart, taunting her with the nickname 'Brain Queen' and shoving her around. She also joined in bullying Allison Taylor, another academically gifted student who briefly rivaled Lisa. Beyond her bullying tendencies, Sarah appears in various school-wide events, such as competing in the Little Miss Springfield Pageant and being present when Milhouse was announced as the new Fallout Boy. During the class photo lice scare, she took part in mocking Lisa further, playing keepaway with her shoes and laughing at her humiliation in front of Principal Skinner. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

title: Olaf
text: Olaf is A minor crossover snowman character appearing in Simpsons specials and dream sequences, based on the Disney film Frozen. Olaf is essentially a cameo character rather than a true member of the Simpsons universe, borrowed directly from Disney's Frozen. He first shows up as one of several random objects Bart hurls at Homer during the Ice Bucket Challenge short. Later he pops up in a surreal dream sequence belonging to Krusty the Clown, where he oddly transforms into Krusty's father, Hyman Krustofsky. He also appears in a non-canon capacity, attending a party at Moe's Tavern to celebrate Disney+'s anniversary, reflecting the show's habit of poking fun at its corporate ties to Disney. In another instance, Ralph dresses up as Olaf within one of Principal Skinner's fantasies, and in a holiday couch gag Homer himself takes on the character's appearance. Olaf never speaks in these appearances, functioning purely as a visual gag or crossover reference rather than a developed character.

title: Shazam
text: Shazam is A DC Comics superhero character referenced within the Simpsons universe, tied to Comic Book Guy's collectibles and pop culture lore. Shazam is a minor, non-original reference to the DC Comics superhero also known as Captain Marvel, appearing only in a background or in-universe comic capacity rather than as an active character in Springfield. He shows up on comic book covers within the show's fictional publishing world, tying him to Comic Book Guy's extensive collection and knowledge. His catchphrase is even cited as one of the greatest quotes of all time according to Comic Book Guy. In a non-canon appearance, someone dresses up as Shazam at a fan convention, poking fun at superhero cosplay culture. Overall, Shazam functions more as an Easter egg for comic fans than a fleshed-out character within the show. Notable quotes: "Shazam!"
quotes: "Shazam!"

title: Montgomery Scott
text: Montgomery Scott is Star Trek character (engineer) appearing in Simpsons parodies/crossovers, not a main cast member. Montgomery "Scotty" Scott is a crossover character from the Star Trek franchise who appears in various Simpsons episodes that parody the sci-fi series. In one parody trailer, he's depicted as elderly and so overweight that he can no longer reach the engineering control panel, poking fun at the aging original cast. He's also referenced through an in-universe autobiography written and fronted by Leonard Nimoy, blurring the line between actor and character. In another episode, he appears in a Star Trek-themed twist on 'A Christmas Carol,' where Captain Kirk orders him to fire photon torpedoes, only for the attempt to fail while showing a vision of his out-of-shape future self. Scotty himself doesn't have much personality development in the Simpsons universe, serving mainly as a nostalgic and comedic nod to Star Trek fandom. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Radio Man
text: Radio Man is Comic-book superhero and predecessor identity of Radioactive Man, appearing in Bongo Comics stories. Radio Man is a Golden Age superhero identity that predates the more famous Radioactive Man, wielding the power to control and manipulate radio waves rather than nuclear energy. The mantle has been held by more than one person, including Claude Kane III, who gained his abilities from a mysterious subway repairman, and later Clarence Kane. Unlike his radioactive successor, Radio Man lacks the telltale lightning bolt protruding from his head, a detail that becomes a plot point when villains exploit his vulnerability to mind control. He fought alongside the Superior Squad against Adolf Hitler during wartime, and in another adventure was forcibly transformed back from Radioactive Man by a villain's ray gun, only to accidentally destroy the device and restore the original hero. As Clarence Kane, he also teamed up with reporter Glenda Grand to trap the villainous Cap'n Bolt after a kidnapping. Overall, Radio Man serves as a nostalgic nod to comic-book history within the Radioactive Man mythos, existing mainly as a legacy identity used in flashback and retro-style stories.

title: Oompa-Loompa
text: Oompa-Loompa is Minor recurring character parodying the Oompa-Loompas from Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, encountered by Homer and Moe. This character is a small, orange-skinned man with green hair, a direct nod to the famous Oompa-Loompas from Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. He first appears working, or at least present, at the Motherloving Sugar Corp., where Homer becomes oddly fascinated by his existence. When Homer finally meets one in person, he finds the encounter unsettling rather than charming, as the Oompa-Loompa is simply sitting on a crate smoking. He later shows up again in a strange cameo on television, prompting Moe to quickly change the channel in discomfort. The character serves purely as a quick pop-culture gag rather than a fleshed-out personality, appearing only briefly across two episodes. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: That guy is freaky.|Homer about the Oompa-Loompa
quotes: That guy is freaky.|Homer about the Oompa-Loompa

title: Purple Haze
text: Purple Haze is A minor superhero character and member of the Superior Squad in the Radioactive Man comic book universe. Purple Haze is a superhero who appears exclusively in Bongo comic book stories tied to the Radioactive Man mythos. He is part of the Superior Squad, a team of heroes who fall into a trap set by the villainous Madame Eczema while trying to meet an ally named Plasmo. Captured alongside his teammates, he is eventually freed by Radioactive Man and joins the fight against Eczema's soldiers. Little is known of his personality or backstory beyond his role in this brief comic arc. His name and visual motif are a nod to the classic Jimi Hendrix song of the same title, fitting the comic's tendency to reference real-world music and pop culture through its hero names.

title: King Quimby
text: King Quimby is Non-canon medieval fantasy counterpart of Mayor Quimby, ruler of the kingdom of Springfieldia. King Quimby is a parody version of Mayor Quimby set in a fantasy, Game of Thrones-style universe called Springfieldia. As the ruling monarch, he commands mages and other subjects, though his leadership seems to be marked by frustration and poor results from his underlings. He appears bad-tempered when his orders are misunderstood, as shown by his reaction to a construction mishap. This character exists outside the show's normal continuity, appearing only in a special non-canon episode. He later became part of the game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, extending his presence beyond the television series. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Dennis Rodman (character)
text: Dennis Rodman (character) is Real-world basketball celebrity who appears as himself in a guest cameo. Dennis Rodman is a real-world athlete who makes a brief cameo appearance in the Simpsons universe, playing a fictionalized version of himself. He's referenced in connection with Bart once mistaking himself for a basketball star while filling in for Lisa in drag. In a non-canon Halloween special, Rodman appears as a couch pacifier alongside Moe, cracking a joke about working off a speeding ticket. His inclusion plays on his real-life fame and eccentric public persona, used mostly as a quick celebrity cameo gag rather than a developed character. He has no ongoing relationships or storylines within the show, appearing only in isolated, comedic contexts. Voiced by Dennis Rodman (Himself). Notable quotes: Dennis Rodman... said he was working off a speeding ticket and wished everybody a Happy Halloween.
quotes: Dennis Rodman... said he was working off a speeding ticket and wished everybody a Happy Halloween.

title: B. F. Sherwood
text: B. F. Sherwood is A family therapist who attempts to counsel the Simpson family. B. F. Sherwood is a therapist brought in to help sort out the Simpsons' dysfunctional family dynamics, though he seems ill-suited for the job. Despite his professional title, he shows little patience for children and an overall lack of professionalism during sessions. He becomes visibly unnerved by odd behavior from the kids, such as Bart returning chewed mints to his mouth. He also appears in a bizarre dream sequence conjured by Bart, where he gives Homer questionable advice that leads to a room being flooded with fish after opening a coffin. His name is a nod to the real-life behavioral psychologist B. F. Skinner, poking fun at his supposed expertise in psychology despite his erratic on-screen behavior. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Mr. Samson
text: Mr. Samson is Minor recurring background character; father of Gerald Samson and husband of Mrs. Samson. Mr. Samson is a minor, non-speaking resident of Springfield known mainly through his family ties rather than any dialogue or storyline of his own. He first appeared in The Simpsons Movie and has since popped up as a background character in several later seasons. One notable moment finds him seated in the audience at Springfield Elementary watching a school play. He is identified primarily by his relationships, being the husband of Mrs. Samson and the father of Gerald Samson. As a silent extra, he contributes to the show's tradition of filling out crowd scenes with recognizable townsfolk who never get a line. His character has no defined job, age, or personality traits beyond his family role and his black hair.

title: Yoko Ono
text: Yoko Ono is Real-world Japanese artist and musician, widow of John Lennon, referenced/appearing as a minor real-world character in The Simpsons. Yoko Ono appears in the show as a real-world celebrity figure tied closely to her late husband John Lennon. She's mostly referenced in passing, such as when an optometrist mentions her in connection with glasses once worn by Val Kilmer, prompting Homer to gripe about her breaking up the Plastic Ono Band. In one memorable moment, a hallucinating Bart imagines a naked Milhouse kissing her after drinking an old novelty beverage, leading Ned Flanders to describe Bart's destructive behavior as going 'Yoko.' She also appears as a wax figure in a rock museum, ends up in archival Beatles footage in a later-referenced documentary, and even co-hosts a fictional version of Krusty's show with Lennon in a tie-in book. In a non-canon story, she guest-stars alongside Henry Kissinger on a radioactive superhero-themed talk show. Throughout her sparse appearances, she functions less as a character with her own personality and more as a cultural shorthand for Beatles history and pop-culture references.

title: The Parson
text: The Parson is A minor recurring character, a friend of Reverend Timothy Lovejoy in Springfield. The Parson is a minor clergy figure and acquaintance of Reverend Lovejoy, known for his connection to Springfield's religious community. He has a shared history with the Lovejoys, recalling Helen Lovejoy from childhood when she went by the name Harold. He's also part of the local bowling scene, having been a member of the Holy Rollers bowling team. Ned Flanders reportedly admires him a great deal, fitting with his devout persona. Visually and stylistically, he draws inspiration from Bing Crosby's priestly film character Father O'Malley. Despite his low profile, he has appeared across many seasons of the show, often in brief or background roles. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Receptionist (There's No Disgrace Like Home)
text: Receptionist (There's No Disgrace Like Home) is Minor character; receptionist at Dr. Monroe's Family Therapy Center visited by the Simpsons. This unnamed receptionist works the front desk at Dr. Marvin Monroe's family therapy practice. Her main function in the story is administrative, greeting and checking in patients before their sessions. She welcomes both the Simpson family and another troubled family, the reformed dad's clan, when they arrive for therapy. Later, she's the one who has to deliver the news to Dr. Monroe that his clients have fled the building, a direct result of chaos caused by the Simpsons triggering a power failure. She's a background, functional character with no defined personality traits beyond her professional role, appearing only briefly in one episode and in archival clip-show footage. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Party Clown
text: Party Clown is A non-canon alternate persona of Milhouse, appearing as a clown in a Bongo comic story. Party Clown is a comic-exclusive identity taken on by Milhouse after retiring from his stint as Houseboy. Existing only in the non-canon 'Once and Future Bartman' storyline, he represents one of Milhouse's many odd career detours in that alternate timeline. His main contribution to the plot comes from watching Bartman's televised announcement, through which he learns that Bartman was mistaken about Numero Uno's true identity as Sideshow Bob. This revelation ties him into the larger conflict involving Bartman's pursuit of justice against the villain. As a background figure, Party Clown doesn't have much characterization beyond his clown appearance and passive role as an observer of the story's events. He appears briefly across two parts of the comic arc before fading from the narrative.

title: Old Scratch
text: Old Scratch is The devil of Hell, appearing in Springfield's various depictions of the afterlife. Old Scratch is the traditional devil figure who presides over Hell in various Simpsons dream sequences and afterlife visions. He first appears when Bart, after being hit by Mr. Burns' car, briefly ends up in Hell instead of Heaven due to a rule violation. He's businesslike and keeps meticulous records, checking Bart's file to confirm he isn't actually due to arrive for decades. Despite his menacing role, he's somewhat matter-of-fact and even oddly hospitable, inviting Lisa to join her cable-stealing family in one of her guilt-driven nightmares. His classic name, "Old Scratch," is simply an old-fashioned nickname for the devil. He's also tied thematically to Mr. Burns, who once credited his own unnaturally long life to a pact with Satan. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Brooke Shields (character)
text: Brooke Shields (character) is Real-life actress who appears as herself in guest spots on the show. Brooke Shields is depicted as a version of herself making cameo appearances in Springfield-related media. She's referenced early on as one of Michael Jackson's celebrity Grammy dates, a detail used by Leon Kompowsky to convince Bart he really is Michael Jackson. Her most substantial appearance has her co-presenting an award alongside Krusty the Clown, where she patiently sticks to the script while Krusty gets sidetracked complaining about a joke. Beyond that, she mostly shows up as a background photo in various Springfield locations, cementing her status as a recognizable celebrity within the show's universe. She's also tied to a minor running joke involving an unnamed husband, referred to only as "The Guy Who Married Brooke Shields." Voiced by Brooke Shields (Herself).

title: Beelzebart Simpson
text: Beelzebart Simpson is Bart Simpson's alternate persona/version of himself while attending school in Hell, from a Treehouse of Horror segment. Beelzebart Simpson is essentially Bart Simpson reimagined as a demonic student after he and Lisa accidentally get transported to Hell through a cursed rune translation. Unlike his usual underachieving self, this version of Bart surprisingly excels academically, earning straight As and even being named class mal-edictorian at the infernal Hellroads school. The character is a one-off Halloween gag that plays on the idea of Bart thriving in an environment built around mischief and torment. He later shows up briefly as an archival image in a couch gag, suggesting he's remembered as a minor piece of the show's Treehouse of Horror lore. Beelzebart also made an appearance as a collectible skin in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, cementing his place as a fun non-canon variant of Bart. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: He who reads this rune translation will be taken to damnation.
quotes: He who reads this rune translation will be taken to damnation.

title: Po
text: Po is A crossover character from the Teletubbies TV series who appears within The Simpsons universe. Po is not an original Simpsons character but a character borrowed from the real-world children's show Teletubbies, appearing occasionally within episodes as a TV show the Simpson kids watch. She has no dialogue and functions mostly as a background or pop-culture reference gag. In one memorable moment, Po and the other Teletubbies chase Homer as part of an angry mob after he fails to pay back donated money, with Po firing lasers from her head antenna. She also appears as a plush toy on Maggie's shelf and as part of a live opening act at a concert. In a non-canon segment, Lisa dresses up as Po while the rest of the family cosplays as other Teletubbies for Maggie's amusement. Overall, Po serves as a running gag referencing the toddler show's presence in the Simpsons' pop-culture landscape rather than as a developed character.

title: John Oates
text: John Oates is Real-world musician who appears as a character in Lisa's dream and a hallucination sequence. John Oates is a real-life American singer and guitarist who makes cameo appearances within the fictional world of Springfield through dream and hallucination sequences. In one episode, Lisa imagines herself performing alongside him and other musicians in a band that narrowly misses the top spot on the charts. He later resurfaces as part of a drug-induced vision experienced by Homer and Ned, standing in as one half of a famous musical duo. Oates never actually speaks in the show, existing purely as a non-speaking, recurring pop-culture reference rather than a fully developed character. His appearances lean on his real-world fame and his association with musical partner Daryl Hall for comedic effect.

title: Ted Nugent (character)
text: Ted Nugent (character) is Real-life musician appearing as himself, briefly considered as a presidential candidate backed by Homer. Ted Nugent appears as a heightened, eccentric version of himself who gets tangled up in Springfield's political and personal chaos. He first surfaces campaigning against a school ban on crossbows, insisting kids need them to fend off charging elk. Later, he's tapped by Homer to be the Springfield Republican Party's presidential pick, joining Homer's show and the Gravy Boat Movement before Homer ultimately backs out of endorsing him. His personality leans into wild-outdoorsman stereotypes—he's shown lugging around dead elk, rigging a treehouse-like sleeping setup on the Simpsons' chimney, and using kids as living target practice with his bow. Despite being politically and personally erratic, he takes rejection in stride, bouncing back quickly when Homer withdraws his support. He's also memorialized in a photo hanging at a local bar, showing his minor celebrity status in town. Voiced by Ted Nugent (Himself).

title: Gwyneth Poultry
text: Gwyneth Poultry is An emotional support chicken belonging to minor character Truth-Anne. Gwyneth Poultry is a brown chicken who serves as an emotional support animal for her owner, Truth-Anne. She doesn't speak, appearing mostly as a background companion during Truth-Anne's various outings around Springfield. Her most notable moment of misfortune comes when Snowball II attacks her at a park designated for emotional support animals, landing her in the hospital and saddling the Simpson family with the vet bill. She also accompanies Truth-Anne on a fateful flight with a budget airline. Her name is a punny nod to actress Gwyneth Paltrow, fitting the show's tradition of silly wordplay for minor characters.

title: Rigellian queen (Treehouse of Horror XXII)
text: Rigellian queen (Treehouse of Horror XXII) is Ruler of the alien Rigellians on Rigel 7, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment parodying Avatar. The Rigellian queen presides over her people on the distant planet Rigel 7, where she oversees production of a valuable liquid resource called Hillarium. She becomes entangled in the show's Avatar-style parody when Bart and Milhouse, disguised in alien avatar bodies, track her down. Unbeknownst to her, Milhouse betrays her location to the human forces seeking to seize the Hillarium supply by force. As a non-canon character confined to a single Halloween special, she has no dialogue and exists mainly as a plot device driving the segment's satire. She later resurfaced as a collectible decoration in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: J. K. Rowling (character)
text: J. K. Rowling (character) is Real-life author who appears as a guest character met by the Simpson family in England. J. K. Rowling appears as a celebrity guest character encountered by the Simpsons during their trip to England. She is portrayed as witty and a bit sarcastic, particularly when dealing with overly enthusiastic fans like Lisa. At one point she briefly works as Lisa's substitute teacher at Springfield Elementary after the school receives a large donation, tasking students with writing an alternate ending to her final Harry Potter book, but she quits once the funding is revoked. Her fame is referenced multiple times through book covers, look-alikes, and even a spot on Lisa's list of admired intellectuals. The character plays on Rowling's real-world status as the creator of the Harry Potter series and pokes fun at fan culture surrounding her work. Voiced by Herself. Notable quotes: Thank you, young Muggle. | He grows up and he marries you! Is that what you want to hear?
quotes: Thank you, young Muggle.
He grows up and he marries you! Is that what you want to hear?

title: She-Wolf
text: She-Wolf is Non-canon monster character; wife of the Werewolf, appearing in a Treehouse of Horror segment. She-Wolf is a minor, non-canon monster character introduced in a Halloween-themed episode. She is defined mainly by her relationship to her husband, the Werewolf, rather than by any independent traits of her own. Her one notable moment comes from jealousy and anger, showing a fierce, possessive side when she catches her husband being unfaithful at a social gathering. This brief but memorable outburst gives her a temperamental, no-nonsense personality despite her limited screen time. She later reappears as a character in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, expanding her presence beyond the original television appearance. Overall, she serves as a background/supporting figure tied to the show's horror-comedy anthology tradition. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Tom Sawyer
text: Tom Sawyer is A fictional tall-tale character based on Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer, appearing in a story told within the show. Tom Sawyer is a character adapted into a Simpsons tall tale, narrated by a singing railroad hobo and loosely based on Mark Twain's classic novel. Alongside Huckleberry Finn, he tricks other children into doing his chores, gets swept up in chaos involving Becky Thatcher's forced marriage, and ends up on the run as a wanted criminal. His adventures take him down the Mississippi River, through narrow escapes, and ultimately to a grim, exaggerated execution for comedic tall-tale effect. The character also appears in a school play performed by Bart and Lisa, where he is portrayed by Nelson and takes part in a whimsical, anachronistic storyline involving lightsabers and giant space worms. Tom's role is largely comedic and parodic, existing to lampoon classic American literature within the show's tradition of tall tales. He also makes a non-canon appearance as a costume for Bart in a mobile game. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: Ramrod
text: Ramrod is Recurring biker character and member of the Hell's Satans gang. Ramrod is a gruff, leather-clad biker who rides with the Hell's Satans gang out of Bakersfield. He first appears causing trouble by helping trash the Simpson household and abduct Marge, though he awkwardly denies any romantic interest in her. Despite his intimidating biker image, he's shown popping up in more mundane settings, including working as a cook at a diner. He's often seen as part of the group rather than as an individual, appearing alongside his fellow gang members at concerts, bars, and other biker hangouts. His appearances span many years, showing he's a durable background figure in the show's rotating cast of recurring characters. Overall, he embodies the rough-and-tumble, slightly comedic biker archetype that recurs throughout the series. Voiced by Henry Winkler.

title: Babe Ruth (character)
text: Babe Ruth (character) is Real-world baseball legend referenced/appearing as a minor character in Springfield lore. Babe Ruth appears in the Simpsons universe as a real historical figure, referenced more often than actually seen. He shows up as an Audio-Animatronic figure at a Duff Days exhibit called "The Alco-Hall of Fame," where he's depicted as brash and competitive, needling Benjamin Franklin. He's also tied into the show's recurring jokes about famous left-handed people, appearing on lists and walls dedicated to lefties. In flashback, he witnessed young Mr. Burns' humiliating childhood performance and laughed at his misfortune. Bart references him while dismissing the value of teamwork, unable to even recall what team Ruth played for. In non-canon material, he's mentioned as deceased and even shows up on a worthless-seeming baseball card used for a scheme involving a valuable lamp. Voiced by Harry Shearer. Notable quotes: "You think you're better than me?"
quotes: "You think you're better than me?"

title: The Penguin
text: The Penguin is A crossover supervillain from Batman comics who appears as an antagonist in a Simpsons episode. The Penguin is a parody appearance of the classic Batman villain, brought into the Simpsons universe as a crossover character. He appears as one of several attackers who ambush Wayne Slater during his special training sequence, working alongside a pair of henchmen. True to his comic book and 1966 TV series origins, he carries his signature umbrella loaded with hidden weaponry. Ironically, Wayne turns this very umbrella against him, using its concealed knockout gas to subdue The Penguin and his men. He is a non-speaking character, existing purely as a visual gag referencing Burgess Meredith's iconic portrayal from the classic Batman TV show. His role is brief, serving mainly as a nod to comic book fans within a single episode.

title: Rib-It
text: Rib-It is Mascot character for the Ribwich fast-food product. Rib-It is a costumed frog mascot created to promote the Ribwich sandwich, memorably covered in barbecue sauce that Homer licked off before eating the burger itself. He's appeared in various promotional and public contexts around Springfield, including a stint in Krusty's holiday ice show. When a beloved food establishment was destroyed, Rib-It joined other mascots in mourning, complete with a black armband, showing a strange sense of camaraderie among Springfield's costumed food icons. He's also popped up in fan culture, with someone cosplaying as him at a convention. In one encounter, Rib-It and fellow mascots turned aggressive, attacking Lisa Simpson when she encroached on their territory while promoting a rival organic vegetable stand, revealing a surprisingly territorial and combative side to these otherwise cheerful costumed characters. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Defonzo Palmer
text: Defonzo Palmer is A jazz trumpeter who recruits Bart into his band. Defonzo "Skinny" Palmer is a jazz musician who plays trumpet alongside his bandmate Marcus "Marbles" Le Marquez. He spots potential in Bart and invites him to join their group, giving him the nickname "Tick-Tock" for his drumming skills. Skinny is shown to be generous and community-minded, organizing a benefit concert to help pay for Bart's arm surgery after an injury threatens his ability to drum. His personal life includes a tragic family connection, as his late sister was once married to his fellow musician Marbles. He appears as a recurring background figure tied to Bart's musical adventures rather than a central character. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

title: Luke Perry (character)
text: Luke Perry (character) is Real-life actor appearing as himself, revealed to be Krusty the Clown's half-brother. Luke Perry appears in Springfield as a version of his real celebrity self, tied into the show's fiction as Krusty the Clown's previously unknown half-brother. He's introduced as one of Krusty's sideshow performers during the ill-fated Krusty Comeback Special, where he's launched from a cannon and survives an absurdly destructive path through several Springfield locations. Despite the disastrous stunt, he takes the mishap in stride and even manages to upstage Krusty at the celebration afterward, hinting at a bit of sibling rivalry or scene-stealing charisma. He remains loosely connected to Krusty's world, later attending his fake funeral and popping up in other Krusty-related media like a Broadway adaptation and a published book. Outside of Krusty's orbit, he's shown participating in a Fox charity fundraiser as a phone operator and is listed among notable left-leaning celebrities in a satirical Flanders-related book. Overall, he functions as a celebrity cameo character whose main gag is his surprising family connection to the beloved but hapless clown. Voiced by Luke Perry (Himself).

title: Red Hot Chili Peppers (characters)
text: Red Hot Chili Peppers (characters) is Real-life rock band appearing as guest characters, booked for a gig at Moe's Tavern and later Krusty's Comeback Special. The Red Hot Chili Peppers appear as themselves in a memorable guest cameo, portrayed as a bit temperamental and easily annoyed by the chaotic booking mishap that lands them a gig at Moe's Tavern instead of a proper venue. They clash with Moe over the venue's laughably small size and restless crowd, showing a mix of professional frustration and rock-star attitude. Bart cleverly manipulates the situation to help them escape the bar gig in exchange for getting him onto the Krusty Comeback Special. Their willingness to perform half-naked on live television, apparently unfazed by the indignity that even shocks Krusty, plays into a running gag about their eccentric, devil-may-care rocker persona. The band's brief appearance ties into the show's tradition of using real musicians as self-parodying guest stars.

title: Sonny Rollins (character)
text: Sonny Rollins (character) is A real-world jazz musician who appears as himself in a guest cameo on the show. Sonny Rollins is a real-life jazz saxophonist who makes a brief animated appearance in the Simpsons universe. In his storyline, he shows up as a hologram dispatched by She-Done-Left-Me Records to discourage Lisa from continuing to send complaint letters to the company. Lisa, being sharp-witted, quickly figures out that he isn't really there in person but is instead a projected image used as a corporate scare tactic. His appearance is brief and largely functions as a cameo nod to real jazz culture rather than a fully developed character. He has gray hair and is depicted as an adult, fitting his real-world persona as an elder statesman of jazz. Beyond this single encounter, he has no ongoing relationships or story arcs within the show. Voiced by Sonny Rollins (Himself).

title: Sakatumi
text: Sakatumi is A minor recurring sumo wrestler character encountered by the Simpson family in Japan. Sakatumi is a burly sumo wrestler who briefly crosses paths with the Simpsons during their trip to Japan. He becomes irritated when Homer insults his weight, leading to a brief scuffle over a pretzel that ends with Bart intervening physically. Despite this rocky first encounter, he later appears as part of a training program run by Wayne Slater, suggesting some connection to the world of sports training beyond sumo wrestling. In a non-canon future timeline, he's shown reaching out to Lisa Simpson through a social media friend request, hinting he holds no lasting grudge. He's a side character mostly used for comedic culture-clash moments involving the Simpson family's misadventures abroad. Voiced by Keone Young.

title: Number 51
text: Number 51 is A minor, background member of the secret society known as the Stonecutters. Number 51 is a barely-there Stonecutter whose entire claim to fame is standing among the group as they sing their signature anthem. He's bald and identified only by his numerical designation, which fans have noted is likely a nod to the infamous Area 51. He shows up briefly in a handful of episodes, mostly through archive footage, and even appears in the audience during a Kang and Kodos routine in a non-canon Halloween segment. It's never revealed whether he continues on to join the rival group, The Ancient Mystic Society of No Homers, leaving his ultimate fate a mystery. He also pops up as a minor character in Simpsons video games like Virtual Springfield and Tapped Out, cementing his status as a background fixture of the franchise's secret society lore. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: Jerry Seinfeld
text: Jerry Seinfeld is Real-life comedian who appears as a fictionalized character/cameo in The Simpsons. Jerry Seinfeld appears as a caricature version of himself within the Simpsons universe, referencing his real-life career as a stand-up comedian, actor, writer, and producer. He briefly shows up as a captcha image on the Wayz app, humorously placed among faces that Lisa must avoid clicking. In another appearance, he's shown hosting his talk show, driving a vintage car and chatting with Krusty about modern political correctness in colleges, until their scene is interrupted by a chaotic cameo from Jay Leno. He's also listed as one of the notable liberal celebrities on Ned Flanders' list of admired left-leaning figures, tying him lightly into the show's satire of celebrity culture and politics. Voiced by Maurice LaMarche.

title: Jesse Pinkman
text: Jesse Pinkman is Crossover character from Breaking Bad who appears briefly in The Simpsons via hallucination and a couch gag. Jesse Pinkman is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover appearance from the show Breaking Bad. He shows up when Homer and Ned, under the influence of U-completeamine, hallucinate themselves as famous duos, briefly imagining themselves as Jesse Pinkman and Walter White. In a separate non-canon couch gag segment, he's shown sitting on a couch with Walter White watching The Simpsons. He also appeared in a live-action couch gag portrayed by actor Aaron Paul, though he had no dialogue in that scene. His presence is essentially a nod to fans of Breaking Bad rather than a developed character within the Simpsons universe.

title: Hugo Simpson I
text: Hugo Simpson I is Ancestor of the Simpson family, son of Howland Simpson, appearing in the family's ancestral records. Hugo Simpson I is a minor ancestral figure in the extended Simpson family tree, known mainly from an old photograph rather than any real appearances. He is the son of Howland Simpson and Gabby Crouse, with siblings Lou, Gaston, and "Old Tut" Simpson, plus a sister named Dulcine. His only notable moment comes when Lisa is doing genealogical research and reacts with visible frustration upon finding his picture, implying he had a shady past or poor reputation. He never speaks and exists purely as a picture-only character. Interestingly, he lends his name to a later, non-canon descendant also called Hugo Simpson, who bears a resemblance to him but with a beard. His inclusion highlights the show's tendency to retcon or reshape its own family history between different media appearances.

title: Skippy Simpson
text: Skippy Simpson is Non-canon future son of Bart Simpson, grandson of Homer and Marge. Skippy Simpson is a future, non-canon child of Bart Simpson and his ex-wife Jenda, appearing in flash-forward episodes of the show. He speaks with a noticeable lisp and is also referred to as Picard Simpson in some scripts, a nod to Star Trek's Captain Picard, paralleling his brother Jiff being named after Captain Kirk. Initially reluctant to spend Christmas with his father, he ends up bonding more with his grandfather Homer instead of Bart. He and his brother Jiff share a playful dynamic, at one point chasing Homer's consciousness through pictures around the house as a game. Skippy also witnesses the ups and downs of his parents' on-and-off relationship, feeling happy when they briefly reconcile. He later appears among the extended Simpson family during a Thanksgiving gathering following Homer's death. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

title: David Silverman (character)
text: David Silverman (character) is Real-world animator, director, and producer who appears as a self-portrayed cameo character in the show. David Silverman is depicted as a version of himself who occasionally pops up within the animated world of Springfield. He's shown as a tuba enthusiast, playing the instrument during chaotic events like a fall off the Escalator to Nowhere and a performance on the Krusty show. His fictional counterpart gets caught up in odd situations, including being mistakenly listed as gay by Kent Brockman and getting his flaming tuba stolen at a Burning Man-style event called Blazing Guy. He's also credited in-universe as the animator who sketched the very first design of Poochie. In non-canon material, he's portrayed as intimidated by an aggressive, perfectionist version of Homer during behind-the-scenes footage for a fictional spin-off show. Overall, his character serves as a playful nod to the real animator's dedication to the franchise, including a nod to his real-life Burning Man attendance. Voiced by Himself.

title: "Old Tut" Simpson
text: "Old Tut" Simpson is Ancestor of the Simpson family; father of Orville Simpson and grandfather figure in Abe's flashbacks. "Old Tut" Simpson is a distant Simpson ancestor originally hailing from Scotland, known mainly through flashbacks and family history rather than direct appearances. He was married to "Happy" Simpson and fathered four children, including his son Orville. His parenting style comes across as harsh and unforgiving, most notably shown when he violently punished Orville out of disappointment in front of a class. Despite this severity, he also had a softer, sentimental side, expressed through his tradition of taking his grandson Abe to Springfield Isotopes baseball games. He voiced hopes that this family tradition of attending ball games would continue for generations to come. His legacy is passed down mostly through family stories and flashback sequences involving Abraham Simpson.

title: Bobby Peterson
text: Bobby Peterson is Dean of Springfield University, appearing in Homer's college storyline. Bobby Peterson is the young, laid-back dean of Springfield University who insists students call him by his first name rather than a formal title. He's the opposite of the stuffy, strict authority figure Homer expects, being hip, easygoing, and reluctant to punish students harshly. Despite his likable nature, Homer irrationally despises him due to preconceived notions from college comedy films. Bobby ends up expelling three nerds for kidnapping a beloved pig mascot, only under pressure from influential figures, and later reverses the decision once Homer confesses his own role in the chaos. He ends up physically injured after being hit by Homer's car, requiring a hip replacement, but the two eventually bond and even team up for pranks together. His character illustrates how misplaced grudges can be, since he never actually fits the stereotype Homer projects onto him. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: "a bit of an ogre"
quotes: "a bit of an ogre"

title: Ayn Rand
text: Ayn Rand is Real-world author referenced within the Simpsons universe, whose works and image recur as background gags. Ayn Rand appears in the show not as a living character but as a cultural touchstone referenced throughout Springfield. Her novel The Fountainhead inspires a bedtime story Marge tells Lisa, and later becomes reading material Smithers uses to soothe Mr. Burns. Her image and legacy pop up in odd places, from a scarecrow on Cletus's farm to a hidden button disguised as her statue in Mr. Burns's secret catacombs. She's also invoked by wealthy or ideologically driven characters, such as The Rich Texan, showing her association with individualist philosophy. Even a local school, the Ayn Rand School for Tots, bears her name, cementing her as a symbol of self-reliance and free-market ideals within the show's universe. She never speaks or appears as an active character, functioning purely as a recurring reference and visual gag.

title: Ring-A-Ling
text: Ring-A-Ling is A minor clown character at Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus, connected to Krusty the Clown. Ring-A-Ling is a background clown performer working for the Ding-A-Ling Bros. Circus, distinguished by the giant clock costume he wears. He was one of several circus clowns that Scuzzo brought in to meet Krusty, blending into the circus's colorful cast of performers. His main function seems to be practical rather than comedic, as he's responsible for waking everyone up in the morning by ringing his clock. He appears throughout circus scenes helping out and performing, though he doesn't have any speaking lines. Like the rest of the circus troupe, he eventually departs Springfield by train when the circus moves on. He later appears in a non-canon capacity in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out.

title: Raoul
text: Raoul is A charismatic man Abraham Simpson met in Miami Beach, later possibly a Springfield resident. Raoul is a suave, smooth-talking older man whom Abraham Simpson encounters while trying to pick up women on a Miami Beach vacation. Despite Abe's assumption that Raoul's swanky penthouse must be a tool for seducing women, Raoul reveals he finds women disgusting, hinting strongly at a same-sex attraction to Abe himself. He shows a peculiar interest in Abe not for his stories, which he finds tedious enough to secretly turn off his hearing aid during, but for the pleasure of simply watching Abe's animated facial expressions. He also seeks physical closeness with Abe, such as walking arm-in-arm on the beach. Raoul later turns up in Springfield at one of Moe's political rallies, suggesting he relocated there after meeting Abe. His brief appearances mark him as a quirky, one-off character with subtle queer-coded traits played for comedic effect. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

title: Primo
text: Primo is A mobster working for the Calabresi crime family, rivals of Fat Tony's Springfield Mafia. Primo, also called Big Alberto, is a mafia enforcer aligned with Dante Calabresi Sr. and Jr. He plays a role in the escalating conflict between the Calabresi family and Fat Tony's organization, taking part in violent retaliation after a misunderstanding about Fat Tony's toughness. His storyline ends abruptly when the Calabresi family is poisoned during a supposed peace-making dinner at the Simpsons' house. Despite his death, he humorously reappears as a background character at a later wedding, playing into the show's habit of ignoring character deaths for comedic cameos. He also briefly appears in a flashback tied to Eleanor Abernathy's backstory. Overall, Primo represents the show's recurring parody of mob family dynamics and dark humor around organized crime. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: George Bernard Shaw
text: George Bernard Shaw is Historical/real-world figure referenced in The Simpsons, depicted as an Irish playwright who appears in flashbacks and parade scenes. George Bernard Shaw appears in the show as a nod to the real-life Irish playwright famous for works like Man and Superman. Rather than being an active character in the Simpsons' world, he's mostly a background or historical presence, showing up as a float figure in Springfield's Saint Patrick's Day parades and in a flashback to Grampa Simpson's younger days in Ireland. He's a non-speaking character, existing purely as a visual reference or cameo rather than someone with dialogue or personal storylines. Lisa is shown reading one of his books at one point, hinting at his intellectual reputation being recognized within the family. His recurring appearances are tied to Irish culture and history rather than any ongoing plot involving the main cast.

title: Number One
text: Number One is Head/leader of the Springfield chapter of the Stonecutters, a secret society Homer briefly joins. Number One is the imposing figurehead of the Stonecutters, presiding over the secret society's bizarre initiation rites and social gatherings with obvious relish. He takes pleasure in subjecting new members to strange, humiliating trials before welcoming them into a club built around drinking, ping-pong, and eating ribs. Though he expels Homer early on for disrespecting sacred Stonecutter property, he quickly reverses course once Homer is revealed to be the group's prophesied "Chosen One." When Homer's leadership ruins the club's fun atmosphere, Number One shows his decisiveness by disbanding the Stonecutters altogether and founding a new exclusive group. He later resurfaces in a minor, comedic capacity online, hinting that his secretive nature persists into the modern age. Despite his authority, he's portrayed as good-humored and eager to keep the good times rolling among his fellow members. Voiced by Patrick Stewart. Notable quotes: You have joined the Sacred Order of the Stonecutters who since ancient times have split the rocks of ignorance that obscure the light of knowledge and truth. Now let's all get drunk and play Ping-Pong!
quotes: You have joined the Sacred Order of the Stonecutters who since ancient times have split the rocks of ignorance that obscure the light of knowledge and truth. Now let's all get drunk and play Ping-Pong!

title: Betty Rubble
text: Betty Rubble is Crossover character from The Flintstones appearing in The Simpsons universe, wife of Barney Rubble and mother of Bamm-Bamm Rubble. Betty Rubble is not an original Simpsons character but a crossover figure borrowed from The Flintstones cartoon universe. Within the show, she appears only in picture form, such as on Bart's Flintstone Phone and Homer's Flintstones-themed map, never actually speaking any lines. Her most memorable use is a running gag involving Captain McCallister, who has a tattoo of his fourth wife that oddly resembles Betty, explaining that's simply how he prefers to remember her. Aside from these brief cameos and mentions, little else is explored about her personality or story within the Simpsons continuity. She functions mainly as a nostalgic nod to classic animation rather than a fleshed-out character.

title: Mav Redfield
text: Mav Redfield is Son of Augustus Redfield and member of the RedStar board of directors, appearing in "Meat Is Murder". Mav Redfield is one of Augustus 'Gus' Redfield's scheming children, siding with his siblings Colby and Sheila in an attempt to oust their father as CEO of RedStar. He's characterized as a reckless, image-obsessed businessman, having organized a disastrous island music festival that resulted in fatalities due to poor planning. Despite his conniving nature, he ultimately fails when Gus outmaneuvers the siblings using Grampa's vote, leading to their expulsion from the company. Mav shows a carefree, hedonistic streak, moving on almost immediately to romantic pursuits after the coup collapses. He is a clear parody of Roman Roy from the TV series Succession, mirroring that character's mix of arrogance and immaturity within a powerful family business. Voiced by Seth Green.

title: Shelby
text: Shelby is A boy from Shelbyville who serves as the Shelbyville counterpart to Bart Simpson, appearing in "Lemon of Troy". Shelby is essentially Shelbyville's answer to Bart Simpson, sharing a similar look and even having his own best friend named Milhouse. His father works at the local impound lot, grounding him in the blue-collar world of Shelbyville. In his main appearance, Shelby takes charge of the local kids after they steal Springfield's beloved lemon tree, gleefully taunting the rival town during a tense standoff at the bluffs. When Bart and his friends cross into enemy territory to reclaim the tree, it's Shelby who steps up to confront him directly, sparking the argument that turns into a citywide chase. Notably, he was never actually named on screen, only receiving the moniker "Shelby" later through a companion guidebook. He has since popped up in archive footage, comics, and other minor appearances, cementing his status as a recognizable one-off rival for Bart. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

title: Joey Jo-Jo Junior Shabadoo
text: Joey Jo-Jo Junior Shabadoo is A minor recurring patron of Moe's Tavern, briefly used by Homer as a fake alias. Joey Jo-Jo Junior Shabadoo is an obscure, largely background barfly whose main claim to fame comes from an awkward, embarrassing moment at Moe's Tavern. Homer invents the name as a cover story while trying to discreetly ask for advice about his attraction to a co-worker, not realizing a real man with that exact name is sitting nearby. The character's defining trait is having an absurdly ridiculous name, which Moe mocks outright, causing the poor man to flee the bar in tears. Barney's sympathetic but useless attempt to call after him only adds to the comedic pathos of the scene. Beyond this one iconic gag, he appears fleetingly in the crowd at a later episode's auction house scene, cementing his status as a one-off joke character who occasionally resurfaces in the background. Voiced by Hank Azaria. Notable quotes: That's the worst name I ever heard. - Moe | Hey! Joey Jo-Jo - Barney
quotes: That's the worst name I ever heard. - Moe
Hey! Joey Jo-Jo - Barney

title: Plaid Piper
text: Plaid Piper is Non-canon superhero alter-ego of Groundskeeper Willie, appearing in Simpsons comic books. The Plaid Piper is a comic-exclusive superhero identity taken on by Groundskeeper Willie after he gains powers from exposure to a nuclear explosion. As a member of a superhero team, he fits into the tradition of Simpsons characters gaining fantastical abilities in non-canon storylines. His name and presumed appearance play on his Scottish heritage, tying his plaid-patterned motif to his everyman identity as the school's short-tempered groundskeeper. Little else about his personality is detailed beyond his origin, since he exists mainly as a novelty twist on Willie for comic book crossover events. He appears specifically within Bongo Comics stories rather than the television series. His inclusion highlights how the comics occasionally explore alternate, exaggerated versions of familiar Springfield residents.

title: Olive Oyl
text: Olive Oyl is A crossover character from the Popeye comic strip who appears in The Simpsons only as a reference/costume, not as an active cast member. Olive Oyl is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed figure from the classic Popeye comics and cartoons. Within the show's universe, she exists only as a point of comparison and a costume choice rather than a speaking role. Marge is once likened to her, being described as having 'Olive Oyl' good looks, tying Marge's homemaker image to the iconic cartoon sweetheart. Separately, Cletus and Brandine Spuckler dress up as Popeye and Olive Oyl for a masquerade ball, playing on the hillbilly couple's penchant for goofy, low-budget costumes. Olive Oyl herself never appears as an active character with dialogue, making her purely a background reference and pop-culture nod. Her inclusion highlights the show's frequent habit of weaving classic cartoon and comic icons into throwaway gags and comparisons.

title: Pinocchio
text: Pinocchio is Crossover character referenced from Disney's Pinocchio; appears briefly in Simpsons non-canon specials and as a nickname mentioned in the main show. Pinocchio is not an original Simpsons character but a borrowed figure from the classic Disney film, appearing only in passing or background moments. In the main continuity, Bart uses his name as a mocking nickname for another character, Paolo Paoletti. Outside of canon, Pinocchio shows up as a silent, picture-only presence in holiday and anniversary specials, once even having his wooden nose used as a snooker cue by Beast. He has no dialogue and no real personality of his own within the show, functioning purely as a visual gag or cameo tying into Disney's ownership of the franchise. His inclusion highlights the show's fondness for crossover references and playful nods to other media.

title: Jeff Sessions
text: Jeff Sessions is Non-canon caricature of U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions, appearing in Simpsons political shorts. This version of Jeff Sessions is a satirical, exaggerated take on the real-life politician, portrayed as a bumbling and almost cartoonishly strange figure within the Trump administration. He's depicted hiding under Donald Trump's bed covers, showing a comically submissive and skittish personality. His antics include escaping through a hole in a wall and, in another appearance, literally flying by flapping his ears after shoving Robert Mueller into a room with Trump. These absurd, surreal actions play into the show's tendency to mock real-world political figures through farcical non-canon specials. As a recurring but minor character, he exists purely for topical satire rather than any deep characterization tied to the main Simpsons cast. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

title: The Raven (character)
text: The Raven (character) is Non-canon character based on Edgar Allan Poe's poem, portrayed by Bart Simpson in a Treehouse of Horror segment. The Raven is a spooky, mysterious bird adapted from Edgar Allan Poe's classic poem, appearing in one of the Simpsons' Halloween anthology segments. In the original tale, it torments a grieving narrator by endlessly repeating the same cryptic word, refusing to answer any of his desperate questions. In the show's parody, Homer imagines himself as the tormented narrator while Bart takes on the role of the taunting raven, frightening Homer both within the story and afterward when he believes he sees the bird outside his window. Beyond this main appearance, the character has popped up in other media tied to the franchise, such as a museum diorama referencing Springfield's founder and as a recurring effect in a video game whenever characters are knocked unconscious. Its main traits are its eerie, single-word repetition and its role as a symbol of madness and grief, rather than having a personality of its own. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright. Notable quotes: Never more | The Raven, Treehouse of Horror
quotes: Never more
The Raven, Treehouse of Horror

title: Bonnie Parker
text: Bonnie Parker is Historical criminal figure (real-world Bonnie Parker of Bonnie and Clyde) depicted in a story told within a Simpsons episode. Bonnie Parker is a fictionalized version of the real outlaw, appearing in a tale narrated by Marge that reimagines her infamous partnership with Clyde Barrow. She's portrayed as a thrill-seeker who craves excitement and danger above all else, quickly growing bored with anyone who fails to keep up with her wild appetite for crime. Her chance meeting with Clyde sparks a violent crime spree across the state, robbing banks together, with Bonnie visibly excited by the chaos they cause. Despite their partnership in crime, she remains emotionally detached, even reconsidering the relationship in her final moments. The character is used for comedic effect, showing that even facing death doesn't stop her from critiquing Clyde's inadequacies. She's grouped among other posthumously celebrated American figures within the show's universe. Voiced by Julie Kavner. Notable quotes: Bonnie then told Clyde to rob a Feed Store to prove that he was bad. | As they were dying, Bonnie told Clyde that she thought they should see other people as he wasn't exciting enough for her.
quotes: Bonnie then told Clyde to rob a Feed Store to prove that he was bad.
As they were dying, Bonnie told Clyde that she thought they should see other people as he wasn't exciting enough for her.

title: Dr. Octuplets
text: Dr. Octuplets is Supervillain alter-ego of Apu, appearing in Bongo comics as a Bartman antagonist. Dr. Octuplets is the villainous persona Apu adopts after an electric shock while fixing a hot dog tray causes him to snap into a maniacal laugh. Teaming up with his own octuplet children, he uses them as tools for crime, exploiting their baby-related messes and affection as improvised weapons against superheroes. He's a clear parody of the Spider-Man villain Doctor Octopus, right down to the punny name. His schemes involve bank and jewelry store heists, which he pulls off by having his babies distract or overwhelm his opponents with dirty diapers or overwhelming cuddles. Ultimately his reign of crime is undone not by force but by a brain freeze from a thrown Squishee, which snaps him out of his evil state. Even after his defeat, his legacy persists as a museum statue and later as a tool used by another villain, the Prince of Crime, who uses his babies against Bartman.

title: The Rappin' Rabbis
text: The Rappin' Rabbis is A minor rap group of rabbis featured on a local Springfield TV segment. The Rappin' Rabbis are a novelty musical group made up of rabbis who perform rap music, positioned humorously as Springfield's Jewish counterpart to the Benedictine monks. They appear briefly as a segment on the local news program Eye on Springfield, watched by the Simpson family. Their existence plays into the show's tradition of absurd local-color acts and fictional entertainers that populate Springfield's media landscape. There isn't much development beyond their single appearance, making them a quick visual and conceptual gag rather than a fleshed-out set of characters. They later resurface in non-canon material as a crowd decoration in a mobile game tie-in. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta, Hank Azaria.

title: Sailor (Boy-Scoutz 'N the Hood)
text: Sailor (Boy-Scoutz 'N the Hood) is An unnamed, minor one-off character who appears in a brief musical gag in a Season 5 episode. This nameless sailor is a fleeting background character who pops up during a musical number involving Bart and Milhouse. He enthusiastically joins their song about Springfield by belting out a line about New York, showing off his own hometown pride. Bart, amused but eager to redirect him, points him toward the actual direction of New York. The sailor politely thanks Bart and presumably wanders off, never to be seen again outside of a clip show reference. He has no defined personality traits beyond his brief comedic interruption, making him a quick visual gag rather than a fleshed-out character. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta. Notable quotes: "New York, New York." | "Thanks."
quotes: "New York, New York."
"Thanks."

title: Paula
text: Paula is A timbersports competitor who becomes Marge's training partner and friend. Paula is introduced as a friend of Patty and Selma, having met them at Burning Woman, and works as a competitive timbersports athlete. She takes an interest in Marge's natural aptitude for chopping wood and takes her under her wing, training her in the woods and encouraging her to channel her anger into her technique. The two grow close over a month of training together for a major bucksaw competition, which sparks some jealous confusion in Homer, who mistakenly worries Marge and Paula are romantically involved. Paula turns out to be married with a child, easing his fears, and the two women go on to win the championship together. She's portrayed as confident, supportive, and a bit dry-humored, taking Homer's awkward comments in stride. Paula is also notable as one of the show's openly lesbian characters. Voiced by Asia Kate Dillon. Notable quotes: Homer then told Paula that if she wanted another kid, they could use his sperm, to which Paula said they'd put him on the shortlist.
quotes: Homer then told Paula that if she wanted another kid, they could use his sperm, to which Paula said they'd put him on the shortlist.

title: Jesse Owens
text: Jesse Owens is Real-world historical athlete referenced in The Simpsons, appearing as a minor character/mention. Jesse Owens is depicted in The Simpsons universe as the famous American track and field athlete known for his real-life achievements at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. In the show's fictionalized retelling, he is credited with beating Adolf Hitler's Zeppelin during the Olympic Games, a comedic exaggeration of his historic victory over Nazi Germany's athletes. He also becomes the target of a time-traveling Radioactive Man, who journeys back to 1936 in an attempt to defeat him at the Olympics, blending real history with the show's superhero parody storylines. Owens himself doesn't have an active speaking role but is referenced as a legendary, larger-than-life figure from history. His inclusion reflects the show's frequent habit of weaving real-world historical figures into absurd, comedic scenarios. He is classified among the show's recurring real-world deceased characters used for background jokes and cultural references.

title: Tig Notaro
text: Tig Notaro is Real-life stand-up comedian referenced/depicted in picture form within the show, not an actual speaking character. Tig Notaro appears in the Simpsons universe only as an image rather than a fully animated character with dialogue. Her likeness shows up on a DVD cover for a fictional special called Everyone Loves Tig, which is shown to be owned by Paula. She's also referenced visually through the 'Vig Notaro' betting service logo, a punny nod to her name. Since she never speaks on-screen, she's classified among the picture-only and non-speaking characters in the show. In real life, she is an American stand-up comedian, writer, radio contributor, and actress who is openly lesbian. Her inclusion in the show is more of a cameo homage than a developed storyline.

title: Retirement Castle nurse
text: Retirement Castle nurse is A recurring nurse who works at the Springfield Retirement Castle. The Retirement Castle nurse is a minor recurring character who tends to the elderly residents of Springfield's retirement home. She's generally shown as somewhat weary and dissatisfied with her job, but not afraid to take drastic action when needed. When an assassin hired by Mr. Burns attacked the home with a machine gun trying to kill Grampa Simpson, she fearlessly fired back with a shotgun to protect the residents. She also cared for Homer during one of his more absurd schemes, when he disguised himself as an elderly resident to avoid an awkward situation with Apu's visiting mother. On another occasion, her frustration with rising costs led her to withhold medication from the residents entirely, showing a more callous or exasperated side to her personality. Voiced by Tress MacNeille. Notable quotes: "our residents are trying to nap"
quotes: "our residents are trying to nap"

title: Sherri and Terri's grandmother
text: Sherri and Terri's grandmother is Grandmother of Springfield Elementary students Sherri and Terri Mackleberry. This elderly woman is the maternal grandmother of twins Sherri and Terri, connecting her to the extended family tree of Jerri Mackleberry. She is a minor, non-speaking background character who appears mainly at community and school events. Her most notable appearance came during a grandparents' day celebration at Springfield Elementary School. She later showed up at the Bounce-A-Thon, suggesting she keeps an active presence in her granddaughters' lives. In a non-canon short, she was also depicted among a crowd of senior citizens during a musical number. Overall, she serves as a recurring but background figure rather than a character with any developed personality or storyline.

title: Renee
text: Renee is Moe Szyslak's former girlfriend, a minor recurring character. Renee is a woman who began dating Moe Szyslak mostly out of pity, since he seemed unable to find anyone else. Despite that unflattering start, the two settled into a genuinely happy relationship for a while. Her tenure with Moe came to an end when she discovered how selfish and cold he could be, particularly regarding his treatment of Homer. She was appalled that Moe would rather spend money on a romantic Hawaiian getaway than help bail out his friend, and things only got worse when he revealed a bizarre, morally dubious scheme to accomplish both. Disgusted by his behavior, she left him for good. Renee later reappears briefly in a civic context, attending a town meeting held by Lisa about Lake Springfield, showing she remained part of the Springfield community even after the breakup. Voiced by Helen Hunt.

title: Mrs. Samson
text: Mrs. Samson is Minor recurring character; mother of Gerald Samson and wife of Mr. Samson, part of the Springfield community of parents. Mrs. Samson is a Springfield mother best known as the parent of Gerald, Maggie Simpson's rival at daycare. She shares her son's distinctive dark unibrow, a trait that marks her as visually memorable despite her minor role. She appeared among a group of judgmental mothers at a gathering hosted by Marge, criticizing the snacks she was served. Interestingly, her portrayal is inconsistent across media: in television episodes she is depicted as slim and somewhat snobbish, while in the Maggie's Crib comic stories she is drawn as plump and friendly toward Marge. Her hair color also varies between appearances, shown as both brown and white in different comics. The rivalry between her son Gerald and Maggie remains a consistent thread across both the show and the comics. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

title: Corporal Punishment
text: Corporal Punishment is Sergeant-at-arms and on-camera security for Krusty the Clown's show. Corporal Punishment is the tough-looking enforcer who keeps order on the Krusty the Clown Show, handling unruly crowds of kids as well as network executives, bookies, OSHA inspectors, and IRA agents. Despite his intimidating bald, muscular appearance, he has a surprisingly soft side, enjoying cotton candy, walks on the beach, and snuggling. He's a man of eclectic hobbies and skills, practicing kickboxing, powerlifting, and bull riding, collecting butterflies, and even cooking gourmet gelato. Before landing his job with Krusty, he tried to join the army but was rejected for flat feet, and instead worked as a bronco buster, bouncer, and mattress tester. He's famously private and stoic, once going 127 days without speaking, and is treated as a non-speaking recurring background character throughout the show. His most memorable on-screen moments include stomping onto the stage to intimidate protesters booing Krusty, and later crying at Krusty's staged funeral.

title: Sasha Reed
text: Sasha Reed is Former Springfield High School student and star of the school musical Marge later revives. Sasha Reed is a former classmate of Marge who was once the celebrated star of a high school musical called Y2K: The Millennium Bug. After graduating, she moved to New York City hoping to become a professional actress, but never landed real acting work and instead ended up as a sales associate at Sephora. Despite this, she maintains a glamorous, boastful persona, claiming to have become a successful star in musicals and plays. Her charm and popularity easily win over old castmates, which stirs jealousy and insecurity in Marge. She had a fling with Barney Gumble back in high school, though he barely remembers it. Ultimately she proves to be good-natured, forgiving Marge for exposing her lie and helping the revived musical go on. Voiced by Sara Chase.

title: Emma Peel
text: Emma Peel is A minor crossover character who appears as a member of the British invasion force in a Simpsons comic story. Emma Peel is not an original Simpsons creation but rather a crossover character borrowed from the classic British television series The Avengers, where she was portrayed by Diana Rigg. In her brief Simpsons appearance, she shows up as part of a British occupying force after Springfield is annexed by the United Kingdom following a constitutional mishap involving Lisa and a gun ban. She has no significant dialogue or personality development within the Simpsons universe, functioning mainly as a nod to fans of the source material. Her presence is a one-off gag tied to the absurd premise of Springfield briefly becoming a British colony. The story resolves when Lisa diplomatically convinces the British to leave, restoring Springfield's American status. Emma Peel's inclusion is emblematic of the show's frequent pop-culture crossovers and references to classic media.

title: Dave Shutton
text: Dave Shutton is Minor recurring character; a journalist for The Springfield Shopper newspaper. Dave Shutton is a hard-nosed print reporter for The Springfield Shopper, easily identified by his old-fashioned fedora reminiscent of a 1940s newshound. He tends to show up at the scene of Springfield's oddities and disasters, chasing stories with a nose for the sensational, such as Bart's discovery of a mutated three-eyed fish. He also covers lighter local news, like checking in on pageant mishaps at Springfield events. Despite his diligence, he's treated as a lesser rival by TV newsman Kent Brockman, who seems to look down on him simply because they work in competing news mediums. This rivalry highlights his role as a background fixture of Springfield's media landscape rather than a major player. His name is a nod by writer John Swartzwelder to a real-life friend.
